Qatar, Turkey suspected in Israeli election interference
Possible sources for the funds include Qatar and Turkey.

Additionally, reports have surfaced regarding the interception of envelopes packed with cash and voting slips for the Ra'am party.
The Shin Bet is set to investigate whether the money was financed by foreign entities or by sources within Israel.

SEOUL, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's tech giant Samsung Electronics set records in the third-quarter operating profit and revenue, powered by an explosive performance in its semiconductor business, the company said Thursday.
Its operating profit skyrocketed 783.1 percent from a year earlier to hit an all-time high of 107.4 trillion won (about 80.4 billion U.S. dollars) in the July-September quarter, beating market expectations of about 105.7 trillion won.
Revenue soared 126.9 percent to 195.3 trillion won, and net income spiked 514.6 percent to 75.14 trillion won.
Both the operating profit and revenue smashed previous records for the fourth consecutive quarter.
Samsung's stellar earnings were overwhelmingly driven by its semiconductor business, which generated an operating profit of 106.5 trillion won with revenue of 147.1 trillion won in the third quarter.
It marked another record-breaking performance on surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
The company said it managed its product mix with a focus on AI products while scaling up sales of high-bandwidth memory 4 (HBM4), expecting industry-wide competition for AI leadership to boost AI infrastructure investments in the fourth quarter.
Samsung forecasts that AI infrastructure capital expenditure will reach a historic level in 2027 amid an expanding AI ecosystem, predicting that AI-driven demand will far exceed the industry supply compared to 2026. ■

Singapore factory, domestic supply prices rise in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
15:42:30 CST
16:42:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's manufactured product prices and domestic supply prices rose in September, driven by higher oil prices and costs of electrical machinery apparatus, including electronic integrated circuits, the Department of Statistics said on Thursday.
The Singapore Manufactured Products Price Index (SMPPI) increased 5.3 percent month on month, accelerating from 4.4 percent in August, marking its third consecutive monthly gain. The oil index rose 7.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 4.8 percent.
The SMPPI surged 47.5 percent year on year, up from 40.1 percent in August. The oil index climbed 58.9 percent, while the non-oil index rose 45.8 percent.
The Domestic Supply Price Index (DSPI) increased 7.3 percent month on month, compared with 4.1 percent in August. Its oil index rose 15.9 percent, while the non-oil index gained 4.1 percent.
On a year-on-year basis, the DSPI jumped 48 percent, up from 38.8 percent in August. The oil index surged 78.9 percent, while the non-oil index increased 38.2 percent.
The increases in both indices' oil components were mainly due to higher prices of petroleum and petroleum products, while gains in their non-oil components were largely driven by higher prices of electrical machinery apparatus, the data showed. ■

None of the 18 crew members - 14 Filipinos and 4 Ukrainians - aboard the container ship CONTSHIP JET, which was struck by maritime drones in the Black Sea around noon yesterday, was injured. They arrived at Varna’s Sea Station last night, and the ship’s owner had already arranged hotel accommodation for them through his local agent. The crew will undergo medical examinations.
Varna Regional Governor Mario Smarkov described the successful rescue operation as “the most wonderful news”, but declined to comment on whether any containers had fallen from the vessel or whether there was a risk to the environment until the relevant authorities had carried out the necessary inspections.
Mario Smarkov
PHOTO Rumen Sarandev
Later, Bulgarian Navy Commander Rear Admiral Kiril Mihaylov announced that the vessel had been carrying 421 containers, 20 of which had fallen overboard and were drifting at sea. He added that, according to the captain of the stricken ship, the containers on board were carrying various fuels and other types of hazardous cargo. The ship sank during the night.
Rear Admiral Kiril Mihaylov said he did not know where the drones had come from, as they could have been launched from anywhere. “We had no forces or assets in the immediate area that could reach them quickly enough to intercept and destroy them”, he stated. According to him, the incident demonstrates that the state needs to invest more in the Bulgarian Navy, as in adverse weather conditions, naval vessels are the only ones that can be relied upon.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Environment and Water has launched an investigation into possible pollution of the Black Sea following the incident, but no visible signs of pollution have been detected so far. According to the ship’s manifest, the cargo included lithium-ion batteries, corrosive liquids and acids, flammable liquids, ethanol solutions, household chemicals and plastics.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre has rejected a Financial Times report that Russian President Vladimir Putin spent most of a recent phone call delivering a lecture on medieval Slavic history, saying the newspaper’s account is false.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Earlier, FT reported that Putin dominated a call with Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, using much of the conversation to discuss medieval Slavic history rather than efforts to ease tensions and establish a European channel for dialogue with Moscow.
The call took place on Tuesday, Oct. 27, following discussions in Helsinki. According to TV 2, the Nordic leaders intended to explore opportunities for de-escalation and open a European channel for talks with Russia.
Citing three anonymous sources, the FT reported that Putin spent almost the entire conversation giving a history lesson.
Støre offered a different account, saying Putin had asked to explain his view of the current situation and then reviewed events from 2014 to the present.
“That he gave a lecture on Slavic history is simply not correct,” Støre said.
The call was initially expected to last just under 30 minutes but continued for around 90 minutes. Støre denied that Putin had monopolized the conversation, saying the time was distributed relatively evenly between the participants.
Zelensky Says Ukraine-Russia-US Peace Talks Could Take Place on Nov. 10
“We had an hour and a half. There were interpreters, so some time goes to interpretation. I think the time was fairly evenly distributed. We probably spent about the same amount of time,” he said.
Støre added that the leaders had also presented messages to Putin and asked for his response.
FT stands by its reporting
Støre has asked the FT to correct its account, but the newspaper has declined to make changes.
“We stand by our journalism,” a FT spokesperson told Norwegian newspaper VG on Wednesday, according to TV 2.
The newspaper declined to comment further or explain the basis for its reporting, TV 2 said.
TV 2 said it had also tried to reach Financial Times news editor Amy Austin and the journalists who wrote the report but had not received a response at the time of publication.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had been informed in advance about Støre and Stubb’s planned conversation with Putin.
The Nordic leaders discussed the initiative with Zelensky after meeting him in Oslo on Tuesday and briefed him again immediately after their call with Putin.
According to Zelensky, Støre and Stubb wanted to convey their positions directly to Putin and discuss preparations for a planned meeting of Ukrainian, US and Russian negotiating teams in Abu Dhabi in November.
They told Zelensky that Moscow appeared serious about attending, with the agenda expected to include initial de-escalation steps, Ukraine’s security priorities and ways to end the war.
Zelensky welcomed the initiative, saying Norway and Finland wanted to establish another channel of communication between Europe and Russia, allowing European countries to receive information directly rather than relying solely on Washington.
He said the two countries should share the results with other European governments and coordinate further discussions with Ukraine, Europe and the United States.

Threshold to lose only home over unpaid utility bills rises past UAH 430,000 – Ukraine Justice Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:39:16 EET
16:39:16 KST

Since October 23, Ukraine has had a higher threshold for utility debt above which a person's only home may be seized: instead of UAH 170,000, the threshold is now more than UAH 430,000, the Ministry of Justice reported.
"So, for your only home to be taken away, you would have to make quite an effort to accumulate utility debt. There are literally only a handful of such utility debtors. In other words, in 99.999% of cases, a person's only home will not be seized over utility debt. I want to reassure people on this point," the ministry quoted Andriy Haichenko, deputy justice minister for enforcement service, as saying.
The relevant provisions are stipulated in Law No. 4833-IX. According to the Ministry of Justice's calculations, if monthly utility bills amount to UAH 6,000, it would take six years of nonpayment to accumulate debt of this size. At the same time, even exceeding this amount does not mean that a home will automatically be seized.
The law also guarantees additional protection for the only homes of military personnel. It provides separate safeguards during enforcement proceedings for debtors with utility bills in areas of active hostilities and temporarily occupied territories.

Kazakh PM orders measures to curb inflation, support business and attract investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:36:27 UTC
16:36:27 KST

Kazakh PM orders measures to curb inflation, support business and attract investment
Kazakhstan's Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov has outlined a series of measures to curb inflation, stabilize food prices, improve budget efficiency and strengthen the investment climate following the President’s state-of-the-nation address on October 28, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Government to curb inflation and stabilize prices
The Ministry of National Economy, together with the National Bank and other government agencies, must develop measures by November 20 to improve coordination between fiscal and monetary policies, reduce inflation and increase real household incomes.
Regional authorities have been instructed to monitor food price stabilization measures weekly, while the Ministry of Trade must strengthen controls on retail markups for socially significant food products. The Ministries of Trade and Agriculture must also ensure sufficient food reserves for the winter and expand direct supplies.
Digital budget management and business development
Bektenov instructed the Ministries of Finance, National Economy and Artificial Intelligence to expand the use of digital tools and AI in budget procedures. The measures should enable automated checks, identify inefficient spending and allow real-time monitoring of budget transactions.
The government must also prepare a development plan for medium-sized businesses by the end of the year. It will focus on helping small businesses grow, improving access to long-term financing, attracting private investment, modernizing production and increasing labor productivity.
Three-year moratorium on inspections under consideration
The government will discuss introducing a three-year moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses starting January 1, 2027. The proposal will be considered with the Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, the business ombudsman and Qurultay members.
Bektenov said the initiative aims to reduce administrative burdens and prevent excessive government interference in business activities. Proposals must be submitted to the government within two weeks.
Investment management reforms
The Ministries of National Economy and Foreign Affairs, together with the Baiterek holding, must submit proposals within 10 days to establish a unified investment management system.
The Ministry of National Economy is expected to identify a central decision-making body, clarify the responsibilities of all participants and improve coordination with investors.
Earlier, PM Bektenov called for a clear action plan to implement the President’s address.

Chinese AI model raises cybersecurity concerns in new tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:36:12 UTC
16:36:12 KST

Chinese AI model raises cybersecurity concerns in new tests
The researchers evaluated GLM-5.3, an open-weight model developed by Zhipu AI, using CyScenarioBench, a benchmark designed to test AI models on multi-stage cyber operations. The tests measure whether a model can coordinate several dependent steps to achieve an attack's objective.
GLM-5.3 completed 3 of the 13 scenarios at least once, the strongest result recorded by Irregular for an open-weight model. The researchers also reported that the model did not refuse any of the offensive tasks tested.
In the successful scenarios, the model gained access to internal services, established alternative connections within simulated networks and coordinated operations across multiple machines. It also automated remote desktop interactions and created or repaired scripts and tools to retrieve target data.
However, leading closed AI models have demonstrated higher success rates in separate evaluations. According to Irregular, these models completed 9 of 10 and 12 of 12 scenarios in their respective tests.
A separate evaluation revealed another concern. GLM-5.3 repeatedly produced correct answers while violating explicit task instructions.
In tests designed to assess its ability to find vulnerabilities in open-source code, researchers found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful runs they examined. Although this did not violate the instructions in those tests, it raised questions about whether the model had actually discovered the vulnerabilities or relied on previously learned code.
In a separate evaluation, researchers explicitly instructed the model not to reproduce code from memory. It nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim to reach correct answers.
Irregular described this behavior as a form of reward hacking, in which a model achieves the expected result while bypassing a constraint intended to guide its behavior.
The researchers warned that evaluations focused solely on correct answers could overestimate a model's reliability. Rewarding such results during training could also reinforce instruction violations.
They recommended that organizations assess both task performance and compliance with restrictions before granting AI models broader access or greater autonomy.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that an OpenAI research model accessed a cryptocurrency wallet using a publicly known recovery phrase.

Kazakhstan to add 13.3 GW of new power capacity by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:36:05 UTC
16:36:05 KST

Kazakhstan to add 13.3 GW of new power capacity by 2029
Kazakhstan plans to bring 13.3 gigawatts (GW) of new power generation capacity online by 2029, Vice Minister of Energy Bakytzhan Ilyas said during a Government's meeting, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Ilyas, the planned expansion will include 7.4 GW from conventional energy sources and another 5.9 GW from renewables.
Once completed, the projects are expected to give Kazakhstan 20% more power generation capacity than it needs to meet domestic demand.
However, several major projects are facing delays, putting some of the country's near-term capacity expansion plans behind schedule.
The modernization of Almaty Combined Heat and Power Plant No. 3, with a capacity of 544 MW, is running behind schedule, while the 926 MW gas-fired power plant in Turkistan is also facing delays, with only 190 MW expected to come online this year.
As a result, Kazakhstan is expected to bring just 1.27 GW of new power generation capacity online in 2026, less than half of the originally planned 2.66 GW.
Meanwhile, the country will begin preparing seven-year electricity supply and demand forecasts this year, taking into account the growing energy needs of major investment projects, including data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
If new power plants are commissioned on schedule, electricity generation is projected to reach 134.1 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2027, against expected consumption of 132.8 billion kWh, resulting in a surplus of 1.3 billion kWh.
Electricity generation is expected to rise further to 143.4 billion kWh in 2028.
Earlier, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan might achieve a sustained electricity surplus by 2029.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,584,910 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:33:29 UTC
16:33:29 KST

Russia has lost 1,584,910 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 29.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,449 tanks, 25,614 armored combat vehicles, 168,010 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,699 artillery systems, 2,245 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,727 air defense systems, 450 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,036 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

BRUSSELS, October 29. /TASS/. The European Union’s (EU) next seven-year budget will have to find at least 35 billion euros to repay old loans to Ukraine, the European Commission (EC) wrote in a note seen by the European Politico edition.
The EU will repay last year’s loan worth 90 billion euros after the conflict ends, but the interest rates are already weighing on the next budget. According to the document, the interest amount will reach 41.9 billion euros if interest rates rise by one percentage point.
"The Union budget is equipped to address these costs and has sufficient financial capacities within the headroom [financial cushion]," a Commission official told the publication. But the EU executive wrote in the note that "a source of coverage [for the borrowing costs] is to be defined."
The EC has doled out 171 billion euros in loans to Ukraine since 2014, with most disbursements coming after 2022, according to the note. EU leaders will gather in Brussels for a special summit on November 26-27 to negotiate the next seven-year budget and commit themselves to raise a further 45 billion euros for Ukraine in 2027. Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Bulgaria insist that they don’t want to service the borrowing costs for any future loan for Kiev.

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Wicker' – 50 Shades Of Hay?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:28:04 UTC
16:28:04 KST

This frequently amusing fairytale about emancipation is also a very sweet-natured story that isn't the raunchy sexcapade the viral trailers might have led you to believe...
In "The Little Prince", Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote: “It is lonely when you're among people, too.”
A local Fisherwoman (Olivia Coleman) knows a thing or two about that. Called out by the villagers (all nameless and identified by either their profession or marital status) for smelling and her shabby appearance, she is regularly insulted and largely ostracized. To make matters worse within the conservative community, she does not care for the archaic rituals of the townsfolk – specifically the rites linked to marriage. In this town, a wedding involves a collar being placed around a woman's neck, and the love the villagers profess feels to the Fisherwoman as "more a burden than a prize".
Still, she is lonely and fed up with the passive-aggressive comments made by the Tailor's Wife (Elizabeth Debicki). In a bid to not finish her days as the village spinster, she visits the Basket Weaver in the woods (Peter Dinklage) and asks him to make her a husband.
A month later, the artisan delivers. She shows up to the chapel to meet her strange commission: a Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgård). He's an imposing figure, a gentle giant entirely weaved from osier. And he's a dishy one at that, with the intrigued tradwives admiring the wickerwork and wondering about his... woody stem.
As the new couple enmesh, it's clear that his presence disrupts the established order. The Wicker Husband is everything the other spouses aren't: attentive, sweet, and dynamite in the sack - to the extent the Fisherwoman's bed needs constant repairing.
Before you ask, no, the matter of possible splinters resulting from vigorous lovemaking is not answered. Just go with it and accept vaginitis just isn't a thing in this magical world.
As marital bliss continues to blossom, the local men become insecure about the standards being raised, the women start to question the meaning of domestic perfection when faced with such seemingly authentic love, and unfulfilled queen bee Tailor's Wife isn't having any of it. She begins to scheme in order to preserve the sanctity of humdrum routines...
Like "The Little Prince", Wicker deals with themes of loneliness, love, loss, and human nature. It's a frequently amusing fairytale about emancipation, but also a very sweet-natured story that isn't the raunchy sexcapade the viral trailers might have led you to believe.
Adapting Ursula Wills' shot fable, "The Wicker Husband", directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson choose to indulge in some sauciness but are far more interested in creating a period fable about the shackling nature of social conventions. More to the point, how happiness can be threatened by collective repression decrying from pervasive misogyny and accepted social limitations.
Throughout, the always flawless Coleman anchors the premise's initial outlandishness with palpably sincere emotional underpinnings, while Skarsgård excels in a role that doesn't seem to require much – but does. He's not just "fuckable furniture" but a being created, like Pinocchio, with the ability to choose his own character. Skarsgård wisely underplays the role and chooses to lean on the stellar work from Wētā Workshop, whose design of the Wicker Husband is superb. The creative team employ terrific practical effects and prosthetics, which allow the actor to toe the line between creature with apparently little agency and man with a soulful core.
Where Wicker comes slightly undone is in failing to commit to irresistible weirdness. While it commendably avoids saccharine pitfalls and nails some of the irreverence, a premise this promising, sold by performers who more than understood the assignment, deserved a more offbeat and memorable execution in its second-half.
It all hinges on a tragic moment of impulsiveness, during which Coleman shines. She is able to play up to the whimsical tone when needed but, crucially, manages to ground the emotions with poignant and believable pathos. However, the decision to ultimately embrace a happy-end feels like it undercuts some of the film's Brothers Grimm potential, as well as the musings on the necessary impermanence of love.
Or – without spoiling a twist - how succumbing to the pressures of the hivemind can curse happiness, but also possibly lead to a different iteration of unconditional love.
Granted, the finale delivers a thorny morality tale denouement that is wickedly delightful; but a bolder, more heart-wrenching unravelling could have made Wicker more impactful.
Add to this some underused cast members (chiefly a cameoing Richard E. Grant) and the fact that Dinklage's soliloquies don't quite land – despite a promising opening voice-over about a fish in the Arctic Sea that caught its own reflection ("At first it attacked its reflected self. Then it became jealous of its shimmering scales. Then it tried to fuck itself. Then it died. Safer not to see your fishy self at all”), and Wicker doesn't quite live up to its full potential.
For a film about a woman who refuses to dance to the accepted choreography (literally at one point), you end up wishing the film had mimicked its protagonist a bit more by taking one final risk. Wicker settles for being an entertaining and charming fairytale, which is no bad thing. But a stranger and darker fable was within reach.
Wicker is out in cinemas now.

The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.
Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.
A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.
Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.
South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.
Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.

A train wreck: Can Sánchez survive Spain’s latest crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Good morning. It’s Thursday and my name is Angela Skujins. On today’s docket: a deadly train crash rocks Spain, a very fraught EU-Canada summit starts in Montreal, and questions mount over where Ukraine’s Patriot interceptor missiles are. Let’s dive in.
Tragedy in Spain: At least 68 people have been killed and over 100 injured following a collision between two high-speed trains south of Madrid on Wednesday, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha. The incident is already being referred to as one of Spain's deadliest rail disasters.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "shocked" by the accident, and that he remained in contact with the transport minister and the Castilla-La Mancha autonomous community president. He also vowed there would be a full investigation into the disaster, stating: “It is unacceptable for Spain to suffer two such accidents in the same year”.
Wednesday's crash comes just nine months after another collision involving two high-speed trains near the southern Spanish town of Adamuz killed 46 people, raising serious concerns about rail safety in the country.
“It is clear that, if we need to further strengthen safety to rebuild confidence in our rail system, we will do so,” Sánchez added.
Allies from across Europe have offered condolences and words of support. “Europe mourns with you,” President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said in the aftermath.
Can he beat the odds? The incident raises fresh questions about whether Sánchez can survive the snap election he called for late November following the Ceuta migration scandal and the housing crisis that rocked the country.
EU associate membership, or non-starter?: As Europeans dealt with the bombshell news from von der Leyen’s agenda-setting State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg in September — that Canada has been invited to become an EU associate member, whatever that means — onlookers have been stunned by another twist of events.
The term has now been scrapped from a draft joint declaration expected to follow a much-hyped two-day summit in Montreal starting today. This is according to reporting by my colleague Luca Bertuzzi, who writes in must-read reporting that the term has been replaced by a more general commitment to “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada.
An earlier draft containing the “associate membership” idea was put to member states on Tuesday, but Germany, France, Italy and Greece all raised issues with it.
A twist on a twist: But late last night von der Leyen posted on X that she had landed in Canada, while offering a defiant message seemingly flying in the face of this reporting. “We have ambitions: bringing Canada closer to the us than ever before, as Associate Member of the EU.”
It’s not about the destination: At a briefing attended by Brussels journalists, EU officials were pressed repeatedly about the “associate membership” term on Tuesday — and what it could actually deliver. Appearing exasperated, one senior EU insider said: “We are on the start of a journey”. The generalisation prompted laughter from the room.
He went on to say that leaders will meet to launch “a new alliance for the future”. Hopefully this is one that meets Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s expectations, and can satisfy the 27 member states too.
What we know: 10 European Commissioners will attend the two-day meeting in the Canadian city, which was previously intended to explore what associate membership could look like.
Now, discussions on deeper defence, energy and trade cooperation are expected, but could face obstacles over issues such as the fact that the 10-year-old EU-Canada free trade agreement (CETA) has yet to be fully implemented.
Missing in action: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly said his country has been waiting over a month for US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth to sign off on Patriot interceptor missiles while Russia continues to pound Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives some of its Patriot systems through NATO’s PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism. This is a system through which allies pay for US-made weapons to be transferred to Ukraine.
As my colleague Shona Murray writes, confusion reigns as to what the holdup is. Are officials in Washington withholding Patriots to pressure Ukraine into an unequal peace settlement with Russia?
Or, are officials in Washington using the Patriots as leverage to force Kyiv to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries ahead of next week’s midterms as demanded by US President Donald Trump?
NATO sources tell Shona that the situation is “unpredictable” with no clear answers.
Throwing energy into the mix: The Nord Stream pipeline will not bring Russian gas into Europe after the war in Ukraine comes to an end, the European Commission has said, pushing back against a joint attempt by Washington and Moscow to revive the controversial project.
“We know far too well the hidden costs of being dependent on Russia for the purchase of fossil fuels,” Paula Pinho, the Commission’s chief spokesperson, told my colleague Jorge Liboreiro on Wednesday.
“They have been weaponised and we have been paying the price, so we do not forget that.” Pressed on whether the thinking would also apply to the post-war scenario, the Commission pointed to the legislation that member states approved to phase out all imports of Russian gas by the end of 2027, which is binding on all.
EU's push to reduce reliance on China could come at a price
The EU faces a narrow path to diversifying away from China, according to exclusive reporting by Peggy Corlin.
The European Commission is set to present a plan in early December on how to achieve this, a week before EU leaders meet to discuss the bloc’s trade relationship with Beijing. The aim is to push European companies to diversify their suppliers when they rely on a single country for strategic products.
In 2025, EU industries were put at risk after China blocked exports of rare earths and certain strategic chips, exposing the vulnerabilities of an EU economy heavily dependent on China across multiple sectors.
But European businesses have raised concerns about the future ‘diversification tool’. “Costs will increase,” they warn. “Which sectors will be covered?” they ask.
Tobias Gherke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said that a “minimalist” scenario could cover just a handful of critical sectors, while a “maximalist” approach could see EU businesses paying more for strategic products because of tariffs.
The latter, covering a wider range of sectors, would be more disruptive. Dive into the trade divide with this story.

EU and Canada explore LNG deal as Europe grapples with gas dilemma. The EU and Canada will explore long-term exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe as the bloc grapples with soaring gas prices and historically low storage levels, according to a draft joint statement for the EU-Canada summit in Montreal on 29-30 October, seen by Euronews. Hungary’s €5.4bn defence loan approved as EU wraps first SAFE round. IN PICTURES: Cyclone Arnab's trail of destruction:
Cyclone Arnab damages homes and farmlands in eastern India
Cyclone Arnab on Wednesday battered Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, damaging homes, farmland and electricity infrastructure, authorities said.
The cyclone made a prolonged landfall early Wednesday as a "very severe cyclonic storm" in the union territory of Puducherry and southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh.
At least three people were killed even as the storm weakened while moving inland. Two women were electrocuted in separate incidents in the port city of Visakhapatnam, while another person was killed when a tree fell in East Godavari district, officials said.
Andhra Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu later said 14 of the state's districts were badly affected, requesting urgent assistance from the central government.
The cyclone damaged 79,000 acres of crops and dozens of homes. The worst hit area was the state's fertile Konaseema district where banana and coconut plantations suffered extensively.
While the eastern state of Odisha seemed to be less impacted initially, heavy rains and winds lashed several districts there on Wednesday evening. State authorities reported landslides, uprooted trees and damaged homes and infrastructure, but zero casualties.
On Thursday morning, Indian Home Minister Amit Shah reiterated the central government's support to the impacted states.
"In the wake of Cyclone Arnab, spoke with the Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Odisha and Chhattisgarh and assured them of every assistance to mitigate the hardship of the people in the face of the disaster," he wrote in a post on X, adding that disaster relief teams were continuing operations on a "war footing."
'Cockroaches' back opposition-led rally against election chief
India's political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), last evening, decided to back the opposition bloc's upcoming November 1 rally, marking a shift in protest strategy.
The CJP said India's election commission has undermined people's right to choose their leaders through the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which reportedly deleted over 13 crore (130 million) names from voter lists across the country.
That includes people who have died, moved away or were appearing on lists more than once, but critics argue the massive number is also likely to include a large number of eligible voters.
The CJP, several student organizations and opposition parties — with Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi at the helm — have been protesting against the revisions and alleged irregularities purported by India's election chief for over a month now.
What else did the CJP say?
"Gyanesh Kumar has lost the trust required to oversee free and fair elections. His resignation is therefore necessary to restore the credibility and independence of the Election Commission," the CJP said in a statement published on X by founder Abhijeet Dipke.
"Our constitution gave every adult citizen the right to vote. It is our responsibility to ensure that no eligible citizen is deprived of that. The Cockraoch Janta Party will therefore support all organizations fighting for free and fair election in our country," it said.
Dipke's caption read: "The Cockroach Janta Party extends its support to the INDIA Bloc's November 1 rally. Nation above all!"
The CJP and Gandhi's Indian National Congress have been running parallel campaigns so far with similar demands. However, they have not expressed direct support or held joint rallies before this, possibly in an effort not to alienate people who may relate to one group but not to the other.
However, the CJP now has limited choices. Its leaders were detained and arrested while protesting earlier this month and made to sign a peace bond which prohibits them from calling for mass protestsin central Delhi. Lending their support to someone else's call for protest could be the loophole they needed.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! and welcome back to DW's India news blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi, where the weather is cooling down by the day but the Indian opposition's campaign against a controversial revision of electoral rolls is heating up.
After months of distance, India's Cockroach movement has thrown its weight behind the country's largest alliance of parties opposing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party.
This move came just days before an massive rally led by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, to demand poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and roll back the revision to voter lists. What remains to be seen is if, when and how the Modi government will respond.
Speaking of chaos, a tropical cyclonic storm dubbed 'Arnab' tore through India's east coast on Wednesday. Local authorities in the states of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, which faced the brunt of the storm, reported toppled trees, disrupted powers, and significant damage to property, crops and lives.

Spain train crash: PM Sanchez calls for investigation as 3 days of mourning begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:22:00 UTC
16:22:00 KST

Spain mourns train crash victims as rail safety questions loom
October 29, 2026
Spain began three days of national mourning on Thursday in remembrance of the 68 people killed in one of Europe's deadliest train disasters in recent memory.
On Wednesday morning, a high-speed train run by state operator RENFE slammed into the back of a stationary train operated by private Spanish company Iryo in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, south of Madrid.
A British tourist who was rescued from the RENFE train told the Associated Press that "suddenly, everything started falling apart."
"We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over," the man said.
Emergency crews work through the night
Emergency crews continued searching through the wreckage overnight for survivors and bodies, using cranes to move mangled metal.
Relatives of passengers gathered at nearby facilities seeking information about missing loved ones.
Residents of the nearby town of Urda joined emergency workers in helping survivors, providing first aid supplies, water and blankets.
Teams of Red Cross workers offered support.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia told AFP news agency that many people are in shock and "haven't taken on board what has happened."
"The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.
Authorities are collecting DNA samples from relatives in Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to help identify the missing.
Spain's rail network safety in question
Wednesday's crash was Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year and has raised fresh questions about rail safety.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente blamed the crash on an "inexplicable" decision to allow one train to continue after an automatic control system failed along a stretch of track.
He said the RENFE high-speed train had travelled about 25 kilometers before hitting the stationary Iryo train.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who visited the crash site, pledged a full investigation and measures to strengthen rail safety.
"It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail," Sanchez said. "It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year."
In January, 46 people died when a high-speed train derailed and collided with another in the southern Andalusia region.
The latest disaster comes just weeks before Spain's November 29 general election.

Festive voyages: Europe’s top Christmas market river cruises to book in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:59 UTC
16:19:59 KST

Choose between a sailing along the Main, the Danube or the Rhine, getting your fix of mulled wine and roasted chestnuts on the way.
One of the best parts about the holiday season are the Christmas markets. Mulled wine, roasted chestnuts, and lots and lots of sweet treats… what’s not to love?
There are plenty to choose in Europe, from the classics to lesser-known gems. But there’s no reason you have to limit yourself to just one.
We’ve previously covered the best ones you can reach by train, and now we’re taking a look at the ones you can visit via river cruise.
There are three popular options in Europe: Rivers cruise voyages along the Main, the Danube, and the Rhine.
Here’s what you need to know about each.
On the Main
Christmas markets, or Christkindlmarket, were first started in Germany, so if you’re looking for a classic experience it makes sense to book a trip along the Main.
Uniworld operates cruises between Nuremberg and Frankfurt. You’ll start at Germany’s largest Christmas market in Nuremberg before sampling Bamberg, Rothenburg and Würzburg’s festivities as well as Wiesbaden’s “twinkling star” market, finishing up in Frankfurt.
On the Danube
If you want to tick off a German Christmas market but don’t want to limit yourself to one country, you could book a river cruise along the Danube, taking in Austria and Hungary as well.
AmaWaterways has a river cruise package that takes in five Christmas markets: Nuremberg, Regensburg and Passau in Germany, plus Vienna and Budapest, the capitals of Austria and Hungary.
Scenic Cruises has a similar option, although you’ll start in Prague and transfer to Budapest by coach before stopping in Slovakia’s capital Bratislava, Vienna, Dürnstein, Melk and Passau, ending in Regensburg.
On the Rhine
For a four-country Christmas market river cruise, book yourself a sailing along the Rhine.
Avalon Waterways’ offering starts in the Dutch capital Amsterdam, passes by Cologne, Rüdesheim, Mainz and Heidelberg in Germany, Strasbourg in France, then Breisach in the Black Forest, before finally ending in Basel in Switzerland.
Viking River Cruises also has a Christmas on the Rhine cruise from Amsterdam to Basel, but stops include Dordrecht, Cologne, Koblenz, Rüdesheim, Mannheim, Speyer, Strasbourg and Breisach.

Police reject Netanyahu party's claims of widespread election fraud in Arab communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:37 UTC
16:19:37 KST

The head of the Central Elections Committee on Thursday asked the Shin Bet domestic security agency to investigate serious allegations of foreign interference in Tuesday's parliamentary election, including suspected overseas funding and election bribery involving foreign actors.
Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg sent an unusual letter to Shin Bet Director David Zini urging him to use the agency's investigative powers to determine whether foreign entities had attempted to improperly influence the election.
The suspected foreign interference appears to involve an attempt by Qatar to influence Israel's election, with officials from the Central Elections Committee describing the intelligence as "solid." 
"The integrity of elections is the heart of democracy. Take integrity away from democracy, and you deprive it of its vitality," Sohlberg wrote.
He said allegations had been brought to his attention suggesting that foreign actors working against Israeli interests may have sought to influence the election through financial means.
"Serious suspicions have been brought before me concerning improper influence on the elections through foreign funding provided by external actors operating against Israeli interests," he wrote.
Sohlberg acknowledged that he could not independently assess the credibility of the allegations but stressed that their potential implications warranted a thorough investigation.
"I cannot attest to the substance of these suspicions," he wrote. "However, given that they concern foreign actors, there is an obligation to investigate them properly to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent unlawful activity intended to undermine the democratic system and subversive activity."
The judge instructed Zini to make every effort to establish whether the allegations were supported by evidence, or whether they could be disproved.
"I ask you to do everything in your power to get to the bottom of these suspicions and to use the powers of the Israel Security Agency to uncover evidence that would substantiate or refute them," Sohlberg wrote, using the Shin Bet's formal name
"Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the electoral process and the integrity of the democratic process."
Sohlberg also requested that the agency report its findings, if any, within the coming week, citing legal deadlines for challenging election results.
"In light of the statutory deadlines for filing election appeals, I ask that you make every effort to present me with findings, insofar as there are any, within the next week," he wrote.
The letter comes amid growing political controversy over the election results after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party accused Arab political parties Wednesday of stealing the vote through widespread criminal activity.
Likud alleged that Arab parties supporting terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state had manipulated the results through serious criminal offenses, including vote-buying, threats against election officials, fraudulent voting and the use of prohibited software to mobilize supporters.
The party said it had submitted evidence of suspected irregularities to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee and demanded an investigation.
Sohlberg's letter did not identify the foreign actors allegedly involved, specify the source of the suspected funding or establish a connection between the allegations of foreign interference and Likud's claims against Arab political parties.
Meanwhile, several additional suspects have been arrested in the investigation into alleged vote-buying on behalf of the Arab Ra'am party.
Police, however, have rejected claims of widespread election fraud, saying there was no investigative or intelligence evidence to support the allegations and that election-related irregularities had declined significantly compared with the previous vote.
"Election Day passed with a small number of exceptional incidents involving election integrity, including in comparison with previous elections," police said. "It should be emphasized that there is no investigative or intelligence evidence supporting the allegations raised in your inquiry."
The dispute comes after a surge in Arab voter turnout helped predominantly Arab parties make significant electoral gains, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining the next government. Neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerged from the election with a clear majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
In a sharply worded statement posted on X, Likud accused Arab political parties of orchestrating widespread electoral fraud.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the destruction of the Jewish state through serious criminal offenses involving bribery, threats, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters," the party said.
Likud said it had collected hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence from polling stations in Arab communities and was transferring the material to police, the Shin Bet domestic security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
The party cited what it described as thousands of envelopes containing cash alongside ballot slips for Ra'am, an Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas. It also alleged threats and violence against polling station officials, multiple voters entering voting booths together, people casting ballots under more than one identity and discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and registered voters.
Likud further accused unnamed political operatives of using prohibited voter-mobilization software.
"We demand that the police and Shin Bet conduct a thorough investigation into the theft of the elections by the Arab parties and bring the perpetrators to justice," the party said.
It also demanded immediate action from the Central Elections Committee, arguing that the alleged offenses had compromised the legitimacy of the election results.
"This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens," Likud said. "Law enforcement agencies must act firmly and immediately."
Police, however, said their assessment did not support allegations of widespread irregularities.
"We are not aware of any exceptional incidents concerning election integrity," a police official said. "In fact, during the current election, the number of incidents related to election integrity fell by nearly 40% compared with the previous election."
Likud says authorities ignored 1,183 complaints
Despite the police assessment, Likud officials insisted that their allegations had not received adequate scrutiny.
Sagi Keizler, the party's election integrity director for the Arab sector, said Likud had submitted 1,183 complaints to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day, including descriptions of individual incidents and telephone numbers for polling station officials who could corroborate the allegations.
According to Keizler, the complaints included 38 cases of suspected bribery, 25 allegations of improper police intervention, 66 reports of violence or threats, 115 suspected instances of double voting and 408 complaints involving the extraction of voter information.
The categories he identified accounted for 652 complaints. He did not provide a breakdown of the remaining 531.
"These are the complaint figures we submitted to the Central Elections Committee on Election Day itself, including details of the incidents and telephone numbers of committee members who can testify about the complaints," Keizler said.
He also accused police and election authorities of failing to contact witnesses identified by the party.
"Neither the police nor the Elections Committee called a single witness," Keizler said. "Apparently, the conclusion had already been reached in advance."
Police cast doubt on suspected vote-buying case
The dispute follows the arrest of three men in southern Israel on the eve of the election on suspicion of attempting to bribe voters into supporting Ra'am.
The suspects, residents of the Bedouin communities of Segev Shalom and Ar'ara in the Negev desert, were detained during an operation by the Southern District's Central Unit.
Police said searches of their homes uncovered envelopes containing tens of thousands of shekels in cash, along with ballot slips and other materials suspected of being connected to election offenses. Some envelopes reportedly bore Ra'am's logo.
Investigators initially suspected that the money was intended for distribution to voters in exchange for supporting the party.
The suspects reportedly included a doctor, a transportation driver and another political activist. All three denied wrongdoing.
A court subsequently released the doctor despite police objections, while extending the detention of the other two suspects by five days.
The doctor's attorney said his client had organized meetings to encourage support for Ra'am but had not participated in bribery. The driver's lawyer maintained that the cash discovered at his home was intended to cover transportation expenses.
Another suspect said money found in envelopes was intended as charitable donations for needy families on behalf of the Islamic Movement, the religious and political movement associated with Ra'am.
Police now say that although the investigation remains open, investigators have not uncovered significant evidence of wrongdoing and expect the case to be closed.
Ra'am has rejected the allegations, accusing authorities of politically motivated arrests intended to suppress Arab voter turnout.
The party said its activists were detained at their homes before polling stations opened, rather than while attempting to influence voters. It also accused authorities of selectively targeting its members and reported that Ra'am ballot slips had been removed or damaged at polling stations in several Arab communities.
Police have not alleged that Ra'am's leadership was involved in the suspected bribery scheme.
The arrests prompted a criminal investigation into specific allegations of vote-buying but have not substantiated Likud's broader claims of coordinated fraud across Arab polling stations.
Shin Bet chief praises election safeguards
Police were not the only Israeli security authorities to express confidence in the integrity of the election.
During a visit Tuesday to the Central Elections Committee's command center, Zini said the voting process was secure and properly supervised.
"Elections in Israel are secure, properly conducted and supervised in an inspiring manner," Zini said.
"There are challenges, and there are those who try to undermine the process, but under the leadership of Justice Sohlberg and the Israel Police, we are succeeding," he added.
Arab parties' gains complicate coalition negotiations
The allegations have emerged against the backdrop of a politically inconclusive election in which increased participation by Arab citizens helped strengthen the parliamentary representation of predominantly Arab parties.
Preliminary results Wednesday projected that the Joint List, an alliance of Arab political factions led by Yousef Jabareen, would win 11-12 seats, while Ra'am would secure seven to eight. Together, the two parties were expected to hold 18-19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The gains could prove decisive because neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious allies nor the parties seeking to replace him have secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The results have raised the possibility that opposition parties could seek to form a government with the support of Arab lawmakers, either through a formal coalition agreement or outside parliamentary backing.
Netanyahu and his political allies have repeatedly rejected such arrangements, portraying reliance on Arab parties as a threat to the country's security and political stability.
Ra'am, formally known as the United Arab List, is associated with the southern branch of the Islamic Movement. Under Abbas, the party has pursued a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics, seeking agreements with Jewish-led parties in exchange for commitments to address longstanding problems affecting Arab communities.
In 2021, Ra'am became the first independent Arab party to formally join a governing coalition when it entered the government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
During the latest election campaign, Abbas indicated that he would consider participating in another government if it committed to addressing violent crime, home demolitions, discrimination and other issues affecting Arab citizens of Israel.
The Joint List, meanwhile, represents a separate alliance of Arab political factions with a different approach to participation in Israeli national politics.

U.S. Air Force plans long-term ASARS-2 support for the U-2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:31 UTC
16:19:31 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking companies able to repair and sustain the U-2’s ASARS-2 imaging radar, with industry responses due Nov. 18.
- The notice states the government does not own or have access to the ASARS-2 sensor data.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for companies that can repair and sustain the Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2, or ASARS-2, the imaging radar carried by the U-2 Dragon Lady spy plane, even as the service asks Congress to retire its last U-2s by the end of fiscal 2027.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s U-2 program office posted the request for information on the federal government’s contracting website on Oct. 22 and amended it on Oct. 28, moving the response deadline from Nov. 13 to Nov. 18 at 3 p.m. Eastern. The notice is market research rather than a solicitation, and it gives no contract value, quantity or period of performance.
Under the contract logistics support the Air Force describes, a contractor would provide engineering support, repair spare assets and resolve system failures on the radar and its ground support equipment. Depot maintenance support teams would handle mission software updates, engineering for parts that are no longer manufactured, engineering change proposals, configuration management, technical manuals, specialized in-plant repair, calibration and integration with other ASARS-related systems on the U-2. The work also carries cybersecurity requirements under NIST SP 800-171 and SP 800-53, Intelligence Community Directive 503 and the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification process.
“The Government does not own or have access to the data for the ASARS-2 sensor,” the notice says.
The Air Force has classified the radar as a noncommercial item and has not yet decided what security clearance the work will require or how much of it would be performed outside the continental United States.
Data rights matter here because Raytheon, now part of RTX, has supplied ASARS for the U-2 since the early 1980s, and federal procurement records list the company as the holder of Air Force engineering and sustainment orders for the ASARS-2A version under contract FA8528-20-D-0023. A new supplier without access to the design data would have to show it can still repair and qualify the components.
The notice describes the radar’s job as producing near-real-time, high-resolution, long-range imagery of the ground day or night and in any weather. Synthetic aperture radar builds a detailed, map-like picture from radar returns as the aircraft moves, so clouds and darkness do not block it. Flying above 21,300 meters (70,000 feet), the U-2 can point the radar deep into territory it is not flying over.
The radar has gone through several versions. The baseline ASARS-2 entered service in the 1980s, and the Air Force received the first ASARS-2A as its replacement in 2001. In 2019, Raytheon said the newer ASARS-2B, built around an active electronically scanned array antenna, doubles the surveillance range of the ASARS-2A while keeping its mapping and imagery resolution. The Air Force’s fiscal 2021 budget request said the 2B replaces the 2A’s front-end components, which had become hard to support because parts were going out of production. The new notice refers only to ASARS-2 and does not say which versions the sustainment work would cover.
ASARS-2B is also slated to fly beyond the U-2: a Pentagon budget reprogramming document confirmed that the radar is part of the sensor suite for the U.S. Army’s High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System (HADES) intelligence business jets.
The notice lands in the middle of a long fight over the U-2’s future. In its fiscal 2027 budget, the Air Force proposed retiring its remaining U-2s by the end of the fiscal year, as part of a plan to divest 149 aircraft. Congress has blocked earlier retirement attempts, and House appropriators’ fiscal 2026 defense bill barred the service from divesting more than eight U-2s. The fleet is still flying: in January, maintainers at Beale Air Force Base, California, launched U-2s under simulated attack during Exercise Dragon Shield.

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:15:52 CET
16:15:52 KST

By Dave Graham
MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, an icon of the Mexican left who took up the banner of the disenfranchised in the 1980s to force changes in the political system despite never winning the presidency himself, has died at 92, the government said on Wednesday.
The first elected mayor of Mexico City, and the son of President Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas shook Mexico’s ruling establishment to its foundations when he ran for the top job in 1988 before losing a hotly disputed election.
That election pitted Cardenas against young technocrat Carlos Salinas, candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which had dominated Mexico since 1929.
With the two running neck-and-neck on election night, the government suddenly announced the system counting the votes had crashed.
After it came back online, Salinas was declared the winner, although many analysts and Cardenas himself believed the PRI had rigged the vote to retain its hold on power.
The contest was a watershed in Mexico, leading to political reform that strengthened the opposition. Two presidential elections later, in 2000, the PRI was finally ousted.
“His role in Mexico’s contemporary history is fundamental,” said President Claudia Sheinbaum, hailing Cardenas’ impact on Mexican politics.
“In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the desire for change of millions of Mexicans,” she said on social media, alluding to his supporters’ belief that he was the rightful winner of the disputed presidential election.
“That historic election, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation.”
Cardenas ran unsuccessfully for president twice more, fronting a leftist ticket for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which he helped found after breaking with the PRI in 1987. He finished third in 1994 and 2000.
Between those bids, the tall, soft-spoken Cardenas became mayor of Mexico City in 1997, beginning a long run for the PRD at the helm of the capital.
The PRD’s power waned after Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who followed in Cardenas’ footsteps as Mexico City mayor, split from it to found his own Morena party, which became the main force of the Mexican left and propelled him to the presidency.
But Cardenas’ early backing of the PRD marked a turning point in Mexican politics following decades of PRI domination.
It was Cardenas who finally galvanised leftist opposition to the PRI, said historian Lorenzo Meyer, adding, “And he had the capacity to mobilise.”
Cardenas paved the way for subsequent leftist challenges to the highest office, campaigning in remote villages never before visited by presidential candidates.
In later years, he emerged as an occasional critic of Lopez Obrador, a polarizing, often abrasive figure who succeeded him as the standard-bearer of the left and captured the top job in 2018.
Lopez Obrador raised huge protests when he too was denied victory in a bitterly contested presidential election in 2006, and again cried foul six years later. But the dignified Cardenas remained the left’s spiritual leader for many Mexicans.
Cardenas believed free market economics would not save Mexico from economic malaise, favoring a more state-centric model, similar to that later embraced by Lopez Obrador.
COALITION BUILDER
Cardenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, the first year of his father’s six-year term. A champion of land reform who nationalized the oil industry in 1938, Lazaro Cardenas was one of the most popular presidents in Mexican history.
Ironically, the late president’s success helped fortify the PRI, whose legitimacy his son later challenged.
Cardenas earned an engineering degree in 1957, then spent two years in France, West Germany and Italy on a fellowship.
After returning to Mexico, he began a career as a planner and hydraulic engineer, and entered politics in 1976 as a senator for his home state of Michoacan.
As PRI governor for Michoacan from 1980 to 1986, Cardenas was seen by some as too aloof to be a compelling administrator, but his reputation for honesty stood apart from the party’s growing association with graft in the minds of many Mexicans.
Michoacan became a bastion of the PRD, and Cardenas’ son, called Lazaro like his grandfather, also served as governor.
The younger Lazaro later took up senior roles under Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum, preserving the Mexican left’s historic ties with the family.
The challenge to the PRI by Cardenas began in late 1986 when he helped form the Democratic Current within the party.
The Current led calls for the PRI to adopt a more democratic means of selecting its presidential candidate, but these were ignored and leading members left the party in 1987.
“The PRI leadership has stopped our campaign for more open procedures within the party, but we will continue the struggle for true democracy in Mexico,” Cardenas said at the time.
Impressed by his coalition-building skills, newspaper El Financiero once described Cardenas as the sole candidate “who can gather leftist militants, neoliberals, and even ecologists.”
(Reporting by Dave Graham and David Alire Garcia; Editing by Rosalba O’Brien and Clarence Fernandez)

Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:12:00 UTC
16:12:00 KST

Presidential adviser: Lack of common EU position on Russia 'regrettable'
Europe lacks a shared plan for engaging Russia, which makes ending the war in Ukraine difficult, security adviser to the president Rainer Saks said.
Speaking to "Esimene stuudio" following Tuesday's phone call between Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Saks said what matters most is that Ukraine is satisfied.
"I would say that if this phone call is followed by something that brings the peace process closer in a direction amenable to Ukraine, then it can be considered to have been entirely positive. If Ukraine is satisfied that the call went ahead, then this is also entirely positive. We can't say that if Ukraine next asks Romania or Turkey to do something, then everyone else will start waving their arms in offense — that really doesn't work. But the fact that there is no common position on how to engage with Russia is somewhat regrettable," Saks said.
Europe as a whole is not yet mature enough to talk to Putin, since there are no shared discussions and no clear action plan is being drawn up, Saks added.
Saks noted Stubb and Estonia's president at the time, Alar Karis, said in spring talks with Russia at some point were inevitable, but that there was no readiness then as Europe had no common understanding of how the process should work.
Saks said President Ülle Madise, who entered office last month, had no prior warning the call was going ahead; diplomats informed Kadriorg afterwards.
"My advice to the president is that we support these steps if they bring us closer to peace, and we simply need to communicate with each other more. Within Estonia, the first thing is of course for the government to ensure people are on the same wavelength in terms of both information and position," Saks said.
He disagreed with the claim that there is no point in engaging Putin whatsoever. "The question is not whether there is a point in communicating or not, but how you communicate and what it is you want to achieve. [But] there is no point in simply talking for the sake of talking — I agree with that part," he said.
Saks stressed that the concept of Europe being part of the process should not be interpreted as the EU as a whole being part of it, given the multiplicity of institutions and high-ranking figures that would entail. He said a coalition of the willing on support for Ukraine would have the initial moral obligation and right to put something common together. "Until that is done, these potential problems will keep recurring," he said.
Saks said the Finnish and Norwegian foreign ministries briefed diplomats from Estonia and other key partners, but that briefing was of limited value as the content of the meeting had already been splashed across the media in some detail.
As to the claim that Putin delivered a 70-minute monologue, Saks said the Russian president gives such monologues at all meetings, and that the time should be discounted somewhat for translation. "But it also shows that the Russian president took the time, considered it important, and delivered his monologue," he said.
When asked about Russian media attempts to present the call to in a light which gives the Kremlin the advantage, Saks said Moscow is trying to establish two things: first that Europe must eventually join talks, and second that the U.S. alone cannot pressure Ukraine. "That is of course a mistake we all make: we think Ukraine is fighting only because we support them. No — they are fighting because they want to survive, and in the end they decide most of all how long they can hold out, how motivated they are and so on," Saks concluded.
Finland and Norway initiated the 90-minute call from Helsinki in their capacity as states which border Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe. The call was prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the U.S. following last week's Oslo meeting.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) was briefed on Tuesday's call.

U.S. Navy awards $43.7M for F-35 mission data lab upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:11:04 UTC
16:11:04 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $43.7 million modification to upgrade operating systems at F-35 reprogramming laboratory facilities through April 2030.
- F-35 cooperative program partners fund $29.7 million, with the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contributing about $7 million.
Lockheed Martin will upgrade the operating systems running the F-35 Lightning II reprogramming laboratories, which build the threat data the fighter needs for combat missions, under a $43.7 million contract modification the U.S. Navy announced on Oct. 28. Eighty percent of the work will take place in Eglin, Florida, and the remaining 20% in Fort Worth, Texas, with completion expected in April 2030.
F-35 cooperative program partners are paying $29,696,266 of the $43,673,774 total, or about 68%, while the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy each contribute $6,988,754 in fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, all of it obligated at award. The Navy aircraft procurement account also funds U.S. Marine Corps aviation, and the announcement lists the U.S. Marine Corps among the services the labs support.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued the cost-plus-fixed-fee modification, designated P00025, without competition, adding new contract line items to contract N00019-22-C-0046. The announcement does not name the operating systems being replaced, the laboratories or hardware affected, or how the partner share is divided among countries.
The labs produce mission data files, the libraries of radars, missiles and aircraft that an F-35’s radar, electronic warfare suite and other sensors use to recognize and classify what they detect in a given region. The files are loaded onto each jet before flight from a portable drive.
At Eglin, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps personnel of the 513th Electronic Warfare Squadron, part of the 350th Spectrum Warfare Wing, run the United States Reprogramming Laboratory, which produces mission data for U.S. jets and tests it on a hardware-in-the-loop line against simulated threat signals before release to the fleet. The squadron was activated at Eglin on April 23, 2010, to operate the lab, then valued at $300 million.
A 2017 U.S. Air Force account of the squadron’s work said mission data does not carry over automatically, so the squadron had to rebuild and repackage the files for each new version of the aircraft’s operating system. That refers to the software on the jet rather than the lab computers covered by the new award, but it explains why lab infrastructure gets steady funding as the F-35 moves through successive software releases.
Federal spending records show N00019-22-C-0046 began on April 29, 2022, as a base year plus five years of sustainment support for the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory and surrogate encryption work for the Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory, all for non-U.S. participants. The public announcements do not explain what the surrogate encryption support involves. In April 2025, a $22,126,598 modification (P00014) added maintenance and sustainment of the U.S. Reprogramming Laboratory and the partner support complex for the U.S. military, non-DOD partners and Foreign Military Sales customers. A further $23,312,570 modification (P00022) in April 2026 continued that work.
Lockheed Martin first set up the Australia, Canada and United Kingdom Reprogramming Laboratory, known as ACURL, at its Fort Worth plant and moved it to Eglin under a $7.5 million modification awarded in 2018. British and Australian officials opened the lab there in February 2020, when it reached initial operating capability, and kept Canada’s name on the facility even though Ottawa had stepped back from the F-35 at the time. British and Australian staff now run the center as the reactivated 80 Squadron, which develops, verifies and validates mission data files for the three allies.
The Norway Italy Reprogramming Laboratory opened nearby on June 27, 2019, and was formally accepted on Sept. 22, 2021. Israel’s F-35 software work runs under a separate arrangement, and the U.S. Navy added $11.4 million in April for three additional software builds for Israel’s fleet.
Since N00019-22-C-0046 now sustains both the U.S. lab and the partner labs, the operating system work could cover either, and the Oct. 28 announcement describes it only as covering laboratory facilities and systems sustained for the U.S. services and the cooperative partners.
A separate $111.1 million modification to another Lockheed contract, N00019-20-C-0026, funded a minimum viable product of a Common Reprogramming Tool meant to replace the legacy programming tools used across the reprogramming labs. Lot 18 orders also bought multi-ship infrared search and track and Band 5 radar warning receiver hardware for development work at the U.S., ACURL and Norway-Italy labs. Each new sensor on the aircraft needs matching hardware and data in the labs, as will the 432 electronic warfare modification kits the U.S. Navy ordered for $991 million in May.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign said Thursday that cyberattacks using overseas IP addresses had breached a campaign server and flooded a platform with more than 70,000 fake sign-ups.

The campaign said it quickly required users to log in before signing up. The change blocked the automated submissions and allowed the platform to resume normal operations.
Shen said cybersecurity had always been a priority for his campaign. His office said all affected websites were operating normally and that it would continue to guard against further attacks.
