'We must learn so that it doesn't happen again': Oct. 7 veterans prepare soldiers for the next war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:39:37 UTC
15:39:37 KST

On Oct. 7, 2023, as Israel awoke to an unprecedented nightmare, these four company commanders were still serving in more junior positions. They rushed from the officer training school, private trips and weekend leave straight into the chaos in communities near the Gaza border, including Be'eri, Kissufim, Nir Oz and the Re'im junction.
They rescued civilians under heavy fire, witnessed scenes they had previously thought existed only in movies and, in some cases, suffered serious injuries. Now, after three consecutive years of intense fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank, they command companies at the Givati Brigade's training base, the Nahal Brigade's training base, the Paratroopers' training program and the squad commanders' course.
The officers are bringing hard-earned operational lessons and insights gained at great personal cost to the training grounds, where they are responsible for educating and shaping the next generation of combat soldiers.
"On Oct. 7, I was a team commander in the Gefen Battalion at Bahad 1," recalled Capt. Y., now a company commander overseeing recruits in the Givati Reconnaissance Unit, referring to the IDF's officer training school.
"We started that morning at 7 a.m., and I drove south with my father to reach the assembly point. I spent my first hours of fighting with two officer cadets, and from there we drove to the Re'im junction area, near the site of the music festival, and then to Nir Oz.
"I separated from the cadets to join my team because I understood that I was responsible for my unit and couldn't let my soldiers fight without me. We brought combat equipment from Bahad 1 and then headed into fighting in Sufa, Nir Yitzhak and the Yesha junction. We spent three or four days restoring control."
One moment from those first days remains particularly vivid.
"There was a moment when we stopped the Humvees, quickly prepared ourselves and the company commander told us to forget what we knew and understand that we were entering a combat zone," Capt. Y. recalled.
"When you're in the Gaza or Lebanon sector and someone tells you that, you understand. But I looked around and saw kibbutzim and Israeli communities. That really struck me. It was a period of tremendous shock and disbelief."
A generation that did not experience Oct. 7
Serious injuries and prolonged combat have become inseparable parts of the commanders' stories.
Capt. N., now a company commander in the Paratroopers' 890th Battalion training program who is set to be promoted to major, fought in Be'eri during the first days of the attack as part of a force known as "Ben-Mosh."
"We ran through Be'eri for two consecutive nights, going from house to house, rescuing residents and fighting in firefights until the community was declared clear," Capt. N. said.
"From there, we moved on to preparations for entering Gaza. A week after the ground offensive began, I was seriously wounded by friendly fire. Shrapnel cut into my windpipe, I was sedated and placed on a ventilator, and I underwent two months of rehabilitation. As soon as I could, I went straight back to my company."
Three years later, the new generation of soldiers is one that did not experience Oct. 7 firsthand as combat troops.
"Today, apart from my deputy company commander, no one serving under me was there on Oct. 7 or at the beginning of the ground offensive," Capt. N. said.
"My job is to help the soldiers imagine what it looked like. We were there, and we remember the initial shock. Our responsibility is to make sure that shock doesn't happen again next time."
Capt. A., a company commander in the IDF's squad commanders' course, puts the cultural and disciplinary lessons in stark terms.
"When I apply Oct. 7 to the training of commanders, I tell my trainees one thing: We must never forget. We must not forget what happened to us and what was done to us, and we must not forget that we failed in our mission," Capt. A. said.
"Alongside heroic battles, there were quite a few professional lessons we must learn so that it doesn't happen again. And it could happen tomorrow morning.
"My trainees were schoolchildren on Oct. 7, and now the responsibility rests on their shoulders. If they forget, we'll fall back into the same assumptions that made us less effective.
"At the tactical level, when I say there could be a war tomorrow morning, it's not a cliché. It's a belief I translate into daily preparations: maintaining constant readiness with ammunition, drills, defensive procedures and readiness at dawn.
"In my view, operational culture is the greatest lesson. Where that culture was lacking, that's where we failed."
'We failed in our mission to defend'
These lessons are shaping the next generation of soldiers from the ground up.
Capt. Y., a company commander at the Nahal Brigade's training base who is currently leading recruits through a week of field training, recalled the moment everything changed for him.
"We entered Kissufim into a full-scale battlefield, with gunfire coming from every direction and rockets in the air," he said.
"As we were driving, a friend who was in the vehicle with me was speaking on the phone with his family in Be'eri, explaining how to tie a shirt into a tourniquet to save their younger brother, who had been shot.
"We went from house to house under fire to rescue families and act as human shields for them. Our mission was to make sure no civilian was harmed, and we failed in that mission."
Capt. Y. of the Nahal training base said today's recruits arrive with a profound sense of responsibility. They understand that they are the country's protective vest, he said, and are eager to learn from the combat experience their commanders have accumulated.
Capt. Y. of the Givati Reconnaissance Unit described his company as part of a "generation of victory," a generation that has fought continuously for three years across multiple fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, and demonstrated levels of resilience and capability rarely seen among soldiers performing mandatory military service.
All four commanders agree that the operational experience gained at such a heavy cost will, in their view, leave the next generation of combat soldiers better prepared to face the most demanding challenges.

====================================================================================================

What European students can learn from their Serbian peers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:39:24 UTC
15:39:24 KST

What European students can learn from their Serbian peers
The Serbian student mobilisation chose a political strategy that ensured its success where others had failed.
While Europe was asleep over the past two years, Serbia was wide awake. A nationwide student movement shook the foundations of a deeply entrenched government and on Sunday, it dealt it an unprecedented electoral blow – something opposition parties had failed to do for more than a decade.
Until the election results came out, the Serbian student movement was largely ignored by international media. The students were seen as naive, irrelevant, disaffected youth.
That they were underestimated by the world and by President Aleksandar Vucic was perhaps to their advantage. But Serbian students did not just rely on their opponent’s overconfidence. For almost two years, they built and practised an alternative model of politics that soon became visible and eventually triumphed at the polls.
The hidden abode of alternative politics
Although the student protests were triggered by one particular incident – the death of 16 people in a train canopy collapse at a newly renovated station in 2024 – their anger had much deeper roots.
Students and their families had been squeezed from all sides: by local elites whose corruption and mismanagement eroded the standard of living and plunged them into precarity; and by international corporations, which fed that corruption, while offering substandard jobs with little prospect of social mobility.
The protests the students started were not the first against Vucic and his government. But what was different this time is that they remained independent: neither aligned with any domestic political party nor any of the four superpowers Serbia is dealing with – Russia, China, the European Union and the United States.
Students managed to sustain the pressure because they did not join existing politics. Most Serbian opposition parties are small, centralised and increasingly detached from the crises people face daily. They are also vulnerable to corruption in a country dependent on foreign investment and credit. Associating with them would have been damaging to the movement.
Instead, the students created their own alternative political scene. Across the country, they blockaded and took over universities, bringing higher education to a standstill. They filled squares with peaceful protests and vigils. They set up their own structures to run their affairs at occupied buildings.
This strong self-reliance was apparent at the Faculty of Technical Sciences in Novi Sad — Serbia’s largest university department, with more than 16,000 students enrolled — which I visited for the first time in March 2025. I was invited there to speak to students.
The faculty looked nothing like it had before. Student guards controlled entrances with communication equipment and metal fencing. LED screens in the corridors announced plenaries and alternative lectures for students. There were rooms stocked with food sorted by type, and medical supplies, with student nurses tending to anyone in need. Kitchens, reading rooms and a student-run administration could also be seen at the faculty.
Discussions on current political and economic issues of interest to Serbia, organised by the students’ alternative education sections, often involved 300 to 400 students and lasted five or six hours, covering topics that would later enter the movement’s electoral programme.
This level of organisation, focused around student plenaries, earned them the respect of the general population, and enabled them to withstand the attempts by the police to evict them. The more the government and its repressive apparatus attacked them, the more the people stood with them.
Introducing direct democracy
As this bond between the students and the wider population grew deeper, democratic participation expanded. By March 2025, suffering more and more attacks, the students called for people to establish citizens’ assemblies akin to the student plenaries, in order to aid them in seeking justice for the 16 killed in Novi Sad.
As the Serbian government continued its repressive strategy, the students realised that a change was necessary and made the first public demand for snap elections.
Their approach to electoral politics was the same as their approach to protest: independent, transparent, and democratic.
The students took decisions collectively. They chose academics and activists whom they had invited to their occupied faculties to discuss and debate with well-known public figures. The gender distribution was equal between men and women and between the various university regions.
It was collectively decided that established politicians would not be nominated. The students made it clear they rejected being incorporated into a type of leadership-based politics that was failing all across Europe.
Candidates were chosen after interviews with students. Last summer, I was invited to one such interview session near Novi Sad. There was a large group of 300 students who questioned each candidate. Phones had to be left outside.
This was the hidden abode of a new kind of politics: decisions were made not at a party headquarters by a select few, but by a network of assemblies, local committees and informal institutions. It was leaderless, and in that particular moment, it worked.
The challenges ahead
The Student List has already started negotiations to form the government. The challenges ahead are numerous. Undoing the damage of the past 14 years would be difficult. But even more challenging is the complex geopolitical arena the new government will face.
The first test will come soon enough. In its electoral programme, the Student List made clear that it condemns the genocide in Gaza and would not be complicit in it. How would this principle translate into practice?
Under Vucic, Serbian-Israeli relations grew closer. After October 2023, Serbian arms exports to Israel jumped from $3.3m that year to $126m in 2025. In September, Vucic opened a factory for the production of Israeli drones.
If the new government is to abide by the Student List electoral programme, it would have to halt arms exports to Israel at the very least.
This would not be a symbolic gesture. It would mean extending political change won at the elections into the economic sphere, unsettling Serbia’s foreign relations and challenging the country’s place in the wider geopolitical order. It could be a truly revolutionary moment.
Given the industrial weight of the arms industry, Serbia’s security cooperation with Israel and its reliance on foreign investment, such a decision could provoke resistance from domestic vested interests and pressure from foreign partners.
In this context, it was no surprise that US-based conservative influencers intervened in the final days of the electoral campaign, framing support for Vucic as a defence of Serbia’s Christian identity against “Islamisation” and the so-called Muslim threat.
Meanwhile, the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) — a powerful US conservative organisation — is set to open a Serbian chapter in November, with Vucic expected to play a central role.
Any shift in Serbia’s ties to the superpowers will test the Student List, its ability to survive as a governing force and its capacity to manage tensions while avoiding conflict within Serbia.
That is why the Serbian case matters beyond the Balkans. Europe, facing its own student movements in Belgium, France, Italy and Spain, has largely ignored what happened in Serbia.
But if civil society begins to collapse in the continent’s core countries under increasing economic strain, the political experiment Serbian students have successfully completed may prove invaluable.
The question is no longer whether lessons can be drawn from Serbia, but whether Europe is ready to learn from them — or once again look away, until the crisis arrives at its own door.

Ousted defense ministry chief to run for Parempoolsed at Riigikogu election

Ousted defense ministry chief to run for Parempoolsed at Riigikogu election
Kaimo Kuusk, former Defense Ministry permanent secretary and former ambassador to Ukraine, is joining Parempoolsed and running for the Riigikogu next spring.
Parempoolsed are seeking to win their first ever Riigikogu seats at the March 2027 election.
Kuusk said via a party press release that he decided to run because he wants to see real impact from his work for Estonia's benefit: "I want my experience, skills and values to serve Estonia's security and defense capability."
He also hit out at what he called undemocratic approaches taken by some of the major parties.
"I can't stand by and watch Estonian democracy being eroded. It's very important to me that Estonia be a state governed by law. I won't accept it if Reform runs the same kind of politics in the country as Center does in Tallinn, where positions aren't allocated via competitions but in the party office," Kuusk said.
Kuusk also criticized the government's decision to hold a planned Ukraine aid conference in late January, which he said, given the situation there in winter, is the least suitable time for Ukraine yet convenient for campaign point-scoring for some of the political parties.
"We're setting the Ukraine reconstruction conference at the least suitable time for the Ukrainians, as Reform and Eesti 200 politicians want to tie it to the front of their election cart. Aid to Ukraine like this is of no benefit to Ukraine," Kuusk added. He noted a worrying trend which he says has emerged in Estonian politics whereby aid to Ukraine is seen primarily as having election propaganda value, at the cost of the state's functioning. "Various state institutions have consequently fallen out with each other. Something has gone wrong when, during a war, the most important question becomes who gets to open a kindergarten in Ukraine."
Kuusk stressed he joined Parempoolsed, founded shortly before the last Riigikogu elections in 2023, as he believes in the party's team and clear plans. "Parempoolsed offer values-based politics that will make Estonia's future better. I like that Parempoolsed dare to decide," he explained.
Parempoolsed chair Lavly Perling said she values Kuusk as a team player. "In addition, Kaimo hasn't worked on aiding Ukraine only on paper, but has been physically on the ground in Ukraine. I also know that as ambassador Kaimo was very active in economic diplomacy, opening doors in Ukraine for Estonian companies," said Perling, a former prosecutor general who has worked in Ukraine.
"Kaimo joining the team makes us even stronger and shows that people believe in Parempoolsed. For the voter who wants a better future for Estonia, the only alternative to the populists in spring 2027 is Parempoolsed," Perling added.
Kuusk, 50, was Estonia's ambassador to Ukraine from 2019 to 2023, ambassador to Lithuania from 2023 to 2024, and Defense Ministry permanent secretary from 2024 until September. Before entering the foreign service he worked for several decades at the Foreign Intelligence Service (Välisluureamet).
Kuusk was dismissed as Defense Ministry permanent secretary in September, weeks after incoming Defense Minister Martin Herem (Reform) made Kuusk's departure a condition of taking up the ministerial spot.
Kuusk's last working day at the ministry was September 15. The government justified his dismissal on the basis of failed cooperation. SDE chair Lauri Läänemets asked the Chancellor of Justice to review the legality of that dismissal. Hanno Pevkur, who resigned as defense minister at the start of September following a defense procurement scandal, said national defense leadership could not be left the victim of mutual distrust.

First seal ring depicting lighthouse of Alexandria found during dig at sunken ancient Egyptian port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:33:54 UTC
15:33:54 KST

A bronze seal ring engraved with an image of the historic Pharos of Alexandria was discovered during underwater excavations, the Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Ministry announced early this month.
The lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was built during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (280–247 BCE). It is believed to have stood at least 100 meters tall, making it one of the world’s tallest man-made structures at the time.
Earthquakes between 956 CE and 1303 severely damaged it, after which it was abandoned and its stones were later used to build the Citadel of Qaitbay in 1480.
Remains of the lighthouse were found in 1994 by a group of French archaeologists, and in 2025, parts of its threshold and foundation paving stones were resurfaced to aid in Egypt’s digital reconstruction effort of the site.
The ring was found at the former island of Antirhodos, which once was part of Alexandria’s Portus Magnus, the ancient royal eastern harbor. The island was also home to the Ptolemaic Egyptian palace.
The island is believed to have sunk around the 4th century CE, following an an earthquake near Crete in 365 that triggered additional earthquakes and a tsunami. The site now lies underwater, off the coast of modern Alexandria, at a depth of approximately five meters.
Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, affirmed that it is the first time an image of the ancient lighthouse has ever been found engraved on a seal ring.
According to Leithy, the lighthouse’s depiction on the ring could indicate that the palace of Antirhodos remained in use until the second century CE for administrative purposes, including those of the lighthouse.
The image is similar to other well-known depictions of the structure seen on coins dated to the second century CE.
Amphorae, oil lamps also discovered during ongoing excavations
Alongside the ring’s discovery, European Institute for Underwater Archaeology Director Franck Goddio explained that several other artifacts had been unearthed by the excavation team during the current season.
Such artifacts include pottery tableware, amphorae, flasks, and oil lamps dating from the 4th century BCE to the 4th century CE. The remnants of glass vessels, dating to the same period, were also found.
The excavations, Goddio noted, are concentrated on four sites in the eastern harbor area, such as the Temple of Isis, the palace site and the western mound on the royal island of Antirhodos, the remains of the obelisk, and the Timonium ("Antony's palace").
Egyptian Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy applauded the archaeological mission for its finds, noting their contribution to enriching knowledge of Alexandria's history.

US elections watchdog restores filing system after cyberattack clouds last-minute spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:33:15 UTC
15:33:15 KST

The Federal Election Commission restored its electronic filing system Wednesday night after taking it offline for nearly 41 hours to contain a cyberattack, which temporarily concealed spending from big donors as political donations ramp up in the final days of the midterms.
Campaign watchdogs sounded alarms as the outage dragged into its third evening. Super PACs and other groups couldn't file mandatory 24- and 48-hour reports showing how much money they are spending to help or hurt candidates at the polls, keeping the most recent political spending out of public view.
"We didn't have access to the last-minute spending, which is really ramped up as the election draws nearer," said campaign finance watchdog Molly White, who tracks crypto and Big Tech political spending. "We have no visibility into that when the filing systems are down."
"It's pretty devastating this close to the election," she added.
Cyberattack on FEC disrupts disclosure of super PAC spending
The outage came at a critical time as daily spending accelerates to its fastest pace in the two-year election cycle, campaign finance experts said. Super PACs, which can accept and give unlimited amounts of money, and dark money groups spent an average of over $50 million per day the week before the outage, OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin said. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added.
The FEC told users that most of the services affected by the outage have been restored. It posted a notice just after 10 p.m. ET on Monday saying it was investigating a problem that caused "major" outages across its systems that process electronic campaign filings.
Reuters could not establish the motive for the hacking effort. Hackers of all stripes regularly target government networks for espionage, financial gain or political motives.
The FEC does not administer US elections, and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.
“Disclosure delayed is disclosure denied,” Hilary Braseth, executive director of nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets, said in a statement released before the system was restored. “When hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money flood political airwaves in the final days before an election, transparency is not an optional luxury, it is a fundamental public safeguard.”
The FEC did not return requests for comment Wednesday or announce any details about the cause of the outage. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.
An FEC officer told campaign compliance firms late Monday that it took those services offline after a "bad actor" tried to breach the agency's systems, according to an email Reuters reviewed.
Campaign finance managers had to reset their passwords before logging in to the system, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.
The timing of the hacking attempt so close to the November 3 elections, and the FEC's lack of information, stirred up conspiracy theories throughout the industry, several people said. White noted that it would be a good way for unscrupulous actors to hide unpopular last-minute spending.
"It's hard to say with any real information that that's what happened, but it's certainly I think where people's minds go very quickly," she said.
Kyle Sandy, the cybersecurity director at IT security firm Logically, said taking the system offline is the right call when dealing with an attack.
"It tells me the FEC detected something they couldn't immediately scope and chose a known outage over an unknown risk," Sandy said, giving the agency time to ensure none of its data was altered by the hackers before bringing it back online.

What is Canada’s climate track record as it seeks 'ever closer' ties with Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:32:14 UTC
15:32:14 KST

Critics say there is a stark contrast between PM Mark Carney's international reputation as a climate champion and his domestic drive to expand oil and gas production.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made an unexpected offer to Canada: to become the EU's first ever “associate member”.
After pushback on the term from member states, most of all Germany, the EU is now pushing for "ever closer association" with Canada, in the latest draft of a joint declaration due to be adopted at the end of the EU-Canada summit which starts today in Montreal.
There is broad consensus amongst member states on closer cooperation with Canada on areas such as defence, critical raw materials, energy, trade and border security.
Just this week the EU's climate chief has told member states they must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, signalling that the Commission is taking climate preparedness seriously. But what about Canada?
Here we look into Canada's policies on oil and gas, the energy transition, carbon pricing and greenwashing.
What is the Pacific Link oil pipeline?
Since taking office in 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has scrapped key policies which would drive down emissions - such as abandoning a planned cap on oil and gas emissions and weakening industrial carbon pricing, according to global NGOs like Climate Action Tracker and Environmental Defence.
At the same time, Carney's government has made it easier for oil and gas projects to get approval. This includes a proposed oil pipeline - the Pacific Link which will carry one million barrels of oil sands bitumen a day from Alberta to the Pacific Ocean off the coast of British Columbia, threatening the habitat of endangered orcas and could increase greenhouse gas emissions up to 18.7 million tonnes.
These decisions mark a significant departure from the climate credentials Carney cultivated as governor of the Bank of England and as the United Nations' special envoy for climate action and finance.
It also raises questions about whether his ambition to turn Canada into a global energy superpower will come at the expense of the country's climate commitments - and whether additional supplies of fossil fuels could slow the transition to cleaner energy in Europe and Asia.
From climate champion to fossil fuel expansion
Carney has a reputation as a skilled statesman and long-time climate champion. This is partly because of his longstanding warnings about the financial risks of climate change.
In 2015, as governor of the Bank of England, he warned that the consequences of global warming could happen sooner than the timelines used by financial markets and lawmakers.
"The catastrophic impacts of climate change will be felt beyond the traditional horizons of most actors - imposing a cost on future generations that the current generation has no direct incentive to fix," Carney said during a speech at Lloyd's of London.
Carney later helped mobilise financial institutions around net-zero commitments.
As PM of Canada, environmental critics say Carney's agenda prioritises energy production, investment and competitiveness over climate policies designed to reduce fossil fuel consumption.
The changes reach beyond his cancellation of consumer carbon pricing, which made households directly pay for their emissions.
Carney's government has also scrapped the electric vehicle mandate, abandoned the proposed oil and gas emissions cap, weakened the national industrial carbon price and relaxed anti-greenwashing standards. Public transport funding has also been massively cut back.
Taken together, the measures risk weakening both sides of Canada's decarbonisation strategy, climate activists argue, citing incentives to move away from fossil fuels and investment in alternatives.
Carney's government has continued to invest in some clean energy projects, but its emphasis on expanding oil and gas production is creating a tension between its climate commitments and its economic strategy.
New oil and gas projects on a faster track
The clearest expression of that shift is the government's push to accelerate approvals for major infrastructure projects.
The 2025 Building Canada Act created a mechanism to designate projects as being in the national interest and exempt them from certain legal requirements.
The legislation was presented as a way to accelerate projects considered strategically important, including developments in critical minerals, renewable energy, nuclear power, ports and hydropower.
But oil and gas projects have featured prominently in the government's plans.
In September 2026, Carney's government introduced a law that would allow projects to be pre-approved in designated regions of national interest, shorten major project reviews to one year and give a federal minister greater powers to remove environmental conditions attached to previously approved projects.
Environmental groups argue that the legislation weakens safeguards for wildlife and reduces public oversight.
LNG expansion and the global race for gas
Carney's energy strategy also includes expanding Canada's Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) export capacity.
The government has backed plans which could double the facility's export capacity from Canada's west coast. It has also signalled openness to developing gas exports from New Brunswick if the province reverses its fracking ban and establishes a domestic production industry.
Ottawa argues it can provide reliable supplies to international partners seeking to diversify their energy sources. Ahead of the EU-Canada summit this week in Montreal, the two blocs are expected to present a feasibility study on long-term LNG exports to Europe, according to a document seen by Euronews.
For Europe, which has sought to reduce its dependence on Russian fossil fuels, additional supplies from politically stable producers could improve energy security. Asian markets are also potential destinations for Canadian LNG.
But greater availability of gas does not translate into a faster energy transition. New LNG terminals and pipelines require substantial investment and can operate for decades. If they encourage long-term gas consumption or divert capital from electrification and renewable energy, they could slow the transition away from fossil fuels.
Esther Bollendorff, fossil-free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network (CAN) Europe, said Canada shouldn’t become the EU’s next gas supplier, but a partner in building an affordable and resilient energy future.
The environmentalist said the proposed feasibility study on LNG exports to the EU is a "dangerous distraction" from renewables-based electrification and energy efficiency.
"It risks locking in fossil fuel infrastructure, stranded assets and higher bills for consumers on both sides of the Atlantic, while undermining Europe’s climate goals," Bollendorff says.
Green activists worry that expanding fossil fuel supply can influence the choices available to importing countries, potentially making continued gas consumption more attractive than investing in alternatives like wind and solar.
An energy superpower - but for whose benefit?
Carney has presented fossil fuel expansion as a way to strengthen Canada's economic independence and attract international investment. Yet the ownership of the industry complicates the claim that expanding oil and gas will necessarily translate into greater Canadian economic control.
A report by Canadians for Tax Fairness found that the four largest Canadian oil sands producers are 60 per cent US-owned. LNG Canada is a joint venture involving Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi and Kogas.
That means a substantial share of the capital and corporate interests behind Canada's energy expansion comes from outside the country.
Carney's argument is that Canada can use its energy resources to strengthen its economic position and reduce its vulnerability to external pressure. But if the industry relies heavily on foreign capital and public support, the distribution of benefits and risks becomes a central question.
Climate targets increasingly out of reach
The retreat from climate policy comes as Canada appears unlikely to meet its emissions-reduction commitments.
According to Climate Action Tracker, planned Canadian policies could reduce emissions by just 14 per cent, well short of the country's target of cutting emissions by 40–45 per cent over the same period.
A September 2026 analysis by the Canadian Climate Institute also concluded that Canada would miss its 2030 emissions target, suggesting the shortfall could persist even towards 2050.

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:26:14 UTC
15:26:14 KST

Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, elder statesman of Mexican left, dies at 92
MEXICO CITY, Oct 28 - Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, an icon of the Mexican left who took up the banner of the disenfranchised in the 1980s to force changes in the political system despite never winning the presidency himself, has died at 92, the government said on Wednesday.
The first elected mayor of Mexico City, and the son of President Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas shook Mexico's ruling establishment to its foundations when he ran for the top job in 1988 before losing a hotly disputed election.
That election pitted Cardenas against young technocrat Carlos Salinas, candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which had dominated Mexico since 1929.
With the two running neck-and-neck on election night, the government suddenly announced the system counting the votes had crashed.
After it came back online, Salinas was declared the winner, although many analysts and Cardenas himself believed the PRI had rigged the vote to retain its hold on power.
The contest was a watershed in Mexico, leading to political reform that strengthened the opposition. Two presidential elections later, in 2000, the PRI was finally ousted.
"His role in Mexico's contemporary history is fundamental," said President Claudia Sheinbaum, hailing Cardenas' impact on Mexican politics.
"In 1988, he led a peaceful democratic movement that channeled the desire for change of millions of Mexicans," she said on social media, alluding to his supporters' belief that he was the rightful winner of the disputed presidential election.
"That historic election, in which he should have been recognized as president, marked the beginning of the democratic transformation."
Cardenas ran unsuccessfully for president twice more, fronting a leftist ticket for the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), which he helped found after breaking with the PRI in 1987. He finished third in 1994 and 2000.
Between those bids, the tall, soft-spoken Cardenas became mayor of Mexico City in 1997, beginning a long run for the PRD at the helm of the capital.
The PRD’s power waned after Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who followed in Cardenas’ footsteps as Mexico City mayor, split from it to found his own Morena party, which became the main force of the Mexican left and propelled him to the presidency.
But Cardenas' early backing of the PRD marked a turning point in Mexican politics following decades of PRI domination.
It was Cardenas who finally galvanised leftist opposition to the PRI, said historian Lorenzo Meyer, adding, "And he had the capacity to mobilise."
Cardenas paved the way for subsequent leftist challenges to the highest office, campaigning in remote villages never before visited by presidential candidates.
In later years, he emerged as an occasional critic of Lopez Obrador, a polarizing, often abrasive figure who succeeded him as the standard-bearer of the left and captured the top job in 2018.
Lopez Obrador raised huge protests when he too was denied victory in a bitterly contested presidential election in 2006, and again cried foul six years later. But the dignified Cardenas remained the left's spiritual leader for many Mexicans.
Cardenas believed free market economics would not save Mexico from economic malaise, favoring a more state-centric model, similar to that later embraced by Lopez Obrador.
COALITION BUILDER
Cardenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, the first year of his father's six-year term. A champion of land reform who nationalized the oil industry in 1938, Lazaro Cardenas was one of the most popular presidents in Mexican history.
Ironically, the late president's success helped fortify the PRI, whose legitimacy his son later challenged.
Cardenas earned an engineering degree in 1957, then spent two years in France, West Germany and Italy on a fellowship.
After returning to Mexico, he began a career as a planner and hydraulic engineer, and entered politics in 1976 as a senator for his home state of Michoacan.
As PRI governor for Michoacan from 1980 to 1986, Cardenas was seen by some as too aloof to be a compelling administrator, but his reputation for honesty stood apart from the party’s growing association with graft in the minds of many Mexicans.
Michoacan became a bastion of the PRD, and Cardenas' son, called Lazaro like his grandfather, also served as governor.
The younger Lazaro later took up senior roles under Lopez Obrador and Sheinbaum, preserving the Mexican left’s historic ties with the family.
The challenge to the PRI by Cardenas began in late 1986 when he helped form the Democratic Current within the party.
The Current led calls for the PRI to adopt a more democratic means of selecting its presidential candidate, but these were ignored and leading members left the party in 1987.
"The PRI leadership has stopped our campaign for more open procedures within the party, but we will continue the struggle for true democracy in Mexico," Cardenas said at the time.
Impressed by his coalition-building skills, newspaper El Financiero once described Cardenas as the sole candidate "who can gather leftist militants, neoliberals, and even ecologists." REUTERS

'Desolation, despair': Spain begins three days of mourning after deadly train crash
Spain entered three days of mourning on Thursday after a high-speed train collision killed 68 people and injured scores. The incident has prompted fresh questions about rail safety and management.
Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second high-speed rail collision this year killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister reported an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.
The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage at night to find further victims on the key line linking Madrid with the southern city of Seville, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, reporters saw.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when "I woke up and I was in the air."
Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, saying that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.
Wearing a bloodstained grey jumper and holding his tattered suitcase, he recounted "a very strong hit... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos".
"I think I've been born again," he said.
'Long and hard hours'
A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones.
Read moreSpain to observe three days of mourning after scores killed in high-speed train collision
Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears, amid crowds of police and journalists from around the world.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said "long and hard hours" were in store because "every person will manage it in their own way.
"We have people who are in shock, who haven't taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.
The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to enable relatives of the victims to provide DNA samples and help identify the missing.
Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims' families.
"What matters most is being with the victims' relatives, that they feel the closeness, because words at a time like this are pointless, but a hug helps," he said.
Recalling how he rushed to the site of the crash, Fernandez said he was confronted with "an image of desolation, despair, uncertainty, death".
'Inexplicable'
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometres (43 miles) of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25 kilometres before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
Read moreRail safety questioned after Spain suffers second fatal high-speed train crash in a year
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.
The latest disaster comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.

Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:25:02 UTC
15:25:02 KST

Europe’s wealth gap: Older households eight times richer than young ones
As protests over living costs and programme cuts spread across Europe, under-35s hold 2.8 percent of household wealth.
Student protests that began in September in France have spread to more than 11 European countries as anger rises over high rents and fuel prices and cuts to public services.
Many young protesters said they no longer expect to be better off than their parents, and household wealth data show a wide gap between generations.
Across the eurozone and two other European countries, households headed by someone under 35 have a median net wealth of about 25,000 euros ($27,870) while those headed by 55- to 64-year-olds are worth about 208,000 euros ($231,882), more than eight times as much, according to the European Central Bank’s (ECB’s) 2023 Household Finance and Consumption Survey.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera compares wealth by age groups across 22 European countries and looks at how much more expensive life has become since 2000.
Where is the wealth gap widest?
The Household Finance and Consumption Survey, run by the ECB and national central banks since 2010, tracks household wealth and debt in the eurozone, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
It measures net wealth, which includes property, cars, valuables and savings, minus debts. Under-35s hold just 2.8 percent of all household wealth in the 22 countries while 55- to 64-year-olds hold the largest share at 24 percent.
In Finland, under-35s hold 0.8 percent of household wealth, the lowest share of any country surveyed, while over-55s hold more than 71 percent. Young people’s shares are also small in Ireland (1.4 percent), Austria (1.6 percent), Greece (1.8 percent) and Germany (2 percent).
Rising housing costs mean many young people cannot afford what their parents or grandparents could.
Wealth is more evenly spread in Central and Eastern Europe. In Lithuania, under-35s hold 13.2 percent, against 15.9 percent for 55- to 64-year-olds. Their share is 12.3 percent in Croatia, 10.1 percent in Slovakia and 9.8 percent in Estonia. Malta, at 11.1 percent, is the exception outside the two regions.
The graphic below shows how household wealth is split between age groups in each country surveyed.
“What we’ve seen is actually a very strong increase in housing prices both in terms of the rental market as well as the ownership market,” Evelyn Astor of the European Social Observatory told Al Jazeera’s Counting the Cost programme.
“All of this is also reinforcing a sense of inequality because ultimately ordinary families are struggling to pay their rents or be able to purchase their homes whereas wealthy people with capital are able to make rather significant investments in the European housing market,” she said.
How much more expensive is it than 2000?
Prices of everyday goods and services, such as food, energy, transport and household bills, have risen by 67.2 percent in the eurozone, Hungary and the Czech Republic since 2000.
Of the countries in our chart, Hungary has seen the steepest rise with prices more than tripling, according to Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
The chart below shows how consumer prices have changed in each country since 2000 with prices in 2000 set at 100 on the index.
Eastern European countries have seen the sharpest increases – particularly since 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began – because many relied heavily on Russian energy supplies.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average until 2022 when annual inflation in the EU hit 9.2 percent.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs. Inflation has since eased, but the price rises of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine have not reversed.

Russia attacked Ukraine with 112 drones; 75% of the jet-powered drones destroyed

On the night of October 29, Russia attacked Ukraine with 112 drones, more than a third of them jet-powered. A total of 97 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed, including 75% of the jet-powered drones. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and where the attacks came from
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, on the night of October 29 (starting at 18:00 on October 28), the enemy attacked with 112 Shahed-type attack UAVs (40 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones launched from the following directions: Oryol, Millerovo — Russia, and the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk.

The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.

Taliban’s poppy ban falters as Afghan farmers say they can’t feed their children
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:19:46 CET
15:19:46 KST

By Mohammad Yunus Yawar , Sayed Hassib and Ahmad Masih Noori
BABA YUSUF, Afghanistan, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Carpets still hang on the walls of Mohammad Dawood’s home in a northern Afghanistan village, and ornate mirrors still catch the light, relics of the years when a single poppy harvest could carry his family through the year.
But the 28-year-old says he now spends his days bent over cotton and wheat in fields that barely provide a living.
“We were doing well,” he said in an interview in his home in the Baba Yusuf village of Balkh province. “Now, my children are malnourished.”
In years gone by, Afghanistan’s poppy fields produced about 80% of the world’s opium, used in the manufacture of morphine as well as in illegal drugs like heroin.
Four years ago, the Taliban began enforcing an opium ban so strict that poppy all but vanished from Afghanistan’s fields. But now their Supreme Leader’s edict is beginning to fray, worn down by a practical problem: legal crops no longer pay and many Afghan farmers say they are struggling to feed their children.
Some are turning back to poppy, and cultivation rose sharply this year, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported on Thursday, in a reversal that could reshape heroin markets as far away as Europe.
Many farmers “don’t have any other choice than to go back to poppy cultivation,” Polleak Ok Serei, UNODC’s country representative for Afghanistan, told Reuters.
Dawood said he is still complying with the ban. But on a bad day, he makes one-fortieth of what he used to make with poppy, he said.
Not all of his neighbours are complying. Balkh, which UNODC found to be poppy-free last year, is growing poppy again this year, the agency reported, although few farmers would dare admit it amid continued Taliban scrutiny.
Cultivation across Afghanistan more than quadrupled this year from 2025 to an estimated 43,300 hectares, according to satellite imagery analysed by the UN. Farmers now hide the poppies from Taliban officials inside cereal fields and behind mud walls.
Cultivation is still only at about a quarter of the 177,000 hectares planted in 2021, the year before the ban was imposed by the Taliban.
But opium sales in Afghanistan generated an estimated $525 million this year, the highest figure since 2018 with the exception of 2022 when the Taliban’s ban made prices skyrocket, UNODC said.
The Taliban rejected the report’s findings, saying actual cultivation was about half the UN estimate and that poppy eradication efforts continued.
The Taliban-run Interior Ministry did not respond to a request for comment by Reuters.
FALLING FARM INCOMES AND CHILD MALNUTRITION
In the country’s farmlands, aid groups say, the economic pressure has become severe.
The toll is increasingly visible among children. UN agencies warned this month that 10 out of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces had critical levels of child malnutrition this year and the number could climb to 14 in 2027.
Despite better harvests, they said, high costs and low crop prices are squeezing poorer farmers and limiting families’ access to food.
Foreign aid cuts and the Taliban’s international isolation over their crackdown on women’s rights have also played a significant role, diplomats say. But at the Alam Khil health center in Balkh, doctors and patients primarily blamed declining farm income for the growing number of severe malnutrition cases the clinic treats.
Outside the clinic, Tahira, whose husband grows cotton, waited for treatment with one of her four children, 7-month-old Benjamin, who was suffering from fever and diarrhea.
“The doctors say he is malnourished,” she said, adding that the family was barely making ends meet. “Our lives used to be good.”
The clinic is surrounded by cotton fields, where white tufts still waited to be picked.
Salima Mohammadi, a nutrition nurse at the clinic, said many families had struggled to find another crop that could support them since poppy disappeared from local fields.
“People own farmland,” she said, “but agricultural yields decrease year after year.”
INTERNATIONAL FALLOUT
What happens in fields like these will have repercussions far beyond Afghanistan. A full return to poppy production would have major implications for global drug markets, analysts say.
“Combine this with the active trafficking networks within the country and the resilient smuggling operations to get the opiates out of the country, and you have a very bleak prediction for the future,” said Paddy Ginn, an analyst with the Geneva-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.
Until the ban, the crop from the country’s poppy fields fuelled health crises across the world, corruption along the trafficking routes that carried it to Europe as heroin and deadly clashes between counter-narcotics forces and smugglers.
After 2022, pre-ban stockpiles initially cushioned the global shortage and blunted price spikes in Europe, giving Afghan farmers less reason to openly defy the ban. But UNODC warned on Thursday that those stockpiles may be running out, strengthening the incentive to plant again.
The Taliban regard the ban as one of their signature achievements and have cited it in their efforts to win international legitimacy.
But Taliban officials themselves have publicly acknowledged the challenges in recent years. Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban’s foreign minister, said at a meeting this month that “support for alternative livelihoods for farmers” was crucial to “ensure the continuation and strengthening of this campaign.”
But UNODC’s Ok Serei said there “was not enough support for alternative livelihoods” either from the Taliban government or the international community.
DROUGHT, WHEAT AND COTTON PRICES SQUEEZE FARMERS
The Taliban’s first ban, in 2000, collapsed about a year later, when US-led forces drove them from power after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
The current ban has lasted far longer, but the farmers expected to uphold it face harsher conditions than a generation ago. Recurring droughts have shrunk rivers and canals.
Drought has choked off much of the fresh water in the fields around Baba Yusuf, said Gul Nazar, a 56-year-old landowner, leaving well water so briny that it damages crops.
Legal alternatives have faltered, too. Wheat barely covers its costs, farmers in Baba Yusuf said. Cotton prices have fallen by about two-thirds amid a sudden nationwide glut, Gul Nazar said, a slump he partly blames on Pakistan’s closure of the border late last year, which cut off a key buyer.
Higher-value crops promoted by aid groups, such as orchard fruit or nuts, take years to establish and depend on reliable water and open export routes.
More than four in five households in Balkh and two nearby provinces reported in a UNODC survey last year that they had replaced none or only part of their lost poppy income.
Gul Nazar said he would not grow poppy again if his family’s living conditions improved. But if they grew worse, he said, he could not promise the same.
“When a person becomes hungry,” he said, “they will do anything.”
(Writing by Rick Noack; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

'It's just cold and silent': Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir on the rise of Icelandic Noir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:16:52 UTC
15:16:52 KST

As crime fiction continues to dominate Iceland's book charts, two of its best selling authors — Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir — sat down with Euronews Culture to discuss why one of the safest countries in the world is so drawn to literary darkness.
In an age of overwhelming uncertainty and anxiety, people continue to seek solace in the dark and gritty worlds of crime fiction.
One of the best selling literary genres across Europe, crime fiction has become especially popular in the United Kingdom and Nordic countries — a recent survey by Storytel Group found that crime and thrillers ranked as the most popular audiobook genres in Sweden, Norway, Finland and Poland.
This will come as no surprise to most, with Nordic Noir a pillar of the genre; known for its atmospheric bleakness, complex characters, and slow-burn procedural thrills — many of which have been turned into popular TV series. But under its umbrella exists Icelandic Noir, a subset of stories that derive their psychological suspense from the country's uniquely isolated geography.
Ragnar Jónasson and Yrsa Sigurðardóttir are often referred to as the King and Queen of this particular genre — one that has become a astonishing phenomenon amongst residents of one of the safest places in the world.
Jónasson, who started out translating the novels of legendary British crime author Agatha Christie, has written eight standalone books alongside two hugely popular series: Dark Iceland and Hulda. The latter was later adapted into The Darkness TV series, starring Lena Olin and directed by Lasse Hallström.
Sigurðardóttir, a civil engineer who began her writing career with children's fiction, has authored 5 standalone crime novels and three major series, including Black Ice, Þóra Guðmundsdóttir and Freyja and Huldar. Two have been made into feature films: Ég man þig (2017) and Kuldi (2023).
Both have sold millions of copies around the world, won multiple awards, and jointly founded the prestigious Iceland Noir festival (alongside author Quentin Bates) in 2013.
At this year's edition of the festival in November, more details will be revealed about an upcoming book they've collaborated on (more on that below).
While recently appearing at London's Taste of Iceland Festival, Euronews Culture sat down with Jónasson and Sigurðardóttir to discuss the unique characteristics of Icelandic Noir, their upcoming projects — and why you should always kill the good guys in crime fiction.
If you had to describe Iceland as a character in a few words, what would it be?
Yrsa Sigurðardóttir (YS): It's just cold and silent.
Ragnar Jónasson (RJ): It's like a tiger, in a way. Beautiful, strong, but it can also be harsh and cruel.
What is it that separates Icelandic Noir from broader Nordic Noir?
RJ: We have this island mentality and we have this pretty awful weather all year long, which I think makes our stories a little bit darker, and a little bit more linked to nature and the elements. We have this big island with a small population, so there's just a different tone to the whole thing. We don't have a big metropolis.
YS: Like Ragnar mentioned, the population is small, so the degrees of separation between people is quite low, meaning that the stories often revolve around more interpersonal things than, for example, syndicated crime or something that we don't have much of. But also, when you have places where everybody knows everybody, reputation is something that matters a lot to people, and people will take desperate measures to keep their reputation intact, which is very often used in Icelandic crime fiction as well.
Despite being one of the safest countries in the world, crime novels have become the most popular literary genre in Iceland. Why do you think this is?
YS: I think the Icelandic reader is really no different from elsewhere, and so crime fiction is a popular genre the world over. It offers the reader the promise that this crime will be solved and justice will be served, in most cases. And that's something that you can't rely on in the real world. So, it's escapism. It also offers the writer and the reader a very good opportunity to test characters. It's a fun way of writing about people, really. So crime fiction does revolve, of course, around the crime, but mostly around character.
RJ: We also have a lot of writing and literature in our DNA. And if we go back to the Icelandic sagas from the Middle Ages, some of those were also thrillers in a way. They dealt with revenge and killings and honour and law and legal battles. And just, you know, people fighting for their position. And these are thrilling stories with a lot of crime drama. We basically started writing crime fiction a long, long time ago, and it's just sort of re-emerged this century as a very popular way of telling stories in Iceland.
You both have very diverse and different backgrounds — Yrsa in civil engineering and authoring children's books, Ragnar in law, reporting and translation. What is it that drew you to writing crime fiction?
YS: I started writing children's books, which were humour based, but then it's just more tiring trying to be funny. It's hard to be fun all the time. So I wanted to write for a more mature audience. And it was really easy to decide to write crime and horror because that's what I enjoy reading.
RJ: I started with the golden age stories of Agatha Christie and her contemporaries as a teenager. I fell in love with that way of telling stories and the puzzles that they presented. And before I went to law school and university, I studied maths at college, and there is something about these types of old puzzles that, in a way, presented like maths problems. These are challenges to the reader. And then, later on, I read Scandinavian noir. In a way, I've tried to merge these two worlds into one in what I write.
You've mentioned how important characters are to crime fiction, but how do you go about developing such complex yet compelling ones?
RJ: When I read crime fiction, the story is very important, but the characters are most important, especially with a series of books, because if you like the characters, you want to come back and you want to know more. And the crime story sort of becomes secondary. And I think that is a very important lesson for anyone who's writing books to learn is that you need to want your readers to come back, not possibly to a series, but to the book. If it's a single standalone book, you want the readers to want to finish the book because they like the characters or they dislike them or they just draw them in for whatever reason. Characters don't have to be likeable. They just have to interesting. They have to be three-dimensional in a way. So, I think that is a good starting point for any crime story, is to create your protagonists.
YS: It's also about keeping characters true to what they're supposed to be like. People don't change overnight. Because most characters in crime stories are in sort of desperate situations, you have to put a lot of thought into how they would react to that in the other scene. Also, I would recommend people who are aspiring writers of crime to 'kill' good people. Nobody cares about bad people. Kill good people, that's much more interesting.
Ragnar, your 2015 novel Dimma (The Darkness) was adapted into a TV series in 2024. What was the process like of translating your words into on-screen action?
RJ: It was unreal to see my character and my scenes come alive and I tried to be on set as much as I could just to experience this and learn and see how it's done. We filmed it in Iceland in winter in a very cold climate, so it was a very memorable experience just being so cold, watching all these fantastic and talented people do their job. I think the most memorable day was [shooting for] a scene in the book where a man is run over by a car. They actually hit a man with a car and they had to do it I think three times to get it right. And at that point I thought to myself, oh my God, I should not have written that scene. I felt so sorry for the poor guy, but he was a stunt man and did it beautifully well and was unharmed.
What changes have you witnessed in the Icelandic literature scene in recent years?
RJ: People keep writing in Iceland as they've always done. They are writing more crime fiction in the past 10 to 20 years than ever before. But also a big change in the last decade or so is that Icelandic fiction is being translated much more and published more widely. If you're writing in Iceland now, the chances of writing for a bigger audience are much better than they used to be. And that goes for probably all Icelandic culture. There is an appetite for Icelandic music or cinema or books at this point, which is wonderful.
Do you have concerns about how artificial intelligence (AI) is infiltrating and impacting the arts?
YS: Yes and no. I mean, AI, it rehashes what's already been done and I think it will become bigger and then it will wind down. I remember when the first drawings came out that AI did and they just looked amazing. But then when you've seen a number of them, they become so soulless somehow. There's something missing that would not be missing if it was done by an actual artist. It's the same with AI written stories. I think people realise the difference between an actual human writing a story and a written story that's, like I said, rehashing something that's already been done.
RJ: The word in Icelandic for culture is menning, and menning is derived from the word human. So, by definition, culture comes from humans and I strongly believe that culture will always be created by humans. And so I think we don't need to worry too much. There would always be an appetite for human-made art.
You have both been working on an upcoming book together, the title and release date of which are yet to be revealed. How did this collaboration come about, and what was the process of it like?
RJ: We've known each other for a long time. We set up a book festival called Iceland Noir in Reykjavik over 10 years ago, and we keep doing that every year now as our contribution to the cultural life of Reykjavik. And throughout this time, we've always thought maybe we should do a book together because we know each other so well. Finally, last year, we had this idea for a very Icelandic Thriller set in a cave and partly set in the Icelandic highlands. We've finally written that book, which will be out next year.
YS: [The process] was so non-confrontational, it was so easy. Ragnar and I, we agree on, I think, almost everything. I don't think we've ever had an argument. We just sort of set the broad strokes and then we went to work and it was really a nice experience. We each came up with our own storyline and then we merged it together. And I think it brings out the best of both of our work, and our strength as writers.
You mentioned the Iceland Noir festival that you set up together, which has become one of the most exciting and prestigious crime fiction festivals in Europe. Could you tell us more about that?
YS: It's a four-day festival [in November]. Even though it's a very small, intimate festival, it's all in English. Our ticket holders, the majority, come from abroad — or about half of them. And we seem to punch above our weight when it comes to the talent that we have appearing. So we've been extremely lucky with managing to get really big and important good authors to appear at our festival. And I really recommend it for book lovers to check out.
RJ: It started out as a crime fiction festival and there was no crime fiction festival in Iceland at that time, and then once we had a lot of crime authors come over we thought we will expand this and we'll include actors and screenwriters and poets and all sorts of creative artists. This year we're doing an Agatha Christie day because it's 50 years since she died this year. So Christie's great-grandson is coming along with her publisher, Lucy Foley, the author who's writing the new Miss Marple book. We have Lee Child coming. We have UK rapper Tinie Tempah coming, so it's all sorts of art forms.
YS: Yeah, and a Japanese manga author. We're embracing storytelling from all sorts of genres and also other media than novels.
The 2026 edition of Iceland Noir will take place from 11 - 14 November across various venues in Reykjavik, Iceland. Find out more here.

Wildfire smoke exposure during pregnancy linked to higher autism risk in children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:12:45 UTC
15:12:45 KST

Exposure to wildfire smoke during pregnancy — particularly during the second and third trimesters — is associated with a higher risk of autism diagnosis in children.
Children whose mothers were exposed to fine particulate matter from wildfires during pregnancy were more likely to receive an autism diagnosis, according to a new study.
Each 0.75-microgram-per-cubic-metre increase in the average concentration of wildfire-related fine particles during pregnancy was associated with a 30% higher risk of developing autism.
The strongest associations with autism happened during the second and third trimesters.
“Pregnancy is a period of rapid brain development, when environmental exposures may interfere with important developmental processes,” said Stefania Papatheodorou, an epidemiologist at the Rutgers School of Public Health and lead author of the study.
Autism is linked to complex neurodevelopmental processes that begin before birth, when the brain is rapidly developing and connections between nerve cells are forming.
She added that the findings highlight the importance of monitoring wildfire events and their potential effects on air quality during pregnancy.
The study included around 900,000 mother-child pairs in the United States, who were followed for an average of 6.3 years.
Wildfire smoke contains fine particles, gases and other pollutants. Its composition can vary depending on what is burning, as fires may consume plastics, electronics and paints that release toxic chemicals into the air.
These particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and contribute to inflammation throughout the body. This is one possible pathway through which exposure could affect pregnancy and fetal development.
“Wildfire smoke can travel far beyond the communities where fires are burning, and exposure may occur even when smoke is not visible,” Papatheodorou said.
It has been linked to several health impacts such as asthma, chronic pulmonary and mental health conditions.
The study was observational and cannot establish a causal link between wildfire smoke exposure and autism, the researchers noted.
“Understanding how prenatal environmental exposures may contribute to autism, alongside genetic and other factors, remains an important research priority,” Papatheodorou said.
Measures to reduce smoke exposure during pregnancy, including improved air-quality forecasting and strategies to limit smoke entering indoor spaces, could help protect maternal and child health.

Finland's unusually mild autumn weather continues
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
08:11:30 EET
15:11:30 KST

As October winds down, the month's relatively mild weather conditions are set to continue this week.
The situation is not at all typical for this time of year, according to Yle meteorologist Matti Huutonen.
In the north nights have been exceptionally mild recently, while a southwesterly wind has kept daytime temperatures unusually high.
On Thursday temperatures in the south will climb above 10 degrees Celsius — in the north they will range between 5 and 10 degrees. In practice, this means most people can safely skip their woolly hats and thick winter jackets; conditions are still mild, even though cloud cover is extensive.
Finland will see mostly dry conditions on Thursday, with chances of local precipitation.
However, in the east and southeast, as well as in a band stretching from Ostrobothnia to southwestern Lapland, it's worth keeping an umbrella handy — or at least being prepared for a bit of rain.
Similar temperatures are expected on Friday, but conditions are set to clear up, as drier air flows in from the west and north — however some local light showers are possible in some places.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Army Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a senior military strategist at the Pentagon, from his post on the Joint Staff, The Hill reported on Wednesday.
Hegseth fired Sylvia, who headed the Joint Staff's Directorate for Strategy, Plans and Policy, known as the J-5, this week, the news outlet reported, citing two US officials familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel issues.

Sylvia’s removal marks another senior military personnel change under Hegseth, who took over as defence secretary in January 2025.

Norway’s Kongsberg doubles new orders in the third quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:07:53 UTC
15:07:53 KST

- Kongsberg’s order backlog reached a record NOK 174.2 billion, about $18.8 billion, after NOK 23.3 billion in third-quarter orders.
- Third-quarter revenue rose 50% to NOK 11.3 billion, helped by missile, NASAMS air defense and remote weapon station demand.
Norway’s Kongsberg ended the third quarter of 2026 with a record order backlog of NOK 174.2 billion (about $18.8 billion), after taking in NOK 23.3 billion (about $2.5 billion) in new orders, more than double the NOK 9.5 billion it booked in the same quarter last year.
The defense group reported on Oct. 29 that third-quarter revenue rose 50% to NOK 11.3 billion (about $1.2 billion), while operating profit, or EBIT, climbed 66% to NOK 1.9 billion (about $205 million). The backlog grew by NOK 16.7 billion during the quarter, and orders so far this year total NOK 67 billion (about $7.2 billion). Its book-to-bill ratio, which compares new orders with revenue in the same period, was 2.06, meaning Kongsberg booked about twice as much new work as it delivered.
The figures cover the defense and Discovery businesses Kongsberg kept after splitting off Kongsberg Maritime as a separate listed company, so they are not directly comparable with group results reported before the split. At the end of the second quarter, the company’s backlog stood at about NOK 157.5 billion and quarterly revenue at NOK 10.4 billion.
“At a time when European security is being challenged, our task is to strengthen defence capabilities through technology, capacity and delivery performance. We are expanding our capacity, including in Poland, to meet growing demand. Our focus now is on executing on our strong order backlog, which provides a solid foundation for continued growth,” said Eirik Lie, President and CEO of KONGSBERG.
Missiles, air defense and remote weapon stations drove most of the demand. In July, the U.S. Air Force ordered more Joint Strike Missiles, the air-launched version of Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile designed to be carried inside the F-35’s weapons bay, and later in the quarter the U.S. Marine Corps signed a framework agreement with the company covering production and sustainment of the Naval Strike Missile. In October, Denmark became the seventh country to announce plans to buy the Joint Strike Missile for its F-35s.
The largest single deal was in air defense. In September, Kongsberg signed a NOK 10 billion (about $1.08 billion) contract to supply the NASAMS medium-range air defense system to Belgium, which became the 18th country to order it, after Belgium agreed in July to buy 10 NASAMS systems through the Netherlands. The Dutch procurement agency signed the contract on Belgium’s behalf, building on the Netherlands’ own record NASAMS and NOMADS order with Kongsberg in 2024.
Kongsberg also won a contract to supply remote weapon stations, gun mounts operated by a crew member from inside the vehicle, for the Canadian Army’s Armoured Combat Support Vehicle program. The company counts those stations as part of its counter-drone offering, which also includes the CROWS C-UAS kit it has fitted to a donor-funded drone hunter vehicle for Ukraine.
The company is also building up its underwater and U.S. business. During the quarter, the U.S. government awarded Kongsberg a $54 million contract related to autonomous underwater capabilities, and U.S. authorities approved its purchase of Sonatech, a maker of underwater acoustic equipment. Zone 5 Technologies, the California missile maker Kongsberg bought in the second quarter to add low-cost weapons that can be built in large numbers, was selected for a $65 million U.S. Navy program during the quarter.
Kongsberg has said it aims to grow annual revenue to NOK 100 billion (about $10.8 billion) by 2029, and it is expanding production capacity, including in Poland, to work through the backlog. The company did not say how much of the NOK 174.2 billion it expects to deliver in the fourth quarter.

Albanese has a sewerage problem and the Coalition loves the stench
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
