analysis
Albanese has a sewerage problem and the Coalition loves the stench
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Anthony Albanese seems to have a bad habit of turning what should've been a one day, or one week, story into a month-long affair.
What is the source of the clog this time? The curious case of a $6m "invitation-only" grant to the Marrickville Golf Club.
When the ABC first published the story last month, the prime minister chided the public broadcaster for it. He declared the funding was to fix the issue of raw sewage flowing into the local river when the plain floods.
He repeated that defence in the House of Representatives. As did Infrastructure Minister Catherine King, as recently as Sunday. But as we learnt this week, that wasn't exactly the case.
Under questioning on Monday, infrastructure department officials confirmed that sewerage works were not part of the project. To make matters worse, that brief was shared with the prime minister's office before the ABC first raised questions about the grant last month.
Albanese was in classic politician form as he got out the mop to clean up the mess the next day. He didn't say he was wrong, but rather "it was not correct" for him to defend the funding with links to sewerage. It was the NSW government that had "stepped in" to tackle the problem.
For the Coalition, his answers stunk. And it's no surprise they've used it as an easy win. The way the story has dragged out over the past month was likened to the never-ending story that was Albanese's ill-fated "melons" remark on the Bush Deep podcast.
It's the same character-chipping exercise Labor ran on an unpopular Scott Morrison over his final term in parliament. The opposition were gleeful at times as they questioned Albanese, pointing to everything from denying he fell off stage during the last election campaign to this grant to paint him as a "serial liar".
Albanese may have been able to shrug off claims he misled the parliament, but the perception that he's not upfront with the public will be harder to flush away.
Taxes, cuts and 'savings'
Of course, every question the Coalition dedicates to the golf club grant is one less on the economy — yet another source of pain for the government.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers isn't having the best of times at the moment. The latest monthly inflation figures, up from 4 per cent to 4.3 per cent in the year to September, have all but locked in a Melbourne Cup Day rate rise.
This would take rates to an 18-year high, and another Reserve Bank board meeting is scheduled for December. Essentially, as Tom Crowley wrote this morning, the worst is still yet to come.
The treasurer maintains that government spending is not to blame, pointing the finger at the war in the Middle East and the AI data centre boom for driving up prices. Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson backed Chalmers up in estimates: "We can only control what we can control."
Nevertheless, Chalmers and Albanese are looking for savings ahead of December's mid-year update. The prime minister says he hasn't directed his ministers to find cuts (sorry, savings), but rather they're all just collectively working together to spend less.
Loading...
Basically, don't expect there to be a pre-Christmas cash splash. Longer term, Chalmers also flagged it could complicate Labor's plan to deliver a larger round of tax cuts in the lead up to the next election.
But speaking of tax cuts, David Shoebridge made his first National Press Club appearance as leader where he again declared his party could take Labor's place.
He came armed with a tax plan that, due to the electoral reality, will never see the light of day and faced questions about internal culture in the party and his opposition to providing military aid to Ukraine.
Loading
'Leave the politics of MAGA in the US'
Angus Taylor released his own costings for a handful of the Coalition's proposed spending cuts. In short, several of Labor's climate and housing initiatives would be scrapped in favour of the opposition's own spending promises such as indexing income tax brackets to inflation.
The Coalition decided to unveil the numbers on Monday; the same day parliament had set aside for reflection and messages of support for independent MP Helen Haines.
Haines remains in a serious but stable condition after an alleged attack outside of her electorate office last week. Her first words afterwards, as shared in the chamber by Allegra Spender, were of concern for staff and gratitude for first responders and bystanders.
For most of the day, you could hear a pin drop in the chamber. MPs of all stripes shed tears as they spoke about Haines and the impact she's had on the parliament.
Among the tributes, another message was braided through.
After months of calling for the temperature to be turned down, Albanese said there was no way to shrug off the "very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse".
"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop," he said.
Taylor was unconvinced by that argument and rejected that there was a link between robust parliamentary debate and political violence. Crossbenchers Zali Steggall and Monique Ryan, who are close to Haines, called his speech tone deaf.
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie's tone differed to his leader's, calling for Australia to "leave the nasty personal politics of MAGA in the United States".
With Haines front of mind, politicians were on their best behaviour during Question Time — only a glass breaking punctured the silence around the speaker.
However as the days went on, things returned to somewhat regular programming. By Wednesday, Speaker Milton Dick was growing tired of MPs trying to up the ante. Nationals MP Llew O'Brien was ejected for swearing.
Watching over it all was the cardboard cockatoo sitting in Haines's vacant seat. A second was also placed at Aussies, the cafe and general store in Parliament House, serving as a gentle reminder of the promises they made on Monday.

How one of Europe’s most polluted cities became a blueprint for nature restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:02:42 UTC
15:02:42 KST

350 football pitches’ worth of degraded urban areas have been restored.
One of Europe’s most polluted cities is getting a verdant makeover. Three million new trees and shrubs will take root in Milan over the next four years, helping to purify its smog-cloaked streets.
An October air quality ranking placed the Italian metropolis seventh in the world’s top 10 most polluted cities – the only European entry on IQAir’s list. This is partly down to its location in the low-lying Po Basin, which limits air circulation, combined with intensive agriculture and emissions as it is an industry-heavy region.
Fondazione Forestami, the organisation behind the project, says more greenery on streets, rooftops and facades is the cheapest and most effective way to filter fine dust, cool the city and improve residents’ wellbeing.
Since it began in 2019, the urban reforestation project has planted nearly 640,000 trees and shrubs, earning its creator – Italian architect Stefano Boeri who built Milan’s famous vertical forest – a European Lung Foundation (ELF) award for his work and commitment to improve air quality.
Now, the project has gained a new accolade: status as a UN World Restoration Flagship. The honour was announced on 29 October during the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
‘One tree for every resident’: Milan one of five new UN World Restoration Flagships
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) says the title recognises Milan’s efforts to bring nature back into “one of Europe’s most densely populated and polluted metropolitan areas”, by “planting roughly one tree for every resident” and restoring about 350 football pitches’ worth of degraded urban areas.
“The initiative is expanding access to green space, engaging schoolchildren and restoring sites including former industrial areas, parking lots and storage yards,” said UNEP in an announcement.
“The World Restoration Flagships… recognise ambitious and promising examples of large-scale, long-term restoration and contribute to global commitments to restore one billion hectares of degraded ecosystems by 2030.”
Forestami was one of just five projects to receive the title at COP17, and the only one in Europe.
Other recipients include Colombia’s wetland restoration initiative, Urban Nature Reborn; the Green Seattle Partnership, a scheme to restore and maintain the US city’s parklands; Ethiopia’s Great Rift Valley Renaissance, reviving one of the Horn of Africa’s most degraded forest landscapes; and China’s Blue Bay Restoration initiative, a large-scale effort to restore the country’s coastal and marine ecosystems.
Nature is making a comeback, UN says – but quicker progress needed
On the same day as the Milan announcement, UNEP published a landmark assessment of global ecosystem restoration progress.
It found that 252 million hectares across 149 countries are being restored – the largest documented global restoration effort to date.
“Today, we are witnessing the makings of one of the largest movements for nature in recorded history,” says Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP. “Yet, at the halfway point of the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, we are still not restoring nature at the scale or speed required.”
There is mixed progress towards the ‘30x30’ goal to protect at least 30 per cent of Earth’s degraded land and sea by the end of the decade.
Restoration of terrestrial ecosystems has reached nearly half the global target, while progress in freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems – which are degrading at the fastest rates – is lagging. Annual restoration finance, meanwhile, must more than quadruple.
Ecosystem restoration is essential for food and water security, climate resilience and human health.
Restoring just 15 per cent of global priority areas could capture and store 30 per cent of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions since the industrial revolution and help avoid 60 per cent of species extinctions.
Reaching global targets could also generate up to an estimated 32 million new jobs worldwide by 2030, according to UNEP.
“We cannot expect to fix nature with one hand while we destroy it with the other one,” says Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat, which co-published the report. “Governments must address the drivers of ecosystem degradation and invest in monitoring mechanisms to ensure the durability of the restoration movement to date.”
The report says governments now need to look beyond individual projects and build “restoration economies”, where sustained recovery also supports jobs and livelihoods in the long run.

Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation

Russia’s alleged sabotage campaign in Europe raises fears of escalation
From drone incursions to alleged attempts to assassinate European defence bosses, Russia is feared to be pressing a shadow war.
Russia appears to have escalated its shadow war in Europe this year.
European officials have alleged that Russian fighter planes have veered inside Polish, Lithuanian and Estonian airspace, testing reaction times. Suspected Russian drones have been downed over Poland, Finland and the Baltic states.
And Moscow has been accused of bringing trouble to the Black Sea.
In two separate operations in October, Ukraine accused Russia of using aerial and surface drones to sink four cargo ships just outside the territorial waters of Bulgaria, a European Union and NATO member, in an apparent warning that Ukraine’s grain exports through NATO territorial waters may not be safe for long.
Russia and Belarus have also been accused of trying to destabilise the Baltic states by making their borders appear fluid.
“Masked and most likely armed individuals on the Belarus side of the border escorted and attempted to push groups of illegal migrants into Latvia,” Ieva Cesniece, Latvia’s ambassador to Greece, told Al Jazeera. “Those individuals expressed threats to Latvian soldiers and border guards. On the same day in a separate incident, masked individuals crossed into Latvian territory and carried out deliberate sabotage. Bborder infrastructure was damaged, and surveillance equipment was removed.”
Latvian media have reported that asylum seekers and undocumented migrants who tried to run back from the Latvian border were rounded up by Belarusian authorities and pushed towards Latvia again.
Cesniece drew a direct link between the Russian war in Ukraine and its shadow war in Europe.
“The weaker Russia appears in Ukraine, the more it tests our resilience, trying to weaken NATO and EU resolve and support for Ukraine,” she said.
As European governments warned of an imminent escalation of a Russian shadow war on the continent, experts said the bloc needs to do more to deter Russia as well as defend itself.
“Protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening intelligence services and preventing attacks are essential, but deterrence is about more than preventing the next incident,” said Olena Tregub, cofounder and head of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission. “It is about convincing your adversary that continuing these operations will become too costly. And I’m not sure Russia currently sees those costs as sufficiently high.”
As an expert on following money trails, she believes European governments have not done enough to identify the networks behind operations, expose the command structures, disrupt their financing and logistics, and impose consequences.
Meanwhile, Russia’s war is going badly on the ground.
Two Ukrainian counteroffensives have blunted Moscow’s main thrust to capture the eastern region of Donetsk and in effect have deprived it of any territorial gains this year.
Since a failed August operation to blow up cargo planes at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, which was later verified by the European Commission as a Russian operation, warnings of further escalation have multiplied.
Czech spy chief Michal Koudelka warned in September that Russia might attempt a military attack on a NATO member in “months, not years”.
Days later, Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova openly declared that European defence industries supplying Ukraine were legitimate targets for Moscow.
“Russia does not necessarily distinguish between the military capabilities Ukraine uses on the battlefield and the European infrastructure that makes those capabilities possible,” Tregub told Al Jazeera.
“From Moscow’s perspective, a factory producing military equipment for Ukraine, a logistics hub transporting that equipment or a company providing critical technology can all become potential targets of disruption.”
This month, representatives of five EU intelligence agencies told the Financial Times that Russia was seeking to “kill” European defence bosses and target their supply chains.
That followed a report from a German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, that Russia had planted incendiary devices in the offices of defence companies Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing in Munich. It also followed a report on the Politico news site in which EU security officials said Russia was planning to move beyond messaging and claim lives on European soil.
European officials have spoken of strengthening the resilience of their data centres, telecommunications, and other vulnerable networks and industries, but they have not spoken of retaliation.
From the Ukrainian point of view, though, Europe has been slow to see sabotage, manned and unmanned military operations, cyberattacks and information warfare as the early stages of a multidimensional war with Russia, and that failure of perception is itself a weakness.
“Where will he stop if he is currently testing all these drones against European countries, even NATO countries?” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked journalists on October 16, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin. “They are not talking about it very loudly yet. They don’t want escalation, … but you will talk very loudly when there are ballistic and cruise missiles and also thousands of drones.”
‘No reaction’ to Russian threats
“Ukrainians don’t know about any war in Ukraine. They know about war in Europe,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a long-serving adviser to the Ukrainian Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs and now a Russian warfare expert with the Royal United Services Institute.
Like Zelenskyy and Tregub, he believes the lack of retaliation to its apparent hybrid war encourages Russia.
“Russians are limited right now only by their capabilities because they do whatever they want. There is no reaction,” he said.
He said he believes NATO needs to place more forward troops in the Baltic states to create “deterrence by denial” and to strengthen Ukraine.
Minna Alander, a leading European researcher in security and defence with the Center for European Policy Analysis, said denying Russians travel visas, carrying out retaliatory cyberattacks, further interdicting the Russian oil fleet and sanctioning Chinese suppliers of defence goods to Russia were all realistic retaliations Europe could impose immediately.
Danylyuk said money remains the most potent tool of deterrence.
“The most direct way to punish Russia is to actually increase support to Ukraine,” he told Al Jazeera. “Each time we detect Russian intelligence operations in Europe, we will increase combined support of Ukraine [maybe] 10 percent, 20 percent.”
Yet Ukraine’s allies are signalling the opposite, he observed.
The United States withdrew its military and financial support in January 2025 and recently placed the dependability of its satellite services in doubt. In France and Germany, the governments trail opposition leaders who want to stop aid to Ukraine.
Ukraine has performed better than many expected.
Since 2023, it has designed and built its own weapons and developed its own strategy to halt the Russian advance. It has punished Russia by striking oil installations and weapons factories deep inside its territory.
To reverse the tide of the war and reclaim its occupied territories, it is asking for more money, and it is asking it from the people providing the vast majority of it – Europe.
“Next year, the war will cost 155 billion euros [$170bn]), and we need at least 70 billion euros [$80bn] more from you,” Zelenskyy told the European Council on October 16.
“We could double or even triple the production of drones,” he said. “Just imagine how much more pressure we could put on Russia if we could do two or three times more.”

EU's push to reduce reliance on China could come at a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

Brussels is preparing a new tool to shield the EU economy from countries weaponising its strategic dependencies. But European businesses fear the costs of diversification - and question which sectors will be targeted.
The European Commission will present a tool in early December, a week before a meeting of EU leaders, designed to push companies to diversify their suppliers and reduce strategic dependencies on a single country.
Although China has not been explicitly mentioned, the future proposal is directly aimed at Beijing, which blocked exports of rare earths — essential for green technologies, digital industries and defence — in 2025 amid a trade war with the US.
The EU car industry was also put at risk that same year after Beijing cut off access to strategic chips during a dispute with the Dutch government over chipmaker Nexperia.
Even as Brussels negotiates with Beijing to rebalance their trade relationship, diversification has become urgent in sectors where dependencies create economic vulnerabilities.
Few details of the future proposal have emerged, but in a consultation with EU businesses that closed on Tuesday, the Commission stated that the new instrument would aim “to address cases where a high level of strategic dependencies on a single supplier country creates a risk for the EU’s security of supply and thus its economic security.”
Increased costs
Some companies warned in their consultation responses that finding alternative suppliers would increase their costs.
“Companies are already doing the maximum to have a cost-effective structure,” Luisa Santos, Deputy Director General at BusinessEurope, told Euronews. “If they are working with certain suppliers it is because they are the ones that have the best offer in terms of the product, regarding its cost and performance.”
However, on 5 June 2026, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič made clear in a speech that industry would be “on the front line” of efforts to diversify suppliers and that business models should incorporate “the cost of resilience.”
“Economic security is a shared responsibility, industry stands on the front line,” he said, “we must have their back, but industry also must do its part.”
He added: “That means diversifying rapidly and strategically, and it means integrating the cost of resilience into business models and treating geopolitical risks as what it is, the core business risks.”
It remains unclear which sectors will be covered and what criteria will be used. Santos, however, stressed that while diversification is necessary to address the risk of the EU's dependencies being weaponised, not all dependencies should be considered problematic.
“We should be focusing more on the areas where we are seeing weaponization. I don’t think that our dependency on Chinese electric appliances for instance should fall within the scope.”
The business representative also stressed that, for products falling within the instrument's scope, alternative suppliers must be available. That is not the case for some critical raw materials, including rare earths, where China dominates production and processing.
“Diversification in that case is not an option, and this needs to be considered unless new sources come into the picture,” Santos added.
The “minimalist” and “maximalist” scenarios
Last June, Šefčovič suggested that the Commission could draw inspiration from the Energy Union, which pushed companies to diversify their energy supplies away from Russia following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine.
“At that time, I remember very vividly the discussions we had about investing in energy terminals and interconnectors and how unpopular it was,” the Commissioner said last June, adding that the investments had raised numerous questions, particularly over their cost, given that Russian gas was cheaper.
“With the hindsight, it was vital for us,” Šefčovič added.
The EU's REPowerEU plan, launched in May 2022 to phase out dependence on Moscow, bans import of Russian oil and provides for an end to short- and long-term contracts for Russian gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG) in 2026 and 2027. EU businesses have had to adapt. Investments have been made in renewable energy, new suppliers have had to be found, joint purchasing has been made possible, and prices have risen for EU consumers.
Tobias Gherke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, sees the energy approach as the minimalist scenario for December's diversification tool.
“The minimalist scenario would be to restrict diversification to a couple of sectors,” he told Euronews, “like they made it mandatory for European energy utilities to diversify.”
The expert pointed to the US defence industry, which was pushed to diversify its suppliers to reduce its dependence on Chinese minerals. Other critical sectors could also fall within the instrument's scope, including dual-use industries and infrastructure such as healthcare and energy grids.
A second, “maximalist” scenario, according to Gherke, would be to say: “ Everyone who is buying more than a certain threshold of a specific product from a single source would face tariffs.”
Gherke added: “Therefore they would be incentivized to buy from a different source.”
Such a scenario would cover a broader range of sectors. If tariffs made supplies of certain critical raw materials more expensive, the consequences would be felt across green technologies, defence and digital industries simultaneously.
“Everyone would be captured,” the expert said.
For EU businesses, this would be what Šefčovič called “the cost of resilience.”

Furious Labour MPs have been lobbying the prime minister and chancellor not to overrule the energy secretary should she decide to block the Rosebank oilfield.
MPs say they are alarmed at the cabinet splits that have emerged over the issue after sources told the Guardian that Miatta Fahnbulleh was minded to refuse environmental permission for the field.
Sources close to the chancellor, John Healey, have since made it clear he is in favour of the scheme, while some in government believe the prime minister, Andy Burnham, also wants it to go ahead.
Backbenchers worried about the environmental impact of the project are now urging their whips and Downing Street not to allow other ministers to intervene in Fahnbulleh’s decision.
Catherine Fookes, a Labour member of the energy select committee, said: “Approving Rosebank will blow a hole in our green credentials. A group of us is making it clear to leadership that this should be Miatta’s decision and I hope they listen.
“Labour MPs are really, really concerned about it – it would go against the thrust of our manifesto.”
Another MP said: “If Healey pushes through Rosebank, there will be blood. It’s economically shortsighted as well as politically explosive – they aren’t listening at all to the discomfort on the backbenches.”
Another commented: “Lots of us have raised this. I think the position Miatta has been put in by these briefings is intolerable.” Concerns are understood to also have been raised with Healey directly in budget meetings with MPs.
Fahnbulleh’s parliamentary aides have circulated a memo to MPs insisting she would have the final say on the proposals, after a number of MPs contacted them to raise concerns that she would be overruled.
“No decision has been made on Rosebank,” the memo said. “The energy secretary will consider all relevant factors in a case before reaching a decision.
“The energy secretary is the only decision maker and will consider all relevant factors as part of the quasi-judicial process. No other cabinet member or minister has any role in this decision and does not see the advice on it,” it added.
Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil drilling, calling the Jackdaw gasfield, which the government approved last week, “a bridge to the future”.
The prime minister insists the decision over Rosebank will be for Fahnbulleh alone to make.
But he prompted speculation about his support for the project on Wednesday, when he told the Commons: “Use of our reserves can support and accelerate a clean energy future, and that was very much the logic behind the decision that the government announced on Jackdaw last week.”
Many in government believe Fahnbulleh can approve the bigger Rosebank scheme without breaching the UK’s carbon commitments, in part because most of its oil would be exported.
The Guardian also revealed on Tuesday that the Treasury had already factored in tax revenues from the scheme, which are expected to hit about £500m by the end of this parliament.
Treasury officials said on Wednesday the money had been included in forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) since 2019, and that doing so would not prevent the energy secretary from blocking it.
The OBR said in its budget forecast on Wednesday: “The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the North Sea Transition Authority’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries.
“The forecast annual pace of decline [in oil and gas production] would be around 14% a year if there were no production from any new fields.”
The memo from Fahnbulleh’s aides added that decisions to score Rosebank as part of the forecast would be a decision for the OBR.
However, some Labour MPs believe the Treasury has been using aggressive tactics to strong-arm the energy department, with one describing the approach of No 11 as “macho bullshit”.
Clive Lewis, another Labour MP, said: “You cannot claim global climate leadership while approving new oilfields simply because you’ve already pencilled in the tax receipts. Tax ‘receipts’, as I understand it, that will be the operator’s estimate and not actual Treasury revenue.”
Analysis by Uplift, a campaign group, found that on the government’s and industry’s estimates, the tax take from Rosebank would probably be limited and could be outweighed by the tax breaks and incentives likely to be offered for the development and decommissioning of the fields.
Areeba Hamid, a co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said: “Any tax revenues from this far-off field in a rapidly declining basin don’t just leave our public services at the hostage of future oil prices, they also leave taxpayers on the hook for the costs of decommissioning for decades to come. The truth is that approving new oil drilling in the North Sea will only add to the costs of climate impacts, costs not fully factored into forecasts such as those from the OBR. Any economist should be able to see that.”
MPs said there would be a significant parliamentary rebellion on Rosebank, unlike Jackdaw, where they were prepared to accept the argument to allow gas to be extracted for domestic consumption.
Fookes said: “The case was made for Jackdaw to some degree and we remained quite quiet over that. Rosebank, however, is a different issue.”

Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard abusive scam compounds, Amnesty alleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards in scam compounds where thousands were forced to work in the online fraud industry, according to a report by Amnesty International.
The global rights group alleged they worked for security companies as part of a system that enabled slavery and rape in the compounds, with some guards using electric batons to keep people trapped.
“For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general.
Based on 151 survivor interviews, visits to 82 scam compounds and social media videos from dozens of guard accounts showing them in company uniform, the investigation said it could link illicit operations with five well-connected private security companies.
“Our findings begin to expose the long-suspected links between Cambodia’s billion-dollar criminal scamming networks and politically connected figures who have remained largely beyond scrutiny,” Callamard said.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped and enforced compliance through fear and violence. Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned.”
Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked into south-east Asia from across the world, according to the UN. In many cases, they have been lured by the promise of an office job and then forced to carry out online scams, targeting victims globally.
Among these is so-called pig butchering, a type of romance fraud where criminals build a fake relationship with a victim, slowly “fattening them up” before stealing their money.
The Amnesty report, titled Official Business: Security companies and authorities at scamming compounds in Cambodia, alleges that a company called Leap Somnang had the largest footprint and was linked to at least 15 compounds across eight provinces. Twelve survivors identified the company’s guards, uniforms or logo, the report says.
Amnesty alleges that Leap Somnang is believed to be controlled by Ban Sophat, who publicly served as its chair while also being a colonel in the armed forces. It provided photos it claimed showed him alongside Leap Somnang guards at two scamming compounds.
The rights group quoted a letter from Ban Sophat denying holding any ownership, director or management role in Leap Somnang, stating that he had “served as an adviser to the company owner”.
“The fact that I may appear in a photograph taken at a particular location does not mean that I have knowledge of, or involvement in, the activities or operations conducted there,” it cited him as saying.
Scam site survivors have described guards administering electric shocks and beatings, detaining people in “dark rooms” and standing guard while compound managers raped women.
Amnesty said it had identified more than 20 members of the military and police who were seen to have an active presence at the compounds, including working openly as guards.
With annual losses estimated at about $100bn – a sum that outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region – international pressure has grown on countries such as Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar to crack down. There are signs that some parts of the industry are moving to South Asia.
In July 2025, Cambodia launched its largest-ever crackdown on scam operations, promising to wipe out the criminal networks. Authorities claim to have shut down hundreds of scam centres, and Amnesty said the industry there was now “dormant”.
“Even if scamming compounds are dormant, our findings clearly show that the infrastructure of impunity has not been dismantled,” Callamard said. “Cambodia will not have ended this abusive industry until it has held to account those who staffed, managed, financed and protected this abusive system.”
Amnesty said it presented its findings to Cambodian authorities, and cited a response from the ministry of interior stating that it had, as part of its ongoing crackdowns, already disciplined 77 police officers, prosecuted six private security guards for using stun batons illegally and detained 17 military, police, and civil officials for colluding with criminals.
Authorities had sent 3,477 suspects to court, the letter says, citing a policy of “no tolerance, no exemption, and no retreat” to ensure Cambodia did not become a “haven or operating base for transnational criminal networks”.
Amnesty said it did not receive a response from Leap Somnang.
The Guardian has contacted Cambodia’s interior ministry, Ban Sophat and Leap Somnang for comment.

====================================================================================================

Liz Truss has brought our divided nation together – in mockery of her | Emma Brockes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:26 UTC
15:00:26 KST

In these times of social and political division, it’s worth doing a quick audit of what keeps us together. Where, as we fight over what constitutes “wealth” and whether or not to go back in on Brexit, are the key sites of consensus? The Celebrity Traitors and the gloriousness of Nigella on Bake Off may offer one area of unity; you can say the words “David Attenborough” to any sample of the population and elicit exactly the same murmur of approval. But, as the recent history of the internet shows, the most forceful bonds are those forged against, rather than in favour of, something. With that in mind, let’s turn to our old friend Liz Truss.
It’s an unusual position, isn’t it, wondering if we might owe a debt of gratitude to the former prime minister who, after tanking the value of the pound in 2022 and otherwise carrying on with the efficacy of someone stopped at random in the street and given the keys to government, is widely regarded as the worst ever to have held office. Truss has a book out this week, her second since leaving office, entitled Bank Job: A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government, and on the evidence of its early reception, it seems likely to prove even more successful in uniting disparate communities of Britain than her previous volume, Ten Years to Save the West.
The government to which she refers in the subtitle is, of course, Truss’s own, which faltered in the wake of her mini-budget four years ago, when she sought to put through £45bn of unfunded tax cuts. Blaming the crash that followed on the Bank of England and the Treasury, the author admits no error, rekindling in observers powerful feelings of fury, mockery, incredulity and shame, plus a release of energy so intense that, like someone kicking in an old TV in a rage room, it might be mistaken for joy.
The Independent’s reviewer called the book “dense, paranoid and peevish”. The Telegraph gave it zero stars and also called it “deranged”. Scottish tabloid the National called it “unhinged”. The Daily Star, which focused on the book’s failure to give an adequate account of the role played by the iceberg lettuce that outlasted Truss’s 49-day tenure, called it “loopy”. Writing on X, Truss’s own former trade minister Conor Burns called her “an international embarrassment with zero self-awareness”, and “financially illiterate”. And so on.
None of these opinions of Truss are new, but condensed as they are into a week of terrible reviews, they perhaps offer us an opportunity to come together to warm our hands around a single point of scorn. Even in a world dominated by horrible characters, this is a rare talent. President Donald Trump, for example, whom Truss has been unsuccessfully trying to suck up to for years, even going so far as to colour-scheme the cover of her last book red (for Republican) rather than blue (for Tory), can do no wrong in certain sections of the US electorate because of what he represents – white supremacy.
But Truss doesn’t represent anything. She is relieved of all political associations. She stands for chaos unrelieved by charm, deepened by the impression she gives of someone receiving orders at a frequency no one else can hear. As an experiment, I tried just now to see if, with a bit of effort, I could drum up some sympathy for Truss, as I have on occasion managed for Theresa May; then I tried to find her funny, as I can sometimes do with Boris Johnson. But no; with Truss it is simply impossible to summon anything but rage and derision.
In light of which, we might say this woman has become a national hero, achieving the seemingly impossible without even trying. In the first weeks after 9/11, Americans in large US cities enjoyed a brief improvement in civic behaviour as reported crime went down. I don’t mean to compare Truss’s premiership to the worst act of terrorism this century, but there is evidence to suggest that when people pull together in the wake of a universally recognised disaster, society briefly improves.
The question, given the damage done by Truss to this country’s standing in the world and to our own sense of political and financial security, is: was it worth it? Obviously not. Still, at the time of writing, as Bank Job sits in the Amazon top 20 and Truss’s belligerent expression stares out, across all media, provoking howls of laughter and explosive diatribes from everyone who looks on her, there are really only two words to say: thank you.
- Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Queen of Spain butterfly invades Britain – but will it become native?

The Queen of Spain has invaded. The enigmatic British visits of this gorgeous golden-coloured butterfly with distinctively shaped, squared-off hindwings have been recorded by lepidopterists for four centuries. Usually there are barely a handful of sightings each summer of a butterfly that is widespread across continental Europe.
This year, thousands have flown in, some from France and Spain that have reached the south coast, and others from the Netherlands, which have fluttered into East Anglia.
These migrants have bred, and British-born offspring have emerged this autumn. Last week, hundreds were spotted at East Tilbury and Linford beside the Thames in Essex.
“It’s a bold attempt at the colonisation of the UK,” says butterfly expert Neil Hulme. “The numbers that have poured into the UK has been phenomenal.”
Will the Queen of Spain become Britain’s 61st native species? It has probably only successfully overwintered here twice in the last 30 years, at Minsmere in Suffolk in the 1990s, and close to Chichester around 2010.
But Hulme is certain that so many arrivals will mean some butterflies will be seen in Britain again next spring. “That’s not necessarily the same as a permanent establishment, but it could gain a foothold with regular top-ups from continental Europe,” he says.
Butterfly-lovers can plant wild and field pansies – its caterpillar’s preferred food plant – to hopefully help this regal arrival conquer Britain once and for all.

Neighbour of new Montenegro embassy in London sues council over impact on mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

It is not a classic neighbour-from-hell dispute, what with the protagonist inviting everyone over for evening drinks and canapés. But the sudden conversion of a five-bedroom family home in Pimlico, central London, into the embassy of Montenegro has triggered a neighbourhood row that has gone all the way to the desk of a high court judge.
The first stirrings of trouble came when one resident argued in a submission to the council this spring that the new embassy’s “flagpole and rather tacky-looking flag stick out like a sore thumb” among Cambridge Street’s Grade II-listed homes.
A second person, who described Montenegro’s red flag with gold border as “gaudy”, suggested the embassy was “out of keeping with the quietly dignified” whitewash late-Regency frontages designed by Thomas Cubitt.
Some of those critics, frustrated by the lack of planning application before the installation of the embassy flagpole and plaque, were somewhat placated when drinks were put on by the chargé d’affairs of the west Balkans state. “Perhaps it would have been diplomatic to have done that at the start,” one resident commented drily.
But the party did not convince everyone, and an involuntary nextdoor neighbour to the embassy has now taken matters to the courts.
Diana Simpson, 35, a Stanford graduate who lives with her parents on Cambridge Street, is suing Westminster city council. She is applying for judicial review and potential damages on the grounds that when the embassy did belatedly seek planning permission for its change of use and flagpole, the local authority failed to take into account the impact on her mental health of the arrival next door of Montenegro, a country that has been involved in recent scrapes with Russia.
Simpson, the daughter of a former US diplomat who has lived on the street for more than three decades, is in receipt of disability benefits after being diagnosed with clinical anxiety, long Covid and a functional neurological disorder. So unsettling has the arrival of the embassy been to Simpson that her nights are regularly affected, she claims in her statement of grounds.
She alleges: “I frequently feel the need to sleep in an alternative to my lifelong bedroom, to gain some marginal relief; sometimes pre-emptively, sometimes in the middle of the night when I cannot reason with my activated primal ‘fear’ brain response (for example, upon hearing a creak, and immediately fearing an intruder accessing my room from the embassy, despite knowing the possibility is very slim and that this response is mostly irrational).”
Citing breaches of the human rights and equality acts, Simpson has said she had considered whether it “remains tenable for me to continue to live in this house, which I had anticipated having the option of living in for the rest of my life”, adding that leaving would wrench her from a “local tight-knit community”.
Simpson told the Guardian she was confident in her case, which alleges the council failed to take into account her conditions, acted irrationally and delivered a flawed public consultation by having a closed mind to objections after the Foreign Office gave its permission.
In its defence statement, Westminster city council denies the allegations and writes: “There is no plausible interference with the claimant’s home or her private and family life.” The council is seeking a summary judgment without a hearing.
A spokesperson for Westminster City Council said: “Councils are legally required to take decisions in line with existing planning policy. It would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”
The case in front of Justice Mould for consideration is perhaps unusual but it has highlighted a more common clash between smaller countries – as they move their embassies due to rent hikes or landlords selling up – and the residents of some of London’s more affluent streets.
The US has its London home in an intimidating purpose-built 12-storey cube structure south of the Thames. But for most of the major nations the natural home is Belgravia or perhaps South Kensington, Knightsbridge and Mayfair. There is a tendency for the lower-tier states to want to be close to these luminaries but spend not quite the same sums on rent.
It is for that reason that Montenegro has alighted in Pimlico, near Victoria coach station, and the Turkmenistan embassy has recently opened in another adapted family home on Victoria Road, in Kensington but a telling 1.4 miles from the splendours of France’s home opposite the Natural History Museum.
The move by Turkmenistan has led to some rancour, too. “I cannot understand the lack of courtesy afforded to immediate neighbours,” submitted one local to a Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea consultation. “I will find out if anything untoward has taken place and, if so, further newspaper action might be necessary.”
The correspondent added of the house in which the embassy is now located, which is owned by Tengku Fahad, 32, the Eton-educated son of the late king of Malaysia, that another location should be found for Turkmenistan, a former Soviet republic in central Asia.
“I was quite happy with the late king of Malaysia [who] lived there and I believe the property is still owned by his son,” she wrote. “We had a family living there for four years who left a while ago for tax reasons but the house has not long been vacant … I have no doubt that they are very pleasant people but, however you bill it, I for one don’t feel totally safe and the idea that there be signage and a flag up leaves me speechless.”
When approached at her home, the complainant, who asked not to be named, said the Turkmens had turned out to be “actually quite quiet” and there had been no problems “so far”.
Risks of such local hostility and scrutiny appear to have led some nations to go another way. North Korea has for two decades had an embassy in something of a place of exile in a seven-bedroom 1920s home off the A406 in Ealing, west London.
Colin Flood, a retired solicitor who lives two doors down, said they never heard a peep from them. A workman renovating the house next to the North Korean delegation added: “They are lovely people – we tidied up their greenery at the front and hope to get more work. Lovely people.”

Rachel Roddy’s pasta with Senegalese-inspired ragu – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

About 30 kilometres south of Naples, the town of Gragnano is surrounded by the Monti Lattari mountain range – the limestone backbone of the Sorrento peninsula. Historically, a series of natural springs fed into a larger stream called Vernotico, which flowed down the mountainside, passing through what was at the time the small village of Gragnano.
The natural slope of the terrain was fortuitous, because it allowed for the construction of a sequence of mills, which started in around 1263. During a visit to Gragnano last month, local historian Giuseppe Di Massa explained how it all worked; how gravity drove the flow of water from one mill to the next, in order to power vertical millstones – a system created for the inconsistent flow. The valley, with its clever water system, became known as the valley of the mills; its role milling grain, which arrived at the nearby port of Castellammare di Stabia, a vital operation to Naples and surrounding towns.
The activity of the 30 mills peaked during the 18th century, but another industry was growing, one that harnessed another natural aspect of the town: its climate. The temperature, humidity and sea breeze were ideal conditions for drying pasta.
Often in strings hung over wooden frames, pasta was dried in the streets of Gragnano, then moved inside when necessary; the skill of the pasta makers and their ability to harness the weather every bit as important as the weather itself. And the industry grew. According to the city of Gragnano website, by 1859 there were 81 pasta factories, requiring ever increasing amounts of hard durum wheat for their pasta, while the mills produced soft wheat. The mills ceased operations in the 1950s, and were largely abandoned until renovation projects turned some of them into small museums.
What has continued to grow in Gragnano, though, is the tradition and art of pasta making; now with its own Indicazione Geografica Protetta, which protects its quality (provenance of wheat, how it is extruded, how long it is dried) and connection with the region. These days, 23 producers – from tiny to vast, 15 of which make up a consortium – make more than 100,000 tonnes of pasta annually in carefully controlled conditions – conditions very different from the open streets, but requiring just as much skill. I returned to Rome with bags of pasta from seven different makers – Di Martino, Faella, Garofolo, Liguori, Afeltra, Antiche Tradizioni di Gragnano, Ducato di alfalfi – all of which pleased me with their nutty scent, porous texture and resilience in the pan.
I also came back from Gragnano with a recipe devised for the town’s Mondopasta festival this year by chef Astou Ndiaye. Born in Dakar and now living with her family in Milan, Ndiaye’s cooking draws both on her heritage and her home. For her beautiful Senegalese ragu, the meat (I used lamb) is marinated in an aromatic blend of vegetables, coriander and cloves before being braised for a stew soft enough to be pasta sauce. I used candele (hollow tubes) made by Garfalo, which I broke into short lengths. It’s a dish that sums up the spirit of pasta di Gragnano, I think; rooted in both Gragnano and Dakar, and at home anywhere.
Pasta with Senegalese-inspired lamb ragu
Serves 4
1 stick celery, trimmed
 
1 small red pepper, trimmed, deseeded and cut into strips
 
1 shallot, peeled
 
1 small bunch coriander
  
2 garlic cloves, peeled
 
3 cloves
  
Salt
  
600g boned lamb shoulder, cubed
 
Olive oil
  
1 large onion, peeled and diced
 
1 tsp paprika
  
1 tsp garam masala
  
400-500g pasta (broken candele, maccheroni, mezze maniche)
Working in a food processor, pulse the celery, red pepper, shallot, coriander, garlic, cloves and a pinch of salt into a rough mixture. Put half the mixture into a bowl, add the meat, then toss so all the chunks are coated. Cover and leave to sit for two to 24 hours (if it’s three hours or more, put it in the fridge).
Working in a large, heavy-based pan, warm four teaspoons of olive oil. Working in batches, brown the marinated meat, then lift out on to a plate.
Add the diced onions to the empty pan, along with the remaining blended mixture and marinade, paprika and garam masala, and stir well, adding more water if it seems too dry. Add the meat, stir again, then add 300ml water. Bring to a simmer, then cover for two hours. By the end of cooking, the meat should be extremely tender and falling apart in just a little thick gravy.
In a separate pot, cook the pasta in salted boiling water according to the packet instructions. Meanwhile, put half of the ragu into the bottom of a warm serving bowl. Lift the cooked, drained pasta on top, toss, adding more ragu as needed, then toss again.

From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court on Wednesday to give evidence in his trial. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters
From sex ‘obsession’ to losing friends, key takeaways from Russell Brand’s testimony at trial
Comedian told jurors he now believed it was wrong to have used his fame for sex and said his life had been consumed by the allegations
Russell Brand was in the witness box for more than four hours on Wednesday at his trial at Southwark crown court. He denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
Six alleged victims say the comedian switched suddenly after appearing charming and forced them into sexual activity in a toilet, a hotel room, workplace corridors and his bedroom, acting as if nothing had happened after the attacks.
Here are the key themes and passages from Brand’s court appearance.
1. Obsession with sex
Brand said in evidence that he had an “obsession” with sex when he was younger, but denied setting himself a “goal” to sleep with 5,000 women.
He said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man and with regard to the latter, with women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond-reckless philandering and idiocy.”
Brand’s former friend, Mark Pinheiro, previously told the trial that Brand had boasted on a car journey to the Labour party conference in Bournemouth about his techniques for “pulling” women and allegedly revealed an ambition to sleep with 5,000 women.
Riel Karmy-Jones KC, prosecuting, asked Brand: “Is it a goal you may have had?” Brand said: “I don’t agree, I don’t recall the conversation you are referring to.”
Brand also suggested a reported conversation in 1999 about never leaving an interaction with a woman without a “conquest” was a riff on a Woody Allen joke.
A court sketch of Riel Karmy-Jones KC cross-examining Russell Brand in the dock. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA
2. ‘Wrong’ to use fame for sex
Brand told jurors he now believed it was “wrong” of him to use his fame for sex. He said: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access which I agree with you was wrong.”
One of Brand’s alleged victims says she was raped after she met him at one of his Hammersmith Apollo standup performances in 2009.
The court heard he stored her name next to the letter T, which he said stood for “tart”. Asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.” He told jurors the woman had not said “no” or told him to stop as they were having sex.
Another allegation is that Brand sexually assaulted a Channel 4 worker in 2009 during a recording session, after she had been forced by members of his entourage to give him a massage. Brand agreed that, while he says he cannot remember that day, it would have been “petulant and childish” to refuse to continue the recording without first receiving a massage.
Asked if he had found thrusting his head into her lap funny, Brand replied: “I don’t remember. I don’t think it’s funny now.”
3. Consent
In his evidence Brand recalled only consensual encounters and told the court that “consent is more important than sex itself”.
The prosecution claimed he had constructed his evidence in response to the allegations. Karmy-Jones accused Brand of staying silent on the accusations in his police interviews so that he “forged” his account around the evidence.
“Were you waiting to see all that evidence before you gave your account?” she asked. Brand replied: “I was doing my best to participate.”
Court sketch of Russell Brand being questioned by his barrister, Ian Winter KC. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA
4. Blamed the media
Brand blamed the media for his public fall from grace after reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and news stories. Asked about the impact of the Dispatches programme, Brand said: “It was devastating.”
Brand told the court that after the programme and the articles he was unable to stay with his son at Great Ormond Street hospital in London when he was having surgery. “Due to material that had been published in the public eye they had to bar my attendance and presence,” Brand said.
He added: “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations.”
5. Shunned by friends
Brand told the court he had been unable to persuade any friend or acquaintance to give evidence on his behalf. The defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked him: “Will they touch you with a bargepole?” Brand replied “No.
Brand described the last few years as “deeply traumatic” and told the court that focusing on the allegations and trying to remember incidents from his past had damaged his personal life.

What’s trending for winter travel? Tripadvisor reveals its top European destinations and experiences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

From snowy escapes to festive breaks, these are Europe’s trending winter destinations and experiences for a chilly getaway.
Looking for some winter holiday inspiration? A new travel index has revealed which European destinations and experiences will be trending this chilly season.
Tripadvisor’s latest study has analysed searches made by travellers in the UK between 1 August 2026 and 31 October 2026, for getaways between 1 November 2026 and 28 February 2027.
Rather than warm winter holidays, its research found that cold weather destinations are on the hotlist, with festive Christmas market towns and Alpine locations topping the list across the continent.
“It’s interesting to see such a strong trend towards cold weather escapes among Brits this winter, with travellers swapping sunloungers for snow boots," Aarushi Kumar, Associate Director of Research & Insights at Tripadvisor Group, said.
“Arctic hideaways, Alpine towns and cosy Christmas market cities taking the top spots just shows that travellers are looking to lean into the colder season rather than escape it.”
Top 10 trending winter destinations in Europe
The trending European winter destinations, according to the Tripadvisor Travel Index:
- 1. Strasbourg, France
- 2. Tromsø, Norway
- 3. Ghent, Belgium
- 4. Saariselka, Finland
- 5. Chamonix, France
- 6. Zakopane, Poland
- 7. Bruges, Belgium
- 8. Nuremberg, Germany
- 9. Salzburg, Austria
- 10. Riga, Latvia
Winter experiences in Europe you won’t want to miss
Topping Tripadvisor’s trending European destinations is Strasbourg in France. It’s famed for its Christmas market, where lights and wooden chalets set the festive scene. This year, the market will run for four weeks starting 27 November.
Alongside the market, Tripadvisor also recommends visiting the Cathedral of our Lady of Strasbourg – a masterpiece of Gothic architecture, stained glass windows and the must-see astronomical clock.
For Northern Lights chasers, book an excursion to Tromsø in Norway. To get prime views of the atmospheric phenomenon, hop on a minibus or boat tour. Visitors should also add reindeer sledding and fjord fishing to their Tromsø itineraries.
Rounding up the index’s top three trending winter destinations, Ghent in Belgium offers a host of cultural and historical experiences. A stop by a key monument like the Castle of the Counts is a must. This medieval attraction stands as Flanders’ only remaining castle from that era with a moat and largely intact defence system.
Here are some of the other experiences to try in the trending destinations this winter:
Saariselka, Finland
• Scenic snowmobile riding
• Go on a husky safari
• Photography experiences to capture the Northern Lights
Chamonix, France
• A trip to the Mont Blanc resort town and scaling Aiguille du Midi
• Go ski touring
• Visit the new Musée du Mont-Blanc
Zakopane, Poland
• Visit Zakopane’s thermal springs
• Stroll along the pedestrianised Krupówki Street
• Take in the views aboard the Gubałówka funicular railway
Bruges, Belgium
• Climb the Belfort medieval bell tower for sweeping views of the city
• Take a walking tour, with a canal cruise and chocolate tasting experience included
• Put on your skates and go ice skating at Koning Albert I-park
Nuremberg, Germany
• Experience a German holiday tradition at Nuremberg Christmas Market
• Visit Kaiserburg Nürnberg medieval castle overlooking the old town
• Go snowhiking
Salzburg, Austria
• Salzburg Christmas Market
• A visit to the Salzburg Cathedral – a 17th-century Baroque landmark
• Attend Winterfest in Volksgarten
Riga, Latvia
• A walking tour around Riga’s old town
• Sightseeing on a canal boat trip
• Snow experiences, like husky sledding

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.
Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.
Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.
The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.
The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.
Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.
“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.
“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”
Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.
“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.
The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.
Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.
For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.
In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.
The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.
Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.
Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.
Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

====================================================================================================

‘There’s nothing scary about it’: Life goes on in Lithuania s troops patrol Russia border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Life in Lithuania’s southwestern town of Vištytis remains undisturbed. Local residents are not troubled either by the threat posed by Russia or by the Lithuanian troops deployed along the border with the Kaliningrad region, who are helping border guards patrol the area.
The military has been assisting the border guards since early October. Around 100 troops are expected to continue doing so until mid-November.
Government officials describe the decision as a precautionary measure in response to the possibility of a new wave of mobilisation in Russia. However, the authorities stress that the threat level along the border has not increased.
“[Potential deserters] will try to cross the state border illegally, both on land and on water. That is why we have stepped up surveillance on land, on water and in the air. As we say here, along the green border, the blue border and in the air,” Rimantas Kundreckis, commander of the Vištytis border guard post, told BNS.
The deployment of troops is estimated to have almost doubled the frequency of patrols along the border with the Kaliningrad region.
The Lithuanian-Russian state border, including the boundary of territorial waters, stretches for almost 300km. It runs through plains, forests and bodies of water.
“There’s nothing particularly scary about it, despite what I read in so many places these days,” Sandra told BNS as she hurried home carrying an armful of groceries.
She is one of just a few hundred residents of Vištytis, in the Vilkaviškis district. Most locals spend the gloomier days of autumn indoors, leaving the town’s central square looking almost deserted, with only the occasional person hurrying toward a nearby shop.
“Nothing has really changed here. You can just see that there are more patrols, but nothing else is happening. The only difference is that the military has arrived, and we see the occasional military vehicle,” the 31-year-old woman said.
She said she was not afraid of the worsening security situation in the region. Nor was her daily life being disrupted by the soldiers recently seen alongside the border guards.
“Life is normal. Everything is just as it was before. There’s no special preparation going on, with people stocking up on supplies or preparing shelters. We’re just living our lives, like everyone else in Lithuania,” Sandra said.
The state border runs through a lake
In Vištytis, a lake separates Lithuania from the Kaliningrad region.
Bright red posts protruding from the water mark the point up to which people who have provided their details to border guards are permitted to sail. Another line of yellow posts, 50 metres beyond them, marks the end of Lithuanian territory.
From the pier where border guard patrol boats moor, you can see a Russian flag flying high just a few hundred metres away.
The lake is monitored by cameras and patrolled by a border guard boat. According to Kundreckis, enhanced surveillance of the lake has helped reduce the number of accidental border crossings.
Previously, people who went out on the water to fish or relax sometimes failed to notice that they were approaching Russian territory. Border guards can now warn them of a potential violation in advance, either by calling them using the contact details they have provided or by approaching them in an official patrol boat.
Accompanying officers on a patrol of Lake Vištytis offers a practical demonstration of how border controls work. When the patrol boat spots another boat, it slows down. Officers observe the person on board and assess the distance from the marked boundary before continuing on their way without making contact.
Such checks are part of the officers’ daily duties.
The most recent border violation recorded by the Vištytis post occurred at the beginning of the year, when two Russian citizens entered Lithuania by walking across the frozen lake. Around 10 similar violations are typically recorded each year.
‘Invaluable experience’
Among those contributing to the border protection mission are troops from the Second Territorial Unit of the Darius and Girėnas National Defence Volunteer Forces (KASP).
Company commander Leonas Ruzgas sees the deployment as an opportunity not only to contribute to the country’s security but also to help soldiers develop their skills.
He was among the first to arrive at the border.
“Border guards have quite a few technological innovations and systems that we do not use, [...] because our work does not require them. So it is good to see how much our border protection has improved, share experience and learn from them,” Ruzgas said.
The commander of the Vištytis border guard post agreed. He said the deployment offered opportunities for professional development not only for officers and soldiers serving on the ground, but also for their commanders.
“The practical experience is truly invaluable. You cannot get it anywhere else, really,” Kundreckis said. “If Day X [war] were to come and the military had to take up a position here, both ordinary soldiers and commanders would already be familiar with the specifics of the area.”
Troops are rotated along the border approximately every four to five days. Different soldiers are usually sent each time, although those who wish to return can do so.
According to Ruzgas, incoming troops adapt to the duty schedules of State Border Guard Service (VSAT) officers, and their powers are largely the same.
Kundreckis said the soldiers assisting the border guards had also brought equipment that was “being successfully used to monitor both land areas and airspace”.
The post commander said he had not noticed any signs of a potential threat, describing activity on the other side of the border as routine daily operations.
“Whether it is a coincidence or not, there has been an increase in military fighter jet flights near the state border. Explosions could be heard somewhere at the training ground towards Kudirkos Naumiestis, and their helicopters have also been flying near the state border more frequently,” the commander said.
‘I was born with the Russians’
Virginijus Dapkus, who owns a farm near Vištytis, told BNS that the authorities’ heightened attention to security made him laugh.
“I was born with the Russians, grew up with the Russians and have dealings with the Russians. I know them very well, and what our authorities, our government, are saying makes me laugh. It is just scaremongering, and they have their own objectives,” Dapkus said as he prepared to go fishing.
He said he felt perfectly comfortable in Vištytis, although he was saddened by the fact that fishing was no longer permitted on the other side of the lake. According to him, the catch now is “like night and day” compared with what it used to be.
“When we were together with the Russians, we used to fish only on the Russian side. Now we fish in a swamp on the Lithuanian side. That is what we call it – the swamp,” he said.
Pranas Stankevičius, a 93-year-old former deportee, also used to fish in Lake Vištytis.
“I used to fish on the lake, but now we are no longer allowed to. You cannot put out a fishing net; they can see everything now. Everything is very restricted,” the pensioner complained.
The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.

The elderly man, who was repairing his car in the street, said he had previously enjoyed travelling to Kaliningrad, where he traded goods with others. Nevertheless, he said he understood the current border controls.
“It is not that bad. A border is a border. What can you do? We belong to Lithuania, so let them guard the border,” he said.
