How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges
John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.
“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.
British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.
Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts.
So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?
The £100 ‘household energy payment’
The government’s biggest bet on offering “breathing space” to struggling households this winter is a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20m households in council tax bands A to D. It is also the measure most likely to deliver real benefit for those in need.
The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey.
Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, said households could face a 25% cost increase from January and shouldn’t expect to feel better off than they do today.
Officials are anxious to avoid handing public money to those who can get by without it but they lack household income data to target proposed support. Using council tax bands is “the least worst proxy”, Lewis said.
The payment will be in addition to the Warm Home Discount, which offers about 6m means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills.
This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.
Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.
A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.
The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.
Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.
A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.
Removing standing charges from gas bills will help two-thirds of households save an average of £45 a year. Photograph: Paul Melling/Alamy
Lower electricity levies
The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.
This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.
This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.
The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.
“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”
Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which add about £200 a year to the average bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.
Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.
Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.
Low-carbon home upgrades
The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.
To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.
The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.
Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.
Energy debt relief
For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.
The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year.
The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.
Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.
More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.

Serbia’s students achieved the impossible. Europe must not fail them now | Srđjan Cvijić
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

As polling stations closed across Serbia on Sunday evening, riot police were deploying around the presidency in Belgrade. Many of us feared the worst: massive electoral fraud, a refusal to recognise defeat or outright violence. After nearly 15 years of Aleksandar Vučić’s increasingly authoritarian rule, a peaceful transfer of power seemed implausible.
I had good reason to feel afraid. I am co-founder of an annual conference on the security and foreign policy challenges shaping the western Balkans, and sit on the international advisory committee of a civil society thinktank, the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy. Such work would be uncontroversial in most countries seeking European Union membership. Under Vučić’s regime, it was anything but.
Over the past two years, our organisation has faced cyber-attacks by actors suspected of links to Russian intelligence, spyware attempts and relentless vilification by pro-regime media. After one attack, investigators documented 28,000 email exchanges that had been hacked. At the same time, Serbian regime propagandists portrayed us as foreign conspirators, while the threat of Russian-style foreign agents legislation cast a long shadow over all of Serbian civil society. Had Vučić won another mandate, exile might have become a reality for many of us.
Others endured far worse. Journalists and activists had their homes set on fire. Students who were detained reported being beaten, females stripped naked and humiliated in police stations while activists were imprisoned for exercising their democratic rights. Among them were the Novi Sad 12 – students and activists prosecuted on politically motivated charges during the protests that followed the November 2024 railway station canopy collapsethat killed 16 people. Six were driven into exile; the other six endured imprisonment and house arrest.
All this happened in a country negotiating EU membership.
And then, on Sunday evening, something extraordinary happened.
Vučić conceded defeat. The student-backed list’s margin of victory was so overwhelming that overturning the result might have proved more dangerous than accepting it.
What convinced a man who had spent nearly 15 years concentrating power in his hands to relinquish it? Fear of popular resistance? International pressure, and if it was this, from where?
Uncertainty over the loyalty of Vučić’s security apparatus may have been a decisive factor. Days before the election, hundreds of serving and former police and intelligence officials, including former security leaders, signed an appeal urging their colleagues to uphold the constitution rather than obey unlawful political orders. It was a reminder that Vučić could not necessarily count on the entire security establishment to keep him in power.
An incumbent accepting electoral defeat is ordinary in an established democracy. In Serbia, it felt almost miraculous.
The students had achieved what many thought impossible. They had forced a system built around the impossibility of losing to accept that it had lost.
Their victory belonged equally to hundreds of thousands who marched, organised and endured intimidation. What began as grief over 16 lives lost in Novi Sad became a movement challenging the foundations of state capture.
For nearly two years, the students dismantled the regime’s most powerful weapon: the belief that resistance was futile, everyone had a price and political change was impossible.
But the significance of their victory is measured not only in votes. It is measured in lives.
I think of Mila, Anja, Doroteja, Branislav, Jovan and Dejan, the six Novi Sad activists forced into exile formore than a year and a half. They may finally be able to come home. Six of their comrades in Serbia are now free from detention and house arrest. But I have friends who have confronted authoritarianism in their countries with equal courage and have no prospect of achieving the same breakthrough. I am thinking of Marika from Georgia, Gökçe from Turkey and Andrei from Belarus. For them, exile remains a condition of life. Their fate reminds us that Serbia’s peaceful breakthrough was not inevitable.
Geography, too, played its part. Serbia lies at the heart of Europe, beyond Russia’s immediate reach and too close to the EU for its democratic struggle to remain Europe’s distant concern.
Serbia’s students deserve the credit, but what happens next also depends on Europe. For years, some European leaders tolerated, and sometimes effectively supported, Vučić’s authoritarian rule, preferring a predictable strongman to democratic uncertainty. Serbia’s breakthrough happened largely despite Brussels, not because of it.
Here lies the irony: while European leaders courted Vučić, much of Serbia’s genuinely pro-European constituency opposed him. Our research found that two-thirds of Serbians who supported EU membership also opposed his government. Brussels was looking for stability in the wrong place.
Serbia’s ability to consolidate its democracy relies on a future in Europe. And Europe now has an opportunity to regain the trust of those who fought for the very democratic values it professes to uphold.
Defeating an autocrat is an event, but dismantling authoritarian institutions is a process. Serbia must restore the rule of law, free its media and ensure that its police and security services serve citizens rather than a political party.
The students have won the right to change their government but the harder task lies ahead. And that means building a country where doing so will never again require such extraordinary courage.
- Srđjan Cvijić is a writer, president of the international advisory committee of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy and co-founder of the Belgrade Security Conference

‘There has to be a bolder shift’: retail and hospitality businesses assess relief in budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

“It is like letting the tyres down and then handing you a pump,” says James Nye, assessing the relief handed to businesses in John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
The managing director of Norfolk’s Anglian Country Inns argues that the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but added more labour costs for already burdened companies.
Nye, who employs 500 people at the height of the season at its 10 venues across Norfolk and Hertfordshire, was among those business owners watching Healey carefully on Wednesday, after two previous Labour budgets under Rachel Reeves had loaded extra costs on to businesses.
Healey aimed to help high street operators by removing the business rates burden from more small businesses and limiting the rise in the minimum wage for younger workers.
The chancellor put a lid on increases to business rates, so they will only rise in line with inflation for two years, and clamped down on VAT dodging by online sellers, among other measures intended to help high streets. However, some businesses argued Andy Burnham’s chancellor could have gone further.
Pets Corner, family-owned retailer
Dean Richmond, the owner of the Pets Corner chain, says the chancellor has not fixed the “fundamental problem” that its costs are rising faster than it can increase sales.
The family-owned business, founded by Richmond’s parents in 1968, now employs 1,200 people and has 159 stores. He does not expect to get much benefit from the increase in the threshold at which business rates begin to be paid.
“It’s a bit ‘moving the deckchairs on the Titanic’ on rates. There has to be a bolder shift if the government is going to help offline retail,” Richmond says.
He welcomed the move to ensure that online marketplaces such as Amazon collect VAT from more sellers, but was disappointed that Healey did not bring forward the end of tax breaks for online sellers, such as Shein and Temu, importing cheaper items from overseas.
“It feels like the world’s against us. When offline retailers all but disappear the world will miss us,” he says.
While he says Reeves’s budgets had been “really damaging, this is safe but isn’t going to change anything”.
“It is not a good news budget with the minimum wage going up,” he says, on top of the previous changes to employers’ national insurance contributions (NICs) and big increases in the minimum wage for employers.
Richmond says the business, based in Crawley in Sussex, had been forced to make “pretty drastic cuts” to the number of people it employed and to reduce bonus incentives, and had shifted to hiring older, more experienced people as there was less incentive to hire new starters.
Herdy, independent retailer and brand
Spencer Hannah is the co-founder and owner of Herdy, which has five shops in Cumbria and sells its cartoon sheep-branded homewares and clothing online and to other retailers in the UK and overseas.
“The chancellor’s key narrative was that he wanted to support British businesses doing business with Britain and we applaud and support that,” says Hannah, whose business employs 28 people directly.
But Hannah says the budget lacked the “seismic difference” to help UK retailers and their local suppliers. He welcomed relief on business rates for smaller shops but says that was “not counterbalancing what’s happened in the last two years”.
“Like everybody else running small and medium-sized enterprises, life has got slowly harder over the last two budgets and some poor choices have been made by the [last] leadership in government.”
He says increases in national insurance contributions, the minimum wage and other costs such as rent and energy have weighed on the business directly, but the “most frustrating thing” has been the impact of the higher costs for his domestic suppliers. He has been forced to ditch some of them, such as its mug manufacturer in Stoke, and look abroad.
Anglian Country Inns, pub and hotel operator
Nye says the budget made a “couple of steps towards helping” but against a very tough backdrop.
He welcomes help on business rates for smaller venues but says this is unlikely to assist Anglian directly. He was disappointed that the chancellor had yet again put up the legal minimum wage from April, which will more than offset the rates change for most.
A failure to cut VAT for hospitality businesses or cut national insurance contributions for younger workers were further disappointments.
Nye hopes that Healey’s support for household energy bills “might help consumer confidence”, but added: “We were expecting a little bit more to offset the massive tax increases hospitality has faced.”
“We are being crippled by taxes as a sector and the cumulative tax burden is horrific. We pay 83% as a percentage of our profits in tax,” Nye says.
“I don’t mind paying people more, but we’re then being taxed on it because the NICs threshold hasn’t changed, and the rate of NICs has gone up, so every time that the national minimum wage goes up, we’re paying more and more in tax.
“The cost of going out is getting more and more expensive. My biggest fear is that hospitality starts becoming a luxury rather than a convenience.”

Thames Water creditors to vote on emergency £2.4bn loan as cash runs low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

A group of creditors to troubled Thames Water are poised to vote on whether to grant an emergency £2.4bn loan to keep the company afloat, as campaigners raise concerns it could add £40 to each household’s bills in interest alone.
A consortium of creditors, called London & Valley Water, will vote on Thursday on whether to increase a funding facility for the debt-laden utility company to £5.4bn to keep it operating to autumn 2027.
The company’s class A creditors, which include BlackRock, Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, last year granted it a £3bn loan at a 9.75% interest rate.
This month, Thames Water said it needed a further £2.4bn cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its extensive debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.
Thames Water has previously said that customers will not be on the hook for the interest on the £3bn loan, but it has almost run out of money and not paid down the debt.
Analysis by the campaign group We Own It showed that the £2.4bn loan, if it is granted on the same terms and added to bills, would cost £40 per household in interest alone, and £454 per household if the entire loan amount was included. London & Valley Water insisted it would not be added to bills.
Andy Burnham is now deciding whether to allow a takeover deal by the water company’s creditors, which would entail writing off fines and reducing environmental commitments. He is also mulling whether to nationalise the company or take another form of state control.
Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners have said Burnham should instead put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.
Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “Since privatisation, £11.9bn has been extracted from Thames Water. They have already had more than enough of our money. If they cannot survive without yet another excruciatingly expensive bailout, this government must let them go bust and bring them into special administration, followed by permanent public ownership.”
The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames Valley. It has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away in 2024, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.
In 2025, Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat MP for Witney, along with campaigners and junior creditors, unsuccessfully took the water company to court over the £3bn loan.
On the proposed £2.4bn loan, he said: “The creditors will likely hand Thames Water yet another massively overpriced rescue loan, which customers will end up having to pay for.
“This is just another short-term fix, paid for by customers and taxpayers. The government has had more than two years to make up its mind. It’s time it did so. Put Thames Water into special administration now.”
The creditors have approved 15 previous consent requests from Thames Water. The company said this month it had so far drawn £2.65bn of the £3bn available under the “super senior” facility.
Prof Dieter Helm, an economist at the University of Oxford, doubted that a turnaround of Thames Water could be “properly funded” and said further loans were merely postponing an “inevitable” special administration.
He said: “The future investment programme for the turnaround will not be properly funded. Thames – and indeed much of the rest of the industry – is caught between a political rock and a political hard place.”
Conquest added: “During a cost of living crisis, this government cannot continue to reward Thames Water’s failures at our expense.”
Burnham has been looking at ways to take control of Thames Water in an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control. He has urged his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a list of policies for the utility company.
One option under consideration is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.
A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Additional liquidity from creditors will enable the investment to continue uninterrupted while the business seeks a recapitalisation. Customer bills are set by Ofwat, and this funding does not add any costs for households.”
A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “No customer bills will be used to pay for the costs of Thames Water’s rescue financing. These costs are borne entirely by the class A creditors.
“Creditors have stepped in to provide the billions of pounds of private capital needed to ensure Thames Water’s record infrastructure investment programme can continue, avoiding the need for any government financial support or taxpayer funding.”

Creative project reimagines history from First Nations perspective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Address to the Nations reimagines history from Indigenous perspective
In the alternate timeline imagined by Address to the Nations, colonisation didn't happen in Australia, and the country is guided by a Ministry of Elders who oversee a democratic system of government.
The project is the brainchild of Yorta Yorta/Wurundjeri actor, writer, producer and director Tony Briggs, best known for creating and writing the musical comedy film, The Sapphires, and his close friend, award-winning artist, curator, producer and writer David Pledger.
To tell the story, which stretches over 300 years, Briggs and Pledger have begun building a portfolio with an art series, TV show, theatre production and video game part of the offering.
They've established the collaborative practice Tomorrow's Pasts under the moniker briggsnpledger and have built a universe that borrows from genres such as alternate futurism, counter-factual storytelling and science fiction to create an alternate Australian history as a way to imagine a better future.
"What if you could travel back in time? What would you do? We had many conversations over a long period of time around that very question," Briggs told PM.
"One of the things that kept popping up was, well, we think we'd like to sort of warn people of the mistakes.
"We can prompt you, [but] you have to find these mistakes for yourself and collect information and come forward and hopefully you come forward with the correct answers for humanity, if you like, [for] all of us, not just a certain sector of the community."
As part of the story, in 2063, the Ministry of Elders, which governs the Great Southern Nations (Australia in our current timeline) sends a message stick 300 years into the past to warn First Nations peoples about the arrival of outsiders (called The Accelerationists) and the potential for race-based conflicts.
The information sent into the past allows for the development of technology, giving First Nations peoples the power to keep control over their lands, regardless of the ambitions of outsiders.
The title of the project invokes the addresses the First Ministers (prime ministers in our timeline) deliver to the country.
Three out of the 10 addresses have so far been recorded. These are set in 1940, 1981 and 2022.
"1940 sets up what's about to happen, which is a race-based civil war in which Aboriginal Australia and its allies [are] contested by a group of [domestic] techno-fascists called the Accelerationists," Pledger told PM.
"Our First Minister in 1981 announces the beginning of the race-based civil war and over the subsequent 40 years there is a contest between Aboriginal Australians [and] allies, and the Accelerationists for sovereignty of the country."
Pledger says technology has a different trajectory in the alternate timeline.
"You have various changes in leadership, and the most significant one is the one that leads us up to the 2022 Address to the Nations, in which a young woman, Alinta Maris, who's a kind of tech genius, who has created HapTik Media and Blockchain over the preceding 20 years, in 2022, she develops non-lethal warfare, which brings the war to an end."
Audiences excited about project
The visual art series was launched in June and has been shown at special screenings in Canberra and Melbourne and will next year be programmed into Australia's premier Indigenous-led film festival, the Birrarangga Film Festival.
Founder and CEO of Indigital Mikaela Jade described the work as "incredible".
"We all have the agency and autonomy to be able to help create this future and I think this is a great catalyst for conversations," she said.
Author and historian Margo Ngawa Neale picked up on the close friendship between Briggs and Pledger.
"What I really like about it is the fact that it is Black and white working together as the only way we're going to move forward,"
she said.
"And these two fellas, their relationship is in fact in itself a model for what Address to the Nations can be."
Impossible choice between friendship and community
Briggs and Pledger first worked together about 25 years ago on the multimedia theatre production K, which Pledger wrote and directed and Briggs starred in.
They became fast friends, and their bond sparked the initial idea for Address to the Nations.
"When David and I first started talking about this idea, it was at the height of the Black Lives Matter movement and a question popped up around having to make a choice," Briggs said.
"What if either of us had to make a choice between our friendships based on our race, based on the colour of our skin, if we were forced to do it?
"And both of us, we both said, well, the first priority will be our families, number one.
"So, we talked around all of that and we sort of imagined the worst being forced upon us and it just sort of kind of cracked open this interesting conversation."
Ultimately, the two agreed they would fight to maintain their close friendship because, as Pledger says, they are like family.
"Family's not just about blood," Pledger said.
"Family's about an extension of the sorts of relationships that you can call familial at least.
"So, it gets very sticky with that kind of question because where's the friendship stop and the family begin?
"And I think that's one of the things where we found so interesting in these sort of discussions is the threshold keeps moving and hopefully it dissolves."

C Next Designers EMEA brings together over 250 professionals for design conference in Almería
For the ninth edition of the C Next Designers design conference, Spanish brand Cosentino brought together designers from Europe, Africa and the Middle East for three days of talks focused on “design as a driver of change”.
The event was held from 13 to 16 October in venues across Almería, Spain and included talks by designers such as Ron Arad, Karim Rashid and design studio Studiopepe.
It is the fourth iteration of the event held in Spain and the ninth worldwide.
This year’s conference focused on the theme Design to Transform, which champions “design as a force capable of reshaping society and adding value to it”, according to the team.
The first day opened with a welcome at the Cabo Gata Beach Hotel.
On Wednesday, the event moved to Cosentino’s industrial park in Cantoria, where Cosentino CEO Pilar Cosentino gave opening remarks.
Architect and designer Ron Arad then spoke with Cosentino commercial director for Europe, Jorge Lope about his career and collaborations with the brand, before the day ended with a guided tour of Cosentino’s facilities, including a local natural stone warehouse.
The day also featured the presentation of the latest product innovations by Valentín Tijeras, global vice president of product.
The second day took place at the Almería Science and Technology Park (PITA) and included presentations by brands Novara, Jung, Speho, TECE and Gaggenau.
Karim Rashid and Studiopepe then gave keynote speeches, which were a highlight of the day.
Dezeen editorial director (special projects) Max Fraser also moderated two panels as part of the event.
The first, held with Dornbracht, focused on hyper-personalisation as a creative tool and featured C’est Ici Design founder Monica Arango, founder of Black Architecture Danko Lekic and head of global channel management at Dornbracht Sascha Bialoian.
The second panel examined how design is changing our everyday habits, and featured Fran Silvestre Arquitectos founder Fran Silvestre, ZHA associate director Bidisha Sinha and founder of AS Architect Ayşin Sevgi Karakurt Macit.
Studio Haus closed the panels, and the event concluded with a gala dinner in the Cloister of Almería Cathedral, which was informed by the Dekton Artik Nodes collection, a new Cosentino material.
Cosentino previously launched Nara, a beige-toned porcelain surface designed to celebrate natural stone and Éclos, which was designed to be free of crystalline silica.
Last year’s C Next Designers conference featured talks by Sabine Marcelis and Peter Ippolito or Nini Andrade Silva.
To learn more about C Next Designers, visit the conference’s website.

Russia Uses North Korean Forced Labor to Sustain War Against Ukraine, Investigation Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:59:09 UTC
13:59:09 KST

A Russian recruitment network backed by North Korean officials is supplying workers to factories supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine, using forced labor to sustain Russian production while channeling much of the workers’ earnings to Pyongyang, a new investigation published Thursday, Oct. 29, found.
The investigation by The Hague-based human rights organization Global Rights Compliance (GRC) uncovered a network of Russian brokers bringing North Korean nationals into Russia on student visas to circumvent UN sanctions prohibiting their employment.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Some workers were placed at factories producing supplies for Russia’s military, including military food rations, according to the findings.
Investigators documented workers facing 12-hour shifts, as few as two days off per month and threats of punishment against themselves or their families if they tried to escape.
The findings expose another dimension of the growing partnership between Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose government has already supplied Moscow with troops and ammunition for its war in Ukraine.
North Korean workers recruited under false student arrangements
The investigation identified a network linked to Moscow businessman Vladimir Sokolov and his Black Horse group of companies, which operates an online platform connecting Russian employers with North Korean workers.
North Koreans entered Russia on student visas, ostensibly to enroll at educational institutions, before being assigned to employers.
Moscow Hit by Massive Drone Attack as Airports Restrict Flights
Brokers received commissions of up to 150,000 rubles ($1,860) per worker, according to the investigation.
GRC researchers used publicly available records, facial recognition technology and undercover inquiries, posing as prospective employers to document how the operation functioned.
The investigation also identified North Korean embassy officials in Moscow inspecting potential employment sites, indicating direct involvement by Pyongyang in arranging the placements.
One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not attempt to flee.
The network’s operations included placements at industrial production facilities, including a factory producing military rations used by Russian forces.
Forced labor finances North Korea’s weapons programs
The investigation found that much of the money paid for North Korean workers’ labor was diverted to the North Korean state rather than reaching the workers themselves.
The arrangement benefits both governments: Russia gains access to a tightly controlled workforce as it struggles to sustain wartime production, while Pyongyang receives foreign currency that can support its weapons programs.
GRC legal adviser Elise Lauriot Prevost said the findings exposed the convergence of two governments’ military interests, linking North Korea’s overseas forced-labor system to Russia’s growing wartime labor demands.
Lead investigator Dyland Carter said workers received little, if any, of the money employers paid for their services, with the proceeds flowing instead to the North Korean government.
The latest findings build on earlier GRC research published in March, which documented systematic exploitation of North Korean workers at Russian construction sites.
Based on interviews with 21 workers across three Russian cities, that investigation found conditions including shifts of up to 16 hours, passport confiscation, physical abuse and mandatory payments to the North Korean government.
Some workers reported earning as little as $10 per month, while others faced escalating state-imposed quotas that trapped them in debt.
The researchers identified all 11 of the International Labour Organization’s indicators of forced labor in the workers’ testimonies.
Moscow and Pyongyang deepen wartime partnership
North Korea has become an important military partner for Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Pyongyang has supplied weapons and ammunition to Russian forces, while South Korean intelligence estimates that more than 10,000 North Korean troops have been deployed to fight alongside Russian forces since 2024.
The two countries signed a strategic partnership treaty in June 2024 that includes mutual defense commitments.
The forced-labor network shows how their cooperation extends beyond weapons transfers and battlefield operations to industrial production and financial support.
The arrangement operates despite UN Security Council sanctions adopted in 2017, which prohibited member states from hiring North Korean workers abroad and required their repatriation by the end of 2019.

North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles into sea
October 29, 2026
North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea's military said.
The missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. local time (0330 GMT) from an area near Wonsan on North Korea's eastern coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement.
South Korea's military said it was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Japan's Defense Ministry said the missiles had fallen outside the country's Exclusive Economic Zone, according to South Korea's Yonhap News Agency.
Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, most recently launching several short-range ballistic missiles on October 12.
Thursday's launch comes amid growing tensions between the two Koreas over a border dispute that has further strained relations between Seoul and Pyongyang.
Why are tensions rising between North and South Korea?
Three South Korean soldiers were wounded on September 21 when landmines exploded in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which separates the two countries.
A joint investigation by South Korea and the United Nations concluded earlier this month that North Korea had planted the landmines south of the military demarcation line more than a year ago.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned South Korean demands for an apology as "despicable." She also rejected Seoul's offer of medical equipment.
Last week, North Korea announced plans to resume propaganda broadcasts along the border and deploy new weapons systems in the area.
South Korea subsequently proposed talks to clarify the border and prevent accidental military clashes. Pyongyang has yet to respond.
What about potential US-North Korea nuclear talks?
The rising tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in potential nuclear negotiations.
Seoul is a key Washington ally, but Trump's approach has fueled uncertainty over South Korea's role in any future talks with the North.
North Korea's previous missile launch on October 12 came a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim Jong Un this year.

Russia restarts grain shipments through Sea of Azov, media reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:54:58 UTC
13:54:58 KST

Russian grain shipments through the Sea of Azov have resumed after a halt of more than three months that followed a Ukrainian drone campaign, according to media reports published on Oct. 28.
Ukrainian attacks prompted Russian authorities to temporarily stop shipping through the Don-Azov Channel on July 10, Reuters reported. Kyiv's military campaign resulted in over 100 Russian vessels being hit in the Azov sea during the summer — negatively impacting Russia's economy and contributing to an increase in global grain prices.
Russia has since restarted granting permits for vessels carrying grain seeking to leave the Sea of Azov. At least one ship had already passed through the Kerch Strait to the Black Sea by Oct. 29, Bloomberg reported.
The Sea of Azov is a strategically important waterway for Russia, used for military logistics and for exports of oil, grain, steel and other goods to international markets. It stretches from Russian-occupied Mariupol to occupied Crimea. The Kerch strait connects the Azov to the Black Sea.
Ukraine launched Operation Molochka in July, a campaign targeting Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea peninsula.
Throughout July, the military reported dozens of Russian shadow fleet vessels being struck in the Black and Azov seas. The Armed Forces said at the time that the targeted vessels supported Russia's military logistics by transporting cargo and servicing port infrastructure. By Aug. 8, Ukrainian drones had struck 218 Russian shadow fleet vessels, including 134 in the Sea of Azov and 84 in the Black Sea, according to the Unmanned Systems Forces.
Ukrainian drone strikes also reached Russia’s main Black Sea export terminals, with all three grain terminals at Novorossiysk, Russia’s leading Black Sea wheat export port, suspending operations over the summer.
The resumption of grain shipping comes as Russia faces growing pressure on its grain-export infrastructure. Krasnodar Krai, Russia's largest agricultural region, declared a state of emergency in September due to an inability to export grain.
Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindauga Sinkevicius called for the EU to impose sanctions on Russian grain, and to ban transit, on Oct. 8, which was followed the day after by a joint letter from the three Baltic prime ministers to put it on the EU agenda.
As Ukrainian strikes shut down Black Sea terminals, Russian exporters shifted much of their grain to Baltic ports, according to Reuters.

Junk food’s impact may go beyond the weighing scale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:48:40 UTC
13:48:40 KST

NEW DELHI: A packet of chips after school, a cookie between meals or a burger as a treat may seem harmless. But a new study suggests that eating more ultra-processed foods may be linked to changes in how children’s brains respond to food, as well as greater gains in body fat over the following year.Published in JAMA Network Open this month, the study followed 46 children who were at a healthy weight at the start. Researchers found that children who got a larger share of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods (UPFs) showed stronger responses in a brain region linked to reward, motivation and habit formation when they saw pictures of tempting foods such as cookies and French fries.These stronger brain responses were linked to greater increases in body mass index (BMI) and body fat over the next year. Children who ate more UPFs also showed an increase in waist size.The findings raise a new concern in the debate over childhood obesity: could the way children’s brains respond to food be part of the link between eating highly processed foods and gaining weight?Dr Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi) and co-author of the 2025 Lancet series on ultra-processed foods, said the findings should prompt a closer look at the foods children eat and how these products are marketed to them.
He said repeated exposure to highly appealing foods could encourage habitual eating.The study, however, did not prove that children become addicted to food or that junk food directly changes their brains.The researchers also found that sugar alone may not explain the link. Many ultra-processed foods combine fat and carbohydrates, which can trigger a strong reward response in the brain. However, when researchers accounted for added-sugar intake, the link between UPF consumption and brain response weakened, suggesting that several factors may be involved.The findings come amid calls for tighter restrictions on advertising foods high in fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) to children. NAPi has sought amendments to the Press Council of India’s Norms of Journalistic Conduct 2022 to prohibit such advertising. The Press Council referred the proposal to the Union health ministry in May 2024, sought comments in June 2025 and sent a reminder in 2026, but NAPi says it is still awaiting a response.
It has also written to the information and broadcasting ministry.Although the study was conducted in the US and its findings cannot be directly extrapolated to Indian children, it raises a key question: should tackling childhood obesity also mean addressing the advertising and food environments that shape children’s choices?
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:46:41 UTC
13:46:41 KST

Fire breaks out at US nuclear weapons facility
A fire broke out at a major nuclear research complex in South Carolina that supports the US nuclear weapons program, the Department of Energy has said.
The fire started at Savannah River National Laboratory, part of the Savannah River Site (SRS) near Aiken, on Wednesday evening and was subsequently extinguished, officials said.
“No contamination has been reported outside the affected facility,” the department said in a statement.
Emergency protocols were activated, with employees not involved in response efforts ordered to suspend operations and shelter in place as a precaution. The site was closed to incoming traffic, while nearby rail, river, and air traffic was restricted.
Officials lifted the emergency declaration at 9:45 PM, saying radiation surveys found no detectable contamination. Protective measures were lifted, and the site was cleared to resume normal operations on Thursday.
Local media reported that the fire broke out in a single room and involved an unfiltered, ground-level radiological release. One employee was reportedly hospitalized with minor injuries.
Established in the early 1950s during the Cold War, the SRS originally produced plutonium and tritium for US nuclear weapons. Although its production reactors have since been shut down, the complex continues to play a key role in maintaining the American nuclear arsenal.
The SRS processes and replenishes tritium, a radioactive isotope of hydrogen used to boost the explosive yield of nuclear warheads. It also manages nuclear materials, treats radioactive waste, and carries out environmental cleanup.
The US government is also developing a facility at the SRS to manufacture plutonium cores for nuclear warheads as part of efforts to modernize the country’s nuclear weapons stockpile.
The incident comes less than two weeks after a fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, killing four soldiers and injuring 39 others during a live-fire training exercise. According to the Canadian military, strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly, overtaking an area occupied by troops.
The Canadian Armed Forces said last week that 27 personnel remained hospitalized, while 12 were discharged. Military police have launched an independent investigation into the incident.

Why US allies in Middle East are accelerating direct talks with Iran

Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:41:41 UTC
13:41:41 KST

Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game.
The clips, which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion.
One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher.
A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster.
“We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed.
They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise.
Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.”
They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.”
The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment.
The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday.
Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush.
The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced.
Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets.
The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang.
It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release.

Military personnel can order NRK amphibious vehicles through Brave1 Market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Military personnel can order NRK amphibious vehicles through Brave1 Market
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Ministry of Defense’s press service.
“A new class of ground-based robotic systems—amphibious robotic systems—is now available on the Brave1 Market platform. The Brave1 defense innovation cluster has created a separate category for them, where the first three products are already featured. The range will continue to expand. Eventually, military units will be able to order these systems through the eBaly program,” the statement reads.
As emphasized by the Ministry of Defense, amphibious RCSs are a new class of robots that expand the capabilities of ground operations. Rivers, canals, and marshy areas can complicate or completely block access to positions. Because of this, delivering provisions and ammunition to troops can be difficult. Amphibious ground drones are advanced logistics robots. They maintain high maneuverability on land and, in a matter of seconds, switch to aquatic mode to continue their route where a conventional ground drone would have to stop. To ensure such solutions reach the front lines more quickly, Brave1, in collaboration with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, is systematically developing the market for amphibious systems.
Back in June 2026, Brave1 launched a separate grant program called “NRK-Amphibians.” Thanks to constant feedback from the military, Ukrainian developers are refining their innovations to meet the realities of the front lines.
According to the press service, the technology’s effectiveness has already been proven on the battlefield. Recently, soldiers from the Alter Ego unit of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade carried out the first-ever combat mission using an amphibious vehicle. The system navigated an extremely challenging route—over 40 km by land and water—and successfully delivered provisions and ammunition to the front lines.
The Ministry of Defense noted that as of mid-August, UAVs had carried out over 100,000 missions on behalf of Ukrainian troops at the front since the beginning of the year.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine conducted large-scale testing of ground-based robotic platforms.

North Korea fires projectile toward sea off east coast, South Korea military says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:30:43 CET
13:30:43 KST

By Kyu-seok Shim
SEOUL, Oct 29 (Reuters) - North Korea fired around 10 ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, as tensions run high ahead of Pyongyang’s end-of-month deadline to activate propaganda loudspeakers along the heavily armed border.
The short-range missiles were launched at around 12:30 p.m. (0330 GMT) from around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast and flew about 250 km (155 miles), South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said.
South Korea was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness for additional launches, while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan, it added.
Japan’s Defence Ministry said North Korea had launched what could be a ballistic missile and that it did not appear to have landed within Japan’s Exclusive Economic Zone.
South Korea’s presidential National Security Office convened an emergency meeting to assess the security implications.
It urged North Korea to halt its repeated ballistic missile launches, calling them a “serious violation” of UN Security Council resolutions, a presidential statement said.
“The launch can be linked to the tensions along the border as part of a broader series of North Korean shows of force, although it is difficult to say the border situation directly prompted the missile launch,” said Kim Yong-hyun, a professor of North Korean Studies at Seoul’s Dongguk University.
Kim said the launch also appeared intended to demonstrate North Korea’s increasingly advanced ballistic missile capabilities to the US, Japan and the broader international community.
TENSIONS RUN HIGH
The launch came as tensions along the inter-Korean border have risen sharply since two mine explosions in the Demilitarised Zone on September 21 wounded three South Korean soldiers.
Seoul says the mines were planted by North Korean forces and has called the incident an armistice violation and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and accused Seoul of fabricating the incident.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced last week that Pyongyang would place loudspeakers capable of blasting anti-South Korean propaganda on standby across the border within days.
She had earlier said the broadcasts would operate along the entire border by the end of October, though analysts in Seoul questioned whether the devices would be activated.
“Rather than being a firm decision to begin broadcasts, North Korea seems to be saying it will have everything ready and watch how South Korea responds,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.
ARTILLERY BATTERIES
North Korea’s military has also deployed artillery batteries visible from across the border, which South Korea’s military said earlier on Thursday appeared largely intended for show.
“We assess that North Korea has several intentions, but the exposure of older weapon systems should be understood as being for show,” JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young told a briefing.
Defence Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said placing artillery where it could be easily seen “makes little tactical or military sense”.
Reuters witnesses this week saw three North Korean armoured vehicles, identified by South Korean experts as self-propelled 122-mm howitzers, positioned near the border with their gun barrels pointed south.
North Korean soldiers were also seen erecting fences inside the DMZ.
Jang said North Korean activity near the Military Demarcation Line bisecting the DMZ was continuing, while South Korean forces were issuing warning broadcasts and firing warning shots during incursions.
Seoul was awaiting a response to its two proposals for military talks and had urged North Korea to return to dialogue, the Defence Ministry said.
North Korea last fired ballistic missiles on October 12. Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year.
(Reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Joyce Lee in Seoul. Additional reporting by Hina Suzuki in TokyoEditing by Ed Davies)

Taiwan grounds Apache helicopter fleet for safety inspections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:30:34 UTC
13:30:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s military has grounded its Apache helicopter fleet for inspections.
Speaking at a special legislative briefing, Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) confirmed on Thursday that the defense ministry received a technical notice from the US, per CNA.
Koo said that in the meantime, the Army would deploy Super Cobra attack helicopters and Kiowa helicopters to carry out missions.
Taiwan currently has 29 AH-64E Apaches stationed in Longtan, Taoyuan; Xinshe, Taichung; Guiren, Tainan; and Feng Nien Airport in Taitung County.
The US Army temporarily paused flight operations earlier this month for its Apaches equipped with improved drive system transmissions for inspections and to complete “corrective actions,” according to Stars and Stripes.
An investigation in May found that “some AH-64E [improved drive system] main transmissions can experience an internal failure resulting in loss of accessory gearbox drive, which can result in loss of tail rotor thrust, electrical power, and hydraulics,” according to an April internal safety document reviewed by Defense One.

Europe’s oil bill: EU pays €10bn more per month than in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:30:07 UTC
13:30:07 KST

Euronews Business takes a closer look at how Europe’s petroleum oil import bill has risen amid tensions in the Middle East - and experts do not expect costs to fall in the near future.
European countries are paying far more for petroleum oil imports this year, following tensions in the Middle East in February 2026. Consumers are already facing higher petrol and diesel prices. Now, the EU’s import bill shows just how sharply costs have risen.
In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent an average of €27.6 billion a month on petroleum oil imports, up 55.8% from €17.7 billion a month in 2025.
But the volume of oil imported barely changed. It rose by just 1.2%, from 36.3 million tonnes a month in 2025 to 36.7 million tonnes.
That means the EU paid €9.9 billion more a month.
The cost per tonne also rose, from €487 to €750 over the same period, returning to its 2022 peak.
Why is the bill rising?
The main reason is the rise in crude oil prices. “The monthly average of the Brent crude price in the second quarter of 2026 is 49.5% higher than the monthly average price of 2025 – a $34 per barrel increase,” Prof. Xiaoyi Mu from the University of Dundee told Euronews Business.
He noted that in 2025, around 20 million barrels of oil and oil products per day – approximately 20% of global daily consumption – were exported via the Strait of Hormuz. “When nearly 20% of world supply is cut, the price must rise to balance the market,” he said.
The cost per tonne tells the story. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU paid €750 for each tonne of imported petroleum oil. That was the second-highest level since 2021, just €2 below the peak recorded in the second quarter of 2022.
At the end of 2025, a tonne cost €435. The price rose to €498 in the first quarter of this year before jumping to €750 in the second quarter.
Szymon Kardas, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), emphasised that the war between the US, Israel and Iran had disrupted oil production and supplies to global markets, pushing prices higher.
“In some weeks, tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns to pre-war levels, only to fall again,” he told Euronews Business.
Kardas said such disruptions hit the EU hard because it was 90–95% dependent on oil imports from outside the bloc. According to Eurostat, this dependence stood at 96.6% in 2024.
Wolfgang Eichhammer, senior expert at the Institute for European Energy and Climate Policy (IEECP), agreed that tensions in the Middle East had the greatest impact, as supplies fell or became less secure. However, he said strong global demand also played a role, with Europe competing for oil with buyers in Asia, notably China.
The chart comparing import value and volume shows how the bill rose while the amount of oil imported remained broadly unchanged. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent €82.7 billion on petroleum oil imports, up from €50.3 billion a year earlier. Import volumes rose only slightly, from 105.2 million tonnes to 110.2 million tonnes.
The same pattern is evident over the past five years. Quarterly import volumes ranged from 105 million to 123 million tonnes, while the bill varied from €38 billion in early 2021 to €91.3 billion in 2022. It then fell to €47.8 billion at the end of 2025 before surging again.
Oil accounts for almost all of the rise in the EU’s energy import bill. In the second quarter of 2026, the EU spent €115.6 billion on energy imports, up from €81.4 billion in the same quarter of 2025. Petroleum oils accounted for €32.4 billion of the €34.2 billion increase, or 95%.
Spending on other energy products changed little. Gas imports rose by €1.6 billion and coal by €0.4 billion, while LNG imports fell slightly, by €0.2 billion.
Drivers pay more at the pump
European drivers have felt the impact at the pump. In the first week of January 2026, diesel cost an average of €1.54 a litre across the EU. Prices rose sharply from March, passing €2 a litre later that month and reaching €2.24 at the end of September. This was above the 2022 peak of €2.03. On 19 October, diesel stood at €2.14 a litre, 38% higher than at the start of the year.
Petrol followed a similar path. Its price rose from €1.60 a litre in early January to €2.10 at the end of September, also above its 2022 peak of €2.03. It has since fallen slightly to €1.99. Filling a 50-litre diesel tank now costs about €107, up from €77 in January.
Impact on households
Mu warned that as consumers spent more on filling their tanks, they would have less to spend on other things, such as food and other everyday goods.
“I would expect the prices of food, public transport and other everyday goods to increase as diesel is widely used in heavy transport and buses,” he added.
Kardas pointed out that the impact would vary across sectors. “Transport, heating, agriculture, and energy-intensive manufacturing will feel an immediate squeeze, passing higher freight, utility, and fossil fuels costs on to end consumers, whereas service-based industries will remain largely insulated,” he said.
How long will it last?
Experts do not expect oil import costs to fall soon. Asked whether costs would remain high in the coming months, Mu said: “Unfortunately yes, as we don’t see a practical way of ending the conflict.”
He also said higher shipping and insurance costs might not yet be fully reflected in the second-quarter bill but could push up costs in the third and fourth quarters.
Kardas expected costs linked to the conflict to “persist in the coming months and may well continue into 2027”.
Eichhammer is also of the view that there's a high risk of oil prices remaining high or rising further.

US Army Pacific readying for potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:29:56 UTC
13:29:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US Army Pacific has made preparations for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year, its commander, General Ronald Clark, said Tuesday.
The threat posed by the Davidson window is “still valid,” Clark said during the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, Stars and Stripes reported. The Davidson window refers to then-US Indo-Pacific Command chief Admiral Philip Davidson’s assessment in 2021 that China would have the military capability to invade Taiwan by 2027.
However, an annual Office of the Director of National Intelligence report said the threat to Taiwan was not imminent, per Stars and Stripes. “Chinese leaders do not currently plan to execute an invasion of Taiwan in 2027, nor do they have a fixed timeline for achieving unification,” the report said.
Clark described the Davidson window as “a period of time for which we’re snapping the chalk line to say we need to be ready by this date.” “So, we’ve embarked upon a strategic approach to setting the theater that we refer to as ‘Army Ready Forward’,” he said.
Under this plan, Army Pacific has rotated troops, equipment, and supplies through islands west of the International Date Line, closer to China, Clark said.
The biggest challenge is balancing “exquisite high-end systems and affordable, mass-producible alternatives,” especially for autonomous systems, he said.

Taiwan High Speed Rail adds 40 trains for local elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:29:53 UTC
13:29:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan High Speed Rail will add 40 trains from Nov. 27 to 30 to meet demand during local elections, CNA reported Wednesday.
Voters will head to the polls on Nov. 28 to elect mayors, county magistrates, and other local officials. THSR will add 18 southbound and 22 northbound trains, bringing the total to 718 over four days.
Tickets go on sale at 12 a.m. Friday through the THSR website, mobile app, and participating convenience stores. Station ticket counters and vending machines will also sell tickets during operating hours.
THSR expects heavy southbound travel on Nov. 27 as people return home to vote. To ease crowding, it will run nine evening trains with 11 non-reserved cars each, allowing passengers to board without booking a seat.
Two to three southbound trains will depart from Nangang or Taipei each hour during the four-hour evening rush period beginning at 5 p.m. These trains will stop at every station through Taichung.
THSR advised passengers to book reserved seats early and collect their tickets before arriving at stations. Those without reservations should check station displays, as the number of non-reserved cars will vary from two to 11 per train.

Modi wrote in a post on X.Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pawan Khera responded by challenging the prime minister to commit to using ballot papers in future Lok Sabha and assembly elections."If Narendra Modi is so confident that EVMs have no bearing on election results, let him prove his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess through action, not rhetoric," Khera wrote on X.He also demanded the suspension of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the restoration of what he alleged were 13.3 crore illegally deleted voters, and action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.NCP (SP) MLA Rohit Pawar also criticised Fadnavis over the deleted post, pointing to the BJP's defeat in Nagpur, where the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) headquarters is located.
"Respected Devendra Fadnavis Saheb, In the Nagpur Graduates Constituency, where you yourself took personal interest and went door-to-door to persuade the rebels to withdraw, in that very Nagpur constituency, in the area where the RSS headquarters is located, the BJP had to face defeat—the meaning of this is clear…… It is indeed regrettable that you had to delete your tweet; but the immense ego of power evident in your deleted tweet is not good at all. Anyway, I can understand. Perhaps you forgot that the election was held via ballot, so the tweet might have been made prematurely… Congratulations to the victorious candidate Abhijit Wanjarri, thanks to the graduates who gave their blessings in the form of votes, and best wishes to all the contesting candidates as well!" Pawar wrote on X.
MVA wins three of five Maharashtra MLC seats
With Wanjari's victory, the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) won three of the five Maharashtra Legislative Council seats contested on October 23, while the BJP-led Mahayuti secured two.NCP (SP) candidates Harshada Deshmukh-Jadhav and Pratapsinh Patil won the Pune Graduates’ and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar Graduates’ constituencies, respectively. Shiv Sena candidate Kiran Sarnaik won the Amravati Teachers’ constituency, while BJP candidate Kaustubh Gawade secured the Pune Teachers’ seat.
The Nagpur result followed more than 40 hours of counting. Kohale had led Wanjari after the second round, but neither candidate secured the required quota through first-preference votes. Wanjari eventually overtook his rival during the subsequent elimination rounds as preferential votes were transferred.The outcome dealt a setback to the BJP in a constituency it had traditionally held. Gadkari represented the Nagpur Graduates’ constituency in the Maharashtra Legislative Council for 24 years, from 1990 to 2014.The results have triggered a political exchange between the BJP and opposition parties over electoral performance and the use of electronic voting machines. While Modi cited the ballot-paper polls to question the Congress's performance, the party has used the results to renew its demand for ballot papers in future elections.

29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded Wednesday to remarks made by French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen during a rally, where she warned that she would not allow the “Mexicanization” of France due to the presence of drug cartels.
“She is misinformed because the ‘Mexicanization’ that should be brought to the whole world is that of the values of Mexico's culture. Of honesty, of love, of solidarity, of fraternity, which are much needed in the entire world today,” Sheinbaum said during her morning briefing.
Le Pen, a prominent figure in France’s far-right National Rally (RN) party and a member of the French National Assembly, launched her campaign over the weekend with a strong message on security policy following the US’s approach of classifying Mexican drug cartels as terrorist organizations and pledging a hardline stance against organized crime.
“We will not allow France to slide into Mexicanization through the presence of cartels. We will eradicate these criminal organizations without hesitation, treating them as terrorists,” she said.
According to the latest security report by the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol), the presence and influence of Latin American criminal groups in the European Union have grown, particularly in drug trafficking, with the groups forming alliances with local European mafias.
Although Le Pen referred to insecurity in Mexico and organized crime as a driving force behind violence in the country, the Europol report does not mention Mexican cartels. Instead, it cites Colombian organizations such as the Clan del Golfo, Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Ecuador’s Los Lobos cartel.
However, Mexican criminal organizations, including the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and the Sinaloa Cartel, have been reported operating in France in recent months. The latter has been linked to a methamphetamine laboratory dismantled last year by the French Gendarmerie.
The term “Mexicanization” has been used by French politicians for years to refer to acts of violence in France. In 2024, French Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau used the term to warn of a growing wave of violence in the country following a shooting at a restaurant.
The use of the term sparked widespread indignation among Mexican officials, prompting a response from the Mexican Embassy in France.
“The use of this expression not only stigmatizes and stereotypes Mexico but also revictimizes Mexican families affected by violence. It also disregards the significant efforts made by the Mexican government to address violence in certain parts of its territory and undermines cooperation among members of the international community, including Mexico and France, to combat the scourge of drug trafficking and its deplorable consequences around the world,” it said.

New Zealand construction costs steady despite sharp rise in diesel prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:13:40 CST
13:13:40 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand construction costs remained relatively steady in October despite a sharp rise in diesel prices, with average construction trade rates increasing just 0.1 percent over the past month, industry data showed on Thursday.
Diesel prices rose an average of 19 percent from the previous month and were 76.2 percent higher than in February. Fuel-intensive construction activities saw more noticeable increases, with excavation costs rising 3.9 percent, while piling and demolition costs both increased 0.6 percent, according to the latest Quotable Value (QV) CostBuilder monthly construction cost update.
The update recorded more than 7,000 data changes across major New Zealand cities including Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin, Hamilton and Palmerston North.
Other price rises included processed timber products, up 6.2 percent, medium-density fiberboard, up 2.8 percent, reinforcing, up 2.7 percent, and roofing and cladding, up 1.6 percent, it showed.
However, some costs declined, including adhesives and sealants, down 4.2 percent, kitchen-related costs, down 1.2 percent, and structural timber, down 0.2 percent, statistics showed.
Rising fuel costs had not translated into broad-based construction cost inflation, as increases and decreases across different products and trades largely offset each other, QV CostBuilder quantity surveyor Martin Bisset said in a statement.
Bisset advised those budgeting for construction work to continue allowing for cost fluctuations, particularly in fuel-sensitive areas. ■

Novikov, also first deputy chairman of the Russian State Duma Committee on International Affairs and deputy chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, said the CPC strives to advance the interests of the people. Novikov stressed that strengthening self-discipline and internal oversight is not an end in itself for the CPC. Rather, the Party's fundamental task is to strengthen ties between governance and society, thereby consolidating public trust in state institutions.
