China Focus: China's sustained housing upgrades keep urban decay at bay
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:13:10 CST
13:13:10 KST

HARBIN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- For the past two months, 53-year-old Hou Fengjun has made regular trips to a construction site in downtown Harbin, watching the run-down 1930s residential building she once shared with 14 other households be reborn from its ruins.
The new four-story building, up and ready for move-in in just two months, marks the first reconstruction project funded by residents themselves in Harbin, the capital city of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province.
"The old apartment was small and shabby, and I didn't hold out much hope for an on-site rebuild," said Hou. Little did she know, the neighborhood would undergo a dramatic transformation. "The new building is of such good quality that I have decided to move back with my family."
The building sits in the city center and neighbors the renowned Baroque architectural complex, the largest and best-preserved cluster of its kind in China. Despite its prime location, living conditions there used to be harsh.
Hou once shared a cramped 25-square-meter flat with three generations of her family in the now-demolished building. Local authorities rated the structure Grade D, the highest danger classification, during the city's building safety check in 2023. After that, residents in the building were ordered to evacuate over safety risks.
The project took shape after residents reached agreement in April to finance reconstruction, backed by a policy from local authorities to give green light to the old building reconstruction mode in February. The city also rolled out fee waivers and support measures to reduce construction costs and help residents reach consensus for the rebuilding.
Hou's family invested more than 100,000 yuan (about 15,000 U.S. dollars) for their new unit, which is around eight square meters larger than their old home. The building comes fitted with an elevator, central heating, piped gas, comprehensive water and sewage systems, and individual kitchens and bathrooms for each household.
Eight projects adopting this resident-funded model have now been launched across Harbin, covering 445 households as of mid-October this year, according to Shan Haibo, an official with the housing authority in Harbin.
The pilot project addresses long-standing hurdles for urban regeneration across China. Small scattered plots often deliver slim returns for commercial developers, and matching residents' compensation expectations has frequently stalled renewal plans, said Wu Songtao, professor at the School of Architecture and Design of Harbin Institute of Technology.
As an old industrial base, Harbin is an urbanization front-runner in China, grappling with a large stock of aging housing. Local statistics show that the city has approximately 71,000 old residential buildings constructed before 2000, including 387 buildings classified as Grade C and D dangerous levels affecting 11,700 households.
The innovative pilot for old building reconstruction charts an alternative path in shantytown renovation in Chinese cities, avoiding large-scale land acquisition and heavy investment from developers.
Nationwide, China is carrying out sweeping residential upgrades as urbanization advances. Official data shows the country's urbanization rate rose from 53.1 percent in 2012 to 67 percent in 2024, with a target of 71 percent set for the next five years.
China's evolving urban landscape has drawn attention from overseas visitors who have shared their impressions online. Eric Garrison, a U.S. YouTube creator with more than 33,000 followers, traveled to China expecting to find neglected, dilapidated settlements.
When he visited an urban village in south China's Guangzhou, he was surprised to find that despite aging housing and narrow lanes, security, sanitation and infrastructure were all well maintained.
His video sparked widespread online discussion, with viewers asking questions like "Why are shantytowns rarely seen in China?" and "How does China deal with low‑income housing?"
"Chinese governments at different levels have invested heavily in renovating old residential communities to meet people's aspirations for improved housing," Liu Lanping, an official with the housing authority in north China's Shanxi Province, told Xinhua.
In coal-producing Shanxi, urban renewal has improved living standards for large groups of industrial workers. Reconstruction began on 180,000 housing units in mining shantytowns across the province from 2006 to 2013 with subsidies from the central government. Local governments and enterprises also provided matching funds.
China addresses challenges of shantytown renovation through refined, orderly governance that respects residents' wishes, Liu said. Funding for shantytown renovation comes from a mix of public and social sources, including central subsidies and local fiscal support.
Between 2019 and 2024, China renovated 280,000 old residential communities, benefiting over 120 million people, according to official statistics.
Looking ahead, China's 15th five-year plan for urban renewal has pledged to roll out safety inspections for urban residential compounds aged 20 years and above and renovate a total of 115,000 old residential compounds.
The plan handles aging residential buildings on a case-by-case basis. It requires structures formally certified as dangerous be demolished and rebuilt, while promoting renovation with age-friendly and smart facilities in other suitable complexes.
The policy push for better housing was outlined at a media briefing by the State Council Information Office in September. The Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development laid out its "quality housing" agenda, prioritizing building new houses of better quality, renovating old houses properly, and delivering quality services.
These higher standards are also written into the newly revised national Residential Building Code, which tightens housing requirements across 14 dimensions. To respond to complaints about cramped interiors, the code raises the standard floor height from 2.8 meters to 3 meters. It also requires elevators in residential blocks of four stories or more to ease access for elderly residents.
As the concept of "good housing" gains momentum, China's real estate sector is expected to shift away from quantity toward quality, raising expectations for both developers and house buyers.
"Thanks to these government policies, we not only get new homes right here where we live, but our property values rise too," said Hou. ■

Hapoel Tel Aviv rolled into Teddy Stadium this week with more than 7,000 fans behind them and rolled out with a dominant 3-0 victory over Hapoel Jerusalem.

Final represents chance to climb back

For Hapoel Tel Aviv, it represents a chance to continue its climb back toward the top of Israeli football after spending time in the Leumit League twice over the past decade. Winning a title against Maccabi would provide another significant milestone in that journey.
Barda understands the importance of the occasion and will have his team ready to compete for the trophy.

Last season, we reached the final but were disappointed with the result. This year, we’re back in another final, with another title at stake. If this club wants to win trophies in the long run, it needs to be competing in these situations consistently. Thankfully, that’s where we are right now,” he said.

We received a red card in the 35th minute, so you have to take that into account when assessing the difference between the teams. That wasn’t a fair reflection of the situation.
“We haven’t discussed the derby until now. No tickets, no talking about it, nothing. Starting Sunday, we’ll begin talking about everything. We’ll approach this game the same way we approach every match. Obviously, it’s a derby, and it’s a final with a trophy at stake, and I’m sure the players understand what’s on the line.”

“Anyone who hasn’t experienced it doesn’t really understand what a Tel Aviv derby is. In my opinion, it’s one of the most intense games in Europe. We’re looking forward to it, especially because there’s a title at stake. That makes it a completely different story, and we’ll arrive fully prepared.”
There should be no shortage of excitement when the rivals meet under the lights at Bloomfield. The derby is always charged with emotion, but the added incentive of a trophy will only intensify the occasion. By the end of the night, one side will be celebrating with silverware in hand, while the other will be left to contemplate what might have been.
Altman, of course, has every intention of being on the winning side.
“Beyond the fact that it’s a cup final and a derby, let’s be honest: it’s the Toto Cup. But winning a derby title means a lot to the players. Lifting a trophy is a dream, and I think every young player dreams of experiencing that moment,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett must put Israel first and talk unity - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:11:25 UTC
13:11:25 KST

Israelis went to the polls on Tuesday in remarkable numbers, with turnout reaching 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades. After months of bitter campaigning, voters have had their say. Now comes the considerably more difficult task of turning those votes into a functioning government.
As the counting continued on Wednesday, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Likud nor his principal challenger, Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot, had a clear path to the 61 seats required to form a government. The final results may yet alter that, but Israel is already confronting the possibility of another prolonged period of political uncertainty.
President Isaac Herzog appeared very much aware of that danger when he addressed the situation on Wednesday, urging political leaders to approach the coming coalition consultations with open minds.
“We must do everything, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said, adding that he expected everyone arriving at the President’s Residence to do so “with an open mind.”
His appeal deserves to be taken seriously by every party leader, regardless of which side of the political divide they occupy.
Why shouldn't Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and Bennett sit down and talk?
There is another possibility worth exploring before coalition negotiations descend into the familiar arguments over ministerial portfolios, political redlines, and personal rivalries.
Why should Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and former prime minister Naftali Bennett not sit down together and talk?
The three men have spent months campaigning against one another, sometimes fiercely. But elections are fought to determine who will govern, and governing requires considerably more than the ability to attack one’s opponents.
As The Jerusalem Post’s Shir Perets argued on Wednesday, the opportunity exists for the broad Zionist government that has been discussed for so long. Such an arrangement would demand compromises, particularly from politicians who have made their opposition to one another central to their campaigns.
Israel’s unique circumstances surely justify making the attempt. The country is still dealing with the consequences of the October 7 massacre, the security challenges posed by Iran and its regional proxies, the burden carried by reservists and their families, and the economic consequences of years of conflict.
For too long, governments have depended on relatively small parties whose demands have often exerted an influence far beyond their electoral strength. Coalition survival has repeatedly complicated decisions on matters of national importance, particularly the question of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) military service.
A broad government could create room for a more equal military service framework, particularly if it can be built without haredi participation, and a consistent approach to national security without every significant decision becoming a negotiation with the most uncompromising coalition partners. Such a government may also find support in Washington.
According to a report published by the Post on Wednesday, American sources said US President Donald Trump wants Israel’s next government to exclude National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. The sources indicated that Trump regards settler violence as an obstacle to his broader regional diplomatic ambitions.
Earlier reports had already suggested that figures in Trump’s circle were encouraging the formation of a broad Israeli unity government.
These reports are significant, particularly given the importance of relations with Washington and the possibility of advancing regional normalization agreements. Israel’s government must ultimately be determined by Israelis, but the diplomatic implications of its composition cannot be ignored.
There are, of course, legitimate objections to a Netanyahu-Eisenkot-Bennett arrangement.
Eisenkot campaigned on replacing Netanyahu, and many of his supporters would regard joining a government under the prime minister as a betrayal. Questions surrounding responsibility for October 7, Netanyahu’s criminal trial, and the conduct of his government cannot simply be brushed aside in the name of unity. Nor should they be.
Any agreement would need clear commitments on the rule of law, institutional independence, military service, and the government’s priorities. The question of leadership would also require serious negotiation.
All parties must be prepared to enter the same room
Yet none of these matters can be resolved unless the parties are prepared to enter the same room.
There is precedent for cooperation. Eisenkot served alongside Netanyahu in the emergency government formed after October 7, while Bennett has previously demonstrated the possibility, and the difficulty, of governing across political divisions.
Nobody is suggesting that a unity government would be easy, or even necessarily successful. But Herzog is right to warn against returning to the ballot box, particularly before every reasonable avenue for forming a government has been exhausted.
The campaign is over. The public has fulfilled its democratic responsibility. Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, and the other party leaders now have a responsibility to examine what can be achieved through negotiation.
Whatever their differences, they owe the country at least a serious conversation.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday, Oct. 28, that a proposed energy ceasefire with Russia had failed because Moscow continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, but welcomed initial progress under a separate US-brokered humanitarian truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten in The Hague, Zelensky said Ukraine had supported US President Donald Trump’s proposal for a halt to attacks on energy facilities, but Russia had not reciprocated.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The energy ceasefire doesn’t work,” Zelensky said.
“President Trump proposed it in the media. We supported this also in the media. And Russia didn’t,” he said.
According to Zelensky, Russian forces launched a massive attack on Ukrainian energy facilities the day after Trump’s proposal, prompting Ukrainian retaliation.
“So now, when they attack our energy, we respond on energy,” he said, making clear that no mutual energy ceasefire was currently in place.
His comments come as Washington seeks to advance negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow, including limited ceasefire arrangements intended to build momentum toward a broader peace agreement.
Zelensky welcomes progress under Oleshky humanitarian truce
Zelensky drew a distinction between the failed energy ceasefire and a separate US-mediated humanitarian arrangement in Russian-occupied Oleshky, in the southern Kherson region.
Dutch PM Says Europe Won’t Return to Russian Gas Amid US Peace Talks
The local ceasefire, which took effect on Oct. 27, is intended to facilitate humanitarian operations, including the evacuation of civilians from the occupied area.
The Ukrainian president welcomed the reported reduction in major attacks, saying even a brief pause in hostilities could bring much-needed relief to civilians.
“We’re happy even when we have two, three days for these people, you know, some ceasefire is great,” he said, noting that residents could once again be seen on the streets.
He thanked Washington for facilitating the arrangement, stressing that the humanitarian mission’s ultimate success would depend on the safe evacuation of civilians.
“This is really their [the US] initiative,” he said. “We will see how it ends. Hopefully, well.”
Abu Dhabi peace talks expected in early November
Zelensky also said Ukraine was preparing for another round of trilateral negotiations with the US and Russia, expected to take place in Abu Dhabi between Nov. 6 and 10.
The meeting would bring together technical-level negotiating teams to discuss practical steps toward ending the war and prepare for possible talks between national leaders.
Zelensky said Kyiv had originally expected another meeting in Brussels, but Washington had postponed it.
“We are waiting for Americans,” he said, adding that he expected greater clarity following the US midterm elections.
The proposed agenda includes ceasefire arrangements, energy infrastructure, maritime security, prisoner exchanges, the release of Ukrainian civilians detained in Russia and the return of Ukrainian children.
“We need to move this war to the end, not just to continue,” Zelensky said.
He expressed hope that one or two technical meetings could create the conditions for negotiations at a higher political level.
Asked when he might meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky said no date had been agreed and that progress depended on Moscow.
“I don’t know when we will have a meeting with Russia on the level of leaders,” he said.
He emphasized that the most sensitive issues, particularly territorial disputes and security guarantees, must be addressed directly by national leaders.
“We are ready also to discuss territories, but on the level of leaders,” he said.
“Nobody can negotiate about Ukraine without us.”
Zelensky insists Europe must have a role in peace talks
Zelensky said Ukraine would proceed with the planned trilateral negotiations even if European representatives were excluded from the initial meeting, but insisted that Europe must help shape any final settlement.
He said Washington had become more supportive of European involvement, while Moscow continued to oppose it.
“What is great now is that nobody is against. And what is good, I think, is that America is very supportive,” Zelensky said.
He noted that previous negotiating rounds had included separate consultations with European national security advisers and representatives of NATO and the EU, suggesting similar arrangements could be made during the upcoming Abu Dhabi talks.
“If we speak about security guarantees for Ukraine, for me, it can’t be without Europe,” he said.
Zelensky also questioned how Russia and the US could negotiate Europe’s future security arrangements without European participation.
“How can you negotiate security infrastructure in Europe without Europe?” he asked. “What will you negotiate with whom? With China? Interesting.”
However, Zelensky made clear that Kyiv would not allow disagreements over the negotiating format to delay the peace process. He also stressed Europe’s role in Ukraine’s eventual reconstruction.
Netherlands pledges more air-defense support
Zelensky’s visit to The Hague also focused on Ukraine’s preparations for another winter of Russian attacks.
The Netherlands announced €500 million in military assistance and €1.2 billion in non-military support over three years, including assistance for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, healthcare and humanitarian needs.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands was reaching out to partners inside and outside NATO to secure additional air-defense interceptors for Ukraine while working to increase missile production.
“Any rocket, even in smaller numbers, is useful today to protect Ukrainians,” Jetten said.

In the Middle East, the next front line is the narrative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

We live in an era where wars are fought not just on battlefields, but also on our screens, in our minds and through the narratives we are led to believe. Narratives are influencing perception while missiles destroy infrastructure. What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself? Who’s controlling the narrative?
Najla Al Midfa, researcher, TRENDS Research & Advisory
When wars end, the fighting over what they meant begins: who won, who was to blame and who can be trusted to keep the peace. These questions are settled less on the battlefield than on screens, in feeds and in group chats. For a Middle East emerging from the war that began on February 28, that contest may decide whether any new security order holds.
The region is now asking what comes after deterrence. That question brought policymakers, military leaders and researchers from the United States, Europe, Asia and the Gulf to the TRENDS 6th Annual Conference, held in Abu Dhabi and organized by TRENDS Global, in collaboration with its global offices. The answer cannot be measured only in missiles and alliances. Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.
What happens when the war for truth becomes more dangerous than the actual battle itself?
The struggle over perception can now matter as much as events on the ground. That is no longer hyperbole. In any crisis today, governments, media outlets, political movements and non-state groups compete in real time to define what is happening. Disinformation, coordinated propaganda and now content generated by artificial intelligence (AI) mean a false account can reach millions before an official one is drafted.
As former BBC correspondent Karen Allen put it at the conference, “Now in an instant, I’m able to influence millions of people,” and algorithm manipulation is what we are increasingly seeing.
This year’s war showed how real that is. Within days of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, an AI-generated video of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa on fire, with crowds fleeing, was viewed tens of millions of times, according to BBC Verify. Fabricated images of damaged U.S. facilities in the Gulf spread just as fast, some posted by Iranian state-linked outlets. UAE Minister of State Noura Al Kaabi later described the attacks on the country as coming “from the sky and behind our screens.” Her government’s answer was to treat “fake news and misinformation as a security threat.”
A more damaging false story was not a single video. It was the idea that the Gulf was a party to the war. The UAE did not want this war and said so. On March 3, Minister of State Reem Al Hashimy said the UAE did not “seek to expand the circle of confrontation,” that it had “repeatedly confirmed” its territory could not be used for any military operation against Iran, and that “returning to the negotiating table is the only rational way forward.” The attacks continued anyway. Reuters reported, citing UAE defense figures, that 186 ballistic missiles and 812 drones were fired at the country in the first days of the conflict.
Information resilience should be treated as security infrastructure, planned and funded like air defense, not managed as public relations.
Tehran sought to blur that record, framing strikes on Gulf cities as retaliation against American aggression. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told NBC News that Iran had “not attacked our neighbors,” only “American bases,” and called the hotels hit in Dubai “collateral damage.” Countering that narrative does not require propaganda of our own. It requires putting the record in front of the world quickly and repeatedly: the UAE’s public calls for restraint before the war, its refusal to let its territory be used against Iran, and the hundreds of missiles and drones fired at it, most of which it shot down. Facts published fast, through verified channels, in Arabic, English and Farsi, are harder to bury than corrections issued too late.
Even after a war ends, the threats do not disappear; they simply take different forms. Ceasefires and reconstruction depend on public trust. If populations come to believe that the peace is a betrayal, or that a neighbor cannot be trusted, no deterrence framework or security pact will survive contact with domestic politics. Spoilers understand this. Their cheapest weapon is a story.
Seen from the Gulf, the lesson of recent years is that speed and credibility beat silence. Crisis communication is not a side function of security. When official channels inform the public quickly, consistently and honestly, rumors have less room to grow. When they hesitate, someone else fills the gap.
None of this is simple. Governments everywhere are still working out where countering disinformation ends and controlling speech begins, and that debate should stay open. But the common ground is wider than it looks: a society cannot be secure if it cannot tell what is true.
The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion: relitigating who was to blame, questioning whether Gulf governments can protect their people, and setting neighbors and communities against each other. Young connected audiences are the main target. They are also the best defense.
Protecting our societies from that influence does not mean closing them. It means official channels fast and credible enough that people turn to them first. It means platforms held to clear rules on labeling AI-generated conflict content, as X began to do in March. And it means a generation of young Emiratis and Gulf citizens equipped to verify what they see and able to tell the region’s story themselves rather than leaving it to others.
The harder test comes now. After a war, influence campaigns shift from shock to slow erosion.
This is not only a Gulf problem. The campaigns aimed at audiences in the Gulf also shape how Washington and Brussels understand the region. The UAE and its partners already work closely on defense and intelligence. Detecting and exposing cross-border influence operations belongs on that shared agenda as a joint effort between governments, platforms and researchers.
Diplomacy, investment, and deterrence will rebuild the region’s security. Whether that security holds will depend on something harder to measure: what people across the region believe about each other, and about who protects them. For the UAE, winning that argument with facts is not public relations. It is part of keeping the country safe.
Najla Al Midfa is an Emirati researcher at TRENDS Research & Advisory, a company under TRENDS Group. Her research focuses on geopolitics, international relations, economic diplomacy and regional security, with a particular interest in the UAE’s foreign policy and strategic partnerships. She holds a master’s degree in Global Affairs and Diplomatic Leadership from the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy, where her thesis examined the UAE’s economic diplomacy through its Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement strategy.

Don’t turn a methane pause into a retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

As Europe’s energy ministers meet in Brussels this week, they are weighing legitimate concerns around energy security, affordability, and the pressures facing businesses and households.
The European Commission’s proposal to delay selected EU Methane Regulation requirements for fossil-fuel importers is now moving quickly through the legislative process. Ministers have an opportunity to keep any adjustment tightly focused, while preserving the policy stability that companies and investors need to plan, invest and manage risk over the long term.
Investors need a stable framework against which companies can plan, manage risk and allocate capital with confidence.
For investors, the question is not whether implementation should be practical. It should. The question is whether a response to current pressures becomes a wider change to a framework that companies have already begun to implement.
Sixty investors, representing over €9.5 trillion in assets under management, have called for the EU Methane Regulation to be maintained and implemented as adopted. That statement pre-dated the Commission’s proposed one-year delay. Its central concern, however, is more relevant now: investors need a stable framework against which companies can plan, manage risk and allocate capital with confidence.
The regulation was designed with phased implementation. It gave companies, importers and national authorities time to prepare for stronger measurement, reporting and verification of methane emissions. It has helped bring methane from the margins into boardroom discussions, where it belongs.
Why methane matters to investors
For investors, methane performance can offer a useful view of how a company is run. It is an indicator of operational discipline, process safety and the quality of management oversight. By setting requirements for measurement, reporting and verification, the regulation can also improve the availability, consistency and reliability of methane data. That gives investors a stronger basis to compare companies and assess whether they are managing risks that could affect long-term value. Maintaining the regulation’s core provisions and avoiding any further delay would protect the progress already under way.
The EU’s position as a major oil and gas importer gives the Methane Regulation particular weight. Clear import requirements can improve the quality and comparability of emissions information across global supply chains. They can help create a more level playing field for companies supplying the European market, rather than allowing weak data or weaker controls to become a commercial advantage.
The choice is not between competitiveness, affordability and effective methane management. Europe can support all three.
This matters for competitiveness as well as climate-related financial risk. Energy affordability is a legitimate concern, particularly for businesses and households facing continued market volatility. But well-designed, practical rules can reward operational excellence, support informed investment decisions and give companies a clearer basis on which to plan, while implementation can be managed in ways that preserve market flexibility and limit unnecessary costs for consumers.
The choice is not between competitiveness, affordability and effective methane management. Europe can support all three. A three-year postponement, however, would not serve institutional investors, companies or Europe’s competitiveness.
Methane is often treated as a narrow technical issue. It is not. Reducing emissions from oil and gas operations is one of the quickest and most cost-effective ways to limit near-term warming. For companies, stronger measurement and reporting can also identify avoidable losses, improve operational performance and strengthen confidence among lenders and investors.
Companies and investors have already begun to respond to the direction set by the impending regulation. Investors are looking more closely at the quality of companies’ emissions data and the systems behind it. A predictable regulatory framework supports that work. Repeated changes to the timetable would do the opposite: they would make it harder to judge preparedness, compare performance and distinguish between companies that are acting now and those that are waiting for the rules to move again.
A longer delay would not remove the work needed to implement the regulation. It would postpone it, weaken incentives for companies and suppliers to prepare, and leave investors with less visibility over how methane-related risk will be managed. It could also disadvantage businesses that have already invested in stronger measurement and reporting, while slowing the development of the market for independent verification services needed to support credible implementation. When the requirements eventually return, the adjustment may be sharper and more costly. That uncertainty carries a cost for companies, investors and the wider market.
Practical implementation, not prolonged delay
The practical challenges facing importers are real and should be addressed through consistent implementation. This includes clear guidance from national authorities, practical ways to link relevant methane data to imported fuels, and clear standards for countries outside the EU whose methane rules are recognized as comparable to EU requirements. This approach would preserve market flexibility and help limit unnecessary costs, without weakening the regulation’s purpose.
If a one-year adjustment is judged necessary, ministers should keep it tightly defined, with a clear end date and no reopening of the regulation’s core provisions. They should use the period to provide the guidance that companies, importers and national authorities need to implement the rules consistently.
The choice facing ministers is not whether Europe should address methane emissions, but whether it does so through a stable framework that rewards preparedness and investment. A limited adjustment may be manageable. A prolonged delay risks creating uncertainty, slowing preparation and leaving Europe less competitive.
Stephanie Pfeifer, CEO, Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change
The views expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of all IIGCC members.

Police find no evidence for Netanyahu’s election theft claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:55:20 UTC
12:55:20 KST

Israeli police reject Likud’s claims against Arab parties
Israeli police have found no evidence supporting claims by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party that Arab parties rigged Tuesday’s parliamentary election, according to local media.
Police received 48 complaints involving suspected fraud and voter impersonation, around 40% fewer than in the previous election. No investigative or intelligence evidence pointed to widespread fraud, i24NEWS reported on Thursday.
“There’s nothing dramatic,” Major General Boaz Blatt, the head of the police’s Investigations and Intelligence Division, said, according to Kan News.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it received around 10,000 reports of suspected electoral irregularities, but around 80% were dismissed as unrelated to election integrity, including false or incorrectly classified complaints. The reports included allegations of photography at polling stations, ballot tampering, and disruptions to voting.
Neither major political bloc secured a parliamentary majority in Israel’s first election since the outbreak of the war with Hamas in Gaza in 2023.
Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win around 52-53 seats, while the rival bloc led by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot was expected to secure 48, according to preliminary tallies. A majority of 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset is required to form a government.
The Arab Joint List alliance and the Islamist Ra’am party were projected to win a combined 19 seats, nearly doubling their previous representation.
Arab citizens make up around 21% of Israel’s population, and their representatives could play a decisive role in coalition negotiations aimed at replacing Netanyahu, who remains caretaker prime minister.
Shortly after the initial results emerged, Likud alleged that Arab parties stole the election through “serious criminal offenses of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries and the use of illegal software to mobilize voters.”
The party said it collected hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence of alleged irregularities at polling stations in Arab communities and demanded an investigation by police and the domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet.
The Arab parties rejected the allegations. Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen accused Likud of attempting to delegitimize Arab voters, dismissing its fraud claims as “the words of losers.” Ra’am also denied wrongdoing, accusing the authorities of politically motivated arrests and attempts to suppress Arab turnout.
In 2021, the Islamist Ra’am party, led by Mansour Abbas, became the first independent Arab party to formally join an Israeli governing coalition, supporting a broad alliance led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
The coalition ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years as prime minister but collapsed in 2022, paving the way for his return to power following another election that year.

Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:54:37 UTC
12:54:37 KST

Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of Virginia Health System
- Summary:
- Researchers have discovered a small group of brain cells that prevents dangerous blood pressure swings, even when average readings appear normal. The finding reveals a hidden source of cardiovascular risk and could open the door to new treatments that protect the heart and brain.
- Share:
Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.
Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.
"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."
A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems
The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.
The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.
"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."
New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated
The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.
Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.
The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

Control of Blood Pressure Variability Across Behavioral States by Brainstem Adrenergic Neurons. Circulation Research, 2026; 138 (4) DOI: 10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.125.326792

Are the midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:43:48 UTC
12:43:48 KST

Are the US midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.
Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.
Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).
Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.
At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.
But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.
Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.
The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).
Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.
Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.
Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies in Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.
Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.
"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.
Loading...
Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.
High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.
Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.
The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.
Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked
American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.
YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.
In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.
But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.
That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.
Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.
If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.
While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.
The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.
The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.
But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?

desert-inspired sensory playground brings kid’s perspective to downtown el paso

desert-inspired sensory playground brings kid’s perspective to downtown el paso
designed by miguel mendoza for the chalk the block festival, desert playgola combines recycled timber, iridescent curtains, and desert-inspired sculptures in an interactive public installation.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DESERT PLAYGOLA BRINGS CHILD-SIZED EXPLORATION TO EL PASO
What does a city look like from just 95 centimeters above the ground? In downtown El Paso, Nómada Estudio Urbano explores this question through Desert Playgola, a temporary pavilion that transforms a traditional pergola into an interactive playground. Designed by Miguel Mendoza for the Chalk the Block public art festival, held on October 3–4, 2026, the installation combines desert-inspired sculptures, iridescent curtains, and recycled materials to create an environment where children can move, touch, and discover at their own pace. Commissioned by the City of El Paso through its Museums & Cultural Affairs Department (MCAD), the project occupies a pedestrian area along W Main Drive, turning an ordinary stretch of the city into a place for unexpected encounters.
The design takes inspiration from Urban95, an initiative by the Van Leer Foundation that encourages architects and urban planners to experience cities from the approximate height of a three-year-old child. Rather than treating children as miniature adults, the approach considers how scale, accessibility, and sensory experiences influence their relationship with public space. For Nómada Estudio Urbano, this perspective becomes the starting point for an environment without predetermined routes or activities. The name Desert Playgola combines ‘play’ and ‘pergola,’ reflecting a structure that offers shelter while leaving room for curiosity, imagination, and a little improvisation.
TIMBER STRUCTURE AND SCULPTURES CREATE A PLAYFUL LANDSCAPE
The pavilion is built around a timber framework supported by concrete block bases, with hanging iridescent curtains and colorful figures made from medium-density fiberboard (MDF). Recycled wooden pallets form a series of raised platforms covered in artificial turf, introducing changes in height and texture across the installation. Freestanding sculptures resembling prickly pear cacti are assembled from interlocking MDF pieces, bringing elements of the surrounding landscape within children’s reach. Together, these components transform the familiar pergola into a small terrain of passages, surfaces, and objects that invite visitors to explore rather than simply walk through.
The Chihuahuan Desert provides the project’s visual vocabulary, with references to prickly pears, ocotillo plants, and the region’s distinctive topography. Some of the hanging elements come together to form a face, giving Desert Playgola an almost character-like presence along the street. From a distance, the installation appears as a colorful figure occupying the urban landscape; up close, its individual parts become objects to navigate and interact with. This shift between recognizable imagery and abstract forms allows the pavilion to operate simultaneously as a piece of public art, a sheltered gathering place, and an informal playground.
SENSORY PLAY REIMAGINES THE CITY FROM 95 CENTIMETERS
Movement, light, and touch play an equally important role in the experience. Wind animates the iridescent curtains, sunlight projects shifting shadows across the ground, and artificial lighting transforms the pavilion’s appearance after dark. Children can pass between hanging elements, climb onto low platforms, examine different textures, or simply find a place to pause. There is no prescribed sequence to follow, and the installation accommodates different ways of engaging with its materials and spaces. The result is a playground that offers possibilities rather than instructions, allowing its youngest visitors to decide what happens next.
Positioned beside La Nube, El Paso’s interactive museum, Desert Playgola extends the idea of playful learning into the surrounding public realm. Its temporary presence during Chalk the Block introduces a different rhythm to the pedestrian route, encouraging visitors of different ages to stop, explore, and share the same space. For Nómada Estudio Urbano, the project reflects a broader interest in making cities more responsive to children’s experiences without separating them from everyday urban life. The studio summarizes its approach with a simple premise: a city that plays is a city that cares. In this case, it begins by bringing the city a little closer to the ground.

designer: Miguel Mendoza 
location: El Paso, Texas, USA

By Bo Erickson and Nandita Bose
CHILLICOTHE, Ohio/MORROW, Georgia, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Neither man is on the ballot but Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former President Barack Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Wednesday, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.
While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering speeches criticizing Trump.
Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats’ chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close.
On Wednesday, Obama appeared in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces a challenge from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican.
While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America’s values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta.
“There is a moral component to the choices we face right now,” Obama said.
“We are not going to fix the system that’s broken, we’re not going to unrig our economy, so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth,” Obama said.
Trump’s public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout.
Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.
Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the president appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown.
Trump attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies the president said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. “The town went to hell,” he said.
Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations local officials repeatedly said were untrue.
TRUMP FACES PROTESTERS
Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined Trump’s motorcade route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners that read, “Republican against Trump,” “Grab them by the ballot” and “GOP: Guardians of pedophiles.”
During the rally, protesters interrupted Trump several times, including at least one who shouted about deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
“I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” Trump said in response.
Trump and Epstein socialized in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s private club in Palm Beach, Florida.
Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump, as well as many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated.
Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security.
In Cleveland on Saturday, Obama poked fun at Trump’s taste in interior decorating, saying, “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” a chain of casual dining restaurants.
Trump defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.
“The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years,” Trump said in Ohio.
ALASKA, MICHIGAN RACES
Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate.
The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan.
Representatives for Peltola did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did,” Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio.
In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energize supporters and boost turnout.
Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit.

Derby and Dawn Kopecki in New York; Writing by Jonathan Spicer and Daniel Trotta; Editing by Scott Malone, Alistair Bell, Donna Bryson and Stephen Coates)

Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:39:27 UTC
12:39:27 KST

Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- Vienna University of Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have defied a long-standing rule of laser physics by generating X-rays with much higher energies than conventional theory predicts. The surprising discovery reveals how two electrons working together can overcome a previously accepted limit, opening new possibilities for quantum research.
- Share:
Scientists have pushed X-ray generation beyond a long-accepted limit in laser physics, revealing a surprising quantum effect that conventional theory does not account for. By directing powerful ultraviolet lasers at helium atoms, researchers produced X-rays with substantially higher energies than the standard model predicts. The breakthrough depends on an unusual interaction between two electrons that allows them to release their energy together.
The discovery comes from a collaboration between TU Wien and the University of California San Diego and builds on research that helped establish the field of attosecond physics. Laser techniques developed at TU Wien in the 1990s contributed to advances recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.
For decades, scientists have understood that directing laser light at certain atoms can cause them to emit extremely short pulses of much higher-frequency light, including X-rays. However, the established theory predicts a maximum energy for these emissions based on the properties of the incoming laser. Beyond this boundary, known as the energy cutoff, X-ray production becomes extremely weak.
The new experiment demonstrates that this familiar limit can be exceeded when two electrons interact in a particular way. The findings were published in Nature Photonics.
How Lasers Generate Powerful X-Ray Pulses
"The mechanism behind short X-ray pulses has been well known for a long time," says Prof. Tenio Popmintchev from the Institute of Photonics at TU Wien. "The laser tears a single electron away from the atom. The electron is then accelerated in the laser's electric field until it eventually collides with the atom again. The energy it loses in the process is emitted in the form of light."
During this process, the laser's electric field drives the freed electron away from its parent atom before bringing it back. When the electron returns and releases its energy, it generates light at frequencies far higher than those of the original laser beam.
Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz used this mechanism in pioneering experiments during the 1990s. Tenio Popmintchev and his colleagues now work at the same TU Wien institute where Krausz conducted his earlier research, but their latest experiment has pushed the process beyond its previously understood boundaries.
"It can be shown that when the electron returns to its atom, it generates a whole range of different frequencies with roughly equal intensity," says Dimitar Popmintchev, postdoc in Tenio Popmintchev's team at TU Wien. "But there is an upper limit. Frequencies above this limit are much weaker; it is simply not possible to exceed a certain maximum frequency."
That prediction describes the conventional process involving a single electron. The researchers wanted to find out whether the outcome would change if two electrons participated instead.
Two Electrons Break the Expected X-Ray Energy Limit
To investigate, the team used intense ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses to interact with helium atoms. Unlike the usual process involving one electron, the experiment allowed both of helium's electrons to be removed in succession.
The first electron was released and accelerated by the laser field, followed by the second. Although the electrons were freed at different moments, their behavior remained connected through quantum correlations. This relationship means their motions cannot be treated as entirely independent.
By carefully controlling the ultraviolet laser pulses, the researchers could arrange for both electrons to return to the atom simultaneously.
"Using UV driving pulses, we can arrange for both electrons to return to the atom at exactly the same time," says Dimitar Popmintchev. "The energy of two electrons is then released all at once. And when more energy is available, a single higher-energy X-ray photon with higher frequency can also be generated."
This coordinated release of energy makes it possible to produce X-ray photons that exceed the conventional energy cutoff. Rather than relying on the energy of a single returning electron, the process draws on the combined energy of two interacting electrons.
An Unexpected X-Ray Signal Confirms the Discovery
The researchers found clear experimental evidence that the two-electron process was producing unusually energetic X-rays.
When they examined the spectrum of the emitted coherent radiation, they identified a second region of sustained emission at much higher photon energies than the standard theory predicts. This additional region, known as a plateau, was weaker than the primary emission but extended well beyond the previously established energy range.
The unexpected signal appeared only when the researchers used helium. Similar experiments involving argon and neon did not produce the same behavior in their outer electrons.
This difference provides important evidence for the proposed explanation. Helium has particularly strong correlations between its two electrons, allowing them to interact in ways that make the simultaneous release of energy possible. The outer electrons of argon and neon did not demonstrate the same effect under the experimental conditions.
A New Window Into Quantum Physics
Beyond producing higher-energy X-rays, the discovery could give scientists a powerful new way to investigate how electrons interact inside atoms and other materials.
The unusual coherent X-ray emission could serve as a highly sensitive spectroscopic "sensor" for electron-electron correlations. By studying the shape of the emitted spectrum, its maximum energy, and how it changes with the polarization of the laser light, researchers could gain information about the behavior of interacting electrons on extraordinarily short timescales.
These interactions occur over attoseconds, with one attosecond equal to one billionth of a billionth of a second. Observing processes at such speeds is essential for understanding how electrons move and influence one another in quantum systems.
Eventually, the same principle might be extended beyond individual helium atoms to molecules and solid materials in which electrons interact strongly.
The technique behind the discovery, known as high-harmonic generation, originally helped make attosecond physics possible. Now, researchers are finding that it can also reveal the complex behavior of multiple interacting quantum particles.
These insights could contribute to research on quantum computing and help scientists understand and design advanced nanomaterials with carefully controlled properties.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Vienna University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Siyang Wang, Jieyu Yan, Alba de las Heras, Sirius Song, Aleksander Prodanov, Zhihan Wu, Luis Plaja, Dimitar Popmintchev, Tenio Popmintchev. Correlated electrons extend X-ray high-harmonic generation beyond the single-electron limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (9): 1092 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01976-2

New York passes law restricting children’s use of AI chatbots
- New York passed a law on 28 October to limit minors’ use of AI chatbots that act as companions. Operators must verify ages and block chatbot traits that seem human or emotional.
- The law stops chatbots from making children think they are “human, alive, or experiences human emotions”, or that they have a “personal relationship” or “authority figure role”. Governor Kathy Hochul said it would stop chatbots acting like “friends, boyfriends and girlfriends”.
- The move is one of the toughest in the US and has split opinion. Tech:NYC called the wording “vague”, while Common Sense Media said it is “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country”.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The governor of New York state signed a new law on Oct 28 preventing minors from using AI chatbots that act as companions, in one of the broadest moves yet for restricting consumer-facing models.
The law requires chatbot operators, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, to verify the ages of users and restrict the use of certain traits by the artificial intelligence interface if the user is under 18.
If used by a minor, chatbots would not be able to produce any content that could leave its user to believe it “is human, alive, or experiences human emotions”, the law states.
It also cannot generate outputs that makes the user think it “has a personal relationship, professional relationship, or an authority figure role”, nor can it frame the content it produces as being a “personal opinion”.
“No longer will minors have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends and girlfriends,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said at a signing ceremony on Oct 28.
“No longer will chatbots be able to keep sensitive information about a minor’s emotional and physical health,” Hochul added.
Other US states including California have also passed laws restricting chatbots, but the law signed by Hochul imposes some of the broadest language in regulating the tech, prompting backlash from AI companies.
Tech:NYC, a tech industry advocacy group for the sector in New York, criticised the “vague language” of the law.
“Keeping kids safe online should not mean cutting them off from tools that help them learn and prepare for careers,” the group said in a statement.
AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to an AFP request for comment on the law.
Common Sense Media, a non-profit advocacy group that provides guidelines for parents about media suitability for children, celebrated the bill’s passage, calling it “the strongest kids’ AI safety bill in the country”.
“AI companies offer chatbots with features that are dangerous, and even deadly, for kids and teens... Now, those harmful features will be outlawed in New York,” Common Sense Media chief executive Jim Steyer said in a statement. AFP

Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

12:34:46 KST

Bluesky is blocking users from opening links to a newly leaked archive of records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, and labels the pages “malicious.”
The files include people’s email addresses and phone numbers, “shared without their authorization,” Bluesky tells WIRED, in violation of its community guidelines. The company says it chose to block the links, rather than remove individual posts, “to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary.”
The DHS records, published Wednesday by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, list employees' and contractors’ names, contact information, and membership in internal groups, tied in some cases to surveillance and undercover operations. A WIRED investigation found that the files lay out in detail how DHS is organized, from senior leadership to individual immigration agents, and in some cases appear to show who has access to certain technologies.
Users who try to open the archive through Bluesky’s website or app land on a page labeled "Blocked Link," which says the URL has been identified as “malicious” and blocked for their safety. Bluesky did not respond to questions about whether the block was imposed automatically or whether any government agency had asked the company to restrict access to the data.
The DDoSecrets homepage loads normally from Bluesky. At least one third-party app, Klearsky, opens links to the DHS archive with no warning.
Bluesky promotes a decentralized approach to content moderation that lets users pick independent services that label or filter posts. Its current community guidelines bar sharing “home addresses, personal contact info, financial or medical data, or identification documents.” (A preview of the DHS leak analyzed by WIRED apparently contained work-related contact information one expert described as details that would be printed “on a business card.”) The same guidelines explicitly protect “factual reporting” on matters of public interest that are “related to government transparency and public officials.”
Bluesky started in 2019 as a Twitter research project, later became independent, and opened to the public in February 2024. By August of this year, it counted 45 million registered accounts, and an estimated 10.4 million people used its mobile app in June. Toni Schneider, the founding CEO of Automattic, has run the company since cofounder Jay Graber stepped down in March. Because the network runs on an open protocol, outside developers can build their own Bluesky apps and decide which of the company’s moderation labels to apply.
Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access to its publications. Twitter suspended DDoSecrets’ account in 2020, prior to the Elon Musk acquisition and X rebrand, and blocked links to its website after the group published BlueLeaks, a 269-gigabyte trove of internal records from hundreds of police agencies and fusion centers. Best says tech platforms often give in to government pressure but insists they cannot prevent the information from spreading. “They can't stop the signal,” they say.
A group calling itself the Department of Peace gave the archive, dubbed “Icepick,” to DDoSecrets and journalist maia arson crimew. crimew also built a website for searching the records, and Bluesky blocks that site in its website and app as well.
At least one of Bluesky’s competitors has taken a different tack. On X, the Grok chatbot built by X’s parent company pointed curious users to the Icepick website, describing it as a “cleaned searchable web tool” and saying that the complete dataset can be downloaded via DDoSecrets’ website or by torrent. X did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Taiwan pushes renewable energy target back to 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:33:42 UTC
12:33:42 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan aims to raise renewable energy’s share of electricity generation to 20% by 2029, four years later than the original target set by the previous administration, Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) told a legislative committee Wednesday.
Kung said the government expects renewables to account for more than 14% of electricity generation in 2026, up from 13.3% in 2025. He added that renewable energy accounted for 4.8% of Taiwan’s electricity generation in 2016, when the government began its energy transition policy, per China Times.
The original 20% target was set by former President Tsai Ing-wen’s (蔡英文) administration as part of its nuclear-free homeland policy.
Taiwan People’s Party Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) questioned the gap between the target and the current pace of renewable energy development. He said the intended power-generation mix was 50% natural gas, 30% coal, and 20% renewables, arguing that a renewable share of just 14% this year points to a structural problem.
Kung expressed confidence that Taiwan could reach the 20% target by 2029, citing progress on several offshore wind farms. However, he acknowledged that concerns surrounding ground-mounted solar photovoltaic projects need to be resolved to keep installations moving forward.
Hung also warned that Taiwan relies too heavily on natural gas and called for nuclear power to be reconsidered as a source of baseload electricity to support economic growth, per China Times.
Kung responded that natural gas is widely used internationally because gas-fired power plants can start up and shut down quickly. He added that procedures to restart nuclear power in Taiwan are already underway.

New York passes law banning harmful AI chatbot interactions with children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:32:03 UTC
12:32:03 KST

The governor of New York State has signed a new law that prevents minors from using AI chatbots that act as companions, one of the broadest moves yet to restrict consumer-facing models.
The law, signed on Wednesday, requires chatbot operators, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, to verify users' ages and restrict certain traits in the AI interface if the user is under 18.
If a minor uses it, chatbots cannot produce content that could lead the user to believe it "is human, alive, or experiences human emotions," the law states.
It also cannot generate outputs that make the user think it "has a personal relationship, professional relationship, or an authority figure role," nor can it frame the content it produces as being a "personal opinion."
"No longer will minors have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends and girlfriends," New York Governor Kathy Hochul said at a signing ceremony on Wednesday.
"No longer will chatbots be able to keep sensitive information about a minor's emotional and physical health," Hochul added.
A violation could expose a chatbot developer to a lawsuit by the state attorney general's office. Penalties could include monetary damages, shutting down the chatbot and destroying data. The law takes effect January 1.
'Vague language'
Other US states, including California, have also passed laws restricting chatbots, but the law signed by Hochul imposes some of the broadest language in regulating the tech, prompting backlash from AI companies.
With Congress doing little to regulate AI, state legislatures are packed with efforts to wield state consumer protection laws to make AI use more transparent and rein in chatbots and rogue AI frontier models.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group that provides guidelines for parents about media suitability for children, celebrated the bill's passage, calling it "the strongest kids' AI safety bill in the country."
"AI companies offer chatbots with features that are dangerous, and even deadly, for kids and teens...Now, those harmful features will be outlawed in New York," Common Sense Media CEO Jim Steyer said in a statement.

El Salvador to send over 2,000 soldiers to Haiti for rescue while elections postponed
PORT-AU-PRINCE/SAN SALVADOR, Oct 28 - El Salvador will send over 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to rescue missing personnel and support anti-gang security operations, its foreign ministry said on Wednesday, while Haiti's electoral council postponed planned presidential elections to next year.
The Caribbean's most populous nation has not held elections since 2016 and its last president was assassinated in 2021. Successive transitional leaders have postponed a vote citing insecurity as armed criminal organizations expand their territories.
Since 2024, foreign troops have deployed under UN-backed security missions intended to help Haitian police secure neighborhoods and pave the way to a secure and credible vote.
In July, Haiti's electoral council scheduled the long-awaited election for December 13, but earlier this month it announced it was reviewing its schedule, without providing a specific timeframe.
The new calendar published on Wednesday by the council has scheduled a first round presidential and legislative vote for July 18, 2027, followed by a second round with local elections on October 4.
This comes just over a week after four Salvadoran aircraft technicians were reported missing after an ambush on their vehicle in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced an operation to rescue them and has since deployed hundreds of soldiers to the Caribbean country, but has not clarified their command structure, length of stay, nor what they will be doing.
El Salvador's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday Bukele had held a phone call with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime and intended to deploy more than 2,000 troops.
Fils-Aime's office confirmed the call in a separate statement, saying the two leaders "reaffirmed their engagement to reinforce bilateral coordination and operational cooperation in the framework of the (UN-backed) Gang Suppression Force, notably to support rescue operations and respond to security challenges."
The office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether this meant the new Salvadoran forces would join the UN-backed mission or operate separately. REUTERS

US: DHS data leak exposes details of more than 40,000 employees
October 29, 2026
In the third major US government data leak in the past month, details on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including officials involved in surveillance, intelligence and undercover operations, were released on Wednesday by a nonprofit leak website.
Distributed Denial of Secrets, a nonprofit data transparency group, said the data was obtained by an entity calling itself "Department of Peace" and provided to the group and "journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew."
DHS said in a statement that it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The agency said it would provide further updates when more information became available.
Transparency group says releasing data justified
The leaked DHS data reportedly includes names, phone numbers and email addresses of personnel from:
- Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
- Customs and Border Protection (CBP)
- US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
- Homeland Security Investigations (HSI)
- the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)
- other DHS agencies
The data transparency group also provided a link to an online search tool that helps the public sift through the data.
Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the leak identifies "key personnel in DHS' ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," according to a statement on their website.
Best said the tool would "replace anonymity with accountability" and aid journalists as well as facilitate congressional oversight.
According to Reuters, the news agency called three DHS employees based on the data and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details.
DHS said in September that it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities," which are known to limit cooperation with federal authorities — as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.
The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that the DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months.
Third serious data breach recently
This is the third major US government data breach in recent weeks:
- Last week, the Defense Department faced a class-action lawsuit over a breach affecting millions of current and former military personnel
- In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen data of thousands of Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) employees.
