This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows an exhibition booth at MIP Africa 2026 in Cape Town, South Africa. The China Pavilion took center stage on Wednesday at MIP Africa 2026, a major film and television industry event in Africa, featuring a diverse range of Chinese audiovisual content, promoting cultural exchange and industry cooperation between China and the continent. (Photo by Xabiso Mkhabela/Xinhua)
CAPE TOWN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The China Pavilion took center stage on Wednesday at MIP Africa 2026, a major film and television industry event in Africa, featuring a diverse range of Chinese audiovisual content, promoting cultural exchange and industry cooperation between China and the continent.
Sponsored by China's State Council Information Office and National Radio and Television Administration and organized by Jiangsu Broadcasting Corporation, the China Pavilion brought together 16 Chinese audiovisual organizations from sectors including broadcasting, film and television production, animation, and cultural media.
Exhibitors at the pavilion showcased more than 50 Chinese audiovisual titles across genres, including TV dramas, documentaries, variety shows and animation, as well as the latest audiovisual technologies.
Wang Xiao, acting consul general of China in Cape Town, told Xinhua that Chinese audiovisual productions had increasingly reached African audiences in recent years, particularly younger viewers, as cultural and people-to-people exchanges between China and Africa continued to flourish.
"Excellent audiovisual works serve as both a window and a bond, fostering mutual understanding and affinity between the peoples of China and Africa," Wang said. "They enable African friends to know more about China, while helping Chinese audiences gain a better understanding of Africa."
Carol Weaving, managing director of RX Africa, the organizer of MIP Africa, said Chinese audiovisual content brought a wealth of storytelling, production expertise and innovation to the African market, spanning drama, animation, documentaries and new digital formats.
"The opportunity lies in identifying stories that connect with African audiences, making them accessible through appropriate language, localization and distribution, and building a deeper understanding of what viewers across our continent want," Weaving said.
Martin Hiller, portfolio director of FAME Week Africa, told Xinhua that the China Pavilion brought not only content for the African market but also expertise that could benefit local industry players.
Hiller expected Chinese content to become more widely available on African streaming platforms, describing the exchange as an opportunity for both sides to share content and knowledge.
MIP Africa 2026 runs from Oct. 28 to 30 at the Cape Town International Convention Centre in South Africa, and has recorded registrations from more than 100 international media companies and over 1,500 attendees, with participation spanning African countries, including South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana. Its theme is "Africa. Untold. Unstoppable." ■

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) President Kassio Nunes Marques said Wednesday that the country's 2026 elections proceeded normally and complied with legal and constitutional requirements.
"I reaffirm the commitment of the entire electoral justice system to the sovereign will of the electorate, who went to the polls and legitimately chose their representatives," Nunes Marques said in a statement on the court's website.
Despite instability in the final stages of voting, measures adopted by the court and the expertise of its technical staff had enabled vote counting to proceed and ensured the election was conducted securely, he said. "All challenges submitted through due legal process will be examined and answered."
The statement came after Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential runoff to incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, alleged electoral fraud in an open letter.
Bolsonaro accused Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (STF) of overstepping the TSE's authority by extending voting by two hours, saying that the order to extend voting hours was communicated only after the official closing time, causing unequal treatment of voters.
He also criticized the TSE, saying it had merely defended the voting extension without providing a credible response.
The STF ordered voting to be extended until 7 p.m. (2200 GMT) on Sunday after both presidential campaigns reported difficulty voters faced in reaching polling stations. The ruling ultimately applied only to polling stations that had remained open at 5 p.m., while those already closed were not reopened.
Lula defeated Bolsonaro by more than 4 million votes in Sunday's runoff. According to Brazilian media, only about 34,300 votes were cast after the original 5 p.m. closing time, far fewer than Lula's margin of victory.
Bolsonaro and his family arrived in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday morning, U.S. media reported. Their plane reportedly landed in the U.S. city after flying from Argentina, with a stop in Ecuador.
His departure followed a ruling by Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordering him to surrender his passports to the Federal Police and barring him from leaving the country.
The ruling is part of an investigation involving Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz on suspicion of money laundering and illegal foreign exchange transactions, Brazilian media reported. ■

TIANJIN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A Thai intern gently slid a fine silver needle into an acupoint on a hemiplegic patient's leg. She lifted, thrust and twirled it -- and the motionless leg twitched.
Salocha Techawanwanitchakorn, an intern at the First Teaching Hospital of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in north China, had just felt what she came to China to learn. "At that moment," she said, "I knew I had made the right choice to study TCM."
Techawanwanitchakorn grew up around the herbal shops of Bangkok's Chinatown, where the air was thick with the scent of Chinese medicine. Her Chinese grandmother was a regular there, buying herbs, and the family relied on TCM to stay healthy.
As a child, Techawanwanitchakorn saw TCM as little more than bitter brews and needles. She didn't understand it, but a seed had already been planted.
Later, Techawanwanitchakorn came to Tianjin for high school. A class visit to the First Teaching Hospital of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine gave her a first close look at TCM.
"I was struck," she said. "TCM doesn't just ease symptoms. It treats the root cause." That visit convinced her to study TCM there, and later she entered Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
Getting to grips with TCM was not easy. In her first year, concepts like meridians and "qi," or vital energy -- invisible and intangible -- left Techawanwanitchakorn baffled. Classical texts full of traditional characters read like a book from another world. None of it deterred the Thai student, however.
The following year, Techawanwanitchakorn began studying acupuncture, practicing on herself first. "I felt soreness, numbness, distension and an electric-like tingle at acupoints on my own limbs," she said. "Only then did I know how to put a patient at ease."
"Even if a patient's symptoms improve by half, I'm happy," said Techawanwanitchakorn, who specializes in acupuncture as a graduate student.
During her clinical internship, Techawanwanitchakorn kept a notebook in her white coat pocket, filled with Chinese and Thai notes on acupoints, prescriptions and the key points her teachers stressed. She came to understand that needling is not just about finding the right acupoint, but about feeling the needle sensation under her hand. Since patients differ in build, the angle and depth of insertion must be adjusted accordingly.
The longer she studied under her Chinese teachers, the more she realized that hands-on skill was only the first step. "A good doctor sees not only the disease but also the person," her mentor told her.
At first, patients took her accent as a sign that she was from southern China. When they learned she was Thai, some greeted her with "Sawasdee kha (hello)," and said "Khob khun kha (thank you)" after she removed the needles. Others said she was the best foreign student at needling they had ever seen. "Experience is built needle by needle," Techawanwanitchakorn said.
In clinical practice, Techawanwanitchakorn has seen more and more patients recover through acupuncture, and has come to appreciate TCM's unique strength in treating the whole patient. Her resolve to study TCM has only grown firmer.
TCM, she believes, remains full of vitality after being passed down for thousands of years. In Thailand, too, many hospitals have TCM departments, and more young Thais are willing to try it.
Techawanwanitchakorn, being one of them, has brought TCM home. Last summer, back in Thailand, she administered acupuncture to her sister, who had back pain. Though afraid of needles at first, her sister later said she felt "much more relaxed." Techawanwanitchakorn also used cupping equipment brought from China to treat her mother. In her daily life, she has adopted TCM-inspired habits, drinking chrysanthemum tea and paying more attention to her routine.
The student is now interning while preparing for China's physician licensing exam. She hopes to stay in China first to gain clinical experience, then return to Thailand to promote TCM.
"China has more patients and more complex cases, so there is more to learn," she said. "I will bring what I learned in China back to Thailand and let more people see the charm of TCM." ■

From infrastructure to AI: President Tokayev’s vision for Kazakhstan in a changing world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:18:25 UTC
12:18:25 KST

From infrastructure to AI: President Tokayev’s vision for Kazakhstan in a changing world
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's October 28 state-of-the-nation address outlined a new phase in Kazakhstan's development, combining a 6.5 trillion tenge infrastructure program with plans to strengthen energy security, develop artificial intelligence and raise living standards, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The address came as governments around the world reassess supply chains, energy needs and the infrastructure required for technological growth. For Kazakhstan, these changes present an opportunity to use its geographic position, natural resources and financial reserves to build a more diversified economy. They also place greater demands on the state, which must translate investment into productive businesses and better public services.
The speech marked a shift in emphasis within Tokayev's reform agenda. Following years of political and institutional changes, including the adoption of a new Constitution approved by 87.15% of voters in March, the President concentrated on what those institutions are expected to deliver.
Infrastructure as an economic strategy
The centerpiece was the People's Construction program, under which approximately 6.5 trillion tenge will be allocated from the National Fund through 2029 to modernize social, transport and engineering infrastructure. Some 1.5 trillion tenge is intended for projects during the remainder of 2026 and the first two months of 2027. Initial plans include around 70 healthcare facilities and nearly 50 education, sports and cultural facilities, along with improvements to utilities and transport networks. Tokayev proposed designating 2027 the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction.
Kazakhstan's priorities reflect a wider international return to infrastructure investment. In 2021, the United States enacted the $1.2 trillion Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, including approximately $550 billion in new federal investment in transport, energy and communications. The programs differ considerably in scale and financing, but both recognize that productivity and technological competitiveness depend on reliable physical infrastructure.
Tokayev's initiative has a particularly strong domestic industrial component. He instructed that National Fund money should not be spent on imports, calling instead for greater use of Kazakhstan-made construction materials, metal structures and equipment, with local small and medium-sized enterprises involved in implementation. This could allow investment to generate demand beyond the construction industry, provided domestic suppliers can deliver the required quality and capacity.
The President also stressed that facilities must reflect the needs of individual regions. This is an important consideration for a program of such magnitude: economic returns will depend not only on how much is built, but on whether the new infrastructure is useful, affordable to operate and completed on schedule.
Energy security in the age of AI
One of the address's strongest economic connections was between artificial intelligence and electricity. Digital competitiveness is often discussed in terms of software and talent, yet data centers and advanced computing also require dependable energy supplies, communications networks and substantial capital investment.
Tokayev said Kazakhstan's annual generation of 123 billion kilowatt-hours was insufficient for its industrial and digital ambitions. He called for a sustainable electricity surplus by 2029, an updated energy balance through 2035 and accelerated development of new generating capacity. Construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant could begin in 2027, while preparations for the proposed Moyinkum facility are expected to advance. The President also raised the possibility of a strategic uranium reserve and stressed the importance of developing domestic nuclear expertise.
He pointed to two supercomputers already launched, a third expected by year-end and the new fiber-optic connection across the Caspian Sea. These projects bring together two sides of technological development: the computational infrastructure needed for AI and the international connectivity needed to make it useful.
The address went beyond infrastructure to consider who benefits from digitalization. Tokayev called for a simplified legal regime for digital employment and pilot projects enabling rural producers to sell through online platforms. If the measures broaden access to markets and employment, digitalization could become a source of income rather than merely a more convenient way to obtain services.
Investment confidence and effective governance
Tokayev also placed considerable emphasis on the institutions that shape investment decisions. His proposals on taxation, business inspections and commercial justice share a central objective: make the rules more predictable while allowing the government to respond to practical difficulties.
Discussing the new Tax Code, the President said it was "not dogma" and directed officials to correct problematic provisions without subjecting businesses to continual rule changes. He also proposed considering a three-year moratorium on inspections of micro and small businesses from January 2027. The proposed pause, not yet enacted, would accompany efforts to strengthen digital oversight and reduce unnecessary administrative pressure.
The announcement concerning Alatau was particularly relevant to Kazakhstan's international investment ambitions. Tokayev proposed establishing an investment court based on the English common law model to hear commercial disputes, with other cases related to the city's special legal regime assigned to a civil court. The government must submit the necessary legislative amendments to the Kurultai by the end of January 2027.
The proposal addresses a consideration that financial incentives alone cannot resolve: investors need confidence that contracts will be upheld and commercial disputes decided predictably. Kazakhstan already operates a common law-based court at the Astana International Financial Centre, giving it relevant institutional experience. Applying a comparable approach in Alatau would build on an established legal framework rather than introduce an entirely unfamiliar model. Its effectiveness will depend on judicial independence, consistent judgments and their enforcement.
More broadly, Tokayev instructed the Presidential Administration to prepare a public administration reform plan by June 2027, emphasizing digital tools and clearer responsibilities. The emphasis on implementation links the country's institutional modernization with the practical requirements of economic development.
Growth that reaches households
The economic agenda included measures with direct implications for household incomes. Tokayev instructed the government to raise the minimum wage from 85,000 to 110,000 tenge on January 1, 2027, potentially benefiting nearly 1.8 million people. He also called for salary increases of up to 40% for eligible primary healthcare workers based on continuous service, affecting more than 77,000 professionals.
The President nevertheless identified inflation as a threat to living standards and called for closer coordination between the government and the National Bank. That warning matters alongside a construction program large enough to increase demand for labor, materials and financing. Higher nominal incomes and new facilities will have a greater effect if prices remain under control.
Kazakhstan enters this investment cycle with significant financial assets. According to figures cited in the address, gold and foreign exchange reserves together with National Fund assets exceed $130 billion. Tokayev argued that public resources should help attract private capital rather than replace it, and urged commercial banks to expand long-term lending to productive businesses. The challenge is to turn this financial capacity into sustainable growth without placing excessive pressure on the budget.
Kazakhstan's place in global supply chains
The international dimension of the address extended beyond technology. Tokayev called for Kazakhstan to move from serving mainly as a transit corridor between China and Europe toward operating logistics companies, consolidation hubs and digital freight systems. Capturing more value from transport would make geographic advantages more useful to the domestic economy.
A similar approach shaped his proposals on critical minerals. The President called for modern geological exploration, a national system for managing strategic metal reserves and partnerships connecting Kazakhstan to more advanced manufacturing. In agriculture, he emphasized better irrigation, long-term finance, modern processing and opportunities for applying AI.
These priorities fit Kazakhstan's multivector economic approach: maintain relations with different markets while building capabilities at home. For a middle power, resilience depends not only on maintaining diverse international partnerships but also on developing the infrastructure, industries and expertise that make those partnerships economically valuable.
From priorities to results
The address set several near-term checkpoints. An initial list of infrastructure projects is due by the end of 2026, Alatau's legislative amendments by January 2027 and the public administration reform plan by June 2027. Larger construction and energy goals extend through 2029.
The proposals are ambitious and interconnected. Better electricity supply would support industry and AI, more dependable commercial institutions could encourage investment, and infrastructure spending could stimulate domestic production while expanding public services. The results will depend on how effectively government agencies, businesses and financial institutions coordinate their work.
Tokayev's 2026 address thus places Kazakhstan's domestic development within a changing global economy. Its distinctive feature is the attempt to bring infrastructure, technological modernization, investment confidence and household well-being into one economic agenda. The measure of that approach will be whether these policies translate into lasting gains in productivity, competitiveness and living standards.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev warned of growing global tensions, a deepening crisis of mutual trust among major powers and the declining role of international law.

KazMunayGas and Exolum join forces to develop aviation fuel infrastructure in Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

KazMunayGas and Exolum join forces to develop aviation fuel infrastructure in Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company KazMunayGas (KMG) and international aviation fuel infrastructure group Exolum have agreed to cooperate on the development and modernization of aviation fuel facilities across Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency cites the press service of KMG.
The agreement was discussed during a meeting in Astana between KMG Management Board Chairman Askhat Khassenov and Ivan Muiño, Senior Vice President for Aviation at Exolum.
The talks focused on opportunities to expand aviation fuel infrastructure as part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to strengthen its transport, logistics and transit potential.
Following the meeting, KMG, KazMunayGas-Aero and Exolum Aviation signed a tripartite agreement outlining the key terms of their strategic cooperation. The document provides for the involvement of international investment, advanced technologies and industry expertise to develop aviation fuel infrastructure at airports across Kazakhstan.
For Exolum, entering the Kazakhstani market will mark the first stage of its expansion into the Eurasian region.
Under the proposed cooperation, the sides are considering the construction of aircraft refueling complexes and specialized aviation fuel storage facilities, as well as the modernization of existing infrastructure. The new and upgraded facilities will be designed to handle Jet A-1 aviation fuel in accordance with Joint Inspection Group (JIG) requirements for quality, safety and operational standards.
KMG will contribute its knowledge of the domestic market, coordinate engagement with aviation industry stakeholders and help identify and develop promising projects.
Cooperation with one of the major international companies in the sector will help accelerate technological modernization, introduce advanced practices in fuel infrastructure management and create conditions for further growth in international air transport through Kazakhstan, said Khassenov.
He also emphasized the importance of transferring Exolum’s expertise and technologies to Kazakhstani specialists, developing local workforce skills and introducing modern approaches to the operation of fuel facilities.
The companies will conduct a comprehensive economic assessment in the coming period. Based on its findings, they will determine specific projects, investment volumes, the allocation of responsibilities and the next stages of cooperation.

Activists accuse Israeli settlers of assault in occupied West Bank
Video footage posted online showed several men, some of them armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X.
Russian activist Adele Shoko has said that Israeli settlers attacked her alongside two of her colleagues in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in the Masafer Yatta area of the occupied West Bank, according to social media posts.
Shoko said on social media platform X that she, US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, and Israeli-Russian activist Andrey X were beaten and threatened by armed settlers who stole equipment and personal items.
“Jasper and I were also beaten. Jasper was then pepper-sprayed and arrested,” Shoko wrote, adding that Nathaniel was taken away by Israeli forces.
Shoko said Andrey X suffered a concussion and lost consciousness multiple times during the incident before being detained by authorities.
“Andrey was severely beaten and lost consciousness several times in front of police. Despite this, he was denied hospital treatment. He was put in an ambulance – but instead of being taken to hospital, he was taken to a police station. He is still there, arrested and being denied medical care,” she wrote.
Video footage Shoko posted online showed several men, some of them armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X. Further video showed Israeli authorities leading away Nathaniel while he shouted that he had just been beaten up.
The assault follows an October 16 incident in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, setting trees on fire and throwing stones using slingshots.
Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the attack, was beaten, robbed, and hospitalised, while a Palestinian man was shot in the leg by Israeli soldiers who arrived on the scene and fired live ammunition and tear gas.
Levine, who was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS”, said settlers repeatedly kicked and beat her on the ground before stealing her passport, phone, and camera equipment. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray condemned the “unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job”, while several US lawmakers called for an investigation and an end to settler violence in the region.

Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm election

Trump and Obama trade barbs in closing week of US midterm election
CHILLICOTHE, Ohio/MORROW, Georgia, Oct 28 - Neither man is on the ballot but Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former President Barack Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Wednesday, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington.
While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering speeches criticizing Trump.
Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats' chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close.
On Wednesday, Obama appeared in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces a challenge from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican.
While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America's values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta.
"There is a moral component to the choices we face right now," Obama said.
"We are not going to fix the system that's broken, we're not going to unrig our economy, so long as we've got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it's OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth," Obama said.
Trump's public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout.
Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022.
Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the president appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown.
Trump attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies the president said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. "The town went to hell," he said.
Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations local officials repeatedly said were untrue.
TRUMP FACES PROTESTERS
Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined Trump's motorcade route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners that read, "Republican against Trump," "Grab them by the ballot" and “GOP: Guardians of pedophiles."
During the rally, protesters interrupted Trump several times, including at least one who shouted about deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago," Trump said in response.
Trump and Epstein socialized in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, Trump's private club in Palm Beach, Florida.
Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump, as well as many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated.
Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security.
In Cleveland on Saturday, Obama poked fun at Trump's taste in interior decorating, saying, "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," a chain of casual dining restaurants.
Trump defended his White House decor and said Obama left the property deteriorated.
"The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can't have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn't been painted in 30 years," Trump said in Ohio.
ALASKA, MICHIGAN RACES
Democrats will need to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate.
The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign's lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan.
Representatives for Peltola did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
"Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did," Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio.
In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energize supporters and boost turnout.
Rogers spent the day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit. REUTERS

‘Feels like we’ve gone backwards’: Indonesia’s choking haze provides spark for wider protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:09:29 UTC
12:09:29 KST

As almost 2m hectares has gone up in smoke in Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, enveloping the region in a thick dystopian haze, 33-year-old university researcher Nurul Amalia has grown increasingly exasperated.
“The government claims to be continuously increasing the number of personnel to extinguish it. But we have yet to see any significant progress,” she says.
“People in Kalimantan continue to report toxic air conditions, and now we hear news of firefighters losing their lives,” she adds, of four volunteers killed fighting fires this month.
On Wednesday, Amalia joined hundreds in Jakarta protesting against the government, the second demonstration in a week. Chief among their demands was that President Prabowo Subianto declare the fires a national disaster.
The demand is just one on a list of grievances amid brewing anger in the world’s third-largest democracy, where analysts say a confluence of policy blunders, economic stress and a government seen as increasingly out of touch is sending Indonesia into a period of volatility unseen for decades.
Civil society groups have criticised the Prabowo presidency for wasteful government programs, increasing militarisation and centralisation of power, deepening patronage, attacks on the press, and what they say is a weakened judiciary.
The government communications agency said in a statement on Wednesday that it welcomed the aspirations of student protesters as part of an effort to nurture democracy, and that concerns raised about the environment, economy and legal reform were being addressed.
Some 70,000 firefighting personnel, it added, had been sent to fire-hit regions, and it was investigating corporations and individuals allegedly involved in starting the fires.
Prabowo marked two years in power this month, but some who voted for him say the country is, at best, stagnating.
“Not only has there been no progress,” says Ika Anastasia, a PR professional and Jakartan mother of three, “it actually feels like we’ve gone backwards.
“In my 32 years, I think this government is probably the worst,” says Aryana, a private-sector employee. “The problems keep coming one after another, and before one is solved, another appears.”
President’s approval rating sinks
Prabowo, a former military general and the ex-son-in-law of former dictator Suharto, ran in 2024 on a platform of continuity, cuddly vibes and a multibillion-dollar free meals program intended to target malnutrition.
Yet the flagship policy has been riddled with controversy.
In June this year the head of the national nutrition agency responsible for rolling out the program was arrested on allegations of corruption. Since it began, thousands of schoolchildren have been inadvertently poisoned after eating tainted meals. Among their complaints have been maggots and glass in their rice.
“This current government is strong at agenda setting in public policy, but it is very weak at delivery,” says Yanuar Nugroho, a former presidential staffer for Prabowo’s predecessor and a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS Yusof Ishak Institute.
“Never have I seen the situation like this,” he adds. “I think this is the worst and the most messy.”
In a statement on Wednesday, the government said it would strengthen supervision and involve local government in implementing the free meals program, with many children, pregnant women and lactating mothers benefiting from it.
But a poll this month by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed that about 62% of Indonesians now oppose it.
The same poll gave Prabowo an approval rating of 44.5%, the lowest of any Indonesian president since polling started 20 years ago.
“It’s just a horrific result. It shows that Prabowo has lost the country,” says Kevin O’Rourke, a longtime Indonesia analyst.
“I think that it’s the programs that he’s put out are failing, and those are things that people see in their communities,” he says, referring to the free meals and a costly village cooperatives program.
Economically, Indonesia is looking a bit wobbly too.
This year the Indonesian rupiah sank to record lows against the US dollar, while the country is up to its third finance minister in two years. In recent weeks footage has shown people forming snaking lines for fuel in Bali, Sulawesi and Kalimantan.
And, in what could be a major setback for south-east Asia’s biggest economy, this month global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “standalone market” status over unclear share ownership and suspected coordinated trading.
The government pointed out the economy had grown 5.29% in the second quarter of this year and poverty had fallen by 8%, while it had accelerated market reforms to address the issues raised by the MSCI.
Some analysts say the MSCI, which is not a regulator, may have gone too far.
The president was pugilistic in his response.
“Our country continues to face all sorts of disturbances, including the MSCI. They are trying to intimidate us,” he told his cabinet. “I simply want to tell MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will never back down.”
Amid the turbulence, analysts say Prabowo has developed a reputation for being stubborn, and reluctant to accept advice. The government disputed this claim, saying Prabowo holds continuous dialogue with various stakeholders.
“I can sense on the one hand, he is detached from the reality,” observes Yanuar Nugroho. “On the other hand, he has very, very strong ideas of him as like a saviour.”
So far demonstrations have been small, but the complaints are adding up.
“There is a lot of uncertainty at the moment and we’ve seen there is a lot of potential for demonstration,” says Kennedy Muslim, an analyst from Indonesian pollster Indikator. “What it needs is a trigger, but that couldn’t be predicted.”
Indonesia is now in a situation unprecedented since its reform era began after Suharto stepped down in 1998, says O’Rourke, noting that in previous administrations there were flaws but more democratic openness, independent institutions and checks and balances.
“In the past, actors always had to respect democracy and the rules of the elections and the rights of opponents in parliament. None of that exists now,” he says.
“Prabowo has a free hand. And so it’s very ugly and very unpredictable, volatile.”

Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:06:41 UTC
12:06:41 KST

Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- SETI Institute
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered seven surprising stages that space rocks go through as they hurtle toward Earth, revealing that melting and violent fragmentation, rather than simple evaporation, determine their fate. The discovery could help explain why meteorites scatter across the ground and how dangerous asteroids explode in Earth's atmosphere.
- Share:
Scientists have gained a clearer understanding of what happens when rocks from space plunge into Earth's atmosphere and survive the journey to the ground. After examining video recordings and photographs of 75 meteorite falls, researchers identified seven stages that describe how these objects transform into meteorites. Their analysis reveals that melting and breaking apart play a much greater role than previously believed in determining how much material a rock loses, how quickly it slows down, and where its fragments eventually land. The findings were published in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.
"We used to think that solid rocks would evaporate from the enormous heat and brilliant light generated in the air collision," said meteor astronomer and lead author Dr. Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames Research Center. "We found instead that first melting and then fragmentation controls how a rock loses mass."
The researchers determined that incoming space rocks pass through seven distinct phases as they travel through the atmosphere. Different physical processes dominate each phase, influencing the rock's appearance, behavior, and eventual fate.
How Space Rocks Become Bright Meteor Fireballs
The journey begins in Phase 1, high above Earth, where the atmosphere becomes dense enough for the incoming rock to generate a shock wave ahead of it. As the rock collides with air molecules, both its surface and the surrounding gas heat up and begin to glow. This produces the streak of light commonly known as a meteor or "shooting star."
During Phase 2, the meteor travels into increasingly dense air, causing its brightness to intensify. Some meteors also display repeating changes in brightness, which can reveal how quickly they are spinning. Among the fastest rotating objects examined, a complete rotation took between 0.5 and 5 seconds.
One of the documented meteorite falls investigated in this study. Fireball produced by asteroid 2023 CX1 over Normandy, France, on February 13, 2023. Meteorites known as Saint-Pierre-le-Viger reached the ground that day and were subsequently recovered. Credit: Image courtesy of G. de Reijke.
By Phase 3, the meteor has become much brighter, developing into a fireball. At this point, melting becomes the primary process responsible for removing material from the rock. The intense airflow strips molten material from its surface, producing droplets that continue to evaporate after separating from the main body.
"In the laboratory, we cannot generate the amount of radiation that occurs in a natural atmospheric entry at those speeds," said Eric Stern, formerly at NASA Ames and now chief scientist at Hyperspace Technologies, Inc. "Rock could aggressively fragment and erode instead, but then we would not expect the observed systematics in how fireballs brighten."
The fireball enters Phase 4 at an altitude of approximately 60 kilometers (around 40 miles), when melting reaches a relatively stable balance. During this stage, the fireball's brightness either remains nearly constant or increases at a steady rate. According to the researchers, melting alone can ultimately remove as much as 40 percent of the original rock's mass.
Why Meteors Shatter as They Approach Earth
As the fireball descends into denser layers of the atmosphere, increasing air pressure begins to fracture the rock. This marks the beginning of Phase 5, when pieces separate from the main body and can produce repeated bursts of light.
One particularly surprising finding was how early this breakup begins. The researchers found that rocks can start fragmenting when the air pressure acting on their leading surfaces reaches only about one-fifth of the strength measured in meteorites recovered on Earth. They suggest that heating during atmospheric entry, along with cracks left by previous collisions in space, may weaken the rocks enough to explain this unexpected behavior.
It is during this stage that the remaining rock begins shrinking rapidly and experiences substantial deceleration. The more extensively it fragments, the faster it loses speed.
"We were able to tie that slow-down from fragmentation to the previous mathematical descriptions based on ablation," said co-author Stu Pilorz of the SETI Institute.
The researchers also discovered that the shape of the surviving rock can influence where smaller fragments eventually land. If its rear section remains intact, the main body creates an area of reduced pressure in its wake, drawing smaller pieces along behind it.
"Our modeling shows that as long as the back of the space rock remains intact, that rock pulls a vacuum in its wake into which fragments tend to flow," says co-author Darrel Robertson of NASA Ames Research Center. "Those small meteorites fall in a narrow strip on the ground."
The Final Explosion and Journey to the Ground
Phase 6 begins when the rear portion of the main rock finally breaks apart. This last major disruption produces a bright flare and sends fragments scattering at greater relative speeds. Because the meteor has already slowed considerably, these final flashes generally appear red, unlike the bright green colors often observed earlier in its descent.
"That final disruption sends fragments flying at higher relative speeds," said Jenniskens. "In past falls, we noticed that meteorites larger than about 20g tended to be scattered wider and many came from close to the surface of the original space rock, which must have been its backside."
The pieces that ultimately survive to reach Earth's surface began as relatively large fragments. Before landing, however, they experienced additional melting and fragmentation while continuing to lose speed.
During Phase 7, these processes continue until the remaining pieces have slowed enough that they no longer produce visible light. Once melting stops, a thin outer coating known as a fusion crust remains on their surfaces. The darkened fragments then complete their descent, with atmospheric winds potentially pushing them away from their original trajectories before they land as meteorites.
What Meteorite Falls Reveal About Dangerous Asteroids
The researchers examined 75 documented meteorite falls involving several different types of space rock. By comparing their behavior, they were able to determine the altitudes at which different materials entered each of the seven phases.
These observations offer more than an explanation of how small meteorites reach the ground. They also provide valuable clues about the behavior of much larger asteroids, including objects ranging from the size of cars to entire city blocks that can produce powerful explosions in the atmosphere.
By measuring how different solid rocks slow down and fragment during atmospheric entry, scientists can better understand the processes that govern these potentially dangerous asteroid airbursts.
"Asteroids up to tens of meters in size are also solid rocks because they tend to spin faster than do the larger rubble pile asteroids," said Jenniskens. "The 20-m diameter asteroid that caused the airburst over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 went through the same phases."
Story Source:
Materials provided by SETI Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Peter Jenniskens, Stuart Pilorz, Darrel Robertson, Eric C. Stern. Bolide light curve systematics from 75 recovered meteorites. Meteoritics, 2026; 61 (9): 2351 DOI: 10.1111/maps.70203

30-year sentence in Minnesota fraud that drew Trump backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

12:00:57 KST

US man gets 30-year sentence for Minnesota fraud that drew Trump backlash
Government says Salim Said ‘hit the jackpot’ in a scheme claiming to feed needy children during the COVID-19 pandemic.
A 37-year-old man who played a key role in defrauding a United States food programme in the state of Minnesota during the COVID-19 pandemic has been sentenced to 30 years in prison in a case that has drawn intense national scrutiny and political pressure from President Donald Trump.
“You took more than taxpayers’ dollars to enrich yourself. You took the reputation of our state down with you,” US District Judge Nancy Brasel said, addressing Salim Said during the sentencing on Wednesday.
The widespread scheme in Minnesota, which resulted in dozens of convictions, has repeatedly drawn attacks from Trump, who ridiculed the Democratic governor for failing to stop the scheme and cited it as grounds for an immigration crackdown in the state’s largest cities.
Said, who operated Safari Restaurant in Minneapolis, was accused of vastly overstating the number of meals when seeking payment for providing food to needy children. The government said he was responsible for $44m in fraud, some of which was committed by others he recruited.
He was claiming a “ridiculous daily distribution of 6,000 meals” while FBI cameras showed 40 people a day collecting food, prosecutors said in a court filing.
“The defendant and his sites did not serve thousands of children; he served a calculated, lucrative lie,” prosecutors said.
Said, who was born in Somalia, denied the allegations while testifying at his 2025 trial, saying many meals were delivered off site. But he changed course and expressed remorse at his sentencing.
Defence lawyer Barry Zone, who had asked for a 12-year prison sentence, disputed the government’s claim that Said was the “architect”.
COVID-19 brought changes to a federal programme that typically fed children through schools. Restaurants could participate, and food distribution was extended to places outside schools.
“For 21 consecutive months, Said made thousands of fraudulent reimbursement claims,” prosecutors said. “Each submission represented meals purportedly provided to underprivileged children, yet the listed children themselves were entirely fictitious.”
The government said Said hit the jackpot, using the stolen funds to buy a $1.2m home, commercial real estate and an $87,000 pick-up truck.
Said was convicted in 2025 alongside Aimee Bock, leader of the Minnesota nonprofit Feeding Our Future, who is serving a 42-year prison sentence for devising the scheme and was ordered to repay $242m.
State auditors found that Minnesota’s education department received numerous complaints about Feeding Our Future but often told the group to police itself. Following relentless criticism from Trump over theft in federally funded programmes, Governor Tim Walz announced in January that he would not run for re-election.

Regulatory tightening in Hong Kong sees delistings outnumber resumptions: report
Grant Thornton says 35 companies were delisted from city’s stock exchange in 12 months to August this year
The tightening of Hong Kong’s securities regulations – in the wake of property developer Evergrande’s liquidation and unrelated IPO frauds – has resulted in more delistings than resumptions for the first time in three years, according to a report by accountants Grant Thornton.
Hong Kong saw 35 delistings in the 12 months to August this year but only 21 resumptions, the report said.
“Regulators have comprehensively tightened resumption requirements,” said Barry Tong, national leader of forensic investigation services at Grant Thornton China, pointing to heightened scrutiny over asset overstatement and misappropriation, bank statement forgery and the illicit outflow of initial public offering proceeds.

James Kunda
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema swore in 24 ministers Wednesday to form a unified Cabinet following his re-election to a second term in the country’s August general elections.
Hichilema also swore in all 10 provincial ministers at a ceremony held at State House in Lusaka.
Among the appointees were Brenda Tambatamba, the mineral-rich nation’s first female mines and minerals development minister, and Elvis Nkandu, the new information and media minister and chief government spokesman.
In Hichilema’s first term, Tambatamba was labor and social security minister, while Nkandu was youth, sport and arts minister.
Frank Moyo was appointed as minster of agriculture, who in the corresponding period was second deputy speaker in parliament.
The 24 joined an initial four who Hichilema appointed to the portfolios of health, finance and national planning, green economy and environment, and foreign affairs and international cooperation two weeks after his inauguration on Sept. 1.
Among the 24 were also ministers who took up portfolios at the newly created ministries of Trade and Exports, Petroleum, Electricity, Industry, Culture and Arts, and Skills and Higher Education under a realigned government system.
Having successfully navigated the southern African nation out of a crippling debt crisis and drought-induced energy shortages among other challenges, Hichilema pinned his second term on the Grow Zambia Agenda, to which he outlined eight sector production targets by the year 2031.
These included the country producing 3 million tons of copper, 10 million tons of grain, 10 gigawatts of electricity and attracting 5 million tourist arrivals, to which he challenged his appointees to showcase deliverables.
“As a government, we have a duty and a responsibility to deliver equitable development to all our people. That is why we have carefully restructured and aligned the establishment of the ministries to ensure that the machinery of government delivers for the people of Zambia,” Hichilema said in a post on Facebook after the ceremony.
Nkandu told reporters following the ceremony that his ministry would intensify public awareness on Hichilema’s agenda to grow Zambia, remarks he echoed when media representatives welcomed him later at his office.

EU and Canada eye now-or-never window to Trump-proof their ties

EU and Canada eye now-or-never window to Trump-proof their ties
Brussels and Ottawa aim for ambitious upgrade in their relationship while the U.S. president is occupied by the midterms — and before Europe’s political landscape shifts.
The EU and Canada are betting they can deepen their partnership while Donald Trump looks inward at the U.S. midterms — and before European elections upend the political calculus.
Their strategy is to push for the broadest possible upgrade and hope Trump is too busy campaigning to respond, four EU officials and two Canadian diplomats familiar with preparations for this week’s summit in Montreal said.
Trump, whose Republican Party is fighting to retain control of Congress in next week’s midterms, has called the EU’s offer of associate membership for Canada “laughable” and threatened “serious tariffs” if the two sides get too close.
Advertisement
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney for two days of talks on trade, security, energy, education and the Arctic on Thursday.
The summit “is a very strong statement,” said Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada and EU Trade and Investment Association. “I don’t think there’s any feeling that this is going to be some discreet get-together.”
Canada is also looking to move before Europe’s politics shift. Ottawa wants changes to the partnership that will outlast Trump and Marine Le Pen, whose National Rally is polling ahead in France and has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact, CETA, said a Canadian diplomat. All the officials and diplomats in this article were granted anonymity to speak frankly about the summit preparations.
Avoiding Trump’s ire
Brussels and Ottawa are pushing to strengthen their relationship, including by cooperating more closely on trade and defense, international engagement and institutional links, according to a draft joint statement obtained by POLITICO.
In her September State of the Union speech, von der Leyen emphasized that the EU-Canada alliance is “not against anyone else.” Yet officials acknowledge that a stronger alliance risks triggering retaliation from Trump.
Von der Leyen, Costa and Carney “are fully aware that the eyes of the world are upon them,” said Camilleri.
Advertisement
The Europeans and Canadians know “the U.S. is watching,” a senior EU official said, adding that the bloc and Canada were nevertheless proceeding with business as usual and pushing for the most expansive possible relationship with Ottawa.
Another possibility is that the summit yields only “nice pictures” and little substance, a third senior official said, making it less likely to “trigger” the president.
European capitals, EU institutions and Canada’s provinces are all waiting to see what von der Leyen and Carney agree on in their meeting, the Canadian diplomat said, adding it was impossible to pre-judge how Trump would react.
Shadow of Le Pen
For Ottawa, pressure comes from another direction: Europe’s electoral calendar and the rise of the far right.
With Spain, France, Poland and Italy all set to go to the polls in the next year, Canadian officials want to secure concrete gains while EU governments remain receptive to closer cooperation and keep the topic front of mind, before elections across the bloc risk shifting priorities and upsetting the political balance.
When Carney came to Strasbourg to lay out his vision for a closer alliance in September, he was heckled from the gallery by the far-right Alternative for Germany MEP Siegbert Droese, who led chants of “USA!”
Advertisement
But it’s France’s presidential election in April — and the prospect of Le Pen in office — that is causing the most concern, according to a second Canadian diplomat.
“It’s very fortunate we’re doing this summit now and not in six months,” the diplomat said, referring to the French election date.
Canada is pushing for big, bold “structural changes” in its relationship with the EU now that will outlast Trump and Le Pen, the diplomat added. Carney has grasped the moment’s rarity and urgency and will not leave the summit without securing major wins, the first Canadian diplomat said.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Canada’s PM Mark Carney at a G7 summit in France on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Evelyn Hockstein via Getty Images
Another question is whether Brussels and Ottawa can upgrade their partnership without eventually drawing the U.S. president’s ire. The midterms might buy them some time, but the vote will not keep Trump busy forever.
Trump might be even more dangerous and more likely to take out his anger on the EU and Canada after the election, given that he will retain many of his tariff and foreign policy powers even if the Republicans lose Congress, the second Canadian diplomat warned.
“At the end of the day, his reaction could be anything,” Camilleri said. “We can only control what we can control.”

Haiti postpones first presidential election in a decade to July 2027
Italy

2026-10-29
03:51:49 CET
11:51:49 KST

By Harold Isaac and Gerardo Arbaiza
PORT-AU-PRINCE/SAN SALVADOR, Oct 28 (Reuters) - El Salvador will send over 2,000 soldiers to Haiti to rescue missing personnel and support anti-gang security operations, its foreign ministry said on Wednesday, while Haiti’s electoral council postponed planned presidential elections to next year.
The Caribbean’s most populous nation has not held elections since 2016 and its last president was assassinated in 2021. Successive transitional leaders have postponed a vote citing insecurity as armed criminal organizations expand their territories.
Since 2024, foreign troops have deployed under UN-backed security missions intended to help Haitian police secure neighborhoods and pave the way to a secure and credible vote.
In July, Haiti’s electoral council scheduled the long-awaited election for December 13, but earlier this month it announced it was reviewing its schedule, without providing a specific timeframe.
The new calendar published on Wednesday by the council has scheduled a first round presidential and legislative vote for July 18, 2027, followed by a second round with local elections on October 4.
This comes just over a week after four Salvadoran aircraft technicians were reported missing after an ambush on their vehicle in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele announced an operation to rescue them and has since deployed hundreds of soldiers to the Caribbean country, but has not clarified their command structure, length of stay, nor what they will be doing.
El Salvador’s Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday Bukele had held a phone call with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime and intended to deploy more than 2,000 troops.
Fils-Aime’s office confirmed the call in a separate statement, saying the two leaders “reaffirmed their engagement to reinforce bilateral coordination and operational cooperation in the framework of the (UN-backed) Gang Suppression Force, notably to support rescue operations and respond to security challenges.”
The office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether this meant the new Salvadoran forces would join the UN-backed mission or operate separately.
(Reporting by Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador and Sarah Morland in Mexico City; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Christian Schmollinger)

Taiwan flags ‘obvious’ threat from 50 Chinese vessels in wide sweep of waters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:51:47 CET
11:51:47 KST

By Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee
TAIPEI, Oct 29 (Reuters) - China has more than 50 navy and other official vessels operating in a wide swath of sea stretching from southern Japan down to Taiwan and off the Philippines, a senior Taiwan official said, calling the threat level “obvious”.
Taiwan, which China views as its own territory, is stepping up efforts to issue details and maps depicting locations where Chinese warships and Coast Guard vessels operate.
“We’re staying vigilant about their activities,” said Joseph Wu, the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council. “The simultaneous threat to Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines is obvious.”
Wednesday’s remarks accompanied a map he posted on X showing the locations of 53 ships, 34 of them navy warships, including the aircraft carrier Liaoning.
The carrier and its accompanying battle group were positioned to the east of the Philippines, with other formations off Taiwan’s east and southeast, along with three off the southern coast of Japan, according to the map.
Wu published a similar map on X in May.
The defence ministries of China, the Philippines and Japan did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
CHINESE CARRIER
On Wednesday, Japan’s Defence Ministry said it had tracked three Chinese warships and a Coast Guard ship a day earlier as they passed through the narrow Osumi Strait off Kyushu island and into the Pacific.
This month, China’s Defence Ministry said the Liaoning was engaged in a routine training exercise not directed at any specific country.
China’s ties with both Japan and the Philippines have tanked in recent months. It has been upset by Japanese support for Taiwan, while embroiled in an increasingly bitter standoff with Manila in the South China Sea.
“We are not happy to see any attempt to project deterrence that could undermine peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region,” Taiwan Defence Minister Wellington Koo told reporters at parliament in Taipei on Thursday.
A senior Taiwan security official briefed on the matter said one thing to watch would be whether the Liaoning carrier group continues north towards Japan after drills in the Philippine Sea.
“If it keeps moving north, that would suggest a stronger intent to put pressure on Japan’s defence posture,” the official said.
USE OF FORCE
China has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, though it says it would prefer “peaceful reunification”.
US Army forces in the Pacific have prepared the Indo-Pacific theatre under the assumption that China could move on Taiwan as early as next year, the US military newspaper the Stars and Stripes quoted their commander, Ronald Clark, as saying.
He made the comments at a forum in Hawaii on Tuesday, it added.
Taiwan was making efforts to build its own deterrence capabilities, Koo said when asked about Clark’s remarks.
“China has never abandoned the use of force to annex Taiwan,” he added.
China recognises no separate sovereignty for Taiwan, whose government says only the island’s people can decide their future and that Beijing has no right to claim it.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee; Additional reporting by Karen Lema in Manila and Tim Kelly in Tokyo; Editing by Clarence Fernandez and Lincoln Feast.)

Strikes on Darfur market in Sudan kill more than 100, rights group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:48:38 UTC
11:48:38 KST

Strikes on Darfur market in Sudan killed more than 100, rights group says
Women and children killed as witnesses say attack struck civilian shopkeepers, RSF forces.
Military drone strikes in southwestern Sudan’s Darfur that killed more than 100 people – mostly women and children – earlier this week targeted a busy city market frequented by paramilitary fighters, witnesses said.
Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence, put the toll from Monday’s attacks at more than 100 dead and 113 wounded.
While Emergency Lawyers reported that most of the victims were women and children, witnesses said on Wednesday that multiple civilian vendors who sold goods to paramilitary fighters were among those killed in the attack in Nyala, the South Darfur city that serves as the de facto capital of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The war between the RSF and the army, now in its fourth year, has created severe poverty, food shortages and the world’s worst displacement crisis.
A cigarette vendor told the Associated Press news agency on Wednesday that hundreds of RSF fighters gathered at the market on the evening of the attack. He said that he moved his stall between gatherings of the paramilitary fighters to sell cigarettes and that a drone struck around 8pm (18:00 GMT), killing dozens of fighters and women selling food.
Another witness told the AP that the explosion was massive and killed many fighters. He estimated that around 14 civilians, including women and children, were also killed, most of them women selling tea and food.
Both spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation.
‘Constant fear of further bombardment’
Mubarak Bekheit, an aid worker in Darfur, said on Wednesday that many people remained missing and some bodies had yet to be recovered from homes in the area after the strike hit a civilian neighbourhood.
“I personally know that war has no morality, but the reality we witness every day is that civilians are the ones paying the highest price. They lose their lives, their loved ones, and their homes, while living under the constant fear of further bombardment,” he said.
Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces fighting with the army, wrote on Facebook that more than “150 militia recruits” were killed at the Dumaya camp, west of Nyala, in what he described as a “precise and targeted air strike”.
Casualty figures from Monday’s attack are unconfirmed and could not be independently verified amid limited information from the city. Sudan Doctors Network, another group that tracks violence, issued a statement on Wednesday preliminarily reporting 21 dead and more than 40 wounded, saying shelling caused most of the deaths.
“The release of this statement was delayed … given the challenges of accessing field documentation sources within Nyala amid ongoing active military operations and security constraints that hinder efforts to monitor and verify the conditions of victims and the injured,” the group said.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said that a second strike hit a civilian neighbourhood after the market attack. MSF said a hospital it supports in Nyala received 36 bodies in the hours after the strike, 21 of them wearing civilian clothing, and that its teams saw more than 150 wounded in the emergency room.
MSF called the strikes “appalling”.
“Markets, homes, and key civilian infrastructure are not targets,” the group said in a statement. “All parties to the conflict must protect civilians.”
Drone strikes have become the leading cause of civilian deaths in Sudan, the United Nations reported, in a war that has pushed parts of the country into famine. In RSF-controlled Nyala, the share of children seeking treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from 5 to 11 percent, according to UN estimates released earlier this month.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Pakistan has reversed its decision to deny Taiwanese airlines access to its airspace, restoring overflight rights for China Airlines and EVA Air, Bloomberg reported Wednesday evening.
According to documents reviewed by Bloomberg, Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority approved the two airlines to use Pakistani airspace from Oct. 28 through March 27, 2027.
The reversal came just hours after Pakistan Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, who also oversees aviation, told Bloomberg that the country’s aviation sector follows the “one China policy,” citing it as the reason for denying Taiwanese carriers permission to fly over Pakistan.
An earlier Bloomberg report described Pakistan as the first country to take such a measure against Taiwanese airlines.
Data from flight-tracking service Flightradar24 showed that China Airlines and EVA Air had not flown over Pakistani airspace since Sunday morning. At least 10 flights operated by the two carriers between Asia and Europe had instead flown over Russia during that period, per CNA.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly condemned Pakistan’s earlier decision and remarks, accusing Islamabad of following Beijing’s narrative, disregarding reality, denigrating Taiwan’s sovereignty, and politicizing and weaponizing airspace.
The ministry said it would remain in close contact with the Ministry of Transportation and Communications. It also said it respects Taiwanese airlines’ decisions to select the most efficient routes based on flight safety, travel time, and cost, per UDN.
China Airlines and EVA Air declined to comment on Pakistan’s earlier restriction. Taiwan’s Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) said it had never prohibited airlines from flying over Russian airspace.
Transportation Minister Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) said Wednesday that airlines submit their own applications to use Russian airspace. The CAA manages flight origins and destinations, while respecting airlines’ applications to use individual countries’ airspace.
Chen said the fact that some airlines had begun flying over Russia indicated that their applications had been approved, adding that the CAA respects the carriers’ routing arrangements.

Michelin-starred Amaze blends heritage and modern technique
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:44:30 UTC
11:44:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant Amaze, winner of Taiwan’s inaugural Michelin Opening of the Year Award, has launched its autumn seasonal menu, “The Full Circle.”
Since opening in 2024, Amaze has earned acclaim for modern Chinese cuisine and refined hospitality. Executive Chef Yang Guang-zong (楊光宗), Chef Huang Jun-ren (黃俊仁), and Sous Chef Chou Chin-hua (周金樺) blend Jiangnan and Zhejiang culinary techniques with Western approaches to reinterpret classic regional dishes.
The menu’s title references the Chinese concept of roundness, symbolizing completeness, reunion, and harmony. Every dish, from appetizers to dessert, subtly incorporates circular visual motifs.
The meal opens with “shrimp and tea,” a variation on classic Longjing shrimp that layers tea aromas using tea powder and fried tea leaves.
Another starter, “smoked egg, scallop, and pepper,” features Sichongxi red-yolk duck eggs smoked with Ruby Black Tea, served over raw Hokkaido scallops with seared tiger-skin pepper sauce and lemon aiyu jelly.
Yang designed several dishes around personal memories and regional traditions. “Caviar and bean puree” pairs Italian caviar with snow vegetable puree, replacing fava beans with edamame and lotus seeds.
“Prawn and fruit” draws inspiration from Taiwanese pineapple shrimp balls, adding coconut for Southeast Asian flavor.
For the main course, “roast duck and seasonal vegetables” features Changhua Rose Duck aged for 15 to 20 days and roasted in the Peking duck style. It is served with basil-spinach wrappers alongside fig, mustard, and pan-seared foie gras.
The centerpiece main course, “wealthy chicken,” adapts traditional Jiangnan beggar’s chicken. Inspired by the Taiwanese practice of using Jiadong leaves in restorative home cooking, the kitchen wraps the chicken with abalone and dried scallops before encasing it in a salt crust, which guests crack open at the table.
To close the meal, Yang offers a radish-based dish inspired by memories of watching his mother-in-law make Hakka rice cakes.
The nostalgic taste once moved a regular guest to tears, stirring up childhood memories, Yang said.
“When a dish carries not just flavor, but culture, memory, and blessings, it becomes a bridge connecting human emotions,” Yang said.
Amaze launches its autumn seasonal menu, “The Full Circle.” (Taiwan News, Lyla Liu video)

Regulators say latest Fukushima discharge will not affect Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:43:49 UTC
11:43:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The latest round of treated wastewater discharge from Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant will have no impact on Taiwan, the Nuclear Safety Commission said Tuesday.
In a press release, the NSC said the plant began releasing a new batch of wastewater on Monday, scheduled to run for 19 days. Japan began discharging treated wastewater containing tritium from the tsunami-disabled plant in August 2023.
Japan’s treatment process reduces most radionuclides in the wastewater to below regulatory limits, but tritium cannot be filtered out and is instead diluted with seawater before discharge, according to Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry.
The NSC said that tritium levels in waters around Taiwan are forecast to “remain below the minimum detectable level of monitoring instruments,” citing Central Weather Administration forecasts. Based on analysis by the Tokyo Electric Power Company, levels of radionuclides other than tritium also met regulatory standards.
The commission added that the recently discharged wastewater is expected to affect mainly waters off Japan’s east coast due to tidal movements.
The NSC monitors seawater radiation in cooperation with other government agencies, and it said that no abnormalities so far have been detected.
Real-time updates on how the wastewater is dispersing is available on the CWA’s website.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten sharply rejected the idea of restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe as part of a potential US-brokered peace agreement with Moscow, calling it a “very stupid idea” and urging Washington to increase sanctions rather than offer economic concessions.
Speaking alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky in The Hague on Wednesday, Oct. 28, Jetten responded to reports that US negotiators had floated the possibility of reviving Russian energy exports to Europe as part of a broader settlement to end the war in Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is clear that we need to push Putin to take the negotiations seriously,” Jetten said, arguing that Russia was suffering mounting military losses and economic pressure from international sanctions.
“The only way forward for Europeans, but also for Americans and others, is to put more sanctions on the Russian regime instead of less,” he said.
“So buying Russian energy is a very stupid idea,” Jetten added.

“I can assure you that there is no European leader willing to buy Russian gas in the next few years,” he said.

Russia Uses North Korean Forced Labor to Sustain War Against Ukraine, Investigation Finds
US explores restoring energy ties with Russia
Jetten’s remarks come amid reports that Washington is exploring renewed energy cooperation with Moscow as part of negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
As Kyiv Post reported Wednesday, citing the Financial Times, US and Russian officials have discussed the possible return of American energy companies to Russia, including joint oil production projects on Sakhalin and renewed Russian crude exports to Europe through the Druzhba pipeline.
Other proposals reportedly include restoring Russian gas supplies to Europe and potentially reviving the Nord Stream pipeline system.
The reported discussions involve economic incentives that Moscow could receive under a peace settlement, although no final agreements have been announced.
US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have been involved in negotiations with Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Europe has already moved to ban Russian gas
The European Union adopted binding legislation in January 2026 to permanently phase out Russian natural gas imports.
Under the timetable, long-term Russian liquefied natural gas contracts are to end from January 2027, with remaining pipeline imports phased out by November 2027 at the latest.
The measures form part of the EU’s REPowerEU strategy, designed to eliminate dependence on Russian energy and prevent Moscow from using energy supplies as political leverage.
Russian gas has not entirely disappeared from the European market. Some EU countries continue receiving Russian liquefied natural gas under existing contracts, but the bloc has committed to ending those purchases.

Kalshi, co-founders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah

Kalshi, cofounders hit with criminal charges in US state of Utah
The charges come after a federal judge ruled that Utah could enforce its anti-gambling laws against prediction markets.
The US state of Utah has announced criminal charges against popular prediction market Kalshi and its two cofounders, accusing the platform and its executives of illegally promoting online gambling.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed the charges against Kalshi, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara on Wednesday, a day after US President Donald Trump’s administration sued the state to block its civil enforcement actions against the platform.
According to the criminal complaint filed in a Salt Lake City court, Kalshi facilitated an undercover law enforcement officer’s wagers on sports events, including games in the NFL.
The charges come after a federal judge in August ruled that Utah was entitled to enforce its stringent anti-gambling laws against online prediction markets, following a legal bid by Kalshi to block enforcement of the law.
The criminal complaint accuses the defendants of 12 counts of online gambling promotion, one count of general gambling promotion and one count of pattern of unlawful activity.
Kalshi and Brown’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Utah has some of the strictest prohibitions against gambling in the US, with its state constitution explicitly barring lawmakers from legalising the activity.
The charges mark an escalation in a showdown between US states and the Trump administration over the regulation of prediction markets.
On Tuesday, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit seeking to block Utah’s enforcement actions against prediction markets, arguing that the platforms fall under federal jurisdiction.
The regulator announced the move after Utah last week filed a civil lawsuit accusing Kalshi of facilitating betting on sports, elections, politics and other outcomes in violation of anti-gambling laws.
Dozens of US states, led by both Republican and Democratic administrations, have argued that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission does not have the authority to regulate prediction markets.
Last month, the state of New Jersey asked the US Supreme Court to rule on whether state or federal authorities have jurisdiction over sports betting on prediction market platforms.
