UN to provide winter assistance to 2.1 million Ukrainians
Matthias Schmale, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ukraine, announced the plan at an event on the UN’s response to the humanitarian crisis caused by Russia’s war against Ukraine, Ukrinform reports, citing its correspondent.
“We plan to provide assistance to 2.1 million people from October 26, 2026, through March 2027. They include nearly 430,000 internally displaced people and 1.7 million people who have remained in their homes. The assistance will include heating support, home repairs, medical services, food aid, and cash assistance. Approximately 84% of the planned assistance will be directed to areas within 50 kilometers of the front line,” Schmale said.
According to Schmale, the plan includes helping vulnerable households cover their winter expenses, as well as measures to ensure the uninterrupted operation of heating, electricity, water supply, and sanitation systems.
In addition, the UN will complement the Ukrainian government’s response efforts in eight cities north of Kyiv, as well as in Odesa and Dnipro. To this end, the organization will work with the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, the Ukrainian Red Cross, and two other partners, Schmale said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukraine’s Minister of Social Policy, Family, and Unity Denys Uliutin and Bernadette Castel-Hollingsworth, the UNHCR Representative in Ukraine, discussed coordination of humanitarian assistance and support for internally displaced people and Ukrainians abroad.

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Mexico is advancing talks with Washington to resolve issues related to the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) on free trade before the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Wednesday.
At her daily press conference, Sheinbaum said Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard is continuing talks with U.S. officials, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson.
She added that regardless of the election outcome, "we are going to continue working with the United States. That work is not interrupted."
The midterm elections, which mark the midpoint of the U.S. president's term, are legislative elections for the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Sheinbaum said that while important progress has been made, no agreement has been reached on priority issues for Mexico, including the reduction of tariffs applied under Section 232 of U.S. trade law on steel, aluminum and the automotive industry.
Numerous issues identified by Washington as non-tariff barriers have been resolved, she said, stressing the negotiations have proceeded without any surrender of sovereignty and are focused on areas of common ground that can strengthen both nations.
In response to U.S. President Donald Trump's recent remarks on the possibility of finalizing an agreement, Sheinbaum urged "great patience and composure" throughout the talks.
The USMCA's periodic review process began on July 1, after the United States opted not to automatically extend the agreement, but instead proposed annual reviews over the coming decade. ■

S. Korea's ABS issuance falls 5.7 pct in Q3 amid drop in real estate project financing assets

SEOUL, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's issuance of registered asset-backed securities (ABS) fell in single digits in the third quarter amid a drop in real estate project financing (PF) assets, financial watchdog data showed Thursday.
The ABS issuance decreased 5.7 percent from a year earlier to 12.51 trillion won (about 9.3 billion U.S. dollars) in the July-September quarter, according to the Financial Supervisory Service.
Despite the quarterly contraction, cumulative ABS sales for the first nine months of 2026 grew 14 percent to 39.1 trillion won compared to the same period last year.
Loan-backed ABS issuance retreated 8.8 percent to 7.54 trillion won as sales of real estate PF-backed ABS plummeted 98.3 percent to just 20 billion won amid the sluggish property market.
Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) sales expanded 13 percent to 5.77 trillion won, but issuance of nonperforming loan-backed ABS declined 11.4 percent to 1.66 trillion won.
Receivable-backed ASB issuance gained 9.9 percent year on year to 4.11 trillion won in the third quarter.
It was bolstered by credit card receivables, which surged 142.2 percent to 3.05 trillion won, offsetting a 92.3 percent drop in installment finance receivables.
By issuer, public enterprises recorded a 13 percent growth in their ABS sales in the third quarter, driven by the Korea Housing Finance Corp., which expanded its MBS issuance.
Financial companies remained relatively flat at 5.76 trillion won, but industrial companies saw their ABS sales plunge 58.7 percent to 0.98 trillion won amid the real estate PF downturn.
At the end of September, the outstanding ABS totaled 246.6 trillion won, up 3.1 trillion won from a year earlier. ■

‘Is he a Mossad agent?’: Inside Israel's global volunteer rescue network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:22:30 UTC
11:22:30 KST

An Israeli hiker's disappearance on Mount Olympus ended in tragedy, but the search revealed a remarkable volunteer network born from another family's loss; operating in 49 countries, the organization has handled more than 230 emergencies and helped save dozens of lives
On September 20, at 4 p.m., Shosh Debi sent a message to her son. Ami Yogev, 46, from Modiin, had flown to Athens a few days earlier on a whim and told her he planned to climb Mount Olympus.
"Since he landed, he had spoken to me every day," she recalled. "Even during the climb, he sent me pictures. After the last photo, when he was on his way to the summit, he stopped answering."
He had managed to read that final message from his mother. The messages that followed remained unopened. From then on, there was only a single check mark on WhatsApp and countless unanswered calls.
Yogev had sent the same photographs to a close friend, telling him how much he was enjoying himself on the mountain. In another message, he mentioned that he had sprained his ankle during the climb. After that, there was silence.
When his family realized they had lost contact with him, they began reaching out to anyone who might be able to help. Within days, dozens of people who had never met Yogev were searching for him.
'We knew that was where we would find him'
Mount Olympus, near Thessaloniki in northern Greece, attracts travelers looking to add adventure to their vacations. The climb can take several days, leading to a summit nearly 3,000 meters (9,800 feet) above sea level, where hikers encounter visitors from around the world.
But in early October, a group of people on the mountain had not come for the views. Several dozen Israelis, some living in Greece and others who had traveled specifically to help, were searching for Yogev, a man most of them had never met.
About 33 of the volunteers had been mobilized through Haverim Mehalzim, or Friends Rescuing Friends, a civilian volunteer rescue network operating under the Israeli nonprofit organization Gvanim. The network assists Israelis and Jews facing emergencies abroad.
The organization's strength lies in its ability to rapidly connect worried families in Israel with people who can help: volunteers and professionals around the world, a coordination center that manages information, and local rescue and medical services. Families receive its assistance free of charge.
That system was put to work in Yogev's case. He had left Israel without travel insurance, and his family financed the search through personal funds and a crowdfunding campaign while also calling for government intervention.
Shortly after the family requested assistance, Haverim Mehalzim issued an appeal to volunteers and professionals in the area. The call reached Liran Aviram, an Israeli woman living in Greece. Through her, Altus, a drone company owned by her partner, Zach, also joined the search.
For days, volunteers worked alongside a Greek rescue unit, searching the slopes and streambeds surrounding Yogev's hiking route. The rocky, steep terrain became particularly hazardous amid fog and rain early that week.
"It seems he set out on the hike without fully understanding the scale of the challenge," said Ron Lavi, co-CEO of Haverim Mehalzim. "He may not have had suitable equipment or known the terrain. But even when we first set out to locate him, we had a fairly good idea of where to search."
On October 9, roughly two and a half weeks after Yogev's last messages to his mother and friend, the search came to a tragic end. His body was discovered in the Mavrolongos riverbed at an elevation of approximately 1,800 meters (5,900 feet). He had apparently fallen from a considerable height during the climb.
"We searched a wooded area along a riverbed with dry waterfalls," said Yiftach Shavit, a co-founder of the organization. "Logic told us that this was the area where Ami might be found. After three days of searching, we found him there, lifeless. We knew what clothing he was wearing and what personal equipment he had from the photographs his family provided, and that was how the team identified him."
Once Yogev was located, responsibility passed from the volunteers to the Israeli consulate in Greece, which is assisting his family with arrangements to bring him home for burial.
'Like roadside assistance, but for emergencies abroad'
The four rescuers who found Yogev in the riverbed had never known him. They would never have been there were it not for another tragedy five years earlier, in a different river.
In November 2021, during a backpacking trip after his military service, Yanai Rimon arrived with friends at a shallow river in Mexico. "He entered the water, was swept away by the strong current and couldn't get out," recalled his mother, Nirit. "They couldn't find him for three days, and then his body was discovered. What impressed me was that dozens of volunteers had worked to find him."
Yanai was 23, a recently discharged combat soldier from the elite Duvdevan unit. He had set off with friends on a long-awaited trip through Central America after three years of intensive military service and a particularly difficult period during the COVID-19 pandemic. "He was, and still is, our second child," Nirit said.
When the search ended and the family received the devastating news, they also understood what had been missing during those days: an organization that could coordinate information, explain what was happening and quickly connect everyone willing to help. Rather than wait for someone else to establish such a network, they created one themselves.
"We were far away. We didn't understand what was happening, and we didn't know what to do with all the people who wanted to help," Rimon explained. "Only later did we understand that, in these situations, time is the most important thing. Whoever gets to the scene quickly can save lives."
"Most of those people didn't even know Yanai. They were simply Israelis who wanted to lend a hand. That's when I understood that we are a special people, a people who feel like one big family," she said. "When something happens, everyone rises to the occasion. And as a family, we understood that we couldn't let that energy go to waste."
In March 2023, Rimon established Haverim Mehalzim in memory of her son under the umbrella of Gvanim, where she now serves as co-CEO. She was joined by Lavi, a specialist in search and rescue operations in difficult environments, and Shavit, who would go on to lead the Mount Olympus search two and a half years later.
"Ron and Yiftach approached us, and together we developed a program designed to give others what we didn't have: not just help with the search itself, but an entire support system, from fundraising to mobilizing people on the ground," Rimon explained.
Lavi himself had not known Yanai. He became involved through Shavit, a longtime friend, and until a year ago was simply a volunteer in the organization he now helps lead.
"Yiftach approached me about six months after Yanai's death and told me they wanted to establish a network to rescue Israelis abroad," he recalled. "The connection with Gvanim was immediate. With their help, we established a worldwide network that includes executives at private aviation, helicopter and drone companies. We really built a professional team with the capabilities to handle these situations."
But what exactly does such a professional team do when an Israeli disappears in a remote corner of the world? Lavi sums it up in a single sentence: "We're like Yedidim, the volunteer organization everyone knows to call when they have car trouble, except we handle extreme emergencies abroad."
The third member of the founding team is Liran Neta, a veteran of the IDF's Unit 8200 intelligence unit, who developed a platform for registering volunteers and managing information during rescue operations.
"This community started as a WhatsApp group, and today it's much more technologically advanced," Lavi said. "It's built around Israelis living all over the world: veterans of elite military units, medical professionals and former members of the intelligence community. When something happens, a message goes out to the group for the country where contact was lost, and people are mobilized. A forward command post is established on the ground, and from there we provide comprehensive support."
Since its establishment three and a half years ago, the organization has received more than 1,000 requests for assistance from Israelis and Jews. Just over 230 involved genuine emergencies across 49 countries.
"Of those, there are around 35 cases where, had we not intervened, the person rescued would most likely not be alive today," Lavi said.
How do local residents react when dozens of Israelis arrive to search for a single person?
"With amazement," he replied. "We encounter only good people who want to help. Locals searching alongside us often ask me, 'Who is this missing person? Is he a Mossad agent? A politician?' And I answer, 'No. He's just an Israeli.'"
From rescue survivor to volunteer
When Lavi speaks of a comprehensive support system, he means everything surrounding a rescue operation, and sometimes assistance that takes the place of a physical rescue altogether.
"We have, for example, a clinical psychologist, gynecologists and even lawyers who become involved when an Israeli man or woman is in distress abroad," he said.
That was the case last December, when an Israeli woman vacationing in Budapest woke up without her wallet or belongings and suspected she had been sexually assaulted. "Within hours, she received comprehensive assistance from us in dealing with the local authorities, with the help of Israelis living nearby who knew how those authorities operated," Lavi said.
Over the past year, the organization has also expanded into mental health support after locating several Israelis experiencing mental health crises who had disappeared abroad.
"Recently, the brother of a discharged soldier called us after receiving a phone call from an Israeli who said his brother was behaving in a frightening way on Koh Phangan in Thailand," Lavi recalled. "We guided him and his sister on how to reach the area and how to speak with him so he would agree to return to Israel. We managed to handle the situation."
In another case, in 2023, an Israeli backpacker jumped from a bridge in Laos, landed badly in the water, lost consciousness and disappeared beneath the river's surface.
"An Israeli woman who was with him saw what happened and started running toward him. Neriya Shukron, another Israeli traveler who happened to be nearby, saw her running and joined her. He took a small boat and pulled the man out of the water unconscious. When he saw that the man was bleeding from his mouth, he called me and asked what to do," Lavi recalled.
"That's when an entire ordeal began. We got them onto a local pickup truck and took him to a hospital, but the staff there barely knew how to treat him, so we flew him to Thailand. Within 24 hours of the fall, doctors drained the bleeding. Today, he's not only healthy, he's one of our volunteers."
A year ago, the organization also assisted Shahar Saadon, a discharged soldier who had fought in Gaza and traveled to India. During a hike in an area known as the Fairy Forest, Saadon fell from a cliff, broke his leg and suffered a head injury. "One of our volunteers heard about the incident from locals and alerted us. Within half an hour, he was brought to a local hospital for lifesaving treatment."
On Mount Olympus, the outcome was tragic. Yet even there, Nirit Rimon said, something happened that captured the very reason the organization exists: dozens of strangers who had never met Ami Yogev dropped everything and climbed the mountain to search for him. His family was not left alone to face unfamiliar foreign authorities and the silence of a phone that no longer rang.
"We built the rescue network to give others what we didn't have at the time," Rimon said. "It was our way of honoring Yanai's memory and allowing something meaningful to grow from our story."
For more information or to volunteer with Rescue Friends, visit the organization's website

Spain mourns after latest train tragedy kills 68

- Relatives are searching for missing loved ones, while Red Cross teams, police and DNA offices are helping with grief and identification.
- Transport Minister Oscar Puente said an automatic control system failed on 69km of track and the decision to resume traffic was “inexplicable”, raising fresh safety fears.
AI generated
URDA, Spain – Spain began three days of mourning on Oct 29 after its second high-speed rail collision in 2026 killed 68 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe’s deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s rail network after the transport minister reported an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash.
The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha in the morning on Oct 28 when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Emergency services combed through the wreckage at night to find further victims on the key line linking Madrid with the southern city of Seville, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, AFP reporters saw.
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when “I woke up and I was in the air”.
Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling AFP that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.
Wearing a bloodstained grey jumper and holding his tattered suitcase, he recounted “a very strong hit... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos”.
“I think I’ve been born again,” he said.
‘Long and hard hours’
A school in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to inquire about their loved ones.
Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears, amid crowds of police and journalists from around the world.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said “long and hard hours” were in store because “every person will manage it in their own way”.
“We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated,” Garcia said.
The Civil Guard has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Cordoba and Seville to enable relatives of the victims to provide DNA samples and help identify the missing.
Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid.
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.
“What matters most is being with the victims’ relatives, that they feel the closeness, because words at a time like this are pointless, but a hug helps,” he said.
Recalling how he rushed to the site of the crash, Fernandez said he was confronted with “an image of desolation, despair, uncertainty, death”.
Safety questions
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Oct 28 that an automatic control system went down on 69km of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to “resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable”, Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25km before striking the Iryo.
The control centre “had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it”, he added.
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain’s railways.
The latest disaster comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on Nov 29. AFP

Pentagon watchdog rejects bipartisan plea to investigate Starlink disruption, AP reports
The Pentagon’s watchdog has refused a bipartisan request by U.S. lawmakers to investigate recent Starlink and Starshield service disruptions to Ukraine, the Associated Press (AP) reported on Oct. 28.
A bipartisan group of nine U.S. senators penned a formal letter on Oct. 15 to the Department of Defense Inspector General, following unexpected disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield services earlier this month. The Department of Defense Inspector General, or watchdog, is an independent office responsible for auditing and investigating official conduct within the Pentagon.
"We urgently request an Inspector General investigation into these incidents," the ators wrote, "including whether actions or decisions by the Department of Defense or its contractors contributed to these dangerous circumstances."
In a response received Oct. 27, the watchdog told the lawmakers that they should turn their concerns to the U.S. Air Force instead, according to AP, which obtained a copy of the letter.
The rebuff is interpreted by sources familiar with the matter as a refusal by the Inspector General to investigate Elon Musk and Starlink.
Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, who signed the initial letter said the response was "concerning" and urged that because "the Trump Administration and SpaceX have provided conflicting accounts of what led to those disruptions" there “must be an independent account and review,” according to AP..
The disruptions occurred on Oct. 14, when Space X abruptly implemented a speed cap on Ukraine’s vital Starshield service.
Ukraine widely uses both commercial Starlink terminals and their militarized version, Starshield.
The limitation occurred amid heightened tensions between Kyiv and the White House, with Trump demanding that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia.
While no actor has taken responsibility for the decision to restrict Starlink, Musk reportedly approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, according to reports by the Telegraph on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Another bipartisan group of Senators penned another public letter directed at Musk on Oct. 23, in which they remind the CEO that Space X is a publicly traded company with legal obligations to disclose information to shareholders and the public.

Barack Obama, speaking at a Wednesday campaign rally in suburban Atlanta, offered a closing argument for Democrats in the final week of the midterm election campaign.
“These are not serious people,” he said of Donald Trump and the Republican party. “And we’re all paying the price for their lack of seriousness.”
Obama came to Georgia to support the campaigns of US senator Jon Ossoff, former Atlanta mayor and gubernatorial hopeful Keisha Lance Bottoms, and an array of down-ballot Democrats as part of his cross-country campaign tour before next week’s election. From 3,500 to 4,000 people filled the Discovery Center of Clayton county for the late election season stop, just south of Atlanta.
Obama has been casting caltrops behind him with each campaign stop, offering pointed criticism of Republican candidates and Donald Trump that has been unusual for the former president. He continued to do so on Wednesday, again invoking the image of Trump’s gilded renovations of the White House and noting Trump’s strident reaction to his crack last week likening it to Saddam Hussein decorating a Cheesecake Factory.
“The Saddam Hussein thing didn’t bother him. But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said. “I mean, it’s all crazy, but this is the crazy part: they mobilized a whole government response to that joke.
“The White House even called the secretary of the treasury,” the former president continued. “The guy who is trying to figure out how to lower inflation … they told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory.”
He also rebuffed Republicans’ accusations of snobbery for referencing the popular chain restaurant.
“I am the father of two daughters,” Obama said. “Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?”
But he turned that discussion to the problems of affordability for American voters, in contrast with the corruption of the presidency.
“We have never seen a president so intent on selling favors,” Obama said. “The guy has made billions of dollars while in office. Understand that this has not been done in modern times.”
The construction of a new ballroom on the site of the former East Wing of the White House featured in the comments of many speakers at Wednesday’s rally, including Ossoff.
“Each day, Donald Trump digs the moral pit deeper,” Ossoff said, accusing the president of leading “the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it”.
“If you’re involved in any of this, next year you’ll be raising your hand to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth,” Ossoff said, in reference to Democrats pledging to impeach Trump if they take control of Congress next year.
The crowd chanted: “Lock him up!” in response.
Bottoms, meanwhile, contrasted her candidacy with that of her Republican opponent Rick Jackson, tying the billionaire healthcare executive to Trump and describing them as “two out-of-touch billionaires who want to keep getting rich on the backs of taxpayers”.
Invoking the legacies of US Representative John Lewis and Coretta Scott King, Bottoms characterized her candidacy as transcending politics. “They may have the money, but they will never overtake our movement,” she said.
Despite a broad wave of Democratic support buoying candidates across the country – and the eight- to 10-point polling lead Ossoff has on his Republican opponent, US Representative Mike Collins – Bottoms is statistically tied in polls with Jackson. If elected, Bottoms would break the state’s Republican trifecta – where the GOP has controlled both chambers of the legislature and the governor’s office – which began in 2004.
Rev Raphael Warnock, Georgia’s other senator, warned of “spiritual wickedness in high places” while describing the effects of deep cuts to Medicaid and Snap nutrition support for children.
“This is about the character of the country,” Warnock said. “This is about who we are and whether we are here for one another … I am concerned about the spiritual health of our country. There is brokenness, because only a broken nation could manage to elect Donald Trump twice.”
Trump, who was campaigning in Ohio at the same time as the Georgia rally, has also been on a national rally blitz, holding near-daily events in the final days of the midterm campaign. Trump has made two appearances in as many weeks in Georgia, both in what would otherwise seem to be congressional districts that are safe territory for Republicans.

Democrats’ Golan rules out forming coalition with Netanyahu
Democrats party leader Yair Golan on Thursday came out against forming a unity government with the Likud party and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying that previous similar attempts "failed spectacularly."
In an interview with Kan public radio, Golan – whose left-wing party is expected to win eight seats when all votes are tallied – made clear that Netanyahu "is going to be sent home," adding that "no business can be done with him."

"I plan to leave no stone unturned, to work in any way and do whatever is needed to actualize the voters' will, and bring forth the establishment of a government of change and rescue for Israel."
Police official says no evidence of election fraud, claims are baseless spin
An Israeli police official and the Central Elections Committee dismissed claims of election fraud on Thursday, saying there was no evidence to support allegations that Arab voters had "stolen" the election.
A senior police official told Haaretz on Thursday morning that there are no indications of election fraud. "These are spin tactics that, so far, have no basis whatsoever," the source added.
According to the official, fewer complaints of fraud and irregularities were received this year than in previous election cycles.

In an interview with Kan public radio, Livneh said the committee was conducting a comprehensive review of the complaints filed, as it does every year.
It's Bibi or Tibi: Israel's future depends on its Arab citizens | Opinion
Now it really is Bibi or Tibi; it's either Ahmad Tibi, a generic name, or perdition.
The future of Israel now depends on its Arab citizens and on the attitude of its Jewish citizens toward its Arab ones. Eighty years after the Nakba and the establishment of the Jewish state, Israeli Palestinians may determine its fate. Is there greater historical justice than that? That is not an exaggeration.
The results of the election have led to a situation in which Israelis must choose between a government led by Benjamin Netanyahu and a government that includes the Arab parties. No other option seems to be shaping up. Voters for the "change bloc," including the racists among them, and there is no dearth of those, must ask themselves who has caused greater damage to the country, Bibi or Tibi? And who will inflict more damage upon it in the future, Yousef Jabareen or Itamar Ben-Gvir, Bezalel Smotrich or Mansour Abbas?

Stephanie Robinson, a mother of three grown children from Ra'anana who voted for the Democrats, says she knew it would be a tight race but is surprised that there was not more anger toward Likud and more of a desire for change among the electorate.

With approximately 91 percent of the votes in the Knesset election counted, Mansour Abbas' United Arab List has climbed from seven to eight seats at the expense of Yousef Jabareen's Joint List, which has dropped from 12 to 11.

Breaking a decades-old taboo, East Jerusalem Palestinians turn out in force
Palestinian turnout in East Jerusalem in Tuesday's Knesset election broke all records since Israel annexed the eastern part of the city in 1967, as more than 10,000 residents exercised their right to vote – with the vast majority backing the Joint List – tripling the rate recorded in the previous election.
The overwhelming majority of the roughly 391,000 Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem are ineligible to vote in Knesset elections. After annexing the city, Israel refrained from granting them full citizenship, instead giving them "permanent resident" status, which grants the right to vote in municipal elections but not national ones.
Despite this, several thousand have obtained Israeli citizenship over the years. Estimates suggest that between 5 and 7 percent of East Jerusalem residents are now citizens and are included in the Knesset voter registry.

He gets to continue to be prime minister for now, and another election serves him since it's likely that his rivals have exhausted their electoral capabilities in the present round.

Airline groups urge US CDC to reconsider Ebola declaration requirements
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:04:20 CET
11:04:20 KST

By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Major American and foreign airlines urged the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reconsider new rules requiring all US-bound travelers to attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days.
The International Air Transport Association and Airlines for America, in separate previously unreported letters reviewed by Reuters, urged the CDC to reconsider the plan announced last week that takes effect on November 3 and is aimed at preventing entry by people exposed to Ebola.
“It is unreasonable for the U.S. government to require all airlines serving the U.S. market to modify their procedures to accommodate the collection of attestations from each individual (passenger and crew) flying to the United States in less than two weeks,” IATA, which represents over 370 member airlines in more than 130 countries, said in the letter dated Tuesday.
The new CDC order requires all US-bound airline passengers and crew members to file digital or paper attestations. The CDC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Airlines for America, which represents United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Delta Air Lines, said in a separate letter to the CDC that the plan was unworkable.
“Changes to check-in systems, digital signatures, station procedures, and training cannot readily be completed in the allotted time,” the group said, calling on the CDC to “reconsider a more proportionate and measured U.S. response.”
Airlines for America said that in 2025, US Customs and Border Protection screened about 130 million air passengers, but fewer than 25,000 of them had a connection to the Democratic Republic of Congo.
IATA also questioned why the plan only applied to air travelers. “The U.S. government has clearly decided that the risk of the importation of Ebola into the United States is high enough to justify this global process. It is difficult to understand why other modes of transportation – maritime and surface – were not included in this mandate,” IATA said.
The CDC in May adopted rules barring foreign airline passengers who had been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the center of the 2026 outbreak, in the prior three weeks. The restrictions were extended to US citizens in July.
Airlines for America urged the CDC to exempt crew members, the US military and jumpseat travelers, calling the plan “overly stringent, costly and burdensome to Americans and the US airline industry.”
As part of the Ebola measures, the CDC since earlier this year has barred foreign nationals from the US if they were in Uganda or South Sudan in the prior three weeks.
The Bundibugyo strain of the virus spread undetected for months before the outbreak was declared in May. It kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC.
(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Tom Hogue and Jamie Freed)

Moscow, Pyongyang back network sending workers to Russian factories, report says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
03:04:03 CET
11:04:03 KST

By Jack Kim
SEOUL, Oct 29 (Reuters) - A Russian network of brokers sponsored by Pyongyang has taken North Koreans to work in Russia in exploitative conditions and in violation of UN sanctions, some at factories that turn out items Moscow uses in the Ukraine war, a rights group said.
The neighbours have boosted military and political ties dramatically since pledging renewed cooperation at a 2023 summit of their leaders, while a mutual defence pact is a cornerstone of a partnership treaty signed the following year.
In its report, the Hague-based group, Global Rights Compliance (GRC), said North Korea reaps funds from the operation, taking much of the wages earned by its workers who are sent to Russia and made to stay under threat of retribution.
The group cites open source information on the operation run by a Russian businessman, facial recognition technology to identify North Korean officials, and evidence gathered by its members posing undercover as prospective employers.
“This investigation exposes a dangerous convergence between two states’ military ambitions,” said the group’s legal adviser, Elise Lauriot Prevost.
These were “North Korea’s use of overseas forced labour to finance its weapons programme, and Russia’s growing reliance on labour to sustain its war economy,” she added.
Russia’s foreign ministry and the North Korean embassy in Moscow did not respond to emails seeking comment.
The rights group said it contacted two Russians identified as key figures in the network, but only one replied, denying the accusation. It did not say if the other responded.
NORTH KOREA SENT TROOPS, SOUTH SAYS
Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians in the Ukraine war, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow’s dwindling armoury while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea’s intelligence agency has said.
To evade UN sanctions that ban member nations from hiring North Korean workers, the latter enter Russia on student visas in the guise of enrolling at colleges, GRC said.
Then they are contracted out to Russian employers, with brokers receiving a commission of up to 150,000 roubles ($1,860) for each, it added.
GRC investigators posed undercover as prospective employers and found the workers were hired at production sites, including a military rations factory.
The workers are forced to stay on the job through coercion and threats of retribution against them and their families.
One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not “run away,” the report said. Workers labour 12-hour days with 2 days off each month, it added, citing such ads.
After North Korea’s sixth and last nuclear test in 2017, a UN Security Council resolution put a blanket ban on the hiring of its workers overseas and mandated their return home.
Russia and China, two permanent members of the Security Council that voted for the ban, have since been accused by South Korea and the West of noncompliance with resolutions.
Such measures, dating back to 2006, banned the flow of goods, energy, weapons and workers with North Korea.
In previous years, Russia employed North Korean labourers in its far east while many North Koreans staffing restaurants in China sent home wages that were channelled to the state treasury, rights groups have said.
North Korea is directly involved in running the network supplying workers in Russia, with officials from its Moscow embassy identified as inspecting work sites for prospective employment, the GRC report said.
“These workers do not come cheap, yet little, if any, of the money paid for their labour reaches them,” said Dyland Carter, a GRC lead investigator.
“Instead, it lines the pockets of the DPRK state,” he added, referring to North Korea by a short version of its official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
($1=80.6455 roubles)
(Reporting by Jack Kim; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

Readers share why and how they are avoiding AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:02:06 UTC
11:02:06 KST

Have you embraced or rejected AI?
We recently asked three AI experts if the idea that "if you don't use AI, you'll be left behind" was true, and found there is a difference between not using, and ignoring, the technology.
Keen to hear more, we invited readers who are avoiding AI to write in and share why.
As a university student, generative AI is all around me and is used by students and staff alike.
I refuse to engage in any use of generative AI, or optional AI. I use browser extensions to block Google's AI summary.
I turn off AI in any program I use. I do not engage with programs like ChatGPT and Claude. And I actively avoid and block any social media content that uses AI.
Society is obsessed with accelerationism without [defining] what exactly we are rushing towards.
I fear that AI is not the answer to our problems and will only make the solutions even more difficult to reach.
AI terrifies me. We had enough trouble knowing what was real, what was true before this, what hope have we got now?
I work for a company that went from "Do not use AI under any circumstances" to "Use AI for everything" in the blink of an eye.
I am greatly concerned about the environmental impacts of AI and have decided to be a conscientious objector on that issue alone.
I have openly declared my refusal to go out of my way to use AI at work (yes, I know it can't be completely avoided) and have been told by local IT that "I will be left behind".
I am also concerned that people will gradually lose the ability to think for themselves on a broad scale. How many of us remember multiple phone numbers anymore? Imagine that on a broad scale, frightening.
Sadly, I know there won't be any satisfaction in being able to say, "I told you so."
I've been a professional driver for 42 years. I developed an ability to read a street map, way before AI or Google came on the scene.
I would imprint this map into my brain and then drive the route as outlaid and with accordance to my experience.
Surprisingly, there were times when I used Google Maps for a bit of fun and indeed, it showed me a better way.
Here's the thing; I used it once to get to an unfamiliar place, then did the drive again without its help and promptly took the wrong exit.
This shows exactly [what I think is] the biggest error in learning via AI: you don't learn, you simply follow instructions.
I probably do use a lot of tech under [the banner of] "AI" but in terms of large language model chatbots and agents and the whole hype of it, I want it to stop.
Thanks to everyone who wrote in to share their thoughts with us. Some comments have been edited for clarity and brevity.

The timing of the next round of three-way talks on a settlement of the Ukraine conflict is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as saying, casting doubt on whether the talks will take place next month as initially proposed.
Ushakov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said on Wednesday that Moscow had not yet proposed a specific date for the talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he hoped that a meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between November 6 and November 10.
"It will also depend on the situation on the battlefield and the situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It just doesn't allow us to hold it in the near future. That's my assumption," Ushakov told journalists, referring to the regional fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Ushakov also said there had been no discussion of having European negotiators in attendance at the next round of talks.
The leaders of Britain, Germany and France said last weekend that Europe would play a role in US-mediated talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy on securing a ceasefire.
"There is absolutely no talk about this, nothing being considered," Ushakov was quoted as saying. "What there is now is an agreement on resuming three-sided consultations with representatives of Russia, Ukraine and the United States."
Lifting sanctions
Ushakov also said discussions with the administration of US President Donald Trump are underway on the US lifting sanctions on Russia's flagship investment fund.
He said the head of the Russia Direct Investment Fund, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, was actively pursuing talks on lifting the sanctions.
"This conversation is going on. It has been going on for a while. I don't know what the outcome will be," Ushakov was quoted as saying.
"Dmitriev is active in his contacts, and that's why the issue is under discussion. It already got into the media a few days ago, and discussions are still proceeding."
The New York Times reported earlier in the day that the Trump administration was considering abandoning the sanctions.
Earlier this month, Trump announced that Russia would provide diesel for the US and world markets, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian fuel. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that a fourth tanker of diesel would depart on Wednesday.
Trump also issued an executive order waiving key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas, that had been scheduled to go into effect under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.

Supreme Court removes October 30 deadline for additions to Delhi electoral roll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:00:02 UTC
11:00:02 KST

Supreme Court asked the Election Commission not to stop adding names to Delhi's electoral rolls by the October 30 deadline
NEW DELHI: In a relief to over 43 lakh voters excluded from Delhi’s draft electoral rolls for ‘permanently shifting out’, Supreme Court on Wednesday asked Election Commission not to stop adding names in the voter list by the Oct 30 deadline and told it to continue distributing and receiving enumeration forms, and Forms 6 (new voters), 7 (for deletion) and 8 (for those who shifted from one constituency to another).A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also questioned EC on why voters whose names were there on earlier electoral rolls but were deleted from the draft rolls were asked to file Form 6, which is meant for enrolment of first-time voters.
Without passing any order, the bench said, “We will examine the issue after two weeks. The effort should be to reduce the 43 lakh (who have been deleted from draft rolls). One suggestion — publish the list of those who are deleted and specify the reason for deletion against each name. Request them to contact the nearest BLO and fill Form 8. You can give them enumeration forms. Tell them that they are welcome to fill either Form 6 or 8.”
How can you insist on Form 6 for person who was voter earlier: SC
During the proceedings on a PIL filed by activist Anjali Bhardwaj, the bench heard advocate Prashant Bhushan’s complaints against EC for insisting on filling Form 6 by those whose names got excluded and, thereby, compelling them to give a false declaration that they were first-time voters.
The bench said, “Right to vote is a vital right. If a person has shifted out from Vasant Kunj to Dwarka, or had gone out of station for a month or so and for some other reason could not respond to the EC notice or could not file the claim for inclusion of name, or did not get enumeration form because of change of address, should EC permanently disable him from voting by striking his name off the voter list?“How can you insist on Form 6 for a person who was a voter earlier? If a person has shifted from one constituency to another within Delhi, it is erroneous to ask him/her to fill Form 6. You must allow similarly placed persons, whose names are deleted on the ground of ‘permanently shifted’, to fill Form 8.”Appearing for EC, senior advocate D S Naidu said the commission had conducted over one lakh camps in Delhi to spread awareness among people on how to re-enter their names in the voter list.
“The situation on the ground is very different. Not a single person has come to fill Form 8. The petitioner is creating a scare on paper in the courtroom. Any person can seek inclusion of his/her name in the voter list of a constituency till the date of filing of nominations,” Naidu said, and clarified that no one has been prosecuted for using Form 6 to restore names in voter lists across states.But EC relented to keep the window open for inclusion of names in Delhi as SC insisted that the Oct 30 deadline for filing claims and objections need not be set in stone as elections were not imminent in Delhi to warrant urgent completion of the SIR exercise.

====================================================================================================

Mark Carney isn’t the climate hero Europeans think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ask European Union leaders what they think of Mark Carney’s climate credentials, and you’ll get a gushing response.
“We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last month, where the Canadian prime minister was the guest of honor.
“Canada and the EU are very, very like-minded,” the bloc’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, told POLITICO in an interview when asked about his hopes for climate collaboration between the two powers ahead of this week’s EU-Canada summit in Montreal.
But this rosy view sidesteps a less comfortable reality: Canada is a major fossil fuel producer whose climate ambitions fall far short of Europe’s.
And under Carney, those ambitions are weakening.
Last year, Canada produced more crude oil than any other country outside the big three producers, Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United States. Oil and gas are Canada’s biggest exports by far, and the industry lobby is an influential force in Ottawa.
In his previous life as a central banker, Carney was considered a climate champion. POLITICO even dubbed him an “eco warrior” in 2018. But since taking over as prime minister last year, he has weakened Canada’s climate policies at a rate few predicted, scrapping a national carbon tax and electric vehicle mandate and opening new oil and gas projects.
The list of climate laws Carney has watered down, repealed and canceled makes the EU’s own recent backtracking on green laws look minor. Some environmentalists argue it is comparable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s wholesale dismantling of environmental protections.
“The track the Carney government has taken on climate and environmental regulation has been a decisive move in the direction of the U.S.,” said Tim Gray, executive director of environmental non-profit Environment Defence. Carney, he said, “seems to be all in on fossil fuels.”
Keean Nembhard, a spokesperson for Canada’s Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, told POLITICO the Carney government is “committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero by 2050 by taking a pragmatic and durable approach.”
“This includes building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, and making significant investment in the low-carbon economy,” he said.
But Gray argued that Carney’s support for fossil fuels and weakening of environmental standards may complicate Canada’s attempts to forge closer ties with Europe, which has some of the world’s most stringent green laws.
Still, in Europe, Carney’s green image persists.
Last week, Belgian member of the European Parliament Saskia Bricmont gave expression to this faith in Carney’s commitment to climate issues when she called on him to lead a global push to put climate back on the agenda ahead of next month’s U.N. climate summit.
“Mr Carney … relaunch the fight against climate deregulation and for the restoration of biodiversity, and re-mobilize the international community around concrete, coordinated measures,” she said.
Carney’s green aura
Carney’s reputation as a climate champion is well earned. As governor of the Bank of England, he led a push among central bankers to take the economic risks of climate change seriously — memorably captured in his 2015 ‘Tragedy of the Horizon’ speech, in which he warned: “The catastrophic impacts of climate change will be felt beyond the traditional horizons of most actors.”
In 2021, after he’d left the Bank of England, he became a United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance and launched a net-zero financial alliance with some of the world’s biggest banks.
But things changed dramatically when Donald Trump took back the White House, and Carney replaced fellow Liberal Justin Trudeau as Canada’s prime minister in 2025. At the time, Trudeau and his Liberals had been way behind in the polls, battered by Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s attacks on his climate policies — in particular an unpopular consumer carbon tax.
Carney’s first act as prime minister was to scrap that tax.
Following his surprise victory in the elections that April, Carney set about promoting Canada as an “energy superpower.” To the dismay of environmental groups, he supported the “Pacific Link,” an oil pipeline costing tens of billions of dollars, designed to carry Alberta crude to Canada’s Pacific coast for export to Asia.
He then pushed for thawing relations with Beijing in January, a not-so-subtle pitch to find a new crude oil client that isn’t the U.S. Germany, rushing to replace its dependence on Russian energy, signed a long-term agreement in July to buy Canadian liquefied natural gas from a proposed port in British Columbia, despite backlash from environmental and indigenous groups.
He also scrapped laws on electric vehicle adoption, dropped plans for an emissions cap on oil and gas companies, watered down an existing industrial carbon price and introduced legislation to weaken environmental permitting rules for big infrastructure projects, which critics dubbed the “bulldoze nature bill.”
A landmark moment, according to Gray, came in November 2025, when Carney signed a memorandum of understanding with the government of Alberta, Canada’s biggest oil-producing province. That document, which promised to turn Canada into a “global energy superpower,” contained a string of promises to promote oil and gas and water down federal climate laws.
So why the dramatic shift?
Carney, who has repeatedly positioned energy sovereignty as a bulwark against Trump’s economic aggression, offered his realpolitik response at an event in the heart of Alberta’s oil patch earlier this month.
“There’s a structural challenge of energy security and the existential challenge of climate change, and these challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and on who they can rely on to supply it,” Carney said in Fort McMurray, Alberta on Oct. 1.
“Even under any plausible net zero scenario, the IEA [International Energy Agency] forecasts the world will still need tens of millions of barrels of crude a day. So the question is: who will emerge as the world’s trusted suppliers? It should be us. It must be Canada.”
Not black and white
Carney, to be sure, is no Trump. Unlike the U.S. president, he has retained his pro-climate rhetoric and promised to develop the country’s mining of critical minerals essential for the clean energy transition.
In May, he unveiled a national electricity strategy which aims to double Canada’s largely clean electricity grid by 2050 to meet soaring demand. “The path to net zero is electrification,” Carney said then.
In August, he announced C$10 billion in federal support for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric project in Newfoundland and Labrador, saying it will be the largest clean energy project in North America, capable of generating enough electricity to light up the equivalent of Canada’s three largest cities.
Nembhard, Environment Minster Dabrusin’s spokesperson, also pointed to new electricity transmission lines, electric vehicle subsidies and a C$2 billion plan to retrofit homes with heat pumps.
Canadian climate activist Alex Cool-Fergus said she does not think Carney “believes that oil and gas is the future,” but is simply being pragmatic about Canada’s economic reality.
“The electricity strategy that came out in May was incredibly important, and actually gives us a better idea of what his thinking is for the future,” she said.
Trudeau’s approach to climate change was “very much values-based, and it was about doing the right thing,” said Cool-Fergus. “I think that’s hit its limits. Carney’s approach makes more sense for the world of 2025-2026.”
The limits of the partnership
Hoekstra, the EU’s commissioner for climate, said he wants to deepen ties with Canada. “Given all the complications the world is facing, it is imperative to team up more closely with your closest partners,” he said. But he’s realistic about how far that relationship can go.
Hoekstra has ambitions of cementing the EU into a global network of economies with carbon pricing regimes. While he conceded nothing is “off the table,” he acknowledged linking the EU’s Emissions Trading System with Canada’s “quite different” version, which varies from province to province: “You’re talking about a completely different horizon, and that is not something we would attempt in the very short run.”
There are, however, other ways Hoekstra believes the EU and Canada can closely link on environmental issues.
“Doubling down, tripling down on electrification, on solar, on wind, on nuclear, on batteries,” he said, adding “that is one area that I think is potentially very fruitful for my portfolio.”
Another is critical raw materials, a key focus of this week’s summit.
Brussels is exploring ways for the European Investment Bank, the EU’s lending arm, to help finance the mining of Canadian mineral deposits that could supply the bloc with an alternative to Chinese-produced metals, with a framework agreement expected to be signed during the summit. Lithium, copper, nickel, and other key ingredients for electric vehicle batteries and clean energy technologies essential for decarbonizing Europe are abundant but often undeveloped all over Canada.
This week’s summit will also explore investing in infrastructure on Canada’s east coast to liquefy and ship Canadian gas to Europe, a move that could help the EU diversify its supply away from the U.S., which, along with Norway, has become Europe’s dominant supplier since it cut off Russian gas imports following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Many EU member countries will welcome success on these goals. But Gray warns that closer ties with Canada could lead to deeper penetration by the country’s powerful fossil fuel lobby, which he described as a “major, major force.”
“They’ll be spending time trying to make sure the alignment with the EU is in a direction that favors them,” he said.
The EU’s lack of oil and gas resources — and, by extension, the absence of a powerful fossil fuel lobby — has kept climate policy relatively bipartisan in the EU. Could inviting a fossil fuel “superpower” into the fold as an “associate member” change that?
“That would depend very much on what is an ‘associate member,’” Dutch Climate Minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said.

Airline groups urge US CDC to reconsider Ebola declaration requirements
- Airlines for America and IATA urged the CDC to rethink new Ebola attestations for all US-bound travellers. They said the Nov 3 deadline is too short and the rules are hard to apply.
- The groups said the plan is “unworkable” and too broad. They questioned why air travel is targeted, while maritime and surface transport are not included.
- The CDC’s rules aim to stop Ebola entry after outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudan. The virus has killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Major American and foreign airlines urged the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to reconsider new rules requiring all US-bound travellers to attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days.
The International Air Transport Association and Airlines for America (IATA), in separate previously unreported letters reviewed by Reuters, urged the CDC to reconsider the plan announced last week that takes effect on Nov 3 and is aimed at preventing entry by people exposed to Ebola.
“It is unreasonable for the US government to require all airlines serving the US market to modify their procedures to accommodate the collection of attestations from each individual (passenger and crew) flying to the United States in less than two weeks,” IATA, which represents over 370 member airlines in more than 130 countries, said in the letter dated Oct 27.
The new CDC order requires all US-bound airline passengers and crew members to file digital or paper attestations. The CDC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Airlines for America, which represents United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Delta Air Lines, said in a separate letter to the CDC that the plan was unworkable.
“Changes to check-in systems, digital signatures, station procedures, and training cannot readily be completed in the allotted time,” the group said, calling on the CDC to “reconsider a more proportionate and measured US response”.
Airlines for America said that in 2025, US Customs and Border Protection screened about 130 million air passengers, but fewer than 25,000 of them had a connection to the Democratic Republic of Congo.
IATA also questioned why the plan only applied to air travellers.
“The US government has clearly decided that the risk of the importation of Ebola into the United States is high enough to justify this global process. It is difficult to understand why other modes of transportation – maritime and surface – were not included in this mandate,” IATA said.
The CDC in May adopted rules barring foreign airline passengers who had been in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the centre of the 2026 outbreak, in the prior three weeks. The restrictions were extended to US citizens in July.
Airlines for America urged the CDC to exempt crew members, the US military and jumpseat travellers, calling the plan “overly stringent, costly and burdensome to Americans and the US airline industry”.
As part of the Ebola measures, the CDC since earlier in 2026 has barred foreign nationals from the US if they were in Uganda or South Sudan in the prior three weeks.
The Bundibugyo strain of the virus spread undetected for months before the outbreak was declared in May. It kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS

One week out: Top mid-term races that will decide who controls US Senate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:53:59 UTC
10:53:59 KST

Voters across the United States are preparing to head to the polls on November 3 for high-stakes midterm elections that will determine Congress's composition and whether President Donald Trump can advance his legislative agenda during his final two years in office.
All 435 House seats and 35 of the Senate's 100 seats are contested.
Republicans currently hold 53 Senate seats against 45 Democrats and two allied independents, meaning Democrats require a net gain of four seats to secure a governing majority.
Competitive races across traditional Republican strongholds have put several seats in jeopardy, while Democrats also defend vulnerable terrain Trump carried in 2024.
Crucial Senate battlegrounds
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican former congressman Mike Rogers for retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters's seat.
A Detroit News/WDIV-TV survey placed El-Sayed ahead 51.4 percent to 45.1 percent. If victorious, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
Maine
Five-term Republican Senator Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, former president of the Maine Senate.
A Marist poll showed Jackson edging Collins 49 percent to 47 percent, with Jackson questioning Collins’s centrist credentials in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024.
Texas
Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton confronts Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico for retiring Senator John Cornyn's seat.
A Univision/YouGov poll gave Talarico a 50 to 45 percent lead. Talarico has accused Paxton of corruption, whilst Paxton benefits from Trump's endorsement and funding from Elon Musk.
Ohio
Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown seeks a Senate return against appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted.
Recent surveys from Fox News and InsiderAdvantage place Brown ahead by three to five percentage points, with Brown campaigning heavily against data centre development.
Alaska
Republican Senator Dan Sullivan trails former Democratic representative Mary Peltola in surveys under the state's ranked-choice system, as elevated fuel costs tied to the Iran conflict burden local households.
Iowa
Republican Representative Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek for the seat vacated by Republican Senator Joni Ernst, with surveys divided as agricultural communities react to fuel prices and tariffs.
Kansas
Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton in a contest drawing $71 million in advertising, with polls indicating a virtual tie in a state that last elected a Democratic senator in 1932.
North Carolina
Former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper holds significant polling leads over Republican Michael Whatley for retiring Senator Thom Tillis's seat, prompting national Republicans to withdraw campaign funding.
Other pivotal contests
In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff leads Republican Representative Mike Collins by eight percentage points in an Atlanta Journal-Constitution survey.
In New Hampshire, Democratic Representative Chris Pappas leads former Republican Senator John Sununu by six points.
Meanwhile, Nebraska features an uncommitted independent challenger, Dan Osborn, leading Republican Senator Pete Ricketts 46 percent to 45 percent, introducing a potential wild card into majority calculations.

Isro to launch NVS-03 on Oct 30, but NavIC has a long way to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:50:06 UTC
10:50:06 KST

NVS-03 is the third satellite in Isro’s next-generation navigation series
BENGALURU: Isro will launch its next navigation satellite, NVS-03, aboard the GSLV-F18 rocket on Friday (Oct 30) at 11.51 pm from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota.GSLV-F18 is the 20th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV). The mission is a crucial attempt to rebuild India’s ailing NavIC navigation constellation, which currently lacks enough operational satellites to provide standalone positioning services.The roughly 50-metre rocket, with a lift-off mass of about 420 tonnes, will place the approximately 2,250-kg NVS-03 into a geosynchronous transfer orbit with a perigee (closest point to Earth) of 170 km, apogee (farthest point from Earth) of 37,023 km and inclination of 20.75°.
Why the launch mattersNVS-03 is the third satellite in Isro’s next-generation navigation series, designed to ensure continuity of the services of the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, now called Navigation with Indian Constellation, or NavIC.NavIC is intended to provide Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) services across India and up to about 1,500 km beyond the country’s landmass, reducing dependence on foreign navigation systems.
“NVS-03 carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured clocks and introduces the L1 signal, in addition to the existing L5 and S signals,” Isro said. The addition is expected to widen compatibility with more user devices and strengthen NavIC’s civilian and strategic utility.But the launch comes at a time when NavIC is operating below its minimum requirement. Earlier this year, union minister Jitendra Singh told Parliament: “After completion of mission life (10 years) of IRNSS-1F, presently the NavIC constellation has three satellites — IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01 — for providing PNT services.To provide basic positioning service, a minimum of four operational satellites are required in orbit.” The govt acknowledged that, as a result, “the NavIC constellation cannot provide standalone positioning service, however timing service is functional.”A troubled programmeNavIC’s difficulties stem from a combination of ageing satellites, atomic-clock failures and a failed replenishment mission. IRNSS-1F completed its 10-year mission life in March 2026; soon after, Isro said its procured onboard atomic clock stopped functioning, removing the satellite from navigation service.The more immediate setback was NVS-02, launched on Jan 29, 2025 aboard GSLV-F15. Although the satellite separated successfully and deployed its solar panels, it could not perform the orbit-raising manoeuvres needed to move from its elliptical transfer orbit to its designated circular orbit.An Isro apex committee traced the anomaly to the spacecraft’s pyro system. It found that the drive signal did not reach the pyro valve in the oxidiser line of the orbit-raising engine, preventing the engine from firing. The committee concluded that the most likely cause was disengagement of at least one contact in each of the main and redundant connector paths.Isro said the panel recommended corrective measures to enhance redundancy and improve the reliability of pyro-system operations, and that these recommendations have already been implemented.
Still a long roadNVS-03’s successful launch would raise the number of navigation-capable satellites, but it will not by itself restore NavIC to full operational strength. The spacecraft must first complete orbit-raising manoeuvres, reach its designated orbit and be validated for service.The govt has said NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in an advanced stage of realisation, meaning further launches will be needed before NavIC regains a robust, redundant constellation.NavIC’s return to standalone positioning service depends not only on NVS-03 reaching orbit, but on Isro executing the post-launch operations that failed for NVS-02, and on the timely induction of the satellites that follow.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Bloomberg, 2 trading firms agree to pay for faster access to Trump’s Truth Social posts: Sources

Bloomberg, 2 trading firms agree to pay for faster access to Trump’s Truth Social posts: Sources
- Bloomberg, Susquehanna and Jump Trading bought faster access to Trump’s Truth Social posts, paying up to US$100,000 a month for a timing edge that could move markets.
- Trump Media says Truth API is an “industry-standard” product, but critics call it unethical and possibly illegal. Democrats want an SEC probe.
- Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation are suing, saying the paid service is “profoundly corrupt” and may block equal access to government information.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Truth Social, the social media platform founded by President Donald Trump, has signed up news and data provider Bloomberg and two Wall Street firms for faster access to the president’s posts, which it sells for up to US$100,000 (S$128,117) a month, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
The firms are Susquehanna International Group and Jump Trading, both high-frequency trading firms focused on algorithmic and automated strategies.
The service gives subscribers a timing advantage to Trump’s posts on Truth Social, which has the potential to create swings in financial markets and to give Wall Street traders an edge not available to everyday investors.
The companies’ purchase of the Truth API service has not been previously reported. An API is a programming interface that is used as a digital bridge that allows one system to connect to another.
Trump Media and Technology Group announced its fastest-access product in July, and pitched it to trading firms and other financial institutions. The deals likely mark the first time a business tied to a sitting president has sold access to their statements, which some critics have called unethical.
While Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan ventures into untested legal territory, Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump in August, seeking to block the White House from posting official government announcements exclusively on Truth Social while the paid feed exists.
The suit, which is ongoing, alleges that erecting a financial barrier to government information is potentially unconstitutional and favours wealthy Wall Street firms.
Bloomberg, Jump Trading and Susquehanna declined to comment.
In a statement, Trump Media said: “Truth Social offers an industry-standard API product for which there is significant demand across industries. We take customer confidentiality seriously.
“This reporting is based on misleading information being peddled by anonymous sources aimed at harming our company, customers and shareholders.”
The president’s family trust owns 41% of Trump Media, and Trump is the trust’s sole beneficiary.
Shares of the company have fallen more than 50% so far in 2026.
The market value of Trump Media has been volatile since it went public; it closed at about US$8 billion in its March 2024 debut, but is now worth about $1.8 billion. The company has lost about $1.76 billion since 2024, including non-cash charges.
Trump Media’s Securities and Exchange Commission filings list Trump Jr, as the trustee of the family trust, with sole voting and investment power.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle said neither Trump nor his family is directly involved in any portfolio investment decisions but did not address the allegations that the president was improperly using his office.
Trump Jr did not respond to a comment request. Questions about his role in the business were referred to the Trump Organization, which did not respond to requests for comment.
Market-moving posts
The service is designed to allow customers to read Trump’s posts more quickly than a human would by constantly checking the app.
The timing advantage, described as 50 milliseconds by Trump Media officials, can matter to trading firms or financial news and data organisations because a US president’s posts can create swings in the value of assets.
High-frequency Wall Street traders employ software that ingests news headlines, company announcements and government statements to search for market-moving information. The software can read, analyse and execute a trade in thousandths of a second.
In one example of how Trump’s posts can move markets, oil futures sank after he announced on Truth Social a ceasefire in the Iran war in April.
In August, Trump Media told investors it had “signed more than 10 customer agreements” which Reuters was unable to confirm. The company did not name the clients, but said they were primarily Wall Street trading firms that are paying between US$60,000 and US$100,000 a month.
Reuters, a financial-news competitor to Bloomberg, said in a statement: “We will assess the service, but have no current plans to subscribe.”
Selling faster access to Trump’s posts has drawn criticism from Democrats and media entities.
Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and California’s Adam Schiff said in July that they had asked the US Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the service violated securities laws.
They described it as a “shocking abuse” of office by a president seeking personal gain, without providing further explanation.
The SEC declined to comment.
A TMTG spokesperson said: “Congressional Democrats continue to mischaracterise Truth API either out of ideological opposition to free markets or a failure to grasp the distinction between public and nonpublic information.”
In the lawsuit against Trump by Intercept Media and non-profit Freedom of the Press Foundation, the plaintiffs described the paid data service as “profoundly corrupt”.
The suit also alleges the service would violate the First Amendment rights of the public who do not have equal access to the information and it would violate the Fifth Amendment by charging “unreasonable sums” for equal access to information guaranteed by law.
The White House’s Ingle did not directly address the lawsuit or its allegations, saying: “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office.” REUTERS

“Together with Yana Lantratova, the Human Rights Commissioner of the Russian Federation, we are continuing to prepare a humanitarian mission to assist the civilian population of Oleshky,” the ombudsman said.
He noted that this work is taking place through the mediation and coordination of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, whose efforts have helped the parties reach the necessary agreements and move toward their practical implementation.
“Since October 27, a ceasefire has been in effect in designated areas, which the parties are observing. Demining of the routes is currently underway. This is an important step for the safe delivery of humanitarian aid and the subsequent evacuation of civilians who wish to leave the city,” Lubinets noted.
Under the agreements reached between Lubinets and Lantratova as heads of the negotiating teams, the parties continue to work on carrying out the mission. The common goal is to provide assistance to people and ensure they can reach safe territory. “We are continuing our work, prioritizing the lives and safety of civilians,” Lubinets added.
As reported by Ukrinform, Melania Trump stated that she had secured a local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which applies only to Oleshky. According to the White House press office, the parties agreed to temporarily suspend all military operations in Oleshky to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through an agreed-upon safe corridor.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that he does not know which side people will choose during the evacuation from Oleshky, but he understands that it is easier to move deeper into the territory temporarily occupied by the Russians. However, he said, many people want to return to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government.
