Australia has highest rates of anorexia and bulimia globally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:00:22 UTC
10:00:22 KST

Australia has highest rates of anorexia and bulimia in world, study finds
In short:
Global cases of anorexia and bulimia nervosa have increased by 71 per cent since 1990.
Australia has the highest rates per 100,000 people for the two eating disorders in the world.
What's next?
Experts suggest more needs to be done, including increasing funding to ensure the numbers do not continue rising.
Cases of anorexia and bulimia nervosa are affecting Australians at a world-leading rate.
The unenviable record comes amid a 71 per cent increase in cases of the two eating disorders globally in the past 30 years.
This jump translates to about 18.1 million people worldwide living with anorexia or bulimia as of 2023, according to a study published today in JAMA Psychiatry.
Australia has the highest rate of any country in the world, with 1,026.5 per 100,000 people estimated to have one of the two disorders.
University of Queensland epidemiologist and study senior author Damian Santomauro said Australia's ranking was "surprising and concerning".
"Usually we do see higher prevalence of eating disorders in high-income settings," he said.
"[But] I'm surprised to see it as high as it actually is compared to the US or other locations in Western Europe."
Eating disorders disproportionately affect younger people and are a mental health condition involving an unhealthy relationship with food.
Butterfly Helpline clinical psychologist Sarah Cox said the study confirmed what people with lived experience of eating disorders, their families and healthcare professionals had been reporting for years.
"Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses that affect a significant number of people in Australia, and that the number of people affected is growing," Ms Cox said.
How data was calculated
The findings are part of the Global Burden of Disease study, the world's largest health project that includes research about the impact of mental disorders on the overall population.
"It was the first of its kind that really highlighted that mental disorders can be on par or if not more burdensome than some physical disorders," Dr Santomauro said.
To calculate the prevalence of these disorders, researchers use surveys rather than treatment data to ensure they capture people who may not have access to treatment.
This allows them to analyse data from around the world since 1990, when the study began.
Worldwide, the researchers estimated 3.92 million people had anorexia and 14.2 million had bulimia. They forecasted cases would keep growing through to 2050 globally.
They also calculated that for the two eating disorders, that led to a loss of 3.81 million disability adjusted life years around the world.
Dr Santomauro noted that Australia's high number of cases may be partially due to the way survey data was collected.
"Almost all the surveys that are done in Australia tend to use a different methodology [to the rest of the world]," he said.
"But I don't think that it's purely because of that type of data."
Ms Cox said the numbers, while high, might also mean Australia had more research and data.
"We might be seeing the problem more clearly than other countries," she said.
Impact higher for youth and females
Dr Santomauro was not surprised cases had increased globally, and said that although there were many factors, one "hypothesis" was increased time online.
"I would expect prevalence to get worse in more recent years because of social media, the Instagram and body image issues that youth are encountering today," he said.
Females accounted for nearly 70 per cent of the 18.1 million global cases and about 41 per cent of all global cases were in young people aged 10 to 24.
Jeanette Chan, an economist and public policy professional who has lived experience with an eating disorder, said people from migrant and non-western backgrounds could have more difficulty gaining help for eating disorders.
"Growing up as a migrant, I didn't have a lot of language or understanding around what mental health was or what mental health issues were," they said.
"In Australia, we're a very multicultural society, and eating disorders are often a very Western conceptualisation of issues surrounding food and eating.
"That affects the way that we make sense of what is problematic."
While Jeanette was able to gain help for her eating disorder, they said more funding for treatment and prevention was needed.
"There's been a lot more investment, but not enough in eating disorders in Australia over the last several years," they said.
Case numbers are underestimated in Australia and abroad
While Australia had the highest rates, the largest relative increases in the incidence of anorexia and bulimia occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and South-East Asia.
The study noted a few limitations, including data gaps for mortality related to bulimia, as well as less information from some low-income countries.
Dr Santomauro said the impact of eating disorders broadly was also underestimated since only anorexia and bulimia were included.
"The numbers … sound very, very large, but it's also really capturing a small proportion of the total eating disorder burden globally.
"There's also binge eating disorder, unspecified feeding or eating disorder and other very prevalent eating disorders that we don't capture."
Ms Cox agreed.
"In Australia, more than 1.1 million people will experience an eating disorder in any given year," she said.
"While anorexia and bulimia are serious eating disorders worthy of attention, we also need to expand the research focus to ensure people living with … other eating disorders are included in the conversation. "
Ms Cox said projections that cases would continue to rise highlighted the need to fund early treatment and prevention.
"We can lower these numbers, and there is more that can be done," she said.
"Getting help early improves the chances of recovery, but many people face barriers to care, including cost, living in regional areas and stigma, and many people with an eating disorder never get treatment."

The National Gallery of Victoria presents the first major Australian solo exhibition of the Melbourne artist, whose work references African studio photography, family archives, Catholic imagery and science fiction, while paying tribute to the myths and traditions of Dinka Bor culture in South Sudan.

Atong Atem is an Ethiopian-born, South Sudanese artist living in Naarm/Melbourne. Her work has been exhibited widely across Australia and internationally
Atong Atem
Wed 28 Oct 2026 21.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 23.08 EDT
Our Neighbour Was a Witch, from the Surat series, 2022
Transforming herself through textiles, paint, costume and symbolic objects, Atem uses her body as a vessel to explore themes of race, gender and colonialism, as well as the beauty and resilience of her Dinka Bor culture and Melbourne’s African diaspora
Men in This Town 01, from the series Men in This Town, 2024

Of the exhibition, Atem said:‘If the body is a terrain, who gets to be the geographer and who becomes the cartographer? My practice as an early career artist has sought to make signposts on the body as a politicised landscape; to document, archive and speculate. These tensions between heritage, identity and place are at the crux of my impulse to make art’
In Dinka Bor culture, names are not owned individually; they are inherited to honour ancestors. Atem’s photographs embody this idea, acting as visual relics that unite a family across time and space
Josephine Margaret Bakhita, from the series Surat, 2022
Surat examines the mythological aspects of portraiture through family photographs. Atem recreates portraits of relatives known to her only through images, using herself as a bridge for memory and ancestral links
In Banksia Atem turns her lens towards African, African American and Caribbean convicts and free settlers who arrived with the first fleet. The work prompts audiences to reconsider the foundations of Australian identity
Scar 2, from the Scars and Constellations series 2024
Scars and Constellations explores the complex relationship between sea, sky and the histories of colonial trade and navigation. Central to the series is scarification, a Dinka Bor cultural practice carrying deep meaning in identity, ritual and healing that is also layered with the histories of conflict
This large-scale wall installation is a world-premiere exclusive commission exploring the stories held in the skies and constellations, weaving together Dinka dance, traditional beading and Catholic iconography. The work also references the astronomical concept of the false cross, which are groupings of stars that mimic the Southern Cross. The work explores how we position ourselves within vast cosmic, historical, cultural systems that surround and shape us
I Have Two of Everything 1, from the series Surat, 2022
Atem’s work has been exhibited widely across Australia and internationally, including at the National Gallery of Victoria, the Art Gallery of New South Wales, London’s Tate Modern and Victoria and Albert Museum, Rotterdam’s Wereldmuseum, Shanghai’s Fotografiska and Saarbrücken’sStadtgalerie
A fully illustrated new monograph produced in partnership with Thames & Hudson Australia will be published to coincide with the exhibition. The book includes essays by Osei Bonsu, Jorge M Pérez, Clothilde Morette; reflections from Atem Yaak Atem and Anna Abul Malual Aguer; an interview with the artist and Natasha Bullock and Anna Honan; and an afterword by Tony Ellwood

What Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs says about the US midterms
The tipping discussion in Tarantino’s 1992 crime thriller was unexpectedly prescient about American capitalism’s trajectory
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Chow Chung-yan began his journalistic career at the South China Morning Post and rose to become editor-in-chief in 2025. 
When I first watched Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs in 1992, I was struck by its inventive opening. Tarantino launched a gritty crime thriller not with a gunfight or a heist but with eight mobsters in a diner, finishing breakfast while bickering over Madonna and tipping etiquette.
By depicting hardened criminals as ordinary men carping about daily trivialities, Tarantino dispensed with the genre’s macho clichés, rendering the characters disarmingly authentic. Decades later, the subject of tipping still dominates daily American life.
On my recent visit to the United States, that famous anti-tipping monologue came back to me like recurring deja vu. Whether in conversation with intellectuals, corporate executives or hard-pressed students, the subject inevitably surfaced. Increasingly, I heard Mr Pink’s voice, the mobster who stubbornly refused to tip, echoed by people born long after the film’s release and by those who have never seen it.

COP31 must amplify people power, not oil lobby voices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

The climate crisis is also a human rights crisis – claiming lives and turning life upside down for countless communities across the world.
But while those profiting from fossil fuel expansion retain privileged access and influence over global climate negotiations, the people facing its harshest consequences, such as Indigenous Peoples or those living in climate-vulnerable communities, remain largely shut out of the decision-making.
As directors of Amnesty International in Brazil, Türkiye and Australia, countries with a leading role in COP30 and COP31, we have seen how effective climate action depends on people being able to speak, organise, protest and participate.
Last year in Belém, fossil fuel lobbyists outnumbered every national delegation except Brazil’s, exposing the imbalance of power within climate negotiations. COP31 should confront corporate capture and expand public participation. Instead, serious concerns have been raised over whether civil society will be able to speak freely and safely in Türkiye.
Rights curbs supercharge climate breakdown
Yet, the human rights needed to confront this crisis and demand justice are being eroded.
Authoritarian practices are supercharging climate breakdown by restricting protest, silencing defenders and shielding fossil fuel interests from scrutiny. Attacks on women, LGBTI+ people or members of other marginalised communities divide societies, weaken collective action and divert public attention while fossil fuel expansion continues.
That is why the assault on civic space in Türkiye, the host of COP31, should alarm every government preparing to attend the summit.
In September, Turkish authorities launched a nationwide operation targeting LGBTI+ organisations, activists and human rights defenders. Homes, venues and offices were raided, people were arrested and imprisoned, and social media accounts belonging to activists, journalists and human rights groups were restricted, including that of Amnesty International Türkiye.
This is part of a decade-long crackdown that has weakened judicial independence, ignored international judgments and restricted peaceful assembly, association and expression. Whoever is targeted, the effect is the same: dissent is silenced and fear spreads.
For COP31 to succeed, Türkiye must end its human rights crackdown.
“For COP31 to succeed, Türkiye must end its human rights crackdown. “
Worrying signals from co-host Türkiye
Against this backdrop, the agreement between Türkiye and the UN on hosting COP31 is alarming.
Article 11.11 requires participants to respect Türkiye’s laws and regulations and refrain from interfering in its “internal affairs”. Article 11.12 reintroduces language on waiving immunity that was omitted from Brazil’s COP30 agreement.
Turkish authorities are already invoking vague notions of “public morality” and “harm to the family” to investigate people and restrict expression. The agreement could therefore have a chilling effect on activists, defenders and journalists.
Could criticism of Türkiye’s fossil fuel policies, its treatment of environmental defenders or its crackdown on LGBTI+ organizations be characterised as interference in “internal affairs”? Nobody attending a UN climate conference should have to ask.
Türkiye and the UN should publicly guarantee that participants can speak, organise, report and protest peacefully without discrimination, intimidation, surveillance, detention or reprisals. Governments ought to challenge the agreement’s flaws before arriving in Antalya.
Brazil offered progress, but not perfection
COP31 must build on Brazil’s approach. Its COP hosting agreement committed to an inclusive and non-discriminatory conference, while its presidency adopted a more open and participatory tone. COP30 saw record participation by Indigenous Peoples, but access did not guarantee influence: many key decisions continued to be shaped behind closed doors.
Commitments made in Belém ultimately depend on domestic political choices, and Brazil’s October election results point to a legislature that may be less willing to uphold them. This could put the rights of Indigenous Peoples, Quilombola and traditional communities at greater risk.
When protections at home weaken, international spaces become even more vital for affected populations to speak out, and hold decision-makers accountable. COP31 must guarantee freedom of expression and peaceful assembly outside the “Blue Zone” (the UN-protected area) and grant civil society greater access to negotiations.
Environmental defenders are driving change
As documented by Amnesty International, communities resisting fossil fuel expansion and building fairer alternatives are facing harassment, surveillance, criminalization, disinformation, violence and restrictions on peaceful protest. They include: First Nations people in Australia challenging offshore oil and gas exploration, artisanal fishers in Brazil’s Guanabara Bay fighting for environmental justice, and activists defending Akbelen Forest in Türkiye from coal mining expansion.
These communities are rights-holders, knowledge-bearers, and political actors protecting territories and forging effective climate responses. Governments must protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say.
Discover more stories of environmental human rights defenders around the world who are standing up for people and the planet:
COP31 must confront fossil fuel power
To protect human rights, governments must use COP31 to advance three urgent priorities.
First, they must end fossil fuel expansion and accelerate a full, fast, fair, funded and human rights-compliant transition away from fossil fuels. States most responsible must go further and faster, ending fossil fuel subsidies and redirecting public resources towards rights-respecting renewable energy.
Second, they must ensure the transition protects rights and leaves no one behind, including by making the Just Transition Mechanism operational, funded and accountable.
And third, they must scale up public, grants-based climate finance for mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage, without pushing lower-income countries further into debt.
COP31 will not deliver these outcomes without the knowledge and expertise of front-line communities.
Brazil must defend the participatory progress made at COP30. Türkiye must reverse its crackdown and protect civic space. Australia, as president of negotiations, should secure an ambitious, human rights-centred outcome while confronting restrictions on peaceful climate protest at home.
The climate crisis cannot be solved behind closed doors. The doors must remain open, and people must have the power to shape what happens inside.
“The climate crisis cannot be solved behind closed doors. The doors must remain open, and people must have the power to shape what happens inside.”

Trump says imported robotics pose national security risks but does not impose tariffs
- Trump said imported robotics and industrial machinery pose national security risks, based on a year-long probe.
- He did not impose immediate tariffs, instead ordering talks with trading partners and a report back in 180 days.
- The move protects US manufacturers for now, but tariffs may still come if talks fail; the FCC also barred new Chinese robots and power inverters.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump found on Oct 28 that imported robotics and machinery pose national security risks but did not impose any immediate tariffs, instead ordering officials to hold talks with foreign governments on import levels.
The decision spares US manufacturers, which rely on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery, from immediate new tariffs but leaves open the threat of tariffs if talks with trading partners fall short.
Following a probe that lasted more than a year, Trump directed the US Commerce Department and US Trade Representative to jointly negotiate agreements with trading partners to address concerns about imported robotics and industrial machinery, and said he could still impose tariffs at a later date.
He directed the agencies to report back in 180 days on the status of the talks with trading partners.
Trump in September 2025 opened a probe to review imported robotics and industrial machinery, such as programmable computer-controlled mechanical systems and industrial stamping and pressing machines.
The robotics probe covered machine tools for cutting, welding and handling workpieces, autoclaves and industrial ovens.
Laser and water-cutting tools and machinery are also included.
The US Federal Communications Commission in July barred imports of new models of Chinese robots and power inverters.
The rule allows existing models of humanoid and quadruped robots to be imported.
Some analysts forecast broad adoption of humanoid robots, topped with AI-enabled “brains”, in consumer and industrial arenas, while booming data centre construction in the US will depend on reliable sources of inverters.
“(Robots) collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots,” the FCC said in July.
The Commerce Department said the United States relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery.
In July, the department completed a probe into imported commercial aircraft, jet engines and parts, and found foreign goods raise US national security concerns. REUTERS

Canada and EU drop associate membership plan in bid to deepen ties
Canada and the European Union will pursue closer ties but have dropped a proposal for associate EU membership, according to a joint declaration ahead of Thursday’s summit in Montreal. Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US, despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Canada and the European Union (EU) agreed to "ever closer association" but dropped the contentious idea of associate EU membership in a joint declaration seen by Reuters ahead of a Montreal summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney starting on Thursday.
The declaration, which officials plan to make public on Friday, said work to define the Canada-EU relationship would continue until another summit next year.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's suggestion of associate membership six weeks ago had been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries on the summit declaration, with Germany leading a group that argued they could not sign up to a concept that had no legal status and had not been fleshed out, diplomats said.
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney's strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on America since US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada's efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.
There is no precedent or legal definition for an EU “associate member”.

Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act,” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week is the launch of further formal negotiations that will take another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an associate member, including an acknowledgement that defining the term would take another year.
The statement includes a joint initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through "new subsea cable infrastructure". It also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.

Julian Karaguesian, a former adviser at Canada’s Finance Ministry, described the summit as “a bit of a show”. “Canada’s effort to be closer friends with the EU is very ill-defined,” he said, adding that increased collaboration with the EU would not necessarily address Carney’s drive to diversify the country's relationships. Canada ships nearly 70% of its exports to the US while the EU accounts for about 9% of Canada’s total trade.

'Highly provocative' statement

“All that talk of multilateralism and support for international law is basically like sticking a finger into President Trump’s eye,” said Barry Appleton, an international trade lawyer and fellow at the Balsillie School of International Affairs in Waterloo, Ontario.

“This is a highly provocative statement from the EU and Canada,” Appleton said.

Albania imposes $6,000 fine for demonstrators present at a protest that turns violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:53:26 UTC
09:53:26 KST

Albania has introduced fines of more than $6,000 for demonstrators who participate in a protest that turns violent, even if they don’t personally commit violent acts, as the government tries to clamp down on the gatherings calling for the prime minister’s resignation.
The capital, Tirana, has been racked by months of anti-government protests that in recent days have deteriorated into pitched battles between the security forces and protesters.
The leaderless movement started peacefully in May, with rallies against a luxury hotel project in a nature reserve, backed by US president Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
It morphed in mid-October into a wave of student-led protests against perceived corruption, shortcomings in the health system and the lack of prospects for young people in the country of 2.3 million people.
On Wednesday, prime minister Edi Rama’s government adopted legislative measures imposing fines of up to 500,000 leks (€5,500, US$6,130) for “anyone who chooses to remain in a crowd” that is carrying out acts of violence or looting in a public space, or “concealing their identity”.
The average salary before tax in Albania is €930 (US$1,026) per month.
Police were also given powers to temporarily restrict gatherings in certain areas, including near educational, healthcare and government institutions if there was a risk of violence. The measures also provide for sanctions against online incitement to violence and compensation for small businesses damaged during protests.
The measures take immediate effect but must be approved by parliament within 45 days to remain in force.
Rama said on Sunday that he was inspired by a French bill, passed by the parliament’s upper house on Wednesday, that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations.
The prime minister has repeatedly blamed “foreign actors” for the violence and accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation. Rama has also called for “dialogue”.

Screwworm infests dog in Arizona, widening US cases
- New World screwworm has infested a dog in Arizona, the third US state affected. The dog had a wound with maggots, and testing confirmed the case.
- The USDA is restricting animal movement near the area, stepping up checks, and releasing sterile flies. State vet Dr Ryan Wolker said: “We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly.”
- The outbreak is spreading again after decades of eradication, with 71 US cases since June and 18 active. It is also complicating livestock trade with Mexico and adding pressure to record beef prices.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – New World screwworm, a parasitic fly that eats warm-blooded animals alive, has infested a dog in Arizona, widening cases to a third US state, the US Department of Agriculture said on Oct 28.
The first detection in Arizona was in Cochise County, which borders Mexico, according to the USDA.
The dog had a wound on its back that was infested with maggots, consistent with screwworm, and scientific testing verified the infestation, the Arizona Department of Agriculture said.
The dog was receiving veterinary care, it added.
“We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly,” state veterinarian Dr Ryan Wolker said in a statement.
The Arizona case marks the latest sign that screwworm, eradicated from the US decades ago, may be regaining a foothold despite federal efforts to contain it, complicating the USDA’s attempts to reopen livestock trade with Mexico and ease record beef prices ahead of the mid-term elections.
The USDA said it was restricting animal movement in a 20km zone around the case, increasing surveillance of live animals and releasing sterile flies that combat screwworm in response to the infestation.
The agency halted livestock imports from Mexico in 2025 to try to keep out screwworm, which advanced north through Mexico and Latin America.
It detected screwworm in a calf in Texas in June and then confirmed additional cases in Texas and New Mexico.
As of Oct 28, the agency had reported 71 screwworm cases since June, and 18 were active, according to its website.
Infestations have multiplied since September, when there were only two active cases.
The import halt helped tighten US cattle supplies and push beef prices to record highs for American consumers, raising concerns about affordability ahead of the midterm elections.
The USDA began to resume livestock imports from Mexico in August and has restarted trade at three ports of entry in Arizona and New Mexico.
The agency has said it next plans to resume imports from Mexico in Nogales, Arizona, on Nov 30, if conditions for safe trade are in place.
Last week, the USDA confirmed the first case of screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Texas. REUTERS

Israel begins counting over 500,000 double-envelope ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:51:21 UTC
09:51:21 KST

Tarek Chouiref
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
 Israel began counting double-envelope ballots early Thursday, with more than 500,000 votes potentially affecting the final distribution of parliamentary seats.
The count was expected to finish by Thursday evening, Israel’s public broadcaster reported.
Double-envelope ballots are used by voters casting their votes away from their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers and displaced residents.
Officials check identification details on the outer envelope to prevent duplicate voting, then separate it from the anonymous ballot before counting.
The remaining votes could change individual parties’ seat totals and the balance between the rival blocs.
After all regular ballots were counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for predominantly Arab parties, according to Channel 12.
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List was projected to secure 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, giving Arab parties a record combined representation of 19 seats.

EU countries block Canada's 'associate membership' plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:49:00 UTC
09:49:00 KST

EU countries block Canada's 'associate membership' plan
October 29, 2026
European Union member states have blocked a proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to grant Canada a special status as an "associate member" of the bloc.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and several other EU leaders pushed to remove the term from a draft declaration ahead of a two-day EU-Canada summit beginning Thursday in Montreal, according to diplomats cited by the dpa and AFP news agencies.
Instead, the revised document calls for a plan to establish "closer ties" between Canada and the EU without membership.
The declaration was approved by EU member states on Wednesday evening and is expected to be published on Friday, at the end of the summit.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen, European Council President Antonio Costa and several EU commissioners are attending the talks.
Why did EU countries oppose Canada's associate membership?
Von der Leyen first proposed making Canada the EU's first "associate member" in September during a speech attended by Carney.
However, the proposal raised questions among member states because existing EU treaties do not provide for such a status.
Diplomats said several governments were concerned about the lack of clarity surrounding the proposed arrangement and insufficient consultation between the European Commission and EU member states.
Germany, France and Italy were among the countries that raised objections, although they broadly support closer cooperation with Canada.
Another concern was that the term "associate membership" had already been used in discussions about Ukraine's potential accession to the EU.
Merz had previously suggested such a status for Ukraine as an intermediate step toward full membership. Under his proposal, Kyiv could participate in EU summits and ministerial meetings without voting rights.
Von der Leyen, however, used the same term to describe a different arrangement for Canada, a country that does not have a legal path to EU membership.
An earlier draft of the summit declaration would have allowed Canada to participate in consultations on major EU political and regulatory initiatives as an associate member.
It also called for the full scope of the arrangement to be defined by the 2027 EU-Canada summit.
Carney, meanwhile, played down the dispute over the wording of the summit declaration.
He said the precise terminology mattered less than the practical benefits closer cooperation would bring to Canadians.
What will closer EU-Canada cooperation involve?
Despite the disagreement over terminology, both sides intend to significantly deepen their partnership.
The revised declaration focuses on an "Alliance for the Future," a term Carney has frequently used to describe relations between Canada and the EU.
The initiative aims to remove trade barriers, facilitate investment and secure supplies of critical raw materials, medicines and technologies during crises.
Both sides also want to strengthen cooperation on energy, climate protection, artificial intelligence, security and education.
Canada could gain broader access to EU programs covering research, education and defense.
A new economic council is planned to bring together businesses from both sides of the Atlantic.
The declaration also calls for a study into the feasibility of increasing Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe.
However, EU governments watered down several economic commitments in the original draft.
An explicit goal of deeper financial market integration was removed. Instead of promising preferential treatment in economic security measures, both sides now intend to limit potential negative effects on each other.
How has Donald Trump affected EU-Canada relations?
The push for closer ties comes amid growing uncertainty over relations with the United States under President Donald Trump.
Trade disputes, US tariffs and Trump's territorial claims have raised concerns in both Canada and Europe about Washington's reliability as a partner.
Both sides hope that closer cooperation will help reduce their dependence on other countries and strengthen their ability to pursue common interests.
Trump previously dismissed the idea of Canadian associate membership in the EU as ridiculous.
He also threatened consequences if the arrangement harmed US interests, warning that he could impose high tariffs or halt trade with Europe in several sectors.

Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre
BENGALURU: Space regulator-cum-promoter Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) has selected six private space-sector entities for seed-fund grants under its AI INSPIRED programme, which aims to encourage the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in space technology.The projects span precision landing, space situational awareness, debris detection, satellite servicing and refuelling, automated target recognition, and spacecraft autonomy. Two other entities have been selected for mentorship and technical support, including access to Isro facilities for technology validation.The programme, announced in Feb 2026 under IN-SPACe’s Seed Fund Scheme, has a total outlay of up to Rs 6 crore, with each selected entity eligible for a grant of up to Rs 1 crore. The funding is intended to help start-ups and micro and small enterprises develop AI-based solutions for space applications.Among the selected projects, Agnikul Cosmos will develop an edge AI-enabled vision-based terminal navigation module for precision landing. The technology is aimed at improving navigation during the final stages of a landing manoeuvre.Digantara has been selected for its Agentic RSO Evaluation Suite (ARES), while EON Space Labs will develop an intelligent optical payload using field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based edge AI.
The latter project aims to enable real-time space situational awareness and detection of space debris.OrbitAid Aerospace will work on machine-learning-assisted pose estimation algorithms for on-orbit servicing and refuelling. Such algorithms can help spacecraft determine their relative positions and orientations, an important requirement for operations involving approaching, docking with or servicing another spacecraft.Omnipresent Robot Technologies has been selected for an automated target recognition project covering applications such as defence and docking. TakeMeToSpace will work on adaptive spacecraft autonomy through an AI modernisation programme for attitude determination and control systems (ADCS), which help establish a spacecraft's orientation and maintain its intended direction.
IN-SPACe has also selected Foucault Private Limited and AkashaVeda Technologies for mentorship and technical support, although they are not listed among the six seed-fund grantees.
Foucault will work on an autonomous collision avoidance system for spacecraft using AI and machine learning. AkashaVeda’s project focuses on AI-based mission management, covering both onboard and ground operations. The two entities will receive opportunities to use IN-SPACe and Isro facilities to validate their technologies. They will also be considered for technology transfer from the Department of Space.As per IN-SPACe, the initiative is part of its efforts to expand private participation in India’s space sector by supporting the development of indigenous technologies and products.

US Justice Department loses initial bid to block votes from alleged non-citizens in California

- Judge David Carter said the request broke constitutional rules and warned it could cause chaos, erode trust, and wrongly strip voters of their rights.
- The Justice Department appealed, while California said its safeguards are strong and the federal claims rely on “suspect data”; similar moves were also made in Alaska and Washington.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – A US judge strongly rebuked the Trump administration on Oct 28 by rejecting a request by the Justice Department to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots for the midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the department alleges are likely non-citizens.
The decision marks the latest setback for President Donald Trump’s effort to boost the federal government’s role in elections ahead of the Nov 3 midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress.
US District Judge David Carter issued the decision after a hearing on Oct 27 in Los Angeles federal court over the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from counting any ballots from the individuals it flagged.
The Justice Department’s lawsuit, filed on Oct 15, was a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before an election and signalled the Trump administration’s willingness to contest the midterm results in court.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon its own constitutional election procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch,” Carter wrote on Oct 28.
The judge, an appointee of then Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department’s last-minute request to exclude more than 20,000 ballots ran afoul of “longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections”.
Carter warned that a ruling in the Trump administration’s favour could create chaos and cause thousands of registered voters to “potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve”.
“Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable,” Carter wrote. “Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the executive (branch) can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.”
The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials,” Justice Department lawyer Bill Essayli said in a statement.
“This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution.”
California has said the state’s safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data” and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.
California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives – 52 – than any other state.
Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its “sanctuary state” policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by non-citizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare.
Appeals court rejected emergency request
The hearing comes after a federal appeals court on Oct 26 rejected an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.
The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.
It had argued that a restraining order was necessary to ensure that California did not impede prosecutors’ ability to enforce a federal law that makes it illegal for non-citizens to vote in federal elections.
But Carter said the Justice Department never explained why counting ballots would impair any prosecutions under the law, as states are not required to help the federal government investigate and prosecute crimes.
Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to competitive races.
In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to prevent certification of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters.
Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot.
In Washington state, the Justice Department on Oct 26 sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens.
Washington’s top election official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results.
California had 23 million registered voters as at December 2025, while Washington had five million registered voters as at 2024, state records show.
Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government’s methods for scrutinising state voter lists to identify non-citizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalised citizens for removal from the rolls. REUTERS

US hospitals and nursing homes are breeding grounds for deadly superbugs – CDC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:45:34 UTC
09:45:34 KST

US hospitals and nursing homes are breeding grounds for deadly superbugs – CDC
More than four in five US deaths linked to drug-resistant infections involve pathogens commonly associated with hospitals and nursing homes, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The agency’s Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report released this week draws on data from 2023 and estimates that 19 types of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths annually in the US. Seven bacterial threats commonly associated with hospitals and nursing homes accounted for more than 42,000 of those deaths, along with nearly $12 billion in healthcare costs.
Antimicrobial resistance occurs when germs develop the ability to withstand drugs designed to kill them, making infections difficult or impossible to treat. Elderly people, those with weakened immune systems, and patients undergoing invasive medical procedures are particularly vulnerable.
Among the pathogens classified as urgent threats is Candida auris, a potentially deadly fungus that can resist multiple medications and survive on surfaces in healthcare facilities. It primarily affects seriously ill patients and can cause dangerous bloodstream infections.
A separate CDC study published in July found that reported cases of Candida auris more than doubled from 2022-2024, rising from 2,882 to 6,197. Most cases for which the type of medical facility was identified were detected in hospitals, including those that provide long-term treatment for seriously ill patients.
The CDC noted that many healthcare-associated infections are preventable, but much of the progress in combating drug resistance was lost during the Covid-19 pandemic, when staffing shortages, overcrowding, and disruptions to infection-control practices contributed to a rise in infections.
The warning comes as US hospitals face mounting financial and staffing pressures. A Harvard-led study published earlier this month found that 432 hospitals closed nationwide from 2010-2025, resulting in a net loss of 216 facilities and more than 24,000 beds.
Nursing homes are also struggling with bed and staffing shortages. An investigation in September by KFF Health News found that declining capacity forced some patients to remain hospitalized longer because suitable care facilities were unavailable.

Discord to make public server messages searchable on Google

Discord to make public server messages searchable on Google
The feature will apply to Discoverable Servers, public communities with at least 1,000 members that anyone can join without an invitation. Discord said on October 27 that the changes aim to make information shared in its communities more accessible to people searching for answers online.
Starting November 16, every Discoverable Server will have a public web page describing the community. These pages may also display automated summaries of public channel discussions, helping visitors understand what members are talking about.
From mid-December, individual messages from public channels may also appear on web pages and in search results. The rollout will be gradual, and messages sent before the launch will not be included.
Server administrators can choose which channels appear on the web or disable the feature entirely. Members can also opt out through User Settings > Data and Privacy. Usernames and profile pictures will not appear alongside messages on web pages.
The rules vary by region. In the EU, the UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia and South Korea, the setting is off by default for members. Users must enable it for their messages to appear online. Teen users are excluded from the feature until they reach adulthood.
Discord said the change could help people find answers to questions about games, strategies, events and other topics that communities discuss on the platform. The company noted that useful information often remains difficult to find because it is buried in server conversations.
The changes will not affect private servers, direct messages or group direct messages, which will remain private.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Reddit, Discord and Roblox expanded the use of biometric age verification technology provided by US-based identity company Persona.

Pakistan makes U-turn on Taiwan airline ban – media
Pakistan has restored overflight rights to two Taiwanese airlines after they stopped using its airspace three days earlier, according to AP, Bloomberg, and Dawn.
On Wednesday, Islamabad issued permits allowing Taiwan-based China Airlines and EVA Air to use Pakistani airspace until March 27, 2027, the outlets reported, citing official documents.
Hours earlier, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif defended restrictions on Taiwanese carriers, citing Islamabad’s longstanding adherence to Beijing’s One-China policy.
“The aviation division follows the One-China policy – only mainland China is allowed,” Asif told Bloomberg. “We have permitted only Chinese airlines to fly over Pakistan.”
According to flight-tracking data, Taiwanese airlines began rerouting flights to avoid Pakistani airspace on October 25. Taipei condemned Islamabad for what it described as undermining Taiwan’s sovereignty and “politicizing and weaponizing airspace,” according to Taiwanese media.
Most countries, including the US and Russia, do not formally recognize Taiwan as an independent state. Beijing considers the self-governing island part of China and seeks reunification, preferably through peaceful means, but has not ruled out the use of force. Washington and several other Western governments maintain unofficial ties with Taiwan and supply it with weapons, drawing condemnation from China.
Pakistan’s restrictions reportedly went further than Beijing’s own rules, which permit some Taiwanese airline operations in mainland Chinese airspace.
China and Pakistan maintain close political and military ties, describing their relationship as an “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership.” China is Pakistan’s principal arms supplier, and Islamabad has consistently supported Beijing position on Taiwan.
Taiwanese airlines largely avoided Russian airspace after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, although neither Moscow nor Taipei formally prohibited them from using it. Following the Pakistani restrictions, several Taiwan-Europe flights were rerouted through Russia.
According to Bloomberg, no country had previously imposed a blanket overflight ban on Taiwanese commercial airlines. In April, Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar withdrew overflight clearances for Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te’s aircraft, forcing him to postpone a visit to Eswatini. How do technology and U.S. militarism shape one another from the past to the present, and what ethical responsibilities arise for researchers, technology workers, and the public? American Anthropologist organized the roundtable to address these urgent questions. This roundtable features Catherine Lutz, Lucy Suchman, and Roberto González in a discussion moderated by Jing Xu and Yang Zhan, associate editors of the journal. The discussion traced the historical expansion of U.S. militarism, the role of science and technology, and shifting cultural beliefs and political economy. ‘Show courage, Eisenkot’: Arab parties offer support but face silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:22:45 UTC
09:22:45 KST

Israel's Arab parties, projected to win a combined 19 seats in the next Knesset, have offered to help replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government, even without joining a new coalition. But despite their potentially decisive role in breaking the political deadlock, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and key parties in his bloc have so far shown little willingness to embrace their support.
The Joint List formally declared Wednesday evening that it was prepared to cooperate with the opposition to establish an alternative government, following an election in which an unusually high turnout among Arab voters significantly strengthened their parliamentary representation.
The offer comes as Netanyahu and his Likud party challenge the legitimacy of votes cast for Arab parties, citing alleged election irregularities, while Eisenkot's opposition bloc remains divided over whether it should rely on Arab lawmakers to form a government.
Neither of the two main political blocs is projected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-member parliament, leaving the Arab parties in a potentially pivotal position. Yet their electoral success does not necessarily mean they will be included in the negotiations that determine the next government.
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen described the election results as a "historic day," saying they demonstrated the growing political influence of Israel's Arab citizens. "We have proven that we are a political force that cannot be ignored, and that no future can be built here without our voice," Jabareen said.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, he made clear that removing Netanyahu from office was the Joint List's immediate priority.
"The public that placed its trust in us wants to change the current reality and bring down the Netanyahu government. The first step is removing Netanyahu and the Knesset speaker," he said.
Jabareen also strongly rejected Likud's allegations of election irregularities, accusing Netanyahu's party of trying to undermine the legitimacy of Arab voters.
"There are people in Israel who want to deny the legitimacy of votes for Arab parties. There were no violations in the election, and Likud's accusations are the words of sore losers," he said.
Jabareen further claimed that Netanyahu wanted to remain in office as caretaker prime minister and drag Israel into another election as early as next March.
Asked about potential cooperation with Eisenkot, Jabareen said the Joint List had not yet examined the opposition leader's plans for forming a government. However, he emphasized that his party wanted to see the current coalition removed from power.
"Ben-Gvir is responsible for the escalation in murders in Arab communities. Bringing down the government means bringing down Smotrich and Ben-Gvir and the government that incites against us," he said. "We need a change in policy and a government without racists."
In a formal statement issued Wednesday evening, the Joint List went further, explicitly declaring its willingness to cooperate politically with Eisenkot's bloc to replace Netanyahu.
"The Joint List will do everything in its power to bring an end to Netanyahu's rule. We are prepared for political cooperation to establish an alternative government that will present a genuine alternative and commit to a fundamental change in the racist policies of the current government," the statement said.
The party also demanded that any future government recognize the rights of Israel's Arab citizens and end what it described as the exclusion of Arab representatives from the country's political institutions.
The Joint List attributed its electoral gains to an unusually high turnout in Arab communities, which it described as a response to the outgoing government's policies.
"Our public understood the significance of this moment and flocked to the polls, from the Galilee and the Triangle to the Negev," the party said, referring to major regions with significant Arab populations.
"Faced with incitement, intimidation and racism, they turned Election Day into an unprecedented show of strength against the Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich government."
The party also said thousands of Jewish Israelis had voted for the Joint List, arguing that the support reflected a broader constituency committed to peace, equality and Jewish-Arab partnership.
It pledged to continue working toward a future based on full equality and genuine political partnership.
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas, whose Islamist party is running separately from the Joint List, also addressed the strong performance of Arab parties, offering an ironic expression of gratitude to members of the outgoing government.
In an interview with i24NEWS, Abbas credited the electoral surge to the very politicians who had been among the Arab parties' fiercest critics. "The unprecedented electoral achievement is entirely thanks to Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and the entire government, which neglected Arab society in Israel," he said.
His remarks reflected a broader argument among Arab political leaders that frustration with the Netanyahu government's policies, particularly its handling of crime and violence in Arab communities, helped mobilize voters.
Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi delivered an even more explicit message to Eisenkot, saying his party was willing to help establish a minority government that would remove Netanyahu from office.
Crucially, Tibi stressed that the Joint List was not seeking ministerial positions or demanding to become a formal member of the coalition. Instead, it was prepared to consider supporting such a government from outside, provided it received commitments on issues important to Arab citizens.
Among those conditions would be a serious government effort to tackle crime and violence in Arab communities, alongside a halt to home demolitions in Bedouin towns and villages. Tibi said the demolitions had intensified during Netanyahu's tenure.
Such an arrangement could allow Eisenkot to establish a minority government supported by Arab lawmakers in parliamentary votes without formally including their parties in the coalition.
Tibi said he had received hundreds of calls and messages since the first exit polls were published Tuesday night, including an approach from what he described as a "significant figure" within the opposition bloc. He acknowledged, however, that Eisenkot himself had not contacted him.
Tibi said he had conveyed a clear message that the Joint List was both "ready" and "willing" to help pave the way for a different government. But for that to happen, he said, Eisenkot and his political partners would have to "show courage."
The appeal comes despite opposition from several prominent parties in Eisenkot's bloc to forming a government that would depend on Arab political support.
Although the Arab parties' projected 19 seats could prove crucial in preventing Netanyahu from securing another term, cooperation with them remains politically contentious among Eisenkot's potential coalition partners.
The 19-seat dilemma facing Eisenkot
The strong showing by the Joint List and Ra'am followed an exceptionally high turnout among Arab voters, approaching 80%, according to election figures cited in the report.
The mobilization helped increase Arab representation in the Knesset and may have prevented Netanyahu's bloc from reaching the parliamentary majority needed to form a government independently.
But it has also created a difficult political question for Eisenkot: How can he replace Netanyahu without relying on the parliamentary strength of the Arab parties?
The dilemma is particularly complicated by the conditions Eisenkot has set for parties seeking to join his government. Those include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and acknowledging Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.
Those requirements could make formal cooperation with Arab parties difficult, even if their support from outside a coalition would not necessarily require them to become government partners.
The Joint List's willingness to consider external parliamentary support offers Eisenkot a potential alternative to a traditional coalition agreement. But it remains unclear whether such an arrangement could overcome the objections of his other political partners or satisfy his own conditions.
For now, the Arab parties are openly signaling their willingness to help bring about a change in government, while Eisenkot has yet to present a framework for cooperation with them.
On Wednesday evening, he reiterated that his priority was establishing what he called a "Zionist government committed to military conscription."
The contrast leaves Israel's opposition facing a central question in the aftermath of the election: whether it is prepared to rely on the Arab lawmakers whose votes could be essential to ending Netanyahu's rule.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s escape to the US: How it happened
- Flavio Bolsonaro defied a court order to surrender his passports after his election defeat and ongoing investigations, sparking confusion and a search for his whereabouts.
- He denied plans to leave Brazil, but later crossed into Argentina with valid travel documents, while Brazilian police said there was no official record of his departure.
- He then flew via Ecuador to Miami, arriving in Florida with his family and a cancelled diplomatic passport, according to US border records.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - Flavio Bolsonaro’s clandestine escape to the United States bewildered Brazil and triggered a frantic search for his whereabouts.
The Supreme Court had ordered the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro to forfeit his passports after his electoral loss on Oct 25, amid fears he would leave the country due to ongoing investigations against him.
But the defeated right-wing presidential candidate failed to hand them in, choosing instead to flee to the US via Argentina and Ecuador.
AFP takes a look at the frenzied 24-hours that left the world scratching its head as Bolsonaro went off the grid.
Refuses to concede
Bolsonaro makes a brief, stone-faced speech from Brasilia on the night of Oct 25 following his electoral defeat to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
He refuses to recognise the result and promises to seek an annulment of the election.
Exit blocked
The next day, the 45-year-old posts a video on Instagram, speaking outdoors in front of a bare wall.
He tells his followers that the Supreme Court has banned him from leaving the country in “a clear attempt to intimidate me.”
“I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” he said.
The ban on his travel is linked to one of several ongoing investigations against him.
Vacant vehicle
On Oct 27, the Argentine outlet Infobae reports that Bolsonaro plans to board a flight in the north-eastern city of Puerto Iguazu.
Journalists including AFP witness Bolsonaro’s official motorcade leaving his Brasilia residence.
It is initially impossible to know whether one of the three black cars is carrying him.
Local media reports the dispersal of the motorcade soon afterward, while the driver of the middle vehicle – usually transporting the politician – rolls down the window and shows that no one is on board.
Going dark
As speculation runs rampant, a police source confirms the cancellation of Bolsonaro’s Brazilian and diplomatic passports to AFP.
American media meanwhile reports that the defeated candidate is en route to the US.
Back in Brazil, confusion reigns, and Bolsonaro’s campaign manager says he has no idea where his boss is.
“I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it,” a dumbfounded Rogerio Marinho tells the press in Brasilia.
Hopping borders
It turns out that while the world had been speculating on his whereabouts, Bolsonaro is still in Brazil.
He only crosses the border into Argentina at 0150 GMT on Oct 28, the neighbouring country’s immigration authorities announce – over 12 hours after the first reports emerge that he has left.
The senator enters Argentina “with valid travel documents and no legal impediment” via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge linking the Brazilian city of Foz do Iguacu with Puerto Iguazu, Argentine authorities say.
Flavio also holds an Italian passport.
It remains unknown how he got to Argentina from Brasilia, more than 1,500km away.
Brazilian police say there is no official record of his departure from the country.
They say they are investigating his failure to hand over his passports, but this does not classify him as a fugitive.
Flight
A private jet then whisks Bolsonaro and his family to Ecuador’s port city of Guayaquil, Argentine immigration authorities say.
The plane makes a brief refuelling stop at the virtually empty airport.
AFP reporters witness the aircraft taking off again, and the FlightAware website shows that it is heading to Miami.
Some 927,000 people track its course via the website Flightradar.
Arrival
Around 12 hours after their departure from Argentina, the Bolsonaro family hits the tarmac at Florida’s Opa-Locka airport.
He enters the United States with his cancelled diplomatic passport, according to the Department of Homeland Security website that tracks border controls.
Flavio Bolsonaro wears a black shirt and shoulders a backpack as he disembarks the plane alongside his wife and two daughters, AFP observes.
Minutes later, a vehicle drives away from the airport. AFP

Leak website releases data on tens of thousands of US govt employees
- Distributed Denial of Secrets said it released data on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security staff, including names, contacts and sensitive job details.
- The leak appears to come from a group called “Department of Peace”, which said it wanted to “limit further harm by the DHS” and support oversight.
- Reuters verified some details and said the files exposed nonpublic information on internal charts and operations, raising privacy and security risks.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets said on Oct 28 it has released data on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees, including details about officials working in sensitive fields such as surveillance and human intelligence.
DHS said in a statement it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively”.
The agency said it was working to ensure its employees were properly protected and would update the public “when more information is available”.
The disclosure – which the non-profit data transparency group says draws on information obtained by an entity calling itself “Department of Peace” – is the third major government data leak to have made headlines in the past month.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed the theft of a massive trove of data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, including sensitive job details and medical information from thousands of bureau employees.
In October, the Defence Department was hit with a class action lawsuit following a breach that exposed data on millions of current and former military personnel.
The DHS data includes names, phone numbers and e-mail addresses of employees from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other DHS component agencies.
Also included in the data were job titles and e-mail groups, which, among other details, showed which agents were assigned to special operations, surveillance jobs, computer forensics and undercover work.
In a statement, Distributed Denial of Secrets co-founder Emma Best said the hacktivist and journalist known as “maia arson crimew” developed a search tool for the data that would allow the public to browse it.
Best said the tool would “replace anonymity with accountability” and empower journalists, guide public records requests and boost congressional oversight.
Crimew said her tool would provide “FOIA material for years to come!”
The Department of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a statement included with the data it said that DHS employees “have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”.
The Department of Peace in March claimed responsibility for hacking DHS and posting documents related to contracts with outside vendors.
Best’s statement said the Department of Peace harvested the data from the Okta sign-on service used by DHS. Reuters could not immediately corroborate the claim.
Okta said in response to a Reuters query: “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised.”
Reuters could not immediately verify the authenticity of the entire data trove, but it was able to match personal information about six DHS employees named in the leak to credit bureau records and breach data carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs.
Reuters called three DHS employees directly and was able to confirm their phone numbers and other details. One said it was the first they had heard of a breach.
In several cases, the data tracked information available on DHS employees’ LinkedIn profiles. But in others, the data revealed nonpublic data about internal DHS organisation charts or previously undisclosed programmes or operations. REUTERS

A Russian disinformation campaign cloned Euromaidan Press to blame Ukraine for Russia’s own strike on Kramatorsk (we took the fake down)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
00:02:14 UTC
09:02:14 KST

Euromaidan Press has been impersonated as part of a Russian disinformation campaign. A copycat website was created, with a hyphen added to our name, which published a fabricated article alleging a Ukrainian drone had killed civilians in Kramatorsk that cites anonymous "Ukrainian OSINT channels" amid copies of our real news reports. In reality, that 8 October strike was a Russian aerial bombing of two public buses that killed 33 civilians.
The fabrication is part of a years-long Russian disinformation campaign to impersonate and clone trusted news brands, predominantly in Europe, and publish false reports under their names. The disinformation research project Gnida tied our case to Storm-1516, one of several overlapping Russian operations, alongside the older Doppelganger, and NewsGuard, which reached out to us while preparing its own debunk, attributes the fake to the same operation. The fabricated Kramatorsk report comes amid an ongoing effort to erode Western support for Ukraine, as Russia's war goes on, and to sow distrust among Western political elites.
The claim and the actual 8 October attack
The fake started circulating on 24 October, one day after the forged publication appeared on our website. It started making rounds on X together with a forged video with a version of our logo claiming that "newly obtained footage" featured the remains of a Liutyi drone that "independent OSINT channels" claimed were "quickly removed from the scene." No specific OSINT channels were named; no sources were linked.
The forged video, apparently produced with AI, and the link were spread by X accounts such as @vick55top, @indiaTales7, @TheWorld_Update, @Wonder_star21, @Theunk5555, @SilentBriefHQ1, and @Suriyakmaps, where it was subsequently removed. The videos on those accounts averaged 400,000 to 500,000 views, far more than the accounts' modest follower counts and their usual engagement would produce, a likely sign of inauthentic amplification.
On 25 October, the Russian disinformation monitor Gnida Project flagged this as a case of the Storm-1516 disinformation campaign. Other recent cases flagged by Gnida included advertisements of Russian Geran drones, claims of the Shamonda virus being leaked from a "Ukrainian biolab," smears against US Democratic candidates, and a fake on a similar copycat "toronto-sun.ca" website alleging that President Zelenskyy purchased a nuclear bunker in Nova Scotia.
As for the actual content of the fake, the real event is one of the most thoroughly documented atrocities of the month. On 8 October 2026, Russian forces struck two public buses in Kramatorsk with an aerial bomb, killing 33 people and wounding about 18. Such attacks are, sadly, a daily occurrence in cities on the frontline. There was no Ukrainian drone and no removed wreckage. The fabrication simply reassigns a Russian mass killing of civilians to its victim, which is the entire point.
The fake site was not a single page. It scraped our entire website, mirroring our genuine articles, and injected the fabricated one among them, so the lie traveled under the credibility of real reporting. The look-alike domain was registered on 15 October, eight days before the fake appeared, according to who.is data.
Storm-1516
Gnida Project identified the fake as part of Storm-1516, a Russian influence operation that clones trusted news brands to spread fabricated stories, and NewsGuard, which contacted us about the impersonation, attributes it to the same operation. NewsGuard has documented the tactic generating some 900 false reports over three years; the same operation has targeted France and Germany and has recently impersonated other outlets, including in Ukraine, such as this fake report on a copycat website pretending to be the New Voice of Ukraine.
Storm-1516 is one of several overlapping Russian operations that impersonate real media. Since 2022, the Doppelganger network has cloned whole Western outlets and government sites, and it is still active, flooding France with more than 200 fake sites before its 2026 elections. Polish fact-checkers literally call the tactic “attack of the clones.” A second operation, Matryoshka, floods social media with cheap fake videos credited to real outlets. Storm-1516, first identified in late 2023 and later named by Microsoft, grew out of Russia's Prigozhin-era troll operations, is the most elaborate of the three, and has overtaken RT and Sputnik as Russia's main disinformation machine. Its attacks combine cloned websites and fake videos.
NewsGuard counts some 906 fabricated reports impersonating 163 outlets from 21 countries since 2023, Euronews, the BBC, Deutsche Welle, and France 24 most of all, as well as the Kyiv Independent. The fakes nearly all bend one way, to erode Western support for Ukraine. Some smear Ukraine's leaders, a fabricated story that 20,000 Ukrainian soldiers evacuated to France had deserted into criminal gangs, invented claims that first lady Olena Zelenska fled abroad. Others, like the one aimed at us, flip Russian actions onto Ukraine. A separate Storm-1516 fabrication, a false claim that Ukrainian officials bought yachts with misappropriated US aid, was repeated in 2023 by JD Vance, then a US senator.
We filed a copyright and abuse complaint with the host, Namecheap, and a phishing report with Cloudflare, and pressed the registrar. The complaints worked: the clone has been taken down.
How to take down a cloned news site
Impersonation is cheap to set up, and any outlet can be next, so here is the procedure our technical team used, which other newsrooms can follow to take a clone down quickly.
- Cut the scraping pipeline. Run a DNS lookup (ping, nslookup, or dnschecker.org) on the cloned domain to expose the hosting IP behind any basic masking, then add a custom block rule in your Cloudflare WAF (Security, WAF, Custom Rules) targeting that IP, which cuts off the scraping scripts in real time. Watch the WAF logs over the next 48 hours in case the attackers rotate to new scraping proxies.
- Unmask the infrastructure and send formal notices. Run an IP WHOIS lookup (ipinfo.io) to identify the host, for example Namecheap or DigitalOcean, and the registrar, then submit DMCA takedown and phishing notices to the host's legal portal or abuse address. Include side-by-side URL comparisons of the original and cloned pages, clear documentation of the brand spoofing and the injected disinformation, and a good-faith legal statement with full contact details.
- Block access and de-index from search. Report the clone to Google Safe Browsing under social engineering and impersonation, which, once verified in 24 to 48 hours, makes Chrome, Firefox, and Safari show a full-page red warning to anyone who tries to open it. Then file a Google Search Console DMCA removal request to pull the cloned URLs out of search results.
- Escalate to the registrar. Submit a registrar abuse complaint demanding a full suspension of the domain, a ClientHold status, on the grounds of bad-faith typosquatting and identity theft, and push your open abuse ticket IDs through your Cloudflare account to skip the standard queue.
Be sure to read the automated replies from the host and Cloudflare and answer them promptly. Those acknowledgments often ask for specific additional information, and a fast, complete reply keeps the ticket moving instead of stalling in a queue.
How to spot Russian Storm-1516 attacks
Many users on X called out the signs: a look-alike domain (our only website is euromaidanpress.com, with no hyphen), a claim sourced to unnamed "OSINT channels," and a story that reassigns a Russian attack to Ukraine.
We never publish an image or video without crediting its source, and we never cite anonymous OSINT experts: our reporting traces to a first source. Trust only reports that name the first source of a claim and label the origin of their images and video. If you cannot trace the source, you cannot trust the report.

No clear winner in Israeli election with nearly 90 percent of votes counted
