Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:58:29 UTC
03:58:29 KST

Iran, Russia move toward joint construction of small modular nuclear reactors
TEHRAN — Iran is moving toward an agreement with Russia to accelerate the joint construction of small modular reactors (SMRs), as the country advances its domestic nuclear capabilities and seeks to expand the role of nuclear energy in meeting rising electricity demand, the spokesman for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) has said.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, who also serves as the AEOI’s deputy for International, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, made the remarks in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) on Wednesday, discussing Iran’s participation in the Sixth Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power in South Korea and the growing importance of nuclear energy worldwide.
Kamalvandi said Iran was in the process of signing a protocol with Russia aimed at accelerating cooperation on the joint construction of SMRs, a technology attracting increasing international attention for its potential to provide flexible, scalable sources of electricity.
“We are also in a good position in the field of small modular reactors,” he said, adding that the proposed protocol would help advance bilateral cooperation in their construction.
Unlike conventional nuclear power plants, SMRs are designed to be built in smaller units and can be deployed individually or in groups, offering countries an additional option for meeting growing energy needs. Their modular design also lends itself to standardized production and the deployment of multiple units.
Kamalvandi said global electricity demand was rising rapidly, driven in part by advances in artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. These developments, he argued, were making the expansion of nuclear power an increasingly important consideration for countries seeking reliable electricity supplies.
Environmental challenges have also heightened international interest in nuclear energy, he said, as countries look for cleaner and more dependable sources of power.
According to Kamalvandi, the world currently generates around 400,000 megawatts of nuclear electricity, while Iran accounts for approximately 1,000 megawatts. He added that announced plans to triple global nuclear power capacity would require the construction of around 1,200 power plants comparable in size to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant in southern Iran.
The AEOI spokesman underscored nuclear power’s capacity to provide a stable, continuous supply of electricity, distinguishing it from wind and solar generation, whose output fluctuates with weather conditions and the availability of sunlight and wind. Such reliability, he said, is particularly important as electricity consumption increases and modern economies become more dependent on advanced technologies.
Kamalvandi also highlighted the broader applications of nuclear technology beyond electricity generation, including nuclear medicine, agriculture and industry, emphasizing its potential contribution to scientific and technological development across multiple sectors.
Reflecting on Iran’s progress, he said his approximately 14 years of continuous service at the AEOI had given him a clear perspective on the country’s achievements in developing its nuclear industry.
“I can say with confidence that the country’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and we have now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants,” he said.
His remarks highlighted Iran’s emphasis on strengthening indigenous scientific, engineering and industrial capabilities, while pursuing international cooperation in emerging nuclear technologies.
The proposed Iran–Russia protocol on small modular reactors represents a further step in Tehran’s efforts to develop its nuclear power sector and broaden cooperation in a field that is gaining prominence as countries confront rising electricity demand, energy-security concerns and environmental challenges.

The New M6 MacBook Pro Has a Serious Price Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:57:22 UTC
03:57:22 KST

Just yesterday, Apple refreshed its 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip inside, and it’s currently available for preorder. This is the first MacBook to get the chip (but certainly not the last), and I look forward to testing this thing out myself. But I do already have a good sense of how well it’ll perform, as I already tested this same chip in the latest Mac Mini. And it points to an issue with the current state of the Mac lineup.
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro currently costs $1,999. That gets you 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Even for as good as these laptops are, that feels like too much money for those specs. Apple raised prices across all Macs earlier this year, but the base 14-inch MacBook Pro got hit the hardest, with a $300 bump. It was already an awkward configuration, as it used the same M5 chip as the much cheaper MacBook Air models. It was such bad pricing that it ended up on my “do not buy” list. The addition of the M6 seems like it’ll add some value, especially with the improvements to GPU performance I saw in the M6 Mac Mini. It also has the dual Neural Engine, which can speed up certain AI tasks in creative applications, especially for content creators. I won’t pretend to make a final evaluation until I’ve thoroughly tested the machine myself.
The Smarter Buy
But consider this. The M6 Mac Mini is on sale for $779 right now, $120 off its retail price. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is similarly $150 off its retail price right now. You could buy both for the same price as one M6 MacBook Pro. That’s kind of insane when you think about it. You miss out on the MacBook Pro’s excellent Mini-LED display and powerful speakers, but to me, it’s a tempting alternative for a $2,000 budget.
It’s even more compelling when you consider how many people are using Mac Minis these days—more as always-on AI agent boxes that you can control remotely with any old MacBook. Pairing the M6 Mac Mini and M5 MacBook air together is a recipe for AI goodness (especially if you configure the Mac Mini up to 32 GB or 64 GB of memory).
Another alternative is the M5 MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip inside for only $200 more. It looks identical on the outside, and has better performance on the inside.
I’m still interested to see how the new M6 MacBook Pro performs, but the price alone makes me wonder if there aren’t better ways of spending your money—even while staying within the Mac lineup.

‘We are a country divided’: Who will feel betrayed by Israel’s next government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:56:43 UTC
03:56:43 KST

‘We are a country divided’: Who will feel betrayed by Israel’s next government?
Israel faces weeks of political uncertainty, as the parliamentary elections did not result in a majority for either side. A unity government could break the deadlock, but at what cost to domestic politics and regional stability?
After months of a fiercely contested race, Israelis are waking up to a political reality that offers little prospect of stability. The question is no longer who won the most seats in the Knesset, but who can form a government – and at what cost.
According to the preliminary results from the Central Elections Committee, which is responsible for counting the 7.3 million votes, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading with a projected 27 out of 120 seats. The former chief of staff and head of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, comes in second, securing 21 seats in the Knesset. These numbers will change as the counting continues.
Divided we stand
For some Israelis, the initial results have already proven disappointing.
“I really hoped that the victory of Eisenkot would be obvious and we could celebrate Bibi’s defeat. The country is tired of this man, we need a change but the results are not encouraging,” Miriam Hassan, a 40-year-old resident of Nazareth, said.
Others share her frustration. “The change bloc [a union of parties aligned against Netanyahu] did everything it could to end the rule of Netanyahu. Arab tried too. They went to the polling stations in their masses but now it is clear that the battle is not over yet. More work needs to be done for us to finally see this man handing down the keys to the premier’s office in Jerusalem,” according to Samer Nasrawi, another Nazareth resident in his 50s.
Ronen Attar, a voter of Yashar in his 30s, said:
“We voted for change, for hope, for the repair of this country. We wanted to see this government that was responsible for October 7 handing down power. Polls indicate our bloc can still form a government but everything is up in the air.”
On the other side of the political divide, Netanyahu’s supporters are celebrating.
“My entire family voted for Netanyahu,” Moshe Keif, a Jerusalem resident in his 50s, said. “He has done so much in these four years. The media and Israeli channels buried him politically, they said he will be crushed but now it is clear, Likud is still the strongest and the biggest party. Netanyahu is unsinkable.”
Itzik Dayan, another Jerusalem voter in his 50s, was less optimistic:
“I think Netanyahu should still be the PM despite his mistakes and vices. But the results show that half of the population doesn’t share these views. We are a country divided.”
Unity as a solution?
With polling stations closed and the count underway, it will take days for the final results to emerge. Even then, weeks may pass before Israel – and the world – learns who will become the country’s next prime minister.
Israel’s political system does not automatically award the premiership to the leader of the largest party. Instead, the president must nominate a candidate capable of assembling a coalition commanding at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
The problem is that neither camp appears to have the numbers.
According to the Central Elections Committee, Eisenkot’s potential partners, the Together bloc led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and Yair Golan’s Democrats – are projected to win 12, 7, and 8 seats, respectively. Together, they would hold 48 seats, 13 short of a majority.
To bridge the gap and secure the premiership, Eisenkot could seek an alliance with the Arab parties: the Joint Arab List and Ra’am, which have won 13 and 6 seats, respectively.
“I voted for them,” Hassan said. “I support the idea of them joining forces with the change bloc to oust Netanyahu from power. Only this cooperation will bring the much needed change.”
Nasrawi agrees:
“It is time for the Arab parties to start cooperating with the Jewish ones. It has been long overdue. They have a chance now. Join forces and remove Netanyahu. Then start cooperating in other spheres, be it tackling high crime rates or the economy.”
Cooperation, however, may be easier said than done. Although Arab party leaders have repeatedly pledged to support initiatives aimed at ending Netanyahu’s premiership, their political priorities remain difficult to reconcile with those of the Change bloc.
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is the clearest example. Arab parties advocate ending the occupation, withdrawing troops from Gaza, and establishing a Palestinian state. Eisenkot and his allies, with the exception of Golan, reject these positions and have pledged to take a tougher approach toward the Palestinians.
Israeli experts consider it unlikely that the Arab parties and the Eisenkot-led bloc will overcome these differences. Without their support, the former chief of staff may struggle to become prime minister. Even if he succeeds, his coalition could prove short-lived.
Netanyahu’s prospects are hardly brighter. Together with his traditional allies, including several religious parties, he commands 53 seats, 8 short of the 61 required for a majority.
To retain power, Netanyahu would need to persuade lawmakers from the opposing camp to defect or convince some members of the Change bloc to join a coalition under his leadership.
He has managed this before. On October 11, 2023, shortly after the Hamas-led attacks, he formed a unity government with Benny Gantz, who set aside his differences with Netanyahu to provide broad legislative support. This time, however, the task will be considerably harder. Several leaders in the Change bloc have already ruled out joining a Netanyahu-led coalition and pledged not to serve in ministerial positions under his leadership.
Yet neither side may ultimately have a viable alternative to a broad unity government.
According to a recent poll, around 60% of Israelis favor a unity government bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together; 33% want the former chief of staff to lead the government, 19% prefer Netanyahu, and 8% say they have no preference between the two.
Political pressure for unity is also mounting. President Isaac Herzog has indicated that he will work to establish a broad coalition between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Netanyahu, too, has urged his opponents to consider the proposal, arguing that unity is the only way to address the pressing challenges facing Israel.
Voters, however, remain deeply divided over the prospect.
“Nobody trusts Netanyahu anymore,” Nasrawi said. “I don’t see how Eisenkot agrees to sit with the man who deceived all his coalition partners in the past.”
“This government needs to go. Striking an agreement with Netanyahu is criminal. If they do so, it basically means they betrayed our trust and threw all our votes out of the window,” Hassan said.
Dayan sees things differently: “I really don’t think there is an alternative but to have a unity government.”
“We still have Iran and Hezbollah on our borders, the situation in the West Bank and Gaza is not stable either, economy needs to be fixed, and all we are doing is dividing the country into pro and against Netanyahu. Only unity can bring a change.”
No bright future in sight
A government of national unity could have consequences far beyond Israel’s domestic politics. Netanyahu previously indicated that if he remains prime minister, he intends to complete what he considers unfinished business in Iran, Lebanon, the West Bank, and Gaza.
The groundwork for further military operations is already being laid. In Gaza, the IDF is conducting near-daily raids and targeted killings. In the West Bank, the military is pursuing a major campaign in the Hebron area aimed at dismantling Hamas infrastructure. These operations could intensify and expand if Netanyahu and Eisenkot join forces.
If they don’t, the future for the region doesn’t look bright either. In the event of a political deadlock, with neither side forming a government, Netanyahu will remain interim prime minister until another round of elections is held, typically within 90 days. Unless there is a war that can push it to a further date.
A war seems to be on the horizon. Reports suggest that Netanyahu planned an attack against Iran on October 10, but was blocked by US President Donald Trump at the last minute.
Experts suggest that he might resume his plans if he remains in office, even for a short period of time.
In the coming days, Herzog is expected to consult the leaders of the various parties before deciding which candidate to task with forming a government. Once given the mandate, the candidate will have 28 days to assemble a coalition, with the possibility of a two-week extension. If the attempt fails, another candidate may get the opportunity.
For now, the clouds of uncertainty hanging over Israel show little sign of lifting. A unity government could offer a way out of the immediate political deadlock, but it would not necessarily heal the divisions exposed by the election.
Israelis who went to the polls hoping for a clear direction may find themselves facing a familiar reality: a country still divided, a government still uncertain, and a future that remains difficult to predict.

Did UK pressure on Israel help Netanyahu, or bring his opponents closer to power? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:55:41 UTC
03:55:41 KST

Just weeks before Israel went to the polls, Britain and some of its allies imposed new sanctions and bans against Israeli settlements. Today’s election results may have exposed the limits of what outside pressure can achieve.
When British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced new measures against Israeli settlements on September 8, he insisted that Britain was not trying to influence Israel’s election.
“I do not want to, in any sense, interfere in that election. The election is for the Israeli people to make their own decisions about their future. I have set out the policy of the British government, and I have made it clear that our quarrel is not with the Israeli people but with the policies of the Netanyahu government,” he told parliament.
Miliband’s answer was in response to concerns expressed by various MPs, including Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat, that the sanctions and their timing would help the campaigns of Israel’s far Right.
He acknowledged the concern but said that the international community could not wait for an Israeli opposition government to change course.
The timing raised an obvious question. With Israelis due to vote on October 27, could sanctions announced by foreign governments help weaken the prime minister they were criticizing, or would they instead reinforce Netanyahu’s argument that Israel was being singled out by a hostile international community?
The answer we see today is not straightforward. Exit polls showed Netanyahu’s bloc falling short of the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority but with, nevertheless, more votes overall than the change bloc. Likud has far surpassed Eisenkot’s Yashar, which pre-election polls had suggested could perform much better.
Of course, neither outcome proves international pressure affected how Israelis voted.
But it does shine a light on a strategy that attempted to change Israeli policy through economic and diplomatic pressure.
The timing was not politically neutral
Britain’s September announcement was more than another expression of diplomatic disagreement. Its government announced measures targeting settlement expansion, including an import ban on settlement goods and restrictions targeting individuals and companies involved in settlement growth.
The British government maintains that these measures target settlement activity, not Israel within its internationally recognized borders.
Britain had already sanctioned National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich in June 2025, as did Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and Norway, citing their alleged incitement of violence against Palestinians in the West Bank. The September 2026 measures were therefore part of a more widespread deterioration in relations rather than an isolated attempt to intervene in an election campaign.
However, the proximity to election day made the political ramifications difficult to ignore. Miliband argued that the international community could not stand by as settlement expansion continued and that Netanyahu was making Israel “less secure.”
That distinction is notable: A government can legitimately seek to influence another country’s policies without explicitly seeking to change its leadership. But when it announces punitive measures just weeks before a significant election and publicly argues that the current leader’s policies are damaging the country’s security, the boundary between policy pressure and electoral pressure becomes more nebulous.
Were the warnings ignored?
A report by The Spectator, subsequently reported by Globes, alleged that British diplomats and intelligence officials had warned the UK government that announcing sanctions before the election risked affecting Israeli politics. According to the report, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar had asked Miliband to delay the measures until after the vote, and some British officials reportedly agreed that waiting was a favorable option.
The concern was reportedly that the announcement could give Netanyahu an opportunity to present himself as defending Israel against foreign pressure, potentially strengthening rather than weakening his position.
And this is indeed the narrative that Likud members peddled in response. On September 8, Sa’ar responded by accusing the UK of “blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and in its electoral process,” calling it a “completely unacceptable attempt by a foreign government to exert external influence in the midst of an election campaign.”
These allegations are worth taking seriously but do not constitute proof that the sanctions were designed to oust Netanyahu. There is a distinction between knowingly accepting a political risk and deliberately seeking a particular electoral outcome.
How might the pressure have played in Israel?
There were at least two plausible, and potentially concurrent, effects. For Netanyahu and his supporters, the measures could have reinforced an age-old argument that foreign governments are hostile to Israel regardless of its security concerns. Sanctions become evidence not of damaging government policy but of international actors attempting to dictate Israeli decisions. Netanyahu could present himself as defending national sovereignty against outside pressure.
His government could then present itself as the defender of national sovereignty against outside pressure.
For Netanyahu’s opponents, the same measures could reinforce the argument that it is his policies that have damaged Israel’s international standing and created consequences that a different government would have to rectify.
Diplomatic isolation may have been seen not as an external attack but as a cost of the current government’s approach to the Palestinians and to West Bank settlements.
Neither mechanism can be assumed to have determined votes. Israeli voters went into this election after years of war and profound security upheaval. The consequences of October 7, confidence in the government’s handling of national security, the future of military-service exemptions for haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men, and the cost of living all offered key incentives to support or reject the Netanyahu status quo.
The election’s high turnout and the weakness of his bloc in the exit polls cannot, on their own, establish which considerations mattered most to individual voters, or that sanctions shifted support between camps.
What, then, did the pressure achieve?
The British government said its measures were intended to restrict the economic activity supporting settlement expansion and preserve the possibility of a two-state solution. The success of those measures should ultimately be assessed against the objectives: whether the restrictions were implemented, whether they affected settlement activity, and whether they changed the calculations of those involved.
If the measures had little practical economic effect, their principal immediate consequences may have been diplomatic and symbolic. If they did impose meaningful costs, they may have influenced Israeli policy regardless of which government ultimately takes office. Neither outcome can be established simply by counting seats.
The broader question is: Can foreign governments apply pressure to Israel without strengthening the very political forces they hope to influence? The election has not supplied a definitive answer.
For now, the evidence supports a more muted conclusion: International pressure became part of Israel’s election debate, but the available electoral figures do not establish that it changed the result. Whether it altered Israeli voters’ calculations, or will ultimately alter Israeli government policy, remains a separate question.

Israel election results: Netanyahu bloc wins 53 seats, opposition holds 48, Arab parties skyrocket
The Central Elections Committee (CEC) announced on Wednesday morning, after almost five million votes were counted, that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is expected to enter the Knesset with 53 seats.
Netanyahu's Likud is projected to enter with 26 seats, while United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Otzma Yehudit are expected to enter with seven seats, and the Religious Zionist Party is expected to enter with six seats, respectively.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and the Democrats, is expected to enter the Knesset with 48 seats, according to CEC data.
Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar is projected to enter the Knesset with 21 seats. B'Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, is expected to enter with 12 seats. Yair Golan's Democrats are expected to enter the Knesset with eight seats, and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu with seven.
The latest CEC results put 19 seats for the Arab parties, with the Joint List at 12 and Ra'am at 7 in the next Knesset.
Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

Unidentified naval drones have attacked another merchant vessel in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea.
Reuters reported the incident, citing a statement by Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov.
According to Stoyanov, three naval drones attacked a Liberian-flagged container ship in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, 20 nautical miles from the resort town of Shabla.
At the time of the attack, representatives of Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia and calling for an end to attacks in the Black Sea that threaten commercial shipping.
The vessel’s crew was evacuated.
Another ship was dispatched to assist the damaged bulk carrier, which was sailing from the Israeli port of Haifa to Constanța, Romania.
The vessel’s owner, Contships Management, confirmed the attack. A company representative said all 18 crew members — 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians — were safe and ashore.
In recent weeks, drone attacks on commercial vessels off the Bulgarian coast have killed about two dozen sailors.
At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
On October 6, the bulk carrier Alfa Watan, owned by a Turkish company, sank off the country’s coast. Ten crew members were reported missing.
On October 13, the vessel HS Dignity sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone following a drone strike. Another 11 sailors were reported missing.
The bulk carriers Able and Chelsea-3 were also damaged. In addition, unidentified drones attacked several vessels off the Romanian coast.
Last week, NATO announced that it would send additional maritime reconnaissance aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten held a meeting in The Hague with representatives from the Ukrainian and Dutch business sectors, specifically in defense, energy, and software, to discuss joint technological and energy projects, as well as the development of satellite technologies and air defense systems.

Houthis say deadly Saudi strikes hit Yemen as they target Aden
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi strikes on a petrol station and a market killed more than a dozen people on Wednesday, while the Iran-backed group targeted the airport in government stronghold Aden, wounding several civilians.
The Houthis last month launched a lightning offensive in Yemen, reigniting a long frozen civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government there.
They have also launched sustained attacks on Saudi Arabia itself, the world's biggest crude exporter, rattling global markets already volatile from the wider Middle East war.
On Wednesday, Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 15 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll", in attacks it blamed on Saudi Arabia in the northwestern Jawf province, where it reported strikes on a market and a petrol station.
In Aden, two ballistic missiles struck the perimeter of the airport, leaving several civilians wounded and causing damage, government forces spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili said on X.
He blamed the Houthis for the attack, describing it as "the sixth such attack on the airport".
A local police source told AFP that one missile fell inside the airport perimeter shortly before the Houthis issued a warning for people to evacuate the area.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden airport to immediately evacuate due to the presence of a military cargo plane belonging to the Saudi enemy transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Telegram.
The first strike happened while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward", the first police source said.
The second attack targeted an area "under Saudi forces' control inside the perimeter of Aden airport", the second Aden police official said.
Both sources spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.

Wars, unhappiness, and loneliness frighten nearly 1 in 2 young people, survey finds
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:49:24 CET
03:49:24 KST

Wars, unhappiness, and loneliness
frighten nearly 1 in 2 young people in Italy, a new survey has
found.
                                    
International geopolitical tension has emerged this year as the
top fear among the younger generations, according to the
Observatory on Generational Fears—an initiative by the portal
Skuola.net—which surveyed 1,000 young men and women aged 11 to
29, asking them to identify which of the various "specters"
presented in the study they found most daunting.
                                    
The results paint a portrait of these generations—known as Gen Z
and Gen Alpha—caught in a double bind: on one hand, the terror
of rapidly escalating global catastrophes, and on the other, a
deep, personal sense of insecurity regarding their own futures
and romantic lives.
                                    
Only 13% of respondents felt confident—or fortunate—enough to
claim they had "none of these fears," with this sentiment being
significantly more common among males (20%) than females (8%).
                                    
Unlike similar surveys conducted in previous years, 2026 shows a
dramatic shift at the top of the list.
                                    
The fear of a nuclear or global war now ranks first, cited by
45% of young people.
                                    
This represents a sharp increase compared to the past, when this
fear stood at 34% (in 2025) and 33% (in 2024).
                                    
At the same time, young people continue to grapple with a
profound sense of inner distress.
                                    
Right behind the specter of war—in second place—is the fear of
never being happy or satisfied, cited by 43% of the sample (a
steady increase from 40% in 2025 and 38% in 2024).
                                    
Rounding out the top three is another concern closely tied to
one's personal life: the dread of never finding love, which has
seen a significant jump to 41%, up from 33% a year ago.
                                    
Further down the list, anxiety regarding financial independence
takes hold: 38% of young people fear not having enough money,
while 37% are frightened by the prospect of failing to build a
life of their own.
                                    
Also at 37%—tied with the previous concern—is a growing worry
about the rise in social violence, which has surged by 11
percentage points from 26% last year.
                                    
Just outside the top tier, at 35%, are the nightmare of being
unable to find work and the fear of climate change—an issue that
has once again begun to weigh on people's minds after remaining
relatively stable at 24% for the past two years.
                                    
Rounding out the list are the fear of having no friends (31%)
and the fear of being unable to travel (23%) to explore a world
that increasingly appears closed off and hostile.

====================================================================================================

The 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player in elite wheelchair sport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:49:00 UTC
03:49:00 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Bayley McKenna to make history as Australia's first non-disabled captain at Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup
There are few athletes in world sport quite like Bayley McKenna.
Shaggy-haired and expressive, he is the kind of player highlights packages are built around, and at 26, he is the youngest-ever captain of Australia's wheelchair rugby league team.
But what really sets him apart is his status as a non-disabled athlete in elite wheelchair sport, with international wheelchair rugby league allowing participation from both people with disability and non-disabled players.
Leading out the Wheelaroos at the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup, starting tomorrow in Wollongong, will undoubtedly be a pinch-me moment for the Townsville world-beater.
But it is also an occasion he approaches with some trepidation.
McKenna received a flood of online abuse during his breakout World Cup in 2022 and is now bracing for more negativity from outside the sport.
"There is such a stigma around able-bodied athletes playing in wheelchairs," McKenna told ABC Sport.
"It is ridiculous … I'd be lying to you if I said I was going into this World Cup not expecting it."
McKenna's journey as a non-disabled player
McKenna's journey towards the Wheelaroos began in 2006, when his father was involved in an accident and became a wheelchair user.
It was a tough period of transition for Darren McKenna, grappling with the realities of his disability and what it meant for his career, family and independence.
He was reluctant to accept assistance from anyone, but his six-year-old son gave him little choice.
"I pretty much said, 'I'm helping you no matter what,'" Bayley McKenna said.
"We did everything together. I was the only person allowed to push him in his wheelchair because I didn't really give him the option.
"I've been his little offsider ever since."
And it was not long before the father-son duo entered the sporting arena, first competing together in wheelchair basketball before finding wheelchair rugby league, which Darren McKenna was integral to growing in both Queensland and Australia-wide.
Participation from non-disabled players is vital to wheelchair sport at a grassroots level, allowing for more teams and competitions for disabled athletes, but wheelchair rugby league is unique in allowing international sides to field up to two non-disabled players at any given time.
This policy ensures that teams at every level of the sport can attract enough players to compete, while also fostering a unique kind of inclusion that flows from grassroots all the way to elite competition.
And the sport is full of stories like the McKennas' — including Australia's Cory Cannane, who shared the field with disabled father Craig at the 2022 World Cup, and non-disabled England legend Jack Brown, who only began playing the sport because of his disabled brother.
Having experienced the benefits of the policy firsthand, McKenna said it was that "inclusion" that provided the game much of its magic.
"I really, really didn't think that anything could have brought us closer together," McKenna said.
"But it did."
Wheelchair rugby league is also a mixed gender sport, although there are no women in the Wheelaroos' squad for the tournament.
Dealing with the 'stigma' of being a non-disabled player
McKenna burst onto the international scene at the 2022 World Cup in England, where his playmaking exploits earned him a spot in the team of the tournament as well as significant attention online.
Aged 22, McKenna's shaggy mullet, uncompromising hits and exceptional chair skills made for ideal social media fodder, with the Australian making regular appearances across the tournament's official channels.
McKenna was taken aback by the vitriol in the online correspondence he received as a result.
"I would have copped about a dozen messages from people all around the world saying, 'you're a fraud, you shouldn't even be in the chair, this is a sport for disabled people,'" McKenna said.
"These guys were coming at me, like, 'you're lucky you're not out there on the street by yourself.'"
It was only after an early-morning conversation with teammate and longtime friend Pete Arbuckle that McKenna began to feel at peace with the abuse.
"Me and Pete were at the gym over in the UK and I got one of these messages and Pete said, 'Don't worry about that bud, don't even stress. You're here representing your country and he's probably at home on the couch,'" McKenna said.
"That put me back in my stride a bit, and it helped me out a lot."
Recalling the conversation, Arbuckle said he reassured McKenna his journey to international competition was a "natural progression" from his early years playing alongside his amputee father.
"I said, 'You don't have to justify anything, you only have to justify yourself to us, your teammates. You don't have to justify yourself to anyone else on the planet,'" Arbuckle said.
"And he didn't let it affect him, and he had a really good World Cup."
Arbuckle, who lost a leg in an accident in 2016, said the contributions of non-disabled players have been vital to the growth of the sport in Australia.
"If it wasn't for the able-bodied players, I don't think we'd have the game here in Australia," Arbuckle said.
"We just wouldn't be feasible … there'd be no Wheelaroos to speak of, or certainly not at the level we're at currently."
McKenna said the rules of the game ensure it is a "level playing field" for all athletes, while both he and Arbuckle described their wheelchairs as equipment needed for the sport, analogous to cricket bats or baseball mitts.
"What people don't realise is this is a wheelchair sport; it's not a disability sport as such," Arbuckle said.
"We play a sport in wheelchairs, and our rules define what can and can't happen."
Wheelchair rugby league's looming watershed moment
The upcoming tournament will provide wheelchair rugby league the kind of exposure most non-mainstream sports could only dream of.
Bundling the wheelchair competition with the men's, women's and physical disability events allows for the World Cups to be marketed as one cohesive product, and for the Wheelaroos to benefit with free-to-air, prime-time coverage.
Well aware of the looming watershed moment, Arbuckle said he hoped the attention would bring more disabled players into the fold.
"It's really going to open our game to people that haven't heard of it before and people that want to choose a physical sport," Arbuckle said.
"I think there's an untapped resource out there."
But the Wheelaroos, and McKenna in particular, are also bracing for the spotlight's burn.
The Australian captain is certain his inbox will once again turn ugly.
But this time, knowing he can call on the support of his teammates and loved ones, he said he will be ready.
"It's just going to be one of those things we move past and move forward, and don't let it get in the camp," McKenna said.
"I've got some damn good mates, bud.
"And they will support me until the cows come home."

Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:46:45 UTC
03:46:45 KST

Five key takeaways from the UK Autumn Budget
The government says its policies are for the ‘working people of Britain’.
The United Kingdom’s government has announced its first budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister and leader of the Labour Party three months ago.
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey unveiled his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, announcing a series of policies that he said were for the “working people of Britain”, who have experienced a dramatic decline in living standards in recent years. Healey said the budget would give the country “breathing space” after years of economic stagnation fuelled by austerity, Brexit, the coronavirus pandemic, privatisation and rising energy prices.
So, what did Healey announce, and what will it mean for the average Brit?
Energy costs
Global fuel prices have soared in recent months because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway through which about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) would normally transit.
In response, Healey said on Wednesday that 20 million households will receive a one-off payment of 100 British pounds ($133) towards their energy bills. People living in homes valued at 88,000 British pounds ($117,000) or less will receive the payment. The valuations are based on prices in April 1991, not current house prices.
Healey also said a temporary cut to VAT – a sales tax – will be extended until 1 July. The measure will reduce the annual price cap by 50 British pounds ($66.50).
However, James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the left-wing think tank Verdant, told Al Jazeera that these measures will not tackle the cost-of-living crisis in “any serious way”.
“There’s quite a lot of small things. These are not nothing. They’re just not approaching the scale of the problem that people are already facing and [which] is expected, according to the government’s own figures, to get worse over the next year,” Meadway said.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), an independent public body that analyses the country’s finances, said it expected no growth in real earnings next year. The body also sharply downgraded its growth forecast for 2027 to 1 percent, from 1.5 percent.
“There are forecasts out there saying that by the end of Parliament, it will be the worst Parliament for living standards in modern history. Put in those terms, what you got in this budget was nothing like enough,” Meadway added.
Defence spending
Healey said he would fund the government’s additional Defence Investment Plan, worth 15 billion British pounds ($20bn), and pledged to plug a gap of 4.7 billion British pounds ($6.2bn) by “reprioritising” budgets across other departments.
However, he did not detail how the government would meet its NATO commitment to spend 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2035, with an interim target of three percent in 2030. Instead, Healey said he would set out how these targets would be met during a spending review next year.
In response, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte welcomed the British government’s budget plan, saying it showed a “strong commitment” to defence.
“Good news on the new budget from MP John Healey with a strong commitment on defence,” wrote Rutte on X.
“The UK role in Transatlantic security is vital, and I welcome this move to put Britain on a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all NATO Allies in The Hague – to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready and able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security,” Rutte added.
Ukraine was also on the agenda during Healey’s budget statement, with the chancellor pledging an additional 10 billion British pounds ($13.2bn) in economic and military aid for Kyiv in its war with Russia.
Salaries
The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will both increase by 3.9 percent in April, at the start of the new tax year. The former currently sets a minimum hourly rate of 10.85 British pounds ($14.44) for workers aged 18 to 20, while the latter sets the rate at 12.71 British pounds ($16.91) for workers aged 21 and over.
Taxes on banks’ profits
To raise funds for additional support for households and businesses, the government will temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from three percent to six percent. The increase will last for 15 months, ending on March 31, 2028. The surcharge is levied on top of standard corporation tax and is expected to raise 1.5 billion British pounds ($2bn).
Housing crisis
Affordable housing is a significant problem in the UK. The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) shows that 35 percent of men aged 20 to 35 were living at home with their parents last year, compared with 22 percent of women in the same age range.
To tackle this, Healey announced a new First Time Buyer savings account. Interest earned in such accounts, commonly referred to as Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs), is tax-free.
The First Time Buyer account will launch in 2029, replacing the current Lifetime ISA. The exact details of the new account are not yet clear. However, like the Lifetime ISA, it will pay savers a bonus of 25 percent on deposits of up to 4,000 British pounds ($5,320). That means savers can benefit from an annual government bonus of up to 1,000 British pounds ($1,330).
Healey also announced that the penalty for first-time buyers using funds from a Lifetime ISA to purchase a house worth more than 450,000 British pounds ($598,853) will immediately be reduced to 20 percent. That means savers will get back at least what they put in. The penalty was previously 25 percent.
A further 432 million British pounds ($574.9m) will also be spent over the next two years to reduce the number of people sleeping on the streets, a problem that Burnham has pledged to end.

Araghchi briefs cabinet on Tehran security summit, warns of risks to global energy markets
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has briefed the cabinet on the latest diplomatic developments, with a focus on a quadrilateral meeting in Tehran involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, emphasizing the need for regional cooperation to safeguard security, prevent escalation and protect national sovereignty.
Araghchi presented his report at Wednesday’s cabinet meeting, chaired by President Masoud Pezeshkian, outlining recent diplomatic consultations on regional and international affairs, including discussions with senior officials from neighboring and regional countries.
The report covered meetings involving a Qatari delegation, as well as consultations with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council; Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defense minister; Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of army staff; and Ibrahim Kalin, head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization.
According to the report, participants in the four-way discussions stressed the importance of strengthening regional cooperation, developing joint security mechanisms and preventing the further escalation of tensions and conflicts.
They also warned against the 'Israeli regime’s destabilizing policies,' including efforts to weaken regional states, expand military aggression, undermine governments and draw the United States into regional conflicts.
The senior officials underscored the need for regional countries to remain vigilant against developments that could fuel tensions and to deepen cooperation in defence of their sovereignty, stability and territorial integrity.
Regional ownership of security
In a message posted on Instagram following the Tehran meeting, Araghchi described the talks as a valuable opportunity to advance dialogue on regional peace and security and address shared threats and challenges. He said the agreement to continue consultations represented an important step forward.
Turning dialogue into lasting cooperation, the foreign minister stressed, would require agreement on common principles, confidence-building, mutual respect for national sovereignty and practical commitments.
Iran’s position, he said, was that sustainable regional security must be achieved through the participation of regional countries, without the military presence or interference of powers from outside the region.
“This approach is based on the responsibility of regional countries to determine their own destiny,” Araghchi wrote.
He also emphasized the need to counter the Israeli regime’s acts of aggression and destabilization, describing this as essential to protecting countries’ independence and sovereignty and preventing the spread of war.
Instagram message concluded with Iran’s diplomatic motto: “Our Neighbors, Our Priority.”
Energy diplomacy and Persian Gulf security
Araghchi also highlighted the energy dimension of Iran’s recent diplomatic engagements, saying the country’s energy diplomacy had advanced during the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, where discussions addressed global gas markets and energy security.
He warned that any military adventurism initiated by Israel in the Persian Gulf could have potentially devastating consequences for international energy markets, making the prospect a serious concern for both gas-producing countries and consumers.
The foreign minister’s remarks underscored the connection between regional stability and global energy security, as well as the importance of diplomatic coordination among regional states in preventing conflicts that could disrupt international markets.

If it feels like (almost) everything is getting more expensive, that's because it is.

The consumer price index rose by 4.3 per cent in the past year, well above the Reserve Bank of Australia's target of 2 to 3 per cent.
Below, we've tracked prices across all kinds of goods and services, including food, electricity, travel and housing.

Turkic nations formalize new audit body TURKSAI in Antalya
The Charter of the newly established Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions of the Member States of the Organization of Turkic States (TURKSAI) has been signed in Antalya, Türkiye, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber.
At the signing ceremony, the Kazakhstan delegation was led by Alikhan Smailov, Chairman of the Supreme Audit Chamber.
The decision to create TURKSAI was adopted in November 2025 in Istanbul at a meeting of supreme audit heads from OTS Member States — Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, and Uzbekistan.
The new organization is designed to elevate audit cooperation across the Turkic world to a new level. It will facilitate sharing knowledge and expertise, enhancing audit practices, conducting joint audits, and implementing collaborative research projects
Practical cooperation under the umbrella of TURKSAI is already underway. Prior to the signing, audit professionals from across the region completed a knowledge exchange program on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It covered the entire SDG audit lifecycle, from topic selection and audit question formulation to drafting recommendations and follow-up monitoring.
Seven auditors from the Supreme Audit Chamber participated in the program. The key takeaways will inform the planning and execution of future SDG audits in Kazakhstan.
Addressing the ceremony, Alikhan Smailov thanked Metin Yener, President of the Turkish Court of Accounts, for warm hospitality and organizing the events. He noted that formalizing the new body was the logical outcome of decisions adopted nearly a year ago in Istanbul.
"Today, we cement our agreements with a foundational document that defines the principles, scope, and operational procedures of TURKSAI," Smailov said. "The organization holds significant potential for practical cooperation. I am confident that signing this charter will serve as a reliable foundation for long-term partnership."
The Chairman of Kazakhstan's Supreme Audit Chamber highlighted that rapidly evolving public finances alongside emerging challenges demand upgraded audit methods and higher standards of public asset management.
"This cooperation, rooted in friendship, trust, solidarity, and the spirit of Turkic brotherhood, will allow our supreme audit institutions to jointly respond to modern challenges and make a meaningful contribution to the development of our states," he emphasized.
Following the ceremony, the delegation heads attended a symposium on the Sustainable Development Goals, focusing on the role of public auditing in advancing SDG targets and leveraging audit outcomes to improve public policy.
As reported earlier, Kazakhstan attaches importance to developing comprehensive cooperation with Türkiye and strengthening ties within the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), with the integration of the Turkic world among the country’s key foreign policy priorities, Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said in an interview with Anadolu.

How do Israeli election results impact timing of possible new Iran war? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:46 UTC
03:38:46 KST

The Israeli election results seem to grant Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a better showing than expected. But they also clearly leave his bloc in the minority with no way to avoid new elections without cutting a deal with Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot.
How do those results impact a possible new conflict with Iran?
In recent weeks, Netanyahu was seriously considering renewing the conflict with Iran.
It seems that a mix of opposition by US President Donald Trump and IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir prevented Netanyahu from doing so, although it is also possible with the hard-to-pin-down prime minister that he just wanted Tehran to think he might attack to deter it from doing anything provocative.
But Zamir’s opposition was only to an attack before Israeli elections were held, and Trump’s opposition was only to an attack before the US midterm elections on November 3.
In fact, Trump has made numerous rumblings about resuming strikes on Iran soon after the US midterm elections, and in his endorsement of Netanyahu, he made reference to wanting Israel involved again as well.
If Eisenkot had won the battle of the blocs over Netanyahu, as forecast by the polls, he might have been able to start to form a government before the US midterm elections.
In such a scenario, it is doubtful that Netanyahu could have ordered a new attack against Iran.
As matters now stand, however, one of Eisenkot’s allies, Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman, will not even start serious talks about forming a government before Friday, when the final vote results are in.
At that point, Liberman must make the excruciating decision of breaking a promise: either making a deal with the Arab parties, making a deal with Netanyahu, or going to a second round of elections.
Even if Liberman moves toward forming a new government, it would just start complex negotiations about what each side would need to do to pave the way to a partnership.
Once there would be agreement on that, there is a whole separate negotiation on who gets what ministries and other jobs.
All of these issues are likely to take more than the four days between Friday and the US midterm elections, given that they usually take weeks or even months.
This means that Netanyahu will likely have the freedom to attack Iran if Trump wants to or would not stop him.
Zamir is in favor of attacking Iran under two conditions: The first has been and remains if Iran was either about to actually strike Israel; and the second was and is if Trump restarted the war first, and Israel had full backing offensively and defensively from the US for engaging in another round of conflict.
Generally, Zamir’s instinct has been that he is ready to strike Iran if it starts recovering its threat capabilities too fast, which it has not yet done, or if such a strike would be part of a well-thought-out and considered strategy to finally push Tehran into making key nuclear concessions to the US.
He was against attacking before the election so as not to undermine Election Day voting by a potential Iranian ballistic-missile counterstrike and to avoid the cloud of impropriety that an attack leading into the election might have been carried out to help Netanyahu’s chances.
Netanyahu's main obstacle would be Trump
Post-election, there is no reason to bar an attack, although Zamir also is not rushing toward an attack, given that he does not view Tehran as having gotten much closer to any growing substantial nuclear or ballistic-missile threat.
To be sure, both issues remain threats, but both have been put off by some period of years due to US-Israeli airstrikes in June 2025 and early 2026.
This means that Netanyahu’s main obstacle would be Trump.
Trump did not want to attack leading into the midterms because the Iran war is already dragging him and the Republic Party down in the polls. But post-midterms, and with him unable to run for a third term, he will be unrestrained and could follow his whim to hit Iran again.
Why might he still not?
His top advisers have been and are mostly against a return to war, and while some think a few days of war might loosen Iran up some, others think Iran’s refusal to crack since February has shown a few more intense days will not sway them either.
So, he may have little to gain, and some of his advisers have also warned that Tehran has shown it is willing to keep firing after a US ceasefire, meaning the conflict might last longer than a few days even if Trump wants to stop.
This could lead Trump to walk away from the price tag of another round and continue his long-term attempt to slowly wear down Iran economically.
In fact, this series of Trump’s dizzying switches from economic pressure to a sudden threat to go to war, to backing down back into economic pressure, happened in August, earlier in October, and at other times.
These inconsistent switches probably have also undermined the viability of his threat in the eyes of the Iranians.
Another possibility is that the Iranians finally get scared by his latest threat of force and offer a real deal on the nuclear issue. That would surely lead to a delay of an Iran attack.
But if Trump ultimately favors attacking, it could not come at a better time for Netanyahu.
If Netanyahu is involved with attacking Iran – as he holds a Jewish majority in the vote count, while Eisenkot and his camp are trying to rally together – a return to a focus on war with Iran would place the nation’s focus where Netanyahu prefers it.
Will Eisenkot and company find it harder to cut a deal with the Arab parties while Israelis have ballistic missiles raining down on them?
Might they feel more ready to cut a deal with Netanyahu if Iran has pushed out the October 7 massacre and haredim (ultra-Orthodox) serving in the IDF as the focus of the national conversation?
None of this means that Israel attacking Iran may not be justified on its own. Until Tehran makes new nuclear concessions, such an attack could be justified in theory, based on the idea of getting it to make those concessions.
And anytime the US offers to assist with cleaning house, many Israelis would say that Israel should not miss the chance to jump on board – as opposed to having to fight Iran solo at some later date.
Still, as long as Zamir is in no rush to strike Iran, Netanyahu would need to justify the attack with more than vague statements about Iran making new progress toward threatening Israel.
It is hard for him to both claim he succeeded at removing the nuclear and ballistic-missile threat in one sentence, and to then demand a new strike now, because time is running out.
How Netanyahu explains a third round of conflict, if it happens during coalition negotiations, will be crucial to the success of any attack and its legitimacy among the wider Israeli public.

US campaign to cripple Iran's economy risks falling short without global partners, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:38:17 UTC
03:38:17 KST

The United States’ Operation Economic Outcast, designed to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime, is falling short of its full potential without greater coordination with international partners, according to a new assessment published earlier this week by two experts from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
According to Michael Jacobson, the Mark and Wayne Levy Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, and Matthew Levitt, the Fromer-Wexler Senior Fellow and director of the institute’s Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, closer coordination with allies on sanctions would strengthen Washington’s efforts to undermine the Iranian regime alongside the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Criticizing Washington for relying on targeted, limited diplomatic efforts to address Iran-linked terrorism, they argued that the results achieved so far have demonstrated the value of a more international approach.
On October 12, the US and 29 other governments issued a statement accusing Iran of orchestrating plots to destroy US air assets at RAF Fairford in the UK, following a similar statement a week earlier in which the US and eight countries in the Western Hemisphere condemned Iran’s terrorist and malign activities in the region.
In June, the US State Department and more than 20 other governments also accused Iran of being behind a series of attacks in Europe, North America, and Australia.
Jacobson and Levitt said some governments had initially been hesitant to condemn Iranian plots, including those on their own soil, because of concerns about Iranian retaliation and the fate of their nationals wrongfully detained in Iranian prisons, but they eventually did so with American support.
US sanctions against Iran-backed groups require stronger enforcement capabilities, experts warn
Washington’s efforts had also helped multiple countries in Central and South America designate or sanction the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hezbollah, and Hamas in recent years, they wrote, adding that such measures carry symbolic weight while giving governments additional tools to counter the groups’ activities.
They cautioned that designations and sanctions must be backed by the material capabilities, skills, and knowledge needed to address the complex Iranian threat, including its sophisticated financial schemes, if they are to translate into meaningful action against the regime.
The Trump administration could use foreign assistance funding to advance these efforts, Jacobson and Levitt wrote, adding that Congress has already allocated almost $300 million to the State Department this fiscal year to strengthen partners’ counterterrorism capabilities.
Although the State Department has publicly committed some of that funding to addressing cartel and gang threats in Central America, similar support could also help countries counter Iran’s malign activities, they said.
US experts urge funding to disrupt Iranian smuggling and terror financing networks
The funding could be directed toward programs to train and equip Syrian border-security authorities to intercept Iranian and Hezbollah smuggling operations, including bulk cash transfers; help Yemeni Coast Guard officials detect and disrupt Houthi weapons and procurement networks; and improve Iraqi financial institutions’ ability to identify illicit Iranian financing schemes, Jacobson and Levitt wrote.
Other initiatives could strengthen efforts by authorities in West Africa and South America to uncover and prosecute Hezbollah’s illicit financial networks, they added.

The US goods trade deficit widened 2.1% month-on-month in September to $134.9 billion, marking its highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday.

These Australians dug into the 'junk' of millions of cells. It could be a drug game-changer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:36:53 UTC
03:36:53 KST

IN BRIEF
- A study of 2,000 Australians found genetic clues linked to 16 diseases, including cancers and Alzheimer's disease.
- Researchers say the findings provide the "building blocks" for new and more targeted drug therapies.
Medical researchers have uncovered new clues about why some Australians develop certain diseases, as well as the "building blocks" for potential future treatments.
Researchers from the Sydney-based Garvan Institute of Medical Research and collaborators led three studies that examined the DNA of 2,000 Australians — recording each person's full genome and measuring gene activity in the 28 different types of immune cells.
Professor Joseph Powell, director of Garvan's Translational Genomics program and UNSW's Institute for Genomics and Health, said the research identified 1,500 genes linked to 16 different diseases.
"We did this for a range of different diseases that were all linked to immune function, so autoimmune diseases, cancers, and inflammatory conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's," he said.
Researchers also identified how DNA variations influence gene activity.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Powell said they identified 21,000 genes and 180,000 DNA positions that act as a "dimmer switch" to control gene expression.
"This gives us the ability to identify how these DNA spots are controlling the activity of genes and then link that to disease," Powell said.
They also found DNA that "turned off" genetic activity, leading to the identification of an extra 350 disease-specific processes that acted as a "type of on-off switch mechanism".
"This is important ... because the way in which you would develop a therapy or treatment to target these is going to be different if the switch is an on-off switch compared to a dimmer switch," Powell said.
The answer in DNA 'junk'
Hope Tanudisastro, a junior medical officer and postdoctoral researcher at Garvan's Centre for Population Genomics and Murdoch Children's Research Institute, said the research also examined DNA "junk".
"A common theme in science is that we always have to challenge assumptions. We always have to look in places that have been understudied or overlooked," she said.
The team analysed DNA stutters, which are tandem repeats within a person's DNA.
While "long written off as junk", stutters could explain how someone's "immune system might be working", Tanudisastro said.
"Yet for years, most genetic studies have set [stutters] aside, and that's partly because they're very hard to read. It's like trying to count identical beads on a string where you can only see a few at a time. At some point, you lose track," she said.
The team measured repeats across the whole genome and tracked their effects in more than five million individual immune cells.
They found more than 69,000 of the repeat switches influencing the activity of genes in the immune system.
Unlocking new treatments for diseases
Tanudisastro said the research identified how changes in DNA and gene activity within "specific immune cell subtypes" can signal when disease is active.
They could now form the "building blocks" for the development of future targeted drug treatments, she said.
The study identified DNA repeats in "more than 200 genes" linked to conditions such as asthma, Crohn's disease, breast and prostate cancer, high cholesterol, and anaemia.
"These are common chronic conditions, and as our population ages, more Australians will be diagnosed with them, which means that better and more targeted therapies are all the more urgent to be discovered," she said.
Powell said the research is just the start, with further studies planned to examine more diseases.
He said the team will seek to develop "approaches for precision medicine".
"There's this well-recognised huge gap in developing new therapies for conditions that don't have active treatments, and for patients where there are treatments that just don't work," he said.
He said the "map" this research has created could help develop new treatments and identify existing treatments for a range of diseases.
"The findings could help researchers identify new targets for drugs and eventually develop treatments better suited to individual patients."

US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:36:20 UTC
03:36:20 KST

US envoy should speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations, Iran says
TEHRAN — Iran’s Ambassador and Chargé d’Affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, has urged the United States to address the facts rather than level 'fabricated accusations against Tehran,' condemning US and Israeli military attacks against Iran and calling for accountability under international law. In a separate address to the UN General Assembly, Darzi denounced unilateral sanctions as economic terrorism and demanded an end to Washington’s decades-long embargo against Cuba.
Speaking at the conclusion of a UN Security Council meeting on Iran, Darzi directly responded to remarks by US representative Mike Waltz, displaying photographs of Iranians killed in US and Israeli attacks.
 
“Let us speak based on facts, not on fabricated accusations,” the Iranian diplomat said, rejecting Washington’s allegations concerning Iran and its peaceful nuclear program.
Iran challenges Washington’s account of the conflict
Darzi said the US representative had failed to provide credible arguments or justification for 'Washington’s blatant act of aggression against Iran.' Instead, he argued, Waltz had resorted to repeated falsehoods and baseless allegations concerning Iran’s nuclear activities to obscure the facts and evade responsibility.
The Iranian envoy stressed that the United States and Israel had carried out repeated military attacks against Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities, which are under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards.
He maintained that Iran was the victim of the conflict, not its instigator, and accused Washington and Tel Aviv of committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
According to Darzi, the attacks had struck a wide range of civilian targets and essential infrastructure, including residential areas, schools, hospitals, bridges, airports, energy facilities, sports complexes, cultural heritage sites and railway infrastructure.
He described the strikes as flagrant violations of the UN Charter, international law and international humanitarian law, holding the United States and Israel responsible for the consequences of their military actions.
“No amount of propaganda can reverse the facts, erase the suffering of the Iranian people, or absolve those responsible of their international legal obligations,” Darzi said.
He emphasized that those who ordered, carried out or facilitated the attacks must be held accountable, warning against allowing those responsible to escape justice.
The Iranian diplomat also criticized Washington for seeking to portray itself as the victim while, in his account, conducting military aggression and inflicting mass civilian casualties.
He insisted that the distinction between aggressor and victim must not be reversed, arguing that the United States could not carry out attacks against Iran and then use the Security Council to present itself as the injured party.
Darzi said the United States and Israel would ultimately have to answer for their actions and the crimes he accused them of committing against the Iranian people.
Iran condemns sanctions as economic terrorism
In a separate address to the UN General Assembly during a debate on the need to end the US economic, commercial and financial embargo against Cuba, Darzi condemned unilateral sanctions as instruments of coercion that undermine national sovereignty, violate fundamental rights and obstruct economic development.
“Sanctions are examples of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law,” he said.
Darzi argued that unilateral coercive measures, including so-called autonomous sanctions, threatened multilateralism, destabilized international relations and undermined the principles enshrined in the UN Charter.
He described such measures as a form of collective punishment that imposed hardship on ordinary people, particularly women, children and older persons, while restricting access to healthcare, food and opportunities for development.
Referring to more than six decades of US sanctions and the economic blockade against Cuba, the Iranian envoy said Washington’s policies had inflicted severe suffering on the Cuban population and impeded the country's development.
He rejected the justification of tightening the embargo in the name of promoting democracy, arguing that the humanitarian consequences contradicted the stated objectives of the policy.
“No government is allowed to dictate the political future of a sovereign nation,” Darzi said, describing economic coercion as unlawful, immoral and inhumane.
He called for the immediate lifting of the embargo, full reparation for the damage inflicted on the Cuban people and accountability for those responsible for maintaining the restrictions.
Tehran links sanctions to violations of international law
Darzi said Iran’s opposition to unilateral sanctions was reinforced by its own experience of US economic coercion and military aggression. He reaffirmed Tehran’s unequivocal opposition to sanctions imposed against sovereign and independent states, including Cuba.
The Iranian envoy argued that invoking human rights to justify economic restrictions was fundamentally contradictory when those measures themselves undermined the rights to health, food, development and a dignified life.
He drew a parallel with the US president’s promise of assistance to the Iranian people, recalling the statement that “Help is on its way.” Darzi contrasted that promise with the subsequent US bombing of a primary school in Minab, which, according to the Iranian diplomat, killed 168 children aged between seven and 12.
He cited the incident as an example of the 'contradiction between Washington’s stated humanitarian commitments and its actions.'
Darzi also invoked Articles 1 and 2 of the UN Charter, emphasizing the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and friendly relations among nations. He cited Article 2(7) in arguing that unilateral coercive measures violate the principle of non-interference when used to force governments to change their domestic policies.
He warned that sanctions deepen international divisions, fuel confrontation and undermine peaceful coexistence, while imposing the heaviest burdens on vulnerable populations.
Concluding his address, Darzi reaffirmed Iran’s solidarity with the Cuban government and people and urged the General Assembly to press Washington to implement the numerous resolutions adopted by an overwhelming majority of member states calling for an end to the embargo.
He called for intensified international efforts to eliminate unilateral coercive measures, warning that their continuation undermined international law and reflected a failure to uphold fundamental legal and moral responsibilities.
