‘Narration of Resistance’ Caravan highlights Sistan-Baluchestan’s cultural riches
TEHRAN – A group of Iranian cultural, religious, media and sports personalities has traveled to Sistan-Baluchestan province as part of a program titled “Narration of the Resistance of the Brave,” aimed at showcasing the region’s cultural diversity, social solidarity and local capabilities.
The caravan, which arrived in the southeastern province on October 25, has organized a series of cultural, Quranic, media and sports activities across several cities, bringing its participants into contact with local residents, community figures, businesses and institutions.
According to reports by Persian media, the program seeks to present a broader picture of life in Sistan-Baluchestan, highlighting its cultural traditions, religious life, scientific and medical facilities, economic activities and the coexistence of its diverse communities.
Among the prominent figures accompanying the caravan are Hojjatoleslam Alireza Panahian, cultural activist Hossein Yekta, writer Vahid Yaminpour, television presenter Raheleh Aminian, travel documentarian Javad Gharai, television host Iman Qiasi, religious program presenter Najmeddin Shariati, singer Hamed Homayoun and several former Iranian footballers.
The initiative combines public gatherings and face-to-face encounters with television production and visits to local institutions, using familiar public figures to draw attention to a province whose cultural and social realities are often less visible in national media coverage.
Quranic gatherings emphasize religious and social ties
Quranic programs have formed a major part of the caravan’s activities, with gatherings involving nationally recognized reciters in Zahedan and Iranshahr.
These events brought residents together around Quran recitation and religious programming, highlighting the role of shared religious traditions in strengthening social connections across the province.
The caravan also included members of the television program “Mahfel,” a Quran-focused show that features reciters and participants from Iran and other countries. The team met with border guards at the country’s frontier.
The visit offered an opportunity to highlight the work of border personnel and their role in protecting Iran’s borders, while bringing media figures into direct contact with those serving in remote areas.
Hossein Yekta also visited Imam Hussein Mosque in Zahedan, where he met residents, including members of the local Sunni community. During the visit, he recalled the late Molavi Rigi, describing him as a figure associated with service to the people and the Quran.
The encounters reflect one of the main themes of the caravan’s program: presenting religious identity and community engagement as common elements connecting residents across different backgrounds.
Visits showcase medical and scientific capabilities
Beyond religious and cultural activities, the caravan has sought to introduce visitors to the province’s medical and scientific infrastructure.
Television presenter Peyman Talebi and Yekta visited Al-Zahra Ophthalmology Hospital in Zahedan, drawing attention to the specialized medical services available in the provincial capital. Media personality Raheleh Aminian also highlighted the province’s medical capabilities in her coverage of the visit.
The program extended to the region’s scientific and technological sector, with Yekta visiting Zahedan Science and Technology Park. The visit focused on the work of researchers, young innovators and technology-oriented businesses, presenting another dimension of the province beyond its geographical location and traditional economic activities.
Such visits are intended to bring greater visibility to local institutions and professionals and to encourage a more comprehensive understanding of the province’s development potential.
Markets and local traditions take center stage
The caravan’s activities have also included visits to Zahedan’s commercial districts, where participants met shopkeepers and residents and observed everyday economic and social life.
These visits provided opportunities to introduce local trades, culinary traditions and the social character of the city’s marketplaces.
Together, the market visits and cultural encounters offered a window into the everyday lives of residents, placing local customs, food, occupations and social interactions alongside the province’s religious and institutional activities.
Television and sports bring programs closer to local audiences
A major feature of the initiative has been the production and presentation of television programs from locations across the province.
Among the activities was the “El Clasico” football program in the Karimabad neighborhood of Zahedan, featuring national television presenters.
The neighborhood event brought sports-related entertainment into a local setting, allowing residents to interact directly with television personalities.
The children’s program “Mal Mal” was also scheduled in Zabol and Zahak, while “Samte Khoda,” a religious television program presented by Shariati, featured Panahian in a public gathering in Zabol.
A football match between a team of former Iranian football stars and a selection representing Sistan-Baluchestan was also announced as part of the program.
The participation of former players, including Nikbakht Vahedi, Mohsen Mosalman, Mohammad Ansari, Mohsen Bengar, Mohsen Khalili, Mehdi Amirabadi, Adel Kolahkaj and Ali Shiri, added a sporting dimension to the caravan’s activities.
A broader portrait of southeastern Iran
Sistan-Baluchestan occupies a strategically important position in southeastern Iran, bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. Its geographical location, diverse landscapes and distinctive cultural traditions give it significance in Iran’s social, economic and regional life.
The province is home to communities with varied cultural and religious traditions, including both Sunni and Shiite Muslims. Its Balochi heritage, traditional clothing, handicrafts, cuisine and local customs form an important part of Iran’s broader cultural landscape.
At the same time, the province faces development challenges, making the visibility of its educational, medical, scientific and economic institutions an important part of discussions about its future. Visits to hospitals, technology centers, markets and community spaces can help introduce these dimensions to audiences beyond the region.
The “Narration of the Resistance of the Brave” caravan brings these themes together through a mix of public engagement and media production. Rather than concentrating on a single event or institution, its activities span religious gatherings, neighborhood programs, cultural encounters, scientific visits and sporting events.
The initiative’s organizers have emphasized resistance, solidarity and the province’s capabilities as central themes. Its coverage of everyday life and local traditions also places the experiences of residents at the heart of the program.
As the caravan continues its activities across Sistan-Baluchestan, the combination of familiar media figures and local encounters is intended to draw wider attention to the province’s people, cultural identity and institutional capacities, presenting a multifaceted view of one of Iran’s most distinctive regions.

Ukrainian AI-Powered UGV Autonomously Travels 19 km During Logistics Mission for First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:20:37 KST

The Lava Unmanned Systems Regiment of the Khartiia National Guard’s 2nd Corps has conducted its first autonomous logistics mission using an artificial intelligence-powered unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) in the Kharkiv sector.
The unit told Militarnyi about the mission.
Integrating AI is intended to reduce the workload on operators and minimize the impact of human factors during missions.
With the new system, the vehicle completed 93% of a 20-kilometer route fully autonomously. The operator took control only for a 1.4-kilometer section.

Before the mission, a specialized system travels along the route and scans the terrain using lidar. The collected laser pulses are used to create a 3D model of the terrain.
As the vehicle moves, its cameras recognize the road, road edges and obstacles in real time. The AI makes its own maneuvering decisions, while the operator can adjust the route and set speeds for individual sections.
Using artificial intelligence reduces UGVs’ dependence on a continuous communications link, including Starlink.
Andrii “Matematyк” Kopach, commander of the Lava Regiment’s UGV battalion, said the system changes the operator’s role from driver to dispatcher. The operator intervenes only when necessary, with the ultimate goal of allowing one operator to supervise several vehicles.
Apex AI is developing the software for the project. Specialists from the Lava Regiment helped define the technical requirements and conduct field tests of the platform.
The next stage in the technology’s development will be its use in evacuation missions. Widespread deployment of such systems would allow personnel to carry out more missions.
Militarnyi previously reported that Khartiia engineers had converted a U.S. M113 armored personnel carrier into an uncrewed platform for mine clearance and logistics.
That vehicle is also equipped with video cameras that transmit live footage to the operator’s screen to monitor its movement.

Rabia İclal Turan
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Wednesday called sanctions imposed on UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese “not acceptable.”
“You can agree or disagree with someone, but you should never ever sanction them,” said Turk in response to a question from Anadolu at a news conference in New York.
“They were appointed by the Human Rights Council as independent experts, and the sanction is just not acceptable,” he said.
He said the sanctions on Albanese and the International Criminal Court (ICC) “are not in line with international law from our perspective.”
“Our call to member states is always to ensure that such sanctions are not only lifted, but that they also use their influence that they get lifted,” he added.
Turk said he will address the ICC Assembly of States Parties in The Hague next week.
“I will say what I have to say about the vital importance of the International Criminal Court for the human rights ecosystem, including for accountability purposes,” he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions on Albanese in July 2025, citing her efforts to arrest American and Israeli nationals, including recommending the ICC arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes in the Gaza Strip.
A US district judge temporarily blocked the sanctions in May, and Washington removed them following the court order. The US then reinstated them after a federal appeals court paused the lower-court ruling, and the appeals court in June allowed the sanctions to remain in effect while her legal challenge proceeds.
On Oct. 9, Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was named winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. 
'Israel has obligations under international law'
Asked about his message for Israel's next government following Tuesday's elections, Turk said: “Don’t continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law.”
“Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them,” he said. He added that he hoped the next government would “change course massively.”

Pakistan’s Artificial Intelligence Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:19:00 UTC
03:19:00 KST

For the first time in its volatile history, Pakistan topped the Global Terrorism Index this year, recording 1,045 terror incidents and 1,139 related deaths in 2025. The fatalities have risen further in 2026, with the third quarter of the ongoing year showing an 83 percent hike in terrorism-linked deaths as compared to the second quarter.
This surge comes amid external security woes. Last year, Pakistan and India came the closest that they have to a full-fledged war since the turn of the century, and reportedly to the brink of nuclear war. Pakistan is also engaged in persistent cross-border clashes with Afghanistan. Meanwhile, the ongoing Iran-U.S. war is reconfiguring militancy in Balochistan, after Islamabad and Tehran exchanged drone and missile strikes on each other’s territories in 2024.
Faced with these multipronged challenges, Pakistan has gradually incorporated artificial intelligence (AI) into its security strategy.
Last year, Pakistan unveiled its National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025 to regulate AI usage. Pakistan’s military forces have already deployed AI to enhance their capabilities through research units, such as the Army Center of Emerging Technologies and the Pakistan Air Force-run Center for Artificial Intelligence and Computing (CENTAIC).
Pakistan has also unveiled a gamut of AI-enabled military weapons, including equipment manufactured by the state-owned Global Industrial & Defense Solutions (GIDS). These include unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs), such as Shahpar-II, and the Spider Anti-UAV system. Pakistan and India used numerous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the 2025 clashes, with Islamabad deploying YIHA-III drones manufactured by the Turkish defense contractor Baykar in addition to Shahpar-II.
Drones are being extensively used along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border according to Pakistan Army sources. “We are facing the double threat – from the Afghan Taliban, and local terrorist groups – and we are countering these by using drones for surveilling and also for striking targets, especially in remote areas,” an official working with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s newly formed Police UAV Division told The Diplomat.
Military sources reveal that Pakistan is also close to deploying robots. “Law enforcement authorities already have robots in bomb disposal units. Robots are also performing reconnaissance tasks, including in border areas. Now we are working on using robots to lead clearance operations, along with transporting ammunition and supplies in military operations in [Khyber] Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan,” said a senior officer.
The security agencies have already run drills with Chinese robotic wolves. There are plans to produce similar machines indigenously, as well as humanoid and bipedal robots.
“To keep pace with India, and to nullify terrorist groups, we are always integrating new technologies in military and law enforcement agencies. However, the biggest challenge is developing our capacity due to the lack of resources and the economic challenges,” Lieutenant General Talat Masood, a former secretary of Pakistan’s Ministry of Defense Production, told The Diplomat. In this regard, Pakistan continues to benefit from Chinese architectural support for CENTAIC. Beijing is also helping Islamabad use facial recognition technology, as Pakistani security agencies gradually expand its deployment to sensitive areas, including border checkpoints and terror hotspots.
Along with fortifying security capacities, however, the Pakistani state is also using these AI-powered technologies to maintain the military establishment’s stranglehold and quell any regional or political dissent. The Diplomat has learned that the military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), is allocating resources for “narrative building.” In addition to producing various forms of media, the ISPR also employs tech professionals to engage in countering what the establishment deems to be “anti-state propaganda,” a misnomer for critiques of the armed forces, the country’s military leadership, and their policies.
“A good chunk of money is going into algorithmic filtering and monitoring, and tools are being used to erase social media anonymity and target individuals accordingly. Many professionals in the IT sector and the media industry are working on these projects,” revealed a senior digital media professional working at one of Pakistan’s largest media houses.
The investment to “counter anti-state propaganda” has significantly increased following the ouster of former premier Imran Khan in 2022. The ensuing anti-army sentiment has meant that Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, and its activists, have especially been under the gun. However, the same digital tools are being wielded to suppress dissidents in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
Similarly, Pakistani citizens are vulnerable to Islamist persecution, with digital blasphemy laws still providing allowance for the use of modern technology to fatally impose antediluvian punishments. This is in stark contrast with the image of moderation and reform that the Pakistani governments wants to show in front of the global audiences, especially as part of its recent role as the mediator between the U.S. and Iran.
A lack of transparency allows the state and the military establishment to deploy technology and AI beyond the realms of the already loosely defined “national security.” The National Security Policy 2022-2026 “has no mention of Artificial Intelligence,” said security analyst Abdullah Khan, the managing director of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “How can we deliberate over its pros and cons, when there is no official declaration of how these technologies are being used?”
Lieutenant General Talat Masood, the former Ministry of Defense Production secretary, said that transparency can only be ensured, and any overreach into the domain into fundamental rights can only be nullified, by having credible checks on the abuse of power. “The command needs to be held by a representative civilian government, which would require a revamp of the state’s power structure, so that the military and civilian can keep charge of their respective domains,” he said.
Those who defend the state’s position argue that compromising on certain freedoms is part and parcel of counterterror policymaking, especially when the situation is as grave as the one Pakistan faces today. But critics maintain that any compromises need to be justified with successful outcomes of technology and AI incorporation. So far, that hasn’t happened.
“All terror trends have increased over the past five years. There are hardly any counterterror successes for us to gauge,” said Khan of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “[The state] is currently in the responsive mode, whereas militants are in the offensive mode” when it comes to using technology.
“We need to change that, and enhance our own capacities beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring. When it comes to actual incorporation of technology in counterterror operations, we are still at the infancy stage,” he added.
As technology impacts the state’s role as a guarantor of its citizens’ security and freedom, it is evident that Pakistan is struggling on both fronts. And it is likely to stay that way, as long as the omnipotent military establishment continues to arbitrarily impose its whims.

Analysis-Israel’s election gives survivor Netanyahu a path to keep power
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:17:26 CET
03:17:26 KST

By Samia Nakhoul
DUBAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pulled ahead on Wednesday as votes were counted in Israel’s election, but the loss of a parliamentary majority leaves his path to another term dependent on drawing rivals into a coalition.
With the turnout in Tuesday’s election at a record high and nearly 86% of votes tallied, Israel’s three main broadcasters put Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties on course to win 53 seats in parliament, with the opposition bloc of rival Gadi Eisenkot trailing on 48.
Both remained short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, or parliament, while parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win 19 seats.
“Maybe it’s hard to say it or to see it, but he’s the winner,” said former Netanyahu adviser Aviv Bushinsky, describing the prime minister’s comeback as a political “resurrection.”
The paradox, Bushinsky said, is that an election that denied Netanyahu a majority in parliament may have restored his political primacy.
Despite the fallout from the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel and criticism of the security failures on his watch that the attacks exposed, Netanyahu won the support of an unexpectedly clear majority of Israeli Jews and has emerged at the head of the largest bloc.
Netanyahu’s achievement was less to win than to survive, said Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer.
Netanyahu’s bloc lost seats and fell short of the 61 needed to govern alone, but Eisenkot’s camp also lacked a viable route to power without the support of Arab parties.
“He won by not losing,” Citrinowicz said. “He managed to survive,” added Citrinowicz.
ARAB ISRAELIS MAKE GAINS
Netanyahu will stay on as caretaker prime minister while Israel’s president decides whom to ask to form a government. Despite not having a parliamentary majority, he retains the power of incumbency and a path to form a coalition government.
The election’s biggest disruption came from Israel’s Arab electorate, whose unprecedentedly high turnout handed Arab parties potentially decisive influence over what comes next.
Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by citizenship, Arab Israelis — who make up 21% of the population — could now hold the balance of power between the rival blocs.
“The Arabs have never been in a position where they held this much power,” said Dennis Ross, a former US Middle East peace negotiator.
Netanyahu’s opponents face a difficult route to removing him. Assembling a government would likely require direct or indirect support from Arab parties, a prospect that could prove difficult for potential right-wing partners such as Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman.
That leaves two broad paths — a broader unity government led by Netanyahu or another election, Israeli political analysts say.
Bushinsky sees a unity government as the most realistic option, particularly if US President Donald Trump presses Netanyahu to bring rivals into government and sideline far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
The United States is Israel’s most important ally, and Trump could use his public backing for Netanyahu as leverage to push for a broader coalition, Bushinsky said.
Failing that, Israel could remain politically deadlocked and return to the polls, a move which several political analysts said could further strengthen Netanyahu rather than change the outcome of the election.
The stalemate, Citrinowicz said, leaves Netanyahu better placed than Eisenkot to be prime minister. With another election unappealing to most parties, he said he saw a Netanyahu-led unity government — potentially bringing in Eisenkot or Bennett — as the most plausible way out.
IRAN LOOMS OVER THE FIGHT FOR POWER
Since the October 7 attacks, Israel has fought wars against Hamas in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, and launched joint attacks with the US on Iran.
In a post-election speech to cheering supporters, Netanyahu called for a “strong right-wing national government” and cast Israel’s military gains as a historic opportunity to eliminate the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all. But ulterior motives must not divert us from this sacred mission,” he said.
Trump, who had urged Israelis to keep Netanyahu in power so the two leaders could “finish the job” in Iran, said the prime minister had done “very well” and credited his own endorsement with helping him.
“It might be winning or tie. The tie is sort of considered a win in that case because it’s a big chess match,” Trump said.
A more consequential question may be whether Netanyahu, fighting to remain in office, again turns to Israel’s security challenges, above all Iran, to reshape the political equation.
A renewed confrontation with Tehran could strengthen his calls for national unity, though any escalation would depend heavily on Washington.
Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, sought to claim that mandate by framing the election as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership.
In a message to Israel’s security chiefs and public servants, Eisenkot said Netanyahu now headed a transitional government that had lost public confidence. “Stand strong and firm against any attempt to challenge you,” he said.
Netanyahu entered the election burdened by a long-running corruption trial, resistance to an independent inquiry into the Hamas attack, escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank and a bitter battle over military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
(Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Alex Richardson and Timothy Heritage)

By Yurii Kovalenko
KHERSON, Ukraine, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Years of near-daily Russian drone and artillery attacks have turned the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson into a battered urban landscape where death is never far away.
On Wednesday, however, the residents who remain ventured cautiously into sun-drenched streets after a US-brokered ceasefire around the nearby frontline town of Oleshky put a temporary pause to the aerial threat.
“Honestly, I can’t put it into words,” kiosk owner Oleksandra Kosenko told Reuters during a visit on Wednesday. “If it stays this way, it would be really wonderful.”
Ukraine said on Wednesday that the six-day ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, was holding, providing a rare moment of relief in the fifth year of grinding war.
The pause in fighting is aimed at paving the way for humanitarian relief for Oleshky, where residents face acute shortages of food and medicine.
CRITICAL RESPITE
For Kherson, a regional capital across the Dnipro River from Oleshky, the ceasefire - which took effect early on Tuesday - brings a brief window of respite.
Since Ukrainian troops recaptured the city from Russian occupation in November 2022, Moscow’s forces stationed on the opposite bank have shelled it regularly and hunted residents with deadly drones, officials say. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
As the attacks continued, residents fled and businesses closed, making daily life increasingly dangerous.
The city still functions, with buses ferrying people around and shops and cafes serving customers. But the scars of the war are plain to see. Some buildings are in ruins, the pavements are largely empty and anti-drone nets are draped over the main roads.
On Wednesday, residents walked their dogs without glancing toward the sky. Elderly men sipped coffee on a bench without the din of distant explosions.
“Kherson, which was constantly under fire, literally came to life,” said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, on the Telegram messaging app.
“People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire.”
Kosenko, the kiosk owner, said she had seen a near-doubling in the number of clients: around 50 in total. She was relieved to no longer be dashing for cover on the way to work.
ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION
On Tuesday, top Ukrainian officials described the ceasefire as a major de-escalation that could build confidence for future agreements.
Yet beneath the relief, Kosenko and others expressed wariness that fighting could erupt again at any moment. Many residents approached by Reuters declined to speak, appearing tense.
Anti-personnel mines dropped by the Russians still pose a danger even when hostilities are paused.
Battles are also raging elsewhere along the 1,200-km (750 mile) front line, where Russia remains intent on capturing the parts of the eastern Donetsk region still outside its control.
Moscow is also continuing its bombing campaign of Ukrainian cities, which has damaged critical infrastructure including in Kherson.
Locals like Olha Chyupikova, who lived through Russia’s occupation of her city, said they had learned to prepare for the worst.
“The Russians have proven that they can’t be trusted,” said the 52-year-old municipal worker.
“So I think everyone subconsciously feels like there could be some sort of provocation at any moment.”
(Writing by Dan PeleschukEditing by Ros Russell)

WINDHOEK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Namibian and Chinese universities plan to expand vocational training in Namibia through Zheng He College, which is expected to begin enrolling students and offering classes in 2027, a university official said Wednesday.
Zheng He College is a vocational education cooperation platform jointly developed by China's Nantong Vocational University and Namibia's Welwitchia University.
The college, housed in a standalone building in Namibia's capital city of Windhoek, will initially offer programs in mechanical manufacturing and automation, and construction engineering technology in the first quarter of 2027, said Amon Haufiku, director of technical and vocational education and training (TVET) at Welwitchia University.
The formal cooperation framework was established on Nov. 27, 2025, when Welwitchia University, Nantong Vocational University and Nami Prefabricated Housing, a local company, signed a tripartite cooperation agreement to promote technical and vocational education and practical training.
Haufiku said the planned programs at Zheng He College would broaden access to technical training in Namibia.
"This will allow Namibian students to access similar technical training locally, while benefiting from the expertise and experience of our Chinese partners," he said.
"As the partnership develops, we also envision student exchanges that will enable students to study in both Namibia and China, deepening cultural understanding, academic cooperation, and practical skills development."
The initiative follows commitments made during Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah's state visit to China in July, during which the two countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in education, technical skills training and technology.
During the visit, the two countries also signed a memorandum of understanding on TVET cooperation to promote exchanges and collaboration between their vocational education institutions. ■

Ukraine Auctions Russian Propagandist’s Kyiv Apartment for $190,000 to Fund Reconstruction
Ukraine has auctioned a confiscated apartment belonging to Russian propagandist and designer Artemy Lebedev in central Kyiv for more than $190,000, with the proceeds designated for the country’s reconstruction.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s State Property Fund on October 28, the property was sold through an online auction for 8.01 million hryvnias (approximately $190,000), exceeding its starting price of 7.07 million hryvnias (approximately $168,000).
The 193.2-square-meter (2,080-square-foot) apartment is located on Saksahanskoho Street in Kyiv’s historic center. It occupies two levels of the top floor of a six-story building and includes three rooms, office spaces, a kitchen, two bathrooms, three balconies, and utility areas.
Two bidders participated in the auction, raising the final price by 936,150 hryvnias (approximately $22,000). The property was transferred to Ukrainian state ownership following a ruling by the High Anti-Corruption Court as part of sanctions imposed against Lebedev.
Under the auction terms, the winning bidder must complete payment within 25 working days after the auction protocol is issued and settle outstanding utility bills before the purchase agreement can be finalized.
The State Property Fund confirmed that proceeds from the sale of sanctioned Russian assets are directed to Ukraine’s Fund for the Liquidation of the Consequences of Armed Aggression, which finances reconstruction efforts.
Lebedev, a Russian designer and blogger known for his pro-Kremlin positions, has faced legal action in Ukraine over his activities during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
In June 2022, he illegally entered the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, where he filmed a report for Kremlin-aligned media about Russia’s seizure of the facility. Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) subsequently notified him of suspicion of justifying Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine.

Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:15:11 UTC
03:15:11 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Loses More Troops in a Month in Ukraine Than USSR Lost in 10 Years in Afghanistan, Stubb Says
Finnish President Alexander Stubb stated that Russia’s offensive in eastern Ukraine would take years to achieve its objectives at the current pace, addressing the UN Security Council on September 23.
Stubb argued that drone warfare has effectively frozen much of the frontline.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking on behalf of the five Nordic countries, Stubb stated that Russian forces had captured roughly 900 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year, while Ukraine had retaken around 800 square kilometers.
“So the line of contact is basically not moving,” Stubb stated.
At that pace, he warned, Russia would need years to seize the rest of Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Stubb also stated that roughly 25,000 soldiers are being killed each month as both sides fight across a frontline that has shifted only marginally.
He compared the monthly losses with the Soviet war in Afghanistan, noting that the USSR lost roughly 18,000 troops over the entire decade-long conflict.
“This, in my mind, is a waste of life,” Stubb stated. “So the continuation of this war is a lose-lose.”
The Finnish president attributed much of the battlefield stalemate to drones, unmanned systems, and near-constant surveillance.
“We haven’t seen anything like this previously,” Stubb noted.
He described stretches of the frontline as roughly 20-kilometer-wide “death zones,” where exposed troops and vehicles face an extremely high likelihood of being detected and attacked.
“We’re seeing unmanned vehicles, we’re seeing death zones of roughly 20 kilometers to which you cannot enter, because with a 95 percent certainty, you’re going to be wiped out,” Stubb stated.
He argued that this environment helps explain why neither side has been able to achieve a decisive breakthrough despite heavy losses.
Stubb also accused Russia of systematically targeting Ukrainian civilians, civilian infrastructure, and humanitarian operations in an attempt to intimidate the population and weaken resistance.
“The aim is to instill fear and wear down Ukraine,” he stated.
The Finnish president called for an unconditional ceasefire, or at minimum limited arrangements covering areas such as energy infrastructure and grain exports, before negotiations on security, territory, justice, and a permanent settlement.
“There has to become a time when the killing stops,” Stubb stated.
Hours after the UN Security Council meeting, Stubb and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a new defense agreement focused on drones, technology transfers, expertise, and joint industrial projects.
“This is not simply a contract or an agreement on the sale and purchase of drones,” Zelenskyy stated. “This is about security—our shared security and joint production.”
Finland has increasingly framed its defense relationship with Ukraine as a two-way exchange, with Helsinki seeking to draw on Ukrainian battlefield experience as it develops its own military capabilities.
“That is exactly why we began saying that this is not a one-way street where we simply provide something to you,” Stubb stated. “On the contrary, it is a two-way process in which we learn from you.”
“By learning from Ukraine’s experience, we are strengthening our own capabilities,” he added.
Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine carried out three major offensive operations in 2026, including Operation Vivaldi in the Donetsk region and Operation VELES near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian troops traveled more than 15 kilometers underground before emerging behind Russian positions.

Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:11:54 UTC
03:11:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Caretaker role could limit Netanyahu but not rule out war with Iran
Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to face more constraints as Israel's caretaker prime minister after Tuesday's election, but experts say his government could still retain significant powers including when it comes to waging war on Iran.
Neither Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is projected by Israeli media to win a majority in the country’s 120-seat legislature. Eisenkot has acknowledged the prime minister was still in office as a caretaker but issued a warning that Netanyahu might use security for political ends.
Netanyahu's office has previously rejected accusations he is using the Iran conflict for political gain. His office did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday.
“If you look at the letter of the law, a caretaker government has the same authority, has the same powers as a regular government,” said Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, adding however that a caretaker government “has a duty of restraint” and more limited discretion to act in some areas.
A caretaker government faces limitations when it comes to issues such as appointments, but has leeway to act in matters where there is a public interest, analysts say.
“In general, security issues are the clearest exception to this duty of restraint,” said Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, noting that Israel's supreme court has previously held that a caretaker government must avoid far-reaching decisions unless they are justified by a pressing necessity.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset convenes and before its committees are formed,” Asher said, adding that “a caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran”.
After the final tally is in, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult party leaders and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government, with the nominee then getting up to 42 days to establish a government.

Austria to launch parliamentary inquiry into use of smart glasses amid privacy concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:11:41 UTC
03:11:41 KST

Burak Bir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Austria is set to launch a parliamentary inquiry into the use of smart glasses amid growing privacy concerns, the country's secretary of state for digitalization said Wednesday.
Alexander Proll presented a three-stage model aimed at regulating smart glasses, which can feature built-in cameras, microphones and artificial intelligence functions, public broadcaster ORF reported.
Under the proposed model, recordings would be prohibited in sensitive areas, including schools, kindergartens, changing rooms, toilets, courts, prisons, and police and military facilities.
Recordings in public spaces would also have to be clearly visible to others, according to the proposal.
Proll said a parliamentary inquiry would be the next step, bringing together experts in science, data protection and technology, as well as representatives of people affected by the use of smart glasses.
He ruled out a total ban on the technology, saying the government aims to allow technological progress while ensuring that people cannot be secretly filmed.
Proll also said manufacturers should be required to make recordings clearly identifiable through measures such as visible recording lights and acoustic signals.  
Meanwhile, nearly 25,000 people have signed a petition calling for a ban on smart glasses, according to ORF.
The Vienna city government also urged federal authorities last week to examine a possible ban on the devices in public transportation, government offices and schools, the broadcaster reported.

Water tariffs will be reviewed under new rules: will Ukrainians’ bills decrease?
Kyiv • UNN
Tariffs will be set by local authorities, while the NEURC will remotely verify their calculations. There will be no automatic reduction in bills.
Ukraine is introducing a new mechanism for monitoring tariffs for centralized water supply and wastewater services. On October 27, the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC) approved a procedure for reviewing decisions on the cost of these services. The regulator will analyze whether the tariffs were calculated correctly and whether the expenses included in consumers’ bills are substantiated.
UNN examined who is now responsible for setting them, how the monitoring will work, and what consumers who doubt the fairness of the charges can do.
Who sets water tariffs in Ukraine
In March 2026, the division of powers in the field of centralized water supply and wastewater services changed in Ukraine. Law No. 4777-IX, which entered into force on March 11, transferred tariff-setting powers to local self-government bodies. Where they have the relevant powers, decisions may be adopted by military administrations of settlements. In turn, the licensing of water utilities and oversight of compliance with licensing conditions were transferred to authorized local state administrations. The NEURC retained responsibility for developing tariff-setting methodologies and verifying the correctness of tariff decisions.
As we can see, the new mechanism does not return to the regulator the right to directly determine the cost of water in each city. Local authorities will continue to adopt tariff decisions, while the NEURC may verify whether a decision complies with legislation and approved methodologies.
Water prices in Ukraine are set by local authorities — Shmyhal21.08.26, 12:55 • 3382 views
How inspections of water supply tariffs will be carried out
The NEURC reported that inspections will be scheduled and unscheduled. Both types of oversight will be conducted remotely: officials will not visit enterprises or local authorities. The basis will be the tariff calculations, documents, and explanations used when the relevant decisions were adopted.
Scheduled inspections will be conducted according to an annual plan published on the NEURC website. Unscheduled inspections may be carried out, in particular, if monitoring reveals inconsistencies in the documents, questionable figures, or grounds for examining a sharp tariff increase.
The oversight process will begin with a request to the body that set the tariff. It must provide the decision, the tariff structure, the water utility’s calculations, and supporting materials. The draft procedure stipulated at least ten working days to respond to a request and no more than twenty working days for the inspection after the documents were received. If the necessary information is insufficient, the deadlines will be suspended in accordance with the procedure.
In addition, the regulator will compare the approved tariff with the calculation data. The result will be a written conclusion. It will serve as the basis for replacing the tariff, but it will not automatically cancel it on the day the document is issued.
What will be examined in the cost of water
The water supply tariff covers the costs of extracting, treating, and delivering water to consumers. The wastewater tariff concerns the collection, transportation, and treatment of wastewater. They are calculated separately, although the vast majority of Ukrainians see a single item on their bills covering payment for water supply and wastewater services.
During the oversight process, authorized officials will verify whether the calculations comply with the established methodology, whether there are sufficient documents to substantiate the expenses, and whether the tariff approval procedure was followed. Particular attention will be paid to the cost of electricity for pumps and treatment facilities, labor costs, network repairs, the purchase of materials, and other economically justified components.
Investment expenses, planned service volumes, and the consideration of the results of previous inspections are separate issues. For example, if an enterprise included certain modernization expenses, it is necessary to determine whether their inclusion in the tariff meets the established requirements.
What will happen if the regulator finds violations
Based on the inspections, the NEURC will draw up conclusions. If the calculations are incorrect or the expenses are unsubstantiated, the conclusion will indicate the violations identified and recommendations for remedying them. They may be taken into account when reviewing, adjusting, or setting tariffs in the future. Once approved, the results must be published on the regulator’s website.
At the same time, local authorities have the right to express their objections to the conclusion.
When discussing the regulator’s recommendations, one more important point should be understood. The NEURC’s conclusions will not mean the automatic cancellation of a tariff or the return of money for services already paid for. A subsequent decision to change the price must be made by the authorized body in accordance with the procedure established by law. The new procedure itself does not establish a separate mechanism for compensating the public for overpayments.
Will water bills become lower, and how can they be challenged?
For household consumers, the new measure will provide an opportunity for additional oversight. If an inspection identifies inflated or incorrectly accounted-for expenses and the local authorities subsequently adjust the tariff, this may affect future charges. However, the regulator does not promise an overall reduction in tariffs.
Consumers should first check the current tariff decision on the website of the city or town council or the service provider. After that, they should determine the date the tariff was introduced, the separate costs of water supply and wastewater services, the consumer category, and whether the bill includes other charges not directly related to the price per cubic meter.
If there are doubts about the calculations, a written request may be submitted to the body that approved the tariff, asking it to provide the decision and an accessible justification. If there are indications of a violation, an appeal may be submitted to the NEURC, including through the "Citizens’ Appeals" section on the regulator’s official website or by writing to [email protected].
The application should indicate the locality, the name of the water utility, the details of the tariff decision, and the specific facts that raise doubts, attaching any available documents.
When the new rules will take effect
The NEURC approved the procedure on October 27, 2026. The text of the resolution prepared for the meeting states that it will enter into force on the day after its official publication on the regulator’s website.
It should also be emphasized that the mechanism is designed to operate during martial law and for twelve months after its termination or repeal. It is connected with the temporary redistribution of powers between the NEURC and local authorities.
Will NEURC oversight make water tariffs for households fairer?
The new inspections make it possible to compare local authorities’ decisions with economic calculations and make identified violations public. However, the effectiveness of the system will nevertheless depend on how fully the authorities provide information and whether they take the regulator’s recommendations into account.
As a reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that Ukrainians and businesses are being offered the option of paying to change their electricity consumption schedule. For example, they could shift the operation of appliances from peak-demand hours to another time. To participate, it will be necessary to conclude an agreement with an aggregator—a company that represents consumers in the energy market.

Constitutional Court rules on conditional early release of life prisoners for military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:40 EET
03:07:40 KST

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine (CCU) on October 28 ruled that provisions of the Criminal Code, which do not provide for the possibility of conditional early release for contract military service for individuals serving life sentences, are constitutional, the CCU's communications department said.
"On October 28, 2026, the Second Senate, at a plenary session, considered the case based on a constitutional complaint filed by Anatoliy Oleksandrovych Luzhynetsky and adopted Decision No. 13-r(II)/2026," according to a statement from the CCU Communications Department, which was received by Interfax-Ukraine on Wednesday.
It is reported that, after reviewing the case, the court concluded that the mechanism for conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service, established by Article 81-1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, is temporary in nature (applicable during mobilization and/or martial law), and its application entails specific consequences due to the possession and use of weapons and military equipment.
Thus, in the court's view, "the conscription of individuals who have committed violent (intentional murder of two or more persons) and other particularly serious criminal offenses entails additional risks to military discipline, subordination, the proper execution of combat missions, as well as the lives and health of other military personnel and civilians."
"In light of the foregoing, the Court has found the provisions of the first part of Article 811 of the Code to be consistent with the Constitution of Ukraine, in that they do not provide for the possibility of applying conditional early release from serving a sentence for the purpose of performing military service under a contract to persons who are serving a sentence of life imprisonment, and exclude the possibility of applying such release to persons convicted of the intentional murder of two or more persons," the court said in its announcement.
The decision and its summary will be published on the court's official website on October 29, 2026.

New city project for Ukraine's reconstruction to be presented at Davos, URC2027 in Tallinn
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:07:09 EET
03:07:09 KST

Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Vladyslav Rashkovan, Presidential Advisor on Reconstruction and Investment Attraction Oksana Markarova, and Executive Director of the New City innovative urban initiative Viktoria Trotska are working on a new city project as part of preparations for Ukraine's recovery.
"For now, I'm mostly providing inspiration, while Oksana Markarova and Viktoria Trotska are already developing the new city project and plan to present the initiative at the World Economic Forum in Davos and at the URC in Tallinn – and perhaps even display a physical model of the city," Rashkovan said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12-18.
According to him, following the example of the construction of the city of Slavutych in 1986-1988, the new city project envisages various districts – conventionally Italian, French, German, Eastern, and others: an international team of German, Italian, French, and Japanese architects is working on the city's design, with weekly coordination meetings.
"So far, they're all working for free. To professionalize the project and anchor it to a specific territory, funding from international organizations is needed. The European Commission likes this idea as a showcase project, since Europe also lacks modern experience in building such new cities," Rashkovan said.
He added that over the next year, with the support of international partners, he wants to prepare a kind of blueprint – a book on the principles of building new cities after the war.
"It doesn't matter whether we're talking about a new city or the reconstruction of districts in Kharkiv, Odesa, Kyiv, or Trostianets. What's important is to establish these principles. Such a resource could be useful not only for Ukraine but also for Syria, Lebanon, and other countries that have suffered war damage. It will also be of interest to European partners, who also need to undertake significant construction projects," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
He said that since reconstruction takes place at the local level, the idea of building new cities seems promising, as 95% of what exists at the state level is already present at the local level.
According to Rashkovan, at the city level, for example, it is possible to implement green, distributed energy systems and inclusivity, put digital democracy tools into practice, and lay the technological foundation from the ground up for the city's effective functioning: rational use of water and electricity, waste management, and transportation organization.
"We would also like to create a self-sufficient city that will not require additional funding from Kyiv, that will itself create jobs and become a magnet for talent and business, serving as a model of deregulation and a favorable investment climate," Ukraine's representative to the IMF said.
According to him, as part of this project, there is ongoing collaboration with Jenny Roe, former former Director of the Center for Design & Health in the School of Architecture, University of Virginia – who is the author of the book "Restorative Cities" about cities capable of helping people heal – as well as with Finnish and Korean experts on the concept of a two-tier safe city, since Finland leads the Shelter Coalition and has one of the best track records in this field.
Rashkovan is optimistic about the prospects for implementing such a project: it must be supported by the government, but 80-85% of it will be financed by private capital, investments, commercial loans, private equity funds, and so on.
Read the full second part of the interview with Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternative Executive Director at the IMF, on Interfax-Ukraine website at https://interfax.com.ua/news/interview/1227277.html.

The US Federal Reserve kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday as policymakers weighed elevated inflation against strong economic growth.
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the decision in a 10-2 vote to support the central bank's dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices, the Fed said in a statement.
Policymakers Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, preferring to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at the meeting.
"Inflation remains elevated," the committee said, pledging that it "will deliver price stability."
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal," it added.
The central bank noted that US economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, supported by resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment despite elevated uncertainty linked partly to geopolitical developments.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce and the unemployment rate has changed little, the Fed said, adding that it is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Expert: Russia must accept reality of NATO’s 32 member countries
Jim Stokes, a senior expert with GLOBSEC’s “Future of Security” program and former director of nuclear policy at NATO (2023–2025), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Russia will therefore have to accept the reality: NATO now has 32 members. Russia can continue talking about this, and NATO can simply respond: “Noted. We are not going to change,” Stokes said in response to a question about whether the Alliance would be willing to agree to the Kremlin’s demands to roll back its military presence to pre-1997 levels.
According to the expert, this seems “absolutely impossible.” He was referring to the new members—Finland and Sweden—not to mention the 16 countries that joined after the end of the Cold War.
“They are not going to agree to leave the Alliance, and the other Allies are not going to agree simply to let them go. That has never happened in NATO’s 77-year history,” Stokes noted.
However, he acknowledged that another question is whether NATO will ever allow new allies to join. Such a decision is made by consensus among all 32 countries, Stokes reminded.
At the same time, the expert emphasized that the main problem right now is that this Russian war is shaping the perception of the threat, and it is precisely because of this war that Finland and Sweden decided to join the Alliance rather than remain mere partners.
“Much of the responsibility therefore lies with Russia. It can blame NATO for expanding closer to Russian borders, and I understand that it is unhappy about it. But Russia had no problem with this in the late 1990s and early 2000s. It turned the issue into a political one, and now it will have to come to terms with it,” Stokes concluded.

The German brigade in Lithuania will monitor Kaliningrad and Belarus using electronic warfare equipment
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:31 EET
03:02:31 KST

The German brigade in Lithuania will monitor Kaliningrad and Belarus using electronic warfare equipment
Kyiv • UNN
The German brigade in Lithuania will use electronic warfare to detect the military activity of Russia and Belarus. The data will update the allies’ databases.
The German brigade being stationed in Lithuania will use electronic warfare systems for the early detection of military activity in the Kaliningrad region and Belarus. This was reported by the head of Germany’s cyber forces, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum, Reuters reported, according to UNN.
Details
The German brigade, whose full deployment is scheduled for next year, will also collect data on Russian and Belarusian military transmitters and radar systems to update electronic warfare databases used by German and allied forces.
"We will enter (the data) into electronic warfare databases, which will then notify all our systems if a new radar appears on the Belarusian side," Daum said.
He noted that Russia’s activities in some regions of Europe had reached what he called a "second phase, whose aim is to cause harm," but which does not cross the threshold of armed conflict.
"There is not yet a war in the cyber-information sphere, but it is no longer peace," said the head of the Bundeswehr’s military cyber unit.
The German army is currently testing electronic warfare systems in Lithuania, including drone detection equipment, signal interceptors, jammers, and sensors designed to transmit battlefield data to analysts.
"Before the war in Ukraine, German military personnel could barely persuade commercial companies to supply them with such systems," said Patrick Jeschke, who heads the Bundeswehr’s cyber innovation center.
According to him, the task has changed: now it is necessary not merely to find suppliers, but to select the most promising technologies from a multitude of offers.
"Over the past decades, we did not invest very much in new capabilities. We used what we had because we were focused on missions abroad—in Afghanistan and elsewhere. Now there is a need to improve our capabilities," Daum said.

Economic freedom should become the foundation of Ukraine's post-war reconstruction – ILI experts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:02:09 EET
03:02:09 KST

The International Liberty Institute (ILI) presented Ukrainian editions of three books by German historian and sociologist Rainer Zitelmann and Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises in Kyiv, and also announced preparations for the publication of another work by Zitelmann. Participants in the presentation emphasized that private property, entrepreneurship, competition and limiting excessive government regulation should become important components of Ukraine's economic recovery.
The books in question are Zitelmann's "In Defense of Capitalism: Debunking the Myths" and "Capitalism Is Not the Problem, but the Solution: A Journey Through the Recent History of Five Continents," as well as Mises' "Bureaucracy." The fourth book, "How Nations Escape Poverty? Vietnam, Poland and the Origins of Prosperity," is currently being edited and prepared for printing, according to the organizers.
In particular, the author of "In Defense of Capitalism" examines ten common accusations against the market economy: from worsening poverty and inequality to environmental problems, monopolies, economic crises and wars. Separate chapters are devoted to the historical experience of socialist economies and the attitudes of citizens in different countries toward entrepreneurship and private property.
"The main idea of this book is to defend an economic system based on freedom, private property, competition and entrepreneurship. Any book that promotes the ideas of economic freedom will have an impact on the improvement and development of our society," Volodymyr Popereshniuk, co-founder of Nova Poshta and the International Liberty Institute (ILI), emphasized at a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Wednesday.
According to him, entrepreneurship creates goods, jobs and prosperity, while excessive government intervention and regulatory restrictions restrain business activity. Popereshniuk also outlined the author's arguments regarding economic inequality, environmental protection, monopolies and the causes of crises.
He separately focused on the sociological part of the publication. According to the presentation materials, Chapter 12 contains a study of Ukrainians' attitudes toward capitalism, while Chapter 13 presents the results of surveys in another 35 countries. According to the results cited by the organizers, pro-capitalist sentiments prevail in Ukraine, Poland, the United States, South Korea, Japan, Nigeria and the Czech Republic.
"Ukrainians perceive economic freedom as their own freedom. These studies give us hope that the ideas of entrepreneurship and competition will prevail in Ukraine," the Nova Poshta co-founder noted, commenting on the results presented in the publication.
Dmytro Dusheiko, PhD in Economics and an expert at the International Liberty Institute (ILI), who served as the academic editor of the Ukrainian edition of "Capitalism Is Not the Problem, but the Solution," in turn emphasized that Zitelmann analyzes the history of countries that chose different economic models under similar initial circumstances. The examples include North and South Korea, the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic, Chile and Venezuela, as well as China before and after the beginning of market reforms in the late 1970s.
The expert drew attention to the differences in the development of West Germany following Ludwig Erhard's reforms and the command-and-administrative system of East Germany. He also cited the experience of market transformations in China and Vietnam after periods of centralized planning.
"We have no right to win the first war for independence and lose the second war — for economic freedom. This very book demonstrates through specific historical examples why reforms will be of decisive importance for the country's development," Dusheiko stressed.
He also pointed out that Zitelmann wrote a special foreword to the Ukrainian edition, in which he emphasized the need for economic transformations after victory in the war for independence.
Dusheiko paid particular attention to the book "How Nations Escape Poverty? Vietnam, Poland and the Origins of Prosperity," on which publishing work is ongoing. In it, the author compares the experiences of two countries that had low levels of personal income at the end of the 20th century but subsequently demonstrated substantial economic growth thanks to reforms.
The economist described the adoption of the Wilczek Act at the end of 1988, which introduced the principle of freedom of entrepreneurship, as an important step in Poland. According to the data presented, the subsequent reforms of Leszek Balcerowicz contributed to 25 years of uninterrupted economic growth in the country between 1992 and 2017. The expert also compared the results of Polish reforms with Ukraine's experience.
"The law did not build anything; it merely allowed people to engage in free enterprise. War and poverty are not a sentence; they are an opportunity for reforms," Dusheiko noted, summarizing the conclusions that, in his opinion, Ukraine can draw from the experiences of these countries.
ILI Director Mykhailo Kamchatnyi presented Ludwig von Mises' work "Bureaucracy," first published in 1944. He recalled that the prominent representative of the Austrian School of Economics was born in Lviv in 1881. According to the institute's director, the first Ukrainian edition of "Bureaucracy" was published in a limited print run in 2021, while the current edition is the second; Mykola Bunyk served as the book's academic editor and translator.
Kamchatnyi explained that Mises distinguishes between management oriented toward profit and consumer needs and bureaucratic management based on compliance with laws, procedures and directives. In his opinion, the problem arises not from the very existence of the administrative apparatus, but when bureaucratic methods are extended to areas where market mechanisms can operate.
"Bureaucracy in itself is neither good nor bad — it is simply a method of management. The most important question is the extent to which bureaucrats interfere in people's lives and in the economy. The main thing we need to do before starting reconstruction is to clearly distinguish the functions of entrepreneurs and bureaucrats. When a former entrepreneur becomes a government official, he begins to act according to laws and regulations rather than the logic of profit," Kamchatnyi emphasized.
According to him, the effectiveness of government bodies should be assessed primarily by how they perform their statutory functions. For example, the amount of tax revenue also depends on the economic situation of a region, particularly its proximity to hostilities.
During the question-and-answer session, participants also addressed the role of private business in the country's defense. Volodymyr Popereshniuk stated that enterprises could participate more effectively in protecting critical facilities, particularly in air defense, but the current procedures, in his opinion, remain excessively bureaucratic.
"This is not a private military company. We do this on a voluntary basis, and the relevant units are subordinate to the military. Companies purchase the necessary equipment at their own expense and allocate personnel, but they operate within the military chain of command," he explained, speaking about business participation in air defense measures.
According to the organizers, the publishing projects presented are intended to encourage discussion about Ukraine's development model, the limits of government intervention and the role of business in reconstruction.

New study explores how money influences interpretations of the Bible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:03 UTC
03:00:03 KST

A new large study reveals that a person’s household income shapes how they interpret the Bible’s teachings on poverty and charity, with wealthier and lower-income believers drawing starkly different conclusions. The research, published in the Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion, shows that highly religious low-income Americans tend to view biblical charity as a call for societal transformation. Highly religious affluent Americans tend to view it as a call for individual philanthropy. These patterns suggest that religious belief often amplifies the economic interests of a person’s social group rather than uniformly justifying economic inequality across all classes.
Sociologists have debated the fundamental nature of religion and its relationship to economic inequality for more than a century. One prominent theory originated with the 19th-century philosopher Karl Marx, who proposed that religion acts as an opiate for the masses. In this view, religious ideas offer a set of comforting illusions that persuade lower-income groups to accept their disadvantaged position.
By framing the current economic system as normal or divinely ordained, religion supposedly drains the motivation to fight for a fairer society. Modern scholars building on this idea argue that religion offers psychological compensators, promising eternal rewards that make present-day inequalities seem less important.
A competing theory takes a different perspective, viewing religion primarily as a tool for binding groups together. Rooted in the work of early sociologist Émile Durkheim, this concept suggests that religious norms and practices serve to unite an in-group and validate that specific group’s interests. Under this framework, religious beliefs do not automatically make people accept the economic status quo. Instead, believers might project their own group’s economic needs onto their theology.
Samuel L. Perry, a sociologist at the University of Oklahoma, wanted to test these two competing frameworks. He designed a study to see if high levels of religious commitment are associated with justifying the current economic system regardless of a person’s own wealth. Alternatively, he wanted to see if religious commitment amplifies different biblical interpretations based on how much money a person makes.
To answer this question, Perry analyzed data from the 2022 Public Religion Research Institute and Brookings Christian Nationalism Survey. This provided a large, nationally representative sample of 5,701 adults living in the United States. The survey included a question asking respondents what they thought Jesus and the prophets primarily meant when speaking about taking care of the poor in the Bible.
Respondents had to choose between two interpretations. The first option stated that biblical teachings on the poor primarily refer to charitable acts by individuals. This represents a more individualized approach to social issues, focusing on personal generosity without challenging the underlying economic system. The second option stated that these teachings primarily refer to an obligation to create a more just society. Scholars often refer to this as structural transformation, which involves altering systemic inequalities.
The researcher looked at two different measures of religious commitment. The first was a private expression of faith, measured by how often the respondents attended religious services. The second was a more public and ideological expression, measured by a person’s adherence to Christian nationalism. Christian nationalism is an ideology that seeks to closely merge Christian identity with American civic life and government policy.
The survey categorized respondents by their annual household income. Perry grouped the participants into three broad economic brackets. These included households earning less than $50,000, those earning between $50,000 and $99,999, and those earning $100,000 or more.
To ensure the results were not skewed by other variables, the statistical models controlled for a wide array of demographic and ideological factors. These included political ideology, political party affiliation, age, race, gender, educational attainment, religious denomination, and geographic region. The control variables performed as expected, with self-identified conservatives and Republicans being less likely to favor the structural-transformation reading of the Bible. In contrast, atheists, non-evangelical Protestants, and highly educated individuals were more likely to affirm the structural reading.
By analyzing these variables together, the study revealed distinct patterns that contradicted the idea of religion acting as a universal opiate. Among Americans in the lowest income bracket, greater religious commitment was linked to a higher likelihood of choosing the structural-transformation interpretation. Highly religious people in this group were more inclined to believe the Bible demands the creation of a just society.
The opposite pattern emerged among Americans in the highest income bracket. For those earning $100,000 or more, high levels of religious attendance and high levels of Christian nationalism were linked to the individualized charity interpretation. As religiosity increased for these affluent earners, they were much more likely to say the Bible teaches that helping the poor is a matter of individual charitable acts.
Middle-income earners fell somewhere in between, though they trended slightly toward the individualized interpretation as their Christian nationalism increased. As their religious attendance increased, they moved toward the individualized interpretation at a pace similar to the highest earners. Overall, the statistical models showed a distinct divide across income groups that widened alongside religious devotion.
The gap in biblical interpretation was widest among the most devout participants. For Americans who rarely attended religious services or scored very low on measures of Christian nationalism, household income was not associated with differing views on biblical charity. Less religious people across all income brackets were about equally split between the two interpretations of poor relief. It was only among highly religious individuals that economic position became strongly associated with a specific theological view.
The author suggests that these results support the in-group cohesion theory over the opiate theory. Instead of deadening the political desires of lower-income people with promises of future rewards, religion seems to amplify the economic interests of whatever class a person belongs to. Wealthy believers favor an interpretation that protects their assets while encouraging personal generosity, while lower-income believers favor an interpretation that demands systemic fairness.
These results come with a few methodological limitations. The survey data is cross-sectional, meaning it captures a single snapshot in time. Because of this design, the study cannot definitively prove that a combination of income and religion directly causes a specific interpretation of the Bible. It is theoretically possible that a person’s theological views might influence their economic position or religious attendance, though the researcher notes this is a less plausible explanation.
Additionally, the study relies on household income as a stand-in for social class. A person’s class is often defined by a combination of factors, including educational background, occupational prestige, and subjective feelings about their own social standing. Future research might incorporate these broader measures to see if the patterns hold up across different definitions of economic status.
The survey also used a single question to measure attitudes about biblical teachings on poverty. Researchers could build on these findings by incorporating multiple questions that ask how participants understand the Bible’s views on getting ahead in life or economic inequality more broadly. Identifying similar trends across a wider variety of questions would provide additional support for the current results.
The study, “Opiate or In-Group Amphetamine? Religion, Economic Position, and the Bible’s Teaching on Charity,” was authored by Samuel L. Perry.
