High-speed train crash in Spain kills at least 64 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:31 UTC
01:41:31 KST

Spain suffered its second deadly high-speed train accident this year when one train on Wednesday slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, with the impact shredding cars and killing at least 64 people.
The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January.
Photo: Reuters
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages.
David Gomez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El Pais.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought,” until emergency services arrived, he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, said the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. It was a source of national pride.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
“It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy,” Garcia said.
Passenger Ignacio Relano was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has “activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities.”
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galan, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was “dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo.”
“Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers,” wrote Sanchez, who faces a national election next month. “All my thoughts are with the victims and their families.”
Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.
“We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo),” the royal couple said. “We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”
Spain’s soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
The January incident shook confidence in the European country’s extensive high-speed rail service.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodriguez, said that the increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodriguez told TVE. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

European gas prices hit 100 euros for first time since 2022
- European gas prices rose above €100 per megawatt-hour for the first time since 2022, driven by Middle East war fears and the need to fill reserves before winter.
- The Dutch TTF benchmark climbed more than 4% to €100.45, though it stayed far below the €345 peak seen during the 2022 energy crisis after Russia invaded Ukraine.
- Analysts said renewed Middle East escalation and weaker wind and solar output are lifting prices, but lower gas use and more renewables should limit power bill spikes.
AI generated
LONDON - European natural gas prices climbed to the highest level since 2022 on Oct 28, topping €100 (S$143) per megawatt-hour, driven by concerns over the Middle East war and the need to fill reserves ahead of winter.
Around 1455 GMT (10.55pm in Singapore), the Dutch TTF futures contract – the benchmark for European gas – rose more than 4% to reach €100.45 per megawatt-hour.
Prices remain far below the peaks of the 2022 energy crisis triggered by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, when they reached €345 per megawatt-hour in March that year.
The jump in gas prices on Oct 28 reflected concerns that the United States could launch a new wave of strikes on Iran after next week’s midterm elections, risking a retaliation by Tehran on energy infrastructure in the Gulf.
Exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Gulf remain very limited, according to analysts.
“Concerns about renewed escalation in the Middle East are driving prices higher,” said Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Global Risk Management.
“However, weather forecasts are also providing support,” he added, as Europe is set for lower wind and solar generation, increasing demand for gas.
Overall, European countries are consuming less gas than in 2022 as they increasingly switch to renewables to generate electricity.
Analysts believe this shift reduces the risk of a gas price spike translating into hikes for electricity bills as severe as those seen in 2022. AFP

United Microelectronics Corp (UMC, 聯電), the world’s fourth-largest contract chipmaker, yesterday said it expects artificial intelligence (AI)-related chips to account for 25 percent of its revenue by 2029, adding that AI revenue is set to meet its US$300 million target this year.
To meet surging demand for a wide range of its technologies from silicon photonics to advanced packaging and AI-related business, the company is allocating an additional US$3.2 billion to accelerate capacity expansion, UMC chief executive officer Jason Wang (王石) said at an earnings conference.
Silicon photonics and advanced packaging are emerging as new growth engines for UMC, as the company aims to address next-generation optical connectivity, power delivery and memory bandwidth requirements for AI infrastructure, Wang said.
Photo: Grace Hung, Taipei Times
In July, the company said it would spend US$5 billion in the next two to three years to expand silicon photonics and advanced packaging capacity.
Most of the new capacity is expected to come online in late 2028 and through 2029, and reach large scale production by 2030, Wang said.
Based on UMC’s expansion plans, it aims to reach a monthly capacity of 18,000 wafers for silicon photonics, 22,000 for deep-trench capacitors and 20,000 for thin-film lithium niobate modulators.
Overall, UMC is upbeat about next year’s revenue growth, as it is negotiating with customers to hike average selling prices by 10 percent to reflect rising raw material costs, persistent capacity constraints and a “richer product and technology mix,” Wang said.
“We expect next year to mark a turning point in our blended average selling prices trajectory, moving from an environment of price erosion toward a meaningful positive uplift,” he said.
This year’s growth momentum is expected to extend into next year, fueled by higher wafer value rather than increased shipment volumes or factory utilization, Wang said.
“We expect the growth momentum to be supported by the healthy demand across our core business and growing opportunity in the flagship technology and high-value applications,” he said.
This quarter, UMC expects wafer shipments to grow by a low-single-digit percentage from last quarter, Wang said.
Average selling prices would remain firm, while gross margin is expected to be comparable to the preceding quarter’s 34 percent, he said.
Factory utilization would remain in the low 90s this quarter, he said.

Advocates call for protecting grassland for owls in Shalun science park project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:29 UTC
01:41:29 KST

Environmentalists yesterday called for protecting grassland for eastern grass owls in the Shalun Science Park development project in Tainan.
The project involving Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s (TSMC) next-generation chip manufacturing fab has been controversial since it was planned last year. Concerns include worries that a major habitat for critically endangered eastern grass owls in Shalun (沙崙) might become fragmented due to the project.
The scoping meeting for the project’s second-stage environmental impact review was completed on Oct. 12, the conclusion of which was that the developer should evaluate whether owl activity hot spots such as zones “Parking 1” and “Industrial 1-2” — the project’s planned parking lot and zero-waste center — can be excluded for ecological avoidance.
Photo courtesy of the National Pingtung University of Science and Technology’s Bird Ecology Lab
Tainan Community College researcher Chao Jui-kuang (晁瑞光) said the two zones collectively have 11.29 hectares of grassland where an eastern grass owl nest has been spotted.
The grassland is also an activity hot spot for ring-necked pheasants and other raptors such as collared scops owls, black winged kites and kestrels, he said.
Tainan Community College researcher Huang Huan-chang (黃煥彰) said the project covers two main ecological areas for eastern grass owls, the Shalun Farm (沙崙農場) and the Erren River (二仁溪) basin.
Grassland around the higher riverbank is home to eastern grass owl nests and should not be considered an ecological compensation site for owls, he said.
The project site is a major habitat for eastern grass owls, because it provides a massive foraging ground, but the project’s discussions have focused only on the breeding ground, he added.
Wetlands Taiwan representative Hsieh Yi-chen (謝宜臻) said eastern grass owls’ habitats can be graded into three tiers: Grassland around high riverbanks are the primary tier, agricultural land such as the “Satoyama” farmland are the second tier, and fish farms, salt fields and other fragmented habitats are the third tier.
What advocates sought to preserve is the primary tier habitat, she added.
Apple Bird Satoyama Conservation Foundation representative Tseng Lung-yung (曾瀧永) said only 63 hectares of land within the science park would be preserved for owl activities, while planned off-site compensation areas are facing challenges in their transition to ideal owl habitats.
For example, the Shalun Farm’s Shenkengzi section (深坑子) is a wooded area that some consider a critical habitat for other species, so trees must not be removed for grassland, he said.
The developer must overcome such challenges early and embark on owl habitat creation before the construction starts next year, otherwise eastern grass owls would soon decrease or disappear from the area, Tseng said, citing the Kaohsiung Science Park as a precedent of the loss of eastern grass owl following land development.

Photo: AP

Taiwan’s AerosoarX collaborates with U.S. firms on AI drones

16:41:24 UTC
01:41:24 KST

Taiwanese drone developer AerosoarX signed strategic cooperation memorandums with US companies Rajant and SiMa.ai yesterday to develop artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled uncrewed systems.
The partnerships combine AerosoarX’s drone platforms with Rajant’s mobile mesh networking technology and SiMa.ai’s onboard AI computing, according to a company statement released at its brand launch event in Taipei.
The combination is intended to let drones process sensor data onboard and exchange information with one another, supporting coordinated operations with less reliance on continuous ground control, the company said.
Photo: Wang Yi-hung, Taipei Times
AerosoarX chairman Max Lo (羅正方) told reporters that the company had already become a supplier of drone platforms and components in the US through its cooperation with Rajant.
His presentation showed that AerosoarX sent personnel to Rajant’s Kentucky facility last month for integration work and was targeting production readiness for its 15-inch AI-enabled first-person-view drone in November.
The planned integration uses SiMa.ai’s Modalix processor for onboard AI tasks such as visual perception and Rajant’s mesh technology for exchanging and relaying data between aircraft.
Lo described SiMa.ai as the only solution that met AerosoarX’s requirements for 50 trillion operations per second (TOPS) of AI computing within its power constraints.
Lo said the choice depended not simply on computing power, but on performance per watt, with AerosoarX cofounder and CEO Jason Wu (吳俊逸) also noting that energy efficiency was critical for drones.
Meanwhile, SiMa.ai founder and CEO Krishna Rangasayee told the event that power efficiency and flight time were “very, very critical for success.”
Rangasayee said his company was working with more than 30 drone companies globally, adding that its processors and software were intended to help partners develop applications more quickly.
Rajant Corp vice president of systems Don Gilbreath said greater onboard computing would allow drones to coordinate tasks, altitudes and separation, reducing the need for an operator to manage each aircraft individually.
“The more computing horsepower we have on the drones, the more we can do,” he said.
Gilbreath said the collaboration had already led to drone sales to US Army and Navy research laboratories interested in the team’s swarm demonstrations.
However, not every aircraft would require the same equipment, Lo said, adding that a drone coordinating other aircraft could carry more capable hardware, with units assigned simpler tasks using less expensive configurations.
On its US business, Lo clarified that AerosoarX was supplying platforms and working jointly with Rajant, rather than acting as the prime contractor. His presentation identified Phase III of the US Drone Dominance Program as a target for next year.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s wartime data plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:22 UTC
01:41:22 KST

The Ukrainian government on Oct. 14 broke the news that Elon Musk’s Starlink services to Ukraine had been throttled, severely impairing Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks. The controversy had erupted amid US criticism of Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy production infrastructure. Although Musk denied it at first, the decision to cut off Ukraine was apparently his own.
This use of private, for-profit services to conduct wars is as old as warfare, but it has taken on a new urgency as private tech businesses run by billionaires with bizarre personal politics assume increasing importance in national defense planning. Taiwan has since 2024 been building an alternative satellite network to Starlink, a wise move in view of recent events. It is unlikely that Musk would permit Taiwan to access Starlink in time of war, given his massive investments in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and his belief that Taiwan should become a special administrative zone of the PRC.
COMMUNICATION STRATEGY
Photo courtesy of the Industrial Technology Research Institute
As part of Taiwan’s alternative communications strategy, the Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) has installed 773 low-earth orbit (LEO) satellite reception stations at key military, police and fire department locations across the country, to serve as back-up channels for nation’s disaster response and critical infrastructure protection. Additionally, MODA has developed Taiwan’s first high-altitude communications balloon, to provide domestic emergency network support.
However, Taiwan is still depending on the tech giants in other ways.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Space Agency
“MODA has identified 18 critical public systems and expects to invest NT$1.34 billion (US$41.9 million) over the next four years (2024 to next year) to promote cryptographic splitting and data backup mechanisms,” the government said in 2024.
Via the nation’s National Digital Resilience Initiative (NDRI), Taiwan has been migrating 18 critical civilian systems, including the household registration and conscription system, land registration and land use system, land survey and land price System, national health records, tax records and defense communications, onto cloud platforms provided offshore by hyperscalers Amazon Web Systems (AWS), Microsoft and Google Cloud Platform (GCP).
The government encrypts this data and then disperses it across data centers located in Japan, Australia and elsewhere. The encryption keys securing the dispersed information remain in Taiwanese hands. Because of the threat to undersea cables from the PRC, the systems are linked by satellite backups.
Photo: Reuters
This program is directly based on Ukraine’s war programs, which were initiated in cooperation with AWS, and by the experiences of the Pacific island of Tonga after its cables were cut during a volcanic eruption. It is intended to enable the government to function in the event that cables are slashed and communications are jammed, isolating Taiwan from the world and the government from its people. In 2023-24 the government explored working with UK’s Eutelsat OneWeb low-Earth orbit satellite and Luxembourg’s SES medium-Earth orbit satellite, according to local media.
Information backup is not the only service provided by these firms. AI tools hosted on these hyperscaling platforms are used by military planners to engage in automated satellite imagery recognition and predictive risk analytics, along with Internet of Things (IOT)-enabled combat systems such as smart naval mines and missile batteries. Taiwan in 2024 began operating a unified digital environment that linked all the branches of the military.
Although the hyperscalers do not do much business in the PRC, and Taiwan prohibits PRC staff or technology in its systems, these systems are at the mercy of regulators and business pressures that Taiwan cannot control. This is noted in an interesting paper by Mahmoud Javadi published last year in the journal Contemporary Security Policy on this topic, which observes that not only are regulatory and business pressures key issues, but “operational tempo and military outcomes become tied to hyperscaler compute and analytics.”
The underlying assumption is that in time of war Taiwan will have access to those resources, but whether even a large hyperscaler like Amazon can maintain multiple services across several nations involved in wars is an untested question.
KMT INTERFERENCE
Readers will recall that the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) held up this year’s government budget until Aug. 14, passing it only after substantial cuts. The digital ministry was among the many government departments to see its discretionary expense allocations slashed to zero. The budget included NT$349.22 million for the cloud backup plan, which covered 16 systems across seven ministries.
The KMT, along with its sock puppet in the legislature, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), has already directed its budgetary ire at the MODA backup information program. The ground station network was sharply reduced when the KMT-TPP coalition froze and cut parts of last year’s budget. MODA’s NT$8.659 billion budget was cut by NT$3.582 billion, about 41 percent, Athena Tong (唐若凌) reported at Thinking Taiwan. She added that the “digital resilience line item supporting non-geostationary satellite communications was hit particularly hard, losing NT$300 million from an original allocation of NT$530 million, a reduction of 56 percent.”
Early last month I wrote about the National Communications Commission (NCC) and its oversight of the radio frequency spectrum (“Taiwan’s drone bill has a kill switch,” Sept. 3). The NCC has been paralyzed by the KMT, which has defunded its operations and blocked new commissioners. Note that the NCC also has authority over the satellite systems that the government’s information resilience program depends on.
On July 13 the Legislative Yuan’s Transportation Committee approved an amendment to Article 36 of the Telecommunications Management Act (電信管理法) that authorized the NCC to grant satellite network operators exemptions from requirements restricting their chairperson’s nationality and foreign ownership, on a case-by-case basis. It was promulgated on Aug. 5. The amendment is expressly intended to support the satellite links necessary to operate the information back up systems. It is clear that the NCC in its current state is probably unable to respond to the complicated demands of case-by-case reviews of satellite operators, which appears to be the intention of the KMT and the TPP. The KMT derailment of governance in Taiwan benefits only the PRC.
Of course, any satellite-based communication system is vulnerable to systems Beijing is putting in place. Not only is jamming the ground systems a solvable problem that Beijing’s researchers have already publicly modeled, but Beijing plans to pressure satellite operators and businesses. It probably already possesses the ability to kill satellites in space.
While the PRC has only limited pressure over firms that do little business in China, it can sometimes muster great leverage over national government regulators. Imagine what pressure Beijing can bring to bear on, for example, the Australian regulators of cloud hyperscalers’ platforms physically present in Australia, especially in time of war. Taiwan and its allies overseas must be ready.
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

Precision metal processing and manufacturing company Kuen Tong Industrial Co (昆桐) said it expects strong business momentum to persist next year supported by its low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-related business and liquid-cooling products for artificial intelligence (AI) servers.
The LEO business covers communications payloads, power systems, propulsion and attitude control, and structural components, Kuen Tong chairman Jeff Lin (林志中) said at a business presentation in Taipei yesterday.
In the first three quarters of this year, LEO satellite business accounted for about 67 percent of the company’s NT$1.53 billion (US$47.2 million) revenue, while bicycle-related products accounted for 24 percent and AI server liquid-cooling products at 6 percent, Lin said.
Photo: CNA
Kuen Tong entered the satellite business in 2017 through a US customer and has since expanded from supplying small-volume ground receiver components into major structural parts and key satellite modules, he said.
The company has secured orders for satellite module-related components for a US customer’s next-generation satellites, Kuen Tong chief financial officer Vibi Shiu (徐絲綺) said, adding that mass production is expected to begin next year.
Kuen Tong said it expects AI server cooling to become its second growth engine after the company entered the business last year.
The company said it is already in volume production of liquid-cooling and manifold-related products for major customers, and its Thai plant has installed three production lines to support its expansion.
Kuen Tong said that it is expanding capacity in Taiwan and Thailand to meet robust demand for its satellite business and liquid-cooling products, as well as high-end precision metal components used in semiconductor production equipment.
Construction of a new plant in Thailand is expected to be completed in the third quarter of next year, with production capacity set to double by the fourth quarter, Kuen Tong president Eden Lin (林純芳) said.
In Taiwan, the company plans to raise capacity by 10 to 15 percent next year by renting facilities before completing its new plant in 2029, she said.
Factory utilization is 100 percent in Taiwan and about 70 percent in Thailand, she said.
Taiwan operations contribute 60 to 70 percent of the company’s revenue, she added.
Kuen Tong’s gross margin reached 45 percent, and earnings per share were NT$11.99 in the first three quarters. The firm is set to debut on the Emerging Stock Board today at a reference price of NT$390 per share.

====================================================================================================

Lula killed  the ‘Donroe Doctrine’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:19 UTC
01:41:19 KST

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s victory in Brazil’s election is a blow to US President Donald Trump’s plan for the Western Hemisphere. The US president was hoping to huddle with client states to the south who mimic his business and mano dura (iron fist) posturing, while further betraying liberal partners. That plan, within reach until Sunday’s vote, is now in tatters.
Disentangling from the world and retreating into a seemingly controllable hemispheric stronghold has been a US dream since the early 19th century. It was inscribed in the Monroe Doctrine, pronounced by then-US president James Monroe in 1823 to warn Europeans against meddling in the Americas, then revived in the 1890s, during the US war against Spain. The inter-American project then moved backstage until Trump tried to revive it once again.
Had Brazil lurched from left to right, the election would have capped an annus mirabilis (a remarkable year) for Trump in the region — in contrast to his debacles elsewhere. The abduction of then-Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro at the start of the year handed Trump a supine client state, following elections in Chile that handed power to the far-right Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast, whose father was a Nazi lieutenant in the Wehrmacht. Then, in Colombia, the left fell to the Trump-backed right-wing candidate, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Illustration: Mountain People
In the wake of these victories, veteran Trump allies such as Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Argentine President Javier Milei are no longer isolated oddballs. A victory for the far-right Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil would have meant nearly a clean sweep for Trump allies south of Mexico.
In November last year, the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy called for a pivot to the Western Hemisphere. Under Operation Absolute Resolve, US forces seized Maduro and licensed his successor in Caracas to give new 100-year concessions to a US firm over 17 oil fields containing 65 billion barrels of proven reserves.
In March, the White House doubled down on hemispheric convergence with the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. Euphemistically called the “Shield of the Americas,” the administration sought a hemispheric alliance to counter the drug trade and organized crime. After a staged event at US Southern Command headquarters in Doral, Florida, 12 Latin American leaders followed Trump to his golf club to celebrate. US officials heralded the coordination to tackle cartels, insurgents and foreign “interference in the hemisphere,” especially by China. In his closing remarks, Trump connected hemispheric security to his strikes against Iran.
The Shield was more than a security pact. Negotiators at Doral emerged from behind closed doors brandishing agreements on Venezuelan gold and oil, and mineral contracts from Chile, all favorable to US companies. The commercial purpose became official in late last month, when Shield signatories added “economic cooperation” to the mission, including “investment screening,” “mineral supply chain” security, and “trusted supplier regulations for digital infrastructure.”
However, even before Lula’s nail-biting victory, Trump’s hemispheric coalition had overstated the strength of the regional alignment. The original head of the Shield of the Americas, Kristi Noem, was sacked in disgrace as US secretary of homeland security two days before the Shield was unveiled. Her demotion to “special envoy” lapsed last month, and the US Department of State has not bothered to designate a successor.
Meanwhile, US ambassadors in Buenos Aires and Santiago have stirred regional contretemps. Brandon Judd, a career US Border Patrol agent who is now Trump’s envoy to Chile, publicly questioned his host country’s sovereignty over the Strait of Magellan and tied Shield support to Chile’s willingness to cooperate with the US. Then there is the squalid, openly corrupt White House infighting over the Venezuelan spoils.
However, the Shield’s bigger weakness is economic. For all the bonhomie among right-wingers, the north and south of the hemisphere have drifted apart economically. The rhetoric about inter-American security masks the broader reality: Since 2000, China, not the US, has become Latin America’s preferred export market. China buys about 28 percent of Latin America’s exports, far surpassing the US’ 16 percent share, which has shrunk substantially.
Driving the new trade axis has been Latin America’s metals, minerals, and energy products. The lithium triangle straddling Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile sends 77 percent of its output to China. Firms such as Tsingshan (the world’s largest stainless steel and nickel producer) operate regional headquarters in northern Argentina, having made massive investments in electrochemicals, industrial plastics (to build enormous chemical storage facilities), and other facilities to support the post-fossil-fuel economy.
South America is also key to China’s space ambitions. To facilitate geostationary orbital solar power stations above the Earth, China is investing in hundreds of telescopes to create an enormous observational park across the same drylands that hold valuable minerals. While Trump indulges visions of “Trump-class” battleships sailing through the Strait of Magellan, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp and sections of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army are building facilities in Patagonia to manage a sprawling fleet of satellites and deep-space power stations.
The Shield of the Americas never addressed what the region needs. Its far-right leaders’ most important task is to pull their countries out of their productivity rut. In the first quarter of the 21st century, labor productivity grew by less than 0.9 percent per year, steadily falling behind the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average. The result is a trap of low innovation, swelling informal sectors, and aging populations — precisely the long-term challenges that populists tend to neglect.
Finally, Latin American debt levels have soared. Hyper-dependency on commodity rents has coincided with lavish borrowing. About 3.5 percent of regional GDP is spent on servicing public debt, a staggering sum that is being siphoned away from investments in public goods or social services. With interest rates climbing, debt-service payments would, too, forcing treasuries to impose austerity.
There was nothing in the Shield to help Latin American partners out of this vice. Lula certainly has his work cut out for him, since he is confronting the same basic challenge. However, with Trump’s grand plan for the Americas in shambles, that work might be somewhat easier.
Jeremy Adelman is director of the Global History Lab at the University of Cambridge and the author, most recently, of The Capitalist Era: The Making and Unmaking of the Global Mind.

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

NT dollar’s drop tied to stocks: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:18 UTC
01:41:18 KST

The New Taiwan dollar’s 3 percent fall this year despite record exports and a widening trade surplus stems from foreign investors cashing in on the local stock market’s technology-driven rally and moving funds overseas, central bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) told lawmakers yesterday.
The NT dollar has become one of Asia’s weakest-performing major currencies this year.
Foreign investors have reaped substantial gains from Taiwan’s surging stock market, prompting them to sell shares and rebalance their portfolios, Yang told a meeting of the legislature’s Finance Committee in Taipei.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Their withdrawals have added to downward pressure on the NT dollar, offsetting support from the country’s strong export earnings, he said.
The benchmark TAIEX had climbed early this year to a high above 49,000 from about 27,000 points, with much of the rally driven by electronics and semiconductor stocks that are heavily held by overseas investors, Yang said.
As returns accumulate, investors are increasingly inclined to reassess their exposure and lock in profits rather than hold their positions indefinitely, he said.
Foreign investors had recorded fund outflows of US$77.6 billion as of Wednesday last week, the central bank said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan.
Yang said that the central bank had intervened in the foreign-exchange market, but rejected speculation that it was defending a specific exchange rate of NT$32.5 per US dollar.
The central bank allows the currency to move with market forces, but seeks to prevent excessive fluctuations, an approach Yang described as the “willow theory.”
The governor also played down the role of the interest-rate gap between Taiwan and the US, saying that US rates had been higher for years amid elevated inflation.
Recent pressure on the NT dollar stemmed more from foreign investors taking profits and transferring funds abroad, while dividend payments by Taiwanese companies had also affected cross-border flows, he said.
Separately, Yang rejected claims that Taiwan was facing a cash shortage, saying that the nation’s financial system had ample savings even as strong economic growth and a buoyant stock market drove up demand for financing.
“I strongly disagree with the claim that there is a cash shortage,” Yang told lawmakers, adding that tighter liquidity at some local lenders reflected their individual funding structures rather than a system-wide lack of money.
Taiwanese banks’ liquidity coverage ratios had averaged at 130 percent in the past, a level Yang considered “unnecessarily high.”
A ratio of about 120 percent would be appropriate, he said.
Tighter liquidity at some banks stemmed from their deposit structures, particularly their heavy reliance on large corporate clients whose funds can be withdrawn at short notice, Yang said.
Banks need to attract more small depositors and issue financial debentures to diversify their funding sources and reduce their reliance on potentially volatile corporate deposits, he said.
Strong manufacturing investment and stock-market activity have increased demand for funds, putting pressure on some smaller borrowers, Yang said.
However, Taiwan’s substantial excess savings remain an important source of liquidity, he said.

FDA identifies nine drugs that pose risks to driving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:18 UTC
01:41:18 KST

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) yesterday identified nine categories of medication that pose risks comparable to driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol, as the agency seeks to raise awareness to improve road safety.
The medications include sleeping pills, anesthetics, pupil dilators, muscles relaxants, anti-anxiety drugs, antidepressants, antipsychotics, some blood sugar and blood pressure medications, some painkillers and cold medicines, and some antihistamines, the FDA said in a statement.
Those drugs can cause slow reaction times, drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination or blurred vision, compromising driving safety, the agency said.
Photo: Taipei Times file
The FDA said it was working with transportation authorities to make educational leaflets on safe driving for people taking common medications.
The information would also be available through the agency’s Web site, weekly newsletter and Facebook page, it said.
The FDA would also urge pharmacists and pharmacist associations to remind people that certain medications could affect their ability to drive, it said.
The Criminal Investigation Bureau has said that driving while impaired by medication could constitute public endangerment.
People should carefully review their doctor’s instructions or warnings that the medication could impair their ability to drive, and assess whether they are fit to safely operate a vehicle, the bureau said.
Under Article 185 of the Criminal Code, drivers who are unable to operate vehicles safely due to the use of drugs, anesthetics or similar substances could be charged with endangering public safety and face up to three years in prison, while those who cause accidents resulting serious injury or death face harsher penalties, it said.
Article 35 of the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例) stipulates corresponding penalties, including fines, the suspension or revocation of the driver’s license and the impoundment of the vehicle.
People can be held legally responsible for driving after taking prescribed medication that impairs their ability to drive and operate a vehicle, the bureau said.

Robust drone supply chains needed: expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:16 UTC
01:41:16 KST

Taiwan’s drone industry needs supply chains capable of sustaining production during a prolonged conflict, rather than relying on stockpiles alone, AerosoarX chairman Max Lo (羅正方) said yesterday, drawing lessons from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Speaking at his company’s first public event since it was established in April, Lo said that a war of attrition could rapidly deplete even substantial inventories and that sustaining operations required production capacity across the entire supply chain.
“Stockpiles can only determine the first month of fighting,” he said, adding that continued production and replenishment would determine who could endure.
Photo courtesy of AerosoarX
He proposed setting up manufacturing operations in different countries that share assembly specifications and interchangeable components. If a conflict or a blockade disrupted one location, others could take over and expand production, he said.
“Defense self-reliance does not mean doing everything ourselves,” said Lo, a major figure in Taiwan’s drone industry and the chairman of the Taiwan National Drone Industry Association.
Lo also suggested cooperation based on common standards, joint procurement, distributed production, mutual maintenance and shared reserve inventories and said that such arrangements should be established before a conflict.
Reflecting on his earlier experience at drone maker Geosat Aerospace & Technology, Lo recalled taking pride in doing nearly 80 percent of the development in-house.
However, that approach is now too slow for rapidly changing requirements, he said.
AerosoarX, dedicated to developing artificial intelligence-enabled uncrewed vehicles and platforms, envisages Taiwan as a hub for system integration, modular design and component kits shipped overseas for assembly, with Vietnam and Malaysia seen as potential supply-chain and assembly hubs.
For company cofounder and CEO Jason Wu (吳俊逸), making that network commercially sustainable requires reaching beyond Taiwan’s domestic market.
“If we only looked at Taiwan from the beginning, frankly, we couldn’t build this supply chain,” he said.
Lo also acknowledged the economic cost of replacing Chinese suppliers, and advocated a gradual reduction in dependence focused on critical supply chain links.
Maintaining a large factory without steady orders would be commercially difficult, he said, adding that focusing on smaller operations serving international customers offered a way to keep production active while retaining the flexibility to increase output during an emergency.

BOOK REVIEW: The definitive portrait of Larry David
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

Larry David agreed to this authorized biography with a five-word e-mail: “Oh Jesus. If we must.” As Blake J Harris tells it, the comedy writer has always been adept at finding reasons not to do something, or to stop doing it, even when there’s nothing to fall back on.
As a peppery standup in 1970s New York, David was notorious for storming off stage if the audience displeased him. He walked out of his first TV job, on the Saturday Night Live clone Fridays, because “I stunk.” He twice quit Seinfeld, the sitcom he co-created in 1989, over meddling by NBC executives and fantasied about the network giving him an excuse to leave for good. In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, he told friends, “Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.” He was only half joking.
David’s career proves that it is in fact possible to be immensely, groundbreakingly successful without ever displaying great ambition. Growing up in Brooklyn amid a boisterous extended family, Lawrence Gene David loved baseball and tall tales but, oddly, not making people laugh.
“I can’t recall him ever saying a funny thing,” remembers his older brother Ken.
After a spell in the army reserve, he drifted through low-effort jobs — limo driver, bra salesman — and dropped out of acting school, partly because his classmate Jeff Goldblum showed him what a real actor looked like.
“Most of the time I was just waiting for other people to stop talking so that I could start talking,” he admits.
Hence standup. In 1977, Variety magazine summed up David’s themes as “sexual fantasies, oriental yodeling, baldness, hypochondria, growing up with Jewish parents, college, porno movies, etc.”
Much as they admired his integrity, his peers considered him too self-destructive and uncompromising to make it. One contemporary says that if you had polled New York’s standups, “Larry would have been voted Least Likely to Ever Accomplish Anything. Including by Larry himself!”
After a few unhappy forays into television, David was already 41 when he began writing a pilot with the amiable, ultra-professional Jerry Seinfeld.
Authorized biographies tend to flatter their subjects, but then there doesn’t seem to be much dirt to dig. Compared with Harris’s last subject, the obnoxious virtual reality entrepreneur Palmer Luckey, David is a pretty solid guy who still has the close friends he made 50 years ago. There is no evidence here of those familiar funnyman archetypes, the sad clown and the secret monster. Harris was therefore able to access every important figure in his life, including fellow comedian Richard Lewis, his best friend, and Rob Reiner, whose company produced Seinfeld, before they died. Augmented by transcripts and memos, the quotes are so plentiful that the book often feels more like an oral history than a conventional biography, especially the Seinfeld section. If you want to read multi-page breakdowns of classic episodes like The Soup Nazi and The Chinese Restaurant (I do), then you’re in luck.
In the self-referential fourth season, Jerry pitches a sitcom, starring himself, that is “about nothing.” Seinfeld itself was never that but it was the first show to root itself in everyday conversations, altercations and humiliations, many of which David had been recording in notebooks for years. One of the pleasures of this book is encountering a funny incident in the 70s that resurfaces on screen 20 years later.
“There are people in this world that funny things happen to,” Seinfeld says. “And he is one of them.”
Jason Alexander once complained to David that his character George Costanza had an implausible storyline: nobody would behave like this in real life.
“What are you talking about?” David replied. “This happened to me, and this is exactly what I did.”
Making Seinfeld was all-consuming (“I missed the whole 90s,” its star once joked) but a creative dream. David, the stubborn catastrophizer, and Seinfeld, the breezy optimist, would write episodes face-to-face across a double desk and almost never argue.
What began as a cult show beneath the dangling sword of cancellation (“too Jewish” was a common critique) suddenly became a cultural juggernaut in season four as David mastered his two great skills: escalating a slim premise into comic delirium and dovetailing multiple storylines with a satisfying click. For a network sitcom, Seinfeld was radically unsentimental — “No hugging, no learning” was the writers’ credo.
“I was shocked that they were letting us do this show,” David admits.
Another curious feature of David’s career is that he didn’t become recognizable until he was in his 50s. Even when he was the showrunner and chief writer of the biggest show on television, with more than 35 million viewers a week, he was effectively unknown. That phase ended in 1998 when the divisively downbeat Seinfeld finale coincided with the abject failure of his first movie, Sour Grapes. For want of a better idea, he decided to return to standup.
Curb Your Enthusiasm began as a one-hour HBO special, framing the routine with a mockumentary, but the frame proved funnier than the picture so Curb turned into a show about “Larry David” at war with the world. Like Seinfeld, it built complex stories out of minute observations and petty grievances but this time there was no script, just an outline to improvise around.
“Your job, basically, is to push Larry David into a corner so that he comes bursting out even more Larry,” explains his friend Ted Danson, who played himself.
As abrasive as David’s buzzsaw voice, Curb made Seinfeld look like Friends. Its success made David famous as his worst self.
“I know people don’t realize it,” says Danson’s wife and Curb co-star Mary Steenburgen, “but Larry really is a sweetheart.”
This is the kind of biography you read for the work rather than the life. Fiercely private and averse to analysis, David doesn’t say much about his divorce in 2007 or Lewis’s death in 2024, nor money (he’s worth an estimated US$400 million), nor politics (he’s a ferocious Trump-basher). Most of the details about his childhood come from his brother Ken. His only hobby is golf. As Harris notes, David is as much an observer of his own life as a participant, turning everything into material.
So what do we learn about Larry David? He’s a loyal friend, a loving father and a generous comedy partner. His comedy idols are Mel Brooks, Woody Allen and Phil Silvers’ character Sgt Bilko. As seen on Curb, he tends to start laughing when people are upset with him and gets absurdly indignant about minor injustices (though less so since becoming a father in 1994). He bypasses niceties — a “social assassin” in Curb-speak. “He’s comfortable being uncomfortable,” summarizes Lewis. “He knows exactly what he wants to do. And he doesn’t need praise.”
Perhaps the key is David’s paradoxical self-esteem. According to Alexander, “At any given moment, he could say, ‘I’m the most worthless, pathetic no-talent in the world,’ and ‘Why is no one giving me my due? I should be doing much better than I’m doing!’ And it was all in the same breath.” Such a person either sinks without trace or, very occasionally, triumphs despite himself.
In 1986 I entered the US Peace Corps in Kenya. As a US government volunteer we had a special US government ID for use in Kenya. Because of our position, we received extensive training in how to behave. This had special urgency for my group of volunteers: we had originally been slated for Nepal, but a US Peace Corps volunteer in another country had criticized that nation’s authoritarian president in public, and all of the Peace Corps volunteers were kicked out. As a result, the next group for that nation got sent to Nepal, and we got bumped to Kenya. The

Airlines are free to choose routes, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

Airlines can choose routes that best suit their operations based on safety, flight time and costs, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said yesterday after two major Taiwanese carriers on Sunday flew flights through Russian airspace.
China Airlines (CAL, 華航) and EVA Airways (長榮航空) had avoided Russian airspace since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
However, CAL Flight CI75 from Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport to Rome entered Russian airspace after taking off early on Sunday morning, marking the first time a Taiwanese carrier had done so in four years.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
EVA Airways Flight BR88 from Paris to Taoyuan also flew over Russian airspace.
Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱) told reporters before a meeting of the Legislative Yuan’s Transportation Committee that the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) oversees the departures and destinations of international flights, while airlines can decide for themselves which routes to take.
Chen was asked whether the airlines had flown through Russian airspace because their requests to fly through Pakistani airspace had been rejected by Pakistan’s aviation authorities.
“The fact that the two airlines were able to fly through Russian airspace means that their applications were approved. They can decide whether to continue using the route,” Chen said. “They can choose routes that best suit their operations after factoring in safety, time and costs. We respect their decisions.”
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday said it had no comment on the airlines’ decisions to fly through Russian airspace.
However, it reiterated the government’s strong opposition to any country invading another sovereign nation, adding that Taiwan complies with international sanctions against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.
Taiwan has been controlling exports of high-tech products to Russia since the war began, the foreign ministry said.
Separately, lawmakers yesterday clashed over Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to shutter Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) and transfer its services to Taoyuan airport.
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lee Kun-tse (李昆澤) said that the number of passengers using Taoyuan airport is expected to exceed 50 million this year.
Annual passenger traffic could top 83.8 million by 2045, Lee said.
Taoyuan “airport’s first and second terminals are designed to accommodate a maximum of 37 million passengers per year, he said.
The third terminal, once completed, can accommodate an additional 45 million passengers, bringing the airport’s annual capacity to only 82 million, he said.
Taoyuan International Airport Corp (桃園國際機場), which operates the facility, would begin planning to rebuild the first terminal, which has been in use since 1979, after the third terminal opens, he added.
CAA data show that 5.62 million domestic and international passengers used Songshan airport last year, Lee said.
The agency estimates that daily passenger traffic at Songshan airport could rise to between 22,000 and 29,000 by 2040, he said.
“Imagine Taoyuan airport receiving an additional 20,000 travelers per day. Whether the high-speed rail system, Airport MRT and freeways could handle the additional passenger traffic warrants careful study,” he said.
The two airports differ in the types of aircraft they can accommodate and their ground operations, while Songshan airport is the main medical hub for about 38,000 people from outlying islands each year, he said.
Additional facilities would need to be in place if all flights at Songshan airport were transferred to Taoyuan airport, he added.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Hung Meng-kai (洪孟楷) said that the central government should not let its vision for Taipei 10 to 20 years from now be constrained by the “status quo.”
Now is the right time to consider Chiang’s proposal, as Taoyuan airport’s third terminal is scheduled to be completed by the end of next year, Hung said.
Chen said that although the first, second and third terminals could collectively serve 82 million passengers per year, the airport would not immediately reach that capacity because the ministry would begin considering renovations to the first terminal after the third terminal is completed.
A third runway at the Taoyuan facility is scheduled to be completed by 2033. The ministry would then begin renovating the first and second runways once the third runway enters service, he said.
“Taoyuan airport was never designed to serve as a domestic flight hub or a medical evacuation hub. If it were to accommodate domestic flights, its operational efficiency would decrease. The airport would also have to undergo a major redesign. All this work takes time,” he said.
Taoyuan International Airport Corp president Fan Hsiao-lun (范孝倫) said the company plans runway and terminal capacity based on the potential growth in international passenger traffic.
“We have never evaluated the possibility of transferring all flights at Songshan to Taoyuan,” Fan said.

“What have wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?” teenaged Marianne Dashwood rhetorically asks in Jane Austen’s 1811 novel Sense and Sensibility.
Her prudent sister Elinor replies: “Grandeur has but little, but wealth has much to do with it.”
Elinor’s wise answer seems to have served as the north star for a new film adaptation, directed by Georgia Oakley and written by Diana Reid. Austen is a regular source material for filmmakers, but the most resonant retellings of her work tend to reflect their era. This latest one, released in US theaters last week, does more to highlight the Dashwood sisters’ financial precarity — a smart creative choice that shows an understanding of what moviegoing audiences are especially attuned to now.
It is clear from the get-go that the girls are extremely short of funds following the death of their father. There are bills they cannot pay. They have been all but evicted from their stately home by its new owners: their half-brother and his odious wife. Elinor writes letter after letter to try and find an affordable cottage. When she finally does secure one, it is dim and cramped — a familiar fate for many a modern renter.
To underline their fall from the 1 to the 99 percent, we subsequently see the Dashwoods growing their own crops, cooking their own food, doing their own laundry and even — unless my eyes deceived me — chopping their own wood. Perhaps it should be mandatory viewing for the tradwife-curious.
It is a harder fate than Austen herself devised for her heroines. However, dialing up the Dashwoods’ money troubles resonates at a time when many moviegoers are feeling the pinch of higher prices for essentials.
Women, always the primary audience for Austen films, feel this acutely. A Pew poll found US women are 11 points less likely than men to say they can pay all their bills; a different survey shows women 13 points more pessimistic about the labor market. Experts suggest women are overrepresented in jobs that could be automated by artificial intelligence.
So, the central problem of so many of Austen’s novels — what does a woman have to do to get a little financial security around here? — hits close to home.
The prosperous 1990s were a different story. The successful Austen adaptations of that era tended to be marketed as Regency rom-coms. Some even gave rise to other rom-coms: 1995’s Pride and Prejudice, which famously shows Colin Firth as Mr Darcy in a wet shirt, inspired the screwball Bridget Jones’ Diary books and films (which, of course, featured Firth again).
For the most part, these adaptations were also explicitly escapist, greeted by critics as nostalgic comfort-viewing for audiences nervously awaiting the turn of the millennium. Adaptations that reached for more gravitas or grappled explicitly with difficult topics — such as 1999’s Mansfield Park, which explicitly included the slave trade as a major theme — struggled to reach audiences of that era.
However, times change, and so do viewer expectations. By the 2005 adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, starring Keira Knightley, viewers were getting a different type of heroine — rather shouty and slightly tomboyish. That was the era of so-called girlboss feminism, when women were encouraged to overcome the odds through pluck, grit and power poses.
That version came out post-dot-com bust, but pre-Great Recession. It was a time when filmmakers were starting to have Austen’s women be more explicit about their financial fears.
“I’m 27 years old,” Charlotte Lucas says in that adaptation, justifying her decision to marry the odious — but financially stable — Mr Collins. “I’ve no money and no prospects. I’m already a burden to my parents, and I’m frightened.”
Those lines were improvised by British film icon Emma Thompson, who consulted on that script — and who won an Oscar for her screenplay for the 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility, in which she also co-starred. That adaptation, directed by Ang Lee (李安), does show the girls’ change in status, but as a much gentler comedown. Their sun-filled cottage is filled with art and knickknacks. They must economize on beef (relatable), but they still have live-in servants (not).
One scene that would have injected a frisson of real danger was eliminated before production began. Thompson had wanted to emphasize the Dashwoods’ vulnerability by showing a fox hunt — with a desperate vixen searching for an escape — but the idea was scrapped.
The 2026 version, by contrast, is crammed with such metaphors. A caged canary rides with the Dashwoods to their dank little cottage; we also get several close-ups of dead birds shot for dinner. Whether it is a grouse or a spouse, everyone is on the hunt for something.
Yet as dire as the Dashwoods’ straits are, it is clear that the answer is not to marry for money. The story is filled with cautionary characters who dug for gold and lived to regret it. Perhaps the film should also be mandatory viewing for TikTok girlies looking to become stay-at-home girlfriends.
Spoiler alert: In the end, Elinor gets her man. However, as punishment for choosing the penniless Elinor, his wealthy mother cuts him out of his inheritance. Grandeur he will not have, but he does find a stable job. In 2026, that is swoon-worthy.

Real Madrid yesterday apologized to China for star striker Kylian Mbappe’s comments poking fun at Mao Zedong, after the star striker’s remarks sparked a social media storm and saw Spanish soccer yanked off state TV.
Mocking former leader Mao — blamed by historians for millions of deaths — is taboo in China, and Mbappe’s remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger Beijing.
In a clip of a video interview with French show The Bridge — since taken down — Mbappe talked about being amused by an Internet meme of his face photoshopped onto “some guy, think he’s a Chinese dictator,” an apparent reference to Mao.
Photo: AFP
Real Madrid “wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any offense caused by the recent remarks of our player Kylian Mbappe,” the club said in a statement.
“The club joins in the public apology issued by Kylian Mbappe, in which the player himself expressed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people,” the 15-time European champions said.
The statement came a day after Mbappe issued his own apology, in French, Chinese and English.
“My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” he said.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun yesterday told a regular briefing: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”
La Liga, which saw the broadcast of its matches suspended in China, on Tuesday said it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappe’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans.”
Earlier, the state-run Global Times said in an editorial that it was “not difficult to see that the club’s longstanding tolerance of such behavior has contributed to Mbappe’s latest offensive remarks.”
Chinese beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s FIFA World Cup ran advertisements with artificial intelligence-generated images of Mbappe, on Tuesday said it had scrapped its partnership with the player, as did dairy firms Mengniu and Milkground.
China Media Group, which oversees public broadcaster China Central Television, said it would suspend broadcasts of La Liga, the world’s second-richest soccer league after England’s Premier League.
Mbappe, 27, yesterday continued to face a torrent of criticism from Chinese Web users, some of it racist.
“His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated,” one user wrote on Sina Weibo.
Mbappe’s original joke about Mao was not reposted — or had been scrubbed — from China’s tightly controlled social media.
Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu froze Mbappe’s account, where he has more than 1 million followers.
Sina Weibo did the same, with a notice saying he had been banned for violating the law or its terms of service.
Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappe-related content on Sina Weibo.
Offline, too, the Mbappe brand appeared to be under threat.
At the Adidas flagship store in Beijing’s Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid shirts were available for sale, but none bearing the striker’s name.

AI boom: ‘one Taiwan, two worlds’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

Taiwan is experiencing an unprecedented economic boom on the surface. Despite surging GDP, stock market and artificial intelligence (AI) exports, why do more people feel they have not become wealthier? This contradictory issue cannot be avoided, and the answer lies in the “K-shaped economy.”
According to data from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, the economic growth rate reached 14.5 percent in the first half of this year, and is forecast to rise 11.05 percent for the full year. However, the income gap between the top and bottom 20 percent of households grew by 6.17 times last year. In other words, while the overall economy is surging, income distribution has not, and AI dividends are enjoyed by a select few.
The K-shaped economy is creating a phenomenon in which Taiwan experiences an economic polarization. At the top of the “K,” there is a minority dominated by AI, semiconductors, servers and high-tech exports. At the bottom, there lies a vast workforce in traditional manufacturing, small and medium-sized enterprises, and the massive service industry.
The nation is not facing an economic downturn, but rather a reshaping of key production factors amid an economic boom — including capital centralizing in high-return AI industries, more talent shifting to high-paying tech sectors, and a crowding-out effect in energy resources, such as electricity and green power. The Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research and industry studies warned that this structural polarization is widening.
This year’s World Inequality Report estimates that the top 10 percent in Taiwan hold approximately 61 percent of the nation’s wealth, while the top 1 percent hold 27 percent. This can explain the surreal disconnect between the booming stock market and grassroots public sentiment.
While the stock market is about capital returns and future profits, ordinary families focus on housing prices, rent, living costs, children’s education and monthly salaries — practical realities of what they can afford and spend. The wealthy with great assets can accumulate more wealth through reinvestment as asset values grow, but those without assets can only rely on wages to keep up with price hikes. The same economic growth figure tells different stories for different people.
The issue Taiwan faces is the lack of social mobility caused by the K-shaped economy. The wealthy are running ahead faster through the accumulation of capital, technology and assets, while the workers are struggling to make a living.
At a time when economic growth is primarily driven by a few industries, enterprises and asset holders, the more impressive the GDP becomes, the more divided society might feel. Therefore, a policy challenge is the only way to transform AI dividends from the “K-peak” of a few sectors into a “K-slope” for the overall economy.
How can the nation enable traditional industries to access transformation capital, allow small-and-medium enterprises to integrate into AI supply chains, boost productivity and wages in the service sector, and equip workers with genuine skills to transition careers? More importantly, how can it provide those without assets an opportunity to accumulate wealth or share the dividends of economic growth driven by the whole public?
While AI has boosted GDP, it has failed to deliver the fruits of such growth to every household. At the top of the “K,” Taiwan is finally riding the wave of today’s AI boom after years of hard work. At the bottom, it should pragmatically confront the pressing issue: resolving the contradictory polarization of “one Taiwan, two worlds.”
Jeff Wu is an economic observer.

Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:08 UTC
01:41:08 KST

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second-largest city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.
Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.
On Sunday, that was more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.
For well over a decade Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the Serbian government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings would have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.
As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?” they put forward a student list of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70 percent — the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 — delivered them a comfortable majority.
What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public — including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vucic support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge toward the bottom of European corruption rankings.
Politically, the priority would be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. However, in the longer term there would be less straightforward debates to be had. Vucic’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. However, on foreign policy issues such as joining the EU and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.
As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Vucic’s Serbia, like Orban’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. However, now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.
