Denmark delays new citizenship screening model – what it means for applicants
The expert group tasked with examining the possibilities for a screening model for citizenship applicants is facing further delays in its work.
The Ministry of Immigration and Integration writes this in a press release.
– Due to the scope and complexity of the work, we cannot manage to deliver our recommendations around the turn of the year. Instead, I expect that we will conclude our work in mid-March next year, says Henrik Thomassen, chairman of the expert group, in the press release.
The granting of citizenship in particular has taken up a significant amount of the political debate recently.
Most recently, the Danish People’s Party entered the debate because the party wants a Pakistani man removed from an upcoming bill that next year will make 2,055 foreigners Danish citizens.
DF’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, has found a Facebook post from 2016 in which the man, according to DF, supported an Islamic execution.
– The government should strip him of the opportunity to obtain citizenship. If they are not willing to do that, they must at the very least be willing to let us meet this man eye-to-eye so we can see the matter for ourselves, Mikkel Bjørn told DR on Thursday.
Last week, Liberal Alliance found a woman who, according to the party, has repeatedly praised Hamas and the former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Therefore, the party wants the person summoned for an interview with the Folketing’s Naturalisation Committee.
The central element in the debate regarding a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 new individuals has been whether they have been sufficiently investigated for anti-democratic views.
Every six months, a bill is introduced in the Folketing granting new individuals Danish citizenship after an often lengthy and comprehensive application process.
This also applied to the then SVM government.
But the latest granting of citizenship coincided with the calling of the general election held in March of this year, and the bill regarding the citizenship of the 2,055 individuals was therefore postponed.
A screening model must be created for people who apply for Danish citizenship to investigate whether they have anti-democratic views. The government announced this earlier in October.
However, the government has ultimately decided that it will introduce the bill before a screening model is ready.
The original bill had its first reading in the Folketing on 5 February, but three weeks later Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen (S) called a general election.
The expert group was established in 2025 and was initially given ten months to complete its work.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

Data on 525,000 people compromised in KU cyberattack
The University of Copenhagen (KU) has been subjected to a cyberattack.
The hackers have gained access to information on approximately 525,000 individuals. Among this is information such as full name, CPR number, work telephone number, private telephone number, and private email address.
The university stated this in a press release on Friday evening.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, just as “other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed”.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness and the Agency for Public Security write in a press release Friday evening that the authorities are monitoring the cyber incidents at the University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University.
The ministry and the agency are working closely with the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalisation and other relevant authorities on the handling, it is stated.
– The incidents emphasize once again that the cyber threat against Denmark is serious, states Minister for Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen (SF) in a written comment to Ritzau and continues:
– The Agency for Public Security generally assesses that universities in Denmark are exposed to the threat of cyberattacks. Among other things because they are leaders within a range of research areas. I know that the universities are working actively to counter that threat.
The minister states that “relevant higher education institutions have been informed about the incidents and have received advice from the Agency for Public Security.”
The attack against the University of Copenhagen was discovered on Tuesday and “was subsequently brought under control”.
The university is in the process of analyzing the exact scope and preventing similar or further attacks from taking place, it is stated.
KU further writes in the press release that at present they have no further comments on the cyberattack, but that “there will be follow-up with further information when a clearer picture of the incident is available”.
Aarhus University stated on Thursday that the educational institution had been subjected to a hacker attack.
The hacker gained access to one of the university’s servers.
Afterwards, the hacker attempted to gain access to and change passwords for approximately 1,700 users – both current and former employees and students.
This did not succeed, as the unauthorized access to the system was discovered.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.
Jacob Harris has been banned from managing or sitting on the board of a company for three years following a ruling by the probate court in Roskilde on Friday.
TV 2 reported the decision, citing trustee and bankruptcy lawyer Morten Bjerregaard.
The ban also means Harris, an independent member of the Danish parliament, cannot own a company unless he accepts personal liability.
The ruling concerns Harris’ activities in Krokodille ApS, a company for which his wife, Tetiana Harris Nielsen, served as director. The court declared the company bankrupt in the autumn of 2025.
According to TV 2, Harris’ wife has also received a three-year bankruptcy ban. The ruling was reportedly based on the couple’s conduct in the company, whose bookkeeping was deficient and entirely absent for 2025.
Krokodille ApS was founded in Hedehusene, west of Copenhagen, in December 2021 under the name Vostok Sokol ApS. A holding company owned by Tetiana Harris Nielsen is registered as its founder. The company changed its name in March 2022 and moved its registered address from the couple’s home to an address in Ringsted in October 2025, shortly before its bankruptcy.

US midterms: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads key Michigan Senate race
Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has opened a six-point lead over Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's closely contested US Senate race, according to a new poll released less than a week before the midterm elections.
The survey, conducted by the Glengariff Group for The Detroit News and WDIV-TV, found that 51.4% of likely voters supported El-Sayed, compared with 45.1% for Rogers, while 3.6% remained undecided.
The poll surveyed 600 likely voters between 19 and 22 October, with a margin of error of four percentage points.
Michigan's Senate contest is among the most closely watched races in the country, with the outcome potentially helping determine control of the chamber, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority.
El-Sayed, a former public health official, is competing against Rogers, a former seven-term congressman, for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
The Democrat's lead narrowed to 4.2% points among respondents who said they would definitely vote on 3 November, with 50.7% backing El-Sayed and 46.5% supporting Rogers.
Independent voters shift towards El-Sayed
One of the poll's most significant findings was a shift among independent voters, who had previously favoured Rogers.
El-Sayed secured 45.5% support among independents, compared with 40% for Rogers, while 15% remained undecided.
The figures represent a reversal from a survey conducted before September, when Rogers led among independents by 42% to 28%.
"This is the first time this election that I've seen El-Sayed ahead among the independents," Glengariff pollster Richard Czuba told The Detroit News.
"This is the sign that I always look for in Michigan in every race. The margin you're leading by among independents tends to be the margin that you win by," he added.
The survey also highlighted the influence of President Donald Trump on voter preferences.
El-Sayed received support from 83% of respondents who disapproved of Trump's performance, compared with 12% for Rogers.
Meanwhile, Rogers secured 92.5% of voters who approved of Trump, against 5.5% for El-Sayed.
Among undecided voters, 77% disapproved of Trump's performance, potentially offering an opening for the Democrat.
"This is all about Donald Trump," Czuba said, describing the president as the central dividing line in the election.
Young and Black voters strongly favour El-Sayed
El-Sayed enjoyed particularly strong support among younger voters, winning more than 77% of respondents under 30 and 59.5% of those in their thirties.
Rogers led among voters aged 65 and older with nearly 54%, and among those aged 40 to 49 with 57%.
The Republican candidate also led among white voters, securing 54% support compared with 43% for El-Sayed.
However, El-Sayed commanded overwhelming support among Black voters, with 88% backing him against just 4% for Rogers.
The Democrat also led among women by 56% to 41%, while Rogers held a narrow advantage among men.
El-Sayed was ahead by 11 percentage points among university-educated voters and by nearly 16 points in metropolitan Detroit.
The poll comes after an expensive Democratic primary in which the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC spent at least $30.6 million opposing El-Sayed.

EXPLAINER - President Herzog takes center stage as Israeli election leaves neither main bloc with majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:54:08 UTC
23:54:08 KST

Attention in Israel is turning to President Isaac Herzog, who will task a member of parliament with forming the next government after preliminary election results left neither main political bloc with a majority.
With about 100% of votes counted Wednesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot. Arab parties won 19 seats.
Neither main bloc had therefore reached the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Official results are due by Nov. 4. Herzog must then consult parliamentary factions and assign the task of forming a government within seven days of the results’ official publication.
Although Israel’s presidency is largely ceremonial, selecting a candidate to form a government is one of its most consequential responsibilities, particularly when the election produces no clear winner. 
Consultations with parliamentary factions
Under Israel’s basic law governing the formation of governments, the president must consult representatives of parliamentary factions before tasking a Knesset member with forming a government, within seven days of the publication of the official election results.
Herzog is expected to hold separate meetings next week with representatives of the 11 parties that won seats in the election.
During these consultations, party representatives typically recommend their preferred candidate to form the government.
Based on the preliminary results, Arab parties could play an influential role in determining who receives the mandate.
The Joint Arab List and the United Arab List could recommend Eisenkot, potentially giving him the backing of a parliamentary bloc exceeding 61 lawmakers.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, could insist that he should receive the mandate on the grounds that his Likud party is the largest in the Knesset under this scenario.
However, the law does not require the president to select the leader of the party with the most seats. 
How does the president choose?
The Israel Democracy Institute, an independent research institution, explains that the first stage of forming a government involves selecting the Knesset member who will be tasked with doing so.
The institute says the president consults representatives of the elected parliamentary factions before choosing a Knesset member to form the government.
It notes that the legislation provides no clear guidelines on how to make that decision, giving the president considerable discretion.
Traditionally, the mandate has been given to the leader of the largest party -- the faction holding the most Knesset seats -- but this is not a legal requirement.
The institute adds that the main consideration is which candidate appears most capable of forming a government that can win the Knesset’s confidence.
It cites the 2009 election, when then-President Shimon Peres tasked Benjamin Netanyahu with forming a government even though his Likud party won 27 seats.
Tzipi Livni’s Kadima party won 28 seats but was not given the mandate.
Herzog’s choice could therefore trigger a political dispute with one of the two camps, given the closely balanced distribution of seats. 
Unity government to avoid another election
Herzog previously pledged to work to prevent another election and raised the possibility of a unity government bringing together Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Israeli television channels reported that the president could invite the two leaders to a meeting to discuss forming a joint government.
They also suggested that Herzog might publicly call for a unity government in a statement to the Israeli public.
This comes as preliminary election results point to difficulties in forming a government with a clear parliamentary majority.
Israel has faced recurring political crises in recent years, struggling to form stable governing coalitions and holding successive parliamentary elections.
The latest election is the sixth since 2019, amid continuing political divisions and disagreements between parties over government formation and alliances.
3 attempts to form a government
Once a Knesset member is tasked with forming a government, a legal process begins that can take days or weeks and involve up to three attempts.
The Israel Democracy Institute explains that the candidate initially receives 28 days to form a government.
The president may extend that deadline by up to 14 additional days if the candidate has not completed the task.
If the first candidate fails, the president can select another Knesset member, who receives 28 days without the possibility of an extension.
If the second attempt fails, a group of 61 Knesset members can request that a third candidate be given the mandate. That candidate then has 14 days to form a government.
If the final attempt fails, Israel heads to another election under the procedures set out in law. 
Can a minority government be formed?
Although governments are usually formed with the support of at least 61 lawmakers, Israeli law also allows minority governments.
The Israel Democracy Institute says Israel’s basic law governing the government does not explicitly require a new government to secure the support of an absolute majority of Knesset members.
It explains that a government can win a confidence vote if more lawmakers vote in favor than against.
However, the institute notes that most governments formed after elections have secured the support of at least 61 lawmakers.
If government-formation negotiations succeed, the Knesset holds a special session at which the prime minister-designate presents the proposed Cabinet and the government’s policy platform.
Lawmakers then hold a confidence vote, and the government formally takes office if it secures the required support.
Until a new government is formed, the outgoing Netanyahu-led government continues to perform its duties.
Whether Herzog gives the mandate to Netanyahu or Eisenkot, or pushes for a unity government, his decision remains the first step in determining the course of Israel’s next government formation.

Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:51:14 UTC
23:51:14 KST

Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure.
Gulf countries have stepped up diplomacy with Iran in a bid to de-escalate tensions across the Middle East, amid fears of renewed US strikes on Tehran and intensifying hostilities between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August – Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – and diplomats from Qatar met with high-ranking Iranian officials on Monday in an effort to prevent the resumption of all-out war.
Underscoring the high stakes, the meeting in Tehran was attended by Saudi Minister of Defence Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, just days after Iran-aligned Houthi fighters struck Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities.
Meanwhile, during a diplomatic visit to the United Kingdom’s University of Cambridge on Monday, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called for a regional security framework, including a “non-aggression pact”, between the Gulf countries and Iran under which the United States would no longer be the primary provider of security.
While Gulf countries appear determined to avoid another round of conflict – which has already restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupted global oil and gas supplies and wreaked havoc on energy facilities and infrastructure in Gulf states – questions remain over whether a regional agreement is possible and where it would leave relations between the US and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
Regional security or de-escalation?
On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated warnings that Washington may carry out another military operation against Iran as rising fuel prices weigh on the US midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Iran would respond more forcefully to any renewed US military action, stoking fears of an even wider escalation.
While this week’s talks in Tehran mark the first high-level contact between Iran and the Mecca mutual defence pact nations since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, reports suggest they have stopped short of landing an agreement.
Reuters reported that Qatari mediators presented Iran with a draft deal on Sunday, which Tehran was expected to respond to by the end of the week. On Wednesday, the news agency quoted Iranian officials as saying Qatar had put forward ideas that were unacceptable and that Tehran would show no flexibility regarding the nuclear issue.
Khaled Batarfi, a Saudi political analyst and academic, said the visit to Tehran indicated that Saudi Arabia was willing to give Iran a “last warning” and “submit to the region’s concerns”, but that Iran has so far refused.
“The gap is [wide] and what makes it worse is that there is no trust,” Batarfi told Al Jazeera.
Observers say diverging views are unlikely to turn the current diplomatic efforts into a lasting infrastructure. “It’s really hard to see a regional security framework coming out in the coming months or even years,” Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told Al Jazeera.
“What we are seeing is more small groups, flexible groups of countries that are taking the lead in trying to reach either bilateral or multilateral solutions,” the analyst said. “A regional security framework would need the same vision for the region, which is not necessarily shared… among the GCC countries themselves.”
Challenges ahead
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye share concerns that a prolonged confrontation between Iran and the US could further destabilise the region.
“The main obstacle remains the fundamental disagreement between Tehran and Washington over the sequence of commitments,” Azizi told Al Jazeera. “The US wants Iranian concessions, particularly on the nuclear issue, while Tehran insists that its conditions for ending the war must be met first.”
“Regional mediation could help bridge this gap, possibly through an interim arrangement, but the willingness of regional actors to facilitate an agreement does not necessarily mean that the two principal parties are prepared to make the necessary compromises,” he added.
As for a new security order, Azizi said regional countries do not share a common understanding of what it should look like and what role the US – which has so far been the GCC’s main security partner – would have left to play.
Iran has long advocated for a regional security architecture that would reduce or eliminate the US military presence. “Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, however, remain deeply integrated into the US security system, and there is little indication that they intend to abandon it,” Azizi said.
“The recent war has certainly raised questions about the reliability of American security guarantees, but this has encouraged these countries to diversify their security partnerships rather than fundamentally redefine their strategic alignments.”

28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Budget includes winter energy payments, higher bank taxes, plans to meet NATO defense spending commitments
- Kyiv welcomes additional financial, military support
The UK announced a £100 ($133) winter energy payment for 20 million households in England and £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in additional support for Ukraine, Treasury chief John Healey said Wednesday.
The measures form part of Healey's first budget, which also includes changes to bank taxation, local government financing and defense spending.
The energy payment will be available to households in council tax bands A to D, which generally cover lower-value residential properties.
Funding will also be allocated to the devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to introduce similar support.
Healey announced measures to increase financial powers for local authorities and regional mayors, describing "fiscal devolution" as a key part of his budget plans.
Under the proposals, local authorities will retain business rates locally by the end of the decade, while mayors will receive a share of income tax revenue from 2028.
The government also confirmed a 3.9% increase in the minimum wage for workers aged 18 to 20, with a smaller increase for younger workers than for other age groups.
The budget includes an additional 3% on the bank surcharge, a tax paid by banks, which Healey described as "time-limited." The increase is smaller than previously expected. 
Defense and aid for Ukraine
Turning to defense, Healey said the UK's defense budget was £14 billion higher than in the final year of the Conservative government.
He said the government would set out in next year's spending review how it plans to meet the UK's NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of gross domestic product on defense by 2035.
A new defense finance task force will examine ways to achieve the target, while the government will seek to increase private investment in defense, including through public-private partnerships.
On Ukraine, Healey announced £10 billion in additional economic and military support following a telephone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier in the day.
Healey said he and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham informed Zelenskyy of the support package during the call.
"He told us 'you've made my day,'" Healey said.
The package includes £500 million in urgent military funding for Ukraine this winter.
Britain will stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes," the UK Treasury chief said. 
Zelenskyy welcomes additional support
Zelenskyy welcomed the announcement and said that the aid package included £7 billion in economic support for Kyiv over the next three years and another £3 billion in British export support.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy described his phone call with Burnham as "great."
He said the export support would be allocated "primarily for the supply of much-needed weapons that will strengthen our protection of lives."
Zelenskyy said the additional funding was separate from the annual assistance London already provides to Ukraine.
He described the decision as a "truly strong" and "very timely" step that came "right as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate."
"Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realizing that it must end this war of its own making," Zelenskyy said.
He added that he and Burnham also discussed sanctions policy.
"I am grateful to Britain, to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team, and to every person around the world who understands that standing with Ukraine is the right thing to do – that it means being on the right side of history," he said.

MOSCOW, Oct 28 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin told African leaders on Wednesday that Russia was their best partner, accusing what he cast as a colonial West of still trying to exploit the continent’s resources and using debt to hold back development.
Putin was speaking at the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, a two-day event attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries, and will hold one-on-one talks with many of the 22 individual African leaders attending on issues such as trade, security, arms and grain.

“Africa is increasingly asserting itself as one of the key players in the global economy and politics,” Putin said.
“However, the emergence of a multipolar world is, of course, no easy task; it faces resistance from countries that are not prepared to accept this reality: those who are accustomed to thinking in terms of their colonial past and to enriching themselves fabulously.”
Putin, whom Western critics accuse of trying to leverage Africa’s colonial past to Moscow’s benefit, did not name the countries he had in mind.
But he spoke of what he called “active attempts by Western countries” to drive Africans back into debt bondage and to force them to accept much-needed financial resources on predatory terms, which he said slowed their long-term development.
RUSSIA READY TO SHARE
By contrast, Putin said Russia was ready to share its know-how, including digital know-how, and localise production rather than just buy raw materials, creating jobs and generating tax revenue.
Russian paramilitary forces have been accused by Western governments of propping up military juntas such as the one in Mali to try to shore up Moscow’s geopolitical influence and squeeze out former colonial powers such as France. Moscow rejects these assertions.
Burkina Faso’s prime minister, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouedraogo, said cooperation with Russia was transparent and ensured both parties’ interests, and that Moscow was not trying to erase African languages and cultures.
“This is completely different from what we had with imperialist France,” he told Russia’s state RT television channel.
Putin told the summit that Russia championed greater African influence in the IMF and World Bank, was ready to embark on joint transport and agricultural infrastructure projects and that Moscow stood ready to supply grain and fertiliser to more African countries.

Thomas Hill Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:48:01 UTC
23:48:01 KST

[Revised entry by David Brink on October 28, 2026.
Changes to: Bibliography]
Thomas Hill Green (1836 – 82) is widely regarded as the founding and most influential figure in the tradition of British idealism that flourished in England, especially Oxford, and Scotland, especially Glasgow and Edinburgh, in the second half of the nineteenth century and early in the twentieth century (see, e.g., Mander 2011). Green’s idealism was systematic, embracing metaphysics and epistemology, ethical theory, political philosophy, and philosophy of history and religion. In metaphysics and epistemology, Green reflected the influence of Immanuel Kant, criticizing the British empiricist legacy of John Locke and David Hume. Green argued that empirical knowledge is the workmanship of the human mind, that reality depends on thought and cannot transcend it, and that the possibility of objectivity requires the existence of a single corporate or divine consciousness of which individual minds are proper parts. The only defensible form of idealism, Green thought, is absolute idealism, in which all aspects of reality are operations of a single consciousness. In ethics, Green embraced a form of perfectionism that identifies the human good with self-realization and the perfection of our nature as moral persons and agents. But self-realization must reflect the way in which individuals participate in associations and communities and, as a result, must reflect the demand that individuals pursue a common good. In articulating this conception of perfectionism, Green sees himself as synthesizing the best elements in two different ethical traditions – Greek eudaimonism and Kantian rationalism. Green’s perfectionist ethics influence his politics. He provides the philosophical foundations for a new progressive form of liberalism that transcends the laissez-faire liberalism characteristic of some strands in nineteenth century British liberalism. The state has a duty to promote the common good, and individual rights are constrained by the common good. This gives the state not just negative duties to refrain from interfering with the freedoms and opportunities of its citizens but also positive duties to provide resources and opportunities for individual self-realization. The ethical and political demand for self-realization, Green thinks, is freedom, properly understood. He believes that moral and political progress in history consists in the gradual and increasingly more adequate realization of the values of perfection, the common good, and freedom. Because Green identifies God with the metaphysical, ethical, and political principles in human nature, he sees God as immanent in the progressive developments in human history. 1. Interview: China becoming engine of global innovation: Merck China president

Unknown Publisher

by Xinhua writer Liu Yinglun
HONG KONG, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is becoming a foundational engine for global innovation, Rogier Janssens, president of Merck China and managing director of Life Science China, told Xinhua in a recent interview.
China is one of the world's most important end markets for life sciences, healthcare and electronics, which are Merck's core domains, Janssens added. This, coupled with China's growing weight in oncology, antibody-drug conjugates and other areas of global drug development, is why the company stays committed to expanding its footprint in the country.
In the latest such effort, the company announced earlier this week that it has signed an agreement with Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) to establish Merck Hong Kong Center, a dedicated physical facility for scientific product supply, technological demonstrations, and expert consultation.
The move came after the launch of the Merck Greater Bay Area (GBA) Innovation and Collaboration Center in Shenzhen in June. Janssens called having two establishments in the GBA a token of Merck's deep commitment to the region, which is spearheading growth across life sciences, healthcare, and electronics.
The centers are assigned different focuses in line with the respective strengths of the two cities, according to Janssens. The one in Hong Kong is primarily focused on early-stage development and early clinical research. Its counterpart in Shenzhen focuses more on manufacturing scale-up for biotechnology and small molecules.
Elaborating on the arrangement, Janssens said that Hong Kong is exceptionally well positioned for clinical research. Its network of hospitals holds rigorous international accreditation, and clinical data generated here is widely recognized by major international regulatory bodies, he said.
On top of mature infrastructure for clinical trials, Hong Kong's established financial markets, vibrant innovation ecosystem and deep talent pool can help Chinese technologies enter global markets, said Janssens.
Multinational firms like Merck can participate in the process by fostering collaborative exchanges and mutual learning between their technical experts and local scientists and startups, as will be the case with the Hong Kong center, according to Janssens.
"The collaboration is about serving science and innovation," said Janssens. ■

Xinhua Headlines: African businesses eye new opportunities as China import expo approaches
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:47:18 CST
23:47:18 KST

* With China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations having taken effect on May 1, African businesses are looking to the expo to tap the Chinese market and move up the value chain through product processing, brand development and other higher-value activities.
NAIROBI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- In Kigali, Rwanda's capital, Grace Mbabazi, founder and CEO of M&M Sozo Ltd., is busy selecting the company's signature honey products ahead of her upcoming trip to China for the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), where she hopes to showcase the Rwandan specialty to a wider Chinese audience.
Scheduled to take place in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10, this year's expo will bring together returning African exhibitors and newcomers alike.
With China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations having taken effect on May 1, African businesses are looking to the expo to tap the Chinese market and move up the value chain through product processing, brand development and other higher-value activities.
NEW FACES, NEW PRODUCTS
This year's CIIE will welcome a number of new African friends, with Gabon making its debut at the national pavilion and Cote d'Ivoire participating collectively for the first time, injecting fresh momentum into China-Africa trade and economic cooperation.
Cote d'Ivoire is seeking to further expand its presence in the Chinese market through the CIIE. Kaladji Fadiga, director of the Cote d'Ivoire Export Agency, told Xinhua that the country would focus on five key sectors at this year's expo: cocoa, coffee, cashew, kola nuts and textiles.
"Our ambition is to make this edition a remarkable showcase that reflects the true potential of our trade with China," he added.
Asnath Adje, head of Cote d'Ivoire's Lya Bissap brand, was delighted to learn that her company had been selected to exhibit at the CIIE. She hopes to introduce hibiscus, a plant familiar to many Ivorians since childhood, to a wider international audience in new forms.
At this year's expo, she plans to showcase hibiscus powder, ultrafine powder and concentrate. The ultrafine powder can be used in food processing and cosmetics, opening up new possibilities for downstream product development, Adje said.
African companies will also bring a diverse range of distinctive products to the expo.
Bansa, a brand from Cameroon, plans to showcase a variety of agricultural and processed products, including roasted sesame seeds, spicy dried meat, sesame brittle made with pure honey, processed cocoa products, shea butter and plantain chips.
"This is my first time participating in the CIIE as an official exhibitor. Last year, I attended as an observer," said Ngoyonga Chaswe Clotilde, a Bansa representative.
Clotilde said she hopes the expo will help promote the brand to a global audience and forge partnerships that could attract investment and support further processing in Cameroon.
NEW GROWTH
China's market has brought tangible benefits for African businesses, with rising export volumes among the most notable.
Kenya's tea exports to China rose from about 2 million kg annually in the past to 12.4 million kg in 2025, and are expected to reach around 20 million kg in 2026, said Willy Mutai, chief executive officer of the Tea Board of Kenya.
Ethiopian coffee company AWO Coffee has also recorded strong growth in China. Its marketing manager, Kaleab Fekad, said the company began exporting to China in 2014, initially shipping only dozens of tonnes annually. In 2025, its exports reached 200 tonnes.
AWO Coffee has expanded its offerings from raw beans to roasted beans and packaged coffee powder. After its first CIIE presence last year, the company recognized the expo's potential for brand promotion and sales, particularly for processed products. It is returning this year to reach more Chinese consumers and further expand its sales, Fekad said.
The CIIE has also helped African businesses forge commercial partnerships.
Wendy Mpendulo, founder of South African nut producer Miante Manufacturing, said that at last year's expo, she met a packaging company manager who expressed interest in appointing her as its representative in South Africa and using the country as a starting point to expand into other African markets.
For Cameroon-based company Africa SARL, the expo has helped establish lasting trade relationships. Its chief executive officer, Pitndap Nchandini Ismaila, said he met Chinese partners at his first CIIE last year, and some of whom have since begun working with the company.
"Thanks to the expo, I was able to meet Chinese partners with whom we now work closely," he said. "Our cooperation has enabled me to expand our plantations and increase exports to China."
China's favorable trade policy toward Africa has provided an additional boost by lowering the cost of accessing the Chinese market.
Mutai said Kenyan tea exporters could save 15 percent in tariffs by obtaining certificates of origin issued by the Kenya Revenue Authority, allowing them to benefit from China's zero-tariff arrangements.
He said inquiries about Kenyan tea have increased noticeably, with Chinese buyers recently traveling to Kenya specifically to seek tea supplies. "It is a big opportunity for Kenya, and we can leverage it to sell more tea," he added.
NEW MOMENTUM
The zero-tariff treatment and China's vast market are also creating incentives for industrial upgrading in African countries. From understanding Chinese demand to raising local production capacity, African businesses are seeking to turn market access into long-term development opportunities.
Repeated participation in the CIIE has helped Zimbabwean leather goods exporter Samuneti Leathers gain a clearer understanding of Chinese consumer preferences.
"We have managed to analyze and understand our customers and what they need, and we are able to give them what they want and need," said Dionne Chibaya, an administrator at Samuneti Leathers.
Building on these insights, the company plans to showcase its finest handcrafted products at this year's expo while gaining a deeper understanding of the market to guide its expansion.
With a long tradition of leather craftsmanship, supported by its livestock sector and diverse wildlife resources, Zimbabwe is seeking to increase exports of value-added leather products. The CIIE offers Zimbabwean producers an opportunity to reach Chinese buyers and explore new business prospects.
Madagascar's mutton made its debut at the seventh CIIE in 2024. The entry into the Chinese market has not only benefited local herders but has also energized the whole "farm-to-table" chain, creating large numbers of direct and indirect jobs, particularly for young people in rural areas.
"From livestock farming and transportation to meat cutting, slaughtering and exports to China, every stage creates jobs for the Malagasy people," Madagascar's Minister of Livestock Riana Nantenaina Randrianomenjanahary said in a recent interview with Xinhua. He said at least 3,000 households benefit from this export-related activity.
Madagascar is stepping up efforts to "improve local production and the value chain, while encouraging a growing number of livestock farmers to join this sector oriented toward the Chinese market," the minister said.
(Video reporters: Deng Bingxue, Chen Shaohua, Fan Haoyu; Video editors: Liang Wanshan, Roger Lott, Wei Yin, Zhang Yuhong, Liu Yutian)■

Finland to launch new mobile emergency alert system

23:47:12 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Finland is set to launch a new public warning system in November, allowing authorities to send emergency alerts directly to mobile phones in specific geographical areas, the Finnish Ministry of the Interior announced Wednesday.
The new system, called FI-Alert, will use cell broadcast technology to deliver warnings instantly to 4G and 5G mobile phones connected to mobile networks in affected areas. Users will not need to download an app or register for the service, and foreign visitors will also be able to receive alerts.
"It is very important that we will be able to warn the public more quickly, reach more people and target warnings to specific areas," Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said.
Authorities can issue emergency warnings when a situation threatens life or health, or risks causing significant property damage. The new system is designed to improve the speed, coverage and reliability of public warnings during accidents, emergencies and other dangerous situations.
FI-Alert will complement rather than replace Finland's existing warning channels, including mobile apps, radio and television broadcasts, and public warning sirens. The ministry stressed that multiple channels remain essential to ensuring reliable communication during emergencies.
The rollout comes amid heightened concerns over airborne threats. Finnish national broadcaster Yle reported that the need for a new warning system had grown following incidents involving warhead-carrying drones straying into Finnish airspace. ■

Feature: Chinese firm helps upgrade Africa's first geothermal power plant in Kenya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:47:12 CST
23:47:12 KST

Staff members inspect the equipment at Olkaria I Geothermal Power Plant at Hell's Gate National Park in Nakuru County, Kenya, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Jianfei)
NAIROBI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Plumes of steam rise above the Olkaria I Geothermal Power Plant in Kenya's Hell's Gate National Park, as a network of pipes channels steam from deep underground to the plant's generating units, where the earth's heat is converted into electricity.
Commissioned in the 1980s as Africa's first geothermal power station, Olkaria I faced growing challenges in maintaining its generating capacity and efficiency as its equipment aged over more than four decades of operation.
Following a rehabilitation project undertaken by SEPCOIII Electric Power Construction Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Power Construction Corporation of China, the plant's total installed capacity increased from 45 megawatts (MW) to 63 MW, while the amount of steam available for power generation remained unchanged.
Located along the Great Rift Valley, Kenya has substantial geothermal potential. Data from Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority show that geothermal power accounts for around 40 percent of national electricity generation, making it the country's leading source of electricity.
Under the Kenya National Energy Compact 2025-2030, the country aims to increase its installed geothermal capacity to 1,681 MW by 2030 and achieve 100 percent clean electricity generation.
Upgrading an existing plant can be more challenging than building a new one, said Zhang Yang, deputy project manager of the rehabilitation project.
"Building a new plant is like painting on a blank canvas, where you can plan everything from scratch. With a rehabilitation project, much of the existing structure has to remain, so you have to find solutions within the space and layout already available," he said.
The project, which began in August 2023, involved upgrading all three generating units within the constraints of the decades-old facility. Engineers had to ensure that new equipment was compatible with existing systems while coordinating mechanical and electrical components within the plant's original layout, Zhang said.
The team also redesigned the steam-field pipeline layout based on steam parameters and optimized several components, including separators, exhaust stations, control valves and cooling systems. These adjustments helped increase the plant's generating capacity without requiring additional steam, Zhang added.
Maurice Awuor, electrical engineering manager at the Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen), said the rehabilitation had raised the plant's installed capacity to 63 MW, equivalent to about 2 percent of Kenya's total installed electricity generation capacity.
"This is the only geothermal rehabilitation project in Kenya over the past three years that has been commissioned and added installed capacity to the national grid," Awuor said.
The rehabilitation also saw the installation of Chinese-made equipment, including condensers, circulating water pumps and cooling towers, to replace aging machinery.
Zhang said that after KenGen personnel visited Chinese factories and exchanged views with manufacturers, they gained a better understanding of the performance of Chinese equipment and its manufacturing processes, paving the way for its adoption in the geothermal project.
"This time, we have introduced Chinese-made equipment into a geothermal project in Kenya, and I believe more projects will adopt Chinese equipment in the future," Zhang said.
Awuor said Chinese companies had strengths in technology and equipment, and cooperation with them was important for Kenya as it seeks to develop its geothermal resources.
Beyond equipment, the project has also facilitated knowledge-sharing between Chinese engineers and their Kenyan counterparts.
Perry Karuri, a Kenyan quality assurance and control engineer responsible for construction inspections, said it was her first time working with Chinese engineers.
During equipment installation and commissioning, she discussed technical parameters, construction quality and on-site challenges with her Chinese colleagues. The teams jointly examined problems and worked out solutions to ensure that construction met the required standards, she said.
"We not only share knowledge and exchange experience, but also learn from each other's different working methods. I have learned a more rigorous approach to work from the Chinese engineers," Karuri said, adding that the cooperation had provided opportunities to develop practical skills and gain experience in operating and maintaining the upgraded equipment.
Zhang Liang, the project manager, said some areas around the plant had previously experienced rotational power cuts due to electricity shortages, and additional installed capacity at Olkaria I has helped strengthen the local power supply.
He added that geothermal power can also complement other renewable sources. While wind and solar generation fluctuate with weather conditions and the time of day, geothermal plants can provide a relatively stable supply of electricity, helping balance the grid when wind generation is low or solar output falls after sunset.
"Geothermal resources are an important domestic energy source for Kenya. Their relatively low generation costs can help reduce the electricity sector's sensitivity to fluctuations in international oil and gas prices," Awuor said.
He noted that the additional capacity at the upgraded plant could help Kenya meet rising electricity demand, support industrial production and manufacturing, and advance efforts to diversify its energy mix and transition toward cleaner energy. ■

Economic Watch: Chinese design gives exports new edge at Canton Fair
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
22:46:59 CST
23:46:59 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Stainless steel has long endured a rather understated existence. It can be found in kitchen sinks, saucepans and rubbish bins, having proved durable and practical but unglamorous. At the 140th China Import and Export Fair in Guangzhou in south China's Guangdong Province, however, a Chinese jewelry maker is giving this metal a different purpose.
Its display of gold-toned, silver-colored and brightly hued ornaments has drawn crowds of overseas buyers at this fair, which is also known as the Canton Fair. These pieces look like fine jewelry, but most are made of stainless steel, offering a polished finish without the price tag of precious metals.
For consumers, the proposition is timely, with gold and silver prices soaring globally. "Some jewelry customers are turning to new product lines," said Chen Danping, deputy general manager of Guangzhou-based Justop Jewelry.
Stainless steel ornaments, Chen explained, combine jewelry-making techniques and appearance with the cost advantage of a much cheaper material.
For Jacob Ruiz Palomo, a buyer from Spain, the appeal is straightforward: the jewelry pulls off a commercial trick, making an inexpensive material look anything but cheap. "Its competitive prices need not come at the expense of good design," Palomo noted.
This trick points to a broader change in Chinese manufacturing. For decades, China's exporters built their strength on scale, speed and cost. These advantages still matter today, but many manufacturers are aiming higher and trying to win the competition via smarter technologies and better designs.
The Canton Fair, China's vast twice-yearly trading floor, offers a snapshot of this transition. Serving as a barometer and wind vane of China's foreign trade, this year's fair, marking its 70th anniversary, has brought together products that seek to compete not only on function and price, but also on intelligence, appearance and design.
The fair's 2026 design innovation award, known as the CF Award, offers a glimpse of where Chinese manufacturing design is heading. This year, 222 products from 174 companies made the cut, with AI-powered products accounting for 32 percent of entries and green, low-carbon products for 44 percent. The top award winners included the ZXMOTO 820RR motorcycle and an intelligent capsule robot for gastric endoscopy.
Yet the value of design is not confined to high-end products. It can also transform the most ordinary household items, making them more functional and distinctive.
At the stand of Guangdong-based brand EKO, a range of stainless-steel rubbish bins showed how thoughtful design can elevate an everyday household item. One model, equipped with an automatic sensor, caught the attention of many buyers.
"The company pays attention to details as small as the angle of a corner and the curve of a lid," said Pan Libin, a representative.
"Thoughtful design can expand a product's uses," Pan added. "A rubbish bin can fit into different settings, from living rooms and kitchens to bathrooms and bedrooms. We can tailor designs to different needs in terms of size, shape, color and available space."
EKO began as an original-equipment manufacturer, making products for other companies. In 2007, it started developing its own brand, betting that design could give it a more distinctive place in the market. One of its products became a Red Dot winner this year, adding international recognition to its effort.
For other Chinese companies, drawing on domestic cultural heritage is another way to differentiate a product.
Zhu Bingren copper art, based in Hangzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province, is a business featuring craftsmanship spanning multiple generations, and has drawn strong interest from overseas buyers at this year's fair. The business incorporates copper carving techniques, recognized as part of China's national intangible cultural heritage, into products ranging from home ornaments to tea sets, thus transforming centuries-old craftsmanship into contemporary designs for global consumers.
"Foreign customers are showing particular interest in traditional Chinese elements," said Gu Dawei, the company's sales manager. "While staying true to our cultural roots, we also pay close attention to the needs and preferences of different markets so that our products can better appeal to consumers around the world."
More than 700 samples brought to the fair have been snapped up by buyers, according to the company.
Industry insiders said the increased presence of Chinese design in consumer products worldwide is underpinned by the strengths of China's manufacturing ecosystem. Its comprehensive industrial chains allow creative ideas to be turned into tangible products quickly, while efficient supply chains enable manufacturers to respond swiftly to changing market demands.
Michael Schjerbeck Jensen, general manager of F&H Asia, told Xinhua that the Danish group's joint product development with Chinese partners has repeatedly turned ideas into reality. In an uncertain world, Jensen said, China's comprehensive, stable and efficient supply chains offer a particularly valuable source of certainty.
"The growing international reach of Chinese design is increasingly evident," said Luo Weiyu, business director of 3&1 Industrial Design. "Backed by China's complete industrial chains, domestic designers can also update their concepts and bring new products to market quickly, making them more responsive to consumer demand. Senators Demand to Know if Dr. Oz Collaborated With Election Denial Groups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:46:35 UTC
23:46:35 KST

With a week to go before the midterms, a group of Democratic senators are demanding that Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), share communications his department may have had with far-right groups promoting a baseless conspiracy theory about left-wing groups stealing votes from residents of nursing homes.
In July, Oz’s agency issued a memo rescinding previous guidance on how staff at nursing homes could help residents to vote by assisting with mail-in voting or transporting residents to polling locations. The memo replaced that guidance with threats of prosecution if staff “engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.” Referring to this memo, election denial groups last month began to boost claims that voter fraud was happening inside care facilities.
That campaign was spearheaded by the Election Integrity Network, a group led by Cleta Mitchell, a former adviser to president Donald Trump. “These left-wing groups go into the nursing homes, and they go into the group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable,” Mitchell said in a recent appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room show.
Now, citing WIRED’s reporting on the nursing home conspiracy theories, a group of senators that includes Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Alex Padilla, Mazie Hirono, Ron Wyden, Kirsten Gillibrand, Jeff Merkley, and Cory Booker wrote in a letter to CMS to ”urgently request that CMS rescind its July 2026 memorandum and reinstate its 2020 and 2024 nursing home voting guidance.”
“This is as low as it gets,” Warren tells WIRED. “The Trump administration’s unfounded allegations of election fraud are inspiring election denial groups to harass nursing home residents and staff. With less than a week until Election Day, every lawmaker in America should be standing up for fair elections and pushing back on this attack on seniors’ voting rights.”
A CMS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the agency’s communications with election denial groups but instead referred WIRED to the July 2026 memo.
In the letter, Warren and her colleagues specifically ask Oz about communications between CMS and Mitchell, the Election Integrity Network, and Project Civica, a New York–based election-denial group. The senators demand Oz “identify each organization and individual involved, the dates and nature of those communications, and any recommendations provided to CMS.”
Mitchell and EIN did not respond to a request for comment. "[We] had no communications or interactions with CMS regarding its memorandum or our Adopt a Care Facility initiative," Kim Hermance, president of Project Civica, tells WIRED. "Our only engagement with the agency's guidance has been reviewing the publicly available information on its website."
In August, Warren sent a letter to Oz questioning the July memo and asking him to reverse the changes. In September, Oz responded in a letter to Warren directly addressing the guidance that was removed from the CMS website in relation to helping nursing home residents with voting.
“Providing neutral logistical assistance, such as helping a resident request a mail-in ballot, completing a ballot per the resident's own expressed wishes, or arranging transportation to a polling location, is not the type of conduct that would give rise to a voter fraud investigation,” Oz writes.
Addressing the apparent contradiction in this response, the senators in their letter to Oz asked: “Why has CMS not reinstated its previous guidance clarifying nursing homes’ responsibilities to facilitate residents’ voting rights?”
With just days to go to the midterms, efforts to boost baseless conspiracy theories about voter fraud continue to gain traction. On Tuesday, Trump said he is willing to accept the outcome of the midterms if they are “honest elections.” But his administration has spent months pushing conspiracy theories about mail-in voting and noncitizen voting, while actively trying to disenfranchise voters.

Montreux Convention helped contain fallout from Russia-Ukraine war in Black Sea: Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:41:26 UTC
23:41:26 KST

Türkiye has strictly implemented the Montreux Convention since Russia launched its war against Ukraine in 2022, helping prevent the conflict from spreading to a wider region and limiting its impact on the Black Sea, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has said.
Speaking on Wednesday at a joint news conference in Sofia after a meeting of defence ministers and chiefs of general staff from Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania, Guler said Ankara remained committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while maintaining channels of dialogue with Russia to prevent further escalation.
Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu also attended the meeting.
Türkiye warns over attacks on commercial vessels
Guler said the war had significantly affected Black Sea security, with commercial vessels coming under attack and threats emerging from drifting mines, unmanned surface vehicles, drones and missile fragments.
He expressed concern over repeated attacks on commercial shipping and said Türkiye had urged both sides to exercise restraint and respect freedom of navigation in international waters.
“We learned today that another commercial vessel was struck by three drones in Bulgaria’s maritime jurisdiction,” Guler said, calling for greater caution from both parties.
He added that Türkiye reserved all legal rights in response to attacks on Turkish-flagged and Turkish-operated vessels and was closely monitoring developments.
Although Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania had the military capabilities to respond to threats, Guler stressed that decisions must account for timing and regional circumstances.
He called for careful diplomacy and rational decisions at both tactical and strategic levels to avoid increasing tensions.
Regional cooperation to counter mines and protect infrastructure
Guler said Türkiye, which has the longest coastline on the Black Sea, considers regional stability and maritime security essential.
He highlighted mine-countermeasure operations conducted by Türkiye’s naval and naval aviation forces to reduce risks to shipping.
He also pointed to the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, known as MCM Black Sea, established by the three coastal countries to tackle the threat posed by drifting mines.
Other countries can contribute to the initiative without deploying vessels, in line with an agreement among its members, he said.
Guler also emphasised the importance of protecting critical underwater infrastructure, noting that amendments to a related memorandum of understanding were signed on July 7 on the sidelines of the NATO Summit.
Türkiye has further demonstrated its commitment to regional cooperation by assuming leadership of the Maritime Component Command under the Ukraine Volunteer Coalition, he added.
Ankara calls civilian shipping a red line
Guler said Türkiye continued to use diplomatic channels to create opportunities for dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, with the aim of protecting maritime trade routes and ensuring freedom of navigation.
Both sides were being repeatedly warned that commercial shipping must remain outside the conflict zone and that attacks on civilian vessels must stop immediately, he said.
He described the coordinated position adopted by Türkiye, Bulgaria and Romania as a clear message that the safety of commercial routes and the security of Black Sea coastal countries must not be compromised.
The three countries have taken joint steps to limit the war’s impact on their security and citizens’ well-being, while maintaining safe navigation, Guler said.
He pledged that Türkiye would continue taking necessary measures to support maritime safety, guided by regional cooperation and the capabilities available to the countries involved.
The joint text agreed upon at Wednesday’s meeting, he added, reaffirmed the three countries’ firm stance on Black Sea security.

Newborn immunisation against respiratory virus could cut infant winter hospitalisations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:39:25 UTC
23:39:25 KST

As the cold season nears, immunisation of newborns against universal RSV could significantly reduce infant hospitalisations across Europe
As the season for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other respiratory diseases approaches, a new report from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) indicates that universal immunisation of newborns against RSV could substantially reduce hospitalisations among infants linked to the disease during the winter season.
‘Protecting infants from RSV in the first months of their life is particularly important,’ said Bruno Ciancio, ECDC Head of Unit. ‘And we have a tool to do just that. Universal immunisation of newborns against RSV can reduce the risk of hospitalisation due to respiratory infections in young children by more than half.’
The models assessed the potential of providing vaccination to expectant mothers, or immunising infants directly with antibodies. Assuming 90% of newborns are immunised with long-acting monoclonal antibodies at birth, models project that 61% of RSV-related hospitalisations in infants can be prevented in the first two months of life. In the same assessment, ECDC estimates that universal vaccination of pregnant mothers would also lead to substantial reductions in RSV hospitalisation among infants in the first two months of life (52%).
As Europe enters the autumn and winter months, RSV, influenza and other respiratory infections can put children at risk of serious illness, while also placing additional pressure on healthcare systems across the region. This makes it all the more important to ensure that newborns are immunised against RSV.

====================================================================================================

Can Singapore Help Europe Rethink Its Indo-Pacific Strategy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:38:00 UTC
23:38:00 KST

On October 27, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Singapore with a message that Europe needs closer partnerships in the Indo-Pacific. Trade, underwater infrastructure, and industrial artificial intelligence may seem like separate policy areas. In fact, they expose the same problem: Europe’s prosperity depends on networks that it cannot secure or shape alone.
Singapore has spent decades making itself indispensable to a global economy in which it has little control over the behavior of the major powers. Germany might be seeking to learn from that example.
At his meeting with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Merz proposed an interregional trade agreement between the European Union and the 12 members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). Together, the two groups account for more than a third of global trade. Wong and Merz also agreed to deepen defense cooperation and industrial AI collaboration under an updated strategic partnership, building on their original agreement from 2024.
The EU already has trade agreements with CPTPP members Singapore and Vietnam in Southeast Asia, as well as with other CPTPP members, including Japan, Canada and New Zealand. Singapore specifically has had a free-trade agreement with the EU since 2019, followed by a digital trade agreement that took effect in February 2026. According to the European Commission, bilateral trade in goods between the EU and Singapore reached 47.8 billion euros in 2025.
Merz’s proposal to link the EU more closely with the CPTPP would therefore need to do more than connect markets that already have bilateral FTAs. Its value would lie in addressing gaps between existing agreements, aligning trade rules where possible, and making it easier for businesses to operate across countries with different regulatory systems. But an interregional agreement would be politically difficult to negotiate.
In the realm of security, Merz and Wong focused on undersea cables, which carry more than 99 percent of international data traffic. These cables support financial transactions, cloud services and government communications, yet they are vulnerable to both accidental damage and purposeful sabotage.
Singapore has taken a leading role in efforts to improve cooperation on critical underwater infrastructure. In May 2026, on the sidelines of the Singapore-hosted Shangri-La Dialogue, 17 countries launched the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defense Exchanges (GUIDE), a voluntary framework for sharing information and exploring practical defense cooperation. Singapore was one of the founding members; European countries, among them France and Italy, accounted for over half of the 17 states that joined at the launch. Germany joined GUIDE during Merz’s visit.
Much underwater infrastructure is built, maintained, and repaired by private operators, making coordination between governments and industry essential. GUIDE provides a framework for countries to share information and improve their response to disruptions that cross national borders. The damage to five undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland in December 2024 illustrated the stakes. Such incidents can disrupt communications, incur substantial repair costs, and leave governments struggling to establish responsibility. For Singapore, a major hub for international data routes, and Germany, whose economy depends on secure digital connectivity, closer cooperation is therefore a practical necessity.
Industrial AI offers a third example of why EU-Singapore connections matter. Germany has deep manufacturing and engineering expertise; Singapore has invested in digital infrastructure and the application of AI.
At their joint press conference, Wong said Singapore was focusing less on building frontier models than on deploying AI in areas such as logistics, healthcare, finance, and advanced manufacturing. The National AI Strategy 2.0, launched in 2023, aims to make the city-state a leading center for AI solutions by 2030. It emphasizes adoption across industry, government and research.
That focus complements Germany’s industrial base. Cooperation could help manufacturers introduce robotics and automation, improve productivity, and bring AI into existing production systems. But the test will be whether cooperation produces systems that businesses actually use.
The EU has spent years declaring the Indo-Pacific a strategic priority. Europe cannot eliminate its dependence on international markets, digital infrastructure, or foreign technology, and it cannot expect Singapore to become an alternative to the United States or China. Singapore’s strength lies in maintaining connections across competing centers of power, not in choosing one at the expense of the others. Europe could learn from that approach. Singapore cannot solve Europe’s strategic problems, but it already has the trade agreements, security partnerships, and technological ambitions that Europe says it wants to build on.
Merz has put forward a vision for closer transregional cooperation, but he has yet to explain how the EU would turn closer CPTPP ties into a workable trade framework. GUIDE remains a voluntary platform, and industrial AI cooperation has yet to demonstrate its economic impact. Merz’s Singapore visit set out the ambition, but the work of implementation has barely begun.
