Implementation of Montreux Convention helped prevent Russia-Ukraine war from spreading: Turkish defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:15:31 UTC
23:15:31 KST

Türkiye has strictly implemented the requirements of the Montreux Convention since the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022, preventing the conflict from spreading to a wider region and keeping its impact on the Black Sea to a minimum, the Turkish national defense minister said Wednesday.
Yasar Guler attended a meeting of the defense ministers and chiefs of general staff of Türkiye, Bulgaria, and Romania in Sofia, alongside Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu.
Speaking at a joint news conference following the meeting, Guler stressed that Türkiye had maintained its clear support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity since the first day of the Russia-Ukraine war.
He said Türkiye had also sought to prevent regional crises from escalating by keeping channels of dialogue with Russia open.
The nearly five-year-long Russia-Ukraine war has had significant repercussions for Black Sea security, Guler said, noting that many commercial vessels had been attacked by the parties and that drifting mines, out-of-control, or struck unmanned surface vehicles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as missile fragments, had been destroyed.
Guler said frequent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were a source of concern and that Türkiye had urged the parties to exercise restraint in line with the principle of freedom of navigation in international waters.
"Indeed, we learned today that another commercial vessel was struck by three drones in Bulgaria's maritime jurisdiction. I believe it would be useful to warn both parties to exercise greater caution," he said.
Guler said Türkiye reserved all its legal rights in response to attacks on Turkish-flagged and Turkish-operated vessels and was closely monitoring developments.
"As countries in the region, we have no shortage of capabilities when it comes to the measures that can be taken. The Turkish Armed Forces, as well as the armed forces of Romania and Bulgaria, possess the capabilities required for all kinds of measures," he said.
"However, it is important that we also take timing and the current circumstances into account. Therefore, it is important to make rational decisions at the tactical and strategic levels through sensitive diplomacy, while avoiding approaches that could increase tensions and risks in the region," he added. 
Türkiye to continue efforts for peace and stability in region
Guler said Türkiye, which has the longest coastline on the Black Sea, considers maintaining stability and security in the region essential.
"As Türkiye, we have strictly fulfilled the requirements of the Montreux Convention regarding Black Sea security since the beginning of the war. In this way, we prevented the war from spreading to a wider region and managed to keep its impact on the Black Sea to a minimum," he said.
He added that Türkiye was also conducting mine countermeasures operations using its naval and naval aviation assets to address the mine threat stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war and help maintain navigational safety.
Guler recalled that the three Black Sea littoral countries had established the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, known as MCM Black Sea, on the basis of regional ownership to address the mine threat.
He said other countries could also contribute without deploying vessels, in line with an agreement among MCM Black Sea task group members.
Guler stressed that alongside the risks posed by drifting mines, protecting critical underwater infrastructure was also important.
"In this context, we signed amendments to the Memorandum of Understanding on July 7 on the sidelines of the NATO Summit," he said.
He added that Türkiye had demonstrated its commitment to regional cooperation by assuming leadership of the Maritime Component Command under the Ukraine Volunteer Coalition.
"In short, Türkiye consistently contributes to strengthening peace and stability in the region and will continue its work and efforts in this regard," Guler said.  
'We have clearly demonstrated our firm stance on Black Sea security'
Guler noted that another critical issue was the targeting of civilian commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
"First and foremost, Türkiye continues its contacts through all channels to create opportunities for dialogue between Russia and Ukraine in order to protect maritime trade routes and ensure freedom of navigation in the Black Sea," he said.
"Both sides are continuously being warned that commercial navigation must be kept outside the conflict zone and that attacks on civilian vessels must stop immediately," he added.
Guler said the unified and resolute stance demonstrated Wednesday in full coordination and solidarity with Türkiye's friends and allies Bulgaria and Romania was important in clearly reminding both warring parties that the security of commercial routes in the Black Sea and of littoral countries was an inviolable red line.
He said the three countries had taken important joint measures to prevent the ongoing war from affecting their security and the well-being of their citizens, while ensuring the continued safety of navigation in the Black Sea.
"I would like to state that, from now on, we will take all additional measures necessary to contribute to navigational safety in the Black Sea, in line with the principle of regional ownership and using the capabilities at our disposal," he said.
"Indeed, through the joint text we agreed on as a result of the consultations held here today, we have once again clearly demonstrated our firm stance on Black Sea security," Guler added.

How we protected the UK and space in September 2026
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:12:49 GMT
23:12:49 KST

How we protected the UK and space in September 2026
This report was issued in October 2026 and covers the time period 1 September 2026 to 30 September 2026 inclusive.
September saw a slightly elevated risk levels to UK interests, with more uncontrolled re-entry and collision hazards but lower space weather activity when compared with August.
All NSpOC warning and protection services were functioning throughout the period.
Re-entry analysis
There was a 7% increase in the number of objects re-entering Earth’s atmosphere monitored by NSpOC in September, when compared with the previous month.
Of the 58 objects that re-entered, 51 were satellites, five were rocket bodies and two were likely pieces of debris.
Collision avoidance analysis
Collision risks to UK-licensed satellites were 16% higher in September than in August but sat well below the 12-month rolling average.
Registered Space Objects (RSOs) analysis
The in-orbit population increased in September, with a net addition of 163 objects to the US Satellite Catalogue.
The number of Resident Space Objects (RSOs) reported may be subject to small adjustments over time as the way objects are tracked is refined. Figures in this report reflect the most current available data and may differ slightly from those published in previous months.
Fragmentation analysis
One fragmentation incident took place in September involving a satellite in Low Earth Orbit. Assessments are ongoing to understand how many pieces of debris were released into orbit.
Space weather analysis
Space weather activity was lower in September when compared with the previous month, consisting of some very limited solar radiation and geomagnetic storms.
Comments
The National Space Operations Centre combines and coordinates UK civil and military space domain awareness capabilities to enable operations, promote prosperity and protect UK interests in space and on Earth from space-related threats, risks and hazards.

Referring to the importance of IRAN CONMINE in introducing the country’s mining capacities, the Chairman of the Iran Mine House said: “This event provides a platform for exchanging experience between domestic and foreign activists, developing international cooperation, and identifying new investment opportunities in the mining sector.”
He continued: “A 13 percent growth in the mining sector is envisioned in the Seventh Development Plan, and one of the main focuses of this year’s exhibition will be examining practical solutions for achieving this goal and removing obstacles to the development of this sector.”
The Chairman of the Iran Mine House announced an increase of about 30 percent in exhibitors this year compared with the previous edition, and said: “With planning and optimal management of the exhibition space, efforts have been made to provide the ground for the participation of a larger number of companies and mining activists so that various parts of the mining value chain—from exploration and extraction to processing—can take part in this event.”
Referring to the international dimensions of the exhibition Bahraman stated: “In this edition, representatives from 36 countries will be present, and the participation of ambassadors and foreign economic activists can help strengthen international communications and expand mining cooperation.”
Pointing to the economic conditions and restrictions caused by sanctions, the Chairman of the Iran Mine House noted: “The country’s mining sector faces numerous challenges, and overcoming these conditions requires realistic decisions, maintaining stability in policymaking, and paying attention to the actual and potential capacities of this sector.”
He emphasized: “To protect existing achievements and prevent damage to mining activities, solutions must be developed in line with the country’s economic conditions, and mining capacities must be properly used to strengthen production, develop processing, and increase Iran’s share in regional markets.”
According to an IRNA report, Iran’s 20th International Exhibition of Mines, Mining, Construction Machinery & Related Industries and Equipment (IRAN CONMINE 2026) opened on Wednesday for four days at the permanent venue of the Tehran International Exhibitions, with the participation of 128 domestic and foreign companies.
In this edition, 128 domestic companies and production units are present alongside foreign representatives from China, Japan, and India.
IRAN CONMINE is one of the country’s specialized mining industry events, providing a platform for introducing machinery, equipment, products, and services related to mining and mining industries.
In early September, the CEO of the Mining Investment Insurance Fund, noting the fund's support for 960 private mines, stated that 2,815 mining machines have been placed on track for procurement and modernization.
Ali Khatibi, in an exclusive interview with IRNA, said: "The majority of active mines in the country are in the hands of the private sector. Out of a total of 6,451 active mines, 6,005 belong to this sector, and the fund has so far supported 960 mines by issuing credit insurance policies."
He added: "The aim of this support is not just to provide financial resources; rather, efforts have been made to reduce investment risk, enabling the equipping of mines, increasing operational capacity, and ensuring production continuity."
The CEO of the Mining Investment Insurance Fund identified exploration as one of the riskiest stages of mining activity and stated: "So far, 1,141 exploration areas have been covered by the fund's insurance, and in the Iranian year 1404 (starting March 2025), 33 exploration investment policies have been issued. Within this framework, about 65,000 hectares of covered areas have entered the exploration activities phase."
Khatibi continued: "Reducing exploration risk allows investors to continue operations such as drilling and trenching with greater confidence, increasing the likelihood of identifying and developing new reserves. Support for deep drilling, especially operations at depths exceeding 1,000 meters, is also on the fund's agenda."
He also identified equipment modernization as another pillar of the fund's support.
Also, in late July, the spokesperson of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade announced the reactivation of 1,200 inactive mines in the country and said: By delegating part of the headquarters' authorities to the provinces, shortening administrative processes, and offering investment packages, the ground has been prepared for a broader presence of the private sector in the mining sector.
Ezzatollah Zarei, in an exclusive interview with IRNA, referring to the high cost of exploration activities, stated: Government financial resources alone cannot meet the needs of this sector; therefore, by synergizing resources and creating economic attractiveness, we must pave the way for private sector entry into exploration and exploitation of mines.
He added: Developing private sector investment both benefits economic actors and secures the government's interests, because with the exploitation of mines, revenues such as state royalties, ownership rights, and taxes are realized.
Zarei, stating that the mining sector, alongside the oil industry, can play a significant role in the country's economy, said: Mining cannot be considered a complete substitute for oil, but this sector has the capacity to have a large, and even greater, share in the country's economy and revenue generation alongside oil.
The spokesperson of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, referring to the goals of the Development Program Law, stated: According to the program, the growth of the mining sector must reach 13.5% by the end of the period. To achieve this goal, a series of actions have been initiated regarding the activation of mines, infrastructure development, and facilitating the investment process.
He continued: In this regard, 1,200 inactive mines have been reactivated. Also, part of the authority related to mining areas, inactive mines, and transfer of permits has been delegated to the provinces so that decisions can be made more quickly.
Zarei explained: Previously, a miner operating, for example, in Chaharmahal-Bakhtiari, had to refer to the ministry's headquarters to follow up on many matters. Now, by delegating authority to the provinces, we have tried to make the decision-making structure agile and shorten the path for investors to enter.

legal action against the chairman of the commission.

forwarded documentation on the case to the anti-mafia
prosecutors in Florence after Rossi's wife and daughter filed a
complaint.
                                    
The Brescia anti-mafia prosecutors are reportedly looking into
economic motives for the homicide possibly linked to cuts to MPS
sponsorship agreements that may have affected the interests of
people associated with the Calabria-based 'Ndrangheta mafia.

Will Pakistan Fight in Saudi Arabia’s Wars?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

The past two years have been significant for Pakistan’s diplomatic revival in Middle Eastern politics. From the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) in September 2025, signed in the backdrop of the May 2025 conflict with India, to the August 2026 Mecca Agreement with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, Islamabad has showcased its ability to navigate multifaceted strategic alignments.
Historically, Pakistan-Saudi security cooperation began during the 1960s when Pakistan deployed its soldiers to train the Royal Saudi Air Force and ground forces. Moving beyond training, Pakistani pilots assisted Saudi pilots in its conflict against South Yemen forces in 1969. Within a decade, Islamabad was once again providing crucial security and advisory assistance to Riyadh countering the 1979 Mecca Grand Mosque seizure.
In 1982, both sides signed a bilateral security agreement for the first time – thus formalizing security cooperation and large-scale deployment of Pakistani military personnel to Saudi Arabia as trainers and advisers. The agreement was put to the test during the 1990-91 Gulf war. Pakistan, taking a pre-emptive approach, stationed a large number of troops in the Kingdom.
A major test of Saudi-Pakistan security ties came during the 2015 Saudi-Houthi war. Islamabad positioned itself as a neutral player and distanced its forces from any involvement in the conflict. The Saudi-Houthi war boiled over again in 2026. On October 5 Pakistan, along with Turkiye, agreed to join hands with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Agreement. However, Islamabad has refrained from direct engagement, restricting its role to assisting Saudi forces without crossing the enemy border.
The Mecca Agreement was signed in the wake of rising Houthi attacks against both Yemeni state forces and Saudi Arabia. It is modelled on NATO’s Article 5 commitment: “an attack against one member is considered an attack against all.” In practice, this three-nation alliance is an expanded version of the Saudi-Pakistani SMDA, with the addition of Turkiye.
The strategic weight of this new alliance stems from the three countries’ substantial combined capabilities. According to the 2026 Global Firepower Index, the alliance has a “combined strength of 1.4 million active troops, 3,400 military aircrafts, 6,000 tanks, and approximately 340 maritime assets.”
The blend of Saudi finance and capital, Turkish defense capabilities, and Pakistan’s military and nuclear posture make for a powerful combination.
Once the Mecca Agreement was activated, Pakistan committed its armed forces to counter Houthi attacks against the Kingdom and Islam’s holy sites, while Turkiye, citing legislative restrictions, has limited its role to supplying technology and missiles. This distanced commitment by alliance members may undermine the basic idea of the security agreement. Pakistan and Turkiye are present in theory but are bringing a shield rather than a sword to the Saudi-Houthi conflict.
The defensive nature of the contribution was acknowledged by Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif. “The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role,” he told Pakistan’s Geo News. “We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces.”
Questions have also been raised over the strength of Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia ever since the SMDA’s inception in September 2025. It took over a year for Islamabad to finally agree to send its troops to Saudi Arabia – that too only under the Mecca Agreement. Even now Pakistan has limited its participation to air attacks and has not committed to direct combat with the Houthis. Rawalpindi seems to be in no mood to sacrifice its forces in a conflict that will divert its attention from its northern and eastern border tensions with Afghanistan and India.
The last time Pakistan fought along with the Kingdom against South Yemen was in 1969 during the Al-Wadiah War. Then too, Islamabad’s role was limited to air warfare, with Pakistan Air Force pilots flying Royal Saudi Air Force fighter jets. Close to half a century later the Saudi-led coalition waged war against the Houthis, but in April 2015, Pakistan’s parliament in a unanimous vote called for strict neutrality, barring Pakistan from engaging in the conflict in any form.
Three years into the conflict, in 2018 Pakistan’s then-Army Chief General Javed Bajwa bypassed the 2015 resolution and sent a contingent of 1000 soldiers to the Kingdom, which he described as a “training and advisory mission.” During all these years Islamabad restricted itself to advisory and defensive deployments to protect Saudi interests within its territory.
In the case of the Houthis – a Shia-dominated group with significant backing from Iran, with whom Pakistan shares close to 900 km of border – Islamabad faces a dual dilemma. First, followers of Shia Islam constitute 20 percent of Pakistan’s population, and this community has in the past stood in solidarity with Iran. Second, given Iran’s security concerns, any regional alignment working against its interest – in this case supporting Saudi Arabia against the Houthis – may be perceived as a direct challenge to Tehran’s interest in the region. Iranian displeasure with Pakistan could result in cross-border skirmishes along the rugged mountains and remote terrains bordering Baluchistan.
How long can Pakistan distance itself from actual fighting? The answer hinges on Islamabad’s larger aspirations to leverage its military influence amid a post-U.S. security vacuum in the region. Another key factor is Saudi Arabia’s long-term financial assistance to Pakistan, which in the future may convince Islamabad to change its peripheral support posture toward a more robust involvement in the regional conflict.
Pakistan’s realist approach to the Mecca Agreement seems to be shared by its partners. Both Riyad and Ankara offered little substantive backing to Islamabad during Pakistan’s recent conflict with Afghanistan. A similar response was received after the SMDA, when Saudi officials emphasized that the bilateral agreement was not against India.
Pakistan may not be comfortable with the diplomatic and political silence from Riyadh following India’s 2019 abrogation of Article 370, which ended the special privileges to the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. Time and again Rawalpindi and Islamabad have drawn global attention to Kashmir by describing the issue as Pakistan’s jugular vein, but Saudi Arabia has offered only limited diplomatic support. That can be attributed to the growing economic ties between New Delhi and Riyadh.
Such developments are a growing concern for Islamabad. Historically, Saudi Arabia sided with Pakistan during the 1965 and 1971 wars with India, and even assisted Islamabad financially in its nuclear program. But Pakistan cannot expect the same level of diplomatic or military support from the Kingdom in a future conflict with India.
Amid the changing contours of the Middle East, Pakistan is trying to balance its approach between war and peace. However, given its domestic security concerns, Pakistan is trying to thread the needle, fulfilling its commitments under the Mecca Agreement without further escalating the conflict.

How party self-governance powers China's economic transformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:06:27 UTC
23:06:27 KST

How party self-governance powers China's economic transformation
TEHRAN- Geopolitical turbulence, rising protectionism, pressure on the global economy and intensifying technological competition are shaping today's world. Within China, industrial upgrading, demographic shifts and the transition to new drivers of growth are placing greater demands on national governance. To maintain steady progress, China needs strategic resolve and the capacity to adapt its institutions, alongside a vibrant market and effective policy implementation.
The ongoing fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) focuses on sustaining full and rigorous Party self-governance. Its significance extends beyond the Party's own development to China's development as a whole.
As President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has emphasized, "China's success hinges on the Party." Understanding China begins with this fundamental political reality: the leadership of the CPC. As the governing party of a country of immense scale, it is responsible for leading state institutions, setting the direction of development, organizing its officials, coordinating action across sectors and guiding social development.
The effectiveness of its leadership, the strength of its organizations and the willingness of its officials to take responsibility shape political unity and social cohesion, the functioning of national institutions, and economic and social development. The principle that running the country well requires first running the Party well follows from this institutional structure.
Through full and rigorous self-governance and the courage to pursue self-reform, the CPC strengthens itself. Discipline, accountability, oversight that identifies and corrects problems, and institutional improvements translate the Party's political and organizational strengths into the capacity to govern.
Connecting Party governance with national governance, and the identification of problems with deeper reform, this process links the Party's leadership system with the country's governance system. It provides important support for institutional resilience, governance capacity and society's ability to advance development.
The Party's inspection system illustrates this connection. After each round of central inspections, inspection teams analyze the problems they have identified, recommend measures addressing both immediate issues and underlying causes, and submit thematic reports to the CPC Central Committee. These reports provide an important basis for national leaders to understand systemic problems in state administration and develop institutional reforms to address them.
The value of institutional reform ultimately becomes clear in development itself. Research by the discipline inspection and supervision team stationed at the Ministry of Science and Technology helped address barriers that had prevented private enterprises from applying for National Natural Science Fund projects. Revised registration rules now allow eligible private enterprises to apply to become host institutions for these projects. Oversight identified a gap in policy, and corrective action helped improve the rules. More businesses gained opportunities to participate, bringing national research resources into closer alignment with enterprises' innovation needs and fostering new drivers of economic development.
Rigorous Party self-governance has also strengthened officials' sense of responsibility and helped put assessments of their performance on a sounder footing. Less paperwork and clearer responsibilities give local officials more time to serve businesses and respond to residents' needs, while making their performance easier to oversee and assess. Tackling pointless formalities and bureaucratism, while supporting officials who take responsibility for reform, helps turn commitment and accountability into practical action to solve problems.
Implementing major initiatives tests a country's capacity to organize work across administrative boundaries. In one case, construction of a bridge linking two provincial-level administrative regions encountered disagreements over design, conflicting approval procedures and unclear responsibilities. Then the discipline inspection and supervision bodies on both sides conducted joint oversight, prompting the transport authorities to assume responsibility together, and parallel approval processes were coordinated. Oversight clarified responsibilities, which in turn improved coordination and enabled the regional development strategy to move forward.
Effective policy implementation often requires unified authority and common rules. China is a unitary state. Local protectionism, violations of rules in investment promotion, and policies skewed toward particular interests can undermine the unity and fairness of the national market. Oversight reaching down to the grassroots, together with accountability, helps ensure that central decisions are implemented and curbs the misuse of local power.
In building a unified national market, oversight has helped correct the creation of market barriers and the granting of improper preferential treatment to particular businesses. This supports local initiative while upholding common national rules, enabling businesses to compete fairly across administrative boundaries. Central authority helps sustain the implementation of long-term strategies across regions, departments and policy cycles.
The effects of rigorous Party self-governance are also evident in improvements to the business environment and relations between government and business. An oversight initiative in Liaoning Province in northeast China helped secure more than 3 billion yuan ($448 million) of contractual payments owed by government agencies, state-owned enterprises and public institutions, and the fulfillment of over 700 unresolved government commitments, according to figures released in June 2023.
Each payment and honored commitment eased immediate business pressures and reduced reliance on personal connections in commercial activity. Government credibility encourages wider respect for commitments, creating better conditions for businesses to operate by the rules and grow through their own efforts. This helps build a supportive environment for long-term investment and sustained innovation.
Rigorous Party self-governance and public participation in oversight reinforce each other, providing a broad social foundation for better governance. Between the 19th CPC National Congress in 2017 and the 20th in 2022, Party inspection bodies at different levels received over 4 million submissions from the public reporting problems, while central inspection teams held 58,000 interviews with officials and members of the public. These channels enabled them to hear people's concerns extensively.
Several provinces have explored arrangements in which residents identify problems, responsible departments take corrective action, discipline inspection and supervision bodies monitor implementation, and the public assesses the results.
Full and rigorous Party self-governance is both a strategic policy of the CPC and an undertaking under its leadership with implications for the country as a whole. As China faces external challenges and profound changes in its development, it connects oversight, reform and implementation, ensuring that the governing party's political responsibilities are fulfilled in practice and that a people-centered approach runs through national governance. This practice has profound significance for political reform and provides sustained impetus for China's economic transformation and higher-quality development.
(Source: CGTN)

How Iran is using espionage threats to crack down on dissent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:03:08 UTC
23:03:08 KST

Espionage threats blur lines between security and dissent in Iran
Iran is using the threat of spy networks to detain and execute political opponents, analysts say.
While two wars on Iran by the United States and Israel have exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security institutions, Iran is using the threat to crack down on dissent, analysts have said.
Saeid Golkar, an associate professor in political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, said the genuine espionage threats faced by Iran were illustrated by the killing of high-level figures, including former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the latest assault by Israel and the US on February 28.
“At the same time, the regime has historically used real or, most of the time, perceived security threats to justify political repression and expand its coercive apparatus,” Golkar told Al Jazeera.
“The current crackdown appears to reflect both legitimate counterintelligence concerns and the regime’s broader efforts to suppress dissent and intimidate society.”
Spy threat
Former Israeli spy chief David Barnea recently said that in the weeks before Israel launched its 12-day war on Iran in June 2025, he had approved the entry into the country of dozens of agents with clear intelligence or sabotage assignments.
“I can’t say that they are here with us. But they are there in Tehran, living their lives,” he told a conference in Israel on October 22.
According to Barnea, who was the director of Mossad for five years until June 2026, Israeli intelligence tried to maximise the number of Iranian citizens arrested by local authorities in order to shield its genuine agents inside Iran.
Just hours after launching the war and killing senior commanders and nuclear scientists, they deliberately released footage of agents inside Iran with a Mossad logo, leading to the arrests of thousands of people with no links to the Israeli intelligence service.
Barnea claimed the strategy worked, and almost all of their assets remained unidentified. Eight months into a second war launched by Israel and the US against Iran, with the stated aim of overthrowing the Islamic republic, Iran’s paranoia remains.
Iranian authorities have significantly accelerated judicial punishments for cases linked to national security since the 2025 war. That has entailed mass arrests, expedited prosecutions, lengthy imprisonment, asset confiscations and executions.
The people targeted include alleged spies but also protesters, journalists, lawyers and minorities. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have documented cases involving coerced confessions, the denial of effective defence and national security charges applied to dissenters.
“The espionage threat facing Iran is very real. The two US-Israeli wars exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security apparatus… Tehran has legitimate concerns about foreign infiltration, sabotage, and intelligence operations inside the country, especially as the threat of another military escalation remains high,” Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said.
“But there is a fundamental distinction between espionage and dissent,” she added. “Espionage involves covertly gathering sensitive intelligence or assisting foreign intelligence operations. Criticising the government, reporting on its failures, engaging with foreign media, or challenging official narratives does not, in itself, constitute espionage. The Iranian authorities have increasingly blurred this distinction, treating political opposition and independent reporting as extensions of foreign intelligence activity.”
‘Hybrid war’
Iranian authorities argue that foreign intelligence operations are aimed not only at overthrowing the government but also fragmenting the country.
Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence said in May that “enemies” were combining espionage, sabotage, hostile media, exploitation of economic crises and fuelling ethnic and sectarian tensions as part of a “hybrid war”.
Judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei has repeatedly invoked wartime conditions and domestic laws to argue for urgent security measures, and accelerated the punishment of alleged collaborators as a means of protecting the country.
Judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said earlier in October that there were active cases involving at least 1,895 people, including 94 media workers, accused of cooperation with Israel or other hostile states. Police had announced at least 21,000 arrests following the June 2025 war, while at least 50,000 people were detained in connection with the nationwide protests in January 2026. Thousands of civilians were killed in the crackdown against antigovernment protests across Iran, according to US-based rights organisation HRANA.
The authorities have referred to the nationwide protests as a “coup” orchestrated entirely by Israeli and US intelligence agencies. The Iranian government also claims that Mossad and other intelligence agents killed protesters. But an independent United Nations fact-finding mission said the authorities committed crimes against humanity during their most violent crackdown since the revolution.
Executions linked with security charges have also increased following the wars and protests. At least 19 people were hanged in espionage-related cases between June and December 2025, according to the UN.
Iran Human Rights, an Oslo-based nonprofit group, said it recorded 16 espionage defendants executed between January and September 2026, alongside 33 protesters and 13 prisoners affiliated with banned groups. The group had tracked at least 604 executions by early October.
Amnesty International reported at least 34 executions this year linked to the January nationwide protests by October 13, including five between September 30 and October 5.
‘Securitising every aspect of life’
Iranian authorities have warned the public about Mossad and other intelligence agencies running cyber-operations to expand their influence in Iran, accusing them of recruiting people through social media and online offers.
Sending images or information to networks deemed to be hostile to the Iranian government – including BBC Persian – could result in sentences of 10 to 15 years in prison and heavy fines. Combined with other offences, it could lead to potential charges of “corruption on Earth”, which carry the death penalty.
The authorities also regard the Starlink satellite internet service as a “tool of war” used for espionage, information gathering and even operating drones by “enemy” agents inside Iran. Tens of thousands of Starlink terminals have been smuggled into the country despite severe punishments for distributing and using the service. Iranian authorities have tried to confiscate or jam them.
For several days during the 12-day war, 20 days during the January protests and 88 days at the start of the current war, Iran imposed a near-total internet shutdown on 90 million Iranians. The official reasons ranged from protecting national assets against cyberattacks to disrupting hostile drones. The global internet remains severely filtered in Iran, and authorities have warned it could be disrupted again in case of military escalation.
University of Tennessee at Chattanooga’s Golkar said that by blurring the line between espionage and political opposition, authorities increasingly treat protesters, journalists and ordinary citizens as potential threats to national security.
“Ultimately, the Islamic republic increasingly treats regime security and national security as interchangeable concepts. While counterespionage is a legitimate state function, it has also become a tool to protect the ruling establishment and expand the influence of security institutions,” he said.
“In brief, and over time, the Islamic republic has transformed into a security-dominated regime that increasingly securitises nearly every aspect of political and social life, including peaceful civic activism, treating even nonviolent expressions of dissent as potential threats to regime survival”.

NATO member Turkey, which has maintained good ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, has repeatedly called on both sides to halt attacks in the Black Sea that have also struck Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned commercial vessels.
Ankara says it is waiting for responses to a proposal it conveyed to Russia and Ukraine aimed at stopping the intensifying attacks and ensuring the safe shipment of grain from the region.

“We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas,” he said, adding that another commercial vessel had been struck by three drones inside Bulgaria’s maritime jurisdiction on Wednesday.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on a Greek container ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
“We also reserve every legal right regarding attacks on Turkish-flagged or Turkish-owned vessels and follow developments very closely… The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels,” Guler added.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on ships and infrastructure facilitating Russian oil and grain exports since July, when Russia intensified its missile and drone strikes on the main Ukrainian grain export hubs of Odesa, Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi.
In a late September meeting, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskiy that attacks by Russia and Ukraine on commercial vessels in the Black Sea were inexplicable and steps must be taken to stop them.
Guler also said Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria — which operate a de-mining operation in the Black Sea — agreed it was important to also focus on protecting critical subsea infrastructure.

By Nate Raymond
BOSTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - A Rwandan-born Ohio man has been convicted of US charges that he lied during a 2019 criminal trial as part of a decades-long scheme to conceal his involvement in the African nation’s 1994 genocide.
A federal jury in Boston on Tuesday found Eric Nshimiye guilty of perjury and obstruction of justice charges stemming from testimony he gave during the earlier immigration fraud trial of a former classmate who was also accused of participating in the atrocities.
Nshimiye, 54, is scheduled to be sentenced on January 26, according to a spokesperson for US Attorney Leah Foley. His lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.
Nshimiye has lived in the United States since 1995, when he gained admission as a refugee. He became a US citizen in 2003. At the time of his arrest in 2024, he was working as an engineer for Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co while living in Uniontown, Ohio.
Prosecutors said Nshimiye falsified and concealed information about himself to hide that he participated in the massacre by the hard-line Hutu regime of an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus during three months of slaughter in his native Rwanda.
Citing witnesses, prosecutors alleged that when the violence broke out, Nshimiye was in Butare, where he had been attending university as a medical student along with his classmate Jean Leonard Teganya.
Prosecutors said both men belonged to the political party that helped perpetrate the genocide, and that Nshimiye during the violence attacked Tutsis and handed Tutsis over to be raped or killed.
Yet when called as a defense witness in Teganya’s 2019 trial, Nshimiye denied participating in the genocide or being a member of the ruling Hutu-dominated party, the National Revolutionary Movement for Development.
Teganya was convicted of perjury and visa fraud charges and was sentenced later in 2019 to more than eight years in prison.
Defense attorney Kurt Kerns told jurors in his opening statement on October 13 that the charges against Nshimiye were based on “fabricated accusations” and that he was not even in Butare when the violence began.
Kerns argued prosecutors only charged Nshimiye after he stepped up to help a friend by testifying as a character witness in Teganya’s case.
“At the time, he trusted that the American system of justice would protect him,” Kerns said. “And that trust, you’ll see in the course of that trial, was betrayed.”

Youssef Siher, a 30-year-old Italian freelance journalist and geopolitics graduate of Moroccan origin, was detained by Milan prosecutors on October 24 on charges of incitement to commit crimes, aggravated by alleged terrorist purposes.
But in a setback for prosecutors who had portrayed him as a dangerous militant, Milan judge Tiziana Landoni said the investigation appeared deeply flawed.
“There are no serious grounds for believing that (Siher) committed the offences with which he has been charged, nor is there a risk of flight,” Landoni wrote in her ruling.
Siher himself always denied any wrongdoing. Prosecutors did not immediately comment, but Meloni was swift to denounce the decision.
“I think this is an unbearable humiliation of the work of the police and investigators,” she said in a video posted on social media.
“I really don’t know how a normal state can defend decent people in the face of these decisions by certain sections of the judiciary,” she added.
In a statement signed by court president Fabio Roia, judges said Meloni’s remarks were “unacceptable”, reflecting what they described as “a poor understanding, whether real or feigned, of the legal institutions of a state governed by the rule of law”.
Italian police had identified Siher as the administrator of the Telegram group “October 17 Movement”, which was created following violent protests in Milan.
According to the detention order, Siher published what investigators described as “subversive content” and messages calling on protesters to gather on October 24 with the aim of carrying out offences against public order.

The newly defined crime carries prison terms of between four and 12 years for organisers of groups that, while taking part in public demonstrations, endanger public safety or cause damage.

====================================================================================================

A mirror trick that adds a sixth finger also changes what people think their hand can grab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:00:56 UTC
23:00:56 KST

Tricking the brain into feeling an invisible sixth finger can quickly change how people judge what their hands are physically capable of doing, according to new research published in Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. After experiencing a brief mirror-based illusion of having an extra digit beside their pinky, volunteers estimated that they could grasp wider blocks and needed larger openings to fit their hand through. The shift in opening-size judgments appeared even among participants who did not consciously feel the extra finger, suggesting that the brain may update its sense of the hand’s physical boundaries partly outside conscious awareness.
Whenever a person reaches through a narrow gap or picks up a wide glass with one hand, the brain automatically calculates how the physical dimensions of the body match up with the surrounding environment. Psychologists refer to these perceived possibilities for action as affordances. Rather than measuring spaces in inches or centimeters, people use their own bodies as a built-in ruler, and this internal gauge adapts rapidly when physical dimensions change. For instance, a 2008 study on movement decisions found that when adults wore a prosthetic that widened their hand by one centimeter, they recalibrated their judgments and selected wider openings as the smallest gap their hand could pass through.
Beyond adapting to physical prosthetics or tools, the brain can also adopt nonexistent extra body parts, known as supernumerary limbs or digits, when visual and touch signals are manipulated in unison. In a 2016 paper describing what is known as the Anne Boleyn illusion, researchers showed that sitting at a mirror and receiving synchronized strokes on both hands alongside a stroke in empty space could trick volunteers into feeling a sixth finger beside their pinky. Building on this technique, a 2025 study on extra-finger illusions indicated that people can experience this phantom sixth digit even when it is angled at biologically impossible postures up to 180 degrees away from the palm, while still feeling their real pinky in its normal spot.
Knowing that an illusory sixth finger can feel independent from the rest of the hand raised an unresolved question: does the brain treat this invisible digit as an isolated sensory quirk, or does it integrate the extra finger into the whole hand when sizing up physical actions? To test whether an illusory sixth finger alters perceived action boundaries, Denise Cadete and her colleagues designed an experiment combining the mirror-box setup with tests of hand width and grasping span. Cadete is an associate lecturer in the School of Psychological Sciences at Birkbeck, University of London, a researcher in the university’s Body Representation Lab and Vestibular×Space Neuroscience Lab, and the lead author of the 2025 posture study. The team preregistered the study’s design, hypotheses, and main analyses before collecting data.
“I first wanted to find a way of having an implicit measure for the experience of having a sixth finger, to overcome the limitations of having self-reported data,” Cadete told PsyPost. “I was interested in the illusory perception of an extra finger beyond the conscious interpretation of that phenomenon. Later, I was very intrigued by using an action perception task that would unravel whether the illusion of having an extra finger would update action representations too.”
The researchers recruited 50 healthy adults, including 32 women, with an average age of 31.4 years. All but one of the participants were right-handed, and every volunteer completed the experiment using their left hand as the target hand across both an illusion condition and a control condition in a counterbalanced order. During each session, participants sat at a table with an upright mirror aligned down the center of their body, placing their left hand out of sight behind the mirror and their right hand in front of it. Looking into the glass created the visual impression that the reflection of their right hand was actually their hidden left hand.
To induce the illusion, a researcher stroked the matching fingers of both hands at the exact same time, brushing back and forth twice from the thumbs to the little fingers. After touching the inner side of the hidden left pinky alongside the top of the visible right pinky, the researcher delivered 20 synchronized strokes to the outer edge of the hidden left pinky while simultaneously stroking the empty table space just outside the reflected right pinky. Because participants saw the stroke land on empty space at the moment they felt touch on the side of their hidden hand, many experienced the sensation of a sixth finger. In the control condition, the researcher followed the same one-minute routine, except the final 20 strokes were applied directly onto both pinky fingers rather than empty air.
Immediately after the one-minute stimulation, the researcher covered the participant’s hands with a box to block visual inspection, and participants kept their hands still so that muscle and joint feedback, known as proprioception, would not disrupt the illusion. Across eight trials per condition, participants first judged aperture passing by watching a wooden frame fitted with black plastic triangles that opened and closed like a camera shutter (from 2.7 to 18 centimeters), calling out when the opening matched the smallest gap their closed left hand could pass through without touching the edges.
Across another eight trials per condition, they judged grasping ability by looking at 16 square foam-board blocks (ranging from 4 to 25 centimeters wide in 1.4-centimeter steps) and stating whether they could stretch their left thumb and fingers across opposite edges to hold each block. Brief top-up strokes were delivered after every two estimates, and at the end of each block, participants rated their conscious sensations on a 0-to-10 scale. At the end of the session, participants physically placed their left hand inside the shutter and grasped the foam blocks so the researchers could calculate an accuracy ratio dividing each person’s estimated size by their actual physical limit, where 1.00 is an exact match, above 1.00 is an overestimation, and below 1.00 is an underestimation.
Questionnaire ratings confirmed that the mirror procedure worked as intended: on the 0-to-10 scale, average scores for feeling six fingers rose from 1.13 in the control condition to 4.36 in the illusion condition. Participants also gave higher ratings during the illusion for feeling two little fingers (3.96 versus 1.24), touch in an unusual place (4.92 versus 1.86), touch off the body (3.55 versus 0.93), and a larger little finger (3.06 versus 1.80). By contrast, a control prompt about feeling an entire extra hand showed no statistically significant difference between the illusion (1.35) and control (1.10) conditions. Ratings across the full group averaged below the scale’s midpoint, in part because 22 of the 50 participants reported little or no sixth finger.
“The illusion is not imaginary, is not a weak sensation or a delusion; it is a vivid sensation of having a sixth finger, created by a trick using visual-tactile stimulation that will map a real touch onto empty space next to the hand,” Cadete explained.
In the action-judgment tasks, experiencing the sixth-finger illusion shifted how participants sized up both their hand width and their grip reach. In the aperture task, the average ratio of estimated-to-actual opening size increased from 0.92 in the control condition to 0.97 after the sixth-finger stimulation, reducing the proportion of participants who underestimated their needed space from 72 percent (36 of 50 people) in the control session to 58 percent (29 of 50 people) during the illusion.
Similarly, though more modestly, in the grasping task, the average ratio of estimated-to-actual grasp width rose from 0.98 in the control condition to 1.01 in the illusion condition, indicating that participants believed they could span wider blocks after the illusion. Participants who showed a larger increase between the control and illusion sessions on the aperture task also tended to show a larger increase on the grasping task.
“These findings point to a flexibility of the mind, not only in perceiving extra body parts that they never had, but also in integrating them immediately into their action perception,” Cadete said. “People change the perception of the action abilities of their hand when experiencing an invisible and illusory sixth finger, as if their hand had indeed six fingers to move and grasp objects.”
Unexpectedly, statistical analyses showed no significant correlation between how strongly participants reported feeling a sixth finger on the questionnaire and how much they adjusted their aperture or grasping estimates. In an exploratory analysis that was not preregistered, the researchers split the sample into 28 participants who consciously felt a sixth finger (scoring between 4 and 10) and 22 participants who did not (scoring between 0 and 2), finding that both subgroups still selected wider openings in the aperture task after the sixth-finger stimulation.
The average aperture ratio climbed from 0.90 to 0.97 among those who consciously felt the extra digit and rose from 0.95 to 0.98 among those who did not, though the shift was roughly twice as large for those who felt the illusion (an average change of 0.07 versus 0.03). In the grasping task, the within-group shifts from 0.97 to 1.00 among those who felt the finger and from 1.00 to 1.01 among those who did not were not statistically significant, possibly because splitting the sample into smaller subgroups reduced statistical power.
The aperture result among participants who did not feel the extra finger surprised Cadete. “This shows that the illusion is updating the perception of action abilities of the hand, regardless of its conscious experience of it,” she noted.
The authors interpret this disconnect between conscious reports and spatial judgments as a sign that the illusion works on two partly distinct levels. In their view, synchronized touch and visual cues beside the hand may update the body schema, the brain’s unconscious working map of body size and posture used to plan actions, even when a person does not consciously experience a sixth finger.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Participants estimated their physical limits by looking at the apparatus and imagining the actions while their hands stayed motionless under a cover, rather than physically reaching out during the illusion. Because imagining a movement and physically executing it rely on partly separate neural pathways, actually moving the hand might produce different results than imagined estimates. In addition, whereas people in prior aperture studies typically overestimated the space their hidden hand needed, participants here underestimated their required opening in both conditions (ratios below 1.00), which the authors suggest may stem from participants watching their hand in the mirror during the stroking routine.
Because spatial judgments shifted even among volunteers who reported little or no sensation of an extra digit, the changes in action perception may reflect a broader effect of mapping touch onto nearby empty space rather than the specific mental image of a sixth finger. Future work will need to examine how this sensory remapping affects real-time physical movement and whether the findings generalize beyond healthy adults in laboratory settings. Even so, the results suggest that passive touch and vision alone can begin reshaping perceived hand capabilities in just 60 seconds, without requiring active movement or mechanical control.
“These findings can help design supernumerary robotics and prosthetics, in a way that updates their body perception but also their action perception,” Cadete added. “At the same time, this shows the flexibility of our mind in the way our bodies are perceived, allowing for additions and including them into a new and extended representation of the acting body.”
“I wish to understand the mechanisms for representing extra body parts and why they seem to have different constraints from real body parts,” she continued. “Ultimately, I want to explore why would humans have this ability, and extend this research into supernumerary robotics, so that they can be better integrated into one’s body representation, overcoming motor limitations due to injury or neurological disorders.”
The study, “Beyond Five: How the Experience of a Supernumerary Sixth Finger Alters Action Perception,” was authored by Denise Cadete, Harriet Morris, Megan Rose Readman, Sally A. Linkenauger, Elisa R. Ferrè, and Matthew R. Longo.

Tale of Brazil's Bolsonaros: Father jailed, mother in senate, sons in congress, third flees to US

The patriarch is under house arrest, his wife is a senator, two sons are in Congress, and a third, who just lost the presidential race to Lula da Silva, started a self-imposed exile in the US.
As Brazil's preeminent new political dynasty, the Bolsonaros are serving up the kind of drama, infighting and ambition.
Many had written off Bolsonarism when former president Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of mounting a failed coup bid after he lost a 2022 election bid to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
But, family fortunes surged again as Flavio Bolsonaro briefly appeared a shoo-in to become president of Brazil, and four other family members were elected to Congress.
But then Flavio Bolsonaro lost in the second round and amid accusations of corruption and money laundering fled into self-imposed exile in the United States.
The patriarch and the coup
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, won a devoted following for his combative style and defense of "God, Homeland, and Family", while drawing criticism for comments demeaning women and others.
The former army officer is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting ways to stop Lula from taking power in January 2023.
Flavio had vowed to free his father if he won, leaving the patriarch's future uncertain.
Flavio, the 'moderate' who fled
The eldest of Jair's five children, the 45-year-old fired up his father's conservative base and less ideological voters, pitching himself as more moderate than his father.
He won a first-round vote and was seen as the favorite ahead of the runoff, before being trounced by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Flavio Bolsonaro is being investigated in several cases, including for alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the financing of a biopic, "Dark Horse," about his father, bankrolled by Daniel Vorcaro.
Flavio at first denied having contact with Vorcaro, but was forced to backtrack after audio leaked of him imploring the banker to make overdue payments.
He arrived in Florida on Wednesday after avoiding Brazilian authorities who demanded his passports.
Michelle, the step-mother
Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, is around the same age as three of her stepsons.
A devout evangelical Christian and devoted wife, she has become a political powerhouse in her own right, and was elected senator representing the capital Brasilia.
During the campaign she aired a public feud with Flavio, accusing him of mistreating her.
In February, after another stepson, Eduardo Bolsonaro accused her of not doing enough to support Flavio's campaign, she shared a picture of fried bananas she was making for her husband.
This was perceived as a dig against Eduardo.
Eduardo then shared a supporter's post saying she should keep frying bananas while he and Flavio worked to "rescue the country."
Eduardo: guns and Trump
Eduardo, 42, moved to the United States in March 2025 where he has met with President Donald Trump and addressed conservative conferences in his push for US pressure on Brasilia.
He lost his lawmaker seat due to his long absence and was sentenced to four years and two months in prison in absentia in June, for his lobbying for US sanctions and tariffs against Brazil.
Seen as the most radical of the Bolsonaro sons, he has shared videos of rifles and guns he has bought, arguing for relaxed gun laws in Brazil.
Carlos, the strategist
Jair's second-eldest son Carlos, 43, entered into politics at age 17 after his father pushed him to run against his mother Rogeria on the Rio de Janeiro city council, a year after his parents divorced.
He won the seat, in an episode he described as "traumatic" and later became his father's social media strategist.
This year he was elected senator for the southern city of Santa Catarina.
His youngest brother, Jair Renan, 28, was elected a lawmaker for the same city.
Jair's brother, 62-year-old Renato Bolsonaro, a retired military officer was elected as a deputy for Sao Paulo state.

Germany is not seeking to decouple from China, but must defend its economic interests, visiting German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in Beijing on Thursday, echoing the line taken by Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his tour of neighbouring countries.
Speaking at Peking University, Steinmeier insisted that Europe’s goal was not to sever ties with the world’s second-largest economy, but to reset the relationship on a fairer footing.
“Our goal as Europeans is clear. We do not want decoupling from China,” he told students and academic staff.

Schneider Electric production base in China starts operation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:29 CST
22:58:29 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows a scene during the completion and commissioning ceremony for the first phase of the Schneider Electric Xiamen Xiang'an Industrial Park in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Xinhua)
XIAMEN, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- French energy technology firm Schneider Electric's largest manufacturing facility for medium-voltage equipment worldwide began operations on Wednesday in Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province.
The first phase of the Schneider Electric Xiamen Xiang'an Industrial Park features a total construction area of about 110,000 square meters, integrating an R&D and technology center, a smart manufacturing hub, and a service training center.
On the same day, construction of the second phase of the project started in Xiamen.
Xu Shaofeng, senior vice-president of Schneider Electric and head of medium voltage and services business in China, said that building on the upgraded manufacturing and operational models achieved in Phase I, Phase II will further expand into key processes and core manufacturing capabilities.
This will consolidate the core manufacturing footprint, focusing on the production of vacuum interrupters, medium-voltage circuit breakers and other products, with increased investment in manufacturing equipment for critical components, he said.
"Supported by this integrated hub for R&D innovation, advanced manufacturing and ecosystem collaboration, we will further capitalize on China's combined strengths in innovation, manufacturing, supply chains and talent," said Yin Zheng, executive vice president of Schneider Electric for China & East Asia operations.
With over two decades of development in Xiamen, the company will further foster an open, win-win industrial ecosystem, Yin added.
China has grown into the second-largest global market for Schneider Electric since it entered China in 1987. The country is also a key supply chain base for the company and one of its four major R&D hubs.
Xiamen occupies an important position in Schneider Electric's industrial layout in China. Since establishing its local presence in 2005, the company has built a comprehensive business portfolio in this coastal city. ■
This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows a view of the first phase of the Schneider Electric Xiamen Xiang'an Industrial Park in Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Xinhua)

Thai central bank holds policy rate at 1 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:27 CST
22:58:27 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged for a fourth consecutive meeting on Wednesday as policymakers maintain an accommodative stance and targeted financial measures to support an uneven economic recovery.
The Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee voted unanimously, with one member absent, to hold the one-day repurchase rate steady at 1 percent, marking its longest pause since the current easing cycle began in October 2024.
"The committee views that the current policy rate is appropriate to support economic recovery," the central bank said in a statement, adding that it would keep watching the inflation outlook and the effects of low interest rates on long-term macro-financial stability.
The bank now expects the Thai economy to grow 2.4 percent this year and 2.1 percent in 2027, up from June forecasts of 2.3 percent and 1.8 percent, citing stronger-than-expected merchandise exports and private investment tied to the global tech and artificial intelligence cycle.
However, growth remains below potential, and the gains are concentrated among businesses and workers in related manufacturing and service industries with limited spillovers to the broader economy, said Don Nakornthab, secretary of the monetary policy committee.
He said private consumption growth was cut to 2.3 percent for this year from 2.6 percent, as high household debt, a fragile labor market, and weak purchasing power weigh on spending.
The central bank also expects foreign tourist arrivals to slip to 32 million this year from 33 million in 2025, partly due to higher oil prices.
Headline inflation is forecast to average 2.1 percent in 2026, down from the 2.8 percent projected in June, and 1.3 percent in 2027, within the bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range.
Inflation is projected to rise through the rest of this year and into early 2027, driven by energy prices and El Nino, before easing due to base effects and weak domestic demand, the bank said. ■

This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows the site of high-speed train collision in Toledo province, Spain. At least 64 were killed in a train accident that occurred on Wednesday in the Spanish province of Toledo, south of Madrid, local authorities confirmed. (Xinhua/Cheng Min)
MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- At least 64 were killed in a train accident that occurred on Wednesday in the Spanish province of Toledo, south of Madrid, local authorities confirmed.
Emergency services continue to search for bodies of the victims with the help of trained dogs, and "even more" victims could still be found among the passengers of the two trains involved in the accident, said Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha which includes the province of Toledo.
According to Spanish newspaper El Pais, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is traveling to the site of the train accident in the province of Toledo to learn firsthand the details of what occurred and the unfolding situation. ■

In pics: agricultural science and technology industrial park in Jinhua City, China's Zhejiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:10 CST
22:58:10 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 27, 2026 shows a night view of a smart greenhouse at an agricultural science and technology industrial park in Jindong District of Jinhua City, east China's Zhejiang Province. The agricultural science and technology industrial park was established in September 2023 as a designated benchmark project for modern agriculture in Jindong District of Jinhua City.
The park covers an area of 198.2 mu (about 13.2 hectares), including modern agricultural smart greenhouses, outdoor standardized planting areas, as well as supporting facilities such as water sources and parking lots. It aims to create an intelligent agricultural comprehensive industrial park integrating seedling research and development, ecological planting, deep processing, brand sales, tourism, and agricultural technology demonstration.
The park has introduced specialty fruit and vegetable varieties of pineapples, dragon fruits, and blueberries to build a demonstration model for high-end tropical fruit and vegetable planting. It has revitalized the idle land resources in the area, optimized the regional agricultural industrial structure. (Xinhua/Xu Yu)

Feature: South Sudanese farmers turn floodwater into rice harvests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:58:06 CST
22:58:06 KST

JUBA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- For years, seasonal flooding has threatened the livelihoods of farmers in South Sudan's Northern Bahr el Ghazal, destroying sorghum crops and undermining household food supplies.
But in Aweil, the capital of Northern Bahr el Ghazal, some farmers are learning to capitalize on the waterlogged land by cultivating rice.
Santino Akech, a 45-year-old farmer, said rice cultivation had offered his community an alternative to traditional crops that struggle to survive in flooded lowlands.
"When flooding came, it affected sorghum, but the rice succeeded," Akech said during a recent interview in Aweil.
Haileselassie Berhanu, head of program at the World Food Program (WFP) Aweil Field Office, said, "We have tried to consider the flood as a potential opportunity, not as a threat," explaining that the WFP and local communities began exploring rice cultivation in waterlogged areas several years ago.
This year, more than 2,100 households were participating in rice cultivation, with approximately 1,000 hectares under cultivation across the wider initiative, according to Berhanu.
Farmers previously cultivated individually but had limited capacity to expand production, said Akech. Through group farming, they pooled resources, expanded their cultivated land and received training in rice-growing techniques from a local partner. In 2025, Akech said that farmers harvested 42 bags of rice weighing 90 kg each from about 1.68 hectares of land.
However, he also identified weeding and harvesting as major challenges, noting that rice cultivation was still a relatively new practice for many community members. Farmers need machinery to prepare waterlogged land, training in improved cultivation methods and access to rice varieties suited to local conditions as well.
In a recent field trip to Aweil, Mutinta Chimuka, WFP country representative for South Sudan, said helping communities produce their own food was an important part of the agency's work to improve food security, alongside the distribution of food assistance.
She described the crop observed as promising, saying the location had retained water despite a dry spell that had affected agricultural production elsewhere.
The crop was flowering and expected to be ready for harvesting soon, Chimuka said.
Chimuka urged closer cooperation with state and national authorities to identify the most suitable locations for rice cultivation and varieties that could perform well under local conditions.
Chinese Ambassador to South Sudan Ma Qiang, who also joined the field visit, said the rice initiative demonstrated the potential to leverage natural conditions, strengthen agricultural production and improve resilience to climate-related shocks.
Ma said that China's experience and agricultural technologies could provide opportunities for further cooperation with South Sudan, including through engagement with national and local governments and other partners.
China has previously donated agricultural machinery to local communities, he added.
Martha Abuk, a 40-year-old farmer who also cultivates rice in Aweil, said that farming and participation in group savings activities had helped her household meet some of its needs, including school fees for the children.
As the WFP and its partners explore ways to expand rice cultivation, the experiences of farmers in Aweil illustrate both the opportunities and the constraints involved in adapting agriculture to climate-related challenges.
Sustaining that progress, however, will depend on farmers' access to suitable equipment, technical knowledge and resources to increase production. ■

Hong Kong lawmaker urges more checks as illegal parking fines top HK$70m a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:58:03 UTC
22:58:03 KST

Hong Kong lawmaker urges more checks as illegal parking fines top HK$70m a year
Lawmaker Mark Chong urges authorities to step up inspections and make use of AI-powered sensors to track repeat illegal parking offenders
Traffic police have issued more than 220,000 tickets for parking-related offences in each of the past three years, raking in at least HK$70 million (US$8.92 million) a year for Hong Kong’s coffers, but a lawmaker said inspections could be enhanced to target more offenders.
In a written reply to the Legislative Council on Wednesday, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said police issued 259,589, 242,550 and 225,489 fixed penalty tickets in 2023, 2024 and 2025 respectively to offenders who breached metered parking regulations.
As fixed penalty tickets carried a fine of HK$320 before January this year, they generated at least HK$70 million per year over the past three years.

Sri Lanka plans 6.01 bln USD capital spending in 2027 to boost investment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:57:51 CST
22:57:51 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka plans to allocate around 2 trillion Sri Lankan rupees (about 6.01 billion U.S. dollars) for capital expenditure in 2027, prioritizing infrastructure and investment-related projects, Deputy Minister of Finance and Planning Anil Jayantha Fernando said on Tuesday.
Fernando said the allocation would focus on roads, railways, rural connectivity, logistics and transport facilities, alongside selected social expenditure.
He said the government's next priority was to move towards economic transformation by strengthening domestic and foreign investment and further developing the capital market.
Fernando said the Finance Ministry had reviewed 12 capital market development proposals submitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission and agreed on most of them, with several expected to be included in the 2027 Budget, due to be presented on Nov. 12.
He also said the government planned to introduce new legislation to restructure state-owned enterprises and establish a common legal framework for commercially operating entities.
The proposed law would allow selected state enterprises to be incorporated as companies with greater autonomy to respond to market conditions, he said. ■

Uganda's Mbale, China's Guiyang agree to establish friendly cooperation ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:57:48 CST
22:57:48 KST

KAMPALA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Mbale City in eastern Uganda and Guiyang City in southwest China have signed a letter of intent to establish friendly exchange and cooperation relations, laying the groundwork for a future sister-city partnership, Uganda's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Wednesday.
The agreement, signed on Monday in Guiyang by Mbale City Mayor Joyce Matuka Kidulu and Wang Hong, mayor of Guiyang, outlines five priority areas for cooperation: smart city development and digital governance, industrial development and investment, agriculture and value addition, tourism and cultural exchange, and environmental sustainability, according to a ministry statement issued in Kampala.
The two cities agreed to establish a joint working group within two months and arrange a technical visit to Mbale to explore investment opportunities in industrial development, coffee processing and tourism, the statement said.
The proposed partnership aims to link Mbale's strengths in Arabica coffee production with Guiyang's expanding coffee industry and expertise in digital technology and green development.
Located near Mount Elgon in eastern Uganda, Mbale is a major coffee-producing area and an important industrial hub. Guiyang, the capital of China's Guizhou Province, has developed a strong presence in big data and digital industries.
The signing took place during a working visit to Guiyang by a Ugandan delegation, which also participated in a coffee trade promotion and business-matching session with the Guiyang Coffee Industry Association.
Uganda's coffee exports to China increased by 224 percent in the 2025/2026 financial year, the statement said, pointing to opportunities to expand market access and promote value addition through the cooperation framework. ■
