Why NASA's Artemis III Mission Will Be One of its Most Complex Flights Ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:14:52 UTC
22:14:52 KST

The last time the folks at NASA tested a crewed lunar lander in low-Earth orbit, here’s how they did it. First, a Saturn 5 rocket lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida carrying three astronauts, an Apollo spacecraft, and a lunar module. Then they got to orbit and the astronauts flew both ships. Then they came home. That straightforward mission was accomplished 57 years ago, during the flight of Apollo 9.
The next time NASA attempts something of the kind—during the planned flight of Artemis III in the summer of 2027—things will be a lot more complicated. First an uncrewed Blue Origin New Glenn rocket will launch from KSC carrying the company’s Blue Moon lander into orbit. Then NASA will launch its prosaically named Space Launch System (SLS) moon rocket, carrying the four Artemis III astronauts aboard an Orion spacecraft. Then the crew will rendezvous with the Blue Moon, dock with it and enter it, checking out its systems before returning to the Orion. Then SpaceX will launch a Starship rocket carrying its own Starship lander, which will also be uncrewed. The astronauts will rendezvous and dock with that ship too, but not enter it since it will not yet be equipped with a life support system. Then they will separate and the crew will spend a few more days running tests on the Orion. All of that work will take up to 17 days from first liftoff to splashdown. And only if everything goes just right with that mission can NASA achieve its goal of landing astronauts on the lunar surface during the 2028 flight of Artemis IV—and in the process, win a new space race with China.
On Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman—along with Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya and Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons—conducted a marathon two-hour press conference at KSC, detailing plans for Artemis III and IV, conceding that the hurdles are considerable, but insisting the goals are within reach. The current NASA, with its tight funding and long timelines, may not be the old NASA that used its generous budgets and garage full of rockets to pop off nine crewed Apollo lunar missions just from 1968 to 1972, but it will be no less successful.
“In that remarkably short span of time, the ambitions of generations once confined to the pages of science fiction became humanity's greatest achievement, and for the first time in billions of years, life born on Earth would set foot on another world,” said Isaacman. “Now, in this incredibly demanding and dangerous business of putting astronauts [back] on the moon, NASA must own the near impossible…That is how we give Artemis IV the greatest possible chance of safely and successfully returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.”
The extreme complexity of Artemis III is owing in part to a pair of decisions NASA made in 2021 and 2023 and in part to the simple limits of known rocket technology. If the engineering physics were perfect—and engineering physics are never perfect—a lunar crew could use just one spacecraft to get to the moon, land, blast back off, and return home. But a spacecraft that could do all of those jobs and remain robust enough to reenter the Earth’s atmosphere would simply be too heavy for a lunar landing and subsequent liftoff. Instead, as in the Apollo days, the job will be divided between two ships—one lightweight one to perform the landing and liftoff and one orbiting mothership to bring the crew home when the lunar exploration is done. During Apollo, the space agency selected Grumman Aircraft Engineering to build its squat, four-legged 23-ft. tall, lunar module (LM). It was a simple ship with a low center of gravity, ensuring a stable foothold on the lunar surface. Grumman inked the contract in 1962 and delivered the goods in time for Apollo 9 and the missions that followed. In 2021, NASA similarly awarded a contract for a crewed lunar spacecraft—this time to SpaceX and its Starship lander. The decision was a headscratcher.
Starship is a silo-like cylinder with a tapered nose cone, measuring 165 ft. tall, calling to mind less an actual spacecraft than the 1953 illustrated book about Tintin’s adventures on the moon. Apollo astronauts used a nine-rung ladder to get down to the lunar surface. Artemis astronauts aboard Starship will use an elevator. Critics and competitors pounced on the plan—not least because of the risk that the giant machine could tip over on the moon—and in 2023, NASA issued a second contract, this time to Blue Origin, which promised to build a lander more in keeping with the low-slung Apollo lunar module. Both companies have continued to produce their landers and both will get a shot to fly on the historic Artemis IV mission—with the winner to be determined by the performance of the ships during Artemis III.
But neither company has had an easy go of things. SpaceX has launched 14 Starships since 2023, only achieving Earth orbit for the first time in September 2026. Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, meanwhile, launched three times from January 2025 to April 2026, before a massive explosion on the launch pad during a test of its first stage engines occurred in May 2026. The disaster marked a major setback for Blue Origin, not least because the pad infrastructure itself was partially destroyed in the blast. The company has been working feverishly since to rebound, and at the Oct. 23 press conference, the NASA brass praised its efforts.
“Blue Origin's New Glenn team has amazed the world with their progress for return to flight after the incident in May,” said Parsons. “We're working closely with them. We have over 100 NASA team [members] engaged throughout return to flight…and I have seen Blue Origin mobilize an absolute army working around the clock.”
Assuming the company can maintain that pace, it stands a good chance of being the winner in the Artemis III sweepstakes. That’s partly because its rival, SpaceX, will not fly a full-up version of its Starship lander during the mission, but rather what amounts to a boilerplate ship equipped with a docking port that will test only whether the Orion and the Starship can meet and link up in orbit. Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander won’t be a fully operational vehicle either, but it will have a functioning crew compartment that will allow the Artemis III astronauts to enter and run tests.
“They're going to open up the hatch. They're going to enter the lander. They're going to evaluate the environmental controls, the life support systems,” says Parsons. “We'll confirm that the spacecraft can maintain the right atmospheric pressure, and we're also going to test emergency scenarios, dual vehicle control, and we're going to put our Mission Control teams through their paces."
For all of the confidence expressed at the press conference, no one at NASA pretends that the Artemis III mission doesn’t have a lot of moving parts and a lot of things that could go badly wrong before the space agency can tee up the 2028 Artemis IV landing. And even if the mission does completely succeed, NASA will still require both competing spacecraft to execute an uncrewed lunar landing and liftoff to prove their mettle further. Only then will the landers be certified to carry crew.
Whether the two companies can perfect the engineering and fly the uncrewed missions in the maximum 18 months that will elapse between the launch of Artemis III and the flight of Artemis IV at the end of 2028 is uncertain. Isaacman, for one, expresses confidence that the target date can be met without slipping into 2029 or later. But he acknowledges that NASA’s years of uncertainty since the Apollo program—with priorities shifting from Skylab to the shuttle to the International Space Station, and with start-stop programs to return to the moon that burned through money but never got anywhere—have set the agency back, especially as it concerns the ongoing competition with China.
“Here we are today, very much in a new space race, and despite decades of accumulated knowledge and extraordinary advancements in technology, this race will be much closer than it ever needed to be,” he says. “That brings us to the moment we find ourselves in today, because the appetite for tolerating and defending the status quo has reached its conclusion. We are here for the mission, and to deliver the outcomes the world expects of the most accomplished space agency in history.”

I've Been Disabled Since I Was a Child. Co-Writing Being Heumann Still Taught Me So Much
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:13:09 UTC
22:13:09 KST

The night before an airline lost my wheelchair was among the most dazzling of my life. I sat at a long table in the back of an L.A. movie theater as talented writers, actors, and creatives read aloud the draft of a movie script I’d co-written with Oscar-winning filmmaker Siân Heder. I felt the thrill of people laughing at just the right moments. I clocked cheeks shiny with tears. But more than anything, I marveled over the possibility that this movie might actually get made. When I was a newly paralyzed kid in the ’90s, with freshly fitted leg braces, I watched Forrest Gump overcome his disability by running so hard his own braces literally fell off. Months after I started college, I watched a recently disabled boxer ask her coach to end her life in Million Dollar Baby. In my formative years, the stories of disability I saw were scarce, unrecognizable, and often harmful.
Our script, Being Heumann, tells the real-life David and Goliath story of a standoff between the U.S. government and a group of scrappy disabled protesters that changed the course of American history. The fight revolved around Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a tiny bit of legislation that reframed how we think about disability in our communities. Instead of positioning its embodiment as a personal tragedy that inevitably excludes people from society, the language of 504 suggested that our exclusion had been largely created and should be corrected. The law passed in 1973, but after years without any moves to implement it, Judy Heumann led over 100 disabled people and nondisabled allies in a sit-in at the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare in San Francisco. They lived in those halls for almost a month as the government tried to push them out, cutting off their water supply and phone lines. When it became clear that they weren’t going to buckle, the government relented, agreeing to implement 504. The very group that had been deemed expendable took on the most powerful and won. It still holds the place as the longest peaceful occupation of a federal building in U.S. history.
Section 504 paved the way for the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), the first civil rights law for disabled people in the world. Thanks in large part to disabled WW II vet and my Kansas Senator, Bob Dole, it passed in 1990 with nearly unanimous bipartisan support and was signed into law by President George H.W. Bush when I was 4 years old. Even if they’re not consistently or completely fulfilled, these laws changed our world in their insistence that physical and mental impairment alone should not and would not preclude us from participating in our communities—going to school; voting; receiving care in a hospital; being considered for a job for which we’re qualified; and accessing our libraries, post offices, public transit, housing, and more. In other words, Section 504 and the ADA protect every American citizen; if there is one thread that binds us together, it is that every single one of us will acquire a disability if we live long enough. Still, I, like most Americans, never heard a whisper of this history growing up.
It wasn’t until I worked on this script that my perspective considerably expanded. It was like putting on a pair of night-vision goggles: the curb cuts, accessible bathroom stalls, and ramps radiated a new story. Someone had fought for me to be here. It didn’t wipe out the inaccessibility and stigma that still exist in my life, but it enriched my understanding of the bigger story I was living inside.
When I first joined the Being Heumann project, I was nervous about earning Judy’s trust. I remember sitting in my car, phone pressed against my sweaty ear, as she asked me questions about my life. “So you went to school with your siblings?” My attendance at the school down the street from my house was never a question, while Judy’s mother battled for years to get her daughter a spot in even a basement classroom. “And what was it like for you applying for teaching positions?” My wheelchair was never mentioned in job interviews, while Judy was denied a teaching license because her wheelchair was deemed a fire hazard. Recapping my life to The Judy Heumann, I saw more clearly than ever before how she and other activists had shaped it. Even as I’d sat on the edges of inaccessible playgrounds or been pushed out of unsustainable work cultures, the full life I live today would not exist if someone hadn’t fought hard for my inclusion before I was born. I wanted Judy to know that my outrage over the exclusion disabled people still face didn’t diminish my appreciation for the gifts she had granted us. I think I convinced her I could hold both stories as true.
While it didn’t make the final cut, one of the scenes performed at our table read told the story of the time Judy was forcibly removed from a plane when the airline insisted she needed a care attendant or a note from a doctor to fly. Someone expressed appreciation that airlines are now more accommodating to wheelchair travelers. Siân looked at me knowingly. “Well, they’re still not great,” she said.
And so when I flew home from the reading, I can’t say I was surprised to find upon landing that my wheelchair, which cost more than my car and is fully customized to prevent pain and pressure sores, was missing. In its absence, I was placed in an airport wheelchair—although, given that it was not self-propelling, it feels more apt to call it a cart. Because airplanes don’t have accessible bathrooms, I hadn’t peed in eight hours, but without wheels that I could push myself, I couldn’t get to a toilet without help. I almost always fly alone, but out of sheer luck, my husband had accompanied me on this trip. We watched the people from the last flights pour out the doors until the floor was empty. Over an hour later, the airline informed us they had no idea where the wheelchair was. I felt like I was being sent home with body parts missing.
The next day, as I sat at my kitchen table, calling the same customer-service numbers again and again, a -familiar feeling thumped in my chest. While we worked on the script, I wanted to capture the frantic helplessness that can come when your basic rights are not in your control. You can hold up a protest sign, put your body on the line, hurl your voice to the sky, write yet another email to legislators, and still, it often feels like you are entirely at the mercy of a few people at the top who aren’t even listening.
Two days later, my husband found the frame of my wheelchair dropped off on our doorstep, scratches across the front, two parts dangling. They never found the wheels. A replacement pair arrived three weeks later.
While I recounted the ordeal to Siân, we marveled at the irony. Here we were, telling the story of a woman who took on the airlines for disabled passengers to have equal access to travel, and 50 years later disabled travelers still take the very real risk of our lives being upended every time we fly. We have come so far. We have so far to go. I saw the dichotomy everywhere. It was my generation’s job, I thought, to build on the progress Judy’s had fought for. What I didn’t realize at the time, however, is that we wouldn’t just be advancing it—we’d be defending it as well.
Almost a year to the date of that hopeful, disastrous flight home, I found out that Apple Studios had greenlighted the making of Being Heumann. I texted Siân gleeful curse words in disbelief. In the coming months, I saw a big film studio prioritize authentic disability casting for more roles than I could count on my hands and ask good questions about how to make the filming process accessible for them. I think I stopped breathing while I watched Ruth Madeley channel Judy’s chutzpah on her audition tape. Every time I thought of my younger self getting the chance to watch this story with these characters, my eyes welled. There is no way to quantify what it would have meant to see bodies like mine do something as ordinary as get dressed, go to work, or receive care, let alone hook up, party, fight, cry and win together. To see the world reflected back to me as I experienced it—pushed out by stairs and curbs, racing wheelchairs down hallways, sitting eye level with butts.
It was right in the middle of this dreamy bubble that I first learned about a new lawsuit, Texas v. Becerra, filed by the attorneys general in 17 states, seeking to make Section 504 unconstitutional or dismantle all of the detailed protections that it lays out. I scoured the internet for any reporting from mainstream news outlets. The silence stunned me. I went directly to the lawsuit itself, and as I squinted into the legalese, I recognized arguments that sounded identical to the ones posed in the 1970s. We’d written these sentiments into the mouths of our most skeptical characters: disabled people are a burden on the rest of us; we shouldn’t be forced to integrate them into our communities.
Over the course of two years, the lawsuit evolved; it was updated as Texas v. Kennedy, the people made noise, and many states dropped out. Then in June, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel issued a memo asserting that Section 504 and the ADA don’t actually mandate that states support disabled people to remain integrated in their communities. Instead, this memo claims, sending people to live in institutions—away from their families, friends, and beds—is an acceptable option. This position is in direct conflict with the way disability-rights law has been interpreted by courts for decades. And, in addition to the human cost, it doesn’t make fiscal sense. For example, according to the Kansas Department for Aging and Disability Services and the Disability Rights Center of Kansas, sending one person with an intellectual or developmental disability (I/DD) to live in an institution can easily cost well over $310,000 a year. Providing home- and community-based services with an I/DD waiver for this same person would cost, on average, $70,000 a year. The discrepancy is similarly steep for someone with a physical disability. So at least in this case, it costs less to include us.
Even so, that memo set the foundation for a joint proposal from the Department of Justice and the five remaining states that ultimately ended the case. They asked the court to vacate critical language about integration, and in September the judge agreed. Now the law remains on the books—only Congress can change the legislation itself—but it’s been utterly gutted, despite the loud outcry from disability advocates across the country and the way it had been applied since the protesters won their fight in 1977. It’s hard not to interpret this move as anything other than a profound disregard for the value of disabled life.
And yet, even as the lawsuit and memo wound their way through the government, the Toronto International Film Festival welcomed Being Heumann as its opening-night film. I rolled across the red carpet in my black sequined dress and scratched-up wheelchair frame, taking in the wide expanse of our embodied disabilities, each of us glammed out and feted for our talents. It felt like living inside two timelines: one where my government undercuts the foundations of laws that have long protected all of us, the other where the hubs of culture celebrate the incredible story behind the passing of those same laws. As Judy’s life’s work is threatened, audiences around the world are learning her name. The past is asserting itself into the present, the future is teetering toward the past, all inside one surreal moment. I’m trying to hold onto the contradiction, never allowing the significance of one reality to eclipse the other.
I wish Judy were here to give us our marching orders—to make the monster lurking around the corner feel a little smaller with the force of her voice. I wish she could take in the wild power of her own story moving across a screen and witness this outpouring of recognition, gratitude, and celebration. She died unexpectedly while we were working on the film. In fact, many of the 504 leaders have passed away—Brad Lomax, Ed Roberts, Kitty Cone, Ron Washington, Hale Zukas. Their generation came of age in a world where doctors routinely told parents they should send their disabled children away to live out their lives in institutions, but their activism fundamentally changed the lives of all of us coming up behind them. Now that we are the adults in the room, what legacy will we leave behind?
I find myself thinking a lot about the work culture can do where legislation drops off. As we continue to fight for the laws Judy and her peers helped make real, I wonder about the ripples of an entertaining movie that isn’t here to force a lesson but bring to life a vivid story of disability as a dynamic, nuanced, deeply human experience. I wonder if one film might beget more. Perhaps this kind of authentic representation of disabled life could be a fixture that younger generations will one day take for granted. Maybe storytelling can insist on our shared humanity in the ways legislation can’t.
Because, even as I see now more than ever how essential laws can be, I don’t want just laws; I also want a society that values disabled people enough to implement them meaningfully and fully. I want whole communities invested in the great, ongoing project of building a world for all of us. I think Judy would co-sign my enormous appetite. I no longer believe human evolution inevitably bends toward including more of us, but if she taught us anything, it’s that we don’t show up because the outcome is guaranteed; we show up because it isn’t.

The Bulgarian Ministry of Defense and Naval Forces have increased surveillance in the Black Sea after four vessels were struck in Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone since October 6, with all sailors from two ships rescued, 11 still missing from another, and the fate of the Alpha Watan’s crew unknown.
The first attacks took place on October 6, when the Alpha Watan and Abel were hit about 70 nautical miles east of Byala. All crew members aboard the Abel were rescued, but the fate of those on the Alpha Watan remains unknown, and the search operation has been called off.
On October 13, drones struck two more vessels, the Chelsea 3 and HS Dignity. The Chelsea 3 was targeted by three unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) about 18 nautical miles east of Byala, while the HS Dignity sank roughly 17 nautical miles east of Krapets.
All sailors aboard the Chelsea 3 were rescued. Of the 16 crew members on the HS Dignity, five were recovered and the other 11 remain missing.
Following the attacks, Bulgaria’s Ministry of Defense and Naval Forces stepped up their vigilance, widened radar surveillance and began surveying the affected areas with unmanned aerial vehicles.

Armenian foreign minister says his country sees no possibility of returning to CSTO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:11:28 UTC
22:11:28 KST

Elena Teslova
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Armenia sees no possibility of returning to the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said Wednesday.
Speaking at a news conference in Yerevan, he said his country had stopped participating in the organization’s activities.
“We stopped participating in the work of this structure a long time ago, froze our membership, and we will not change our position. We do not see ourselves returning to the CSTO,” he said.
CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov earlier said that the issue of expelling Armenia could be raised at a meeting of the organization’s Collective Security Council in Moscow on Nov. 11, 2026.
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has also said he would support the country’s expulsion, adding that Yerevan does not intend to increase its engagement with the organization over the next five years.
Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO in 2024. Pashinyan said in December of that year that relations between Armenia and the organization had passed the point of no return.

Judge orders release of creator of 'October 17 Movement' social media channels
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:10:59 CET
22:10:59 KST

A preliminary investigations judge
(GIP) on Wednesday ordered the release of Youssef Siher, a
30-year-old Italian researcher and freelance journalist with
Moroccan roots who has been accused of being the creator of the
"October 17 Movement" social media channels set up after the
shocking rioting and looting that took place in Milan on the
weekend of October 17-18.
                                    
GIP Tiziana Landoni rejected a request from prosecutors to
impose pre-trial detention, saying that while Siher talked about
"forms of protest" against "current government policies" on the
October 17 Movement Telegram channel and even "alluded to acts
of 'civil disobedience'"; this does not "translate into the
adoption of violent or, more generally, criminal behavior, but
rather into the simple planning of weekly demonstrations,
intended to raise awareness and involve as many people as
possible".
                                    
Siher is accused of incitement to commit a crime, with the
intent to commit terrorism an aggravating factor.
                                    
His wife, a cultural mediator, is also under investigation for
the same alleged crimes.
                                    
Prosecutors said Monday that Siher possessed a level of
technical expertise that would have enabled him to "develop a
revolutionary strategy" in their arguments in favour of his
being remanded in custody.
                                    
His lawyers, Benedetto Ciccarone and Yasmina Abu Shara, however,
asked the GIP to let him go, saying he "did nothing wrong".
                                    
"There was no incitement to violence, there is no terrorism,
there is no crime," they said.
                                    
The lecturer who supervised Siher's degree thesis at Milan's
Statale University is among the people who have stuck up for
him, saying he is being scapegoated for the unrest, prompting
the institute to stress that she was speaking on a personal
level and not on behalf of it.
                                    
The lecturer, Professor Elisa Giunchi, told Tgcom24 that Siher
"has been subjected to shameful media pillorying and has already
been convicted by some newspapers, while the investigations are
still ongoing.
                                    
"He is absolutely not a violent person," she added, describing
him as "very polite, reserved, shy and certainly not the street
agitator he has been portrayed as in the media over the last few
days."
Conservative newspapers have dubbed Siher "The Ayatollah of the
Maranzas" (youth gang members) and said that he is an Islamist
conspiring to bring down the Italian State.
                                    
The street violence in Milan and other cities overshadowed
initially peaceful protests by students against school
conditions, the cost of living and housing, wars and other
hot-button social issues.

What happens next after Israel’s election?
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:06:40 CET
22:06:40 KST

By Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track to win the most seats in Israel’s parliament after Tuesday’s election, though neither he nor his main competitor, Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a majority.
Votes are now being tallied, followed by potentially long negotiations as parties try to assemble a governing coalition. If those talks fail, Israel could head to another round of elections.
With around 77.6% of votes tallied on Wednesday morning, Israeli media forecast Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties winning 54 seats in parliament, far surpassing 49 for Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
WHEN WILL WE KNOW IF ANYONE WON?
Israel’s Central Election Committee was still tallying votes on Wednesday, and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election are known.
The committee will also tally hundreds of thousands of ballots by Israeli soldiers, as well as diplomats, who voted from outside the country.
The committee’s tallying followed exit polls from major Israeli TV channels. Those polls can help give a general sense of each party’s relative strength but are not considered a reliable barometer of precise results, particularly in Israel’s fragmented political system.
The final vote tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
WHY IS IT SO COMPLICATED?
The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE RESULTS ARE PUBLISHED?
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.
(Reporting by Maayan Lubell and Rami Ayyub; Editing by Timothy Heritage and Alex Richardson)

====================================================================================================

Iranians cut essentials and put dreams on hold as war-hit economy bites
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:06:31 CET
22:06:31 KST

By Parisa Hafezi
DUBAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Iranian families are cutting back on food, housing and education as the eight-month-old war with the United States fuels one of the country’s worst inflation surges in decades, eroding incomes and pushing households to the brink.
The strain is being felt far beyond the country’s major cities. Workers say wages no longer cover basic expenses, while businesses face rising costs and weakening demand as families spend most of their budgets on food, rent and other necessities.
The conflict, triggered by US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and followed by Tehran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf, has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.
Reuters spoke to more than two dozen people across Iran from different social and economic backgrounds who said worsening conditions had left them struggling to afford food, housing, healthcare and education.
“We have no money, no future and no hope. We’re tired of living in fear, fear of another US attack and fear of not being able to make ends meet at the end of every month,” said Mohammadali, a 47-year-old shopkeeper and father of two in the northeastern city of Mashhad.
Iran’s Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh on Tuesday apologised for the mounting cost-of-living pressures facing Iranians, state media reported, saying pensioners, workers and civil servants were bearing the brunt of soaring prices and high inflation.
Iran’s inflation surge has shown little sign of easing. Consumer prices in September were nearly 90% higher than a year earlier, while annual inflation accelerated to 73.6%, according to official data and figures reported by state media.
Food prices have risen even faster. The cost of food and beverages was 121.8% higher than a year ago, forcing many families to cut spending elsewhere.
PRICES OUTPACE PAYCHECKS, JOBS DRY UP
For Mahmoud, a 44-year-old government employee in the central city of Isfahan, the gap between wages and living costs widens every month.
“With my salary of less than $100, you can survive only for 10 days … My wife and I lie to our daughters all the time when they ask for a toy or new clothes,” he said.
Official estimates put the minimum monthly cost of living for a three-person working-class family at around $336, more than three times the average monthly wage of roughly $92 at the free-market exchange rate.
As wages fail to keep pace with inflation, many families have exhausted savings, cut consumption or borrowed money to cover daily expenses. Government-mandated pay increases have been swiftly overtaken by rising prices.
For many Iranians, the challenge is no longer preserving their standard of living but avoiding financial collapse.
“We had to move to my parents’ house last month because my husband got laid off from a small tile factory in May. We spent all our savings. But my husband is still jobless and we could no longer afford rent,” said Hamideh, a 39-year-old mother of two in the northern city of Rasht.
Rising housing costs have added to the squeeze on family budgets. Rents in September were 32.8% higher than a year earlier, while housing, utilities and fuel costs were up nearly 38%, according to official data.
The pressure extends to the labour market. The official unemployment rate climbed to 9.1% in the spring, up 1.8 percentage points from a year earlier. The economic participation rate fell to 40.7%, indicating fewer working-age Iranians were employed or actively seeking work. Nearly a quarter of young people aged 15 to 24 are unemployed.
“I have been looking for work since graduating in advertising, but after months of searching I’ve started to lose hope. Companies are cutting budgets, not hiring. Most of my classmates are either unemployed or working in fields unrelated to what they studied,” said 23-year-old Firouzeh, who lives with her parents in the northwestern city of Urmia.
STUDYING ABROAD A DISTANT DREAM
The weakening rial is also closing off opportunities once seen as pathways to upward mobility. Iran’s currency has lost more than half its value over the past year, putting overseas education beyond the reach of many families.
“Both my parents are government employees. Their dream was to send me abroad to become a medical doctor. But after two years studying in Turkey, I could not pay the tuition for this year and I am returning home,” said Shahriyar, 25, in Istanbul. He said several of his friends were in the same situation.
Washington’s expanded sanctions, announced on August 24 as part of “Operation Economic Outcast” and aimed at cutting Tehran’s funding for the war, have added to the economic strain on ordinary Iranians, analysts said.
Businesses are under pressure. Sanctions and war-related disruptions have increased the cost of imports and restricted access to foreign currency and raw materials, while retailers and small businesses face higher operating costs just as demand weakens, threatening revenues and jobs.
For Iran’s rulers, the challenge is maintaining essential imports and public services while financing a costly conflict. Central Bank Governor Abdolnasser Hemmati said in mid-October that US claims Iran’s economy was collapsing were “an illusion”.
The deterioration in living standards also presents a growing political challenge for the authorities, who remain wary that worsening economic conditions could reignite nationwide unrest.
Economic grievances have fuelled repeated waves of protests in recent years, leaving officials sensitive to signs that war, inflation and rising unemployment are further eroding public patience.
The clerical establishment responded to previous outbreaks of unrest with a sweeping crackdown that, according to Iranian officials and rights groups, killed thousands in January.
(Additional reporting by Emily Giles, Writing by Parisa HafeziEditing by Ros Russell)

China Focus: Chinese smart cars accelerate from test track to commercial competition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:02:28 CST
22:02:28 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Racing from the test track to the vast arena of commercial application, China's booming smart vehicle models and technologies are breathing new life into the intelligent connected vehicle (ICV) market.
Industry insiders have noted that the focus of China's ICV industry is shifting from technology validation to scaled commercial competition. Commercial viability, per-vehicle cost and data compliance have become the make-or-break factors for market competition.
As of Oct. 16 this year, a fleet of BAIC Motor's Arcfox AlphaS vehicles, the Level 3 version, had accumulated more than 150,000 km of road operations.
This model is one of the first two Level 3 conditional autonomous driving models which received product admission approval from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in December 2025, marking China's Level 3 autonomous driving endeavor officially moving from closed-venue testing to road pilot validation.
Level 3, or conditional driving automation, allows vehicles to perform dynamic automated driving tasks while requiring a human driver to remain available to take control when requested.
In January 2026, the pilot fleet began scaled on-road pilot operations on designated routes, including the Beijing Daxing Airport Expressway.
Amid real traffic circumstances, this fleet has been continuously collecting data on complex scenarios such as vehicle cut-ins and traffic flow fluctuations, repeatedly validating perception, decision-making and vehicle-road coordination capabilities.
Beyond advancing new ICV models through road pilot validation, major Chinese automakers are also turning new technological achievements into real-world application, driving the country's auto industry shift from scale advantages to core technology strengths.
These automakers have moved to the global technological forefront in vehicle integration, power batteries and intelligent cockpits, with combined driving assistance features becoming increasingly widespread. Major progress is being made across technologies spanning smart-driving chips, fast charging, vibration damping and real-time communication.
By July this year, 70.5 percent of new passenger vehicles in China were equipped with Level 2 combined driver-assistance functions, while 34.2 percent of automobile models provided the Navigate on Autopilot (NOA) driving functions, Guo Shougang, an MIIT official, said at a press conference.
The MIIT will accelerate diverse moves to boost progress in the ICV sector. These include scaling up the deployment of network infrastructure such as direct communication, promoting onboard applications of technologies like direct-to-satellite connectivity and the BeiDou system, and expanding multi-scenario connectivity adaptability.
The ministry will also promote digital upgrades of traffic signals and road markings, advance pilot applications of vehicle-road-cloud integration, speed up scaled applications of vehicle-grid interaction, and actively explore sustainable business models, according to Guo.
Weng Youling, an official with the Ministry of Transport, said the ministry will work with relevant departments to deepen implementation of innovation initiatives and continuously expand intelligent driving application scenarios.
Meanwhile, efforts will be made to strengthen digital-intelligent infrastructure support, and drive steady progress in the integrated development of ICVs and the country's transportation sector.
The MIIT and eight other government departments in early September jointly released a plan for the development of the intelligent connected new energy vehicle (NEV) industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
The plan proposes that, by 2030, China will further consolidate its advantages across the entire intelligent connected NEV industrial chain and join the ranks of the world's auto powerhouses.
Intelligent connected NEVs are the main direction for transforming and upgrading the country's automobile industry, typical examples of new quality productive forces, and key components in building a modern industrial system in China, the plan notes. ■

Sixteen years of drills to secure three minutes to safety at rural Chinese school
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:01:48 CST
22:01:48 KST

XINING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven-year-old Tenzin Wangso was curled up on his dormitory bed, too frightened to move, when his math teacher Karma Tenzin found him.
The teacher grabbed a quilt, wrapped it around the boy and carried him downstairs to the playground. He then rushed back into the building to make sure no children had been left behind.
A 7.0-magnitude earthquake had struck Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Oct. 22, sending strong tremors through neighboring Jieduo Township of Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture in Qinghai Province in northwest China. Most of the 120 boarding students at the township's rural boarding school were already asleep when the quake hit.
Within about three minutes after the quake struck, all 120 had reached the playground, according to the school's surveillance footage. None was injured.
The school, more than 4,200 meters above sea level on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, had been practicing for such an emergency for 16 years.
Chime Tsering, principal of Jieduo Township Central Boarding School, still remembers the morning of April 14, 2010.
He had arrived as vice principal just a month earlier. Back then, the school consisted of two rows of single-story buildings, one for classrooms and the other for dormitories.
When a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Yushu that morning, teachers and students were attending morning study sessions. Nearly 2,700 people died across the region.
"We had no experience dealing with an earthquake. Everyone was terrified," Chime Tsering recalled.
Teachers and students made it to the playground. Subsequent inspections found cracks in both buildings, which were later demolished and rebuilt.
This experience prompted the school to rethink its emergency procedures. As local education authorities called for more earthquake drills, Chime Tsering and his colleagues began working out how to get students to safety.
At first, they simply designated evacuation routes. Early drills took six or seven minutes. As teachers identified problems and revised the procedures, that duration fell to three or four minutes, and eventually to under three.
They also began holding drills at different times of day, including at night, when children would have to be woken and guided out of their dormitories.
Teachers were given specific responsibilities: waking students, directing them at stairwells and guiding them through exits.
The school now holds emergency drills at least once a month, covering both earthquakes and fires, with two or three nighttime exercises each semester. Its most recent earthquake drill was held roughly two weeks before the Oct. 22 quake.
The dormitory building has two designated evacuation routes and the teaching building has three. Each teacher is also assigned a group of 13 students to look after in daily school life, as well as specific rooms or classes to oversee during emergencies.
Karma Tenzin, who has taught math at the school for three years, was grading homework when the tremors began.
"The ground was shaking violently, and the tables and chairs were moving," he said. It was the strongest earthquake he had felt in recent years.
He and other teachers headed for the student dormitories.
Karma Tenzin was responsible for checking five rooms in the boys' dormitory. Moving from one room to the next, he was most worried about younger pupils, who might be slow to react or fall during the evacuation.
Among them was Tenzin Wangso, the first-grader he carried to safety. The boy had started school only in September.
Another teacher, Pema Wanggyal, also carried a first-grader out of the building.
On the playground, children gathered in coats and quilts while teachers checked attendance and comforted those who were frightened.
The school put up temporary tents that night. Parents began collecting their children the next day.
Most of the school buildings had been rebuilt after the 2010 earthquake. They remained largely intact, although fine cracks appeared in some walls.
"Only through repeated practice can we stay calm when something really happens and protect every child," Chime Tsering said.
The school has more than 170 students, most of them children of local herding families. Many live in remote pastoral areas where mobile phone reception is unreliable.
With in-person classes temporarily suspended, teachers began visiting students' homes on Oct. 25 to inform parents of the arrangements and find out whether the children had the equipment and internet access needed for online lessons.
"We have to visit families one by one," Karma Tenzin noted. "We also need to understand their circumstances before deciding how online teaching can be arranged."
For him, the greatest relief was that the drills had worked when they were needed, and that every child had come through the earthquake unharmed. ■

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2026) and Colorsoft (2026) Review: Best for Accessories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

It's a good day to be a Kindle fan. Amazon announced the arrival of a new generation of devices earlier this month, and the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are available today. A question now presents itself: Should you upgrade?
The most intriguing reason to upgrade isn't the devices themselves—the Paperwhite and Colorsoft both have base plastic versions with 16 GB of storage and aluminum-backed Signature Editions with 32 GB of storage and extra features—but the little extras could go a long way for certain readers. Namely, the ability to add page-turn buttons with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80)—which is compatible only with the new Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft.
Color also plays a big role in the Signature Editions compared to the new base models. Not a color screen, to be clear—that's still Colorsoft only—but the color of the device itself, which Amazon has said was a huge driver for Kindle users to upgrade to a new model after the brand released colors like Matcha and Raspberry in 2024. The 2026 line has one color for each of these 7-inch e-readers that's only available with the Signature Editions.
It's worth noting that while the price of these new models is the same as the 2024 editions, it's because Kindle raised the prices of its 2024 versions back in August. At first, it seemed like this was intended to make Amazon sales look better than they actually were heading into Prime Day and Black Friday, but now it's clear it was probably a way to make these new models feel worth buying, since you won't find a cheaper model as easily. And it's a valid move: These models will be my new picks, because if you're spending the same amount, why wouldn't you want the latest model?
But that doesn't necessarily help you decide if it's worth upgrading. It might be worth it if you're desperate for page-turner buttons, which is easily my favorite part of this new line of Kindles. If you don't have a Kindle already and are on a mission to select your first one, this latest version of the Paperwhite remains a good choice unless you're determined to splurge on a color screen. The warm light is a big benefit for anyone who reads in the evening, and you'll have to choose one of these two models from Kindle's lineup to get it anyway.
The Base Lineup
The Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are, to some degree, the same device. You'll see a similar laundry list of features: a 7-inch screen, a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth, and 16 GB of storage in the base models. Both have the same new look of a flush-front screen and ever-so-slightly-smaller body when compared to the 2024 Paperwhite and 2025 Colorsoft (the first Colorsoft in 2024 was later renamed the Signature Edition, and a cheaper base model came out in 2025).

Britain told it can lead world in metamaterials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:00:57 GMT
22:00:57 KST

Britain can become a global leader in metamaterials if it acts now to turn its research into commercial products, and the Ministry of Defence’s chief scientific adviser has welcomed a new government roadmap setting out how, according to the Institute of Physics.
Metamaterials are engineered materials whose properties come from their internal structure instead of their chemical composition, which lets them respond to energy in ways conventional materials cannot. British-developed examples are already being applied to knee implants, impact protection, fifth generation connectivity, noise reduction and electric vehicle batteries, and the field holds potential for earthquake shielding, wireless charging, targeted ultrasound and cloaking against radar and the human eye.
Professor Tim Dafforn, chief scientific adviser at the Ministry of Defence, said: “MOD is encouraged by this government signal designed to translate metamaterials opportunities created by the world-leading UK academic base, to drive commercialisation in this important dual-use emerging technology domain.
“In line with the Strategic Defence Review and UK Industrial Strategy, this strongly supports UK freedom of action, resilience, and advantage economically and for defence and national security, at a time of heightened global uncertainty.”
The Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap, published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, warns that the global race to commercialise the technology is already running and that Britain’s window is closing, with countries across Asia, Europe and North America competing for the economic and national security benefits. Earlier research by the Institute of Physics found Britain ranked third in the world for academic papers on metamaterials, behind only China and the United States, but fourteenth for patents.
Tom Grinyer, chief executive of the Institute of Physics, said: “The UK has the outstanding research foundations, underpinned by physics, to be a world leader in metamaterials. What we need now is the ambition and coordination to turn that unique advantage into innovations that deliver the UK’s strategic priorities and economic growth, beginning with a properly developed funding plan from research to commercialisation.
“If we get this right, uniting public and private sectors behind long-term priorities to unlock the scale of investment needed, the UK can lead the way for the next global technology revolution through metamaterials. If we don’t, we risk the UK falling behind and becoming just one part in the pipeline of an extraordinary future.”
Chris McDonald, the Minister for Science, Innovation and Investment, said: “Metamaterials represent a significant opportunity to strengthen the UK’s technology and industrial base, supporting economic growth, and solving societal challenges. Realising this opportunity will depend on our ability to translate cutting-edge research into commercially viable products and new industrial solutions.
“I welcome the publication of the Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap and its vision for accelerating innovation, attracting investment and building the partnerships needed to position the UK at the forefront of the transformative potential of metamaterials.”
The roadmap identifies fragmented funding and investment, limited manufacturing scale-up, skills gaps and a lack of standards as the barriers, and sets a ten year plan to build the world’s first integrated manufacturing value chain for the technology, with scaled manufacturing and commercialisation capabilities in place by 2035. It builds on more than £80 million of government investment through the National Materials Innovation Programme.
The Metamaterials Strategy Action Group behind the work includes the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory alongside the business department, the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, Innovate UK, the Institute of Physics, the UK Metamaterials Network, the High Value Manufacturing Catapult and the National Physical Laboratory.
Professor Alastair Hibbins of the University of Exeter and Dr Claire Dancer of the University of Birmingham, who co-lead the UK Metamaterials Network, said: “Building on the UK’s world-leading academic excellence, research, training, and metamaterials community the launch of the UK Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap represents a defining moment, positioning the UK at the forefront of an enabling and transformative technology.
“We see the Roadmap charting a course towards the UK becoming a global leader in commercialising metamaterials research and innovation, contributing to our nation’s security and prosperity. Realising this ambition depends on coordinated community action, driven by the community activities of the UK Metamaterials Network’s c.1300 academic, industry, and government members, to fully harness the UK’s competitive advantage in metamaterials.”
