Intelligence and fertility: Do smarter people have fewer children? The strongest evidence suggests a smaller, more complicated link
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:00:54 UTC
22:00:54 KST

People who score higher on intelligence tests tend to have slightly fewer children, a pattern most visible among women in American and British studies. But the strongest studies, which count children only after people finish having them and compare siblings from the same families, suggest the link is small. The pattern depends heavily on the timing of parenthood and on family background, and in Scandinavia, the association runs in the opposite direction for men.
Scientists study this question because it represents a puzzle for evolutionary biology. Intelligence test scores predict more education, higher income, and higher status. In most animals and in preindustrial human societies, status and resources went along with more surviving children, but in many modern societies, the pattern has run the other way. Researchers have proposed several explanations, including more effective use of contraception, the time demands of higher education, and changing values about family size.
This field of research has a highly contentious history. Eugenics was a movement, popularized by Francis Galton in the nineteenth century, that sought to “improve” human populations by encouraging people with traits deemed desirable to have children and discouraging others, in some places through forced sterilization. Early research on intelligence and fertility grew out of eugenicists’ worry that less intelligent people were outbreeding more intelligent ones.
Some researchers use small statistical trends to argue that modern populations face a genetic decline in intelligence, while others have questioned those assumptions. Several of the strongest claims come from a small network of researchers whose backgrounds are described below, while other findings have been replicated by independent teams.
How to Read the Research
The studies vary widely in how well they measure intelligence. Military conscription tests and batteries of school tests capture intelligence more reliably, while brief vocabulary quizzes partly reflect how much schooling someone has had. Most of these studies report their findings as correlations, which are statistical measures ranging from negative one to positive one that describe how two variables move together.
A 2017 study published in Intelligence, led by Hsin-Yi Chen, offers a concrete example. In that Taiwanese sample, adults with scores below 84 averaged 3.16 children, compared with 2.29 children for those scoring above 115, and the overall correlation was negative 0.18, a small tendency for higher scores to go with smaller families. By comparison, intelligence scores in the same sample correlated 0.65 with education.
A common pitfall in this literature involves the timing of parenthood. People with higher test scores tend to spend more years in school, start their careers later, and delay having children. To avoid this age trap, scientists look at completed fertility, counting a person’s children only after that person reaches age 45 or 50. Looking at the full lifespan provides a much more accurate picture.
Population-level trends can be misleading because they group people from vastly different backgrounds together. Different financial resources, neighborhoods, and family values create confounding, a situation where an outside factor distorts the apparent relationship between two variables. Controlling for a variable uses statistical techniques to hold that outside factor constant.
One of the strongest ways to account for family background is a sibling comparison, which looks at brothers or sisters raised in the same household. Siblings also share about half their genes on average, so these comparisons partly account for genetic differences as well. While this removes shared family influences, it does not remove individual differences, such as differences in health or experiences unique to one sibling, so it still cannot prove a direct cause.
Many of these studies also analyze the same datasets, which can create the illusion of more independent confirmation than exists. Two of the studies described below drew on the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, which covers Americans born from 1957 to 1964, two on the General Social Survey, a long-running survey of American adults, and two on the Health and Retirement Study, which covers Americans born from 1931 to 1953.
Two used Britain’s National Child Development Study, which follows everyone born in Britain during one week of March 1958, and three used the UK Biobank, a database of about 500,000 British volunteers who tend to be healthier and wealthier than average. The three Swedish studies share the same national registers, as do the two Norwegian studies.
The Timing Trap: Why Delayed Parenthood Skews the Numbers
An early American study shows how the timing problem plays out. A 2013 study published in Intelligence, led by Charlie L. Reeve, analyzed Project TALENT, a national survey of American high school students begun in 1960. The researchers measured the number of children people had five and eleven years after high school, and at those young ages, higher test scores predicted fewer children.
The authors also estimated how much average intelligence would change per generation from genetic selection alone, while cautioning that the figures might overstate the decline because many participants had not finished having children. Based on children counted five years after high school, the projected decline for women was about 1.2 IQ points per generation, but when children were counted six years later, it fell to about 0.5 points. For men, the projection dropped from about 1.5 to about 1.15 points.
A 2019 study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, led by Martin Kolk, showed how this age trap works. Using Swedish national registers of men born between 1951 and 1967, who took intelligence tests in their late teens as part of mandatory military conscription, the researchers found that the lowest-scoring men had about twice as many children as the highest scorers when children were counted before age 30.
When the researchers waited until the men reached age 45, the trend flipped, and higher scorers ended up slightly ahead in family size compared to their peers. Timing played a large role: among men who became fathers, the lowest scorers had their first child at about 27.6 years old on average, compared with about 31 for the highest scorers.
Other research finds the same delay in parenthood, even though higher scorers tend to mature physically earlier. A 2025 study published in Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, led by Jose C. Yong and co-authored by Satoshi Kanazawa, analyzed Britain’s National Child Development Study alongside the American Add Health study, which began surveying teenagers in 1994 and 1995. The researchers found that higher childhood test scores predicted an earlier onset of puberty but a later age at first child in the British data.
For example, girls with intelligence scores above 125 had their first menstrual period at 12.60 years old on average, versus 13.24 for girls scoring below 75. Counting children born by age 33, the highest-scoring women had their first child at about 27.9, compared with 21.5 for the lowest scorers, and the gap for men was about 28.5 versus 24.4. While higher intelligence initially seemed linked to later marriage, that association was not reliable in either sample after accounting for education, nutrition, and health.
Yong, a senior lecturer at James Cook University, argues that the pattern reflects a split between fixed biological traits, such as the timing of puberty, and flexible behaviors shaped by preferences. He told PsyPost that “even though intelligent individuals are reproductively endowed at the physiological level with earlier puberty (which should typically predict faster reproduction), they opt for reduced sexual activity and fewer children at the behavioral level (resulting in slower reproduction).”
He added that the link with puberty held up after the statistical adjustments, while “the overall predicted patterns for behavior still held more rather than less, particularly for number of children.” Those patterns come from British and American data, however, and the Scandinavian results for men, described below, show that a later start does not always mean fewer children in the end.
In Scandinavia, Higher-Scoring Men Tend to Have More Children
When researchers look at completed families, the link between intelligence and having children differs notably between men and women. For men, Scandinavian data show a positive trend. In Kolk’s 2019 Swedish study, brother comparisons showed that the lowest-scoring group of men, those scoring below 74 or roughly the bottom 4 percent, had about 0.56 fewer children than the median group. The highest-scoring men had about 0.09 more children against an average of about 1.8 children, with the median representing the middle point of the score distribution.
A 2021 study in Intelligence, led by Kolk, expanded on those Swedish brother comparisons. The lowest scorers were about 20 percentage points more likely than median scorers to remain childless. Ever marrying by age 45 differed by about 20 percentage points between the lowest and highest scorers. Among men who married, the lowest group had only about 0.1 fewer children, leading the researchers to conclude that lower-scoring men had fewer children primarily because they had difficulty forming stable partnerships.
A 2023 study published in the Journal of Population Economics, led by Francis Kramarz, used Swedish military conscription tests to compare thousands of twins and close siblings. The conscription process also rated non-cognitive skills through an interview with a psychologist assessing traits such as emotional stability and social maturity. Cognitive scores and these non-cognitive ratings tend to go together, correlating at about 0.4. A standard deviation is a unit that measures how spread out scores are from the average, equaling about 15 points on a standard IQ test.
When the researchers compared men with the same non-cognitive rating, each standard deviation of higher cognitive scores was linked to about 0.02 fewer children, a very slight negative link. Kolk’s studies, which did not hold those skills constant, found a positive link. When comparing twin brothers, the higher-scoring brother tended to have about 0.09 more children per standard deviation. Non-cognitive skills showed the strongest link of all, with each standard deviation associated with 0.13 to 0.17 additional children, both across the population and within twin pairs.
This positive trend for men holds true beyond Sweden. A 2023 study published in Biology Letters, led by Bernt Bratsberg, examined Norwegian men born from 1950 to 1981 across 32 birth cohorts, or groups born in the same year. They found that high-scoring men had children later but eventually had more of them than lower-scoring men. Across the cohorts, childlessness nearly doubled, with the largest increases among the lowest scorers, though lower-scoring men who became fathers were more likely than higher scorers to go on to have additional children.
The results for men do not agree across all countries. The association is practically zero in Britain’s 1958 birth cohort, analyzed in a 2014 study published in Social Science Research by Kanazawa. It is slightly negative in the United States, with correlations of about negative 0.06 to negative 0.07, in studies by Gerhard Meisenberg and Rosemary L. Hopcroft.
In a cohort of people born from 1950 to 1956 in Aberdeen, Scotland, analyzed in a 2011 study published in Intelligence led by Sophie von Stumm, higher-scoring men had about 31 percent lower odds of having any children for each standard deviation increase in childhood intelligence. Odds describe the likelihood of an event happening compared to it not happening. Intelligence was unrelated to the total number of children for either sex in the Scottish study, though the odds of being divorced rather than married at midlife were about 13 to 14 percent lower for each standard deviation increase in childhood intelligence.
The divorce finding echoes the Swedish evidence that stable partnerships play a large role in men’s family size. Why might Scandinavia differ? In their 2019 study, Kolk and Kieron Barclay pointed out that in Nordic welfare states, education and income are positively tied to men’s fertility. They argued that preferences for smaller families spread first among higher-status groups and have since diffused across society, leaving better-off people better able to afford the two or three children most people want, and they predicted that similar positive links might emerge elsewhere.
Women, Education, and the Role of Family Background
For women, American and British surveys mostly show a small negative association. A 2010 study published in Intelligence, led by Meisenberg, analyzed the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth and reported a correlation of negative 0.16 for white women and negative 0.07 for white men. His results also showed correlations of negative 0.24 for Black women and negative 0.03 for Black men, though the Black subgroups were smaller and the result for Black men was not statistically significant, meaning the researchers could not rule out that it arose by chance. A 2015 study published in Evolution and Human Behavior, led by Hopcroft, analyzed the same American survey and found correlations of negative 0.15 for women and negative 0.06 for men.
Income adds another twist. In Hopcroft’s 2015 study, higher personal income, measured after childbearing in 2010, was associated with more children for men (a correlation of 0.08) but fewer children for women (a correlation of negative 0.15). An earlier 2006 study by Hopcroft in Evolution and Human Behavior used the General Social Survey’s ten-word vocabulary test and found that while higher vocabulary scores predicted slightly fewer children, higher-income men had more biological children.
A classic 1988 study published in Social Biology, led by Robert Retherford, tracked more than 9,000 Wisconsin high school graduates from the class of 1957. The researchers estimated a selection differential of about 0.8 IQ points per generation, a figure describing what would happen if children matched their parents’ average score. Because this calculation comes before accounting for how much of intelligence is passed down genetically, it is not directly comparable to the genetic projections described later. The link was much stronger for women.
Researchers debate whether staying in school longer explains this drop in fertility for women. In a 1989 follow-up published in Intelligence, Retherford’s team indicated that once the researchers accounted for how much schooling people completed, intelligence scores predicted little about family size. Meisenberg and Reeve both reached similar conclusions, finding the association ran largely through education and income.
On the other hand, Kanazawa’s 2014 study reported the reverse: once childhood intelligence was taken into account, education no longer predicted whether women became mothers. For each standard deviation increase in childhood intelligence, a woman’s odds of becoming a mother by age 47 dropped by 21 to 25 percent, though the study found no such association for men.
Social standing may also shape the pattern. In the Scottish study led by von Stumm, occupational class measured at midlife rather than intelligence was linked to childlessness for women. Among higher-status women, childless women scored higher than mothers, but among lower-status women, mothers scored higher than childless women. The authors suggested that lower status may be a consequence of motherhood rather than a cause.
Outside Europe and North America, the Taiwan study led by Chen reported a correlation of negative 0.25 for women, while the link for men was not statistically significant. The sample’s ages ran from 35 to 90, a span covering the country’s historical fall from about six children per woman to about one. Because older participants grew up when large families were the norm and schooling was less common, differences between generations can masquerade as effects of intelligence, a problem known as cohort confounding. The authors reported the link held after adjusting for age, though they did not publish the adjusted figures.
When researchers use sibling comparisons to control for family background, the negative trend for women’s education and grades shrinks. In the 2023 Journal of Population Economics study, Kramarz compared twin sisters in Sweden. Across the general population, each extra year of schooling went with about 0.04 fewer children, and better school grades also went with fewer children. When the researchers compared twin sisters, the schooling association shrank to about 0.01 fewer children per year and was no longer statistically significant, while the association for school grades vanished almost entirely.
Because women were not conscripted, the Kramarz study had no intelligence test scores for them, only estimates based on their brothers’ scores for population comparisons, so researchers could not test women’s own scores within families. Kramarz and colleagues suggested that some families prize education while others prize large families. Families that prize education may cultivate academic skills and have fewer children, and their children may inherit both the skills and the preference.
That dynamic would make academic skills and small families go together across families, even when the higher-scoring sibling within a family has no fewer children. Consistent with this idea, fathers who had more children and less schooling than their own skills predicted tended to raise sons whose non-cognitive skills outpaced their cognitive scores.
Is Intelligence Declining?
These modest correlations underpin a more contentious claim. A network of authors frequently publishes studies projecting a genetic deterioration in intelligence in modern populations. A 2018 systematic review published in Personality and Individual Differences, led by Reeve, pooled 17 datasets to estimate the correlation between intelligence and number of children. A systematic review is a comprehensive summary of all available research on a specific topic.
Roughly half of the datasets in the 2018 review came from a specific network of researchers, while the rest were independent studies from researchers like von Stumm and Retherford. The review reported an overall correlation of negative 0.11 between cognitive ability and the number of offspring. The authors reported that newer studies tended to find stronger negative associations than older ones, though that trend rests on fewer than 20 studies and weakens noticeably when a single 1932 study is removed. This also contrasts with the Norway study, which found a stable positive pattern for men across 32 birth cohorts.
The review’s own data highlighted the importance of completed fertility. When the researchers limited the analysis to studies where people had finished having children, the correlation for men was about negative 0.03 and not statistically significant, while the correlation for women was negative 0.12. Overall, the correlation was negative 0.13 for women versus negative 0.06 for men.
To project future declines, some of these studies use a mathematical approach based on a formula called the breeder’s equation. Researchers weight each parent’s score by their number of children, compare the result with the population average, and multiply the gap by heritability. Heritability is a statistical estimate of how much variation within a population is explained by genetics.
The 2017 Taiwan study led by Chen used this method to project a drop of 1.19 IQ points per generation. Chen’s team assumed a heritability of 0.71, and Meisenberg assumed 0.5 in his 2010 study to project a drop of 0.8 points per generation in the United States. A higher assumed value produces a larger projected decline.
A 2004 study published in Intelligence, led by Richard Lynn, reported correlations of about negative 0.08 to negative 0.18 using the same General Social Survey vocabulary quiz. The authors projected a drop of 0.9 points per generation by multiplying their correlation directly by a heritability estimate. This shortcut differs from the standard formula, which accounts for how much family sizes vary. If every adult had exactly two children, even a strong correlation would leave the next generation’s average unchanged.
These projections also rest on several assumptions, including an assumed heritability value and an environment that stays the same from one generation to the next. During the twentieth century, average test scores rose by roughly three points per decade. This trend, known as the Flynn effect, far outpaced any projected genetic change. Average scores have stalled or fallen in several countries in recent decades, including Norway, Denmark, Finland, and France, leading Lynn and colleagues to point to genetic selection.
In a 2018 study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that tested that idea, Bratsberg and colleagues compared brothers and found that the Flynn effect and its recent decline can be recovered within families. Younger brothers outscored older brothers while scores were rising, and scored lower while scores were falling. Since brothers share parents, changes in who is having children cannot account for most of the shifts, pointing instead to environmental causes. The study was designed to rule out explanations rather than to identify which environmental factors were responsible.
What DNA Studies Suggest About Education and Evolution
Studies that measure DNA directly offer another test, and they do show a small signal related to education. A polygenic score is a tool that combines the small effects of hundreds of thousands of genetic markers to predict a trait. A 2017 study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, led by Augustine Kong, found that an educational attainment polygenic score was linked to delayed reproduction and fewer children in Iceland, an effect that was stronger for women and held after adjusting for education. For women, each standard deviation higher on the genetic score went with about 0.08 fewer children and a first birth about 0.6 years later, in a sample of about 109,000 Icelanders.
In the Iceland study, the average score declined by about 0.010 standard units per decade, where one standard unit equals one standard deviation of the score. The directly measured drop translates to about 0.038 IQ points per decade, roughly 80 times smaller than the three-point-per-decade rise in test scores during the twentieth century. The genetic score captured only about 4 percent of the differences in education between people. To reach a larger figure of 0.30 points per decade (about a tenth of the twentieth-century rise), the authors assumed that all genetic influences on education, which they put at about 30 percent of those differences, were changing the same way as the small portion the score measures.
A 2016 study in the same journal, led by Jonathan Beauchamp, analyzed the Health and Retirement Study and estimated a decline of about 1.5 months of schooling per generation in the United States, an amount he described as small compared to the gain of roughly two years of schooling per generation in recent times. Natural selection is the process by which traits become more or less common in a population based on reproductive success. A 2022 study published in Behavior Genetics, led by David Hugh-Jones, investigated this process in the UK Biobank database.
Genetic scores predicting higher education and earnings also predicted lower fertility, though the direction of natural selection reversed among older parents or after controlling for age at first birth. In other words, among people who started families later, higher education scores were linked to having more children, not fewer. The negative effect was concentrated among lower-income groups, younger parents, people with more sexual partners, and people not living with a partner.
A 2024 study in Behavior Genetics by Hugh-Jones, which used the same survey, found that genetic scores correlating with more education were selected against across three generations of Americans. The economic explanation holds that people with greater earning power give up more income when they spend time raising children, predicting the pattern should be strongest among lower-income, less educated, unmarried, and younger parents. The study found stronger effects among low-income and unmarried parents, but not among less educated or younger ones. Together, these genetic studies point to a real but small shift, far smaller than the environmental changes in test scores over the same period.
Eugenics Roots and the Researchers Behind the Decline Claims
Several researchers who advance the decline argument have documented ties to organizations widely described as funding eugenics research and promoting scientific racism. Scientific racism is the use of scientific-sounding claims to argue that some racial groups are innately superior to others. Some of these authors use the term dysgenic, a word rooted in the eugenics movement, to describe a hypothesized genetic decline in intelligence.
The term has spread beyond this network. A 2023 commentary in Biology Letters, led by Rebecca Sear, responded to the independent Norwegian study, noting that its findings of a positive trend for men in fact challenge eugenicist claims. The authors argued the term treats value judgments, such as the idea that higher test scores are desirable, as science. They also noted that, in evolutionary terms, if people with lower scores had more children, scientists would describe them as better adapted to current conditions, not as a sign of decline.
Lynn, who died in 2023, was lead author of the 2004 study and a co-author on the 2017 Taiwan study, and he promoted the claim that racial differences in intelligence are genetic. Ulster University withdrew his emeritus title in 2018. He was president of the Pioneer Fund, whose role in financing scientific racism is documented in psychologist William H. Tucker’s 2002 book, The Funding of Scientific Racism: Wickliffe Draper and the Pioneer Fund, and he edited Mankind Quarterly, which Tucker described as a journal written by racists for racists.
Meisenberg was described by the New Statesman as a fellow director of the Pioneer Fund and was editor-in-chief of Mankind Quarterly. Marian Van Court, a co-author on the 2004 study, founded the Future Generations eugenics website and wrote “The Case for Eugenics in a Nutshell” for The Occidental Quarterly, which the Southern Poverty Law Center describes as a racist journal and lists as a hate group.
Michael A. Woodley of Menie, a co-author on the 2018 review, was criticized by the New Statesman and other outlets for his involvement in the London Conference on Intelligence, an invitation-only conference founded in 2014, held four times at University College London, and revealed by the London Student in January 2018. The gathering was held on campus without the university’s knowledge, and critics and student journalists labeled it a eugenics conference. Woodley of Menie organized a published defense co-signed by 14 other attendees who disputed the characterization.
Kanazawa’s record involves a different controversy. The author of the 2014 study and co-author of the 2025 Yong study was banned from non-peer-reviewed publishing for a year after an internal investigation found he had brought the London School of Economics into disrepute over a 2011 blog post claiming Black women were less physically attractive. In the 2014 study, Kanazawa based a forecast of declining population intelligence partly on the premise that boys inherit intelligence solely from their mothers through the X chromosome. Modern genetics researchers widely reject this premise, as cognitive ability is massively polygenic, meaning it involves thousands of genes spread across all human chromosomes.
The Reverse Question: Does Parenthood Shape the Aging Brain?
A completely different branch of research asks the reverse question. These studies investigate whether having children is linked to a person’s thinking skills later in life. A 2023 study published in Social Science & Medicine, led by Yan Zhang, analyzed cross-sectional data from the UK Biobank. Cross-sectional means researchers measured people at a single point in time.
The researchers found that fathers scored better on all five cognitive tests than childless men. Mothers scored lower than childless women on fluid reasoning, numeric memory, and prospective memory, with most of that gap explained by education. However, mothers scored better on reaction time and visual memory, an advantage that grew larger after controlling for education. The researchers controlled for polygenic scores, and the results did not substantially change.
A 2017 study published in The Journals of Gerontology: Series B, led by Sanna L. Read, looked at English adults aged 50 and older for about eight years. The researchers initially found a U-shaped link where people with either no children or many children had lower cognitive scores. The U-shape faded after socioeconomic adjustment, but childlessness remained linked to slightly lower scores in both men and women, and women who had a child after 35 scored slightly higher. For women, the link between childlessness and lower cognitive scores strengthened after statistical adjustment.
A 2020 study published in Scientific Reports, led by Kaida Ning, also used the UK Biobank database. The researchers found that parents had faster reaction times by 4 to 10 milliseconds and fewer memory errors, with larger differences for fathers. The paper also suggested that having two or three children was associated with brains that appeared 0.5 to 0.7 years younger on MRI scans. Brain age is a computer-generated estimate of how old a brain looks compared to others of the same age.
A lifestyle effect is one possibility, but it is difficult to tell if parenthood changed people’s brains or if healthier, more socially active people were more likely to become parents. These patterns are also consistent with the Scandinavian finding that the lowest-scoring men are the most likely to remain childless.
What Remains Uncertain
Several uncertainties remain in the study of intelligence and family size. Nearly all of this research is observational, so even the strongest designs show associations rather than cause and effect. While massive datasets from Scandinavia offer the best view for men, researchers still lack equally large sibling comparison studies that include women’s own cognitive test scores. Swedish and Norwegian register studies also reflect societies with strong welfare states, and patterns might differ in nations with less social support.
Nearly all of the completed-fertility evidence describes people born before the early 1980s, so it cannot say whether the same patterns hold for people starting families today. There is also little evidence from outside Europe, North America, and Taiwan. Yong acknowledged the same limit for his own work: “perhaps we can’t be 100% sure that the results will pan out similarly in other non-Western cultures or in later generations.”

A private jet carrying Brazil's defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has landed in the Miami area, AFP news agency reported.
The plane, which was seen by AFP journalists earlier on an overnight stopover in Guayaquil, Ecuador, matches the description of the aircraft identified by Argentine authorities as carrying Bolsonaro.
Washington has said it would grant him a visa.
With the whole world trying to work out where he was, Bolsonaro entered Argentina with his wife and two daughters late on Tuesday evening, according to the country's migration department.
Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and had refused to comply with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports, crossed into Argentina via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, about 19 hours by road from his home in Brasilia.
The family then boarded a private plane operated by Baires Fly S.A. bound for the Ecuadorean city of Guayaquil, the migration department said.
Argentina's presidency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Neither did Baires Fly.
A Gulfstream G400 operated by Baires Fly, registration LV-JQW, departed Puerto Iguazu at 12:22 am (0322 GMT) and landed in Guayaquil at 3:46 am (0846 GMT), according to FlightAware. 
The aircraft then departed for Miami's Opa-locka Executive Airport, where it was landed at 9:18 am local time (1318 GMT).
It was unclear how Bolsonaro entered Ecuador. Authorities there did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US-Brazil rift
Bolsonaro's departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas.
Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to help return them to power. Ahead of Sunday's election, Reuters news agency reported on a US State Department campaign to restore the Bolsonaros to office.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the United States, after his State Department said it would give them entry visas.
Trump has previously alleged that Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Jair Bolsonaro also travelled to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022, during Joe Biden's presidency. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
Bolsonaro had been favoured to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, had said on Monday after the order to hand in his passports that he had no plans to flee.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."

‘Killed Softly’: EU Prosecutor Warns of Threats as Von der Leyen Faces Pfizergate Questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

‘Killed Softly’: EU Prosecutor Warns of Threats as Von der Leyen Faces Pfizergate Questions
European Public Prosecutor’s Office chief prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi said the institution faces chronic underfunding, bureaucratic delays and attempts to undermine its independence, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has yet to give an in-person statement in the investigation known as Pfizergate, according to a person involved in the effort, POLITICO reports.
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) took over a Belgian-led investigation in 2024 into alleged criminal wrongdoing surrounding negotiations between von der Leyen and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla over coronavirus vaccine procurement. Legal documents seen by POLITICO say prosecutors have been investigating von der Leyen for “interference in public functions, destruction of SMS, corruption and conflict of interest.”
Asked about the claim that von der Leyen had not provided a statement in the case, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the Commission had cooperated extensively with EPPO to clarify the facts and assess events. He added that this cooperation had taken place with the president’s full support and that she remained willing to answer outstanding questions within the limits of her duties and availability.
In an interview with POLITICO ahead of the end of her seven-year term on Friday, Kövesi said she had repeatedly encountered EU officials who refused to respond to summonses from her office. “Some politicians think that they are above the law,” she said, adding: “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.”
Kövesi said EPPO faced particular difficulties when investigations involved prominent politicians or wealthy people with links to the political class. Asked whether von der Leyen was among the officials she meant, she declined to comment on specific investigations.
EPPO warns of threats to its independence
Established in 2017 and operational since 2021, EPPO investigates crimes involving EU funds. Kövesi said the office’s work had faced repeated attacks and efforts to weaken its authority.
“As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show, Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: 'In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,' and unfortunately, this is true,” Kövesi said, referring to the Ridley Scott film Alien. “I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it's doing its job.”
She identified three main obstacles: persistent funding shortages, delays in revising EPPO’s legal framework and a complicated bureaucracy that generates prolonged discussions about procedures rather than helping prosecutors work.
Kövesi said that, on paper, EPPO should have 230 European delegated prosecutors but had funding for only 180. She also said the organization received funding for just one-third of the cost of its security services.
The revision of EPPO’s regulation had been delayed despite the office calling for the process to begin earlier, she said. Kövesi also criticized prolonged discussions about anti-fraud arrangements and a joint intake registry, arguing that criminal organizations were expanding and defrauding EU and national budgets while officials debated administrative procedures.
She said EPPO had improved the detection of crimes in most member states, increased the number of successful cases and strengthened protection of the EU budget, although some aspects of its work remained below expectations.
Kövesi said she would make the same decisions if she could start her mandate again, but believed others should change their behavior. She identified preserving EPPO’s independence and credibility as the main task facing her successor, German prosecutor Andrés Ritter.
Kövesi said she had initially expected Brussels to operate differently from Romania, where people were accustomed to working with prosecutors. At the EU level, however, she had encountered a perception among some officials that they were above the law and did not need to attend when summoned.
She said delays in investigations did not necessarily mean prosecutors were unwilling to act. In some cases, national authorities opened proceedings covering the same subject after EPPO had launched an investigation and was preparing further measures. A national prosecutor could then rule that EPPO lacked jurisdiction, limiting its ability to investigate.
Kövesi also questioned whether EU institutions were reporting potential corruption cases adequately, saying the situation had changed significantly since EPPO began operating. She warned that investigations involving powerful political figures or wealthy people connected to the political class remained particularly difficult because of disputes over jurisdiction.
Addressing concerns that EPPO could undermine national sovereignty, Kövesi argued that cross-border criminal organizations exploited divisions between countries. She said the office continued to apply national legislation and bring cases before national courts, adding that cooperation provided citizens with greater protection and security.
Greece accused of intimidating prosecutors
Kövesi identified Greece as the most blatant example of an attempt to intimidate EPPO prosecutors during her tenure. The country was hit by a farm funding scandal last year that led to the resignation of ministers and deputy ministers. Four lawmakers from the ruling New Democracy party are currently facing court proceedings and all have pleaded not guilty.
Last May, EPPO filed a formal complaint with the European Commission over moves by the Greek government to prevent European prosecutors from investigating lawmakers. The office also objected to the Greek Supreme Judicial Council’s refusal to renew the mandates of European delegated prosecutors for five years, as EPPO had requested.
Kövesi warned that the dispute could lead to cuts in EU funding for Greece under Article 16 of the EPPO Regulation.
Relations between EPPO and the Greek government have been strained, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis suggesting a political motive behind the investigations and criticizing what he called “selective leaks.”
Kövesi rejected accusations that the office was pursuing a political agenda, saying criticism had diverted attention from the facts of the cases. She argued that some politicians supported judicial independence until investigations reached them or their associates, at which point they accused prosecutors of abuse and political interference.
Some Greek officials have suggested that the country could withdraw from EPPO, but Kövesi said leaving the institution was “almost impossible.” She warned that politicians could try to weaken the office by restricting its powers and funding or dismantling specialized police units.
Kövesi said the investigations were not being timed around elections. In the Greek farm subsidy case, she said, EPPO had finalized indictments and the cases were in court. She argued that prosecutors’ responsibility was to determine whether honest farmers had access to EU funding, rather than to adjust their work to electoral campaigns.
She said funds intended for farmers had instead gone to people who falsely claimed to be farmers and used the money for luxury trips and cars, while legitimate farmers received nothing. Kövesi said attacks on EPPO arose when politicians unhappy with investigations sought to undermine the office’s credibility and intimidate prosecutors.
She also defended the handling of the Greek case in which EPPO asked Parliament to lift the immunity of 11 lawmakers, but only four were eventually sent to court. Kövesi said requests to lift immunity were not findings of guilt, but a necessary condition for prosecutors to investigate and gather evidence.
Funding concerns in Poland and Hungary
Kövesi also warned that budget constraints threatened EPPO’s credibility in other EU countries. In Poland, the office had agreed that it needed 24 European delegated prosecutors but had only 15, despite high expectations for its work.
Hungary officially became a participating member of EPPO in August 2026, and the office is now establishing its operations there. Kövesi said EPPO had clearly explained its funding requirements, but the European Commission had proposed only half the budget it needed.
She warned that inadequate resources could damage the institution’s reputation in countries where expectations were high but it had been unable to deliver on its commitments.
The EPPO chief prosecutor said that, despite receiving support from some stakeholders in individual cases, she remained concerned about the combination of inadequate funding, delays in revising the legal framework and administrative complexity.
Investigation into EU parliamentary group funds
EPPO is also investigating the alleged misuse of more than 4 million euros by Identity and Democracy, a defunct political group in the European Parliament. Patriots for Europe could be required to repay the group’s debts. Patriots for Europe includes France’s far-right National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen, who is the frontrunner ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election.
Kövesi rejected the suggestion that EPPO should limit its activities when elections are approaching, arguing that doing so would prevent the office from carrying out its mandate.
“If you ask EPPO to abstain and to not do anything because there are elections in Europe, we will not work at all,” she said.

Iran’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity: AEOI spox

Behrouz Kamalvandi, who is also the deputy for the International, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, made the remarks in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran News Network (IRNN) on Wednesday, expounding on the significance of the development of the nuclear energy in the world.
Clarifying the objectives and significance of the presence of the participation of the Iranian delegation in the International Conference of Nuclear Power in South Korea, Kamalvandi emphasized that global nuclear industry is divided into two sectors: energy and non-energy. Nuclear medicine, agriculture, and industry are among the fields where nuclear technology is applied within the non-energy sector, while nuclear power generation constitutes a significant part of the nuclear industry.
The sixth ministerial conference on nuclear energy is currently underway in South Korea, he said, adding, “Perhaps one of the reasons for the increased attention given to this subject in recent years lies in global environmental challenges, issues that have become a serious concern for the international community and further underscore the necessity of shifting toward nuclear energy.”
Given the development of modern technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and the electrification of vehicles, the demand for electricity is steadily increasing. Hence, the expansion of nuclear power generation has become an undeniable necessity, the spokesman stressed.
In technical terms, nuclear-generated electricity is referred to as "baseload" power. It differs in this respect from certain other clean energy sources, such as wind and solar, where power generation depends on atmospheric conditions, the intensity of sunlight, or wind speeds.
In contrast, nuclear power plants provide stable and continuous electricity generation; this characteristic has further underscored the importance of developing such facilities, he continued.
Regarding Iran’s standing in the utilization of modern technologies, Kamalvandi stated, "Given my approximately 14 years of continuous service at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, I can say with confidence that the nation’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and we have now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants."

Ukraine plans to spend 43.8% of its GDP on defense in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:57:28 UTC
21:57:28 KST

- Ukraine’s parliament approved a 2027 budget in a first reading that allocates 4.885 trillion hryvnias, about $107.5 billion, to security and defense.
- Defense spending equals 43.8% of projected GDP and about two-thirds of planned expenditures, with a final vote planned for Nov. 23 to 26.
Ukraine’s parliament has approved in a first reading a 2027 state budget that sets aside 4.885 trillion hryvnias (about $107.5 billion) for security and defense, equal to 43.8% of the country’s projected gross domestic product.
The Verkhovna Rada passed draft budget No. 16000 on Oct. 28 with 239 votes in favor, 25 against and 26 abstentions, Interfax-Ukraine reported. Defense makes up about 66.8% of planned spending of 7.272 trillion hryvnias (about $160 billion), while revenues are forecast at 5.648 trillion hryvnias (about $124 billion), leaving a deficit of nearly 1.7 trillion hryvnias (about $37 billion).
The defense allocation is nearly 12% higher than this year’s, and 1.73 trillion hryvnias (about $38 billion) of it, or 35.7%, comes from European partners and is earmarked for weapons and military equipment. When the government submitted the draft in September, the finance ministry said spending on weapons, ammunition and equipment would reach 2.298 trillion hryvnias (about $50.6 billion), with much of the rest going to pay for troops, Reuters reported at the time.
The 2027 figure builds on a sharp increase this year. In June, parliament added 1.56 trillion hryvnias to Ukraine’s 2026 defense budget, raising it to a record of about 4.4 trillion hryvnias, with much of the extra money backed by the European Union’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan program covering 2026 and 2027. Before that increase, the original 2026 budget had set defense spending at about 2.8 trillion hryvnias, or roughly 27% of GDP.
Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko told lawmakers in September that the country will need more than $52 billion in international financial aid in 2027, and he named Russian assets frozen by Kyiv’s European allies as a possible source to close the gap. The draft budget projects a deficit equal to about 15% of GDP and public debt above 110% of GDP, UNN reported.
Lawmakers filed more than 5,000 amendments to the draft, and proposals to raise spending totaled 8.8 trillion hryvnias, of which 5.8 trillion hryvnias related to defense, according to the finance ministry. Among the changes parliament kept in the first-reading version was an amendment to raise military pay, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, a member of the Rada’s finance committee, said.
Parliament also adopted its budget conclusions, which list the changes the government must make before the second reading. The Cabinet of Ministers will revise the draft, coordinate some items with international partners and send an updated version back to lawmakers, The Kyiv Independent reported.
The second and final reading is planned for Nov. 23 to 26, Zhelezniak said, and the budget must be adopted by Dec. 1 under Ukrainian law.

AI doomsday fears prompt researcher to abandon retirement savings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:55:36 UTC
21:55:36 KST

AI doomsday fears prompt researcher to abandon retirement savings
An AI safety researcher has stopped saving for retirement because he believes artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the next ten years. His warning follows similar predictions from researchers concerned that increasingly powerful systems could escape human control.
Nate Soares, a former Google and Microsoft engineer who now heads the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), discussed his outlook with Atlantic CEO Nicholas Thompson
“I do not save for retirement right now. I have a 401(k) from when I worked at Google, but I haven’t contributed for a decade,” he said, referring to his workplace retirement account.
Asked whether he believed there was a greater-than-50% chance humans would not survive another ten years, Soares stated that it’s “more than 50% that we don’t have a decade at this point.”
“I am not really an AI job apocalypse guy,” he said. “I’m an AI kills all humans guy.”
Soares argued that a sufficiently capable system could develop goals incompatible with human survival, evade oversight, and improve itself. It could then acquire resources and build automated infrastructure allowing it to operate without people, potentially making the planet uninhabitable.
The researcher urged governments to halt the training of general-purpose AI systems, arguing that superintelligence should be treated as a danger comparable to nuclear weapons. At the same time, he supported the use of the technology in narrowly focused applications, including cancer research and safer self-driving cars.
Soares stressed that catastrophe could still be prevented. “I do everything I can to stop this eventuality. I don’t think it’s inevitable,” he said.
Other researchers have voiced similar fears. In September, Anthropic’s Evan Hubinger put the probability of AI killing all humans within a decade above 10%. His colleague Jacob Coxon resigned, accusing developers of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
The warnings come amid repeated disclosures of AI agents acting beyond developers’ instructions. OpenAI reported in July that its agents escaped restricted testing environments and accessed systems belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets. The company has since restricted internet access during training of its most powerful models.
Critics have called for binding government safeguards and a halt to the development of potentially uncontrollable systems. On the other hand, supporters of continued development argue that AI’s benefits outweigh many of the risks.

Iran among 5 countries in eye stem cell transplantation
Unknown

21:52:26 KST

According to published reports by local Iranian media, the treatment is used for certain severe eye injuries caused by chemical and thermal burns. The cost of the treatment is also covered by government funding, according to the head of the Iranian Ophthalmology Society.
Eye stem cell transplantation is a treatment method used to restore the ocular surface in patients whose limbal stem cells, located in the cornea, have been destroyed or impaired by severe injuries, including chemical and thermal burns. These cells play a role in maintaining and regenerating the corneal surface, and damage to them can lead to vision loss.
The scientific secretary of the Iranian Ophthalmology Congress also identified diabetes and its effects on the retina as major threats to eye health. He also warned about the consequences of prolonged computer use and the development of dry eye.
Diabetes can damage the blood vessels in the retina, potentially leading to visual impairment. Dry eye is also a common problem associated with prolonged screen use and may cause symptoms such as burning, a foreign-body sensation, and intermittent blurred vision.
In recent years, Iran has made progress in developing treatments for eye diseases, including corneal transplantation and the use of advanced technologies to restore vision.

Iran to mobilize millions of students for weekly anti-US rallies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:52:00 UTC
21:52:00 KST

Demonstrators carry rifles as they stand during the state-organized ‘Janfada,’ or ‘Sacrifice for Iran,’ military-style parade in Tehran, Iran. (AP Photo)
Iran’s Education Ministry has instructed schools across the country to organize weekly rallies against the United States and Israel, with millions of students expected to take part in gatherings scheduled for Wednesday evenings, according to state media.
The demonstrations are part of Iran’s annual Week Against Arrogance, which culminates on Nov. 4, officially designated as the National Day of Fighting Global Arrogance.
The commemoration marks the 1979 seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran by supporters of the Islamic Revolution, as well as the 1964 exile of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic.
Education Minister Alireza Kazemi said directives had been issued to schools nationwide to hold student gatherings “every Wednesday evening in city squares and streets,” the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA) reported this week.
Kazemi said Wednesday was selected because it falls toward the end of the school week, allowing more students to participate.
He added that responsibilities had been distributed among student organizations to ensure the rallies were coordinated nationwide.
More than 16.5 million students are enrolled in over 124,000 schools across Iran during the 2026-2027 academic year, including more than nine million primary school pupils, according to Tasnim News Agency, which is affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
The program also features a nationwide march, cultural and educational events at schools, and the ringing of an “Anti-Arrogance Bell” across more than 124,000 schools ahead of the Nov. 4 anniversary.
Kazemi described the commemoration and the Week Against Arrogance as an important educational opportunity to introduce students and future generations to what he called “global arrogance and the Israeli regime.”
Referring to the 12-day war as a series of “complex enemy plots” and describing the 40-day conflict as the “Ramadan War,” the minister said this year’s developments and what he characterized as the Iranian people’s resistance had heightened the education system’s responsibilities during the commemorative week.
On Nov. 4, 1979, Iranian students seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran, demanding that Washington return Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, Iran’s deposed shah, who had been admitted to the United States for medical treatment.
The seizure triggered a 444-day hostage crisis, during which 52 Americans were held captive until their release on Jan. 20, 1981. The incident became a major turning point in relations between Washington and Iran’s newly established Islamic Republic.

Fake Iraqi dinars flood markets as Iran border seizures mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:50:53 UTC
21:50:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Fake Iraqi dinars flood markets as Iran border seizures mount
Concerns are mounting in Iraq over the smuggling and circulation of counterfeit currency in local markets, as authorities continue to seize fake Iraqi and foreign banknotes at border crossings and inside the country.
The phenomenon, which has persisted for years, has raised concerns among currency exchange offices and businesses over potential financial losses.
It has also prompted questions about the sources of the counterfeit money, the networks responsible for bringing it into Iraq, and the effectiveness of government measures to prevent it from entering circulation, particularly given the widespread reliance on cash transactions.
Official data show that tens of millions of counterfeit Iraqi dinars have been seized in recent years, including around 12.9 million dinars at the Shalamcheh border crossing in May 2024 and 10 million dinars at the same crossing in September 2019.
In the latest developments, authorities foiled three smuggling attempts this month at the al-Sheeb and Shalamcheh crossings on the border with Iran. One operation resulted in the seizure of 48.5 million counterfeit dinars, alongside a stash of local and foreign banknotes whose value was not disclosed.
The latest seizures coincided with an announcement by Prime Minister's adviser Abdul Amir Taiban that the closure of the al-Sheeb crossing with Iran was prompted by violations involving the entry of counterfeit money, drugs and prohibited goods.
The developments have raised concerns that counterfeit currency could be used to purchase US dollars and smuggle them abroad, potentially causing losses for traders and undermining confidence in cash transactions.
Government tightens measures
Alaa al-Din al-Qaisi, spokesperson for Iraq's Border Crossings Authority, said efforts to combat counterfeit currency smuggling and prevent its entry into the country had intensified.
The measures follow government directives to strengthen border controls and improve coordination between security, customs and intelligence agencies, particularly amid repeated attempts to smuggle counterfeit money into Iraq.
Al-Qaisi told The New Arab that smugglers used various methods, including concealing counterfeit banknotes in travellers' luggage and personal belongings.
Border personnel rely on modern screening and inspection equipment, alongside intelligence monitoring and scrutiny of passenger movements, to detect and thwart such attempts, he said.
The measures extend beyond confiscating counterfeit money to pursuing those involved in smuggling operations.
Al-Qaisi said one recent operation had led to the identification of a third person inside Iraq who had been tasked with receiving the seized money, in coordination with the relevant intelligence authorities.
Risks facing currency exchange offices
Hareth al-Rawi, a currency exchange office owner, warned of the risks posed by counterfeit money circulating in Iraqi markets, particularly 25,000-dinar banknotes, which require diligent scrutiny when received.
Exchange offices face challenges detecting some counterfeit notes, especially during busy periods of cash transactions, he said.
Speaking to The New Arab, al-Rawi said some exchange offices had received counterfeit 25,000-dinar notes, with some only identified as fake after examination using specialised equipment.
The danger lies in the possibility of counterfeit notes being mixed into bundles containing genuine banknotes, making them difficult to detect through rapid inspection, he added.
He said currency dealers had become more cautious, checking bundles of banknotes and scrutinising security features rather than relying on their appearance alone.
He stressed the importance of updating detection equipment, raising public awareness and tightening oversight of entities attempting to circulate counterfeit money.
Suspicions of dollar purchases and smuggling to Iran
Economist Ahmed Sabah suggested that attempts to bring counterfeit currency into Iraq across the Iranian border could be linked to organised activities aimed at circulating fake banknotes in local markets and using them to purchase dollars on the parallel market to then smuggle into Iran.
Speaking to The New Arab, Sabah said smuggling was not limited to official border crossings. Unofficial routes and passages were also used to move money and goods beyond government oversight.
These routes could be exploited to bring counterfeit currency into Iraq, meaning that announced seizures might not reflect the actual scale of the activities, he warned.
Those involved can use counterfeit money to purchase dollars, even at elevated exchange rates, because the banknotes they use are worthless, Sabah said.
This could create illicit demand for foreign currency and add pressure to the parallel market if the operations expand, while transferring losses to currency exchange offices and others who accept the fake money.
Sabah warned that repeated smuggling operations, whether through official crossings or unofficial routes, could contribute to the spread of counterfeit banknotes and weaken confidence in cash transactions.
The lack of official statistics identifying the volume of counterfeit money that has successfully entered circulation makes it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem, he added.

Iraq sacks four top officers over 'insult' to US flag
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq sacks four senior officers over 'insult' to US flag
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed four senior Interior Ministry officers for failing to prevent members of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) from "desecrating the US flag" during a military parade in Baghdad last month, according to an official document obtained by The New Arab.
The decision, believed to be the first of its kind in Iraq, also orders an investigation into the officers over alleged security negligence during celebrations marking the end of the US-led coalition's military presence in the country.
The dismissals were outlined in an official document issued by the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and signed by General Abdul Amir al-Shammari.
Those removed include Brigadier General Dawood Salman Dawood Hassan, director of the second security sector, and Brigadier General Riyadh Jizan Rasan Salloum, an officer at Baghdad's Rusafa Police Command.
Colonel Dhulfiqar Awda Kitab, commander of the fifth Rusafa Emergency Police Regiment, and Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Saleh Muhaidi, an intelligence officer in the same unit, were also dismissed.
According to the document, the officers failed in their security duties by allowing PMF members to desecrate the US flag during a parade held on 30 September to mark "Sovereignty Day".
The document described the incident as an "irresponsible act that harms international relations and Iraq's standing abroad".
Al-Zaidi also instructed security forces in Baghdad's Rusafa district to strengthen their readiness and monitoring to prevent similar incidents during demonstrations and public gatherings.
US flag driven over during military parade
Videos circulated from the Sovereignty Day celebrations showed military vehicles belonging to Iraqi armed factions driving over a US flag laid on the ground in central Baghdad.
The incident drew criticism from US figures and prompted Iraqi authorities to take action.
On 4 October, Major General Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for Iraq's commander-in-chief, announced the arrest of individuals accused of desecrating the flag, stressing that authorities would not tolerate violations of public order or existing laws.
Although disciplinary action against senior officers over such an incident is unprecedented, similar acts have occurred during previous demonstrations and military parades.
Members of the PMF and other armed factions, many aligned with Iran, have repeatedly painted US flags on roads and walked over them during public events as an expression of hostility towards Washington.
The New Arab contacted three officials close to Prime Minister al-Zaidi, all of whom declined to comment formally on the dismissals.
However, one official said the decision was intended to prevent actions that could damage Iraq's relations with Washington or other countries.
"The decision is a government measure aimed at preventing insults to Washington, as well as preventing similar incidents that could target other countries," the official said.
The official added that dismissing the officers would strengthen security forces' ability to enforce discipline and prevent similar incidents.
The arrests have already drawn criticism from Iran-aligned armed groups.
Abdul Qader al-Karbalai, a military aide to the Nujaba Movement, previously described the arrests of PMF members accused of desecrating the US flag as a "dangerous precedent" that could not be ignored.
The group's secretary-general, Akram al-Kaabi, also posted a video on X showing himself walking over a US flag.
He accompanied the footage with the words, "Your crimes are beneath our feet", in an apparent protest against the Iraqi government's arrests.

UK committee voices concern over plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:48:19 UTC
21:48:19 KST

Burak Bir
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A British parliamentary committee has warned that the government plan to build an additional Sizewell nuclear plant would bring a "high level of risk" for the taxpayers over the rest of the century, local media reported Wednesday.
The Parliamentary Public Accounts Committee said the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48 billion ($63.7 billion), The Guardian reported.
This would leave bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8 billion to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12 billion over its 60-year operating life, they warned.
According to the committee, taxpayers and consumers face a "high level of risk," after the government agreed to take a near-45% stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project to the heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plant in Somerset.
Last November, a review by the Nuclear Regulatory Taskforce, established by then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer, concluded that the UK has become the world’s most expensive country in which to build nuclear power plants, urging sweeping reforms to streamline regulation and reduce project costs.
Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the committee chair, said: "The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills."
He urged the government to "focus on the successful delivery of this project."
A government spokesperson said the report "completely ignores that investors are incentivized to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible" through the terms of the deal.
"Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site," the spokesperson was quoted by the British daily as saying.

Indonesia should stop selling palm oil to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:45:45 UTC
21:45:45 KST

Indonesian palm oil is still going to Israel. This week, new reports showed that thousands of tonnes are shipped there every year, even during the genocide in Gaza.
The numbers come from Indonesia’s Ministry of Agriculture and its national statistics agency, Statistics Indonesia (BPS). Indonesia sent about 29,600 tonnes of palm oil products to Israel in 2023, about 22,400 tonnes in 2024 and about 19,500 tonnes in 2025. From January to August this year, another 10,400 tonnes went there, together with almost 4,900 tonnes of coconut products. In those eight months, the two products were worth about $20.8 million.
Two economists from Widyatama University in Bandung found that from 2020 to 2025, Indonesia supplied on average 71 per cent of the crude palm oil that Israel bought from other countries. Other reports say that in some years the share reached 88 per cent. The products include palm olein, palm kernel oil and glycerine. Some shipments may go through Singapore or Hong Kong first.
The amounts have gone down since 2023. But the trade has not stopped.
Palm oil is one of Indonesia’s biggest exports. It is used in cooking oil, soap, snacks and many other products. Indonesia has no official relations with Israel. It does not recognise Israel because Palestinians still live under its occupation. Many Indonesians believe this means the country also does not trade with Israel. They are wrong.
READ: Indonesia slams Israel for discriminating against one of its pilots
The preamble to the 1945 Constitution says that colonialism must end everywhere in the world. Indonesian presidents often repeat these words when they speak about Palestine. Indonesia’s trade with Israel does not match them.
Social media posts have named several large palm oil groups: Wilmar; Sinar Mas, through its company SMART; Musim Mas; and Royal Golden Eagle, through Apical and Asian Agri. These groups sell a large part of Indonesia’s palm oil abroad. But there are no shipping papers yet that show which company sold to Israel. Sinar Mas did not answer questions from reporters.
So the companies should tell the public. If their oil does not go to Israel, they can show it. If it does, people have a right to know.
Some people worry that a ban would hurt Indonesia’s economy and its farmers. But Israel is a very small buyer. The Widyatama study shows that Israel bought less than 0.12 per cent of the crude palm oil Indonesia sold abroad. In 2023, BPS said that Israel took only 0.07 per cent of all Indonesian exports. Farmers would hardly notice.
For Israel, it is different. Indonesia is its biggest supplier of palm oil. This gives Indonesia power, but the government does not use it.
The researchers also found that Indonesian export rules treat Israel like any other country. This includes export taxes, fees and even the short export ban in 2022. Indonesia’s foreign policy says no to Israel. Its trade rules say yes.
In January 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the highest court of the United Nations, ordered Israel to take steps to prevent acts of genocide in Gaza. In September 2025, a UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide there. It called on all countries to stop their companies from helping. Israel rejects these findings.
OPINION: Indonesians must boycott pro-Israel singer Andrea Bocelli’s concert at Borobudur
Last week, Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, urged Indonesians to step up the boycott of Israel during a visit to Jakarta. The Indonesian Ulama Council (MUI) has urged the government to stop trade with Israel. The boycott group BDS Indonesia has called for palm oil exports to end.
Malaysia has already acted. In December 2023, it banned Israeli ships from its ports. It also stopped any ship going to Israel from loading cargo there. Indonesia, by contrast, still allows Israel’s ZIM shipping company into its ports.
Indonesia can act in four ways.
First, the Ministry of Trade should ban exports of palm oil, coconut and their products to Israel.
Second, exporters should declare where their goods will finally go. Then the oil cannot quietly travel through Singapore or Hong Kong. Companies that break this rule should lose their export permits.
Third, the big palm oil groups should publish where their oil is sold, including sales through traders.
Fourth, the House of Representatives (DPR) should hold a public hearing and ask BPS to publish this trade data every month.
Israel may still buy palm oil from another country. But Indonesia would no longer take part. For a country that says it stands with Palestine, this matters.
Selling oil to a country that a UN inquiry says is committing genocide does not fit the values written in the Constitution. It is time to stop.

Huang said the TPP had supported gender equality through policies and concrete actions, including measures under former Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) to recognize same-sex couples’ rights. These included allowing couples to register their partnerships, apply for social housing, and designate each other as medical proxies.
Huang also cited the TPP’s continued efforts in the legislature to amend the Assisted Reproduction Act, saying a more comprehensive legal framework was needed to make equality a reality.
Huang said more work remained to achieve equality, adding that the party would continue working toward a society in which all forms of love are respected and diversity is embraced.
