Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:11:52 UTC
21:11:52 KST

Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
Fire salamanders secretly glow under ultraviolet light, revealing a mysterious ability that could help them communicate and defend themselves.
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology
- Summary:
- Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released.
- Share:
Fire salamanders are among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black and yellow coloring and the poisonous substances they release to deter predators. Despite their familiar appearance, scientists are still uncovering surprising details about their biology. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as "vulnerable" on its Red List of Threatened Species. Fire salamanders typically inhabit damp forests, streams, and mountainous regions, where habitat destruction and fragmentation increasingly threaten their survival.
New research has revealed that fire salamanders possess an unexpected ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet light. The glow is most pronounced on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. Researchers traced the fluorescence primarily to glands in the animals' skin and the substances those glands release. Remarkably, these secretions can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after leaving the salamander's body.
"It is fascinating that such a well-studied species still harbors unknown phenomena like this. It reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools," says Bernat Burriel, a researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona and the study's first author.
The phenomenon occurs when compounds in the salamander's skin absorb ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see, and reemit that energy as visible light. This process produces vivid green and cyan colors. Known as biofluorescence, it requires an outside source of illumination and should not be confused with bioluminescence. Animals such as fireflies produce their own light through chemical reactions, while fluorescent organisms must first absorb light from their surroundings.
Scientists once believed that biofluorescence occurred almost exclusively in marine organisms, with scorpions standing out as an unusual example on land. More recent studies have challenged that assumption, identifying fluorescent properties in a growing variety of terrestrial animals, including reptiles, birds, and amphibians.
Why Do Fire Salamanders Glow?
Although researchers have confirmed that fire salamanders fluoresce, the biological purpose of this ability remains uncertain. One possibility is that the glow serves as a form of communication, helping individuals recognize one another or assess potential mates. Another is that it makes their warning coloration more noticeable to predators.
"Fluorescence meets several criteria that suggest a communicative function. It could help salamanders detect each other in nocturnal or particularly dense environments, or act as an additional defense signal," says Martin Kaltenpoth, director of the Department of Insect Symbiosis at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-author of the study.
The discovery that toxic skin secretions are also fluorescent raises additional questions about how salamanders interact with predators and other animals in their environment.
For now, these proposed functions remain hypotheses. Animals with particularly sensitive vision may be able to detect the green and cyan fluorescence even when it is extremely faint. Humans, however, need a UV lamp to observe the effect.
In the forests where fire salamanders live, nighttime illumination comes primarily from moonlight and starlight. Researchers note that full moonlight contains a greater proportion of ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight, which has a more evenly distributed spectrum. Under these conditions, fluorescence could create small green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings, potentially making them easier for other salamanders to spot.
Could the Fluorescent Glow Warn Predators?
Another possible explanation involves aposematism, a defensive strategy in which animals display conspicuous colors to advertise that they are poisonous or otherwise dangerous. Fire salamanders already use their distinctive yellow and black patterns as warning signals, and fluorescence might provide an additional visual cue.
Scientists established a connection between salamander warning colors and chemical defenses more than a century ago when they identified samandarines. These highly toxic steroidal alkaloids are produced from cholesterol precursors and contribute to the animals' chemical protection.
Despite decades of research into salamander toxins and skin chemistry, the newly observed fluorescence came as a surprise.
"The presence of this fluorescent compound was surprising because salamander skin secretions have been studied chemically for decades, and we were unaware of any published reports on fluorescence," says Andrés Brunetti, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and a co-first author of the study.
The Mysterious Chemical Behind the Glow
One of the biggest unanswered questions concerns the substance responsible for the fluorescence. Researchers have not yet determined its chemical identity, although the evidence suggests it may be a molecule not previously recognized in fire salamanders.
"We still don't know what the compound responsible for this fluorescence is, but everything indicates that it is a molecule unknown until now in this species. Identifying it will be key to understanding its origin and function," adds Salvador Carranza, a researcher at the IBE (CSIC-UPF) and another co-author of the study.
The team is now working to identify and chemically characterize potential compounds responsible for the effect. Determining which molecule produces the glow could help explain how the fluorescence develops and whether it plays a meaningful role in salamander behavior or survival.
A New Discovery With Implications for Amphibian Conservation
Beyond revealing an unexpected feature of a familiar species, the findings demonstrate how new research techniques can uncover biological traits that have escaped scientific attention for decades.
Understanding whether fluorescence influences communication, mating, or predator avoidance could also contribute to conservation efforts. Such information may help researchers better understand the behavior and ecological needs of fire salamanders, which already face significant threats from habitat loss and fragmentation.
The research also involved scientists from the Institute of Subtropical Biology and the Catalan Society of Herpetology. It forms part of a pioneering amphibian conservation project in Catalonia supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.

Timeline: Major Chinese cultural relics returned from overseas in recent years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:40 CST
21:09:40 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The National Gallery of Australia (NGA) handed over two Chinese cultural relics to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration in Canberra on Wednesday.
The two relics are the head of a military official statue and the head of a civil official statue, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127). According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province.
The following is a timeline of major cultural relics returned to China from overseas in recent years:
Sept. 17, 2026:
-- The United States returned 64 Chinese cultural relics and paleontological fossils to China.
May 16, 2025:
-- The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art officially returned the Zidanku Silk Manuscript volumes II and III: Wuxing Ling and Gongshou Zhan from the Warring States period to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration.
Nov. 9, 2024:
-- A total of 56 lost Chinese cultural relics were returned from Italy.
June 27, 2024:
-- The Chinese Embassy in Argentina received 14 pieces of cultural relics returned to China from the South American country.
April 18, 2024:
-- China's relentless quest to retrieve lost cultural relics from overseas received a significant boost, as 38 artifacts were returned by the Manhattan District Attorney's Office. The prized haul comprises mainly Tibetan Buddhist objects spanning from the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368) to the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911).
Feb. 7, 2024:
-- An ancient bronze ritual vessel that had been lost overseas after being stolen 40 years ago finally made its way home.
Unearthed in 1978 at an archaeological site dating back to the late Western Zhou Dynasty (1046-771 BC) in Famen Township of Baoji City, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, the bronze vessel, named "Feng Xingshu Gui" was classified as the top-grade cultural relic of the state.
May 10, 2023:
-- The Consulate General of China in New York received two illegally transported Chinese cultural relics from the Manhattan District Attorney's Office.
The returned cultural relics are two stone-carved tomb beds dating back about 1,100 to 1,600 years, according to the National Cultural Heritage Administration.
Dec. 1, 2020:
-- A bronze horse head sculpture, a treasure of China's Old Summer Palace that went missing after Anglo-French allied forces' looting 160 years ago, returned to its original palace home. ■

In the first three quarters of this year, mainland imports of agricultural products from Taiwan rose 18.5 percent year on year, while fishery product imports increased 35.5 percent, he said.
From April to September, Fujian imported 19,100 tonnes of fishery products from Taiwan, with a total value of 585 million yuan (about 87 million U.S. dollars), up 35.9 percent year on year.
The mainland will continue to share development opportunities with Taiwan compatriots and assist in addressing practical difficulties, Chen said.
The goal is to enable people on both sides of the Strait to gain greater benefits from cross-Strait economic and trade cooperation and integrated development and enjoy better lives, he added. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: WHO regional director highlights China's role in global health
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:09:33 CST
21:09:33 KST

RIYADH, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Hanan H. Balkhy, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean, has highlighted China's contribution to global health, describing the country as an important partner for the WHO.
In an exclusive interview with Xinhua, Balkhy cited China's public health achievements, medical teams working alongside health professionals in other countries, and its capacity to manufacture vaccines, medicines and other health products, calling for stronger cooperation between the WHO and China in areas including access to health products, South-South cooperation and antimicrobial resistance.
The WHO official pointed to China's malaria elimination as an example of how national public health experience can contribute to global health. The WHO certified China malaria-free in 2021, while the country's "1-3-7" surveillance and response model has been incorporated into the organization's technical guidance.
She said stronger regulatory systems, reliable supply chains and sustainable regional manufacturing partnerships, including South-South cooperation, could help developing countries strengthen resilience and improve access to vaccines, medicines, diagnostics and other health technologies.
"No region should be at the back of the queue when the next crisis comes," she said.
Balkhy also highlighted lessons from health emergencies in the Eastern Mediterranean, saying that WHO responses in Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and Afghanistan had reinforced the importance of preparedness, the protection of health workers and facilities, and the maintenance of essential public health services during crises.
Citing Gaza as an example, Balkhy said WHO worked with national authorities and partners to help vaccinate more than 600,000 children after the territory recorded its first paralytic polio case in 25 years in August 2024.
On pandemic preparedness, Balkhy said global health security should be built on strong national capacity backed by international solidarity.
She highlighted surveillance, laboratories, trained health workers, reliable supply chains and trusted relationships with communities as essential elements of preparedness, while stressing that equitable access to vaccines, diagnostics and treatments should be planned for before a crisis.
Meanwhile, Balkhy also warned that antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains a major global health threat.
She said antimicrobial misuse in both human and animal health, together with inadequate infection prevention, poor sanitation, overcrowding and conflict, is accelerating the spread of resistance.
"The gap now is not knowledge; it is implementation," she said, calling for properly funded national action plans covering surveillance, infection prevention and control, responsible antimicrobial use, and reliable access to diagnostics, medicines and new antibiotics.
Addressing broader challenges facing the organization, Balkhy, WHO director-general candidate nominated by Saudi Arabia, called for more predictable and flexible financing, a broader contributor base and clearer responsibilities across the organization's three levels, while stressing the need to protect its scientific independence.
She said the WHO must also demonstrate the importance of international cooperation at a time when multilateralism is under pressure. ■

Germany and Japan will explore possible cooperation on the development of a next-generation fighter jet, Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed on Wednesday.

Switzerland considers direct US arms purchases after problems procuring F-35s from Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:07:41 UTC
21:07:41 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Switzerland is considering buying military equipment directly from US defense companies instead of relying on Washington as an intermediary, following complications involving its F-35 fighter jet purchase, the country's defense procurement chief said Wednesday.
Urs Loher, head of the Federal Office for Defense Procurement (Armasuisse), told Swiss daily Neue Zurcher Zeitung that the experience had exposed weaknesses in the existing procurement system.
"That is one of the key lessons learnt from the F-35 purchase," he said.
Under the US Foreign Military Sales program, Switzerland purchases American military equipment through the US government, leaving buyers with limited options to resolve pricing disputes or seek compensation for delayed deliveries.
Loher said direct contracts could offer greater flexibility, although they would require approval from US authorities.
He suggested that certain components of the Patriot air defense system might be purchased directly from manufacturers, while acquiring advanced fighter jets such as the F-35 through this route would not be feasible.
"As this is a system that has been tried and tested for years, selected components are certainly available directly from the manufacturer," said Loher.
The shift comes as Switzerland faces a five- to seven-year delay in receiving its Patriot missile systems, with Washington prioritizing deliveries to Germany.
Switzerland has already paid more than 1 billion Swiss francs (over $1.2 billion) in advance for the systems.
Loher said the country expects to recover at least part of that amount, although the timing remains uncertain.
Swiss authorities have also assessed an alternative air defense system, with the Federal Council expected to make the final decision.

From Pushkin’s ancestor to Mandela’s envoys: The untold story of Russia-Africa ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:07:05 UTC
21:07:05 KST

From Pushkin’s ancestor to Mandela’s envoys: The untold story of Russia-Africa ties
In 1944, an unusual pavilion dedicated to the Soviet Union opened in Johannesburg, South Africa. Visitors could discover more about life in the USSR, view exhibitions, relax in a tea garden, and even stop by a vodka bar. The pavilion was very popular and attracted a total of about 250,000 visitors. This little-known episode is just one example of the rich and varied history of Russia-Africa relations. From Russian officers at the court of the Ethiopian emperor to African students who studied in Russia under the patronage of Nicholas II, the New Moscow Cossack settlement on the Red Sea coast, and the son of a Russian officer who became one of Ethiopia’s first pilots, we explore some of the highlights of Russia-Africa relations below.
From Peter the Great to New Moscow in Africa
Perhaps the most famous African figure in the history of the Russian Empire is Abram Gannibal, the great-grandfather of the great Russian poet Alexander Pushkin. In the early 18th century, the African boy found himself at the court of Peter the Great, who became his godfather and later sent him to study in France. Gannibal received military training, became an engineer, and eventually rose to the rank of general. Historians still debate the exact location of his birth, with modern-day Cameroon and Eritrea among the possible locations.
However, Gannibal was far from the only African at the Russian court. Africans appeared in Russia as early as the 17th century, and later, a specialized court position was instituted: ‘Arap (Moor) of the Imperial Court’. Some of them feature in paintings depicting the life of Russian monarchs.
For a long time, Russians had a limited understanding of Africa, largely shaped by books and traveler accounts. Russian pilgrims traveled to Egypt, merchants traded with North African ports, and scholars gradually discovered Africa’s geography and history. However, by the late 19th century, interest in Africa began to take on a more practical dimension.
One of the most unusual expressions of this interest was Nikolay Ashinov’s expedition. Ashinov called himself the ataman (leader) of the free Cossacks. In 1889, he landed with a group of like-minded individuals on the shores of what is now Djibouti, proclaiming the creation of a Russian settlement called ‘New Moscow’. They raised the Russian flag over it, but it soon turned out that the territory fell under French colonial interests. French military forces commanded the settlers to abandon the fort; when the latter refused, the French shelled the area and detained the expedition members. The Russian government, which did not support Ashinov’s initiative, distanced itself from the endeavor, and that marked the end of one of the most peculiar attempts at establishing a Russian presence in Africa.
Russians at the court of the Ethiopian emperor
Russia’s relationship with Ethiopia fared much better. Ethiopia was one of the few African nations that managed to retain independence during the era of European colonial expansion. Russia and Ethiopia shared the Christian faith, and Ethiopian Emperor Menelik II viewed Russia as a potential partner that did not seek to encroach on his territories. One of the first Russians to establish personal contact with him was military officer Viktor Mashkov. In 1889, he traveled to Ethiopia (formally as a correspondent for the newspaper Novoye Vremya) and managed to secure an audience with the emperor. Upon returning to St. Petersburg, Mashkov brought back a personal letter from Menelik II to Alexander III, along with gifts, including ceremonial weapons. He later returned to Ethiopia with a reply from the Russian monarch. These visits laid the groundwork for the establishment of official diplomatic relations between the two countries in 1898.
Cooperation swiftly extended beyond diplomacy. Following the Ethiopian army’s victory over the Italians at the Battle of Adwa in 1896, a medical mission from the Russian Red Cross Society arrived in Ethiopia. Menelik II was highly impressed by Russian doctors. According to the reports of Russian diplomat Pyotr Vlasov, during a visit to a hospital in 1898, the emperor didn’t just inspect the wards; he donned a hospital gown, attended a surgical operation, questioned patients, and examined medical instruments. The partnership in the field of healthcare became one of the most enduring traditions in Russia-Ethiopia relations.
The story of the first Ethiopian students in Russia is less well known. In 1897, Menelik II reached out to Nicholas II, requesting that several young Ethiopians be accepted to study in Russia. The Russian emperor agreed, and five young men, aged between 17 and 20, made their way to Russia. They were supposed to study medicine and various trades and then return home. However, the Russian education system wasn’t adapted to the needs of African students. For example, two of the young men were expected to enter a vocational school that typically admitted boys aged 12 to 15. The new students were significantly older and didn’t speak Russian, necessitating special language classes and high-level discussions about funding. In April 1898, Finance Minister Sergey Witte appealed to Nicholas II to allocate 250 rubles annually for the education of the students and an additional 1,200 rubles for their instructor. Sixty years before the establishment of the Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia, the Russian emperor personally supported this small group of African students.
Equally intriguing is the story of the Babichev family. In the late 19th century, a Russian officer named Ivan Babichev traveled to Ethiopia and decided to stay there permanently. He joined Menelik II’s service, married an Ethiopian woman, and eventually rose to the rank of fitawrari (commander). His son, Mishka Babichev, became even more famous. When soon-to-be emperor Haile Selassie began building Ethiopia’s aviation program in the late 1920s, young Babichev became one of its pioneers. He received flight training in France and became one of Ethiopia’s first military pilots. He later played a significant role in establishing the country’s civil aviation. After the Second World War, Mishka Babichev was appointed as Ethiopia’s diplomatic representative to the Soviet Union.
From Transvaal to the Soviet pavilion in Johannesburg
In the same period, the attention of Russian society also turned to South Africa. The Anglo-Boer War broke out in 1899. In the course of this war, two small republics – Transvaal and the Orange Free State – fought against the British Empire. The Russian public strongly sympathized with the Boers (Afrikaners, descendants of Dutch settlers); newspapers extensively covered the situation on the front lines, charity drives were organized, and some Russians volunteered to fight in South Africa. Approximately 200 individuals from Russia fought alongside the Boers. Among them was Evgeny Maximov, who led a contingent of foreign volunteers and was promoted to the rank of general by the Boers, as well as Aleksey Guchkov, who would later become chairman of the State Duma and Minister of War in the Provisional Government.
The most enduring impact of the Anglo-Boer War on Russian culture is reflected in the song ‘Transvaal, Transvaal, my homeland, you’re all on fire!’ which became popular in Russia at the turn of the century. The song, based on Galina Galina’s poem, quickly gained popularity throughout Russia. It was later often heard in movies.
Decades later, the relationship between Russia and South Africa took an unexpected turn. During WWII, the Soviet Union and the Union of South Africa became allies. In South African cities, various organizations emerged to collect aid for the USSR, and the Society of Friends of the Soviet Union held large-scale events to support the efforts.
In July 1944, the University of the Witwatersrand hosted a two-day congress promoting African-Soviet friendship that brought together about 600 delegates. In November 1944, a Soviet pavilion opened in Johannesburg, featuring exhibition halls, a tea garden, and even a vodka bar. But South African support for the USSR extended beyond donations and exhibitions. In July 1944, Dmitri Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony, known as the Leningrad Symphony, was performed in Johannesburg, and two months later, in Cape Town. Proceeds from both concerts were sent to the Soviet Union.
Nine students and Mandela’s secret mission
In the post-war years, collaboration in the field of education became a cornerstone of Soviet policy in Africa. In 1960, the Peoples’ Friendship University was established in Moscow. It was later named after Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of independent Congo. However, African students studied not only in Moscow, but also in cities throughout the USSR, such as Leningrad, Kiev, Kharkov, Odessa, Minsk, Voronezh, and many others. For many of these students, the trip to the Soviet Union was the first journey outside their home country and an opportunity to experience an entirely different culture and lifestyle. Everything was new – from Russian winters and dorm living to Soviet cafeterias and the challenge of learning a new language.
In January 1962, nine young activists from the African National Congress movement gathered in a house in Johannesburg. To their surprise, Nelson Mandela, who had gone underground, showed up at the meeting. The activists planned to go abroad for military training, but Mandela explained that the movement had other priorities. He tasked them with traveling to the Soviet Union to learn how free education, healthcare, affordable housing, and public transportation were organized, hoping this knowledge would aid in building a future democratic South Africa.
To cross the border discreetly, the young activists posed as a table tennis team headed to a tournament. After an extensive journey across Africa and Europe, they finally reached the USSR. Among them was Sindiso Mfenyana, who traveled to study economic planning in Kiev. But for him, the trip proved life-changing in more ways than one; while traveling by boat to a Black Sea resort, he met Rita, a Soviet woman studying aerospace engineering. They began corresponding, and in June 1963, they were married in Kiev. Later, they welcomed a son, whom they named Nikita. Years later, Mfenyana became full secretary to parliament in democratic South Africa.
The story of Mfenyana isn’t unique. In 1981, around 34,000 African students were enrolled in Soviet universities. In total, about 90,000 Africans received higher education in the USSR from 1960 to 1990. Among these graduates were future ministers, diplomats, and presidents. Angolan President Joao Lourenco studied at the Lenin Military-Political Academy, Ghanaian President John Mahama attended the Institute of Social Sciences under the Central Committee of the Communist Party, and Namibian President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah graduated from the Higher Komsomol School. This means that some of the officials present today during negotiations with Russian officials had spent their youth in Moscow, studying at Soviet universities, and being immersed in Russian culture.
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia-Africa relations entered a period of minimal engagement. However, certain connections persisted through personal relationships, joint projects, and educational ties. In the 2000s, Russian companies began re-establishing a presence in Africa, including in countries where Soviet geologists, engineers, and educators had worked decades earlier. The first Russia-Africa summit took place in Sochi in 2019, followed by a second summit in St. Petersburg in 2023.
Today, Russia-Africa relations encompass more than just official meetings and economic initiatives. Approximately 35,000 African students are enrolled in Russian universities, and it’s increasingly common to see Africans working in the fields of trade, services, and delivery in various Russian cities. Meanwhile, the number of Russians traveling to African nations is gradually rising. These daily interactions lay the groundwork for new friendships, familial bonds, and both professional and personal relationships. In the future, these stories may be as captivating to read as the adventures of Russian travelers in Ethiopia or the experiences of African students in the Soviet Union.

In Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, where Israeli airstrikes remain a regular occurrence despite a cease-fire, residents were closely following Israel’s election results, hoping that anyone but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would lead the next government.
“All of their policies toward Gaza are tough, but we choose the lesser of two evils,” resident Ayman Ahmed said.
Ahmed said he hoped Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, would prevail, adding that he supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s roadmap for Gaza.
The plan calls for disarming Hamas and installing a new U.S.-backed government. It also requires Israel to withdraw its forces from the territory and allow reconstruction to begin.
Most of Gaza’s 2 million people remain displaced, living in the bombed-out ruins of their former homes or in squalid tent camps.
Netanyahu agreed to Trump’s plan but never implemented it beyond the initial stage, which involved a partial withdrawal and increased aid in exchange for the return of the remaining hostages held by Hamas, both living and dead.
The plan has been largely frozen for nearly a year.
In the rubble-strewn streets near Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, Mohammed Abed said a Netanyahu victory would be seen as a triumph for his agenda but that he did not expect major changes regardless of who took power.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, favors tough responses to “Israel’s enemies.”
“An Eisenkot victory will not dramatically change the situation, because their policies are almost similar,” Abed said. “In the end, it will be the same.”
Underscoring Abed’s pessimism, two strikes in Khan Younis on Wednesday killed one man and wounded at least six others, according to health officials at Nasser Hospital. Israel’s military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
More than 1,550 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by the Israeli military since the cease-fire between Israel and Hamas began in October 2025, according to the blockaded Palestinian enclave’s Health Ministry.
The ministry says women and children account for roughly half of those killed.
The Gaza genocide began following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages.
Israel’s retaliatory offensive killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza.
Hasan al-Masri, who was displaced from his home in Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, said he desperately hoped the election would bring change to the territory.
“We pray to God that these elections bring a positive outcome for us,” he said. “We have been utterly devastated; nothing remains. They have killed our children, destroyed our homes, and everything we had is gone.”
The future of Gaza was barely discussed during Israel’s election campaign. The only major candidate to advocate for a two-state solution was Yair Golan, head of the small Democrats party.
Asked whether the prospect of a future Palestinian state was something Gaza residents hoped for, Ahmed said, “only people outside Gaza care about these topics,” adding that their main concern was finding enough food to eat.
He said he feared a Netanyahu victory would bring more war and suffering.
“We support any effort to bring down Netanyahu,” he said.

Drones hit container ship off Bulgaria, crew safe and ashore
Reuters, Oct 28 - Sea drones struck a container ship off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Wednesday, the ship's owner and the government said, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised concerns about the growing scope of Russia's war in Ukraine.
It was not clear who carried out the attack on the Greek ship that was sailing under the Liberian flag in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ), or what the vessel's 421 containers were carrying.
"A container ship was hit...with three naval drones, approximately 21 miles southeast of Shabla," Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters on the sidelines of a regional security meeting.
Bulgaria's transport ministry said in a statement that four naval and police boats had been dispatched to assist the vessel, which was travelling from the Israeli port of Haifa to Constanța in Romania, and that the 18 crew members had been evacuated.
The ship's owner, Contships Management, confirmed the attack and a company official said all the crew of 14 Filippinos and 4 Ukrainians, were safe and ashore.
A maritime security source with knowledge of the matter said the ship had been badly damaged and was listing.
INTERNATIONAL CONCERN
Drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria have likely killed some two dozen international seafarers in recent weeks, according to government statements on missing crew members. At least six merchant vessels have been attacked.
The strikes have been in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, an area that stretches beyond Bulgaria's waters but where the country holds sole rights to explore and manage resources.
The attacks have prompted international condemnation and concern about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine. Bulgaria, a member of the European Union and NATO, has sought allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Ukraine has blamed the attacks on Russia and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appear to benefit Russia, but Moscow has denied involvement.
In a sign of the international concern, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler warned Russia and Ukraine on Wednesday against carrying out attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. He said Ankara reserved the right to take legal action against the strikes. REUTERS

How TIME and Statista Determined America's Best Brands, According to Each Generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:05:28 KST

The ranking "America's Best Brands, According to Each Generation" is based on surveys of more than 33,000 Americans, featuring Baby Boomers, Gen X, Millennials, and Gen Z. The analysis was primarily based on user experience, customer service, reputation for quality, and likelihood of recommendation.
Methodology
The America’s Best Brands According to Each Generation 2026 rankings were identified from the results of an independent survey of participants who have either made purchases, used services, or looked for further information about a brand within the past three years either in person or online. Customers evaluated several brands: in total over 220,000 cross-demographic evaluations were collected.
The survey was conducted on brands and service providers from 112 categories, providing results for a broad spectrum of customer experiences across demographic groups via a national online panel. For each category, the most relevant brands were included in the scope of the survey according to user experience, customer service, and reputation for quality.
For most categories, brands must be available to U.S. consumers. Categories involving location-dependent services must be present in at least two census regions. In total, the survey took an average of 10 minutes to complete, and the field period ran from March to May 2026.
The final assessment and rankings were based on the Likelihood of Recommendation (50% of the final score) and three equally weighted evaluation criteria (also 50% of the final score):
1. User Experience: measures the end-to-end journey, including easy access, clear information, meaningful personalization and intuitive technology.
2. Customer Service: measures the speed of responses, the knowledge and relevance of the support provided, and the accessibility of priority options.
3. Reputation for Quality: measures consistent and reliable performance that foster trust and safety, alongside transparent communication regarding return policies and warranties where applicable.
The top 3 to 5 brands based on category size receiving the highest scores in each category and generation were awarded as America's Best Brands According to Each Generation 2026. See the full list here.
Disclaimer:
The rankings are comprised exclusively of brands that are eligible regarding the scope described in this document. A mention in the ranking is a positive recognition based on customers’ evaluations and the data sources available at the time. The ranking is the result of an elaborate process which, due to the interval of data-collection and analysis, is a reflection of the last three calendar years. Furthermore, events following August 31st, 2026, and/or pertaining to individual persons affiliated/associated to the brands were not included in the metrics. As such, the results of this ranking should not be used as the sole source of information for future deliberations. The information provided in this ranking should be considered in conjunction with other available information about the brands or, if possible, accompanied by a visit to the brand's stores or websites. The quality of brands that are not included in the rankings is not disputed.

The Blood Between Us: Syria After the Fall of Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:03:03 UTC
21:03:03 KST

On his way to the airport to leave Damascus, Robin Yassin-Kassab’s car is stopped at a checkpoint by a guard who is friendly, briefly checks the boot and then waves them through. Yassin-Kassab was visiting the new Syria under the transitional government, and his driver told him that under Bashar Al-Assad there had been six checkpoints operated by different security agencies on the route to the airport. You had no way of knowing who you might come across or if any of them would take you away. Now there is one checkpoint and the guards are polite. Yassin-Kassab writes: “Friendly checkpoints are most definitely better than terrifying checkpoints, and one checkpoint is better than six. The difference between this year and last is the difference between the earth and the skies. But still a checkpoint remains to be dismantled.”
The Blood Between Us: Syria After the Fall of Assad is Robin Yassin-Kassab’s account of his travels in, and analysis of, the new Syria. The book has bleak parts covering events such as the March 2025 coastal massacre against Alawites and the July 2025 massacre of Druze in Suwayda, but it also has many hopeful moments, including elections and civil society initiatives. But fundamentally, the book is not purely musings on where Syria is going; if read closely, it is a subtle call to action.
Syria is a pluralistic society, and the pressure of the 2011 revolution was towards democratisation. Syria can still fulfil this desire. Indeed, as Yassin-Kassab observes throughout the book, there are many indicators of Syria’s democratisation, but he is clear-eyed about the challenges, and critical, honest and nuanced about what is unfolding in the Mediterranean country. Whether optimistic or pessimistic, Yassin-Kassab dismantles simplistic thinking and offers concrete analysis.
Like most Syrians and observers of Syria, Yassin-Kassab did not expect the Assad regime to collapse when it did. As he recounts, on Friday 29 November 2024, he and his family were in Edinburgh for the day visiting the oddly appropriate Museum of Illusions. While he was walking through a swirling light vortex installation and losing his balance, events in Syria were taking a sharp turn. A rebel offensive that had begun a few days before had captured the city of Aleppo and driven the Assad regime into retreat.
When he arrived home, Yassin-Kassab heard the news and, like many, was in a state of disbelief: “Like most Syrians, however near or far they were from Syria, I’d spent most of the previous decade absorbing the fact the Syrian Revolution had been defeated…Now, as I watched videos of men and women running through the open gates of Aleppo’s prisons, I thought of the multiverse theory…Tonight it felt like not only I but all of us had jumped from one existence into a parallel universe, one which a lot more was possible.”
BOOK REVIEW: A History of Modern Syria
In some ways, this is a key message of the book. Syria defies expectation, and it remains a place where more is possible than meets the eye. “The change was radical and total. Nothing like it had happened before in the Arab World. Against all odds, it was the most successful, most thorough revolution of the twenty-first century.”
But as Yassin-Kassab observes, the new Syria is still afflicted by old wounds, and trauma still runs through society. Sectarianism remains an issue in the country, and it has led to catastrophic events, including two major massacres and a number of violent incidents.
Unlike some, Yassin-Kassab does not essentialise the sectarian violence; he does not see it as centuries in the making, and he demonstrates the ways in which sectarianism was utilised in recent history, from the French mandate to the Assad regime. Understanding this history and addressing the problem is essential for building a Syria for all Syrians.
The new Syria offers the possibility for this type of dialogue to happen, as Yassin-Kassab’s conversations with other Syrians reveal. In one conversation, a man tells Yassin-Kassab that there is now a situation where people from different sects are sitting together and openly talking about their experiences. This would not have been possible in 2024 under the old regime.
The Blood Between Us blends personal memoir with sobering analysis of the first year of a country in transition. It makes for a thoughtful reflection on both the hopes and fears of millions of people. It doesn’t offer simple answers, but it does give us very real reasons to pay close attention to what unfolds there. Syria is a place where hope and despair, trauma and resilience brush up against one another, and I can think of no book that captures this quite like The Blood Between Us.

The 70th Anniversary of Italy’s Permanent Mission in Geneva

At the Palais des Nations in Geneva, the long history of collaboration between Italy and the United Nations is currently being celebrated with the opening of an exhibition that traces its key moments, thanks to the extraordinary documentary and multimedia collection provided by the Farnesina, the Istituto Luce, and the UN Office in Geneva.
                                    
On December 14, 1955—as a statement from the Mission recalls—Italy acceded to the United Nations Charter, becoming a member of the Organization, and in 1956 the Italian Permanent Mission began its work in Geneva: “70 years of continuous commitment to supporting multilateral dialogue and promoting a global order based on rules and the protection of human rights.”
As noted by the Permanent Representative, Luigi Maria Vignali, the exhibition tells a story rich in major diplomatic events in international Geneva and bears witness to Italy’s active participation in multilateralism. Geneva has, after all, always been inextricably linked to Italy’s history, from the Risorgimento to the welcoming of anti-fascist exiles, who later became the founding fathers of the Republic.
                                    
The exhibition—as the press release specifies—includes an extremely valuable first edition of Cesare Beccaria’s *Treatise on Crimes and Punishments*, confirming Italy’s long tradition of developing a body of international norms to protect human dignity. And it is precisely through the United Nations that Italy has taken decisive steps in its campaign for the abolition of the death penalty, as summarized in various documents on display.
                                    
Just a few days before the International Day commemorating the founding of the United Nations, the event thus traces the deep connections between Italy and the diplomatic community (and beyond) in the city of Geneva, the press release concludes.

Amazon Adds an Alexa Photo Frame and a Bedside Clock to Its Echo Family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:01:00 UTC
21:01:00 KST

Panos Panay, Amazon’s senior vice president of Devices and Alexa, says a couple hundred million people now use Alexa+, the revamped version of the decade-old voice assistant, on its Echo devices. He says people talk to Alexa+ two to three times more than before its AI glow-up, cook with it five times more, listen to music three times more, and create routines twice as much.
To keep that momentum going, Amazon has new Echo products to deliver a richer Alexa+ experience, including minor refreshes on existing hardware and entirely new categories. Announced Wednesday and available for purchase now, they include the Echo Dot ($100), Echo Studio With Home Camera ($250), Echo Show 16 ($500), Echo Time ($200), and the first Alexa Photo Frame ($200).
“I don’t think anyone’s really doing AI at all in the home, and if they are, they aren’t doing it well,” Panay says at an intimate media-only event in New York City. As people have “deeper” conversations with Alexa+, Panay says devices need to be in premium shape—a strategy Amazon has been focusing on after announcing more premium Kindles and Alexa Tablets in early October.
You can see that premiumization in the hardware pricing: The Echo Dot—once the affordable, entry-level $50 smart speaker—now starts at $100. That’s higher than the marked-up prices on existing Amazon devices from this summer, which the company blamed on the memory shortage.
Echo Dot
Panay says Amazon has sold more than 100 million Echo Dots, and in 2026 alone, people spent more than a trillion minutes listening to music on the diminutive orb. So, the main goal for the new Dot? Boost the sound. The full-range driver reportedly delivers 50 percent stronger bass performance and crisper vocals.
With four beamforming microphones (up from three) and Amazon’s AZ3 chip, Alexa can isolate your voice in a noisy environment and track your commands more effectively. It also has Omnisense like last year’s Echo Dot Max, which can sense the environment to, say, detect when you walk into the home and turn on the lights.
The Dot now supports the Matter standard and works as a Thread border router, turning it into a hub for setting up and controlling smart home devices. If you have an Eero router, it can also turn into a Wi-Fi extender.
It comes in four colors, three of which are calming pastels. Amazon’s design head Chris Green tells WIRED that’s intentional, to evoke a calm, softer aesthetic, citing recent data showing nearly half of US adults are stressed once a week. Alternatively, you can buy the Kids Echo Dot, which has the same hardware but in fun designs, plus Amazon Kids+ for age-appropriate content.
Echo Studio With Home Camera
The new Echo Studio is the first Amazon smart speaker with a camera—a feature once limited to Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays—allowing Alexa to identify the person making the command (along with voice recognition) for more personalized responses. That’s especially important these days as Alexa+ can connect to email or calendar apps and needs to verify who’s speaking before divulging personal information.
It also lets you use Live View to check in on your home and monitor pets, or video call friends and family. With no display on the Echo Studio, you’ll need to pair it with a Fire TV or use your smartphone to view the camera feed of the person you’re calling—as seen in the picture above when Panay used the Studio to Drop In on his dad. This “Drop In” feature will arrive later through a software update.
The camera enables what Amazon calls “Advanced Room Adaptation,” which tunes the sound to the room. Even if you move around the space, the volume will stay consistent. And it can also be used for visual intelligence—just like how you might use your phone to identify an object with Google Lens, you can pick up an object and show it to Alexa through the camera, and it can identify it and answer questions. For example, show a board game you’ve decided to play and ask Alexa to explain the rules.
While no privacy shutter physically blocks the camera, you can press a button to turn off the mics and camera, and an LED lights up when the camera is on and in use. If you don’t want yet another camera in your home, Amazon says you can buy the standard Echo Studio. The speaker is otherwise very similar to the 2025 model and is meant to be the top-end option for folks who want even better audio quality.
Alexa Photo Frame
Digital photo frames are a well-established category now, with companies like Aura and Skylight leading the market. Now Amazon’s entering the fray with the Alexa Photo Frame. Yes, you can still talk to Alexa just like any other Echo device, but the 10-inch display will always show your photos—nothing else. The bottom edge lights up when Alexa activates, and you can ask it the weather or to show you pictures of your dog last Halloween.
The caveat is that you need to use Amazon Photos. Once your images are in Amazon Photos, you can choose who and what appears on the frame—even newly captured photos so Mom can see the latest pics from your vacation before she even asks. The display is a semi-matte, anti-glare touchscreen that adjusts brightness based on the room’s ambient light, and you can swipe the screen to see more images. Tap an image to play a voice note tied to the picture—that’s something you can add in the Amazon Photos app, but a future update will let users add voice notes to images straight on the Alexa Photo Frame.
Smart curation happens in the background to choose the best photos. For example, if you have a lot of vertical images, it will stack them side by side and group familiar faces together. Maybe that means a pic of your kid when they were 8 years old, and the pic on the right of when they’re 14. (Though Google has been doing this for years on its smart displays.) Alexa knows to choose pictures of people smiling, and understands timing—you’ll be served last year’s Halloween pictures around this time of year.
Amazon says it’s easy to set up for someone else—like your grandparents—and the frame comes in three styles: black, birch, or walnut.
Echo Time
The other entirely new product is the Echo Time. It’s similar in size and sound to the Echo Dot, but with a digital clock screen. No cameras here—it’s designed for the bedside table, after all—and the 3.2-inch circular display can dim as low as 0.3 nits (the same as Apple’s new HomeView).
It’s hardly the first time Amazon has dabbled with clocks on an Echo (see the Echo Spot), and Amazon even sold a bedside sleep tracker before discontinuing it barely a year later.
The Echo Time doesn’t track your sleep, but it can help you start a bedtime routine as you wind down. The embedded ultrasonic transducer can detect your breathing to identify when you’re in a light sleep stage and gently wake you up within 10 to 60 minutes of your alarm, rather than forcing you out of deep sleep. These “Smart Alarms” are increasingly common on fitness trackers, like Google’s Fitbit Air, but the pitch here is that you don’t need a gadget on your wrist. Sadly, these features work only for the person closest to the Echo Time; with two people in bed, you’ll need two Echo Time units—one on each nightstand.
You can choose from hundreds of clock faces, set up alarms with Alexa+, and ask the assistant to remind you about certain things when it wakes you up—like grabbing lunch from the fridge before heading out. Alexa can play soothing soundscapes to lull you to sleep like a sound machine. And when you wake up, you can tap the top of the device to snooze it (up to four times).
There’s a Kids Echo Time with wacky designs and more limited features constrained to Amazon’s Kids+ service. Kids can set their own alarms, ask for the weather forecast, and customize clock faces, but the main highlight is Sleep Studio. This connects to content from apps like Calm, Headspace, and Moshi to help kids wind down and fall asleep.
Echo Show 16
Finally, there’s the Echo Show 16. Yes, it’s a bigger smart display, but Panay says Amazon has redesigned the entire experience from the ground up. This specific model is designed to be wall-mounted, though you can buy a kickstand if you’d prefer. It starts at $500, but Amazon has introductory pricing of $400; the version with the Nanomatte anti-glare display (like the one on the Alexa Tablet Pro 12) costs $550.
It has slimmer bezels, a thinner frame, and an entirely new audio system with eight woofers and two tweeters. The 13-megapixel camera can supposedly identify people from up to 17 feet away, so you won’t have to walk really close to the screen to see your personalized information. It also supports night vision, so you can use Live View to check in on your home and still see in the dark.
A full built-in Fire TV experience lets you watch as much content as you want while cooking, or follow along with recipes with Alexa. One big focus of the redesign was letting users prioritize the features they use the most. Want to use it as a smart home controller? There’s a dashboard that shows all your controls as your primary “Screen Style.” Parents who prefer to use it as a calendar can set the “Family Organizer” screen as the main display. Or just let it turn into a digital photo frame with the Photos Screen Style.
More unique is the AI-generated interface Amazon is debuting with Alexa+ called “Neo.” Instead of a basic chat transcript like most other chatbots, Alexa+ will create charts, generate images, and offer other visuals to zhuzh up its responses during more complex conversations. (That’s something Google and OpenAI have also played up with recent updates to Search and ChatGPT.) These “Cards" will also appear in your Alexa app so you can revisit them at any time.
A Reuters report earlier this year revealed details that Amazon was working on a smartphone, codenamed Transformer, with Alexa+ as the focus of the experience and a generative user interface. “Neo” on the Echo Show 16 gives us a first glimpse of what that might look like, and paired with many of the Alexa+ features introduced on the recent Alexa Tablet Pro 12, it feels like the Amazon smartphone is closer than ever.
I asked Panay point-blank whether Amazon was making a phone, and while he said there was “no intent," he pointed out that all of the new software experiences are “scalable.” He then asked to look at the iPhone Duo I was holding and remarked that it was similar in size to the Surface Duo, which Panay helmed at Microsoft. There may be “no intent” on paper, but it sure seems like he wants to make a phone again.

A strong emotional bond with a mother predicts resilience after childhood trauma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

People who experience childhood abuse exhibit a wide variety of biological, psychological, and social outcomes in adulthood. While trauma often leaves lasting scars, many individuals manage to demonstrate remarkable resilience. A large new study published in Stress and Health found that early factors like a strong emotional bond with a mother figure and lower amounts of sedentary time predict better adult adaptation following childhood trauma. These results highlight the need to target specific lifestyle habits and family dynamics to support vulnerable adolescents.
The concept of resilience describes how some individuals manage to adapt and function well despite experiencing severe stress or trauma. Historically, health researchers have looked at physical health, mental health, or social success in isolation. The biopsychosocial model offers a broader framework by suggesting that biological, psychological, and social factors constantly influence one another to shape a person’s overall well-being.
Early life adversity can cause a cascade of physiological changes that disrupt the body’s stress response systems. This accumulated physical toll is often called allostatic load. When a child experiences ongoing abuse, their body stays in a constant state of high alert.
Over time, the stress hormones that help them survive the immediate threat begin to damage their cardiovascular and immune systems. This can leave individuals vulnerable to later biological issues, such as heart disease or metabolic problems. It can also increase the risk of psychological conditions like depression, along with social difficulties like failing to secure a stable income.
To understand how these different areas of health align or diverge as people grow up, Yuxiao Zhao and colleagues at the Shanghai Mental Health Center and Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine set out to track these outcomes together. They wanted to identify different patterns of adjustment in adulthood following childhood abuse. They also aimed to see if specific behaviors or social environments during adolescence could predict which pattern a person might eventually fall into.
The researchers analyzed data from a large longitudinal project called the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health. This dataset tracked 5,112 participants from adolescence, beginning between the ages of 11 and 21, into early adulthood, ending between the ages of 24 and 33. During the adulthood phase of the project, participants answered questions about any history of emotional, physical, or sexual abuse by caregivers before age 18.
Emotional abuse included feeling unwanted or unloved. Physical abuse included being hit or thrown down. Sexual abuse included being forced into sexual contact.
To assess biological health, trained interviewers visited participants in their homes to collect physiological data. They measured blood pressure, heart rate, waist circumference, and body mass index. They also took blood samples to check cholesterol, blood sugar, and markers of immune system function.
These measurements were combined into a single score representing cardiometabolic risk. The researchers measured adult psychological health using a standardized depression questionnaire that asked how often participants felt sad, bothered, or happy over the previous week. They evaluated social functioning by looking at educational attainment, ranging from less than high school to college graduate, and personal income levels.
Finally, the research team looked back at data collected during the first wave of the study, when the participants were adolescents. This earlier information included demographic details and self-reported lifestyle habits. For example, participants estimated how many hours they spent watching television, watching videos, or playing computer games during the past week to measure sedentary behavior.
The survey also asked about the quality of parent-child relationships, having participants rate their feelings of warmth and relationship satisfaction with their parents. They used a statistical technique called latent profile analysis to organize this information. This method identifies hidden patterns within large datasets, grouping people who share similar characteristics.
By applying this technique, the researchers could categorize participants based on their combined history of childhood abuse and their adult health outcomes. The research team then used a statistical tool called multinomial logistic regression to see which adolescent factors predicted membership in the adult profiles. This allowed them to isolate the impact of specific variables while adjusting for overlapping influences.
The statistical analysis revealed five distinct profiles among the participants. The majority of the sample fell into a low-risk group with positive adult outcomes. A second group experienced low levels of abuse but still struggled with high depression and lower income in adulthood.
A third, small group reported medium levels of abuse but showed the worst outcomes across all biological, psychological, and social categories. The researchers noted that this group also experienced high family income strain during adolescence. Financial hardship might combine with abuse to cause widespread health problems across multiple physical and mental systems.
The remaining two groups reported high levels of childhood abuse. One of these high-risk groups suffered from poor mental and social health in adulthood. The other high-risk group, which made up roughly 13 percent of the total sample, demonstrated strong resilience.
Despite their trauma, these resilient individuals exhibited healthy psychological and social functioning as adults. When looking at the adolescent predictors, the researchers found that biological sex and family income played a role in future outcomes. Female participants and adolescents from lower-income families were more likely to end up in the groups characterized by poor psychological and social health.
Lifestyle habits also emerged as strong predictors of adult well-being. Adolescents who spent more time engaged in sedentary behaviors, such as watching television or playing video games, had a higher chance of poor adult outcomes. Physical activity, measured separately by the frequency of engaging in sports, did not show a protective effect.
This suggests that sedentary behavior acts as an independent risk factor for poor health, separate from a simple lack of exercise. Family dynamics provided another layer of protection. Having a close, warm relationship with a mother figure during adolescence predicted positive adult outcomes.
Adolescents who reported feeling emotionally close to their mothers were much more likely to show resilience in adulthood. Other parenting factors, such as the amount of time spent together or the frequency of communication, did not show a similar protective effect. This indicates that the emotional bond is more impactful than simply sharing activities.
These findings have practical implications for public health and clinical interventions. Addressing the consequences of childhood trauma often requires looking beyond basic mental health counseling. Strategies that encourage adolescents to reduce their sedentary screen time could provide physical and psychological benefits. Helping families build warmer emotional connections, even in the presence of other stressors, might foster better long-term adaptation.
Retrospective reports of abuse can be influenced by memory biases, as adults may misremember or reinterpret childhood events. The study measured the total amount of abuse but did not pinpoint exactly when the maltreatment happened. Because the exact timing is unknown, it is impossible to say whether a warm relationship with a mother preceded the abuse or happened afterward.
A close maternal relationship might help heal the effects of trauma, or it might simply reflect a period of safety before the abuse began. Future studies will need to track the exact timing of childhood adversity to map out how early protective factors actually work over time.
The study, “Profiles of Childhood Abuse and Biopsychosocial Outcomes in Adulthood: A Nationally Representative Sample Analysis,” was authored by Yuxiao Zhao, Jingyi Liu, Wenhong Cheng, and Xiaoning Sun.

Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:17 UTC
21:00:17 KST

Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- Istanbul Technical University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered evidence of a previously unknown volcanic system that formed roughly 100 million years ago in what is now northwestern Iran. The discovery reveals a missing chapter in the region's geological history and offers new clues about the powerful tectonic forces that shaped ancient oceans and continents.
Mountain ranges contain valuable records of Earth's distant past, preserving traces of vanished oceans, shifting continents, and the geological processes that transformed the planet over millions of years. However, these records are often difficult to interpret because later tectonic activity, erosion, and layers of buried sediment can conceal evidence of much older events.
An international team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has now identified remnants of an ancient continental magmatic arc that had previously gone unrecognized. Named the Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc, the system formed during the Late Cretaceous period in a region that is now part of the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone.
The research, published in Geoscience Frontiers, indicates that the volcanic system was active approximately 101 to 97 million years ago, when the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean was undergoing major geological changes. Over time, tectonic deformation, erosion, burial beneath sedimentary basins, and a younger episode of volcanic activity during the Eocene obscured much of the evidence of its existence.
Ancient Rocks Reveal a Lost Volcanic System
To reconstruct this overlooked chapter of Earth's history, the researchers examined volcanic and plutonic rocks collected from multiple locations across northwestern Iran. Much of their investigation focused on formations along the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault.
The team used several advanced techniques to determine when the rocks formed and where their original materials came from. These included zircon U-Pb geochronology to establish their ages, Hf isotope analyses to investigate their sources, and whole-rock geochemistry to examine their chemical composition.
Together, the results revealed signatures consistent with continental arc magmatism, a geological process that occurs when one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, generating magma that can rise through the overlying continental crust.
Dr. Ali Mohammadi, the study's corresponding author at Istanbul Technical University, explained: "This study shows that the magmatic history of northwestern Iran is more complex than previously recognized. By integrating geochronological, isotopic, and geochemical evidence, we identified a Late Cretaceous continental arc that was subsequently obscured by later tectonic processes."
The international research effort also involved scientists from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research and Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences; ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Karadeniz Technical University, Türkiye; and Damghan University, Iran.
A Missing Piece of Iran's Geological History
Previous reconstructions of Iran's ancient magmatic activity have largely centered on two major geological features: the Sananda-Sirjan Magmatic Arc and the Urumieh-Dokhtar Magmatic Arc.
The newly identified Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc adds another important piece to that history. Its discovery suggests that northwestern Iran experienced a separate episode of continental arc activity during the Late Cretaceous, expanding scientists' understanding of how the region developed.
The findings also point to a potentially important role for the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault. Researchers suggest that this fault may mark a major tectonic boundary connected to changes in the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean system.
Those changes may have included slab rollback, a process in which a descending tectonic plate retreats as it sinks into Earth's interior, as well as the migration of volcanic arcs to new locations. Such movements could help explain why this particular episode of magma formation lasted for a relatively short period.
New Clues About the Disappearance of an Ancient Ocean
Beyond Iran, the discovery provides a broader lesson about how Earth's geological history can become hidden over immense stretches of time.
Ancient magmatic arcs do not always survive as continuous, easily recognizable formations. Tectonic movements can break them apart, erosion can remove exposed rocks, and sedimentation can bury what remains. Later volcanic activity can further complicate the record, making older systems particularly difficult to identify.
By recognizing the surviving fragments of these ancient structures, scientists can better reconstruct how tectonic plates descended beneath one another, how volcanic arcs shifted, how continental crust grew, and how once-vast oceans eventually closed.
The Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc offers new evidence for understanding the Late Cretaceous evolution of northwestern Iran and the larger Neo-Tethyan region. It also helps researchers refine geological models of an area shaped by repeated episodes of ocean closure and continental collision.
The ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean played a major role in the geological development of the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Western Asia. Its eventual disappearance helped shape the modern landscapes of these regions.
By uncovering a volcanic system that had been largely erased from the geological record, researchers have added another piece to the complex story of how Earth's continents and oceans evolved over millions of years.

12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Ocean’s ability to absorb carbon is weakening as climate change intensifies, UN warns
The ocean absorbs around 30 per cent of human-caused carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions and 90 per cent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. But climate change has already reduced its capacity to absorb carbon by approximately six per cent, a new UN report warns ahead of the COP31 climate conference in November.
The report was a collaboration between the UN’s environment agency, UNEP, and the UN climate secretariat, UNFCCC, which co-organises COP31.
“For a long time the ocean has been doing us an enormous climate service, but that service is under increasing pressure,” Sara Traerup, lead author of the report, told UN News.
Rising temperatures and changes in ocean chemistry, circulation and ecosystems are weakening its ability to absorb and store carbon, leaving more CO₂ in the atmosphere.
And this process “can definitely accelerate” in the foreseeable future, Ms. Traerup warned.
Bridging our knowledge gap
A major challenge is the lack of reliable ocean monitoring data, particularly in the Southern and Indian Oceans, the Arctic and many coastal regions.
The report therefore calls for stronger “ocean carbon intelligence” – using science, technology, data and local knowledge to better understand and manage ocean carbon systems.
“As of now, we don’t have full information about the ocean, and what we don’t know, we cannot manage and protect,” Ms. Traerup explained.
From sensors to seagrass
UNEP looked at three main types of ocean climate technologies, each offering different opportunities and risks.
The first is ocean monitoring: observation systems, sensors, data systems and modelling. Ms. Traerup called these the most mature technologies and the most immediately needed.
The second is blue carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes. They already sequester around 407 million tonnes of CO₂ a year, and restoring them could add significantly more. They also protect coastlines, support biodiversity and sustain livelihoods.
The third is marine carbon dioxide removal, which aims to extract CO₂ from the atmosphere and store it over the long term. While potentially promising, these approaches remain highly uncertain and require further research, monitoring and regulation.
“We shouldn’t treat ocean-based technologies as a shortcut,” Ms. Traerup cautioned, as they must complement, not replace, emissions reductions and ecosystem protection.
Islands leading the way
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) contribute less than one per cent of global emissions, yet are “on the front line of ocean and climate impacts,” Ms. Traerup noted.
The report called for greater access to finance, technology transfer and capacity-building to enable these countries to develop ocean solutions tailored to their needs. Some islands are already showing how this can work.
In 2015, Seychelles, for instance, benefited from a debt-for-nature swap, which involved restructuring part of its foreign debt in exchange for marine conservation commitments. This enabled the country to set up a trust fund to finance marine conservation, climate resilience and the sustainable blue economy.
In the Pacific, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu received support to map seagrass meadows and mangrove forests, and measure how much carbon they store. As a result, more than 100 people were trained in blue carbon assessment, giving governments data to feed into their national climate plans.
The report also stressed the importance of integrating local and Indigenous knowledge.
“Communities have been coping with climate change for many, many years,” Ms. Traerup said, pointing to their experience in protecting coastlines through natural habitats and in managing fisheries and coastal resources sustainably.

Record heat-related deaths in 2023, WHO-partnered report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Record heat-related deaths in 2023, WHO-partnered report finds
Climate inaction continues to harm and kill people in all countries with a record 710,000 estimated deaths globally from heat in 2023, a UN-partnered report warned on Wednesday. For the first time, more than seven in 10 fatalities were attributable to human-caused climate change.
The latest Lancet Countdown report in association with the World Health Organization (WHO), finds that health harms from climate change are accelerating, with expanded fossil fuel extraction holding back progress and threatening “catastrophic” health risks.
“Heat-related deaths, drought and other climate-related risks (are) increasing faster than a decade ago, even as clean energy investments and climate action begin to deliver health benefits,” the report’s authors state.
Key findings:
- Heat exposure caused the loss of 573 billion potential work hours in 2025, costed at $1.07 trillion
- Clean energy jobs grew 2.3 per cent in 2024, almost twice direct fossil fuel employment
- Cleaner air is preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year in 70 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen
- National laws on climate change and health have risen roughly 50-fold since the year 2000 and most have been since 2016
- Wealthy nations accounted for 55 per cent of climate–health laws in 2025, compared to two per cent in developing countries
Other findings indicate that the global area affected by extreme drought “has grown more than 700 per cent faster than it did in 2006–2015”, with droughts affecting 51.8 per cent of land on earth for at least one month in 2025.
The report also examines the link between rising temperatures and rainfall patterns to dengue transmission, finding that conditions suitable for dengue transmission by Aedes albopictus mosquitoes increased by 24 per cent between 1981-90 and 2016-25, while suitability for transmission by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes rose by seven per cent.
Drilling down
And in a warning that too little is being done to mitigate climate change, the report also notes that the world’s 100 largest oil and gas companies plan to produce “150 per cent more fossil fuels by 2040 than is compatible with keeping warming to 1.5°C [above pre-Industrial Revolution temperature averages], up from 138 per cent a year earlier”.
These and other worrying findings highlight the urgent need to formally recognize climate change as a global health emergency, the authors maintain, in support of stronger, health-centred climate action ahead of the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
Priorities include accelerating reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, increasing support for adaptation and expanding investments that strengthen health system resilience.
Action on climate
WHO responds to climate-related health risks through surveillance, early warning systems, health adaptation planning, technical guidance and emergency response teams.
The agency is also closely following the expected health impacts of the ongoing El Niño event through a global incident management team, mobilizing expertise, health intelligence and support to countries most at risk.
WHO also oversees the work of ATACH (the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health), the only network of health ministries and partners working together to develop climate-resilient, low-carbon and sustainable health systems at the country level.
Scientific approach
The report – produced by researchers and institutions from all over the world and led by University College London – analyses global trends across 54 indicators linking climate change and health.
It shows that heat-related deaths increased by nearly 36 per cent in the years following the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change compared with the previous decade. The report also highlights worsening drought conditions, increasing exposure to water-related extremes and substantial economic losses linked to heat exposure.
Premature deaths protection
In more positive developments, important progress has been made in resisting the health impacts of climate change, the report notes, pointing to a record $2.1 trillion global investment in clean energy last year.
“Many countries that have lowered fossil fuel-related air pollution are estimated to be protecting thousands of people from premature deaths each year,” it adds.
The report also notes advances in climate-resilient health systems, including increased adoption of national health adaptation plans and climate-based early warning systems.
Around one in four countries now have a national plan for adapting health services to climate change, up from just 14 WHO Member States in 2015; 47 have separately completed a vulnerability assessment to underpin plans.
The development follows a warning by the UN World Meteorological Organization (WMO) that levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases accumulating in the atmosphere reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increase for the planet.
