Third child dies in Morocco diphtheria outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:18:01 UTC
20:18:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Third child dies in Morocco diphtheria outbreak
A twelve-year-old boy has died of diphtheria in northern Morocco, prompting parents to demand urgent action against the contagious bacteria infection in schools.
The boy died on Tuesday at Lalla Meryem Provincial Hospital in the northwestern city of Larache after he received intensive treatment for the disease.
The boy was not vaccinated against the disease, Hespress reported. Two other children in northern Morocco have recently died of the disease.
Parents' associations are now calling for an urgent vaccination programme, and health monitoring in schools.
96% of people in Morocco have received three doses of the diphtheria vaccine, according to estimates from the World Health Organisation (WHO).
The WHO now recommend that children are given six doses of the vaccine before adolescence, though they do not record data for vaccinations past the third dose.
The vaccine is often given in combination with vaccines against other diseases like tetanus and polio.
Diptheria is caused by an infection of a bacteria called Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which makes a toxin that kills healthy tissue.
The bacteria can be spread between people through respiratory droplets, often from coughing and sneezing.
Typical symptoms of diptheria include fever, difficulty breathing, swollen glands, and puss-filled blisters on the skin. In rare cases the toxin can enter the blood stream, damaging vital organs.
Diphtheria can usually be treated with antibiotics or other medicines, though it proves fatal in approximately 10% of cases, even with treatment, according to Oxford Vaccine Group.
Morocco's Ministry of Health announced in September that they have identified two clusters of diphtheria involving children who have not been fully vaccinated against the disease.
Before the recent outbreak, Morocco had not reported diphtheria cases in three decades.
The most recent outbreak of Diptheria reported by the WHO was in Guinea in 2023. That outbreak caused 13 confirmed deaths.
The WHO has not yet reported current the outbreak of Diptheria in Morocco

At Least 50 Dead in High-Speed Train Collision in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:17:14 UTC
20:17:14 KST

At least 50 people were killed and many others injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain near Toledo, south of Madrid, on Wednesday morning, Spanish authorities said, as rescue operations continued and officials warned that the death toll could rise.
Local media reported that 46 people had died, citing emergency services, although that figure had not been confirmed. More than 500 people were aboard the two trains, according to a spokeswoman for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government.
The crash occurred shortly after 9 a.m. local time in the province of Toledo. Images from the scene showed severely damaged carriages lying on their sides after tumbling down an embankment, while footage shared on social media showed debris scattered beside the tracks and at least one carriage apparently completely derailed.
One train, operated by AVE, was reportedly carrying 397 passengers, while the other, operated by IRYO, had 146 people on board, the regional government spokeswoman said.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia confirmed to national broadcaster TVE that the collision involved a high-speed impact but said it was too early to establish the final number of casualties. "We are expecting this to be a major tragedy," she told TVE.
Garcia also said that medical facilities in the area needed intensive care capacity, adding, "We don't just need help from nearby hospitals, we need nearby hospitals that have ICU beds."
The mayor of Urda, Manuel Galans, said two trains had collided and people had been injured. Jesus Perez, mayor of nearby Los Yebenes, described the accident as "serious" in comments to Spanish television.
A spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the initial reports were deeply concerning: "The information we are receiving is not good at all."
A reporter for TVE described the scene as one of "absolute chaos," with ambulances and other emergency vehicles arriving continuously. The El Pais newspaper cited witnesses who reported numerous injuries and the arrival of emergency medical teams.
Spanish emergency services said they were mobilizing all available resources, including "several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units," an emergency services spokesperson told AFP.
In a post on X, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was "shocked" by the accident and was in contact with the transport minister and the president of the Castilla-La Mancha autonomous community.
Rail operator Adif announced on social media that services on the high-speed line connecting Madrid with Andalusia had been suspended following a rear-end collision between the trains. Rail services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were also halted.
A passenger named Miguel told local radio station COPE that those aboard felt the collision before realizing what had happened. "We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds as if the train were about to derail," he said.
Miguel said he then saw the wreckage of another train through the window on his right: "Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one."
Authorities had not immediately established what caused the collision.

Economic Watch: China's Canton Fair opens a wider door to shared gains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:58 CST
20:14:58 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- When German businessman Can Yildirim first walked into the Canton Fair 23 years ago, he was young and unsure how to find the right business partners. As luck would have it, a stranger named Jimmy Chen noticed that he seemed a bit lost and offered to help him navigate the fair.
That first meeting really stuck with him. Yildirim and Chen have kept in touch, and Yildirim has been connected to the Canton Fair ever since.
"It's about being open-minded and making friends," said Yildirim, who now keeps a long list of suppliers he has met through the fair. "When we have to cope with a difficult period, none of my Chinese suppliers has ever left me on my own," he said.
The China Import and Export Fair, better known as the Canton Fair, has grown and thrived through openness for 70 years. Now, it's back in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, for its 140th edition. Running in three phases from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4, the fair has grown into China's largest and longest-running international trade event, with buyers coming from more than 220 countries and regions and cumulative transactions reaching 1.6 trillion U.S. dollars.
Often seen as a barometer for China's foreign trade, the fair has enjoyed enduring success that underlines China's unwavering commitment to expanding high-level opening-up and the practical need for economies to draw on each other's strengths and work together for mutual benefit.
Official data showed that China's foreign trade maintained solid momentum in the first three quarters of this year, with total imports and exports rising 18.8 percent year on year during the nine-month period, the highest level for the same period in five years.
Smarter and greener products are helping drive China's export growth, a trend on full display at the Canton Fair. The first phase of the fair drew more than 12,000 exhibiting companies, about half of which were high-quality firms such as specialized or innovative enterprises. The number of new products, AI products and green products on display were up 6.7 percent, 20.5 percent and 13.5 percent respectively over the same period of the previous edition.
For international buyers, the expanding range of products and technologies offers fresh opportunities for growth.
"China is like a gold mine. The deeper you dig, the more you get," said Anis Sajan, a buyer from the United Arab Emirates. His company imports more than 500 containers of goods from China every month, helping his business grow 30 percent this year.
Such trade is increasingly about more than importing finished goods. More countries are relying on China's products, technology and capital to improve their own industrial systems and lift their high-end export capacity, accelerating industrial upgrading and steadily climbing the global value chain.
At the booth of Bodor, a Shandong-based company specializing in laser cutting and welding, several buyers from Southeast Asia watched closely as a machine sliced cleanly through aluminum alloy. "We don't just need cutting equipment," said one buyer from the sheet metal industry. "We want equipment that can help drive digital upgrading across our whole industry. A complete digital solution like this is exactly what our current transformation needs."
China's push for more balanced trade is also creating opportunities for exhibitors to tap further into the Chinese market. The Canton Fair has hosted an import section since 2007, giving foreign companies a direct channel to Chinese and global buyers.
During the second phase of the fair, which had just concluded, the import section brought together 213 companies from 27 countries and regions, including national pavilions from nine countries, such as Egypt, Thailand and Pakistan, showcasing kitchenware, household goods and gifts.
Dominik Bledzki, general director of the Polish-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, comes to the Canton Fair twice a year and finds something new each time -- new buildings, new suppliers and new products, all of which help him expand his business.
"China is a global buyer, but it's also a global seller," Bledzki said. "If you look for your products, if you want to do business, you have to be here. China is not only manufacturing goods; it is manufacturing ideas, new technology and new designs," he said. ■

HANOI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The 17th People's Council of Vietnam's capital Hanoi approved a plan to adjust the administrative boundary between the city and the northern midland province of Phu Tho at its seventh session on Wednesday, the Vietnam News Agency reported.
The plan covers the transfer of more than 4,000 hectares of land and 1,057 residents from Phu Tho to the capital, incorporating the areas into Ba Vi and Yen Xuan communes, according to the report.
The boundary adjustment comprises over 2,500 hectares of Ba Vi National Park and 1,477 hectares of its buffer zone, aiming to align territorial administration with park management, improve forest protection and biodiversity conservation, and strengthen forest fire prevention and control, water resource protection and ecological conservation.
According to the municipal people's committee, more than 2.4 million households, or 94.97 percent of the total consulted across 126 communes and wards, supported the proposal, which will take effect after approval by the National Assembly. ■

World Insights: Flavio Bolsonaro's reported departure for U.S. after election failure sparks political reactions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:38 CST
20:14:38 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Flavio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, reportedly left Brazil for the United States on Tuesday after failing to meet a Supreme Court deadline to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports, which were subsequently canceled amid a money laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing.
Flavio Bolsonaro was defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday's presidential runoff and his reported departure from Brazil has sparked heated reactions.
AFTER ELECTION
Brazil's 2026 general election culminated in a presidential runoff on Sunday, following the first round of voting on Oct. 4. Neither candidate won outright in the closely contested first round. With all votes in the runoff counted, Lula received 51.79 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.21 percent for Bolsonaro, according to the official tally.
Lula's victory secures him a fourth term as Brazil's president, with his inauguration scheduled for Jan. 5, 2027, for a four-year term.
After Lula's victory, Bolsonaro, speaking in the Brazilian capital of Brasilia, said it is "impossible" to recognize the results and called for the annulment of the election, alleging unequal treatment of voters following a two-hour extension of voting hours at polling stations affected by public transport disruptions and heavy rain.
Bolsonaro argued that the decision had disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and that his legal team would challenge the results.
However, the Liberal Party, to which Bolsonaro belongs, formally acknowledged Lula's victory on Monday. Other right-wing and center-right parties that had supported Bolsonaro during the election, including the Republicans, the Brazilian Democratic Movement and the Progressives, also acknowledged Lula's victory, making clear that they did not support calls to annul the election results or hold a new election.
PASSPORT OR U.S. VISA
Brazilian media reported Monday that Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to the Federal Police and barred him from leaving the country.
The ruling is part of an investigation involving Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz, according to Brazil's public news agency Agencia Brasil. The probe reportedly involves suspected money laundering and financial links to businesses connected to the sports betting industry.
Additionally, Bolsonaro is under investigation over the financing of a biopic about his father. The probe examines the source of funds for the film's production.
Bolsonaro confirmed on the same day that he intended to comply with a request to surrender his passports and denied plans to flee the country following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, serving a 27-year-and-three-month sentence for plotting a coup after his 2022 election defeat and remains under investigation in related cases.
However, he failed to surrender the documents before the deadline expired on Tuesday, and the passports were subsequently canceled. Bolsonaro was then reported to have left Brazil for the United States, though his exact route remained unclear.
Meanwhile, U.S. media reported Tuesday, citing a senior State Department official, that the department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the United States.
POLITICAL REACTIONS
In response to the news, Lula told supporters who gathered outside the Alvorada Palace: "I regret that he left Brazil ... And his decision to leave Brazil is shameful."
Lula also criticized Bolsonaro for failing to comply with the court order to surrender his passports, saying he should have stayed in Brazil to address the allegations against him. Recalling that he had surrendered his own passport when ordered to do so in 2018, Lula said he had chosen to remain in Brazil to prove his innocence.
Bolsonaro's departure has not been officially confirmed.
Brazilian media reported that there was no record in the country's immigration control system indicating that he had left Brazil through regular border controls. The Federal Police were investigating whether and how he might have left the country.
Argentina's migration department reportedly said on Wednesday that Bolsonaro and his family boarded a private plane bound for Ecuador late on Tuesday, but the Ecuadorian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to the statement.
The current location of Bolsonaro and his family remains unclear.
Earlier Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump said Brazil's presidential election "looked like another rigged election" and that the decision to extend voting hours was "very strange."
Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin on Monday rejected Trump's claim that Brazil's presidential election appeared to have been "rigged," saying there was no evidence to support the allegation.
"First, one does not interfere in the politics of another country. That is a fundamental principle," Alckmin said. "Brazil, in fact, is an example to the world in terms of electronic voting and legal safeguards. This is how democracy works: you win an election, you lose an election, and it is the people who decide."
Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered the Federal Police on Tuesday to open an investigation into possible foreign interference in the country's electoral process.
The decision issued by the court's Justice Flavio Dino points to signs that algorithms on digital platforms were manipulated to benefit the conservative candidate Bolsonaro. ■

====================================================================================================

mixes sci-fi horror and small-town politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:14:32 UTC
20:14:32 KST

John Scalzi has developed a reputation in science fiction for comitting to the bit. Whether with meta-explorations of killable side characters in Redshirts or a world in which the moon literally turns into cheese in When the Moon Hits Your Eye, you can count on Scalzi seeing a concept through to its wildest implications. In his latest romp, corporate greed, lovable cows and hideous monsters converge in Richland, Ohio. It’s a small, exploited town on its last legs—but the first tentacles will be arriving shortly.
Fresh off a red-eye flight after winning his fourth Hugo Award, Scalzi stopped by to chat with us about his newest novel, Monsters of Ohio.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If you had to pitch Monsters of Ohio to someone who has never read a John Scalzi novel, what would you say?
I describe it as “cozy Cronenberg.” The slightly longer version of that is “Stephen King and Nora Ephron are made to violently kiss.”
When you last sat down with us, you described your niche in contemporary science fiction as taking “a really absurd idea and then [trying] to apply real life to it.” Monsters of Ohio seems to be no exception. How did we get here?
Well, thanks to Stephen King and Stranger Things and all of that sort of stuff, we have all seen the idea of monsters in a small town, right? I thought it would be fun to take a lot of the dressing of that and put a new spin on it, where the idea was not necessarily horror but to see what some of the consequences would be if, all of a sudden, there were monsters in your town and yet you were still trying to get through the rest of your day.
What did your research process look like? How much digging did you do for the more scientific aspects of the book?
A lot of my “research” is not directed research. It is literally “Oh! I remember this one thing I read one time on the internet!” And either that comes in handy while I’m writing, or it will pop up in my head and will keep going around and around and around until I write something about it. My brain is a rat’s nest of judicial decisions, fun facts about small mammals, and lots and lots of astronomy stuff.
I think, in many ways, I was uniquely designed to be a novelist, because when people are like, “When will you ever use that information?” I’ll be like, “Well, as it turns out, I will use it while I’m writing up a book called Monsters of Ohio.” So there you have it.
How important is scientific plausibility to you when writing science fiction?
It’s very important to me that people remember that science fiction has two parts to the phrase. There is the science, but there is also the fiction. I want to get the science at least broadly correct and reasonable so that, when I step into the fiction part, you can see it as a natural extension. Now you may or may not always agree with how I’ve decided to step off into the fiction part, but you can see, at least, [how] I got there.
I am always very hesitant to call myself a hard science-fiction writer because so much of that basically requires an advanced degree—and I have a B. A. in philosophy, so all I know is how to find things. That said, I’ve always also had a real interest in science and a real interest in talking about how science interacts with our lives. And so, when you are writing a story where, you know, [highly unlikely monster shenanigans redacted by editor], you want to be able to do it in a way that is, at least, scientifically plausible. I mean, [a written event] always happens because plot, but mine is rooted in specific things that happened in the natural world, as opposed to “and then magic” or “and then gods and demons.” There’s nothing wrong with gods and demons, but, in my case, I’m a science-fiction writer, so that’s where my brain goes first.
Monsters of Ohio is your 20th novel, and it feels paradoxically cynical and hopeful at the same time.
A lot of that cynicism plus hopefulness comes out of the experience of modern life and day-to-day life.
We live in a world where there is private equity strip-mining small towns. We live in a world where the interests of the moneyed class really are at odds with the interests of the people going day-to-day. [Take] where I live right now. In this moment, we are having a huge discussion about [how] they’re going to put power lines somewhere through Darke County, [Ohio], which is also the county that’s in the book. They swear to us that [the lines] are not to power the huge data centers that are being put up in our state right now, but come on. And part of the problem is that one of the routes is literally my street.
The hopeful part is the part where the people who are dealing with the consequences of that look toward their community, look toward their friends, look toward the people around them for support, for help, for unity—all of those sorts of things. The way that I think the little guy is going to get through this is to look at his neighbors and realize that all the messaging and disinformation that is designed to keep us angry and suspicious at our neighbors is, in fact, designed to keep us angry and suspicious of our neighbors and, in fact, [that] we need our neighbors’ help and that we need to help our neighbors and support them as much as we can during this time.
This is already helping, because I thought the takeaway of the book was that the proverbial little people were going to get through this by exploding.
I mean, why not both?
Getting to the really important questions now: You have often asked musicians to write theme songs for your books. Have you done that here?
I have inquiries out, which is, I think, the only thing that I can say at this time. But it would make sense to do it because the protagonist was very briefly in a very briefly famous emo band. So I would like to have that set up. Unfortunately I may have missed the window for the hardcover release, but there’s always the trade paperback release in about a year.
Chappell Roan would do a great rendition of the protagonist’s signature song, “Red Wine Massacre,” in case you’re taking suggestions.
I think she might be a little bit out of my price range. When you commission something like that, you do have to pay your artists, and I think Chappell Roan might be just a little pricey for a humble science-fiction author.
What would it take to get you to write a book about someone from Michigan?
I would be happy to have a character from Michigan. Will my neighbors burn my house down if I do it? Possibly. But that is the risk one takes for true literature.

====================================================================================================

Animal-borne Shamonda virus infects and kills a human for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:14:22 UTC
20:14:22 KST

A person has contracted and died from the Shamonda virus, a disease-causing microbe that had been thought to only infect animals, for the first time. The incident, while unlikely to herald a more widespread outbreak, is a potent reminder of the potential for pathogens to jump from animals to humans—with deadly consequences.
The Shamonda virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in 1965. Spread by bites from tiny insects called Culicoides midges, it causes several symptoms in the animals, including fever, diarrhea and reduced milk production. The virus has also been known to infect sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. Previously, cases have been detected in some African countries, Japan and—for the first time this summer—Europe. But the virus doesn’t even seem overly contagious and isn’t deadly in adult animals. (Infected pregnant animals can transmit it to their fetus, however, which can result in miscarriage, stillbirth or birth defects.)
Yet for the first time in the more than six decades since it was discovered, Shamonda was detected in humans. A 61-year-old man who was undergoing treatment for leukemia at the Civil Hospital of Lyon in France contracted the disease. According to a case report published in Eurosurveillance, the man had undergone a stem cell transplant and experienced fatal encephalitis, or brain swelling. He showed symptoms, such as blindness and confusion, that the report authors say were likely caused by the virus. The man fell into a coma and succumbed to the disease on October 9, 2026, after life support was withdrawn. He is the first person ever known to have contracted the disease and died as a result. There are no vaccines to protect animals or people from Shamonda infections.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Experts emphasize the need for caution. “At this stage, there is no evidence that the Shamonda virus will become more common in humans,” says clinical virologist Grégory Destras. He is affiliated with the same hospital in Lyon and is a co-author of the report. Destras notes that the virus may have spent several weeks incubating and multiplying in the patient before the neurological symptoms appeared.
In a joint statement, the French Ministry of Health and Ministry of Agriculture said that they suspect the patient contracted the disease from a midge bite in eastern France, where the disease has been found in several animals. Officials have reported their findings to the World Health Organization and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
Shamonda has been found in livestock in 14 European countries. Two new clades of the virus, SHAV-EU1 and SHAV-EU2, were detected earlier this year, and genetic testing revealed traces of the first type in the deceased person’s cerebrospinal fluid, urine and saliva, among other samples.
The Shamonda virus is part of the Simbu serogroup and belongs to the genus Orthobunyavirus—the same serogroup and genus as the Oropouche virus, or sloth fever, which caused 9.4 million human infections in Latin America and the Caribbean regions from 1960 to 2025.
Indiana University School of Medicine virologist Natasha Tilston-Lunel highlights the Oropouche cases, but notes that the Schmallenberg virus, which is closely related to Shamonda, has been found to be widespread in livestock but not humans. She believes that, based on current information, Shamonda may also have limited infectiousness among people. Continued surveillance of livestock and their aborted fetuses, insects and genomic sequencing of human samples, however, will be critical to detecting any changes to Shamonda’s risk in people, she says. Tilston-Lunel was not associated with the new study.
Veterinary virologist Martin Beer of the Friedrich Loeffler Institute in Germany is part of a team that has conducted several studies of the Shamonda virus, including a recent preprint on the first evidence of its presence in European sheep and goats. Beer says that the main transmission route of viruses of the Simbu serogroup are biting midges, which can rapidly spread infections, especially in the summer and autumn. “In winter the transmission cycle stops since the number of biting midges is very low and temperatures below approximately 12 degrees Celsius do not allow efficient virus replication,” he says.
A spokesperson for the ECDC told Scientific American that the agency needs clarity regarding the transmission of the virus and the role of vectors in infecting people. Destras suggests that retrospective analyses of stored samples from immunocompromised people could identify asymptomatic infections and the true scale of Shamonda in France.
Beer points out that novel cases of unexplained encephalitis have occurred in immunocompromised people who were infected with other orthobunyaviruses, such as the Jamestown Canyon virus or the Cache Valley virus. More studies to analyze antibody prevalence against Shamonda in people could give a clearer picture of whether this particular virus made the leap to humans before and we just didn’t realize because no one died.

AI generated
Jerusalem – Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is known for his unassuming and mild manner, but all eyes will soon be on him as he decides who to task with forming the next coalition government.
The decision is a weighty one, given that partial results show neither the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his rival Gadi Eisenkot securing a majority in Parliament.
After the official announcement of the results, Herzog will consult party representatives and name a candidate who has the best chance of forming a government – not necessarily the one whose party holds the most seats.
Under the law, the president, whose position is otherwise largely ceremonial, is afforded broad discretion, with no guidelines on how to make the choice.
Just ahead of the pivotal vote on Oct 27, Herzog acknowledged there would be tremendous pressure, but vowed not to let outside influence, notably from Donald Trump, sway his decision.
“I don’t think the president of the United States or anybody else can intervene in my discretion,” he told US outlet MS Now.
“It’s Israel’s democracy and Israel’s Constitution, and that’s what counts for me.”
Herzog also told MS Now he would do everything he could to avoid a fresh election – a possibility if neither camp can cobble together a coalition – including backing a unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
‘Worthy and wonderful man’
Modest, diplomatic and with a strong political pedigree, 66-year-old Herzog was sworn in as Israel’s president in 2021 after being elected by lawmakers in a landslide.
Yair Lapid, now a member of Eisenkot’s bloc, praised Herzog at the time as “a worthy and wonderful man who is always focused on the good of the country and the Jewish people”.
As president, Herzog has faced pressure from Trump to grant Netanyahu a pardon in his long-running corruption trials, which could land him in prison if he loses power.
In April, Herzog invited Netanyahu’s lawyers and prosecutors to his residence for talks on the issue.
Before he served as head of state, Herzog was elected to Israel’s parliament in 2003 and held portfolios including housing, tourism and welfare.
In 2015, as leader of Israel’s centre-left Labour party, Herzog vied to oust Netanyahu as prime minister, presenting himself as a subdued, even-keeled alternative to the bombastic “Bibi”.
Netanyahu, now 77, is Israel’s longest-serving premier, having governed on and off for nearly two decades.
The Oct 27 election was seen as a referendum on the veteran leader’s tenure after he pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023, attack.
‘Bring a real change’
In an interview with AFP in March 2026, Herzog said the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran marked a “historical juncture”.
“There comes a moment that after well over a generation of endless wars, bloodshed and terror, the root cause of it, which comes from Tehran, will be blocked and stopped, and the whole direction of the region will change,” he said.
“Let’s help us bring a real change so that there will be a different future in the region.”
He also stressed the importance of talks with Lebanon, with the two sides sitting down in April for direct negotiations that are still ongoing.
Herzog’s Irish-born father, Chaim Herzog, served as head of Israel’s military intelligence, then went on to become its ambassador to the United Nations and finally its sixth president, from 1983 to 1993.
Herzog’s grandfather and namesake – Rabbi Yitzhak (Isaac) HaLevi Herzog – was the first chief rabbi for Israel’s Ashkenazis, the branch of Judaism whose roots are in eastern Europe.
At the helm of the Labour party, Herzog worked to steer its focus back to peace with the Palestinians.
He answers to the nickname “Bougie” – reportedly given to him by his Egyptian-born mother, who mixed the French word for doll “poupee” with its Hebrew equivalent “buba”. AFP

Israel election: What we know so far

Breadcrumb
Israel election: What we know so far
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his chief rival Gadi Eisenkot are expected to win a governing majority following Tuesday's election, which saw huge voter turnout and delivered historic gains for Palestinian parties.
With almost 90% of the ballots counted on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu's far-right bloc was on 53 seats while the Eisenkot coalition had 48. Arab parties make up the difference and are on course to win 19 seats between them.
The vote - the first since the Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023 and Israel's subsequent genocidal war in Gaza – was seen largely as a referendum on Netanyahu's rule and the turmoil of the past three years.
Here's what we know so far about the Israeli election results.
Netanyahu leads but neither side has a majority
Netanyahu's far-right bloc was leading on Wednesday morning, with 85.6% of votes counted, but was projected to fall short of a governing majority.
The Likud leader's coalition was on course to secure 53 seats, compared with 48 for the anti-Netanyahu bloc.
Netanyahu's Likud was set to remain the largest party in the Knesset with 26 seats, while Eisenkot's Yashar was in second place with 21.
Both leaders have vowed to form a government, despite neither having a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Addressing supporters, Netanyahu claimed his coalition had won a "decisive majority" and called for the formation of a "national right-wing government".
Eisenkot, meanwhile, declared an end to Netanyahu's rule and the beginning of a "new era" for Israel.
"The Israeli street has chosen change," he told supporters at his party's headquarters.
Arab parties hold the balance of power
A surge in Arab voter turnout has propelled the two Palestinian parties to historic gains, leaving neither of the two main blocs with a majority.
The left-wing/nationalist Joint List alliance is expected to become the joint third-largest group in the Knesset with 12 seats, while Ra'am is projected to secure a record seven seats.
Despite the historic result, it remains unclear whether Arab parties will play a role in forming the next government.
Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas has indicated he would be willing to join an Eisenkot-led coalition, although his party's support alone would not be enough to secure a majority.
The Joint List is unlikely to enter a governing coalition, but its leader, Yousef Jabareen, has suggested he could support an Eisenkot-led minority government to keep Netanyahu out of power.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Jabareen told Israeli media on Wednesday.
Voter turnout reaches highest level since 1999
Figures from the Central Elections Committee showed turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in an Israeli election since 1999.
This was 7.1 percentage points higher than in the 2022 election, which brought to power the most far-right government in Israel's history.
Far-right parties fall short of expectations
Israel's far-right parties appear to have fallen short of the gains forecast ahead of the vote, with Jewish Power and Religious Zionism now projected to win six seats each.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power had been expected to secure eight seats, a significant increase on its performance four years ago.
However, the surge in Palestinian voter turnout appears to have reduced the party's share of seats, leaving it short of its target.
What happens next?
The remaining votes are expected to be counted by Friday, with official results due to be published by 4 November, a week after the election.
Once the final results are confirmed, Netanyahu and Eisenkot will seek the support of smaller parties in an attempt to secure a 61-seat majority.
President Isaac Herzog will consult parliamentary factions before deciding which lawmaker has the best chance of forming a government.
The chosen candidate will initially have 28 days to assemble a coalition, with the possibility of a 14-day extension.
With neither bloc appearing to have a straightforward path to a majority, a minority government remains a possibility.
A national unity government involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot is another option, although it appears unlikely given their political rivalry.
If coalition negotiations fail, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.

India invites Pakistan to SCO forum a year after stand-off
India has invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) meet in Delhi, the first such invite since the armed stand-off between the two nuclear-armed South Asian countries last year.
New Delhi invited Pakistani Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurangzeb Khan Khichi to the first SCO civilizational Dialogue Forum to be held on November 20-22.
This is the first time a Pakistani minister is being invited by India since the clash. The stand-off, dubbed Operation Sindoor by New Delhi, followed a terror attack in Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir that killed more than a score of Indian civilians.
If Khichi accepts the invite, it will be the first time since the SCO foreign ministers’ meeting in Goa in 2023 – attended by Bhilawal Bhutto – that a Pakistani minister would visit India. The forum is aimed at promoting cultural relations between member countries and promoting mutual understanding.
Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh, who announced the invites at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, also voiced New Delhi’s apprehensions about facilitators of terrorism but without mentioning Pakistan.
“There should be no double standards in dealing with terrorism, and no place for those who finance, support or provide safe havens to terrorists. The entire ecosystem of terrorism must be firmly and collectively dismantled,” Singh said in the presence of Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar.
The SCO comprises ten member states – Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan – and 15 dialogue partners, in addition to Afghanistan and Mongolia as observers.

Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:08:25 UTC
20:08:25 KST

Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- University of St. Andrews
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of St Andrews have identified a previously unknown process that may help explain how Earth entered past ice ages. Their findings reveal a surprising connection between ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere and ocean changes near Antarctica, suggesting that cooling in one part of the world could trigger a chain reaction affecting the entire planet.
The study, published in the Journal of Climate, offers a possible explanation for how growing northern ice sheets influenced ocean circulation and sea ice in the Southern Hemisphere. These southern changes are known to help reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), an important factor in the development of ice ages. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain how processes occurring at opposite ends of the planet could be so closely connected.
One of the main forces behind Earth's past ice ages was a reduction in atmospheric CO2 as more carbon became stored in the oceans. Much of this process was controlled by changes in the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica. However, a major question remained unanswered: How could expanding ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere, initially driven by natural variations in Earth's orbit, cause the distant Southern Ocean to absorb more CO2?
How Northern Ice Sheets Could Trigger Changes Near Antarctica
The researchers propose that the answer lies in the movement of ocean water between the hemispheres. As large ice sheets spread across northern regions, they cool nearby waters in the North Atlantic. Over time, these colder waters circulate southward, eventually reaching the Southern Ocean.
If the cooling is sufficiently strong, it could alter ocean circulation around Antarctica in ways that allow more CO2 to be stored beneath the ocean's surface. As atmospheric CO2 declines, the planet cools further, potentially helping intensify an ice age.
To investigate this possibility, the team used computer simulations of ocean circulation. Rather than lowering temperatures across the entire planet, they cooled only the northernmost latitudes (mimicking the effect of a large ice sheet) and examined how the Southern Ocean responded.
The results were striking. Cooling the far northern regions alone produced 74% as much CO2 drawdown as a separate simulation in which the entire planet was cooled. This suggests that temperature changes in the Northern Hemisphere could have a powerful influence on the Southern Ocean and its ability to store carbon.
A Missing Link in Earth's Ice Age Mystery
The simulations provide strong support for the proposed connection between expanding northern ice sheets and changes in the Southern Ocean. They suggest that colder water originating in the North Atlantic could eventually influence circulation around Antarctica, helping remove CO2 from the atmosphere and contributing to the global cooling associated with past ice ages.
For decades, much of the research into ice age climate changes has concentrated on the Southern Ocean because of its important role in controlling atmospheric carbon dioxide. Only more recently have scientists begun to recognize how changes in distant ocean regions might influence these processes.
Lead author Dr. Madison Shankle, from the University of St Andrews School of Earth and Environmental Science, explained the importance of the findings:
"Essentially, we've produced evidence of a plausible mechanism connecting these two far-flung puzzles pieces - Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Hemisphere ocean circulation changes leading to CO2 drawdown - which has been a tricky thing to explain in our theory of Earth's past ice ages. Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field."
What Ancient Ice Ages Reveal About Today's Climate
Understanding how past ice ages developed offers scientists a valuable way to study Earth's natural carbon cycle. These periods reveal how carbon dioxide moves between the atmosphere and oceans, and how changes in that balance can influence global temperatures.
By identifying another mechanism that may have helped reduce atmospheric CO2 during ancient ice ages, researchers can develop a more complete picture of how Earth's climate system operates.
That knowledge is especially important today, as scientists work to understand how the planet's oceans and other natural systems will respond to the additional carbon dioxide now entering the Earth system.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of St. Andrews. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Madison G. Shankle, Graeme A. MacGilchrist, Andrea Burke, Alice Marzocchi, Malte F. Jansen, James W. B. Rae. Isolated Northern Hemisphere Cooling in an Idealized Model Promotes Ocean Carbon Storage and Glacial-like Ocean Features. Journal of Climate, 2026; 39 (22): 6471 DOI: 10.1175/JCLI-D-25-0355.1

Egypt's Saudi support raises fears of economic fallout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:04:59 UTC

Breadcrumb
Egypt's Saudi support raises fears of economic fallout amid pound slide and rising prices
The Egyptian parliament's authorisation of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support Saudi Arabia and defend its territory against external aggression has raised concerns over the move's potential impact on Egyptian markets, amid fears of further pressure on the pound, financial markets and commodity prices.
The decision, approved on Monday 26 October, occurs as the economic fallout from the US-Israeli war on Iran and its regional impact threatens to intensify, with Egypt already facing pressure on its currency and foreign investment inflows. Consumers could also face higher prices for goods and fuel, alongside rising living costs.
Mohammed Ali Al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi's political council, described the Egypt's authorisation as a "declaration of war" against Yemen, saying it contradicted declared efforts to reduce regional tensions.
The remarks came as the Houthi intensify attacks against Riyadh.
On Tuesday, the group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the Yemeni armed forces had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Meanwhile, the dollar surpassed 56.50 Egyptian pounds at banks on Monday. On Tuesday, it returned to the black market at 56.67 pounds for buying and 57.90 pounds for selling, increasing the risk of higher import costs.
The Egyptian stock market also fluctuated, showing downward trends. Analysts estimate that around $4 billion in foreign investment in government debt instruments exited the market between 15 and 26 October, with outflows accelerating over the final two days.
Traders hoard goods
The New Arab has observed several major traders and suppliers, particularly in commercial centres in downtown Cairo, withholding goods from distributors and shops.
The products include foodstuffs, consumer goods and durable goods, with traders waiting for the dollar exchange rate to stabilise and for Egypt's position on the war to become clearer.
Analysts warn that the conflict could affect consumers through higher oil, shipping and insurance costs, as well as increased production input and food prices. This would further undermine the purchasing power of ordinary families, who are still struggling with previous waves of inflation.
Meanwhile, revenues from tourism and Suez Canal and Red Sea shipping traffic also remain vulnerable to regional escalation, potentially putting further pressure on Egypt's foreign currency resources.
Hisham al-Dajwi, head of the foodstuffs division at the Chamber of Commerce, attributed what he described as traders' "greed" partly to the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade's failure to fully implement the "Carry On" system, intended to distribute affordable food and subsidised commodities through around 40,000 outlets nationwide.
Distributors said the recent price hikes in goods and products were down to merchants' hedging against price increases, based on a dollar exchange rate exceeding 60 Egyptian pounds. With the increased risk of war, some were hoarding products in the hope of reaping substantial profits if the conflict escalates or they are unable to replenish stocks.
Minister of Supply and Internal Trade Sherif Farouk appealed to traders not to raise prices and to display prices on their products, pledging that the government would secure essential commodities for between three and six months from domestic stocks.
New prices expected
Economist Abdel Nabi Abdel Muttalib said several agents and suppliers had informed retailers last Thursday that no new indicative prices had been issued, while anticipating that new prices would take effect at the beginning of the following month.
He told The New Arab that some suppliers had begun delaying deliveries while waiting for new contracts, allowing them to price products according to future costs.
Abdel Muttalib cited sanitary products for the elderly, which he described as essential for health reasons, noting that some retailers had raised prices over the past two days, only to revert to the former prices after being informed that sales would be suspended until the end of the month.
These practices had contributed to higher prices, he said, warning that they could intensify pressure on consumers, particularly those purchasing essential goods.
Abdel Muttalib warned that continued dollar appreciation could revive the currency black market, with rising exchange rates encouraging expectations of further increases.
He said he had previously ruled out the dollar exceeding 55 pounds, but subsequent increases had heightened concerns over further depreciation.
A weaker pound should theoretically reduce imports by increasing the cost of imported goods and lowering demand. However, this does not apply equally to production inputs, raw materials and essential commodities that Egypt cannot do without, including oil, gas and wheat.
He said the government could have limited price pressures by temporarily coordinating with traders to prevent price increases and penalising violators, or by imposing fees, taxes and levies on capital seeking to exit the country, thereby limiting its profits and preserving state resources. A combination of the two approaches was also possible.
Abdel Muttalib suggested the government may have avoided such measures to preserve Egypt's image as a market allowing foreign investment to enter and exit freely, and to avoid such restrictive measures affecting the IMF's assessment during its latest programme review.
Saudi financial support expected
Abdel Muttalib said the parliamentary authorisation could strengthen ties between Egypt and Gulf states, potentially helping offset capital outflows if it led to new financial inflows or investments from Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Such inflows could compensate for some outgoing funds, he said, while warning that unfavourable regional developments could place Egypt under greater pressure.
He considered a wider regional war relatively unlikely, but said an expansion of the confrontation could exacerbate economic risks, particularly if accompanied by continued foreign capital outflows and rising prices.
Financing and investment expert Wael al-Nahhas warned that a regional confrontation lasting up to six months could intensify financial pressures on Gulf economies and affect Egypt through higher import costs and reduced foreign currency inflows.
He said the dollar's rise from below 50 pounds to more than 56 pounds in a short period represented pressure beyond normal exchange-rate fluctuations.
Nahhas warned that households were already facing cost-of-living pressures, warning that reduced supplies could intensify price increases even without comparable rises in global markets.
Nahhas also cautioned against interpreting temporary stock market gains as a definitive sign of recovery, given uncertainty over the war, US interest rate decisions and corporate earnings.
If stock prices continue to fall, investors may lose confidence, making it harder for the government to sell shares in state-owned companies, including Banque du Caire, as investors demand greater discounts to compensate for risks or choose to postpone investing.

Xi Focus: Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:03:46 UTC
20:03:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) — The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee on Monday started a four-day plenary session in Beijing, which focuses on strengthening Party self-governance.
This marks the latest move by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core to strengthen the Party through full and rigorous self-governance.
Xi, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has emphasized that exercising full and rigorous self-governance is an enduring task for the Party.
“One has to be very strong if he wants to strike the iron,” Xi said shortly after his election to the post of general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in November 2012. He later warned at a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that if corruption is allowed to grow unchecked, “it could spell the end of both the Party and the state.”
As China entered the new era, the CPC, the largest governing party in the world, faced unprecedented challenges in ensuring reform, development and stability, and addressing problems and risks confronting the nation.
Xi has stressed that China’s success hinges on the Party, and has made clear that the CPC must continuously strengthen itself through self-governance.
In 2014, he explicitly put forward the concept of “exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance” as part of the Party’s four-pronged governing strategy, alongside building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform and advancing law-based governance.
He has made full and rigorous Party self-governance a long-term strategy, as he considers it vital to the Party’s long-term governance, the country’s enduring stability, and the people’s happiness and well-being.
BREAK NEW GROUND
In December 2012, Xi began strengthening Party self-governance by introducing a code of conduct that became known as the “eight-point rules.”
It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power.
Its implementation has helped curb longstanding malpractices, with effects extending beyond Party and government offices to wider society.
“The eight-point rules have indeed brought about fundamental changes over the years,” Xi said last year, when the Party launched a campaign to reinforce this code of conduct and consolidate the improvements it had brought about.
Xi also launched an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept every corner of public office, netting both high-ranking “tigers” and lower-level “flies.” Some of the most senior officials — including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago — have been brought to justice.
The anti-corruption campaign has continued unabated, with Xi stressing that the fight is an ongoing endeavor. In 2025 alone, 115 officials at ministerial level or above were placed under investigation, while 627,000 people were disciplined in cases involving misconduct and corruption that affect the people’s immediate interests. The same year, China also opened investigations into more than 500 cases of cross-border corruption.
At a plenary session of the CPC’s top disciplinary body early this year, Xi again warned that corruption remains a problem that arises all too easily and frequently.
“We must see the fight against corruption through to the end, no matter how great the resistance or how high the cost,” he said. “No one who engages in corruption will be shown leniency, regardless of who they are, how high their rank or how great their contributions.”
EFFECTIVE APPROACHES
To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, it is imperative to uphold the Party’s overall leadership.
Over the past 14 years, the Party’s leadership has been further affirmed in both the Party Constitution and the country’s Constitution. Central commissions have been established to oversee key areas including reform, national security, cyberspace affairs, and financial and economic affairs. Working mechanisms for central decision-making and coordinating bodies have also been strengthened.
Strengthening theoretical education is another approach. With Xi at the helm, the CPC has launched nine Party-wide major education campaigns.
The latest one, launched in February this year, prodded Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance, aiming to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records.
This campaign built on the gains of previous ones on Party discipline and implementing the eight-point rules, among others, to advance the Party’s self-governance.
These efforts have gone hand in hand with institution-building. Under Xi’s watch, the Party and state oversight systems have been improved.
The National Commission of Supervision and local supervisory commissions were established to bring everyone in public office, regardless of Party membership, under supervision.
And Xi has made discipline inspections a key instrument of intra-Party oversight.
The inspection system allows higher-level Party authorities to send teams to examine how officials exercise power and carry out the central leadership’s policies. Inspectors interview officials and members of the public, review documents and receive complaints. They report their findings to Party authorities.
After each round of inspections launched by the Party Central Committee, Xi reviewed the reports in detail, assessed the problems uncovered and pushed for further improvements in inspection work.
Since 2012, the Party has also formulated or revised an unprecedented number of internal regulations, building a comprehensive framework of rules to confine power in “a cage of institutions.”
Noting the progress, Xi also warned that in some localities, rules were poorly enforced while “hidden rules” prevailed. He stressed that regulations must become “high-voltage lines” and that power must be exercised transparently, leaving no room for such hidden rules.
All these mechanisms are part of the integrated efforts to ensure officials, in Xi’s words, “do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to become corrupt.”
LEADING MODERNIZATION DRIVE
Full and rigorous Party self-governance serves a broader purpose: strengthening the Party’s capacity to lead China’s modernization drive.
“To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development,” Xi told senior provincial- and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year.
He urged Party officials to become more capable of pursuing high-quality development, serving the people, and guarding against and defusing risks.
China has entered a critical period for achieving the goal of basically realizing modernization by 2035, and still faces rising uncertainty abroad and mounting challenges at home. At such critical junctures, strong Party leadership is vital to chart the course.
All Party members, Xi said, must remain true to the Party’s original aspiration and mission, and lead the nation to “create new historic glories.”

Asen Vassilev, leader of We Continue the Change (PP) and a former finance minister, said on Nova TV on Wednesday morning that he expects Bulgaria’s 2027 budget to be significantly worse than the 2026 version, questioning Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s promise to submit it by the end of the month, before the presidential runoff.
Vassilev expressed doubt that Radev would meet the legal deadline, arguing that delaying the budget until after the election would leave the government asking the public to trust its assurances. “If it comes after the elections, it will be a case of 'trust me' [a famous catchphrase used by Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, which helped him win the 2001 elections – Ed.]. People trusted Mr. Radev once, and we saw that 900,000 of them ended up very disappointed. If the new budget were actually any good, they would have presented it on time, as required by law,” Vassilev said.
In the first round of the presidential election, Iliana Yotova received 915,000 fewer votes than Progressive Bulgaria won in the parliamentary elections. Vassilev said he suspected the country’s budget outlook would deteriorate from 2026 onward, but argued that it was better to wait for concrete details rather than speculate. He noted that no tax legislation had yet been submitted to Parliament.
Vassilev also rejected Radev’s claim that the European Commission was preventing the Bulgarian government from increasing social spending. He said the Commission focused on overall budget figures, while decisions on how funds were spent remained a national responsibility. Vassilev called for scrutiny of whether capital expenditures had increased despite claims that there was insufficient funding for salaries and pensions, and whether spending was directed toward people rather than areas vulnerable to theft.
The end-of-month deadline for submitting the budget to Parliament falls on a Saturday, Vassilev noted, while the presidential runoff is scheduled for Sunday. He said the proposal would first need to pass through the tripartite council for social dialogue before receiving approval from the Council of Ministers, with at least 24 hours required between the two steps.
Vassilev said the state could not directly control shop prices through a “price committee” of the kind used during the communist era. However, he argued, the government could avoid increasing base prices under its control, including electricity and gas costs, which directly affect prices paid by consumers.
“We removed the VAT on district heating and provided additional compensation to businesses. We lowered the price of road vignettes - though they are now being raised again. We also offered a discount on fuel. There are base prices that can be adjusted; the government has control over these,” Vassilev said. He added that a 20% to 30% increase in base prices would feed through to other prices.
He disputed the argument that rising personal incomes were driving inflation, saying that explanation might apply to a large, closed economy but not to Bulgaria, which is part of the EU and accounts for a very small share of the European market. Vassilev added that incomes rose faster than inflation in 2022, 2023 and 2024, whereas income growth is now lagging behind inflation.
“For the first time, a budget includes a provision for the impoverishment of Bulgarian citizens,” Vassilev said.
He cited what he described as unusually large expenditures approved by the current government, including 40 million euros per kilometer for construction of the Struma highway.
The PP leader also criticized the distribution of public spending, saying administrative operating costs had risen much more sharply than salary funding. He questioned why operating expenses were being increased by 35% while salaries were rising by only 5%, noting that operating costs cover electricity, water, minor repairs and supplies, and that these expenses had been raised by 1.5 billion euros. “There is money for operating costs, but none for salaries,” he said.
Vassilev also addressed the presidential runoff between Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov, arguing that the result would be determined by voter mobilization rather than agreements between political parties. With turnout at 22%, he said, the outcome remained open, as it was not yet clear how many people would vote in the second round or who they would support.
“Personally, I believe that the president should be elected by Bulgarian citizens, not by party headquarters. Each party is free to make its own decision, but it cannot be a matter of backroom deals within party headquarters,” Vassilev said, rejecting the idea that party leaders should negotiate support for a particular candidate.
He accused the ruling authorities of using fears of war to gain political advantage and distract the public from economic problems.
Martin Dimitrov, a Democratic Bulgaria member of Parliament, separately criticized the government’s budget plans in a Facebook post, accusing the authorities of preparing substantial tax and social security increases without meaningful cuts to public spending.
Dimitrov said the government’s proposed revenue measures for 2027 totaled 1.96 billion euros, equivalent to 1.39% of gross domestic product.
The planned social security changes include raising the maximum insurable income threshold from 2,300 to 2,400 euros, as well as increasing minimum insurable income levels and thresholds across various economic sectors.
For businesses, the proposals include a new 33% tax on excess profits for banks, insurers, retail chains, telecommunications companies and other sectors. The so-called “weekend tax” would rise from 3% to 7%, more than doubling. The deduction of tax losses would be limited to 70% of positive taxable financial results, while mandatory VAT registration would apply to certain transactions involving new buildings and regulated land plots.
The proposed measures affecting citizens include a new 7% tax on food vouchers, including the portion previously exempt from taxation, and faster increases in excise duties on tobacco products. The plans also envisage a new excise duty on high-powered vehicles exceeding 250 kW when first registered or imported, along with new restrictions and fines of up to 2,000 euros for home distillation of rakia, a fruit brandy.
Dimitrov also warned that property tax valuations would be raised in stages, effectively doubling by 2029 and paving the way for higher local real estate taxes.
He said the new measures were expected to generate nearly 2 billion euros in additional revenue by 2027, while the planned net reduction in government expenditure amounted to just 57 million euros.
Dimitrov accused the authorities of seeking to collect more money from individuals and businesses instead of tackling inefficient public spending, arguing that the proposed changes would increase taxes, social security contributions and the overall burden on taxpayers.
