The layoffs will affect 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members and will take place in stages.
Most employees will leave at the end of January 2027, while the remaining dismissals are scheduled for approximately 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, Norwegian’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The dismissals are happening out of necessity.”
Last week, aviation news outlet Check-in.dk reported that 125 employees at Norwegian’s Copenhagen base were at risk of losing their jobs.
The airline plans to reduce the number of aircraft based in Copenhagen during the summer season from 16 to 14.
According to Norwegian, the decision reflects significant seasonal differences in passenger demand.
The airline currently needs 16 aircraft during the busy summer months but only 10 during winter.
Despite the reduction in Copenhagen-based aircraft, Norwegian says it will maintain its existing number of summer departures from the Danish capital.
Some routes will instead be operated using aircraft based in Spain.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline last year, accounting for 15 percent of passengers, according to the airport’s latest financial statements.
SAS held the largest share at 38 percent, followed by Ryanair in third place with nine percent.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest operating base after Oslo.
Last year, the airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen Airport.
Danish Minister steps down as minister due to stress
A change in the government happened overnight, with a member of the government stepping down from her role for health reasons.
Signe Munk is stepping down as Denmark’s minister for cities, rural areas and transport after becoming ill with stress, the Prime Minister’s Office announced.
Munk, 36, a member of the Socialist People’s Party, known as SF, said she needed time to recover and find a better balance between work and family life. “I have become ill with stress. And I have decided to step down as minister,” she wrote on Facebook, adding that she intended to remain in politics.
Munk became a minister when the government was formed this summer, after years of working alongside SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr to rebuild the party following its crisis in 2014. Fellow SF politician Karina Lorentzen Dehnhardt, who has served as the party’s justice spokesperson, will replace her.
Lorentzen Dehnhardt first entered Denmark’s parliament in 2007, though she was out of office from 2015 to 2019. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen praised Munk’s contribution to the government negotiations, while Olsen Dyhr expressed full support for her decision to step down.
Nils Brøgger, an SF senior adviser and former campaign manager, will take Munk’s parliamentary seat during her sick leave. Having served less than a year as minister, Munk will not qualify for a ministerial pension but will receive six months of post-service pay.
Three senior doctors leave Rigshospitalet after being sent home following patient safety warnings
Three senior doctors who raised concerns about patient safety at Rigshospitalet’s transplant department are leaving the Copenhagen hospital after management sent them home, according to Danish broadcaster DR.
They were among five senior doctors who wrote to hospital management and the Capital Region, which oversees the hospital, expressing concern after two surgeons left the department earlier this year.
Nurses and doctors have also raised questions about professional standards at the Department of Transplantation and Diseases of the Digestive System, Denmark’s only unit performing liver transplants.
At a meeting Monday, hospital managers assured regional politicians that the department still had the quality and capacity needed to treat patients properly.
Regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt welcomed that assurance but said the departing doctors’ expertise would be difficult to replace. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj said it was too early to determine whether guidelines for experimental surgery had been breached. Those guidelines cover how procedures are documented and how patients are informed and involved.
An external investigation will review previous treatments to assess whether the department followed the guidelines and met professional standards.
Bank deposits in Denmark fall for two consecutive months
Danes’ bank deposits fell for a second consecutive month in September, reaching 1,309.3 billion kroner, according to figures from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank.
That was down from 1,317.7 billion kroner in August and 1,323.2 billion kroner in July. Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension provider Sampension, said the last decline lasting two consecutive months occurred in January 2023, but cautioned against treating the latest figures as evidence of a broader trend.
Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, said September declines were common, occurring in 16 of the past 20 years. He suggested loan payments and spending on autumn and winter clothing could help explain the fall, while noting that September does not bring large child benefit payments or tax refunds.
Despite the recent declines, deposits remained above the 1,283.1 billion kroner recorded at the beginning of the year. Dalsgaard expects savings to grow again, saying uncertainty about personal finances could encourage Danes to put more money aside.
Copenhagen Airport warns of continued security delays into next week
Passengers traveling through Copenhagen Airport could face longer waits at security checkpoints during busy periods over the weekend, with delays potentially continuing into next week.
The airport issued the warning Monday afternoon in a written statement to Ritzau from communications director Lise Agerley Kürstein.
The delays follow an inspection by Trafikstyrelsen, the Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority, which prompted the airport to introduce additional security measures temporarily.
The airport has brought in extra staff to help manage queues while maintaining security standards.
“Copenhagen Airport has called in extra staff and is doing everything we can to get passengers through security control as quickly as possible, while naturally maintaining the necessary high level of security,” Kürstein said.
Passengers are advised to follow their airlines’ recommendations and arrive at least two hours before flights within the Schengen Area, Europe’s passport-free travel zone, and three hours before flights outside it.
Neither the airport nor Trafikstyrelsen has explained what prompted the additional security requirements.
However, the airport previously told Danish broadcaster DR that the measures were not introduced because of external factors.
Speaking to Ritzau on Friday, Kürstein acknowledged passengers’ questions about the changes but said details of security procedures could not be disclosed.
“I understand the curiosity about there being some changed security considerations right now, but we cannot go further into details about our security procedures. But it is important to say that security is always top-notch, and that it is safe to fly,” she said.
Trafikstyrelsen will determine when normal security operations can resume or whether the airport must make permanent changes to its procedures.

The University of Copenhagen (KU) shut down several administrative systems Monday after another cyberattack, just days after hackers gained access to personal information belonging to approximately 525,000 people.
The university confirmed the latest attack on its website, reporting disruptions to several administrative systems and difficulties accessing university websites on Monday evening.
The previous breach exposed personal information including full names, CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and private email addresses.
The university has not provided further details about Monday’s attack.
Denmark’s Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization, Christina Egelund of Moderaterne (the Moderates), expressed serious concern about the repeated incidents.
“It is the second time in a short period, and it does not become less serious that it comes in the wake of several attacks on our universities,” she told Ritzau.
Several Danish universities, including the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Aarhus University, have also experienced cyberattacks in recent weeks.
Egelund said the incidents highlighted the seriousness of the security situation.
“It is an attack on our knowledge institutions, which are an absolutely crucial pillar of society in Denmark,” she said.
The minister summoned leaders from Denmark’s eight universities to a meeting Monday to discuss cybersecurity.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, explained that universities hold large amounts of personal and research data, making them attractive targets.
Their public visibility also increases their exposure to cyber threats.
“That makes us potential targets for both cybercriminals, foreign states, and activist groups,” he said in an Aarhus University press release.
New Danish media outlet Projekt Y to launch with AI-written news
A new Danish news outlet, Projekt Y, launches today at 1 p.m. with an approach that combines artificial intelligence-generated articles with traditional editorial oversight.
Editor-in-chief Michael Dyrby describes the content as AI-assisted rather than fully automated.
Human editors select stories, determine their angles, review AI-generated drafts, make revisions and choose images before publication.
“We could have made it so that AI did everything. But it doesn’t,” Dyrby said.
AI assistants will also help identify potential stories from research reports, press releases and other news outlets.
The aim is to produce more journalism with fewer resources while maintaining editorial control.
“We will find out,” Dyrby said, describing Projekt Y as an experiment in journalism’s future.
Initially, the outlet will cover Danish politics, business and international affairs from a broadly center-right perspective, although Dyrby says it will not follow a rigid ideology.
Its target audience is primarily adults aged 28 to around 60.
Dyrby, who graduated from the Danish School of Journalism in 1989, previously helped launch TV 2 News in the mid-2000s.
Projekt Y has received media subsidies and will also generate revenue through advertising.
Coverage could eventually expand to sports and culture.
Beyond publishing news, the company plans to develop technology that allows others to establish their own media outlets.
“The ambition is to create a technology that is so simple that everyone can use it and create their own media outlet, and in that way help democratize the use of media,” Dyrby said.
Additional publications are planned throughout the remainder of this year and into 2027.
Danes expect businesses to benefit more from AI than workers
Two-thirds of Danes believe artificial intelligence will benefit Danish companies, while only about half as many expect employees to gain from the technology.
The findings come from a new survey by TrygFonden, a Danish foundation supporting safety and social initiatives.
Frederik Olsen, a senior analyst at Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, an economic institute linked to the labor movement, said there was not yet evidence that AI benefited companies more than workers.
Even in occupations expected to face job losses, employment is developing similarly to the broader labor market, he said.
Olsen described AI as a productivity improvement but said investment in continuing education and skills development was necessary for both workers and employers to benefit.
The survey also found concern about young people entering the labor market.
Six in 10 respondents ages 18 to 35 feared that AI would make it harder for young people and recent graduates to find jobs. Across the full population, 46 percent shared that concern.
A September analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank, found that youth employment grew more slowly at companies using AI than at companies that did not.
However, young workers who might previously have joined AI-using businesses generally found employment elsewhere.
Nationalbanken expects companies to introduce AI gradually enough for affected workers to find other jobs.
It nevertheless said uncertainty remained high and could not rule out AI reducing Danish employment over the longer term.
Danish publisher bans AI tools for work on manuscripts
Danish publisher Lindhardt og Ringhof has prohibited employees and external partners from using artificial intelligence to complete work for the company.
The ban applies to proofreaders, editors, manuscript readers and consultants, according to a letter distributed by the publisher.
“It is not permitted for any purpose to use AI tools for tasks that one as an external partner solves for Lindhardt og Ringhof,” the letter states.
Manuscripts and other documents provided by the publisher must not be uploaded to AI systems under any circumstances.
The company said even apparently harmless uses, such as asking AI to summarize a manuscript, could create legal and copyright risks.
“Texts that are uploaded into AI tools can subsequently be copied and data mined, even if the provider claims otherwise,” the publisher said.
Literary director Sune de Souza Schmidt-Madsen told Danish public broadcaster DR that Lindhardt og Ringhof was not aware of external partners already using AI for its assignments.
However, he said the publisher expected the issue to emerge eventually and wanted to establish its rules in advance.
The restrictions also apply to the publisher’s own employees, Schmidt-Madsen said.
Denmark issues safety guidance for vulnerable people after CPR data leak
The Agency for Societal Security has published new guidance for people who may face increased risks following the leak of 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers and other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The advice is aimed at people who have previously experienced harassment, hold jobs that could attract criminal attention or are publicly known and at risk of having their names misused.
It also covers people whose names may expose them to harassment or identify them as members of vulnerable social, ethnic or religious minorities.
“The leak means that persons among these exposed or vulnerable groups of people must have a greater awareness of, among other things, their surroundings, behavior on social media and the security of their homes,” the agency said.
People who believe they face physical danger because a specific person may now know their address can consider applying for name and address protection.
The agency also recommends considering contact with police, a crisis center, the Danish Stalking Center or another specialized counseling service.
People can additionally request a hidden, secret or unlisted telephone number.
A hidden number prevents the recipient of a call from seeing the caller’s number.
Secret and unlisted numbers are also excluded from public telecommunications services, directory assistance and online telephone directories.
Power fault causes train delays and cancellations across Zealand
Passengers should expect longer travel times on most train services across Zealand because of a power fault at Copenhagen Central Station.
Three tracks at the station were without traction power Monday morning, DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said.
The fault caused several cancellations and reduced services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
“Banedanmark is working on resolving the fault,” DSB wrote on X.
Banedanmark is the state agency responsible for maintaining Denmark’s railway infrastructure.
Danish traffic service P4 Trafik reported at 10:50 a.m. that trains at Copenhagen Central Station had temporarily stopped because of the missing power.
Services were expected to resume shortly, although passengers would continue to experience delays and occasional cancellations.
Copenhagen’s S-train network was not affected and continued to operate normally.
Strong winds and high water to ease as calmer weather reaches Denmark
Denmark’s week will begin with strong winds and elevated coastal water levels before calmer and sunnier conditions arrive around Thursday.
The strongest winds Monday morning were along Jutland’s west coast between Blåvandshuk and Skagen, Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Mette Zhang said.
Some areas continued to experience storm-force gusts, although the wind was expected to weaken during the day.
DMI maintained warnings for elevated water levels around the Wadden Sea, the central western coast of Jutland and parts of the Limfjord.
Water levels in the Wadden Sea reached more than three meters above normal overnight but were beginning to fall.
Western Denmark will experience the most clouds Monday, while eastern areas will have clearer conditions. Showers are expected in several places before conditions improve later in the day.
Temperatures will range from 9 to 13 degrees Celsius.
A new front will bring clouds, rain and stronger southerly winds overnight into Tuesday. Winds could reach gale force along the west coast, although less rain is expected than during the weekend.
Wednesday will bring a mixture of rain, showers and sunshine.
A high-pressure system is expected to stabilize the weather from Thursday, bringing less wind, drier conditions and more sunshine.
Fog may form overnight into Thursday and Friday. Clearer skies will also increase the risk of overnight frost, particularly heading into Saturday.
Denmark investigates suspected Shamonda virus infection in cattle
Statens Serum Institut, Denmark’s national infectious disease institute, is investigating a suspected case of Shamonda virus in Danish cattle.
The suspicion is based on new information from the agricultural industry, SSI said. The institute has not previously detected the virus in Denmark.
The investigation follows the first confirmed human infection identified by French health authorities.
The French patient, who was severely immunocompromised and lived in an area with known infections, later died. The information provided did not establish whether the virus caused the death.
SSI said it was monitoring developments but currently saw no reason for concern among the general population.
The risk of human illness is assessed as “very limited.”
“It cannot be ruled out that the virus can also occur in Denmark, but it is important to emphasize that even if the virus is found in this country, it does not necessarily mean that people become ill,” SSI said.
Shamonda virus usually affects livestock and spreads through small blood-sucking midges.
It was first identified in Nigeria during the 1960s and has since been found occasionally in animals in Africa and Japan. In 2026, it has spread among cattle in Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
Farmers and veterinarians are being asked to report unusual illness or reproductive problems, including fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, abortions and stillborn or deformed calves.
Danish Crown confirms slaughter without stunning at Polish subsidiary
Danish Crown has confirmed that its Polish subsidiary Sokolow uses kosher slaughter without prior stunning at one of its facilities.
The practice occurs on a limited basis at a slaughterhouse in Tarnow in southeastern Poland, Danish financial news outlet Finans reported.
Kosher slaughter follows Jewish dietary rules and involves cutting an animal’s throat without first stunning it.
The method is legal in Poland but has been prohibited in Denmark since 2014, when prior stunning became mandatory.
Danish Crown said the Polish facility slaughtered 69,000 cattle in 2025. The company said only “a minority” were slaughtered using the kosher method but declined to provide a specific number.
Several animal welfare organizations criticized the company’s involvement.
Søren Kent Pedersen, a veterinarian with animal welfare organization Dyrenes Beskyttelse, described the practice as animal cruelty and accused Danish Crown of hypocrisy because the company publicly emphasizes animal welfare.
Danish Crown’s website states that “good animal welfare is the core of our business” and that the company protects animals’ well-being from farms through slaughter.
Sokolow chief executive Przemyslaw Gostkiewicz said Poland has a particular tradition of kosher slaughter that allows Jewish people to follow their dietary rules.
“We use the slaughter method, even though it naturally raises dilemmas regarding animal welfare, regardless of the fact that the method is fully legal,” he said.
Danish Crown did not say whether it would continue permitting the practice.
Parents urged to check children’s electric scooters after illegal riding cases
Danish road safety authorities are urging parents to check electric scooters used by their children after police stopped underage riders and scooters capable of greatly exceeding the legal speed limit.
Riders must be at least 15 years old to use an electric scooter alone in traffic. Scooters may travel no faster than 20 kilometers per hour, and helmets are mandatory.
Children under 15 may ride in traffic only when accompanied by an adult.
The Danish Road Safety Council identified 21 reported cases between September 13 and October 13 involving children who were too young or scooters that could travel too fast.
The figure came from media coverage and police reports rather than a complete national count.
Children as young as nine were stopped, while some scooters could reach speeds of up to 90 kilometers per hour.
“Parents should take it seriously and check the rules before saying yes to an electric scooter,” council chief executive Jakob Bøving Arendt said.
Emergency departments in Odense and Svendborg have treated 811 people injured in electric scooter accidents since 2021. Twenty-five percent suffered serious injuries.
Odense University Hospital physician Jens Lauritsen said crashes can cause severe injuries even at legal speeds.
Modified scooters capable of traveling 60, 80 or 100 kilometers per hour could endanger both riders and others, he said.
Denmark to cull 27,000 turkeys after bird flu outbreak on Lolland
Danish authorities will cull 27,000 turkeys Monday after highly pathogenic avian influenza was detected in a flock in Stokkemarke on the island of Lolland.
It is Denmark’s second confirmed outbreak of the highly contagious disease within one week, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said.
Another outbreak was identified Friday in a flock in Bøgelunde in Slagelse Municipality.
“It is therefore extra important at this time of year that everyone who keeps poultry or other birds does everything to prevent contact between their animals and wild birds,” agency veterinarian Mette Kirkeskov Sie said.
Owners should prevent wild birds from reaching their animals, drinking water and feed. The agency also recommends changing footwear before entering areas where birds are kept.
Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the infected flock on Lolland. Poultry owners within those areas must follow stricter disease control requirements.
The restrictions will remain until authorities complete their investigations and determine that the risk of further transmission has declined.
The agency said avian influenza only very rarely spreads to humans.
However, people should avoid touching sick, weakened or dead wild birds.
Denmark’s current threat assessment for highly pathogenic avian influenza transmitted by wild birds remains at the medium level.
Danish authorities urge companies to strengthen personal data protections
The Agency for Public Security has urged Danish authorities and companies to reduce the risk of personal information being systematically retrieved from their IT systems.
The warning follows several major incidents involving unauthorized access to personal data.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and a major business association, said the advice applies beyond systems directly connected to the national CPR register.
It covers any system where identification details, such as a CPR or customer number, can be used to retrieve names, addresses or other personal information.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The warning follows the leak of 8.8 million CPR numbers and separate cyberattacks affecting the University of Copenhagen and telecommunications company 3 Denmark.
The university said hackers accessed information involving approximately 525,000 people. Meanwhile, 3 Denmark said unauthorized parties may have accessed names and addresses belonging to as many as 400,000 private customers.
“The special thing about the threat is that the perpetrator does not necessarily need to break into a system,” Dansk Industri cybersecurity expert Jeppe Engell said.
Access can instead be misused to conduct unusually large numbers of searches, he added.
Dansk Industri recommends identifying systems that retrieve personal data, removing unnecessary access, reviewing logs for suspicious patterns and limiting the number of searches.
Companies should also decide in advance who is responsible for investigating and shutting down suspicious access, including systems operated by external suppliers.

Struggling with Denmark’s dark winter? A researcher says we should embrace it
As Denmark switches back to winter time this weekend, the evenings will suddenly feel much darker. But instead of fighting the darkness with more artificial light, a Danish researcher suggests we learn to appreciate it.
If you are new to Denmark, the dark months can take some getting used to.
When the clocks go back one hour during the night leading into Sunday, sunrise and sunset will both come an hour earlier. That means more daylight in the morning – but also an earlier start to the long, dark Danish evenings.
For many internationals, the lack of daylight can be one of the more challenging parts of living in Denmark.
But Mette Hvass, a researcher in darkness at Aalborg University, argues that darkness itself is not necessarily something we should try to eliminate.
“We have become used to thinking that more light is always better. But the opposite is often the case,” she said in a press release.
“Too much and incorrect outdoor lighting can be harmful to both humans and animals. Therefore, we must become better at appreciating the darkness and the experiences it gives us.”
Less light can sometimes feel safer
It may sound counterintuitive, but reducing artificial light can in some situations actually make people feel safer.
Hvass points to an experiment at a light rail station in Aarhus, where lighting was reduced by around 80 percent.
According to Aalborg University, people waiting at the station reported feeling safer after the change because the lower brightness made it easier to see the surrounding area instead of only the brightly lit space immediately around them.
Hvass is not suggesting that Denmark should simply switch off its lights.
“We do not need to choose between light and darkness. But we must become better at using light thoughtfully,” she said.
What you notice when the lights go down
Darkness also offers experiences that artificial lighting can easily obscure.
Stars, planets and the Moon become more visible, while dusk itself makes it possible to experience the gradual transition from daylight to night.
Our other senses also become more noticeable. Sounds, smells and changes in temperature can feel stronger when vision is no longer dominant.
And according to Aalborg University, our eyes can often adapt to darkness better than we expect.
For people who associate darkness with insecurity or discomfort, spending more time outside after sunset can also make it feel more familiar.
“When we make room for the darkness, we gain access to experiences, senses and natural phenomena that otherwise disappear in the light,” Hvass said.
So as Denmark enters the darkest part of the year, perhaps the answer is not always another lamp.
Sometimes, it may simply be to give your eyes – and yourself – a little time to adjust.

Strong winds bring unusually cheap electricity to Denmark this weekend
Electricity prices are expected to fall sharply across Denmark on Saturday as strong winds boost production from the country’s wind turbines.
If you have a variable electricity contract, Saturday could be a good day to run the washing machine, charge an electric car or use other power-hungry appliances.
The average spot price of electricity is expected to be around DKK 0.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) on Saturday, according to energy company Norlys.
That is significantly below the average price so far in October.
“It is actually the first time in all of October that electricity prices consistently stay below one krone per kilowatt-hour for a full 24-hour period, and that is primarily because we are getting plenty of wind,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
So far in October, average electricity prices have been DKK 1.16 per kWh in western Denmark and DKK 1.19 in eastern Denmark.
Wind power pushes prices down
Denmark’s electricity market is divided into two price areas: western Denmark, which covers Jutland and Funen, and eastern Denmark, which includes Zealand and Copenhagen.
Prices can therefore differ slightly depending on where you live.
On Saturday, prices are expected to remain below DKK 1 per kWh throughout the day. The highest price is expected at around 19:00, when it will reach approximately DKK 0.75–0.76 per kWh.
The particularly low prices are being driven by strong winds and increased production from Denmark’s wind turbines.
The Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI, has warned of severe gales in parts of western Denmark during the night from Saturday to Sunday.
Norlys says this could also keep electricity prices low on Sunday.
“There is a good probability that we will also have low electricity prices on Sunday,” Trolle said. “Even though weather forecasts and electricity prices can always change, much points right now to consumers getting another day with cheap electricity hours.”
Your actual electricity bill will be higher
The quoted prices are wholesale spot prices and are not the final price consumers pay for electricity.
Grid charges, tariffs, subscriptions, supplier mark-ups and VAT are added to the spot price.
How much you can benefit from Saturday’s low prices also depends on your electricity contract. Customers on hourly or other variable-price contracts can benefit directly by moving electricity consumption to cheaper hours, while customers on fixed-price contracts generally will not see the same immediate effect.

New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Epistemic Ecology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:51:00 UTC
19:51:00 KST

Catherine Elgin’s Epistemic Ecology is an important book. It is a wide-ranging tour of the central issues in epistemology, a tour that is anchored in the treatment of knowers as agents in their environments rather than spectators of those environments. According to Elgin, “autonomous agents extend, modify, and adapt to their environments, both natural and social, in order to frame and promote their epistemic ends” (3). It is in this sense that Elgin’s approach to epistemology is ecological: Epistemic Ecology consistently treats the activity of coming to know as a way in which epistemic agents relate to and cope with one another and to their natural environments.
In developing this ecological epistemology, Elgin relies on a number of key interconnected concepts, including ‘understanding’, ‘acceptance’, ‘commitment’, and ‘reflective equilibrium’. She applies these concepts seriatim to a variety of apparently distinct problems so as to articulate a unified holistic and internalist account. The issues in epistemology that Elgin focuses upon prominently include the autonomy and sociality of epistemic agents, testimony and the acceptance of testimony, the conditions on the reasonableness of disagreement, and the character and legitimate ends of teaching.
Significantly, Elgin’s ways of handling each of the various topics that she treats hang together with one another, and with her ecological approach to epistemology in general, in a reflective equilibrium of mutually supporting commitments, thus exemplifying the thesis of Epistemic Ecology. As the book has this overall structure of a set of mutually supporting commitments in reflective equilibrium, and the central node in this network is Elgin’s commitment to the ecological model of epistemology, the remainder of this review will focus on the most important implications of the ecological approach, and her reasons for accepting that model, rather than going through each of the topics discussed by Elgin.
Of the key concepts that she employs, ‘understanding’ is the most central. For Elgin, ‘understanding’ names the basic epistemic end of cognitive agents. She uses the word ‘understanding’ as both a noun and a verb:
An understanding of a topic is a network of commitments in reflective equilibrium. To understand a topic is to accept such a network—that is, to be willing and able to use it in non-trivial inferences and actions when one’s ends are cognitive. (231)
It is also central to Elgin’s concept of ‘understanding’, however, and thus to her ecological epistemology, that the commitments that are included in such networks of understanding include more than mere commitments to the truth of fact stating propositions, and that many of these additional elements that an epistemic agent accepts when she understands an area are neither true nor likely to lead to truth. An understanding of a topic
is a network of commitments that includes not just commitments about matters of fact but also acceptance of models, idealizations, and thought experiments that are known to diverge from the truth, as well as methods, norms, and standards that are not truth apt. (288)
That for Elgin the reflective equilibrium of a network of commitments that constitutes the understanding of a group of phenomena includes commitments to models, methods, norms, etc., that are apt to lead in turn to even greater understanding of those phenomena, but which themselves are neither true nor conducive to uncovering truths, leads to some of her most striking and distinctive claims. As a particularly telling example, in Epistemic Ecology, Elgin develops an extended account of her long-held position that models are best seen as “felicitous falsehoods”, misrepresentations that, suitably employed, enhance a more fruitful understanding of the phenomena that they represent.
In the course of developing that account, Elgin suggests that the felicitous falsehoods introduced by the sciences’ use of models are essential to those sciences, in that the epistemic end of science is better viewed as understanding, rather than as true and complete representation of the world.
I contend that models enable us to understand reality in ways that we would be unable to if we restricted ourselves to the unvarnished truth. The point is not just that the features that a model skirts can permissibly be neglected. They ought to be neglected. Too much information occludes patterns that figure in an understanding of the phenomena. The regularities a model reveals are real and informative. But many of them show up only under idealizing assumptions. (265)
A critic might think that there is a certain perversity involved in Elgin prioritizing understanding as the crucial end of inquiry rather than truth. After all, isn’t coming to know the world as it actually is the entire point of inquiring about the world, and doesn’t knowing the world as it actually is require coming to have a representation of the world that is true? The best that Elgin can promise for understanding, a critic might assert, is a reflective equilibrium of commitments that is productive in inference, action, and further understanding, but, for all that, quite possibly contains misrepresentations of the world. Elgin is sensitive to this concern, and addresses it directly in the course of providing reasons to accept her preferred ontological position, ‘constructive nominalism’. For Elgin, nominalism differs from realism in respect of their characterizations of what is involved in epistemic agents establishing the identity conditions on individuals and sorting those individuals into kinds.
To determine what there is we need to settle which differences matter, thereby marking out individuals, properties, and kinds…The issue that divides realists and nominalists is whether—or perhaps to what extent—such scientific work is creation or discovery. Do the scientists draw the lines, or do they discover where nature draws them? Realists maintain that nature draws the lines. The scientists and other investigators simply find what is there to be found. (248-249)
The nominalism that Elgin champions, on the other hand, is the “rejection of the idea that reality privileges any specific universals. All of the extensions are equally real…The kinds we recognize evolve in tandem with our emerging interest, methods, and resources” (244).
Elgin’s case for prioritizing understanding rather than truth as the central epistemic goal turns on her case in favor of constructive nominalism. If we should accept nominalism, then, arguably, what is epistemically important is understanding, which crucially involves the way that epistemic agents, in light of their interests and needs, carve the world into individuals, and sort those individuals into kinds, rather than faithfully and truly mirroring a hypothetical pre-existing structure of the world.
Elgin’s constructive nominalism is pervasive in Epistemic Ecology, but her most explicit consideration of the position appears in Chapter 10. Faithful to her commitment to the reflective equilibrium of a set of mutually supportive commitments as a primary epistemic virtue, Elgin’s case for constructive nominalism has the form of highlighting the role that it plays in the system of views she lays out in the other sections of the book, rather than a deductive argument.
Elgin begins this consideration by emphasizing her original starting point, the ecological model of epistemic agency. Knowers are organic agents that, as organisms, need to cope with and survive in their environments. As such, what is important to epistemic agents are those facets of the world that are relevant to their ability to interact successfully with their environment, a success condition which is fixed in detail by the kind of organism that they are and the specific character of their environment. One of the ways in which such coping takes place is through niche construction, the activity in which the agent not only adapts to its environment but also adapts that environment to its needs. So, the epistemic agent also has an interest in coming to understand how it might alter its particular environment so as to serve its other interests.
Organisms both adapt to an environment and alter the environment to make it a more suitable ecological niche. The choice of phenomena that epistemic agents seek to understand is a function of both the environment and the epistemic resources that epistemic agents bring to it. Epistemic agents adjust their interests to what is accessible, given their resources, and modify their resources as a result of the information they access. (241)
On Elgin’s account, finite epistemic agents are thus limited in their ability to access information about the world and selective concerning which information about the world they have an interest in accessing. But that world, according to Elgin, is fecund in regard to kinds. Although she doesn’t put the point in quite this way, on her view everything in the universe is both like and unlike everything else in the universe in an infinite number of ways, so there are also an infinite number of kinds. Any particular organism, however, only has the informational resources to access a limited set of similarities among individuals, and only a relatively small subset of all similarities is relevant to the needs and interests of any organism. So, taking the production of a complete and accurate representation of the world to be the legitimate end of inquiry is neither plausible nor, indeed, useful for finite epistemic agents.
Rather, it makes more epistemic sense to aim at an understanding of those similarities that help the agent to successfully navigate her environment, together with an understanding of the patterns of relationships among those similarities, the ways in which those similarities are related to and dependent upon one another. In coming to have such an understanding the agent comes to be able to leverage that understanding in successfully gaining access to the resources she needs from her environment and to reconstruct that environment in a manner that is beneficial to achieving her goals. As Elgin also points out, the similarities and patterns among similarities that are important for an epistemic agent might, or might not, align with those kinds that a physicist or chemist might think of as natural kinds. To cite one of Elgin’s examples, those individuals that fall into the kind ‘toxic to humans’ share very little physically or chemically, although coming to know which individuals fall into that kind is of great importance for any individual which happens to be a member of the set of humans.
Epistemic Ecology makes a compelling case for a distinctive and important way of thinking about epistemological issues. It does so by displaying how consistently applying an ecologically informed epistemological stance can help to provide illumination on a wide variety of issues in current epistemology, rather than by attempting to produce air-tight arguments for her position, or against her opponents’ views. Elgin’s writing style is remarkably lucid, and her treatment of alternative positions is always clear and fair-minded, even when she is critical. Epistemic Ecology is highly recommended.

BAE Systems test-fires new deck launcher for U.S. Navy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:48:26 UTC
19:48:26 KST

- BAE Systems completed the first live-fire test of its Adaptable Deck Launcher, a deck-mounted launcher for Evolved SeaSparrow missiles, at China Lake, California.
- The launcher uses Mk 41 electronics and Mk 25 Quad-Pack canisters and can be reloaded at sea with standard shipboard equipment.
BAE Systems has completed the first live-fire test of its Adaptable Deck Launcher, a deck-mounted missile launcher that lets U.S. Navy and allied ships carry more Evolved SeaSparrow air defense missiles and reload them at sea with standard shipboard equipment.
The company announced the test on Oct. 27 from China Lake, California, home of the U.S. Navy’s main weapons test range in the Mojave Desert. BAE developed the launcher under a U.S. Department of War contract for the NATO Seasparrow Project Office, the multinational program that manages the Evolved SeaSparrow Missile, or ESSM, and it has not released details such as how many missiles were fired or which ESSM version was used.
The launcher sits on a ship’s deck and fires from fixed-angle canisters, so it does not need the deep below-deck wells required by the Mk 41 Vertical Launching System, the standard missile launcher on U.S. Navy cruisers and destroyers. It still uses the Mk 41’s electronics and logistics suite, which BAE says keeps operating costs low and gives it the same reliability as a vertical launcher. The ADL is fully compatible with the Mk 25 Quad-Pack canister, which holds four ESSM interceptors, the missiles ships use to defend themselves against supersonic anti-ship missiles, aircraft and other aerial threats.
Reloading is the main selling point. Because the canisters sit above deck, crews can replace spent ones at sea using normal shipboard equipment, so a ship can keep firing without returning to port to rearm.
“The successful demonstration of the Adaptable Deck Launcher is a major milestone in our commitment to enhancing the Navy’s combat effectiveness and readiness,” said Jason Casciotti, vice president of Weapons Systems at BAE Systems.
BAE designed the launcher for aircraft carriers, amphibious ships and other surface combatants, and it offers compact configurations for medium unmanned surface vessels, the smaller robotic ships the U.S. Navy has been testing as additional missile carriers. On carriers and amphibious ships, which were built without large vertical launch systems, the ADL could add air defense missiles without new below-deck construction.
The launcher grew out of the U.S. Navy’s Next Generation Evolved SeaSparrow Missile Launch System program. In 2023, BAE received a $37 million contract to design prototype deck launchers for the NATO Seasparrow Project Office based on its ADL concept, with the goal of fielding the newer ESSM Block 2 on carriers and other large-deck ships. ESSM Block 2 adds an active radar seeker, letting the missile guide itself to a target in the final phase of flight.
BAE serves as the mechanical design agent for the Mk 41 family and builds the canisters used in it, work that has included recent production contracts for Mk 41 canisters for the U.S. Navy and allied navies, including those of Australia and Japan. That role gave the company a ready supply chain and a common canister design for the new deck launcher.

Mbappe's Mao remarks expose costs of crossing China's red lines

2026-10-28
10:46:47 UTC

News analysis
Kylian Mbappe’s Mao Zedong remarks expose costs of crossing China’s red lines
- Kylian Mbappe’s Mao remarks triggered fast backlash in China, with sponsors cutting ties, CCTV removing ads, and social media limiting his accounts.
- The case shows a common China pattern: online outrage, official pressure and corporate distancing after a remark is seen as crossing red lines.
- Analysts say the rules are unclear, so brands and celebrities need cultural awareness, training and crisis plans to avoid sudden damage.
AI generated
SHANGHAI – Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe’s rapid fall from favour in China after remarks about Mao Zedong followed a familiar pattern: online outrage, corporate distancing, platform restrictions and official intervention.
Within 24 hours of a podcast clip surfacing in which the France captain referred to Mao as “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”, sponsors including Mengniu Dairy, Shanghai Milkground and energy drink-maker Eastroc ended cooperation with the footballer.
State broadcaster CCTV removed Mbappe-related advertising and Chinese social media platforms restricted access to his accounts. Mbappe apologised on Oct 27, describing his remarks as “ill-judged”.
The speed of the fallout will be familiar to companies, brands and celebrities with exposure to China. Analysts say the episode is the latest reminder of a business risk that remains difficult to manage despite years of similar controversies.
Foreign brands have repeatedly faced public backlash in China, from Dolce & Gabbana’s cancelled Shanghai fashion show in 2018 and apologies by Versace, LVMH-owned Dior and Tapestry’s Coach in 2019, to boycotts of H&M, Nike and Adidas over Xinjiang cotton and the NBA’s fallout with CCTV after a Houston Rockets executive expressed support for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
The details differ, but the pattern is similar: a remark, image or statement gains traction online, commercial partners come under pressure to respond, and reputational damage quickly outgrows the original offence.
“You don’t need to think like a Chinese person to succeed in China, but you do need to understand how Chinese audiences will react and the cultural implications of not self-policing,” said Michael MacRitchie, founder of MGI Group, which connects global celebrities with Chinese brands.
A matter of respect
A central question in such episodes is how much of the backlash reflects genuine public anger and how much is amplified by state media, online platforms and official actors.
The Mbappe case illustrates how difficult that distinction can be to draw. As the controversy unfolded, the original comments about Mao were largely inaccessible on China’s heavily censored internet.
Many consumers were therefore exposed less to what Mbappe said than to reports that sponsors had dropped him and official media were condemning him.
“What we’ve had in this situation is to a certain extent a manufactured outrage,” said Mark Dreyer, a sports analyst and author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s sporting ambitions.
Even so, Dreyer said it would be unwise for leagues, clubs and athletes to underestimate the reaction such incidents can provoke.
“They can’t be seen to be giving a stated directive to their players not to say anything that could offend China,” he said. “Of course, behind the scenes, I’m sure people are being told, just be careful, be sensible, be aware that these sorts of reactions can happen.”
Zak Dychtwald, founder of BridgeWorks Global, which advises multinational organisations, said that although these controversies remain relatively common, they are preventable.
“If you are participating in this market, the expectation is that you respect China’s self-narrative and you have a basic understanding of what it is. Red line education should come at the foundation of it,” he said.
Another challenge for brands, leagues and celebrities, however, is that while China’s political and cultural red lines are broadly understood, they are rarely clearly defined.
That uncertainty can encourage companies and commercial partners to distance themselves from controversial figures before the scale of any offence has been fully established.
“There is no rule in black and white for what crosses a line,” said Wei Kan, founder of consultancy Conduit Asia. The line shifts depending on “how consumers feel, the wider mood in society, and how platforms and media amplify a story”, he said.
For foreign businesses, China’s sensitivities should no longer come as a surprise. Yet analysts say political and cultural risks are still often treated as secondary considerations rather than routine commercial hazards.
MacRitchie said his firm includes behavioural and reputational clauses in endorsement contracts; others point to market-specific briefings, media training and crisis-response planning as increasingly necessary safeguards rather than optional precautions.
“When it goes well, everybody celebrates,” Dychtwald said. “But when you get (China) wrong, it can be extraordinarily painful and swift in its retribution.” REUTERS

Mounting censorship across the industry has forced adult creators to get more creative when it comes to protecting their livelihoods. Sixteen states, almost all of them with majority Republican legislatures, have likewise adopted resolutions declaring porn a public health crisis, with some, like Alabama, passing “porn tax” legislation on adult sites that operate within its jurisdiction. Free-speech advocates argue that age-verification laws, which have also been enacted in the UK, are making the internet less safe.

Breadcrumb
Syria and Jordan reopen border crossing after deadly air strikes that killed seven civilians
Syria and Jordan resumed passenger and commercial traffic through the Nasib border crossing on Wednesday, following a temporary closure triggered by Jordanian air strikes in southern Syria that killed seven civilians, including children.
The reopening comes as Damascus and Amman agreed to establish a joint security committee to investigate the strikes, which targeted areas in the southern Syrian provinces of Daraa and Suwayda on Monday.
Mazen Alloush, director of international relations and cooperation at Syria's General Authority for Land and Sea Ports and Customs, confirmed that passenger movement and commercial activity had returned to normal on Wednesday morning, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syrian authorities had suspended traffic in both directions on Tuesday, citing concerns for the safety of travellers and border personnel following the strikes.
The Nasib crossing, which connects southern Syria with Jordan, is a major route for passenger travel and overland trade between the two countries.
The reopening signals an effort by both governments to contain tensions following the Jordanian military operation, which Damascus said had not been coordinated with Syrian authorities.
Joint investigation into deadly strikes
The decision to establish a joint security committee followed a telephone conversation between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and his Jordanian counterpart Ayman Safadi.
According to a joint statement issued by the two foreign ministries on Wednesday, the committee will examine the circumstances surrounding Jordan's recent military operations inside Syrian territory and assess their consequences.
It will also develop mechanisms for field and intelligence coordination to address security threats and prevent further civilian casualties.
Both ministers emphasised their commitment to strengthening bilateral relations and resolving disagreements through dialogue, recognising the interconnected security interests of their countries.
Jordan's armed forces said Monday's strikes targeted sites linked to the Islamic State group (IS), which it accused of posing an imminent threat to Jordanian security.
The operation followed a deadly attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the Jordanian city of Karak on Friday, which killed at least nine people and wounded 34 others.
IS claimed responsibility for the church attack, prompting Jordanian security forces to launch an investigation and arrest three suspects.
Jordan subsequently carried out air strikes against what its military described as IS hideouts in southern Syria.
However, the strikes also hit civilian areas, killing seven people, according to Syrian civil defence authorities. Five members of one family, including three children, were among those killed.
Syrian emergency and disaster management teams responded to attacks at four locations in Daraa and Suwayda.
Jordanian authorities initially maintained that the operation had been coordinated with Damascus, but Syrian officials disputed that account.
Safadi later expressed deep regret over the civilian deaths during his conversation with al-Shaibani, while reaffirming Jordan's commitment to Syria's sovereignty and stability.
He maintained that the strikes had been based on intelligence concerning suspected threats to Jordan.
The disagreement over whether the operation had been coordinated highlighted tensions between the neighbouring countries, despite their stated commitment to security cooperation.

Burnham’s government unveils its first UK budget: What to expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:42:52 UTC
19:42:52 KST

Burnham’s government unveils its first UK budget: What to expect
UK chancellor to present an autumn budget amid rising living costs and energy bills.
British Chancellor John Healey will set out the country’s autumn budget, the government’s tax and spending plans, the first under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s premiership amid high inflation and government spending levels.
While the budget will be announced in parliament on Wednesday at 12.30 GMT, speculation about what it will lay out has ranged from a series of tax announcements to commitments to defence spending.
But the country continues to deal with a rising cost-of-living crisis and energy bills are expected to see their biggest rise in four years in January due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
As total United Kingdom borrowing broke through the 3 trillion pounds ($3.99 trillion) barrier for the first time in September, the country is already spending 100 billion pounds ($133bn) each year just on servicing that debt.
Despite that challenge, the chancellor has said the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain”.
In a speech last month, Healey said that he and Burnham were in “lockstep” in meeting fiscal rules, “to balancing the books, with a buffer to protect against uncertainty, to control borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.
Gregory Thwaites, interim chief economist at the British think tank, Resolution Foundation, told Al Jazeera he is expecting a “relatively small budget given the limited room for maneuvre the government has”.
“A bit of action to offset high living costs,” but “most big decisions postponed to next year.”
Following the two budgets from former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which included big tax and spending increases, Healey’s budget is expected to take a more “steady as she goes” line, which some say is the wrong approach.
Here’s how he will be expected to achieve that.
Defence spending
On Monday, Burnham said Healey would set out a plan to fully fund the government’s defence plans and commitments, telling ITV’s Good Morning Britain that his government’s first challenge was financing the already announced defence investment plan.
Announced in June, the plan is backed by 298 billion pounds ($396bn) of investment and will transform the armed forces as the country moves to “warfighting readiness” and stepping up “European security”, according to a government policy paper.
But Burnham said it was “crucial that we have a funded plan that we can then implement, and we will set out more details on Wednesday as to how we’ve done that”.
He added that NATO commitments of spending 3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence spending by 2030 and 3.5 percent by 2035 are included in the pathway, explaining that national security issues were “at the top of the priority list”.
As it stands, Britain spends about 2.6 percent of its GDP on defence.
The Guardian reported that on defence spending, Healey aims to close a 4.7-billion-pound ($6.2bn) funding gap in the government’s plan inherited from the previous Labour Party leader, with cuts to other departmental budgets likely to fund it.
Inflation
Government borrowing and inflation continue to rise, which is a potential spanner in the works for proposed spending.
Last week, UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest levels in a year.
According to the Office for National Statistics, borrowing was nearly 25 billion pounds ($33bn) last month alone, “a little higher than a year earlier, as spending, including higher debt interest costs, increased more than government income, partly reflecting the impacts of inflation”.
ONS added that in the financial year to September 2026, borrowing remained below the same period last year, but it was higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecast.
According to Jasper Kenter, a professorial research fellow in ecological economics at Aberystwyth Business School, for the government to grow the economy without raising inflation levels, there needs to be an understanding of what kind of economy is created.
“The strongest policies improve prosperity, resilience and sustainability at the same time,” Kenter said.
“Growth is less likely to be inflationary when it comes from increasing the economy’s productive capacity rather than simply boosting spending. Measures that improve skills, reduce energy dependence, strengthen local economies and regenerate ecosystems are likely to deliver more lasting benefits than short-term stimulus,” he added.
Moreover, Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said in a media release ahead of the budget that Healey “faces a forecast in which borrowing is still expected to fall in coming years, and the fiscal rules are still being met”.
“Despite that, a ‘steady-as-she-goes’ budget is not an option available to the chancellor. Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
Tax on banks, online sellers
The budget is also expected to reveal new taxes on banks and online marketplaces such as Amazon, Temu and eBay, as well as a funding boost for mayoralties and local authorities.
The biggest four banks collectively made about profits of 15 billion pounds ($19.9bn) in the first six months of this year. Trade unions are calling for higher taxes on those earnings, the BBC has reported.
According to the BBC, the Treasury is leaning towards changing a 2023 surcharge rate on banks, which would raise about 2 billion pounds ($2.6bn).
On marketplaces such as Amazon, Healey is reportedly looking to crack down on foreign sellers who avoid paying VAT – a UK sales tax – which is expected to raise as much as 1 billion pounds ($1.3bn) and help fund business rate cuts for high street shops, The Times reported.
Paying for social care and benefits
According to The Guardian newspaper, Healey is expected to allocate about 1.42 trillion pounds ($1.8 trillion) this year for day-to-day spending and public investment, with about 100 billion pounds ($132.8bn) going on debt interest.
Kenter, of Aberystwyth Business School, told Al Jazeera that he expects “targeted support rather than large-scale tax cuts or rises” in the budget announcement.
“The government appears keen to signal empathy with the pressures many people are facing. Addressing the harsh cliff edge in carer’s allowance and expanding parental pay are good examples of this,” he said.
Some of the budget’s contents have already been announced, including ending the carers’ allowance limit and removing tariffs on a range of food items, including chocolate and beans, to make them cheaper for shoppers.
Pensioners are also expected to be shielded from income tax through the introduction of a new personal allowance, while Healey is expected to add another 1 billion pounds ($1.3bn) to the 39 billion pounds ($51.8bn) planned for social and affordable housing in England over the next decade.
“Pensioners will benefit from another substantial increase in the state pension, while low-paid workers will benefit from increases in the minimum wage. For most households, the bigger determinants of living standards will remain wages, inflation and energy costs rather than any new tax measures announced in the budget,” Kenter explained.
Last month, Burnham announced a new national care service to provide free personal care for elderly people. As costs of care for the elderly have soared in the UK, this was a major issue from the outset of Burnham’s premiership.
He said the plan would be introduced in phases and would be fully funded from public spending and savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock – an annual increase in state pension that goes up with inflation, wages or a fixed rate of 2.5 percent, whichever is highest.
A report on how this will be implemented is due in summer 2027.
Energy bills
Amid high gas and oil prices as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, energy prices worldwide have increased, with Brent crude futures at $115.90 a barrel on Wednesday.
In the UK, energy prices are predicted to reach nearly 2,000 pounds ($2,655) a year for households in January after energy consultancy Cornwall Insight projected in its latest forecast last month that the government’s cap on energy prices is expected to increase by 16 percent.
On energy bills, reports suggest the chancellor is expected to announce help for households in the budget by scrapping standing charges for energy supply, among other things.

Plato’s Moral Realism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:42:00 UTC
19:42:00 KST

In Plato’s Moral Realism, Gerson defends two connected claims: Plato is a metaethical non-naturalist realist, and his ethical realism necessarily depends on his metaphysics. As quickly emerges, Gerson’s Plato is also a Moorean—after a fashion. Just as Moore used his open-question argument to argue that intrinsic value must be sui generis and unanalyzable lest we fall prey to the naturalistic fallacy, so Plato—on Gerson’s reading—believes the Idea of the Good must have no essential content (it must be “beyond essence”, as Gerson translates ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας (Republic 509b9)), or else we can always ask why any of its essential properties (or the instantiations of those properties in the world) are themselves good. We might think of Gerson’s Plato as aiming to avoid an essentialistic fallacy—and this Platonic version of the open-question argument serves as an argumentative refrain throughout the book (e.g., 16-19, 33, 49, 66-67, 90, 96, 130, 143, 156, 170, 173, 182). Often explicitly associated with Moore, the argument provides key motivation for Gerson’s central theses: Plato’s superordinate Idea of the Good has no essence, and only such a sui generis metaphysical entity can adequately ground Plato’s normative theory.
After establishing his metaphysical framework at the start of Chapter 2, Gerson draws out its consequences: the identification of the Good with the One means I more fully instantiate the Good the more I realize integrative unity in my life (Chapter 2); the knowledge necessary and sufficient for virtue is a grasp of the Idea of the Good (Chapter 3); that the knowledge relevant to virtuous activity is rooted in Plato’s metaphysics shows the normative theory of the ‘so-called’ early Socratic dialogues is not eudaimonist/prudentialist (Chapter 4); wrongdoing occurs when I fail to act in accordance with my recognition of the Idea of the Good’s normative authority (Chapter 5); the Philebus and Statesman show how the concept of integrative unity provides a contentful normative theory (Chapter 6); and all this has important results for our understanding of Plato’s theology and political philosophy (Chapter 7).
My brief survey risks masking the richness of Gerson’s work, which touches on a staggering array of debates in contemporary Plato scholarship. Given a project this daring—Gerson aims to upend the widely-held assumption that Platonic (and, distinctly, Socratic) ethics can be understood independent of Plato’s metaphysics—it is hardly surprising that some choices in presentation and argument invite objection.
It is often difficult, for instance, to distinguish when Gerson believes he is reconstructing Plato’s own positions using direct textual evidence from when he is ‘filling in the gaps’ in Plato’s theory, whether on the basis of later Neo-Platonism or his own philosophical intuitions. Gerson also makes a number of bold claims without offering the kind of sustained defense one might hope for. For example, Gerson claims that for anyone who believes “the source of all being is no guide to the attainment of the good for human beings…the only possible guide to that which is really good is how that appears to each one” (45)—a striking reductio, but hardly supported by the argument he provides.
Furthermore, when engaging with other perspectives in the secondary literature, Gerson sometimes mistakes the point in dispute. A key example is his engagement with defenders of Socratic eudaimonism (which Gerson calls ‘prudentialism’) in §4.2. Gerson claims that prudentialism reduces to “a probabilistic argument in defense of Socrates” (129); that is, eudaimonist arguments for the life of virtue reduce to virtue being the most likely/reliable way to ensure one’s happiness. However, when scholars like Irwin claim Plato is a rational eudaimonist, they are fundamentally interested not in how we determine whether I have reason to perform this or that action (prudentialist deliberative frameworks might, but need not, involve probabilistic reasoning), but rather in what grounds my reasons (answer: my own good, rather than the Good). By insisting on the non-universal nature of practical maxims derived from probabilistic calculations, Gerson fails to engage with the more fundamental question of the structure of practical reasons—and his criticisms of prudentialist readings miss their mark.
However, because I believe Gerson’s underlying theses are true—Plato is a metaethical non-naturalist realist, and we isolate his normative theory from his metaphysics at our interpretive peril—I want to focus on how Gerson chooses to defend them, namely, by presenting Plato as a Moorean (of a sort) avant la lettre. I have my hesitations about attributing Moore’s open-question argument to Plato some two millennia before Moore, but let us grant that Plato has such an argument available to him and that it structures his conception of the Good throughout the dialogues. We should then ask why, when facing the same theoretical choice points, Gerson’s Moorean Plato opts for such different paths from Moore—which will in turn draw our attention to several key challenges for Gerson’s interpretation.
Moore was an intuitionist, believing we identify intrinsic goodness by employing our innate intuition in conjunction with the Principia’s method of isolation. Importantly, this intuitionism allows us to preserve the unanalyzable character of intrinsic goodness (and thereby avoid the naturalistic fallacy) while still making evaluative determinations.
I found it surprising that Gerson says nothing about the Philebus’ method of isolation (see e.g., 20e-22b) in his chapter on the Philebus and Statesman, especially given the dialogue’s importance for Moore’s own project. More surprising still, while Gerson believes Plato endorses a form of Moorean intuitionism (our vague knowledge of the Good is a “permanent endowment in rational creatures” (166 n.43)), he does not appeal to this intuitionism as the ultimate justification for first-order normative claims. Instead, Gerson attributes several seemingly-essentialist properties to the Idea of the Good, for instance, that it is one, and claims these generate “criteria” or “heuristics” by which we can determine whether the Good is instantiated (43).
Gerson believes that saying “the Good is the One”, or that integrative unity is an ‘index’, ‘criterion’, or ‘heuristic’ for the Good, is different from claiming that “the Form of Justice is part of the Good”. The latter, Gerson claims, is an unacceptable essential predication vulnerable to open-question style objections, whereas the former preserves the essence-less character of the Idea of the Good. It was not at all clear to me by the end of the book that Gerson had earned this distinction—and if he has not, then I find it puzzling why his Plato appeals to such heuristics and identity statements, thereby at least appearing to commit the essentialistic fallacy, when he might instead appeal (like Moore) to direct applications of our valuative intuitions.
Moore also takes the primitive ‘object’ in his axiology to be a form of value—intrinsic value itself is sui generis and unanalyzable. Moore believes the open-question argument applies to what he calls ‘metaphysical ethics’ (turning on non-natural metaphysical objects like Platonic Forms) just as much as to natural properties, because we can still ask why instantiating the Form of the Good is itself good. Of course, this theoretical decision comes with costs—Moore is infamously vague about intrinsic value’s ontological status and chary of questions about its source. Gerson’s Plato, on the other hand, does not take his unanalyzable primitive to be value itself, but rather the source of value. As Gerson repeatedly emphasizes, the Idea of the Good is not itself good, but the source of all goodness (224). This contrast between Moore and Gerson’s Plato raises two issues.
First, it is ultimately unclear how value enters Gerson’s picture. Drawing on Proclus, Gerson distinguishes between the co-ordinate Form of the Good (the genus of all perfections) and the super-ordinate Idea of the Good (the source of all value). When I say that, for instance, ‘justice is good’, I can mean two things: that justice perfects human beings and so participates in the Form of the Good; and that justice is, for human beings, a kind-relative form of integrative unity and thereby a way of instantiating (however imperfectly) the Idea of the Good. Participating in the Form of the Good by being just is a form of self-perfection; instantiating the Idea of the Good by being just (which is, for humans, a form of integrative unity) is good simpliciter and therefore, Gerson’s Plato argues, necessarily also good for me. Gerson believes the former claim is vulnerable to open-question challenges (why is self-perfection good for me?), but the latter is not. Yet it seems to me that these two claims should stand or fall together: I see no principled reason why instantiating the essence-less Idea of the Good through my kind-relative integrative unity is any further removed from the essentialistic fallacy than participating in the Form of the Good by realizing kind-relative perfections. In both cases, we are left asking why such relations are valuable—and merely asserting that the Idea of the Good is the source of value (though not essentially!) cannot resolve this worry.
This raises a second Moorean challenge for Gerson’s account. Precisely because he thought non-natural, metaphysical grounds of value were equally susceptible to naturalistic fallacy-esque objections, Moore deliberately constructed his ethics to be independent of metaphysics: to get his normative theory off the ground, he thought it only necessary to posit an unanalyzable form of value that was intuitively accessible. That Moore built his ethics on such metaphysically-abstemious grounds challenges the stronger of Gerson’s interpretive claims about the relationship between metaphysics and ethics in Plato’s thought, namely, that Plato’s normative theory not only depends on his metaphysics as a matter of historical fact, but that such metaphysical dependence was philosophically necessary—there being no other way, Gerson claims, to construct a robust realist metaethics to undergird the normative theory we find in the dialogues. Couldn’t Plato, like Moore, construct his normative theory by a similar route, avoiding appeal to his metaphysics? He may not in fact have done so—but that does not license Gerson’s bolder claim of theoretical necessity (Gerson calls the Moorean solution “untenable” early in the book (11n.33), but by the end, it was unclear whether his objection amounted to anything more than a question of philosophical taste).
Finally, Moore builds a consequentialist normative theory on the back of his metaethical non-naturalist realism: what makes an action right is that it promotes intrinsic goodness in the world, and our notion of agent-relative value is reducible on analysis to whatever agent-neutral value is found in a particular life. Gerson’s Plato endorses many of consequentialism’s hallmarks (for instance, that the good is prior to the right (§1.4)) and identifies the good-for-me with the Good, but Gerson nevertheless insists that “Plato’s moral realism is unalterably opposed to utilitarianism” (226). His motivating worry is that consequentialist theories (and Gerson here uses ‘utilitarianism’ and ‘consequentialism’ interchangeably) eliminate all universal moral laws except for a principle of maximization, which may require me to sacrifice my own good or harm others for the sake of maximizing overall goodness—both possibilities that Gerson’s Plato would emphatically reject.
This rejection is justified by appeal to the Idea of the Good’s superordinate character, which ensures my good is identical with the Good and consequently will never require my harming others—and Gerson explicitly contends that for Plato “the identity of ‘good’ and ‘good for me’ does not support consequentialism” (19n.51). However, he provides no clear means of resisting Moore’s consequentialist conclusions. Insofar as I aim to ensure (perhaps maximize?) the Idea of the Good’s instantiation in the world and this instantiation is identified with my good, I see no reason to prefer that I instantiate it in my own life rather than the lives of others. The result is ironic: in making Plato a Moorean, Gerson may also have inadvertently made him a utilitarian (insofar as my interest in the Good’s instantiation should not prioritize its instantiation in my life alone)—or, in what would represent an equally repellant conclusion for Gerson, a prudentialist (because the only justification for prioritizing the achievement of my own integrative unity would seem to be pragmatic/probabilistic, insofar as my good is the good I can most effectively or reliably achieve).
All this is not to detract from the accomplishments of Plato’s Moral Realism. Gerson’s magisterial grasp of the ancient commentary tradition and contemporary scholarship is on constant display, and the book serves as a clarion call to re-evaluate our understanding of the relationship between Plato’s ethics and metaphysics. Even if one ultimately decides Plato is no Moorean, Gerson’s arguments deserve careful attention.
