Everything you need to know about bats but were too afraid to ask
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:26:28 UTC
19:26:28 KST

Bats are not the world’s most beloved creatures. Mostly night animals, they’ve become a symbol of Halloween—associated with vampires, death and general ghoulishness. Sure, a few bat species do, in fact, feed on animal blood. Some bats have a face only a biologist could love. And yes, bats can be reservoirs of disease. But in their more than 50 million years on Earth, these maligned creatures have developed some admirable qualities, too.
For one, they’re everywhere: bats live on every continent except Antarctica. They echolocate, using sound to navigate their world—and they are the only mammal to evolve true flight. They also eat insects such as mosquitoes—contributing billions of dollars in value annually for the world’s farmers—and are critical pollinators of tropical plants.
“We need them,” says Emma Teeling, a professor and founding director of the Center for Irish Bat Research at University College Dublin.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
So, in honor of spooky season, here are seven bat facts you may not know:
Bats are “super agers.”
In nature, larger animals, such as elephants and whales, tend to live longer than smaller animals, such as mice and shrews, Teeling says. Bats are an exception.
“Bats are some of the smallest mammals in the entire world and can live for this extraordinary long time,” she says. Some of the oldest bats have been known to live for decades.
Teeling and other bat researchers are studying aspects of the animals’ longevity, including bats’ ability to repair their DNA and harbor viruses without getting sick, for clues in order to enhance our own lives.
Vampire bats could help us treat stroke victims.
When vampire bats such as Desmodus rotundus, also known as the common vampire bat, feed on birds and other mammals, they bite their prey and lick the wounds, Teeling says. An anticoagulant in their saliva prevents the blood from clotting up.
Researchers have studied this protein in the hope that it may offer a way to treat blood clots in stroke victims—while lowering the risk of causing brain bleeds. Although drug development stalled a decade ago after lackluster results, the treatment may still have potential, according to a recent review.
There are about 1,500 bat species—and counting.
Bats are incredibly diverse—across all mammals, bats include more species than all but one other group, rodents, says Rachel Page, a scientist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. In fact, there are about 1,500 known bat species worldwide.
Some, such as the vampire bats, drink blood. Others eat nectar, while others still eat insects, fish and even frogs.
Some bats “eavesdrop” on their prey’s mating calls.
For the frog-eating bats, meals can be treacherous. Some frogs are poisonous. Others are so big they could pose a danger. To meet this challenge, the fringe-lipped bat, Trachops cirrhosus, “eavesdrops:” the bats listen for the loud, “conspicuous” nighttime mating calls of their prey and then attack, Page says.
“They exploit those calls. They use them to detect, to locate, and then also to assess those prey” for size and toxicity, she says.
Bats likely evolved in Europe.
In September, Teeling and more than 130 other scientists across the world published a paper in Nature in which they sequenced genomes across all 21 bat families.
By pairing these genetic data with fossil records, they made a breakthrough—bats likely evolved in Europe and then spread to Africa and around the world, they found. Until then, it was thought bats might’ve emerged somewhere in North America, among other theories. “We rewrote evolutionary history,” Teeling says.
Many bats have a signature scent.
Across bat species, 9 percent are known so far to have odor-producing glands and other structures, but research on this is sparse, according to a 2021 paper in Mammal Review co-authored by Page. T. cirrhosus males employ a “pungent” golden crust with a “musky” scent on their forearms, likely to attract females, Page says.
Vampire bats will throw up to feed a friend.
If a vampire bat doesn’t feed for about two nights in a row, it will die, Page explains. “It doesn’t have the energetic reserves to make it beyond that,” she says. But research shows that if a vampire bat comes back to its colony hungry, other bats will step in and regurgitate blood to share—a costly but lifesaving sacrifice.

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
The midterm elections are fast approaching, and as usual, science is all over the ballot. Scientific American breaking news reporter Adam Kovac has been keeping an eye on how topics in science and tech have shown up in debates and campaign messaging, and he’s here to tell us more.
Hey, Adam. Thanks so much for coming on to chat with us.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Adam Kovac: Thanks for having me, Rachel.
Feltman: So the midterms are coming up, and you’ve been talking to a few candidates about how science factors in. Why don’t we start, kind of, more broadly, you know, what are the big science issues that, you know, have people going to the polls this midterm?
Kovac: I think it kind of depends on where you stand. If you’re in the sciences or you’re a science enthusiast like many of our listeners probably are, you’re probably really worried about the big changes that have come to a lot of the governmental scientific bodies. You know, there have been huge changes that have come to the NIH [National Institutes of Health], that have come to the NSF [National Science Foundation], changes to how science gets funded.
Some people are really worried about the politicization of science. But, you know, more broadly, health care, that’s a science story, and people are really concerned about health care costs. People are really concerned about food safety. I mean, look at the Cyclospora outbreak that we had earlier this year. People are really worried about changes to the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] that have happened under Robert [F.] Kennedy, Jr. So some of the biggest issues that are going on in this election are, at their heart, science stories.
Feltman: Right. I was thinking about it, and it’s, it really has not been that long since it was sort of a question of, you know, whether your candidate said climate change was a hoax or not. And now there are so many science and tech issues that are, you know, being discussed at the micro level in debates and, you know, that people really care about going to the polls. Kovac: So I think the big name that most people would know is ...
[CLIP: Abdul El-Sayed speaks on a phone call: “Hey.” Kovac on the call: “Hi, is this Abdul?” El-Sayed responds: “This is Abdul.”]
Kovac: I spoke to Abdul El-Sayed, who’s running for Senate in Michigan.
He has a degree from medical school. He was never a licensed physician, which has been kind of a story that’s dogged him for the last couple of weeks. But that’s because he chose to go and get, also, a Ph.D. in public health. And so he was the head of public health in Detroit and in a county in Michigan. I, I think it’s safe to say he’s an expert in public health, and that’s really, kind of, been a core component of his messaging during the campaign, is really talking about how health policy affects the everyday person. He’s really made that, kind of, the linchpin of what he stands for in a lot of ways.
Feltman: Yeah. And how have voters been responding to that and reacting to it?
Kovac: It’s hard to say. I’ve actually never been to Michigan, so I can’t really tell you, boots-on-the-ground. You know, from my little echo chamber on my online spaces, you know, people seem to be really into it. But it does appear to be a very close race. It’s not a blowout for sure. I don’t think that Democrats are celebrating a victory in Michigan quite yet.
But it’s just become very high-profile just because, you know, he’s really good at social media, so a lot of his videos have gotten traction. You know, he is a Muslim candidate running against a white opponent. Neither candidate has really held back in their criticisms. In a lot of ways, it’s been a really ugly race, so it’s gonna be interesting to see how voters, you know, respond to the tone of the race when it comes to trying to cast their votes.
Feltman: Yeah. So as a, a public health expert, you know, what are some of the topics that he’s been making a big part of his campaign?
Kovac: So he’s kind of chosen a little bit of an interesting path because when you talk to a lot of scientists, they get very dismissive of the MAHA [“Make America Health Again”] movement. They focus on, kind of, the pseudoscience aspects of it, the focus on supplements that aren’t necessarily FDA-approved or of RFK, Jr.’s workout routines and his cooking show and his general hostility toward vaccines.
But what Abdul El-Sayed is doing is really interesting because he’s focusing on what MAHA has gotten right. He’s acknowledged that there’s a lot of distrust to the medical establishment, and he believes that’s rightfully so. You know, he lays a lot of the blame at big pharma, you know, people feeling that they can’t afford the medications or the treatments that they’re told they need.
And so, of course, you’re gonna distrust an establishment where you feel that these people don’t have your best interests at heart. That’s kind of been an interesting component of his messaging, is talking about what MAHA gets right and then trying to kind of guide them back toward more conventional medicines by trying to make that, you know, saying he wants to make this more accessible to the average person.
Feltman: So what were some of the highlights of your, uh, conversation with him? You know, were there, were there any surprises?

Kovac: You know, he’s really taken a lot of cues from Bernie Sanders on that front.
[CLIP: Bernie Sanders talking on his Youtube channel: “To my mind, uh, our current health care system is dysfunctional, it is broken, it is wildly bureaucratic. We spend twice as much per capita as any other country on health care. I think we need to move toward a Medicare for All, single-payer system.”]
Kovac: And so there’re politicians who talk a lot about the benefits of Medicare for All, but [what] we don’t really talk about is the how of it all.
And something that I don’t think a lot of people realize is just how big of an employer private health insurance is in the United States.There are hundreds of thousands of jobs that are directly in the industry and then many, many, many more that are indirectly related to it.
You know, that’s a lot of people who rely on it to pay their mortgage, pay their rent, put food on the table. So what happens to those people when you lessen the reliance on private health insurance for people to go get their health care? That’s a lot of jobs that are at stake.
So he seems pretty confident that there is still going to be a place for private industry, in terms of how Medicare for All gets administered—and, you know, jobs that are lost in one area can be made up for in other areas—and that on the whole, this would probably be neutral or a net gain of jobs. But I just want to get that kind of into the conversation because, you know, we talk a lot about the cost of implementing this but not a lot about, kind of, the downstream effects that could be felt.
Feltman: Sure. No, it’s interesting. John Oliver recently had a Last Week Tonight episode about UnitedHealthcare and just how many arms of it there are ...

And I hadn’t really thought about, you know, [how] the flip side of that is: How many people are employed? And that is an interesting question to get at.
What else came up in your conversation with him?
Kovac: So I asked him about, you know, what things outside of just the immediate health care system can affect people’s health—because he talks a lot about, kinda like, the systemic effects on people’s well-being and people’s health. And so there’s a lot of things he wants to touch on, you know?
I got the impression he doesn’t wanna be, like, a one-trick pony. He wants people to know that, like, he’s thought about policies in other areas. So one thing he pointed out was energy systems. We all rely on electricity, clearly. But think of some of the negative effects that can come from it. If you live near a coal-powered power station, the air you breathe can have negative effects on your health. So he really wants to focus on building high-quality renewable energy that isn’t going to have these effects on people’s health. So [he’s] really talking a lot about the social determinants of health, and I thought that was pretty interesting.
Feltman: Well, I know you also talked to a GOP candidate, and I’m curious: How was science coming up for them in the race?
Kovac: So it actually took some time to get somebody from the GOP to talk to me. Feltman: Interesting. What are some science issues that are, kind, of riding on this election that, you know, you’re gonna be keeping an eye out for when we see those results?
Kovac: There’s two ways to think about this: there’s short-term and long-term. I think over the long term, if the Democrats come ahead in the House and maybe also the Senate, we could be seeing a lot of hearings of senior administration officials who are in the science-related departments. You know, Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., will probably be spending a lot of time testifying about some of his policy decisions. Trump: Putin-Zelensky talks to be set up ‘very soon’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:25:03 UTC
19:25:03 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump met with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Türkiye, Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (AP Photo)
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 28 that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, would be set up “very soon.”
The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters.
Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that a trilateral meeting between Kiev, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Meanwhile, a local truce aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct. 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents told AFP last month that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
“The possibility of evacuation from Oleshky is very good news for me and for the people who are trapped there,” Olga, a former resident, told AFP on Oct. 27.
“My acquaintances are ready to leave,” she said.
Announcing the truce last week, U.S. first lady Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require.”
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
AFP was not able to immediately verify details about the humanitarian mission or whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
The Russian military does not routinely grant international media, including AFP, access to areas under Russian occupation.
Right-leaning U.S. cable network Newsmax said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city.

Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers to meet in Ankara on Thursday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:24:25 UTC
19:24:25 KST

Muhammet Tarhan and Busra Nur Cakmak
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Participants expected to approve administrative and financial documents related to the organization’s operations
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) on Thursday as part of the organization’s 13th summit.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, foreign ministers of the member states will convene for the fifth time this year, with one regular and four informal council meetings, at the gathering in Ankara on Oct. 29-30.
The meeting is expected to include consultations on areas of cooperation within the organization and efforts to strengthen its institutional structure.
Participants are also expected to approve several administrative and financial documents concerning the organization’s operations at the end of the meeting.
Fidan is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the gathering.
In his address, Fidan is expected to emphasize that political dialogue and the capacity for joint action among Turkic states have been strengthened under the organization's umbrella, while shared historical, linguistic and cultural ties and bonds of brotherhood have been translated into concrete cooperation.
During Türkiye’s chairmanship of the organization, Fidan is expected to underline that priorities will include enhancing the organization’s institutional capacity, improving the human and financial resources and capabilities of its secretariat, and strengthening coordination among Turkic cooperation organizations.
He is also expected to stress the importance of translating economic and strategic cooperation into tangible results, particularly in energy, trade, investment, digital transformation and the defense industry.
Fidan is expected to highlight the importance of strengthening the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor to improve connectivity between Asia and Europe and reinforce economic resilience.
He is also expected to draw attention to developments in Afghanistan and their implications for regional security, stability and connectivity, emphasizing the need to increase consultations and coordination on the issue among member and observer states.
Organization of Turkic States
The organization was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States under the Nakhchivan Agreement signed on Oct. 3, 2009, by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its name was changed to the Organization of Turkic States at the Istanbul Summit in 2021.
Its main objectives include strengthening mutual trust and political solidarity among Turkic states, developing and deepening economic and technical cooperation, and documenting and promoting the historical and cultural heritage of the Turkic world.
Headquartered in Istanbul, the OTS has five members -- Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan -- and four observers: Hungary, Turkmenistan, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) and the Economic Cooperation Organization.
13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States
The OTS’s 13th summit will be held in Ankara on Oct. 29-30, hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Inspired by Erdogan’s vision of the Century of the Turkic World and the motto of Ismail Gasprinski, the summit will be held under the theme Turkish Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action.

Australia returns 2 cultural relics to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:21:53 CST
19:21:53 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 28, 2026 shows two Chinese cultural relics, the head of a military official statue (L) and the head of a civil official statue, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127), returned from Australia, in Canberra, Australia. The National Gallery of Australia (NGA) handed over two Chinese cultural relics to China's National Cultural Heritage Administration in Canberra at 2:52 p.m. local time on Wednesday. According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province. (Photo by Chu Chen/Xinhua)
CANBERRA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Australia returned two Chinese cultural relics to China at a handover ceremony held at the National Gallery of Australia (NGA) in Canberra on Wednesday.
Tang Wei, deputy director of China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA), Liu Jinsong, Chinese Ambassador to Australia, and Nick Mitzevich, director of the NGA, attended the ceremony and delivered remarks.
The two relics are the head of a military official statue from the Yongyu Mausoleum and the head of a civil official statue from the Yongchang Mausoleum, both dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127). According to the NGA, both relics are made of limestone and originated from central China's Henan Province.
The Chinese side said that returning displaced cultural relics to their countries of origin is an important step towards safeguarding cultural heritage, respecting the cultural rights and national sentiments of peoples around the world, and protecting the achievements of human civilization.
Noting the handover as a significant outcome of China-Australia cooperation in implementing international conventions and protecting cultural heritage, the Chinese side said it would further promote people-to-people exchanges and empathy between the two peoples.
The Australian side said that the return represented more than the physical transfer of cultural objects, reflecting respect for cultural heritage, a sense of responsibility and the importance of international partnerships. It added that the handover would help strengthen Australia-China relations and encourage continued cooperation in cultural heritage protection.
In 2025, the NCHA, working with China's Ministry of Public Security and cultural heritage and public security authorities in Henan Province, submitted a memorandum and supporting evidence to the NGA, formally requesting the return of the two relics.
The successful return was achieved through close coordination between the NCHA and the Chinese Embassy in Australia, within the framework of the UNESCO 1970 Convention on the means of prohibiting and preventing the illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property, a bilateral memorandum of understanding on cultural heritage protection signed by China and Australia in 2009, and the NGA's 2021 policy on due diligence and provenance research. ■

China willing to work with Switzerland to inject more certainty into world economy: spokesperson
China

18:21:30 CST
19:21:30 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is willing to work with Switzerland to deliver more benefits to the two peoples, create more favorable conditions for enterprises from both countries, and inject greater certainty into the world economy, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Wednesday.
Spokesperson Guo Jiakun made the remarks at a regular press briefing when asked about China's view of current China-Switzerland relations and its expectations for the upcoming visit by President of the Swiss Confederation Guy Parmelin.
China welcomes Parmelin's visit, during which Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet with him, the spokesperson said.
Guo said this year marks the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Switzerland innovative strategic partnership. China-Switzerland relations are currently enjoying sound development, with fruitful cooperation across various fields, particularly in free trade, which has become a major highlight of bilateral relations.
Switzerland was the first continental European country to sign a free trade agreement with China. Since the agreement entered into force more than a decade ago, it has played a positive role in promoting bilateral economic and trade exchanges, the spokesperson said.
"In August this year, Switzerland once again became the first European country to conclude negotiations with China on upgrading their free trade agreement," Guo added.
China is willing to work with Switzerland to leverage the steady development of bilateral relations to deliver more benefits to the two peoples, provide more favorable and convenient conditions for enterprises of both countries, and inject greater certainty into the development of the world economy, Guo said. ■

Norway's premier says call with Putin was effort to present European views

Norway's premier says call with Putin was effort to present European views
OSLO, Oct 28 - Norway's prime minister defended on Wednesday a three-way call with Vladimir Putin and Finland's president, saying it was intended to ensure the Russian leader heard European as well as US views.
Tuesday's call between Russia's Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian premier Jonas Gahr Stoere broke a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin, and was criticised by allies including Denmark's Mette Frederiksen.
The 90-minute call came ahead of what are expected to be the first face-to-face talks since February between Ukrainian and Russian officials, in Abu Dhabi next month.
"We (Stubb and I) were focused on looking forward, what must happen for this war to not continue endlessly for months, with people dying ... and it is even more difficult to find a solution," Stoere told public broadcaster NRK.
"I don't think (Putin) will change his mind, but he gets to hear our position very clearly. I am worried that some of these messages do not reach him when the Americans talk to him," he said.
Norway, said Stoere, was keen to introduce de-escalation steps such as stopping attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine, halting strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain and conducting prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Asked whether there could be peace without Ukraine ceding territory, Stoere said: "Today Russia controls nearly 20% (of Ukrainian territory). Ukraine will never sign a deal that recognises that they have lost territory, but whether they can take the current frontline as a reality and as a starting point, that is a different question."
"And the big question is what kind of security guarantees can there be for the country (Ukraine) after a peace deal? Putin recognises that this is the big question."
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said Tuesday's call offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process. REUTERS

Iran, Russia near agreement on joint development of small modular nuclear reactors
Iran is finalizing a protocol with Russia to accelerate joint development of small modular nuclear reactors, Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman and deputy for international, legal and parliamentary affairs at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, has announced.
Speaking to Iran's Shabakeh Khabar television network, Kamalvandi said the agreement would facilitate closer cooperation on the construction of small modular reactors, a technology attracting growing international interest as countries seek reliable, low-carbon electricity sources. SMRs are far smaller than traditional large-scale reactors.
Kamalvandi also highlighted rising global electricity demand, driven in part by artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. He said nuclear power could provide stable baseload electricity while helping reduce emissions.
He claimed Iran's nuclear industry had reached a mature stage and said the country had developed substantial domestic capabilities in nuclear plant construction, fuel-cycle technology and nuclear safety. He also stated political pressure had delayed some Iranian projects but had not halted the country's nuclear activities.
Kamalvandi made the remarks while discussing Iran's participation in an international ministerial conference on nuclear energy in South Korea. He said the Iranian delegation was using the event to promote international cooperation and argue that countries party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty should have their rights respected alongside their obligations.

Cost of Iran war rises to an estimated $47 billion
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

EU prosecutors still await von der Leyen’s statement in Pfizer vaccine probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:20:07 UTC
19:20:07 KST

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has yet to receive an in-person statement from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as part of its investigation into the bloc’s COVID-19 vaccine procurement, news outlet Politico reported Wednesday, citing a source familiar with the matter.
The investigation, known as “Pfizergate,” concerns alleged criminal wrongdoing linked to vaccine negotiations between von der Leyen and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla.
EPPO took over the Belgian-led investigation in 2024.
Legal documents cited by Politico indicate that prosecutors have been examining allegations of “interference in public functions, destruction of SMS, corruption and conflict of interest.”
Von der Leyen has yet to give an in-person statement to EPPO as part of its investigation, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Asked about reports that von der Leyen had not provided an in-person statement, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the institution had cooperated extensively with EPPO.
He added that the cooperation had taken place with the full support of von der Leyen, who remained willing to address outstanding questions within the limits of her duties and availability as commission president.
Meanwhile, EPPO Chief Prosecutor Laura Codruta Kovesi said some EU officials had refused to respond to summonses issued by her office.
“Some politicians think that they are above the law,” Kovesi told Politico in an interview. “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.”
She said her office faced difficulties exercising its investigative powers, particularly when cases involved high-profile politicians or wealthy individuals with political connections.
However, Kovesi declined to comment on whether von der Leyen was among the officials she was referring to.
Established in 2017 and operational since 2021, EPPO is responsible for investigating and prosecuting crimes affecting the financial interests of the European Union.

Govt brings in new cut in diesel duties of 4.9 cents per litre
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:18:19 CET
19:18:19 KST

A new cut in diesel duties worth 4.9
cents a litre was published in the official gazette on Wednesday
as part of the government's efforts to help households and
businesses cope with the rise in fuel prices linked to the Iran
war.
                                    
The first such cut was approved in March in the wake of the
war's outbreak and in recent months there had been a
17-cent-per-litre reduction in diesel duties, which was
gradually brought down to 12.2 cents and then to 6.1 cents
before expiring early this month.
                                    
The new cut in duties will last until November 7.
                                    
Farmers, fishers, taxi drivers and truckers are among the groups
who have staged strikes and big protests in Italy in recent
weeks to highlight the difficulties they are enduring because of
the high fuel prices.
                                    
Encouraged by the government, at the start of October
State-owned energy giant Eni imposed a cap on fuel prices in its
gas stations, currently 2.25 euros for a litre of diesel and
1.99 euros per litre for unleaded petrol, and several other
companies running petrol stations in Italy followed suit.
                                    
Last week Eni said its cap will continue until the end of the
year, as will that of Kuwait's Q8 company.

Sofia Heating Rollout Begins as Temperatures Fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

Sofia’s district heating operator Toplofikatsia Sofia will begin switching on the city’s central heating system on October 29, with schools and kindergartens to be connected first, followed by residential and administrative buildings.
Plamen Mladenovski, chairman of the Energy and Water Regulatory Commission (EWRC), said in response to a journalist’s question that the phased activation would start by the end of the week, with most buildings in the capital expected to have heating by Monday.
Regulations require the average daily temperature to remain below 12°C for three consecutive days, alongside forecasts from the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (NIMH) confirming a sustained decline in temperatures. These conditions have already been met in Sofia.
The weather forecast for the next seven days points to further cooling, with average daily temperatures expected to fall below seasonal norms. The price of district heating and hot water in Sofia was last raised by 5.5% in July.
Toplofikatsia Sofia said customers who want their heating activated later must submit a formal request at one of the company’s customer service centers. The request must include the minutes of a decision adopted by the General Meeting of the condominium owners.
The company also urged customers to finish repairs to their internal heating systems and refill them if they have been drained. Buildings whose internal systems have not been refilled will not receive heating.
Residents should turn their radiator control valves to the maximum setting to avoid the need for additional radiator bleeding. They should also check the displays on their electronic heat cost allocators and contact their heat metering service provider if a device shows no reading.

Russia ready to play part in ‘second awakening’ of Africa – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28

Russia ready to play part in ‘second awakening’ of Africa – Lavrov
Russia is ready to expand cooperation with African countries and regional organizations through new partnerships in business and other sectors, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Speaking at a meeting with the heads of leading African media outlets on Tuesday, Lavrov said Moscow was open to developing additional forms of engagement with the African Union, individual countries and regional blocs.
“Our partnership is already quite extensive, and there is certainly room to enrich and refine it; we are fully open to that,” Lavrov said.
The minister also stressed that Russia seeks to strengthen ties with Africa on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, helping countries develop domestic industries and become more independent in global finance and technology. He said Moscow’s approach follows UN principles of mutual respect and non-interference.
Lavrov argued that Africa’s next major transformation will be economic, noting that many countries remain dependent on former colonial powers despite having gained political independence.
“The second awakening [of African countries] will, of course, be economic, including achieving a situation where the richest resources of the African continent are not simply extracted and exported as raw materials, but are used in Africa itself so that added value is created there, rather than in the former colonial powers,” he said.
Turning to UN reform, Lavrov opposed increasing Western representation on the Security Council, arguing that Western countries already occupy six of its 15 seats despite their declining share of global economic output.
“Like China and many other countries, we [Russia] maintain that only nations from the Global South should be granted new seats—whether permanent, non-permanent, or a mix of both,” Lavrov said.
The 15-member UN Security Council has five veto-wielding permanent members and ten elected members serving two-year terms. Africa currently holds three seats, occupied by DR Congo, Liberia and Somalia, with Zimbabwe set to replace Somalia in January 2027.
The remarks came at the four-day Russia-Africa Media Forum, which opened in Moscow on Monday. The gathering comes ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the accompanying Economic and Humanitarian Forum, taking place on Wednesday and Thursday in Moscow.

Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”
NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.
The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.
Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”
One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.
Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.
Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.
In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.
Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”
Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.
Since I first reported on the creep of AI in the publishing world, I’ve heard from staff at all of the Big Five who claim that executives are pushing them to use AI tools, even as Hachette, Macmillan, and Penguin Random House Verlagsgruppe (its German-language division) are suing some of the leading AI companies for copyright infringement.
At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.
At Penguin Random House (PRH), the largest of the Big Five after the 2013 merger between Penguin Books and Random House, several workers say they’ve been encouraged to use ChatGPT Enterprise in AI learning sessions, even though PRH’s German division is suing OpenAI for copyright infringement.
In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”
Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.
“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”
Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”
Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.
“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.
“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”
Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”
All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.
“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”
Following WIRED's previous reporting, several high-profile authors condemned the adoption of AI tools in publishing. “I have never looked down on other publishing models (zine girly from way back) & every day, self pub looking ever more possible for future work,” Mo Ryan wrote on Bluesky. Her most recent book, Burn It Down: Power, Complicity, and a Call for Change in Hollywood, was published by HarperCollins.
John Scalzi, the sci-fi novelist who signed a 10-book deal with Macmillan’s Tor Publishing Group in 2024, wrote, “I would be EXTREMELY annoyed to discover my PR is ‘AI’-generated, and as someone bombarded with dozens of ‘AI’-generated emails daily, I assure you the stink of ‘AI’ is immediately noticable [sic] and immediately dismissible. Publishers are not doing their new books any favors in using it.”
Bestselling authors who have already accumulated huge readerships say they don’t need the institutional support of a Big Five publisher to sell copies. Brandon Sanderson, for instance, publishes some of his fantasy novels through Tor Books, an imprint of Macmillan, but raised more than $15 million in 24 hours from his readers on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.
“Publishers have always seen authors as a bit of a nuisance, and now there’s a desire to make us obsolete,” says one bestselling Big Five author. “What’s fascinating to me is that in the process of trying to make authors obsolete by using AI, the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.”

Philippines holds oil storage talks with Saudi Arabia, Russia, US
The move is aimed at hedging against surges in fuel prices due to the Iran war and the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon
The Philippines is in talks with Saudi Arabia, Russia and the United States to store oil in the fuel-import-dependent nation, in a bid to hedge against fuel price spikes driven by the Iran war.
The Southeast Asian nation, which imports nearly all its energy needs, also planned to increase diesel and gas-fired power output to make up for an estimated 60 per cent decline in hydropower and 20 per cent fall in solar output in the first half of 2027 due to the El Nino weather phenomenon, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said.

28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Italy’s latest military aid package for Ukraine remains on hold as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government awaits the outcome of next week’s US midterm elections, Italian daily La Repubblica reported Tuesday.
The 13th package is ready but has yet to receive final approval, the newspaper said, citing government sources. Italy’s previous aid shipment to Ukraine was last December, according to the report.
Rome had assured French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that it would approve the package by October, with missile deliveries expected by the end of the month.
However, the parliamentary committee overseeing intelligence services, known as Copasir, had not convened to examine the decree as of Monday evening.
The package includes Aster 30 air defense missiles sought by Ukraine to protect Kyiv and other cities from Russian attacks.
The decree requires signatures from Defense Minister Guido Crosetto, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, and Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.
Crosetto and Tajani support approval, while some government sources suggested Giorgetti was hesitating over potential opposition from League leader Matteo Salvini, the report said.
The final decision rests with Meloni, and Crosetto had privately warned of a political obstacle that needed resolving.
Approval has already been delayed several times, with expectations shifting from July to September and then until after the League’s party congress.
Government sources now favor waiting for the US midterm elections next Tuesday to assess Washington’s future approach and adjust Italy’s position accordingly.
Domestic political considerations are also contributing to the delay, including opposition to arms supplies from former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte and concerns about giving political momentum to Roberto Vannacci.
Italian officials have informally asked their Ukrainian counterparts to remain patient, according to the report.

Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, mainly in DR Congo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:03:30 UTC
19:03:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases, mostly in DR Congo
The latest outbreak of Ebola in the African continent has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, the vast majority of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Congolese health authorities said on Tuesday, with almost 5,000 fatalities.
According to the DRC's figures, 10,060 people have been infected and 4,887 have died since the virus was first detected in May in the vast central African country's deadliest outbreak in its history.
Cases have likewise been detected in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, with the World Health Organisation warning that Africa faces a "complex" task to contain an outbreak spanning the east, west and centre of the continent.
While some 2,684 have recovered from the virus in the DRC, the epidemic's fatality rate appears to be close to 50 percent, according to the Congolese National Institute of Public Health.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
After spreading under the radar for weeks, the virus was first detected in the northeastern Congolese province of Ituri, kicking off the DRC's 17th outbreak of the disease.
It has since spread across swathes of the country's north and east, which is plagued by a litany of violence by various armed groups and where trust in a faraway and long-absent state is low.
Ituri and the eastern North Kivu province, the latter of which is partially controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 militia, account for the majority of reported cases.
Swiss woman evacuated
After registering a total of 20 cases and two deaths, neighbouring Uganda was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in late August.
Kenya, which had not reported a single case of the contagious virus until October 6, has now seen two virus deaths from nine cases, most of them from recent travellers to the DRC.
The only case so far confirmed in Nigeria, a 42-year-old Swiss woman who contracted the virus following a trip to Uganda with her husband, was evacuated to a hospital in Geneva on Monday.
Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Congolese Jean Kaseya, told AFP his organisation was still trying to track how the patient came into to contact with the virus.
"We saw that the genomic sequencing of the Kenyan case is similar to the Nigerian case. And we discovered that yesterday with some cases in Beni," he explained. "Today it's an outbreak in three regions. We didn't see that since we started to have experience of Ebola outbreaks. We were not thinking that Nigeria could be an at risk country."
When the outbreak was declared, just three zones of one province were affected, he said. "Today we are talking about eight provinces, more than 66 health zones. To give you an idea, it's like twice the size of the UK."
Fifty-three of the patient's contacts have been identified by the Nigerian health authorities, in a bid to stop the virus spreading across Africa's most populous nation.
Some experts are worried that the virus—caught through contact with bodily fluids—could have spread after the Swiss couple landed back in Nigeria on 3 October.
The WHO said the patient, the wife of an employee of the Swiss embassy in the capital Abuja, developed symptoms on 7 October.
She then sought care in Abuja on 11 October, before testing positive for Bundibugyo on 20 October.
A Ugandan government spokesperson dismissed the idea that the Swiss woman could have contracted the disease while in the African Great Lakes nation.
Nurse killed
The response to the DRC's outbreak has been hampered by the distrust of parts of the population.
A nurse was killed and a health worker seriously wounded in the northeastern Tshopo province on Saturday, according to the WHO.
Doctor Marcel Likolo, chief medical officer of the Bafwasende health district, told AFP that young people from the area had accused the victims of trying to infect locals with tablets before attacking them.
The Ebola treatment centre where the incident took place has since shut down, he said.
Since it first emerged half a century ago, Ebola has killed more than 15,000 people across Africa.
Testing of the Ervebo vaccine, which has already proven to be effective against the more common Zaire strain of the virus, has begun in recent weeks to determine whether it could also provide protection against the Bundibugyo variant.

One proposal under consideration is to establish multiple working groups simultaneously, with different member economies serving as conveners and reviewing applications in parallel rather than sequentially.
If the bloc adopts parallel reviews, Taiwan could be assessed alongside other applicants, an approach the foreign ministry is working to promote, he said.
The foreign minister added that the ministry hopes to establish a mechanism requiring any member opposing an applicant to provide specific reasons, CNA reported. Without such a mechanism, some members may be reluctant to support Taiwan publicly because of political pressure, he said.

The Amarna letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

First discovered in Egypt in the late 19th century, the collection of clay tablets known as the Amarna letters is one of our richest windows into the ancient world. The letters are extraordinary not only for their contents – diplomatic communications exchanged between Egyptian pharaohs and other nearby rulers in the 14th century BCE – but also for their script: they were written not in Egyptian hieroglyphs but largely in cuneiform, a writing system most often associated with ancient Mesopotamia. In this video from the British Museum, the always entertaining Assyriologist Irving Finkel details how the letters came to be and how they were discovered, and delves into the fascinating correspondence itself, which includes petty disputes over perceived slights, leaders lobbying for military support and more than a few requests for gold.

Horror isn’t just intense fear, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:50 UTC
19:00:50 KST

Reading a news headline about a violent tragedy can provoke an unsettled, sickening jolt that feels very different from the anxiety of facing a personal threat. A new study published in Cognition and Emotion suggests that when descriptions of harm involve extreme outcomes or vivid, gory details, they tend to heighten horror much more than fear, in part because they make the event seem more abnormal. The findings provide evidence that horror is not merely an intense version of fear, but a distinct emotional reaction to events that violate our basic expectations of how the world works.
In everyday conversation and dictionary definitions, horror is often treated as a synonym for extreme fear. In psychology, however, the two terms can represent different ways of interpreting and categorizing a harmful event. Fear functions as a threat-detection system that alerts a person to potential danger and motivates self-defense or escape. Some emotion researchers define real-world horror, by contrast, as an emotional and mental shock experienced when witnessing or learning about actual harm that contradicts a person’s fundamental assumptions about human safety and how the world operates.
“‘Horror’ is one of dozens of English words we have to label our emotional responses to harm, but it remains largely unstudied,” study author Pamela Marie Taylor, an assistant professor in the Faculty of Global Connectivity at Akita International University, told PsyPost. “This neglect might be because research in the 1980s categorized horror as a subtype of fear, or because it has become closely associated with the fictional genre of horror films. However, people use the word ‘horror’ to describe their responses to real events, and do so in a way that is meaningfully different from how they use the word ‘fear’.”
“For example, ‘horrified’ is often paired with verbs like ‘learn’, ‘realize’ and ‘discover’ that indicate a response to extreme novelty or abnormality (e.g., ‘I was horrified to learn’),” Taylor explained. “In contrast, people typically use the word ‘fear’ to describe the anticipation of some possible harm (e.g., ‘fear the worst’, ‘fear of snakes’). This study was done to test if horror can be differentiated from fear based on how abnormal a harmful event is seen to be.”
How people evaluate unusual events plays a central role in shaping their emotional reactions. In a 1986 theoretical paper, psychologists proposed that people judge how unusual an event is by comparing it against their mental norms, and that bad outcomes preceded by abnormal circumstances provoke amplified emotional responses. Building on this idea, a 2022 experimental study by Taylor and a colleague found that people reported greater fear when facing common, mild, or personally relevant threats, whereas they reported greater horror when learning about extreme or abnormal harm that had already happened, even when the victims were strangers.
Encountering accounts of bizarre or extreme harm often leaves people struggling to reconcile the event with their worldview. Some research suggests this tension can shape how people seek explanations. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that individuals with higher morbid curiosity about unsettling events and dangerous people are more likely to seek out and believe conspiracy theories as explanations for threatening occurrences.
Although the 2022 research linked horror to abnormal harm, its experimental scenarios blended together the severity of the injury and the graphicness of the wording, leaving it uncertain which feature actually made the harm feel abnormal. To isolate these factors, Taylor designed two experiments examining how harm severity and graphic language independently shape perceptions of abnormality. She defined graphicness through the distinction between abstract and concrete language.
Taylor reasoned that abstract descriptions use broad, familiar categories, such as stating that “a person was murdered,” which allows the mind to file the event into existing mental frameworks, whereas concrete descriptions include specific sensory details, such as “a camper was slaughtered by his friend who sliced into his chest with a rusty axe,” which are harder to fit into normal expectations.
Taylor also wanted to test whether perceived abnormality is what truly separates horror from fear, or if the difference comes down to physical arousal. In psychology, arousal refers to the level of physical activation or agitation in the body’s nervous system. If horror is simply an intense form of fear, then heightened physical arousal alone should explain why people label their reaction to gruesome news as horror rather than fear.
In the first study, Taylor recruited 60 adult native English speakers in the United States through the online platform Prolific. The participants had an average age of 35.5 years, ranging from 21 to 69, and the sample was 70 percent female and 71.1 percent White. Each participant read four text stimuli presented as real news headlines adapted from The Daily Mail tabloid describing a person being harmed, with each headline remaining on the screen for seven seconds before rating questions appeared. Taylor preregistered the main prediction that severe harm and graphic descriptions would increase horror more than fear.
The headlines were systematically varied across two dimensions: the severity of the harm (moderate injuries that heal versus extreme, permanent harm such as death) and the graphicness of the description (abstract, general wording versus concrete, tangible details). After reading each headline, participants rated the perceived abnormality of the harm on a 5-point scale from 1 (“not at all”) to 5 (“extremely”) using four items assessing how unusual, abnormal, or unheard-of the event seemed.
They also rated their emotional reactions on the same 5-point scale, where scores for “horrified” and “shocked” were combined to measure horror, and scores for “scared” and “afraid” were combined to measure fear. To measure physical arousal, participants selected one of five illustrated figures ranging from a calm, closed-eyed figure to a wide-eyed figure with jagged lines depicting intense bodily activation.
To account for individual tendencies to score higher or lower on rating scales, Taylor analyzed the repeated measurements while statistically controlling for baseline differences between participants. Across the 5-point scale, where the overall average abnormality rating was 3.40, shifting from moderate to extreme harm increased perceived abnormality by 0.89 points, and shifting from abstract to concrete language increased it by 0.88 points.
Both factors also elevated horror much more strongly than fear. Across all conditions, the overall average emotion rating was 2.69, with horror averaging 0.98 points higher than fear; describing extreme rather than moderate harm boosted horror by 1.09 points compared to a 0.45-point increase in fear, while concrete rather than abstract descriptions raised horror by 0.70 points compared to a 0.22-point increase in fear.
Participants also rated the general harmfulness of each event based on whether someone suffered bodily pain or injury, and in the first study, these general harmfulness ratings predicted horror and fear equally, as the difference between the two emotions was not statistically significant. Taylor then used mediation analysis, a statistical technique that estimates how much of a relationship between an experimental condition and an outcome passes through an intermediate step, to test whether perceived abnormality explained the rise in horror.
Perceived abnormality accounted for 39 percent of the total effect of harm severity on horror and 76 percent of the effect of graphic language on horror, while explaining 63 percent and 83 percent of why severity and graphicness increased horror more than fear. In one Study 1 model, the effect of graphic language on horror over fear was no longer statistically significant once physical arousal was taken into account, and when physical arousal and perceived abnormality were tested side by side as parallel pathways, both independently explained a portion of the shift toward horror.
To verify whether these patterns would hold up in an independent sample, Taylor conducted a second study with another 60 adult native English speakers in the United States recruited via Prolific. Participants in the second group had an average age of 42.57 years, ranging from 21 to 75, and the sample was 70 percent female, 30 percent male, and 75 percent White. The procedure and rating scales were identical to the first experiment, except that one headline from Study 1 involving an animal attack was replaced with an interpersonal attack so that all four headlines depicted one human harming another.
The second study closely replicated the core findings regarding abnormality and horror. Around an average abnormality rating of 3.42 on the 5-point scale, extreme harm raised perceived abnormality by 0.85 points and concrete graphic descriptions raised it by 0.89 points. Extreme harm increased horror ratings by 1.01 points compared to 0.39 points for fear, making the effect on horror more than 2.5 times larger, while concrete descriptions increased horror by 0.62 points compared to 0.14 points for fear, an effect more than four times larger.
Unlike the first study, general ratings of bodily harmfulness in Study 2 showed a stronger association with horror than fear, though the author noted that because every headline involved harm, 12 percent of participants in Study 1 and 22 percent in Study 2 gave identical harmfulness ratings across all four headlines, limiting the precision of that specific measure.
Where the second study diverged most notably from the first was in the role of physical arousal. When arousal was tested on its own in Study 2, it again helped explain the shift toward horror, but once abnormality was added to the model, the arousal pathway was no longer statistically significant, with indirect effects of 0.11 for harm severity and 0.06 for graphicness. Perceived abnormality, by contrast, remained a strong, consistent pathway in both studies even after controlling for self-reported bodily activation. Taylor argues that whereas fear tends to arise from uncertainty about potential danger, horror arises from an excess of concrete information about severe harm that is hard to square with a person’s understanding of a safe world.
For everyday news consumers, the findings highlight how subtle shifts in phrasing can alter how a story lands emotionally. “When the same harmful event in a news headline was described using concrete language, it was rated as more abnormal than when it was described using abstract language, and caused an increase in horror that was three-to-four times greater than the increase in fear,” Taylor noted. “In other words, a person’s emotional reaction to a news event is influenced by the language with which it is told.”
“In terms of practical significance, it seems that a lot of online and political rhetoric uses abnormality to capture attention, shape discourse and influence interpretations,” Taylor said. “Therefore, people should be aware of how their emotional responses to events can be shaped by how events are described. We are increasingly aware of the dangers of online misinformation, but that focuses on the factuality of what is described. These results indicate that even in factually accurate descriptions, the language with which the event is described can influence our perception of how normal or abnormal it is, and consequently our emotional response to it.”
“We would not argue that using concrete language is bad or that headlines that use it are necessarily manipulative,” Taylor added. “The current findings examined how concrete and abstract language elicit different emotional responses without investigating the appropriateness of the language. Another way to read this study’s findings is that describing harm with abstract language can normalize it, which also has consequences when reporting on harmful events.”
There are a few additional caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because adding vivid sensory details requires extra words, the concrete headlines were naturally longer than the abstract ones, meaning word count could have contributed to the impact of the graphic descriptions. In addition, the experiments only examined short tabloid headlines about harm happening to strangers in ordinary, everyday settings, without a non-harmful baseline condition. It remains an open question whether severe harm in settings where danger is already expected, such as a combat zone, would feel less abnormal and elicit less horror.
Perceived abnormality was measured rather than manipulated, and the analyses testing it as a pathway were exploratory, added after the main results were known. The horror measure also combined “horrified” with “shocked,” a feeling that may overlap with judging an event as unusual. Both studies used nearly the same set of headlines and newly created two-item emotion scales, so it remains to be seen whether the results hold with other materials and measures.
Methodologically, participants rated perceived abnormality, physical arousal, and their emotions at the exact same time after each headline, so the statistical models cannot establish a strict chronological sequence of events. Physical arousal was also assessed through a single visual self-report scale rather than biological measures like heart rate or skin conductance.
Additionally, both study samples were 70 percent female and restricted to native English speakers in the United States. Because not all languages separate horror and fear into distinct everyday words, such as Japanese, which uses the term osore for both, future research could explore whether horror functions as a culturally specific emotion concept.
“Because many conspiracy theories seem to involve attempts to make sense of a horrifying event, I am interested in investigating if feelings of horror play a role in conspiratorial thinking,” Taylor said. “For example, can conspiracy theories act as a form of emotion regulation that people use to turn the helplessness of horror into anger, with the latter associated with a greater sense of control?”
The study, “Gruesome Details: Graphic Descriptions and Extreme Harm Differentially Elicit Horror (vs Fear) via Increased Perceptions of Abnormality,” was authored by Pamela Marie Taylor.

Israel election results: Can you form Israel’s next coalition government?
Israel has only ever been governed by coalitions. Can you put one together that reaches 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats?
Israelis voted on October 27 and, with more than 90 percent of the vote counted, there is still no clear winner.
The next government, like every government in Israel’s history, will have to be a coalition.
The question now is who can secure at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats to form a government and become Israel’s next prime minister.
Al Jazeera has built an interactive tool that lets you test different combinations of parties. It starts from the latest official results, and you can also enter your own seat numbers. Add parties until your coalition reaches 61 seats. You can add an entire bloc at once or select parties individually.
Who is ahead?
On the Central Elections Committee’s count, Likud is ahead as the largest single party, with 26 seats.
Netanyahu’s bloc stood at 52 seats, against 48 for Eisenkot’s. The Arab-led parties held the remaining 20.
Neither bloc is close to a majority. Netanyahu is nine seats short and Eisenkot 13. These figures are provisional and will shift as the final ballots, including those cast at diplomatic missions and in hospitals and prisons, are added to the count.
How many seats are needed?
Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. Parties win seats in proportion to their share of the national vote, provided they clear the 3.25 percent threshold to enter parliament.
A government needs the support of at least 61 politicians to secure a majority.
Neither of the main blocs has reached that number in the exit polls or the initial count. The next step is to find enough parties willing to join forces to make up the difference.
Why is forming a government so difficult?
The Arab-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List hold the balance of power, with 20 seats between them on the current count. They are the only bloc with enough seats to carry either side past 61.
On the arithmetic alone, that makes them kingmakers. In practice, analysts say they are unlikely to play that role, because the refusal of other parties to govern with them works as a political veto.
Netanyahu has described a coalition with Arab parties as “shameful”, while leading figures in the Jewish-led opposition have also ruled out governing with them. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have rejected a partnership, citing a lack of shared values.
That leaves potential coalitions that may work on paper but face serious political barriers.
Which parties belong to each bloc?
Netanyahu’s bloc spans Likud, the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism, and the far-right parties Religious Zionism, led by Bezalel Smotrich, and Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc includes his Yashar party, the Together list associated with former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
What happens next?
Once the results are certified, the president gives the mandate to the member of the Knesset considered most likely to assemble a majority.
That politician has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of up to 14 days. If they fail, another lawmaker can be given a chance. If no one can form a government, Israel may have to hold another election, as it did repeatedly between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, with 19 years in office across three stints, remains caretaker prime minister while coalition negotiations unfold. He is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
Official results are due on November 4. Negotiations to form a government could take considerably longer.

Türkiye to host Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers' meeting in Ankara
Unknown

2026-10-28
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara on October 29 2026.
The meeting will be hosted as part of the organisation’s 13th summit, scheduled for October 29-30.
The meeting will bring OTS foreign ministers together for the fifth time this year, following one regular and four informal council meetings.
Ministers are expected to discuss cooperation within the organisation and efforts to strengthen its institutional structure. Several administrative and financial documents related to the organisation’s functioning are also expected to be approved.
In addition, Fidan is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the meeting.
In his address, Fidan is expected to highlight the strengthening of political dialogue and joint action among Turkic states, as well as efforts to turn shared history, language, culture and fraternal ties into concrete cooperation.
He is also expected to outline Türkiye’s priorities during its OTS chairmanship, including strengthening the organisation’s institutional capacity, developing the Secretariat’s human and financial resources, and improving coordination among Turkic cooperation organisations.
Fidan is expected to emphasise the importance of translating economic and strategic cooperation into tangible outcomes, particularly in energy, trade, investment, digital transformation and defence industry.
He is also expected to underline the importance of strengthening the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor to improve connectivity between Asia and Europe and enhance economic resilience.
The foreign minister is expected to draw attention to developments in Afghanistan and their implications for regional security, stability and connectivity, calling for greater consultation and coordination among OTS member and observer states.
The OTS was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States under the Nakhchivan Agreement, signed on October 3 2009, by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its name was changed to the Organization of Turkic States at the Istanbul summit in 2021.
