How Lula defied Latin America's rightward shift to win Brazil's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:15:19 UTC
18:15:19 KST

Brazil's incumbent president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, secured an unexpected victory in Sunday's presidential runoff, overturning a first-round deficit to win an unprecedented fourth term.
No Brazilian presidential candidate had previously won a runoff after losing the first round. Yet Lula, the 81-year-old Workers' Party leader who once worked as a shoeshiner, gained more than 10 million additional votes in just two weeks.
The first round ended with Flavio Bolsonaro leading Lula 47 percent to 45 percent. Bolsonaro also secured a crucial endorsement from centrist Avante party leader Augusto Cury, who received 2.89 percent of valid votes.
The contest unfolded amid a broader rightward shift across Latin America, with right-wing leaders recently elected in Colombia, Chile, Peru and Bolivia, while Argentina already had a right-wing president.
How, then, did Lula overcome these odds?
Analysts say voter mobilisation, aggressive digital campaigning, and the 81-year-old politician’s personal appeal helped secure his unprecedented fourth presidential term in Brazil.
A Supreme Court decision to extend voting by two hours because of torrential rain and flooding in parts of the country may have also helped Lula. But the turnout figures alone do not fully explain his unexpected victory.
Nearly three million more voters turned out for the runoff, while an estimated 1.8 million people who had cast invalid ballots in the first round were assumed to have voted for one of the two candidates in the second.
Yet Lula secured 10.4 million more votes than in the first round. Even if all 4.8 million additional valid votes had gone to him, that would still leave 5.6 million votes to be explained by shifts in support among those who had already voted in the first round.
For Alfonso Insuasty Rodriguez, director of the GIDPAD research group at the University of San Buenaventura, the decisive factor was Lula's ability to transform “an existing electoral base into a broader social mobilisation”, attracting not only left-wing supporters but also a significant share of centrist and conservative voters.
Between the two rounds, Lula attracted new voters, mobilised those who had previously abstained and “secured support from people who had voted for other candidates”, Rodriguez tells TRT World.
But what persuaded so many centrist and right-wing voters to back Lula?
According to Rodriguez, two factors were particularly important: his campaign's nationwide political mobilisation, including a stronger presence on digital platforms such as WhatsApp, and “fears about a further entrenchment of Bolsonarismo”.
He says these concerns reflected growing anxiety among “broad sections of the popular classes” about their living conditions under a liberal government.
Despite his victory, Lula faces the challenge of governing without a legislative majority, with right-wing parties holding considerable influence in both chambers of Congress.
“Ultimately, Lula has won the presidency, but not a corresponding legislative majority. The central question is whether he can turn electoral legitimacy into effective transformative capacity without sacrificing the social programme in the name of governability,” Rodriguez says.
Appealing to populism
Lula also benefited from political campaigners with working-class backgrounds, including Andre Janones, a former bus conductor who used social media to launch aggressive attacks against the Bolsonaros.
Janones portrayed the father and son, both publicly aligned with US President Donald Trump, as defenders of Brazil's wealthy elite who favoured cuts to social welfare spending.
In the three weeks after the first round, Janones' pro-Lula WhatsApp channel reportedly grew from 50,000 followers to nearly 11 million, underscoring the leftist camp's digital campaign's intensity.
Rodriguez says Lula's victory also raises broader questions about the changing nature of populism, which has gained traction across Europe and the Americas.
“The concept requires clarification: populism is not exclusive to either the right or the left,” Rodriguez says.
He explains that both left-wing and conservative movements can appeal to populist sentiments and demands.
“Lula prevailed because he did not confront this current through ideological debate alone. He combined a political record recognised by sections of the popular classes, a defence of social policies and an electoral mobilisation strategy that adapted as the campaign progressed,” says the political analyst.
“The initial setback forced his campaign to correct its course and compete more vigorously across digital spaces, in everyday public debate and for the votes of those who did not fully identify with the Workers’ Party.”
The Workers' Party's campaign messaging also shifted between the two rounds. Its posters increasingly featured green and yellow, the colours of Brazil's national flag, rather than red, traditionally associated with the political left.
Lula also adopted a position long advocated by the Bolsonaro camp, announcing his support for lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16.
External factors
Beyond his appeal to populist sentiments, Lula also benefited from longstanding Brazilian opposition to foreign intervention, particularly as Bolsonaro strengthened his ties with the Trump administration, according to analysts.
US President Donald Trump described the right-wing candidate's first-round success as a “great victory”, reinforcing perceptions of Washington's support for Bolsonaro. He was allegedly fled from Brazil after his election loss, according to new reports.
The Trump administration's political rhetoric, coupled with its “bellicose actions” towards Venezuela and Cuba and its so-called “drug boat” strikes in the eastern Pacific, “all tainted Bolsonaro by association,” James E. Mahon Jr., a professor of political science at Williams College and an expert on Latin American politics, tells TRT World.
Unlike Bolsonaro, who advocates a Trump-style economic model similar to that pursued by Argentina's Javier Milei, a staunch Washington ally, Lula has emphasised social programmes, strategic autonomy and regional cooperation as safeguards against foreign intervention.
The leftist leader has also championed BRICS, a grouping of major emerging economies, while strengthening Brazil's relations with China, which has increasingly challenged US influence in global economic and political affairs.
Lula has sought to expand Brazil's diplomatic influence on the global stage, drawing on the country's position as Latin America's most populous nation and largest economy, as well as its considerable natural resources, including rare earth minerals. He has also condemned Israel's actions in Gaza and other Palestinian territories as genocidal.
“Lula clearly articulated the direction he intends to pursue by stating that Brazil aspires to be a central, rather than a peripheral, nation,” Martin Alejandro Martinelli, a historian and sociologist who heads the Geohistorical Observatory at Argentina's National University of Lujan, says.
Martinelli says this vision resonated with Brazilians' aspirations for their country to play a greater role in global affairs.
“In this vein, he proposed developing domestic artificial intelligence capabilities and building national data centers, thereby reducing reliance on both China and the US,” Martinelli tells TRT World.
According to Martinelli, Lula's emphasis on technological self-reliance also helped broaden his electoral appeal.
Martinelli says his victory could have a “continental impact” with global implications, showing that governments that can build common ground with their populations can withstand US pressure.
“Brazil can coordinate positions with Mexico and other regional governments, providing both continuity and an alternative to a policy of unreserved alignment with the United States.”
Rodriguez also sees Lula's victory as significant for the wider region.
“The result places a political limit on Trump’s project of expanding US influence across Latin America through ideological alliances, trade pressure and security agreements,” he tells TRT World.
“The victory therefore weakens the regional advance of the Trump-aligned right, but neither closes the cycle of authoritarian politics nor guarantees structural transformation.
“It creates an opportunity for Latin American integration, although its reach will depend on coordination between governments, social movements and popular organisations.”

The biennial elections for these Graduate and Teacher constituencies across Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, and Maharashtra were held via ballot papers on October 23, 2026, with counting beginning on October 27, 2026.
NEW DELHI: Congress faced a major setback in the legislative council elections on Wednesday, failing to secure a victory in the seats declared so far across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra, even as counting continued in several constituencies.The biggest setback for the Congress came in Karnataka, where it failed to win a single seat despite being in power in the state. The BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats, with the BJP retaining three constituencies and the JD(S) wresting the Bengaluru Teachers’ seat from the Congress. The defeat was particularly significant for the ruling party as it lost its sitting seat in Bengaluru Teachers’ and failed to make gains in any of the three BJP-held constituencies.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP and Samajwadi Party (SP) registered wins, while in Bihar, Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj Party opened its legislative council account by defeating the Congress. The RJD also scored a victory in Bihar, wresting the Patna Teachers’ seat from the BJP.Counting for 28 legislative council seats across Uttar Pradesh (11), Bihar (8), Maharashtra (5) and Karnataka (4) began on Tuesday following polling on October 23.
The elections were held for graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies, with results declared for several seats and counting continuing in others.
Here is a state-wise look at the latest results and counting trends.
Karnataka (4 seats): BJP-JD(S) alliance sweeps all four, Congress draws blank
The BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats in Karnataka, dealing a setback to the ruling Congress. The BJP retained the North-East Teachers’, South-East Graduates’ and West Graduates’ constituencies, while its ally JD(S) wrested the Bengaluru Teachers’ seat from the Congress.JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated sitting Congress MLC Puttanna by 908 votes in Bengaluru Teachers’. Ranganath secured 10,810 votes against Puttanna’s 9,902.BJP’s Shashil G Namoshi retained North-East Teachers’ by 3,297 votes, securing his fifth victory from the constituency with 15,596 votes against Congress candidate Sharanappa Mattur’s 12,299.In South-East Graduates’, BJP candidate K M Suresh defeated Congress nominee Shashi Hulikunte Mutt by 23,098 votes. Sitting BJP MLC S V Sankanur retained West Graduates’, defeating Congress candidate Mohan Limbikai by 9,323 votes.The results marked a clean sweep for the opposition alliance, with the Congress failing to win a single seat despite campaigning by chief minister D K Shivakumar, former chief minister Siddaramaiah and other senior leaders.However, the results are not expected to affect the stability of the Congress government or significantly alter the balance of power in the 75-member Legislative Council.
Uttar Pradesh (11 seats): BJP wins four seats, SP secures two
The BJP won six of the 11 Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured five. The BJP won the Agra Graduates’, Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers’, Lucknow Teachers’, Meerut Teachers’, Meerut Graduates’ and Gorakhpur-Faizabad Teachers’ constituencies.The Samajwadi Party won the Allahabad-Jhansi Graduates’, Varanasi Teachers’ and Agra-Aligarh Teachers’ constituencies.In the Agra Graduates’ constituency, BJP candidate Manvendra Pratap Singh (Guruji) was declared elected.The BJP retained the Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers’ seat, with its candidate Hari Singh Dhillon defeating SP nominee Danish Akhtar by 17,676 votes. Dhillon secured 21,672 votes against Akhtar’s 3,996 after all five rounds of counting.The BJP also won the Lucknow Teachers’ constituency, where its candidate Umesh Dwivedi defeated SP’s Sushil Kumar by 6,992 votes. Dwivedi secured 13,179 votes against Kumar’s 8,371.In Meerut, the BJP won both the Teachers’ and Graduates’ constituencies. Its candidates Dinesh Kumar Goyal and Shri Chand Sharma were declared winners in the Graduates’ and Teachers’ seats, respectively.The BJP also retained the Gorakhpur-Faizabad Teachers’ constituency, with its candidate Dhruv Tripathi defeating Independent candidate Rajiv Yadav by 307 votes. Tripathi secured 14,887 votes against Yadav’s 14,580.However, Yadav alleged that the election had been manipulated to ensure his defeat. Claiming that around 1,000 votes had been stolen, he said he would approach the Election Commission and the court to challenge the result. He also demanded a forensic examination of 1,612 votes counted in the fourth round, alleging irregularities in the counting process.The MLC polls are being viewed as a prestige battle between the ruling BJP and the opposition SP ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. Voting for the 11 seats, comprising five Graduates’ and six Teachers’ constituencies, was held on Friday, with counting beginning at 8 am on Tuesday.
The Bihar Legislative Council elections delivered several upsets, with five sitting MLCs losing their seats and the Jan Suraaj Party securing its maiden victory in the Upper House.Of the eight seats, which went to polls on October 23, the BJP won three, Independents secured two, while the RJD, Jan Suraaj Party and NDA partner JD(U) won one seat each.Jan Suraaj Party candidate Suresh Prasad Rai defeated sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha in the Darbhanga Teachers’ constituency, marking the party’s first win in the Bihar Legislative Council.BJP candidate Narendra Prasad Singh won the Tirhut Teachers’ seat, defeating CPI MLC Sanjay Kumar Singh, who had the support of the INDIA bloc.In another major upset, RJD candidate Sanjeev Kumar defeated veteran BJP MLC Nawal Kishore Yadav in the Patna Teachers’ constituency, ending the latter’s long hold on the seat.Independent candidate Rahul Raj also defeated sitting MLC Afaq Ahmed in the Saran Teachers’ constituency.Meanwhile, JD(U)’s Neeraj Kumar retained the Patna Graduates’ seat for a fourth consecutive term, defeating his rivals despite a challenge from within his party. BJP candidates Sarvesh Kumar and N K Yadav retained the Darbhanga Graduates’ and Kosi Graduates’ seats, respectively.Independent candidate Bansi Dhar Brajwasi also retained the Tirhut Graduates’ constituency, while two other seats went to the BJP and Independents as part of the overall tally.The Congress, which contested five seats, failed to win any and is now left with just one member in the 75-member Bihar Legislative Council.The polls saw 90 candidates contesting four Graduates’ constituencies and 60 candidates in four Teachers’ constituencies. The four Graduates’ seats had 4.92 lakh eligible voters, while the four Teachers’ constituencies had 40,253 voters.
Maharashtra (5 seats): Congress retains Nagpur graduates’ seat, defeats BJP
The BJP-led ruling Mahayuti won two seats in Maharashtra, while the opposition NCP (SP) bagged two, as results were declared for all five Legislative Council seats.Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP’s Sudhakar Kohale by 3,271 votes to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates’ constituency, ending more than 40 hours of counting. Wanjari secured 67,231 votes against Kohale’s 63,960.
Also read: Congress opens account in MLC polls as Abhijit Wanjari retains Nagpur seat after nail-biting contestKohale, a former MLA, had led Wanjari by 4,294 votes after the second round of counting on Wednesday. However, with no candidate securing the required quota through first-preference votes, the counting proceeded to second-preference votes, allowing Wanjari to overtake his rival during the elimination rounds.Shiv Sena candidate Kiran Sarnaik won the Amravati Teachers’ constituency, while BJP candidate Kaustubh Gawade emerged victorious in the Pune Teachers’ constituency.In the Pune Graduates’ constituency, NCP (SP) candidate Harshada Deshmukh-Jadhav won, while party candidate Pratapsinh Patil secured victory in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) Graduates’ constituency.The polls, held on October 23, saw 182 candidates contesting across three Graduates’ and two Teachers’ constituencies. The results were closely watched amid rebel candidates, alliance differences and efforts by the BJP-led Mahayuti and the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi to consolidate support.

Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom eyes Asian alternative to Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:14:04 UTC
18:14:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chunghwa Telecom is considering an alliance with Asian telecom operators to develop a low-Earth orbit satellite network, aiming to strengthen Taiwan’s communications resilience amid rising geopolitical risks and concerns about reliance on foreign satellite services.
Chunghwa Telecom Chairman Simon Chien (簡志誠) said Wednesday that the proposed “low-Earth orbit satellite constellation alliance” remains an idea, with no specific partners identified, per CNA.
Ukraine has relied heavily on Starlink and the military-grade Starshield satellite services provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX during the Russia-Ukraine war, according to Mirror Media. A recent slowdown of the networks, which Musk said was due to an alleged breach of terms of service, affected Ukrainian drone operations and combat capabilities, highlighting the importance of communications autonomy during wartime.
Chien said an alliance with Asian telecom partners could raise NT$20 billion to NT$30 billion (US$626 million to US$939 million) to launch 48 or 64 low-Earth orbit satellites, potentially providing round-the-clock communications coverage across Taiwan, Mirror Media reported. Chunghwa Telecom also hopes to enlist major technology companies to help ensure Taiwan’s communications autonomy, he said.
The investment would cover the satellites and supporting infrastructure, Chien said. He acknowledged that the project would require government support.
Chunghwa Telecom is already active in the satellite communications market and is the only Taiwanese telecom operator with access to satellite networks in high, medium, and low Earth orbits, per CNA. It has obtained commercial licenses for Eutelsat OneWeb low-Earth orbit satellites and SES’s O3b medium-Earth orbit satellite network, and has a strategic partnership with US satellite company Astranis to develop Taiwan’s first dedicated satellite.
Chien said President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) has repeatedly stressed the importance of national resilience, particularly digital and communications resilience, according to Mirror Media. Chunghwa Telecom is pursuing a multilayered network combining undersea cables, fiber-optic and mobile networks, microwave links, and satellites in different orbits to reduce reliance on any single communications system.
Chien said the company is focusing on maintaining connectivity in worst-case scenarios, not just improving network speeds under normal conditions, per Liberty Times. If undersea cables fail, terrestrial backbone networks must reroute traffic, while microwave links and satellites should provide backup when disasters disrupt ground-based mobile infrastructure.
Government agencies, hospitals, transportation hubs, and other critical infrastructure must also maintain basic communications during emergencies, he said. Chien added that some resilience investments may not generate short-term revenue or ever be needed, but are essential to Taiwan’s security and the continuity of critical services.

Taipei Nuit Blanche to feature art and performances around Yuanshan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:13:54 UTC
18:13:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei's Nuit Blanche will take place Saturday, featuring more than 30 artworks and 50 performances around Yuanshan and Taipei Expo Park, with events continuing until 2 a.m. Sunday.
This year's festival, titled “NIGHT KA SHI,” draws inspiration from the Nakashi tradition, in which musicians traveled between venues to perform. The theme explores how music, art, and social interaction shape Taipei's nighttime culture, per a press release.
Taipei introduced Nuit Blanche in 2016, adapting the international nighttime arts festival first held in Paris in 2002. The event invites visitors to explore public spaces and neighborhoods through art installations, performances, and light displays.
The festival's program spans Yuanshan Natural Landscape Park, Taipei Expo Park, Tatung University, Minzu East Road, and the Qingguang Market area. The event combines public art with music and cultural activities designed to encourage visitors to experience the city after dark.
Taipei MRT will extend service at Yuanshan, Minquan West Road, and Zhongshan Elementary School stations until 2 a.m. Sunday. After regular service ends, additional one-way trains will run about every 20 minutes from Yuanshan to Taipei Main Station and from Zhongshan Elementary School to Minquan West Road, per a Taipei MRT press release.
During extended service, only the three designated stations will allow passengers to enter and board trains. Shuanglian, Zhongshan, and Taipei Main Station will permit passengers to exit but will not offer boarding or transfers.
Yumen Street north of Yuanshan MRT Station will also be closed to vehicle traffic from 2 p.m. Saturday until 2 a.m. Sunday. Intercity buses serving Keelung, Taoyuan, and Yilan will be rerouted, with passengers directed to temporary stops instead of the Yuanshan Transfer Station’s Yumen stop.
Taipei MRT will also adjust train frequencies according to crowd levels in response to other large events scheduled for Saturday, including a Taipei Dome concert and the Taiwan LGBT+ Pride parade.
To manage crowds, the metro will establish a command center at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall Station and deploy staff near Exit 5, which connects to the Taipei Dome. Escalators may be temporarily stopped when platforms or entrances become overcrowded or when large crowds are expected.
Passenger-flow displays, colored floor markings, and LED signs will help guide travelers through the station and direct them toward less congested routes.

Taiwan warns common medications can make driving dangerous
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:13:46 UTC
18:13:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Food and Drug Administration warned Wednesday that some common medications can make driving unsafe, with impaired motorists potentially facing criminal charges.
CNA reported that some medicines can cause drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, and slower reactions. These side effects can affect driving ability even when medication is taken as prescribed.
The agency identified nine groups of medications that may affect driving, including sleeping pills, anesthetics, eye drops that dilate pupils, and muscle relaxants. Certain medicines for diabetes, high blood pressure, pain, colds, allergies, anxiety, depression, and psychiatric conditions can also pose risks.
The warning follows concerns that police drug tests may detect substances found in legally prescribed medications. Two drivers in Taipei tested positive in roadside saliva screenings earlier this year, but subsequent urine tests linked the results to medication use, per UDN.
The Criminal Investigation Bureau said drivers could face criminal charges if medication leaves them unable to drive safely. It said previous court rulings have held motorists responsible even when they took medicine as directed by doctors, per CNA.
Under Article 185-3 of the Criminal Code, drivers convicted of qualifying drug-related driving offenses face up to three years in prison and a possible fine of up to NT$300,000 (US$9,400). Those whose offenses cause serious injury or death face heavier penalties.
The Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act also provides for fines, driver's license suspension or revocation, and vehicle impoundment for certain drug-related driving violations. Taking prescribed medication alone does not automatically constitute an offense.
The administration and transport ministry have prepared educational materials on medication and driving safety, including guidelines for drivers. The agency said it would continue sharing safety information online and had asked pharmacists to warn patients about possible side effects.
Drivers should read medication labels and consult doctors or pharmacists about whether and when they can safely drive. Those experiencing side effects that affect driving ability should avoid driving and use public transport or other alternatives.

Trump’s Ukraine policy sends warning to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:13:17 UTC
18:13:17 KST

President Donald Trump’s support for Ukraine has been extremely shallow and increasingly appears to be approaching abandonment.
Since his inauguration in January 2025, US military, financial, and humanitarian support has been sharply reduced.
In recent weeks, Trump has multiplied his verbal attacks against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Meanwhile, it has been reported that Ukraine’s access to Starshield — a militarized version of Starlink — was limited following an order from within the White House.
Like Ukraine, Taiwan faces military pressure from a more powerful neighbor and depends heavily on American support for its defense. Washington’s treatment of Kyiv therefore raises concerns about how it could approach Taipei when that support conflicts with other priorities.
Although Trump has not yet adopted such a disruptive stance toward Taiwan, several similarities between Washington’s approaches to Kyiv and Taipei are worrying.
The first parallel concerns military support.
Ukraine has experienced repeated interruptions, including the suspension of military assistance in March 2025 and the withholding of some weapons in July 2025. Washington is now also delaying approval for transfers of Patriot interceptor missiles from partner countries.
Taiwan faces a similar challenge. A US$14 billion (NT$454 billion) arms package from the United States, which would be the largest ever, has remained on hold for months and has been described by Trump as a “negotiating chip” with China.
Worse, the issue extends beyond the delayed arms sale. By directly discussing arms sales to Taiwan with China, the current administration has weakened the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) and profoundly undermined the commitments made under the Six Assurances, allowing Beijing to influence decisions about Taiwan’s defense.
Another similarity is Washington’s use of military support to extract economic gains.
Although US economic pressure is not unique to Taiwan and Ukraine, both depend heavily on Washington for their national security. This dependence makes it harder for them to resist economic demands without worrying about consequences for military support.
Early in his second term, Trump pressed Ukraine to compensate Washington for its military support, ultimately resulting in the US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, commonly referred to as the minerals agreement.
Similarly, in 2024, Trump said Taiwan should pay the United States for its defense.
Investment in American semiconductor production increasingly appears to fill a similar role.
Trump has repeatedly claimed that Taiwan stole the chip industry from the United States, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said the administration aims to bring 40% of Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain and production to the US during Trump’s term.
Lutnick also said Trump is vital to protecting Taiwan and that the country therefore wants to keep him happy.
The current administration has also shown an appetite for making deals with aggressors in a more conciliatory manner.
Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel as part of an agreement intended to lower fuel prices, despite the risk of providing Moscow with additional revenue to finance its war.
Moreover, US Ambassador to China David Perdue said Trump asked Chinese leader Xi Jinping during his September visit to the US whether China would like to buy American weapons. The White House and State Department later denied that there was any plan or offer to sell weapons to China.
Nevertheless, the episode should raise concerns among US partners in the Indo-Pacific.
Another recurrent pattern has been shifting responsibility for tensions or war onto the threatened partner.
Trump’s meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin in August 2025 and Xi in May 2026 were followed by antagonistic remarks toward the countries facing pressure, respectively blaming Zelenskyy for failing to end the war and calling on Taiwan to “cool down.”
By placing responsibility on the threatened partner, Washington reduces pressure on the aggressor and signals that its support for partners can be inconsistent.
Taiwan and Ukraine’s security cooperation with the United States is therefore increasingly tainted by uncertainty and unpredictable commitments.
However, Taiwan’s situation remains different from Ukraine’s in several important respects.
First, Taipei is a longstanding ally of Washington, unlike Kyiv, which has only more recently become a major US defense partner.
Before the TRA, the US-Taiwan Mutual Defense Treaty was in force from 1954 to 1979. Those were certainly different times, but the security relationship between Washington and Taipei has deep roots.
This is reflected in Taiwan’s steady and strong bipartisan support in the United States.
Taiwan, as a central component of the First Island Chain, also benefits from its importance to US regional interests.
Should China successfully invade Taiwan, the Indo-Pacific balance of power would be profoundly disrupted and American interests challenged.
Ukraine is certainly relevant to European security, but less central to the United States. Washington’s principal strategic competition is with Beijing, not Moscow.
Taiwan’s central role in this competition means that concessions over its security could strengthen the very power the United States is seeking to counter. This places Taiwan in a different category of strategic importance and gives Washington an additional reason to maintain its support.
Equally important, Taiwan’s leverage over the United States is greater than Ukraine’s.
With its semiconductor industry and the growing importance of artificial intelligence, Taiwan carries considerable weight in Washington’s strategic calculations.
Nonetheless, Taiwan’s importance does not remove the risks created when Washington uses the vulnerability of threatened partners to extract concessions while making their security negotiable with their adversaries.
A profound upheaval in Washington’s posture toward Taiwan remains unlikely, but concessions such as the delayed arms package still weaken Taiwan’s defense and encourage Beijing to test how far American support extends.
How long will it be before economic concerns open another negotiating window for China to convince Trump to make a deal?
The Russian diesel agreement shows how pressure to lower prices can give Trump an incentive to accommodate an aggressor despite the consequences for a threatened partner.
Taiwan needs stability. Its national defense depends in large part on Washington’s support.
The commitments made to Taipei must therefore remain reliable rather than depend on what Beijing might offer Washington in the future.
The shift in how Washington treats its partners, and the weakening of longstanding commitments to Taiwan, could have effects lasting beyond Trump’s presidency.
Future administrations could inherit diminished confidence in American support and a precedent that encourages Beijing to press for further concessions over Taiwan’s security.

Historic gains for Arab parties in Israel election: exit polls

Strong and historic gains for Arab-majority parties in Israel vote: exit polls
The first exit polls from Israel's pivotal general election on Tuesday showed strong gains for the country's Arab parties, whose voter base turned out in high numbers.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning around 20 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
As more than 60% of the count has been done, the Netanyahu-led bloc holds 56 seats, about five seats shy for 61—the threshold for a majority.
In response to these gains by the Arab parties, Yair Golan, the head of Israel's main but very tiny left-wing party, called on Wednesday for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as partial election results showed their support would be crucial to reaching a governing coalition.
"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," he said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
The history gains by the Arab parties occurs despite scaremongering by Netanyahu and other extreme right-wing politicians.
Netanyahu remained defiant early Wednesday as he seeks to remain the country's longest-serving prime minister. He dismissed the idea of a partnership with Arab parties—whose constituents make up 20% of Israel’s population—as treasonous.
“We must establish a strong, right-wing, nationalist government,” Netanyahu said. “We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties.”

US hints at expanding Russian diesel deal

Unknown Publisher

18:10:37 KST

US hints at expanding Russian diesel deal
More Russian diesel fuel could enter global markets as part of a trade agreement between Moscow and Washington struck earlier this month, Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said. He claimed the shipments could be a “carrot” for Moscow to scale back fighting in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump announced the landmark diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on October 9, saying Russia would release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 tons in November, another million afterward and potentially 3 million more, depending on refinery capacity.
Trump called lowering fuel prices for American consumers his “greatest priority” ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, where the Republicans are at risk of losing their congressional majority.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky condemned the surprise deal as a “weak decision,” prompting an angry response from Trump, who suggested that Ukraine replace Zelensky with someone willing to negotiate peace with Russia. Trump has also repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, something Kiev has refused to do.
Speaking to CNBC on Tuesday, Wright described the diesel deal as an “incentive” for Moscow to stop hostilities with Ukraine, adding that more Russian tankers could “quite possibly” depart under a six-month sanctions waiver.
“It’s trying to put a carrot in front of Russia,” he said, arguing that reduced hostilities would allow Moscow to export more diesel and marginally ease global fuel shortages.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying diesel are already en route to the US, with a fourth expected to depart Wednesday. On Sunday, he offered to supply as much as buyers wanted within Russia’s available export volumes, saying: “We can supply all of it.” He previously said Russian diesel exports could reach 3.5 million tons monthly by year-end.
During a meeting with Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff last week in St. Petersburg, Putin noted that global diesel prices fell 5%-6% after the deal was announced. Earlier this week, Reuters reported that Russia’s daily diesel output rose from 160,000 tons in early October to 180,000 tons after the introduction of new export quotas.
The agreement has nevertheless met bipartisan resistance in Washington, with a group of senators calling it a “gift to our adversary” and a betrayal of Ukraine. Novak pushed back on Tuesday, singling out Democrats and wondering why US lawmakers were acting “not in the interests of the residents of the United States.”

Russia test-fires Bulava from one of its newest missile submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:10:19 UTC
18:10:19 KST

- Russia’s Generalissimo Suvorov submarine fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
- The missile was launched from underwater toward the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, and the Pacific Fleet said its warheads arrived on schedule.
The Russian Pacific Fleet’s ballistic missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile from beneath the Sea of Okhotsk on Oct. 28, sending it across the country to the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry said the launch was carried out from a submerged position as part of the crew’s planned combat training, and the Pacific Fleet said that, according to tracking data, the missile’s warheads arrived in the designated area at the planned time. The flight path took the missile from Russia’s Far East to the far north of its European territory, a route the Pacific Fleet uses to test the readiness of its strategic submarines.
“The crew of the Project 955A Borei-A class strategic nuclear-powered missile submarine Generalissimo Suvorov of the Pacific Fleet, in accordance with the combat training plan, test-fired a Bulava intercontinental ballistic missile aimed at the Chizha test range in the Arkhangelsk region,” the Russian Defense Ministry said.
The K-553 Generalissimo Suvorov is one of Russia’s newest strategic submarines and the third of the upgraded Borei-A class, a fourth-generation design from the Rubin Central Design Bureau in St. Petersburg. The Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk laid it down on Dec. 26, 2014, and the Russian Navy commissioned it on Dec. 29, 2022. Before entering service, the submarine fired a Bulava from the White Sea on Nov. 3, 2022, with the warheads striking the Kura test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the opposite direction to this week’s flight.
In 2023, the submarine sailed from the Northern Fleet to the Pacific along the Northern Sea Route and arrived at its permanent base in Vilyuchinsk on Kamchatka on Oct. 16, 2023, where it joined the 25th submarine division. TASS reported that the boat’s imported components have been replaced with Russian-made equipment.
Each Borei-class submarine carries 16 Bulava missiles. The Bulava is a solid-fuel missile developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Engineering, the design bureau behind the Topol-M and Yars land-based missiles, and it is launched from underwater so the submarine does not have to surface and reveal its position. Each missile can carry multiple nuclear warheads that separate and fly to individual targets, and the Barents Observer has reported that each Bulava carries six. Russia formally accepted the missile into service in May 2024 after years of testing that began with a first launch in 2005.
The Sea of Okhotsk-to-Chizha route has been used before by Pacific Fleet submarines. In December 2020, the Borei-class Vladimir Monomakh fired a salvo of four Bulava missiles from the same sea toward the same range in the Arkhangelsk region, the first time a Borei had launched four missiles in a single salvo.
Russia’s Borei and Borei-A submarines are replacing the Soviet-era Delta-class boats that carried the naval leg of Russia’s nuclear deterrent for decades, with the Generalissimo Suvorov and its sister ships forming the core of the Pacific Fleet’s strategic submarine force at Kamchatka.

Bulgaria Seeks Transfer of German Suspects in Starlink Arson Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:09:00 UTC
18:09:00 KST

Bulgarian authorities identified the two German citizens suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas near Sofia on October 10, a day after the incident, but their detention in Germany required a European Arrest Warrant issued on October 19, Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The two officials were scheduled to answer questions from lawmakers about the arson during an extraordinary National Assembly session, but the meeting could not proceed because there was no quorum. The government then decided to disclose the information to journalists outside Parliament.
Radev praised the security services and the Ministry of Interior for identifying the alleged perpetrators within hours, despite their having already left Bulgaria. He said Bulgarian agencies had contacted their counterparts abroad to have the suspects monitored.
The prime minister said the authorities could not disclose the suspects’ names earlier, responding to criticism over the lack of information at a previous parliamentary hearing on October 14. He said doing so could have prompted the suspects to flee the country where they were staying.
“It was not possible to share all the information immediately; had the security services and the Ministry of Interior disclosed the names of the perpetrators, they would most likely have fled the country where they were located,” Radev said. “Sometimes, patience is required to ensure we can apprehend the perpetrators.”
Radev also said partner intelligence services had helped identify and apprehend the suspects, while their motives remained unclear. He rejected claims that a government press office statement offering advice to the media on covering his appearances amounted to censorship.
“We have never engaged in censorship; on the contrary, as you can see, we are here - we have never refused to speak with the Bulgarian media,” he said.
Asked about the MPs who did not attend the session, Radev said lawmakers from across the political spectrum were occupied with the election campaign, although some were present in Parliament.
Demerdzhiev said Bulgarian authorities had established the suspects’ identities and identified the vehicle they used to travel by October 10. Information was passed in stages to law enforcement counterparts in every country they crossed while returning to Germany, where they arrived later that day.
German authorities knew who the suspects were by October 10 but could not arrest them before the European Arrest Warrant was issued. Demerdzhiev said the procedure had been accelerated as much as possible, with the warrant issued on October 19 and the relevant documents translated and transmitted afterward.
“The procedure was expedited as much as possible. The warrant was issued on October 19, the documents were translated and transmitted, and our German counterparts located and apprehended the perpetrators at the first available opportunity,” Demerdzhiev said.
The minister said Bulgaria expected the suspects to be handed over to its authorities so that investigative and procedural steps could continue. He confirmed that both were German citizens permanently residing in Germany and said information gathered about their previous activities had been shared with German authorities.
The suspects, Zeka Islam and Tirpan Beytulla, are both 19. They were detained in Duisburg on October 23, according to the information provided by Bulgarian authorities.
Demerdzhiev said the two had criminal records in Germany but had not previously been associated with this type of offense. He added that available information indicated they may have carried out a similar act in another European Union member state on October 18.
“The full details regarding their stay and activities will be clarified during the course of the criminal proceedings,” Demerdzhiev said.
The minister explained that the suspects had left Bulgaria legally, passing through border checkpoints according to established procedures. Authorities had no legal grounds to stop or detain them at that time.
The arson took place on October 9 at a Starlink antenna installation in the Plana region near Sofia. The suspects have been charged, and the Prosecutor’s Office has said the offense carries a possible prison sentence of up to 12 years. Their transfer to Bulgaria is pending, while the investigation continues into the circumstances and motives behind the attack.
The incident was also discussed after an extraordinary parliamentary session failed to convene, with many MPs from the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party absent. Radev addressed comments by Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chair of Yes, Bulgaria, who was the first to report the incident, explaining why the authorities had not released further details when requested on October 14.
The suspects are also under investigation over a possible similar incident in Lithuania. On the night leading into October 18, an attempted arson targeting Starlink antennas and a control unit was reported at a facility near Vilnius.

Iran sees only unacceptable ideas in latest mediation to end war, official says
DOHA – Qatari mediators have presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
The official briefed on the negotiations, who is not from Iran, said a new draft peace proposal for the eight-month-old conflict was presented on Oct 25 and was being considered by Tehran, with a response expected by the end of the week.
Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and recently spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran’s and Washington’s concerns, laying out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.
Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented only “unacceptable ideas and not an offer”, and that Tehran’s policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Oct 28 that Tehran remained in close contact with intermediaries to review ideas that could ensure the implementation of its own seven-day proposal aimed at ending the war in the Middle East.
He said Iran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed, adding that Tehran’s seven-day plan could be implemented in less than a week.
Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme to be part of negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions – which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.
Attack on Saudi oil refinery
In late September, Iran presented its seven-day proposal under which Araqchi said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Oct 25 was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. The official had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.
Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on Feb 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.
In recent weeks, Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia - a key US ally and the world’s largest crude exporter - opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.
Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than US$115 a barrel on Oct 28 after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over supply risks.
Fighting with the Houthis intensified in September as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.
Concerns about risk of new strikes
The official briefed on the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of the Oct 25 meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for another term in a general election, could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.
On Oct 23, Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.
On Oct 26, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of de-escalation efforts. Qatar said on Oct 27 that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.
Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.
The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has eroded Trump’s approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as deaths near 4,900 in DRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:02:00 UTC
18:02:00 KST

Africa’s latest Ebola outbreak has infected more than 10,000 people, with nearly 4,900 deaths reported in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Congolese health authorities said Tuesday.
According to figures from the DRC, 10,060 people have contracted the virus and 4,887 have died since the outbreak was detected in May. It is the country’s largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic.
Cases have also been reported in Kenya and Nigeria, while Uganda, which recorded cases earlier in the outbreak, was declared Ebola-free by the World Health Organization (WHO) in August. The WHO has warned that containing the outbreak across several countries presents a complex challenge.
In the DRC, 2,684 people have recovered from the disease, according to the country’s National Institute of Public Health. The reported figures put the outbreak’s fatality rate at nearly 50%.
One of the main challenges facing the response is the lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus, the strain responsible for the outbreak. Researchers have begun testing whether the Ervebo vaccine, which is effective against the more common Zaire strain, could also protect against Bundibugyo.
After spreading undetected for weeks, the virus was first identified in the northeastern Congolese province of Ituri, marking the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak.
It has since spread across parts of the country’s north and east, where violence by armed groups and limited trust in state institutions complicate efforts to contain the disease.
Ituri and North Kivu province account for most reported cases. Parts of North Kivu are controlled by the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group.
After reporting 20 cases and two deaths, Uganda was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in late August.
Kenya, which had not reported a confirmed case until Oct. 6, has recorded nine cases and two deaths. The cases have been linked to a traveler who arrived from the DRC via Uganda.
Nigeria confirmed one case on Oct. 20 involving a 42-year-old Swiss woman who had traveled to Uganda with her husband. She was subsequently evacuated to a hospital in Geneva, Switzerland. Authorities are investigating how she contracted the virus, as she had no known travel history to the DRC.
Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told Agence France-Presse that the organization was investigating the source of the infection.
“We saw that the genomic sequencing of the Kenyan case is similar to the Nigerian case. And we discovered that yesterday with some cases in Beni,” he said.
“Today it’s an outbreak in three regions. We didn’t see that since we started to have experience of Ebola outbreaks. We were not thinking that Nigeria could be an at risk country.”
When the outbreak was declared, only three health zones in one province were affected, Kaseya said.
“Today we are talking about eight provinces, more than 66 health zones. To give you an idea, it’s like twice the size of the UK.”
Nigerian health authorities had identified 53 contacts of the Swiss woman as they sought to prevent further transmission.
Some experts have raised concerns that the virus could have spread after the couple arrived in Nigeria on Oct. 3.
The WHO said the woman developed symptoms on Oct. 7, sought medical care in Abuja on Oct. 11 and tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus on Oct. 20.
Ugandan officials have rejected suggestions that she contracted the disease while in Uganda.
Efforts to contain the outbreak in the DRC have been hampered by mistrust among some communities.
A nurse was killed and another health worker seriously wounded in the northeastern province of Tshopo on Saturday, according to the WHO.
Marcel Likolo, chief medical officer of the Bafwasende health district, told AFP that young people in the area accused the two workers of trying to infect residents with tablets before attacking them.
The Ebola treatment center where the attack occurred has since closed, Likolo said.
Since Ebola was first identified in 1976, the disease has killed more than 15,000 people across Africa.
Researchers are testing whether the Ervebo vaccine, which has demonstrated effectiveness against the Zaire strain of Ebola, could also provide protection against the Bundibugyo virus.

6 in 10 Belgian nuclear companies postpone investments amid energy policy ‘uncertainty’

Melike Pala
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Six out of 10 companies operating in Belgium’s nuclear sector are postponing investments due to uncertainty over the country’s energy policy, according to a survey by technology federation Agoria cited by broadcaster VRT on Wednesday.
The companies are calling on the government to provide a clear and predictable energy strategy, including concrete decisions and timelines for future nuclear projects.
Belgium has been moving toward a nuclear phase-out over the past two decades.
However, the nuclear sector continues to account for more than 8,000 full-time jobs and generate over €9 billion ($9.9 billion) in annual turnover.
Agoria said the sector has significant growth potential but needs clarity from the government on its nuclear ambitions.
“We need clear decisions and a concrete schedule for nuclear projects so that companies can prepare for the future,” Agoria CEO Bart Steukers said.
He stressed that businesses remain uncertain about which types of nuclear facilities the government intends to develop, where they would be built and when construction could begin.
“It is currently completely unclear what is going to happen and when,” he said.
Steukers said the government should clarify whether it plans to build large-scale nuclear power plants or small modular reactors (SMRs), as well as specify locations, timelines and regulatory conditions.
Agoria estimates that a clear and predictable policy could generate an additional €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in turnover and create 500 new jobs in the sector within two years.

Sudan market drone strike kills at least 36 as Darfur crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

At least 36 people have been killed in a drone strike on a crowded market in Sudan’s Darfur region, a medical aid organization said Tuesday, as attacks on civilian areas intensify and the country’s humanitarian crisis deepens.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said Sudanese armed forces struck a market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, on Monday evening, causing what it described as “complete devastation.” A second drone strike hit a residential area.
The MSF-supported Nyala Teaching Hospital had received 36 bodies by Tuesday, including 21 people dressed in civilian clothing, the organization said. More than 150 injured people had also been treated in the hospital’s emergency department, many suffering from shrapnel wounds and severe burns. Children were among the wounded.
The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan’s military since April 2023, gave a substantially higher toll, saying 188 civilians had been killed and another 356 injured. The figures could not immediately be independently verified.
The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had not commented on the attack as of Tuesday.
MSF called on both sides to protect civilians and refrain from attacking markets, residential buildings and essential civilian infrastructure.
The strike is the latest in a series of deadly attacks on civilian gathering places. At least four people were killed and many others injured in a similar drone strike on another market in Nyala on Oct. 16. A separate attack on a market in the Abyei region, near the border with South Sudan, killed at least 80 people.
The United Nations has also reported drone strikes at several locations in the capital, Khartoum, in recent days, including an area near the airport. Other attacks have been reported in West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan.
Drones have become an increasingly prominent feature of Sudan’s civil war. According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, drone strikes killed at least 1,120 civilians during the first half of 2026. Both sides have been accused of carrying out attacks that have endangered civilian lives.
The conflict, which erupted in April 2023, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million, creating one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The latest violence comes as Sudan’s government seeks international accountability for atrocities in Darfur, where the RSF’s takeover of El Fasher has left civilians facing severe food shortages, displacement and widespread reports of abuses.
Sudan’s Ambassador to Türkiye, Nadir Yousif Eltayeb, said Tuesday that the international community had failed to take an impartial approach to the conflict and had not done enough to address the suffering of civilians.
Speaking at a meeting on Sudan at the Foundation for Political, Economic and Social Research (SETA) in Ankara, Eltayeb said El Fasher had endured a complete siege for about 30 months, leaving residents dependent on limited aid deliveries.
“About 1 million people were surviving on aid delivered by the armed forces by air. People could not access enough food, to the point that they had to eat tree bark,” he said.
Eltayeb said Sudanese government forces had made more than 200 attempts to break the siege but had failed to restore access to the city.
“The international community has taken a biased approach to this issue, preventing it from being resolved,” he said.
The RSF captured El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, on Oct. 26, 2025, after about 18 months of fighting and a siege that began in May 2024. The city had been the last major urban center in Darfur under the Sudanese army’s control.
Eltayeb accused foreign countries of supporting the RSF, arguing that the paramilitary group would not have been able to advance without outside assistance. He also alleged that armed groups had deliberately targeted particular tribes in El Fasher.
“What happened in El Fasher is genocide,” he said.
He added that the full death toll in El Fasher and the wider Darfur region remained unknown.
Eltayeb further alleged that pressure from the United Arab Emirates had prevented Sudan from submitting reports on the killings to the U.N. Security Council. He accused Abu Dhabi of supporting armed groups involved in the conflict but acknowledged that the allegations had not been proven.
The UAE has repeatedly denied accusations that it supports the RSF.
“We are seeking justice for Sudan,” Eltayeb said, thanking Türkiye for its support.
The fall of El Fasher marked a major shift in the conflict, but the fighting and its aftermath have left the city’s remaining population facing dire conditions.
The U.N. Human Rights Office said more than 6,000 people were killed during the first three days of attacks after the RSF seized the city. Subsequent reports described killings, forced displacement, torture and sexual violence against civilians.
The U.N. has warned that abuses against civilians, including women and children, have continued, citing reports of executions and sexual violence.
The takeover also triggered a mass exodus. About 138,200 people were displaced from El Fasher and surrounding settlements between Oct. 26, 2025, and March 1, 2026, according to figures provided in the humanitarian assessment.
Before the war, El Fasher had a population of more than 1 million. Its population is now estimated to have fallen below 70,000.
Those who remain face continuing insecurity and severely restricted access to food, medical care and other essential services. The departure of tens of thousands of residents has further strained already limited humanitarian operations across Darfur.

Atlas drops seven hundred paratroopers into Germany
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:25 GMT
18:00:25 KST

Around seven hundred paratroopers have been dropped onto a German drop zone from four Atlas C1 transports across multiple waves, bringing back battlegroup-level airborne insertion using the aircraft for the first time, according to the Royal Air Force.
Exercise Rhino Titan brought together the RAF Air Mobility Force and 16 Air Assault Brigade Combat Team as a Joint Airborne Task Force, with British, French and German troops taking part. Airborne operations have long been part of British military capability, and the difference here lies in the scale and in soldiers travelling with their stores in the same aircraft.
Squadron Leader Luke, a flight commander on 30 Squadron and the airborne mission commander, said: “Rhino Titan demonstrates the return of large-scale airborne insertion as a capability. The Atlas allows us to deploy combat forces further, faster and more efficiently than previous generations of aircraft, giving Defence the ability to project force rapidly wherever it is required.”
Stores previously needed aircraft of their own, so carrying personnel and equipment together generates more combat power from the same number of airframes, and lets troops become operational almost immediately on landing. Paratroopers board carrying parachute equipment, weapons, communications systems and bergen loads of up to fifty kilograms, with air loadmasters and parachute jump instructors supervising the process before departure.
Squadron Leader Nick, officer commanding the Parachute Training Squadron at RAF Brize Norton, said: “By the time soldiers board the aircraft, a significant amount of planning and preparation has already taken place. Parachute Jump Instructors will have delivered specialist ground training, while detailed planning between aircrew, dispatchers and ground forces coordinates every aspect of the mission.”
He added: “It takes RAF aircrew, engineers, Air Loadmasters, Parachute Jump Instructors and support personnel working alongside the Army to deliver that capability safely and effectively.”
Getting to this point took eighteen months of increased activity between Brize Norton, Weston-on-the-Green and Salisbury Plain, progressing from basic parachuting serials through formation flying and simulated mass drops to integrated delivery of personnel and stores. Aircraft, crews and instructors had to be dedicated to that training while global operational commitments continued.
Squadron Leader Luke said: “The harder we train in exercises, the easier it is to deliver the capability when it’s needed.”
Pathfinders went in ahead of the main force to validate the drop zone and provide reconnaissance and surveillance before the larger force arrived. The RAF said the exercise builds on work done with NATO allies through activities such as Exercise Falcon Leap, where Atlas operators and other tactical airlift nations develop common tactics and procedures, and that dropping troops by parachute lets forces deploy beyond established infrastructure.
The A400M Atlas entered RAF service in 2014 and operates from Brize Norton with 24, 30, 70 and 206 Squadrons. The type will also be fitted for firefighting under the package the government announced last week, which is to give Britain an aerial firefighting capability permanently based in the United Kingdom for the first time.

US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

US and China share a love of “new things and innovation” says Ma Yansong
Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.
Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.
“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.
The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.
“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.
Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.
“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”
His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.
At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.
Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.
The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.
Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.
The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.
Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.
He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.
The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.
“You create a dream. That’s important.”
The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.
Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.
“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.
“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”
Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.
“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”
“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”
For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.
“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”
“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”
At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.
The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.
“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”
“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”
“I like the future, but not the cold future”
The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.
Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.
And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.
“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”
Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.
“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.

Two high-speed trains collide in Spain, at least 10 dead
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:58:10 CET
17:58:10 KST

By David Latona, Guillermo Martinez and Michael Francis Gore
URDA, Spain, Oct 28 (Reuters) - At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain’s second fatal rail crash this year and Europe’s deadliest since 2013.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a televised address from near the accident site south of Madrid that “all of Spain” was in mourning, while the opposition People’s Party said it had cancelled all campaign events for the day ahead of an election next month.
Sanchez said the “terrible tragedy” would be investigated and vowed to address any failures that came to light, adding that the causes of the two crashes appeared to be unrelated.
“If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sanchez said.
RED SIGNAL
Spain’s transport minister said the crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue its journey despite an active red signal due to a stationary train ahead.
Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, and an erroneous decision had been made to restart the Renfe train.
At the scene, ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters had parked next to one of the trains on an elevated track section, while twisted metal and wreckage were strewn across an embankment down which at least three carriages had plunged.
The head of Castilla-La Mancha’s regional government said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescue workers were still going carriage by carriage looking for other crash victims.
Passengers, some splattered with blood or bandaged, were evacuated along a nearby road in the aftermath of the accident, which Spain’s health minister Monica Garcia said on social media had injured 80 people, 15 of them very seriously.
Salvador Arriza described the chaos in his carriage.
“I was very close to the door, but (other passengers) were breaking the windows to be able to get out. Some people practically couldn’t move because they were trapped amongst the seats,” said the 62-year-old.
INVESTIGATION UNDER WAY
The accident, the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela in which 80 people died, follows another in January between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people.
In that crash, a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, prompting a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance.
Renfe said in a statement on Wednesday that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know”.
“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
Iryo and Adif did not respond to requests for comment.
PASSENGERS SENT FLYING
A Castilla-La Mancha regional spokesperson said 147 people were on board the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe service, which crashed at around 9 a.m., causing two Iryo carriages to derail.
Passenger Rafael Barcelo said he felt lucky as he had stepped away from his seat for a coffee, adding there had been at least eight victims from his carriage.
“We were having breakfast, drinking a coffee when we felt a very strong impact and we were sent flying,” he said.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols.
At a school in Urda where relatives of those missing were being sent, a woman who gave her name as Ana fought back tears as she said there was no news of her husband Pepe and his name was not on the list of those identified, but police had found their dog, Trece.
MAINTENANCE SPENDING
The causes of the January accident are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period last year, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain’s competition authority.
Meanwhile, accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year, according to Spain’s railway safety authority.
European Commission data shows Spain’s maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000 km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged other large European countries.
Although Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any other country, most of this was to build new infrastructure with only around 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.
(Reporting by David Latona, Emma Pinedo, Mireia Merino, Corina Pons, Victoria Waldersee, Benjamin Mejias, Joan Faus and Pietro Lombardi; Writing by Charlie Devereux and Alexander Smith; Editing by Toby Chopra and Alison Williams)
