The banker, the basketball star, the cardiologist and the chemist: meet Serbia’s potential new leaders
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:57:40 CET
17:57:40 KST

BELGRADE, Oct 28 (Reuters) - After a leaderless student-led protest movement swept Serbia’s former President Aleksandar Vucic from power in a historic snap election on Sunday, the country is waiting to hear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key ministerial positions as it forms a government.
Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students’ list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade’s Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution’s independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic’s government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, pointing to Serbia’s standing and declining scores on international transparency metrics, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions.
Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policy amendments of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement’s lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement’s “Guardians of the Constitution” bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system “at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients”. In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building “a better Serbia, nothing else is important”.
He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Tuesday wrote on X that he had held a “good” telephone conversation with Srdanovic, saying that the priority is to establish a new government without delay.
Some of Srdanovic’s policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of those of the previous government. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. During the campaign he also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national “existential survival”.
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement’s most prominent public speakers.
He described Sunday’s election as a fight “for the return of a country that has been hijacked”.
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan “We have our God, his name is Bodiroga.”
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students’ election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a “citizens’ victory”.
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic’s resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was “occupied from within” and said he was ready to put “even his life” at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a “temporarily occupied territory” and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic’s recent resignation from the post.
(Writing by Aleksandar Vasovic, editing by Kirsten Donovan and Edward McAllister)

Ebola disease: Providing mental health support to patients and their loved ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:57:30 UTC
17:57:30 KST

In Butembo, in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Kasoki Zawadi spends her days with her husband, who is being treated for Ebola disease. A plexiglass window separates them, but they can talk to each other. In Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) treatment centres, psychological support is available to both patients and their loved ones.
In the corridor of Kitatumba's Ebola treatment centre in Butembo, North Kivu province, Kasoki Zawadi sits on a plastic chair facing the window that separates her from her husband, Victoire. He has been in hospital for 13 days. On the other side of the plastic screen, he smiles from time to time.
The hospital where Victoire is being treated is one of the facilities where MSF supports treatment for patients with Ebola disease. In Butembo, 1,472 cases were confirmed and 735 deaths recorded between May and 22 October 2026.
The outbreak is hitting people already facing insecurity and economic hardship. Many families are sheltering relatives displaced by fighting in neighbouring areas, while movement restrictions and reduced trade have made daily life even harder.
At the treatment centre, teams provide support not only to patients but also their loved ones, as they cope with fear, uncertainty, and the wait for test results. From the moment of admission, psychologists are there to listen to concerns, explain the care being provided, and help families manage the mental strain of hospitalisation.
Every morning, Kasoki arrives at around 6.30 am and stays until 6.30 pm. Her brother-in-law takes over at night.
“We manage to communicate despite the window,” she says. “We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.”
We manage to communicate despite the window. We’re allowed to see each other, and this brings us comfort.
Kasoki Zawadi, whose husband is receiving treatment for Ebola disease
Since her husband was admitted, she has stopped working as a teacher. Their family is supporting them during this time. She also worries about her own health. And when she leaves the centre, the separation weighs heavily on her.
“In the evening, when I go home and can’t see my husband, I find it hard to sleep,” says Kasoki.
A few days later, Kasoki explains that a negative test result had given them hope that they would soon be able to go home. But a second test came back positive.
“When he tested positive again, we were exhausted, mentally and physically,” she says. “Fortunately, the psychologists’ support helped us feel calmer, and we managed to wait.”
Staying in touch during hospitalisation
The disease and hospitalisation can be distressing for both patients and their loved ones. In Butembo, Patrice Muyisa Kokotz, mental health activity supervisor, provides psychological support. He describes people who arrive not only fearing the disease, but also worried about what awaits them at the centre. Some fear that isolation means they will be abandoned.
“We give them time to express themselves, talk about their past and their emotions,” explains Patrice. His team introduces people to how the centre works, explains the care provided, and organises visits. He says seeing other patients and their caregivers helps reassure families.
Some suggest that psychological support can have an impact on patient outcomes.
“Ebola disease is traumatic and sudden; it is a viral illness. So you are under stress, always expecting death at any moment,” says Rachel Kashimoto, a clinical psychologist working with MSF in Beni, also in North Kivu. 
“If you are not mentally stable and not well cared for, even physically, things may not go well,” says Rachel. “But if you are mentally stable, well supported, and well monitored, there will also be physical improvement. Because when you have hope of recovering, you follow all the instructions the medical staff give you, and then there can be rapid improvement.”
Supporting the return home
Psychological support does not end when patients leave the centre. In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, it continues through the survivors’ clinic.
“We organise individual consultations as well as group discussions,” explains Phoebe Zueya Yonkeu, who manages mental health activities at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Mongbwalu. 
“Many tell us they faced stigma when they returned home, lost their jobs or were rejected by their communities, who believed they were still contagious,” says Phoebe. “Others feel guilty towards loved ones who did not survive the disease, and they even wonder whether they were the ones who infected them.”
While some patients face stigma and the trauma of having come close to death after leaving the treatment centre, returning home can also bring immense relief to them and their loved ones.
In Butembo, on the twenty-third day of Victoire’s hospitalisation, the couple learns that he is due to leave that same day. The positive result, following the first negative result, prolonged their wait: now that he has finally tested negative twice.
Kasoki and Victoire say they are very happy to finally be going home.
“Kasoki’s presence really is part of my care,” says Victoire. “I feel comforted. When I see her, it reduces my stress.”

Turkish defense giant ASELSAN adds $7.5 billion in orders in one quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:56:16 UTC
17:56:16 KST

- ASELSAN’s order backlog reached a record $30.7 billion after the third quarter of 2026, rising $7.5 billion from the previous quarter.
- Nine-month revenue rose 28% in real terms to 151.5 billion lira, while new export contracts grew 34% to $1.9 billion.
ASELSAN, Türkiye’s largest defense electronics company, ended the third quarter of 2026 with a record order backlog of $30.7 billion, after adding $7.5 billion in a single quarter and passing the $30 billion mark for the first time in its history.
The Ankara-based company reported its results for the first nine months of the year on Oct. 27 in a disclosure to Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform. Revenue reached 151.5 billion Turkish lira, up 28% in real terms from the same period of 2025, and new export contracts rose 34% to $1.9 billion. ASELSAN reports in inflation-adjusted lira, a requirement for Turkish listed companies, so the growth figures are measured after accounting for the country’s high inflation.
The backlog figure is the headline number because it shows how much work the company already has under contract and has yet to deliver. ASELSAN said its book-to-bill ratio, which compares the value of new orders signed to the revenue recorded in the same period, rose to 4.4, meaning it booked more than four times as much new business as it billed. The company reached the $30 billion level ahead of its own forecast: in August, when it reported a first-half backlog of $23.2 billion, chief executive Ahmet Akyol said ASELSAN expected to see levels of $30 billion from next year onward. At the end of the first quarter, the backlog stood at $20.7 billion, when the company also posted its strongest quarterly export performance in years.
“2026 is not just a year in which ASELSAN has grown, it is the year we redefined the very scale of our growth,” said ASELSAN CEO Ahmet Akyol.
Air defense, radar and electronic warfare systems led revenue in the period, alongside underwater systems, AI-powered urban security systems, guided munitions, electro-optics and communications equipment. ASELSAN’s recent product launches span much of that portfolio, from a trailer-mounted version of its 35 mm counter-drone turret to the KILIÇ underwater strike system and TUFAN unmanned surface vessel unveiled at SAHA 2026 in Istanbul in May.
Profitability rose with sales. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, a common measure of operating profit, climbed 38% to 40.6 billion lira, and the margin improved by 1.9 percentage points to 26.8%. Akyol attributed the gain to the use of artificial intelligence in company processes, digital transformation and a growing share of higher-value products, and said revenue per employee rose 4% in dollar terms.
ASELSAN is spending heavily to turn that backlog into deliveries. Capital investment at its new Oğulbey Technology Base and existing campuses rose 228% to $684 million in nine months, which Akyol said is nearly twice the company’s total capital spending for all of 2025. The first phase of Oğulbey, whose foundation was laid in 2025 and which the company describes as the largest single defense industry investment in the history of the Turkish Republic, came into operation during the period, along with a new Guided Ammunition Systems Production Center and expanded robotics and automation for air, naval and land systems production.
Research and development spending increased 36% to $1.3 billion. ASELSAN said it is directing that money toward low Earth orbit satellites, quantum computing, underwater technologies, high-power microwave systems, microelectronics, and smart munitions and propulsion. The satellite effort, called ASTRALINK, was presented for the first time at the International Space Congress in Antalya.
“ASELSAN which has provided Turkish Armed Forces’ communications on land, at sea and in the air since its founding, will now also provide satellite communication services,” said Akyol.
Operating cash flow reached 23 billion lira, financial liabilities stood at 14% of total assets, and financing expenses fell 10.3% from a year earlier. ASELSAN’s equity ratio was 55%, its return on equity rose 4 percentage points to 16.6%, and its return on assets reached 9%.
ASELSAN has also climbed in international rankings this year. In August it rose three places to 40th in Defense News’ Top 100 list of defense companies and became the first Turkish defense firm included in the Forbes Global 2000.
“Our primary responsibility moving forward is to convert this portfolio into timely deliveries, expanded production capacity, and sustained technological superiority,” said Akyol.

Syria reopens Jordan border crossing after mending ties

Syria reopens Jordan border crossing after mending ties
- Syria reopened the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 after both sides tried to calm tensions caused by a deadly Jordanian strike.
- Jordan said its raid targeted “Daesh sites” after a church attack killed nine people in Karak, while Syria called the strike an “unacceptable violation” of sovereignty.
- Civilian deaths in southern Syria deepened anger, and a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet soon to discuss action against IS.
AI generated
Damascus – Syria reopened its main border crossing with Jordan on Oct 28 as the two countries reaffirmed ties that were strained by a deadly retaliatory strike by Jordanian forces.
Jordan’s strike – a reprisal against a gun attack on a church – sparked the worst crisis between the two countries since the ousting of long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Syria condemned the strikes on the country’s south as an “unacceptable violation”, while Jordan said it killed more than 20 jihadist fighters in its raid.
Jordan sought to ease tensions on Oct 27, saying it had “great respect” for its neighbour and expressed regret for civilian casualties.
The main Nassib border crossing, known as Jaber on the Jordanian side, was closed following the strikes, but passenger and commercial movement will return to normal as of the morning of Oct 28, senior Syrian customs official Mazen Alloush told state news agency SANA.
Last week, gunmen opened fire during a funeral service at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan’s Karak governorate, killing nine people and wounding 25 – prompting a military response from Amman.
While Jordan insisted it coordinated its airstrikes with Syria, Damascus denied the claim, and Syria’s civil defence agency said the raids killed seven people, including three children.
On Oct 27, Jordan’s Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi spoke to his Syrian counterpart and emphasised Jordan’s “full respect for Syria’s sovereignty... and security”, while also expressing “sorrow and grief over the death of innocent civilian victims”, according to a joint statement.
The two officials also discussed the raids against what the statement branded as “Daesh sites”, using an acronym to refer to the Islamic State (IS) group.
Earlier, Jordan’s government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani had said that “the preliminary results... indicate significant losses among Daesh’s ranks – estimated at more than 20 fighters”.
He also said “a large weapons depot belonging to the organisation” had been destroyed.
‘Blatant violation’
Earlier, Syria’s foreign ministry issued a “condemnation and rejection” of the strikes, calling them “an unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination”.
It also said the raid was “a blatant violation of the principles of good-neighbourliness and Syrian national sovereignty”.
In the coming days, a joint Syrian-Jordanian security committee will meet to discuss the operations against IS, a government source told Syrian state news agency SANA.
Syria said five people, including a woman and three children, were killed in the village of Al-Taf in Daraa province, which borders Jordan, with two other people killed elsewhere in the south.
“We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children – two boys and a girl – were killed,” said Nassouh al-Salim in Al-Taf, staring at a grey body bag.
An AFP reporter saw a huge crater in the family’s destroyed home, with school books, clothes and the remains of furniture strewn among the rubble.
Syrian Emergencies and Disaster Management Minister Raed al-Saleh said on Oct 27 that both sides were handling the dispute through “diplomatic and legal channels” with the aim of securing justice for the victims.
‘Dark ideologies’
On Oct 26, Amman said the authorities had arrested three Jordanians accused of the church killings, two of them brothers and the other related by marriage.
The authorities said the suspects were hospitalised after being wounded in a shootout with security forces.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three percent of the population.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” King Abdullah II said.
IS was territorially defeated in Syria in 2019, after it seized swathes of territory during the country’s more than 13-year civil war.
But remnants are still present, and the group occasionally claims attacks, mainly targeting Syrian security forces.
The group has previously been present in parts of Daraa province. AFP

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:50:55 UTC
17:50:55 KST

Canada signs trade deal with UAE in push for non-US markets
The agreement aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Canada and the United Arab Emirates have signed a comprehensive trade deal to lower barriers between the economies and boost investment, the governments have said.
The deal comes as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to expand trade and investment ties amid tension with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) on Tuesday, which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has pledged to double Ottawa’s non-US trade over the next decade as US President Donald Trump’s tariffs have rippled through Canada’s economy.
Subsequent attempts to reach a deal with Washington have broken down, which has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
“Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99 percent of current Canadian exports to the UAE,” the Prime Minister’s Office said in a statement.
“That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators.”
“The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors,” it said, adding that CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
Multiple deals
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
“We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing – all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” the UAE’s Foreign Trade Minister Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart, Maninder Sidhu.
The UAE is the largest Middle East market for Canadian exports and a major buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery.
Two-way trade between the countries was worth 3.5 billion Canadian dollars ($2.48bn) last year. It has been growing at 10 percent annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE also committed up to $50bn in investment in Canada last year.

Dadgar elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation
TEHRAN – Ali Dadgar has been elected president of Iran’s Shooting Federation after securing a majority of votes in the federation’s electoral assembly.
The election was held under the chairmanship of Mohammadshervin Asbaghian, Deputy Minister of Sports and Youth for Championship and Professional Sports Development.
Dadgar was elected as the federation’s new president after receiving 26 votes from the 51 members of the assembly.
Six candidates had initially been approved to contest the election: Ebrahim Barkhordari, Ali Dadgar, Hossein Zakizadeh, Salar Mohammadnia, Abbas Mohammadipour, and Masoud Nosrati Qazvininejad.
However, Barkhordari, Mohammadnia, and Nosrati Qazvininejad withdrew their candidacies before the voting began, leaving Dadgar, Zakizadeh, and Mohammadipour to compete for the presidency.
In the first round of voting, Dadgar received 25 votes, followed by Zakizadeh with 19 and Mohammadipour with five. One ballot was declared invalid.
As no candidate secured an absolute majority in the first round, the election proceeded to a runoff between Dadgar and Zakizadeh.
In the second round, Dadgar narrowly defeated Zakizadeh by 26 votes to 25, securing the presidency of Iran’s Shooting Federation for the next four years.
Dadgar has previously served as president of the federation.

Collingwood has announced a review of its struggling AFLW program, saying it remains committed to ensuring the club is ready for success.

What's next?
Collingwood will finish its season against Essendon on Sunday.
Collingwood has pledged to thoroughly review the wreckage of its AFLW program, admitting "we haven't got it right".
The day after announcing that women's coach, Sam Wright, is about to leave, the Magpies said they would bring in a consultant to help with the strategic review.
Collingwood is a perennial AFLW under-achiever, winning only one game so far this season to be second-last.
Including the last two seasons, their record is five wins and 29 losses.
With Wright about to leave and captain Ruby Schleicher about to return home to WA, there are also reports of a mass player exodus once the season ends.
"Our AFLW program is an integral part of Collingwood, and we are committed to ensuring it is positioned for sustained success," president Barry Carp said in a club statement.
"The board, together with the executive team, acknowledges that we haven't got it right — we take responsibility for that and are committed to getting better, both on and off the field.
"Engaging an expert outside Collingwood is important for us to provide a broader perspective, challenge our existing approaches and identify what needs to improve or change."
He added the expert would work with their AFLW sub-committee to ensure the women are set up for long-term success.
"We have a responsibility to our players, coaches, staff, members, supporters and the wider game to listen to feedback and be prepared to make meaningful, considered changes across the club to build a stronger AFLW program for everyone at Collingwood," Carp said.
Wright will coach Collingwood for the last time on Sunday against Essendon at Windy Hill. It will also be Bombers coach Natalie Wood's last game.
St Kilda are also looking for a new AFLW coach after Nick Dal Santo's departure, and expansion team Tasmania are the fourth team in the market.

A “very severe” cyclone slammed into India’s east coast on Wednesday, killing at least five people as winds of up to 150 kph uprooted trees and knocked out power. More than 180,000 people were evacuated before the storm hit.
Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast of Andhra Pradesh state near Yanam between 2 and 8 AM, with sustained winds of 125-135 kph. It weakened to a “severe” cyclone after moving inland, the India Meteorological Department said.
Satellite images show Arnab’s broad cloud bands stretching across large parts of eastern and southern India. Although its winds weakened after landfall, the authorities warned that heavy rainfall could continue through Thursday, raising the risk of further flooding.
The six-hour landfall battered coastal districts, including Kakinada, Konaseema, and West Godavari. Strong winds brought down trees and electricity poles, blocked roads, and disrupted power supplies. studio loutsis integrates timber wayfinding into snøhetta’s theodore roosevelt library
studio loutsis designs an environmentally compliant wayfinding and signage system for the theodore roosevelt presidential library, integrating custom typography, heavy timber pylons, and flush-mounted interior details across the badlands campus.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
WAYFINDING system FOR Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
Located in Medora, North Dakota, the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library is embedded directly within the terrain of the Badlands. Designed by Snøhetta with architect of record JLG Architects, the library campus connects three institutions across expansive indoor and outdoor environments. Studio Loutsis was commissioned to develop the comprehensive signage, wayfinding, and donor recognition system spanning the site, treating graphic wayfinding as an architectural and landscape-driven extension of the campus.
graphic maps, architecture, and landscape into a unified system
To unify varied scales, from monumental exterior markers to pedestrian trail placards, Studio Loutsis collaborated with Commercial Type to engineer a bespoke typeface, paired with a custom iconography system. Exterior wayfinding incorporates heavy timber pylons, directional panels, campus maps, and dark metal dimensional lettering engineered to withstand North Dakota’s extreme climate while weathering alongside the building envelope.
Fabricated under stringent Living Building Challenge sustainability parameters, all materials, non-toxic coatings, and mechanical assemblies adhere to strict ecological standards. Indoors, signage mounts directly to vertically articulated timber partitions using custom-milled infill blocks, while the central lobby’s ‘Wall of Gratitude’ integrates flush donor wood panels into the primary architectural cladding.

India invites Pakistan to SCO dialogue in Delhi for first time since four-day war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:44:06 UTC
17:44:06 KST

India has invited all 10 member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), including Pakistan, to participate in its inaugural Civilisational Dialogue Forum, scheduled to be held in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, Indian media reported on Wednesday.
The invitation marks the first time since the four-day war between India and Pakistan last year that India has invited a senior Pakistani minister to the country.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh announced the initiative at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20, confirming that all member states had been invited to participate.
“At the end of this year, India will host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum. We invite all SCO countries to participate in it,” Singh had said.
Pakistan Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar was present at the meeting.
Pakistan’s Minister for National Heritage and Culture Aurangzeb Khan Khichi has been invited to the forum, according to diplomatic sources cited by India Today. The forum aims to strengthen cultural ties and foster mutual understanding among SCO member states.
The invitation comes against the backdrop of strained relations between India and Pakistan following their four-day war, launched by India in May 2025 in what it described as a response to an attack in India-administered Kashmir’s Pahalgam, for which India blamed Pakistan. Pakistan firmly denied the accusations, for which India has provided no evidence.
If Khichi attends the event, it would mark the first visit by a senior Pakistani minister to India since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari participated in the SCO Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Goa in May 2023.
The proposed forum is aimed at deepening cultural engagement and promoting greater mutual understanding among the countries in the grouping.
Pakistan has yet to issue any official statement regarding its possible attendance.
Pakistan assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term on September 1. It took over the position from Kyrgyzstan following the SCO summit held in Bishkek.
The SCO has 10 member states: Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India became a full member of the organisation in 2017.

Two high-speed trains rear-end in Spain, rail operator says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:43:13 UTC
17:43:13 KST

At least 68 people dead in Spain’s second major train crash this year
MADRID – At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Oct 28, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain’s second fatal rail crash this year and Europe’s deadliest since 2013.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a televised address from near the accident site south of Madrid that “all of Spain” was in mourning, while the opposition People’s Party said it had cancelled all campaign events for the day ahead of an election in November.
Sanchez said the “terrible tragedy” would be investigated and vowed to address any failures that came to light, adding that the causes of the two crashes appeared to be unrelated.
“If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because what is unacceptable for a country like Spain is to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” Sanchez said.
Red signal
Spain’s transport minister said the crash happened after a Renfe train was authorised to continue its journey despite an active red signal due to a stationary train ahead.
Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, and an erroneous decision had been made to restart the Renfe train.
At the scene, ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters had parked next to one of the trains on an elevated track section, while twisted metal and wreckage were strewn across an embankment down which at least three carriages had plunged.
The head of Castilla-La Mancha’s regional government said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescue workers were still going carriage by carriage looking for other crash victims.
Passengers, some splattered with blood or bandaged, were evacuated along a nearby road in the aftermath of the accident, which Spain’s health minister Monica Garcia said on social media had injured 80 people, 15 of them very seriously.
Salvador Arriza described the chaos in his carriage.
“I was very close to the door, but (other passengers) were breaking the windows to be able to get out. Some people practically couldn’t move because they were trapped amongst the seats,” said the 62-year-old.
Investigation under way
The accident, the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela in which 80 people died, follows another in January between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people.
In that crash, a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, prompting a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance.
Renfe said in a statement on Oct 28 that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know”.
“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
Iryo and Adif did not respond to requests for comment.
Passengers sent flying
A Castilla-La Mancha regional spokesperson said 147 people were on board the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe service, which crashed at around 9am, causing two Iryo carriages to derail.
Passenger Rafael Barcelo said he felt lucky as he had stepped away from his seat for a coffee, adding there had been at least eight victims from his carriage.
“We were having breakfast, drinking a coffee when we felt a very strong impact, and we were sent flying,” he said.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols.
At a school in Urda where relatives of those missing were being sent, a woman who gave her name as Ana fought back tears as she said there was no news of her husband, Pepe, and his name was not on the list of those identified, but police had found their dog, Trece.
Maintenance spending
The causes of the January accident are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period in 2025, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain’s competition authority.
Meanwhile, accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 in 2025, according to Spain’s railway safety authority.
European Commission data shows Spain’s maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000km of high-speed lines has lagged other large European countries.
Although Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any other country, most of this was to build new infrastructure with only around 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades. REUTERS

Damaged Cargo Ship Drifts Into Bulgaria’s Black Sea Zone as Regional Security Talks Begin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:42:30 UTC
17:42:30 KST

Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said Bulgaria would propose a joint security coordination mechanism with Romania and Turkey to respond more quickly to threats in the Black Sea, as the disabled cargo ship Khoryv drifted into Bulgaria’s maritime zone following a drone attack off the Romanian coast.
Speaking before a trilateral meeting in Sofia with his Turkish and Romanian counterparts, Stoyanov said the three countries needed a common approach to protecting navigation and responding to further incidents involving commercial vessels. He said Bulgaria had prepared political proposals and military measures for discussion, with the aim of agreeing on a joint position.
The meeting brings together Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov and Chief of Defense Admiral Emil Eftimov; Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea and Deputy Chief of Defense Lieutenant General Dragoș-Dumitru Iacob; and Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler and Chief of Defense General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu, along with their delegations.
Stoyanov thanked his counterparts for accepting his invitation and said the talks had been prompted by attacks on commercial vessels in exclusive economic zones, territorial waters and nearby areas.
He said the three countries should establish a coordination mechanism to make decisions faster when maritime security is threatened, adding that such cooperation would serve the interests of all three NATO members and help protect freedom of navigation.
“The risks are growing with each passing day, and we must respond adequately - the three nations together. We need to address every situation in a way that ensures freedom of navigation. We must not allow lines of communication to be severed. That is our goal,” Stoyanov said.
He expressed hope that the talks would lead to sustained cooperation rather than remain a one-time initiative, saying further meetings would be useful to develop a joint response mechanism.
Stoyanov said the discussions focused on political statements and military measures, not on a memorandum directed at Russia or another country. Responding to a question from BNT about plans to increase naval deployments in exclusive economic zones despite legal constraints, he said Bulgaria did not exercise sovereignty in its exclusive economic zone.
He declined to reveal the military proposals before they had been agreed upon by all three countries. Regarding the investigation into the attacks on commercial vessels, he said only the competent investigative authorities could disclose established findings.
The meeting coincided with the entry of the damaged cargo ship Khoryv into Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. The vessel was attacked by a kamikaze naval drone off Constanța on October 23 and is now partially submerged and drifting southward without a crew or navigation lights.
The incident was first reported at around 9 p.m. when the vessel was spotted 13 nautical miles east of Cape Sivri Burun, the northernmost point of Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. The Ministry of Transport and Communications issued a navigational warning, advising other vessels to keep a distance of at least five cables, or approximately 0.5 nautical miles, and exercise heightened caution.
Bulgarian authorities are tracking the ship in real time and are preparing further measures. A naval vessel may be sent to its location, while drones will also be used for surveillance. Bulgarian authorities had begun preparing for a possible intervention on Tuesday, when the ship was about five to six nautical miles from the boundary between the Bulgarian and Romanian exclusive economic zones.
Forecasts of stronger northerly and northeasterly winds in the coming days have added to concerns about the vessel’s movement.
The Khoryv, which sails under the flag of the Comoros, caught fire after the attack and sent a distress signal. There were 13 people on board, including 10 Ukrainian and three Azerbaijani citizens. Nine sailors were rescued, one was killed and three remain missing. Bulgarian sailors aboard the vessel Sartor took part in the rescue operation.
The cargo ship can carry ore, coal and petroleum products, raising concerns about possible marine pollution if fuel or cargo leaks into the sea. However, no environmental incident has been confirmed, and it remains unclear what the vessel was carrying when it was attacked.
The incident is part of a series of attacks on commercial vessels in the western Black Sea during October. Other ships affected include Alfa Watan, Able, Chelsea-3 and HS Dignity. The Alfa Watan and Able were struck inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on October 6, 2026, at around 3 a.m. Bulgarian authorities have not established the origin of the drones involved in those attacks.
The Bulgarian Navy has increased surveillance of maritime areas where commercial vessels were targeted, including with unmanned aerial vehicles, Nova TV and BGNES reported. NATO also announced last week that additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones would be deployed to the Black Sea following the attacks, which were linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine, Reuters reported. At least five cargo ships have been struck near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts over the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported dead or missing.
Stoyanov said the Council of Ministers was expected to decide on two memoranda. One concerns Bulgaria’s participation in an initiative to counter low-altitude threats, particularly drones, while the other covers the purchase of MICA anti-aircraft missiles for Bulgarian patrol vessels.
“At the Ministry of Defense, we continue working on the modernization of the Bulgarian Armed Forces and, consequently, on joining projects that are appropriate for addressing modern-day threats,” Stoyanov said.
The minister’s announcement comes after Prime Minister Rumen Radev told the National Assembly in mid-October that Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were working to improve coordination and interoperability in surveillance, situational awareness and rapid responses to incidents in the Black Sea. Radev said the three countries already had an operational communication channel through their Multinational Mine Countermeasures Group.
Earlier this month, Stoyanov held telephone conversations with his Romanian and Turkish counterparts, and he later said the priority was to develop a common strategy for action in the Black Sea region.
Former Deputy Foreign Minister Milen Keremedchiev and journalist Mohamed Khalaf, speaking on NOVA NEWS, argued that the trilateral meeting should result in concrete steps rather than political declarations.
Keremedchiev said the meeting was overdue because Romania and Turkey had already taken independent measures to address regional risks. He argued that Romania had a substantial advantage over Bulgaria in maritime and territorial defense capabilities and said Bulgaria was behind in developing a collective Black Sea security framework.
Keremedchiev also referred to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin about potentially establishing safe shipping corridors. On the investigation into the drones used in attacks on commercial vessels, he said the lack of an official conclusion did not necessarily mean it was taking too long. Citing an investigation in Germany that lasted 28 days, he noted that Bulgaria was on the 22nd day of its inquiry.
Khalaf took a more critical view, saying Russia was behind the attacks despite the lack of a publicly announced finding from the official investigation. He called for Bulgarian authorities to state clearly what action they intended to take.
Keremedchiev also called for the three NATO members to agree on a common position, arguing that concrete action required identifying the specific threat first.
The two commentators also discussed protests in several European countries. Khalaf said Russia was seeking to destabilize Europe through military action and influence over domestic political processes, while Keremedchiev noted that economic difficulties were also contributing to public discontent.

Netanyahu likely to win most seats in Israeli polls: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:39:00 UTC
17:39:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies appear on track to win the most seats in Israel's parliament after an election this week, though neither he nor his main competitor, Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a majority.
Votes are now being tallied, followed by potentially long negotiations as parties try to assemble a governing coalition. If those talks fail, Israel could head to another round of elections.
Israel's Central Election Committee was tallying votes on Wednesday, and it will likely take until Thursday before definitive results of the election are known.
The committee will also tally hundreds of thousands of ballots by Israeli soldiers, as well as diplomats, who voted from outside the country.
The committee's tallying followed exit polls from major Israeli TV channels. Those polls can help give a general sense of each party’s relative strength but are not considered a reliable barometer of precise results, particularly in Israel’s fragmented political system.
The final vote tally is expected by Oct. 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on Nov. 4.
Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25% of the national vote to secure seats.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers.
If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present Cabinet staying on as a caretaker government.

Flavio Bolsonaro on way to Ecuador from Argentina after fleeing Brazil
Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro was on his way to Ecuador after fleeing Brazil, Argentina's government said on Wednesday.
Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's runoff election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, entered Argentina on Tuesday night before boarding a flight to Ecuador, the country's National Directorate of Migration said on X.
The 45-year-old entered Argentina "with valid travel documents and no legal impediment," it added, despite a court order banning his exit.
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters boarded "a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador," the government agency said.
According to data from the Flightradar24 website, the flight took off just after midnight (0300 GMT) on Wednesday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country's northeast.
Baires Fly did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment.
US media citing anonymous sources had earlier reported that Bolsonaro had arrived in the United States on Tuesday.
The US State Department said it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family but did not confirm their travel plans.
Brazil's Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports.
He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.
A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled, but the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP.
'Shameful'
Reports of Bolsonaro's exit from Brazil came as a shock to his political camp.
"We still don't have any news about his whereabouts," Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho told reporters in Brasilia on Tuesday.
"I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it," he said. "That was the only communication we had."
Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Instagram a day earlier that he "never had any intention of leaving the country" and the ban on his exit was a scare tactic.
Lula, who won the election with 51.8 percent of the vote, called fleeing the country a "shameful" act.
"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration.
Following his loss, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting.
Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro over bad weather in parts of the country.
US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Flavio's father and Brazil's former leader Jair Bolsonaro, said that the elections were "rigged."
All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month.
He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival's inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later.

Most of Britan’s nuclear missile submarine fleet now at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:37:38 GMT
17:37:38 KST

Three of the Royal Navy’s four Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines are at sea at the same time, an arrangement naval sources described as unusual, according to reporting in The Times.
One of the boats is understood to be conducting the deterrent patrol, carrying Trident II D5 missiles, which is the task the Royal Navy has maintained without a break since 1969. The other two are believed to have been on sea trials and preparing to take over the patrol. HMS Victorious, the fourth boat, is at Devonport undergoing maintenance and was not among those at sea.
The Ministry of Defence declined to comment.
Having three boats out at once is not a sign of extra capacity, though, as the Vanguard class was designed around a four boat cycle in which one submarine is on patrol, one is working up or recovering, one is in training or trials, and one is in deep maintenance, and the fourth hull is what keeps continuous at sea deterrence going as the submarines age. Running three at sea at the same time means the cycle has been compressed, and it is as consistent with pressure on availability as it is with a deliberate signal.
The Times was told by a former senior naval source that the service had been operating in what submariners call 2BA, or two boat availability, for a prolonged period. In that condition only two of the four boats are available for operational tasking at any time, which leaves no margin, because a defect on the boat at sea has to be covered by a single relief.
The strain is visible in how long the boats are staying out, Navy Lookout reported in March 2025 that a Vanguard class submarine had returned to the Clyde after 204 days, breaking a record set in 2023, and patrols of more than two hundred days have since been reported again. Deterrent patrols were historically planned around three months. Crews now routinely spend five months or more submerged with no contact with their families.
Forces News reported last week, in an account of life aboard the boats, that Commander Roger Ireland, a retired submariner who served on the earlier Resolution class, described the length of modern Vanguard patrols as horrendous. Resolution boats carrying Polaris went out for around eight weeks at a time.
Maintenance has been the other great difficulty, and HMS Vanguard emerged from a refit at Devonport in 2023 that took around seven and a half years against a planned three and a half, after an unscheduled nuclear refuelling pushed the cost from roughly £200 million towards £500 million, as this publication reported when she sailed.
The four Vanguards entered service between 1993 and 1999 and were designed for around twenty five years each. All four are now beyond that, and they must hold the deterrent until the Dreadnought class arrives from the early 2030s. The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, covering Dreadnought, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the infrastructure behind them.

Villa Ginori, Versilia home of marquis Puccini dedicated La Bohème to, goes on market
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:34:42 CET
17:34:42 KST

Villa Ginori, a historic residence in the coastal Versilia area of Tuscany, in the province of Lucca, has gone onto the market with Lionard Luxury Real Estate (https://www.lionard.com/exclusive-historic-villa-on-lake-versil ia-hinterland.html). 
The home once belonged to Marquis Carlo Ginori Lisci, heir to the celebrated Ginori porcelain factory at Doccia and a close friend of Giacomo Puccini, who dedicated La Bohème to him. 
Overlooking Lake Massaciuccoli in Massarosa, the villa remains in the hands of descendants of the Ginori Lisci family. 
It preserves rooms once frequented by the composer, who lived across the lake in Torre del Lago, as well as Liberty-style decorations by Francesco Fanelli, a painter who studied under Giovanni Fattori. 
The estate owes its present appearance to Carlo Ginori Lisci. In 1887, the marquis acquired Lake Massaciuccoli and the surrounding land from the Minutoli family, transforming an existing building into a residence in the Tuscan neo-Gothic style. 
The villa's architectural character is defined by its direct relationship with the water. The lake extends beneath the building's great arches to a private covered boathouse, making it possible to reach the residence directly by boat. 
The same relationship continues inside, where the large windows of the loggia and winter garden open onto the lake. Irises, botanical motifs and Oriental-inspired lines by Fanelli, who was asked in 1900 by the marquis to decorate several rooms, echo the surrounding landscape across the walls. 
The estate comprises approximately 4,000 square metres of built space across eight buildings and 10 hectares of private land. 
Alongside the main villa, which measures about 1,200 square metres, stand an 800-square-metre 19th-century residence and a clubhouse created from a former boat shelter, as well as a chapel, a limonaia and other service buildings. 
The park, dotted with historic palm trees and exotic botanical species, is crossed by navigable canals. 
"The most authentic expression of Made in Italy is not only what we produce, but also what we have been able to build, preserve and pass on," said Dimitri Corti, Founder and CEO of Lionard Luxury Real Estate. 
"Villa Ginori represents a dimension of luxury that goes beyond the material value of a property. A building can be restored, transformed and adapted to new needs. What cannot be recreated is its history, its relationship with the people who lived there, and with the land to which it belongs. That is what makes certain places truly irreplaceable."

====================================================================================================

Chinese team reveals how brain neurons support flexible decision-making
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:56 CST
17:33:56 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese research team has revealed how brain neurons support flexible decision-making. According to a study recently published in Science, rule-related information and sensory information are compared within the same neuron, which itself takes part in cognitive computation.
Traditional theory holds that neurons are the basic structural and functional units of the nervous system. For a long time, most studies treated each neuron as a simple point-like unit that performs summation.
However, researches in brain science and artificial neural networks have found that higher cognitive functions such as flexible decision-making require the integration of massive contextual information and abstract rules, as well as dynamic adjustment of output. Such complexity is difficult to explain with the simple structure of point-like neurons.
Xu Ninglong, a researcher at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and his team designed a series of experiments in which mice heard different sounds and had to infer hidden rules. Once the mice had learned the current rules, the team changed the rules to see how quickly the mice adapted to the new logic. The team used two-photon microscopy to observe neurons in the mice's auditory cortex.
A neuron is like a tree with many branches. The cell body is the main part of the neuron, while dendrites are branch-like extensions. The distant branches are called apical dendrites.
The experiments found a clear division of labor within the same neuron. Apical dendrites mainly encode the abstract rule inferred by the mouse, while the cell body more strongly represents external auditory sensory input. The two types of signals undergo nonlinear integration within the neuron, producing a decision output that drives behavioral choice.
The experiments demonstrated that a single neuron is itself a microcomputer and that the interactions between a neuron's dendrites and cell body can perform decision-related cognitive computation. Only after a hypothesis has been verified multiple times and confirmed to be reliable does the brain slowly strengthen neuronal synapses and store the rule permanently.
The team found that although AI can also use context and existing information to adjust its answers, its mechanisms differ greatly from those of the brain. Large models mainly develop capabilities through training on data, whereas the brain combines experiential learning, internal states, and real-time information processing. Even a single neuron has a rich internal computational structure.
The team also found that the brain can support flexible behavior while using limited energy. Its biological mechanisms are worth studying for insights that could help make AI systems more flexible and more efficient. ■

Seven Chinese golfers set for Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:42 CST
17:33:42 KST

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Seven Chinese golfers, including four debutants, will compete at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship (AAC), which begins Thursday at Te Arai Links in New Zealand.
The 17th edition of the championship runs from October 29 to November 1 on Te Arai Links' South Course, with 120 players from 39 countries and regions competing in the 72-hole stroke-play event.
The winner will earn invitations to the 2027 Masters Tournament, the 155th Open Championship and the 131st Amateur Championship.
China's seven-player contingent comprises Zhou Ziqin, Wu Qiyou, Li Zhi, Hou Zenghao, Wang Yixiang, Liu Yiming and Cui Jingguo. Li, Wang, Liu and Cui will make their tournament debuts, while Zhou will be competing for the fifth time.
Zhou, 20, is ranked No. 55 in the World Amateur Golf Ranking and finished runner-up in 2024, one stroke behind compatriot Ding Wenyi.
"That was really close, just one shot back. But honestly, that was two years ago, and I believe my game has improved this season," Zhou said Wednesday.
"I wasn't playing my best for a period, but I played really well last season, and my game is starting to come back now."
Zhou said he was confident in his preparations but expected putting to play a decisive role on the links-style course.
"I think I did a good job preparing for this week, and I'm really ready. We have beautiful courses, and I feel like it's going to be a putting contest this week," he said.
Li, making his championship debut, said he was eager to test himself against the region's leading amateur golfers.
"I'm very happy to have the opportunity to play in the Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship. Receiving the invitation is a recognition of my ability at this stage," Li said. "I believe I'll learn a lot and benefit from the experience."
Li added that the fairways, undulating greens and coastal winds would present a stern challenge.
"The fairways and greens are very firm, and the greens have considerable slopes. Combined with the wind, these factors will make the course challenging," he said.
Thailand's Fifa Laopakdee returns to defend his title in a tournament that has helped launch the careers of several leading golfers from the region.
Chinese players have won the championship five times, with Guan Tianlang claiming the title in 2012, Jin Cheng in 2015, Lin Yuxin in 2017 and 2019, and Ding Wenyi in 2024.
The championship was established by the Asia-Pacific Golf Confederation, The R&A and the Masters Tournament. ■

California governor signs orders to prepare for El Nino storms
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:31 CST
17:33:31 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed two executive orders, easing environmental requirements for flood-prevention work and requiring a risk review of Highway 1 ahead of potential El Nino storms.
The orders were signed at Crystal Cove State Park in Newport Beach, Southern California, following a statewide emergency declaration issued on Sept. 21, according to the governor's office.
One order allows the suspension of state requirements for eligible public-agency work to limit flooding, landslides, debris flows and erosion, while requiring advance eligibility approval and safeguards for fish, protected species and waterways.
The second order establishes a Highway 1 Task Force, convened by state transportation and natural resources agencies, to prepare the corridor for El Nino storms and address longer-term climate threats.
Highway 1 runs about 1,056 km along California's Pacific coast and has suffered repeated landslides and closures in the Big Sur area in recent years.
On Tuesday, the U.S. National Weather Service warned of significant coastal flooding in Orange and San Diego counties in Southern California until Thursday.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center said on Oct. 8 that there was a more than 83-percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Nino through January to March 2027. ■

Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:33:27 CST
17:33:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Most childhood physical abuse in Australia occurs within families and before children turn 10, according to an Australian study.
The study analyzed Australian Child Maltreatment Study data from 8,503 Australians aged 16 and older, focusing on 2,623 individuals who reported experiencing physical abuse during childhood, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Curtin University.
One in four Australians aged 16 to 24 reported experiencing physical abuse by a family member. Family members were responsible for 85 percent of reported perpetration, while 4 percent occurred in institutional settings and 5 percent involved both family and institutional settings, the study found.
Among children abused before age 10, both parents were identified as perpetrators in one in three cases. Abuse involving both parents was also associated with the earliest onset and longest duration, according to the findings published in the journal Child Maltreatment.
Childhood physical abuse remains a major public health concern globally and is associated with substantial adverse mental, physical and social outcomes across the lifespan, said the researchers, noting that prevention efforts must extend beyond institutions and place greater emphasis on the home. ■

AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.
The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.
“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”
Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.
The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.
“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”
Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.
As climate disasters become more frequent and widespread, there have been numerous examples of flawed human communication scrambling an emergency response. In 2016, for instance, adjacent counties in California issued a “voluntary evacuation” and a “mandatory evacuation” for the same wildfire. In Australia in 2019, officials warned about wildfires by using the phrase “Watch and Act,” which the government later said caused “significant confusion” because no one knew what it meant.
In some cases, inadequate communication can mean the difference between life and death. This happened in Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire. A few weeks after the fire, a heavy rainstorm produced a deadly mudslide. The government of Santa Barbara County struggled to communicate the risk to residents still traumatized from the blaze and experiencing a phenomenon that Sutton calls “warning fatigue.” The county sent alerts to everyone in the “voluntary evacuation zone” for wildfires, telling residents to “stay alert to changing conditions and be prepared to leave immediately.” Most of those residents should have left immediately, but to many the evacuation notice was optional; others just didn’t want to evacuate for a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others.
Governments that put out bad warnings are apt to lose the public’s trust, said Sutton. “They're losing the opportunity to be that voice to help people to be safe.”
In theory, alerts are a perfect use case for artificial intelligence, and in particular for the generative AI systems that have developed at a dramatic pace over the past few years. FEMA provides training sessions for emergency managers to learn best practices for synthesizing and sending alerts, but many officials don’t remember all their training when an emergency arrives. A large language model is different. It can read hundreds of thousands of alerts in mere minutes, digest all the research on what works in similar scenarios, and then apply that to edit a human alert in seconds.
“If you’ve only sent one [alert] in your life, and that was 15 years ago, and you need to remember all your training, and you’re thinking ‘Hey, there's a chemical plume coming my way, the phone's ringing, the radio's blaring, I need help,’ the AI is probably gonna do a better job than you are,” said Rob Dale, a former meteorologist who now runs the emergency management department in Ingham County, Michigan.
Dale has already used AI to draft a few practice alerts behind the scenes, but he’s never had to send one out. Ingham County is a small county in central Michigan, and it’s immune from major weather events like hurricanes and fires. If such an event did happen, Dale said he would have no issue allowing a chatbot to draft his incident communication, but he’d still want control over sending the alert out.
Some experts believe the technology is already good enough to deploy. EM1, a startup that produces AI software for emergency managers, has used Sutton’s research to train a model that its executives say is already better than almost any human emergency manager. The company has tested this in-house model on a number of scenarios including wildfires and tsunamis. It can already match or exceed human capabilities on most benchmark tests.
Sutton gave Grist an example of how the software works: Grist provided her with a recent alert sent by a New Mexico county that was trying to warn residents about flooding on the San Juan River.
The original alert read, “Breeched banks. The water is rising. EVACUATE NOW. McGee Park open for people and pets, RV.” Sutton asked the EM1 model to evaluate and revise the alert. In a few seconds, it produced what she said is a far better alert, one that checks all the main boxes of disaster communication.
The new alert read: “San Juan County: Floodwater is rising near [location]. People in [evacuation area]: LEAVE NOW for higher ground. Do not walk or drive through floodwater. McGee Park is open for people and pets. Check [official update source] for updates.” The model identified and fixed several problems with the original text, which does not say who is sending the alert, name the specific location where flooding is happening, or clarify who needs to evacuate and give advice on how to do so safely. It misspells the word “breached,” and it doesn’t provide any guidance on where residents can seek further information.
EM1 has contracts with around a hundred government agencies and school districts, but none are using it to automate their extreme weather alerts just yet. For the moment, they’re only using it to workshop plans and internal preparations. Even so, all the experts interviewed for this story said they are certain that many emergency managers are already using chatbots to write messages, even if they won’t admit it. Sutton said that the emergency managers who take her alert training sessions often present her with high-quality alerts they have drafted in seconds using ChatGPT or Gemini.
“Official adoption is pretty low, but people are unofficially using it, absolutely,” said Sarah Miller, a professor of emergency management at Pierce College in Florida and a longtime instructor at the National Disaster Preparedness Training Center. “They're using their own personal accounts, or they're using free ones.”
It sounds like an easy trade-off: if AI is better and faster than humans, and the difference between a good alert and a bad alert can be life and death, we should be using AI for every heat wave and wildfire. Yet even researchers who are bullish on chatbot technology say that making the switch could backfire. Members of the public who are skeptical of AI or who don’t trust the government in the first place may spurn agencies that publish AI-generated graphics or social media posts. In Syracuse, New York, for instance, a union of public employees sued the local government for using an AI service to answer non-emergency 911 calls.
“We trust things that we perceive [are] authentic and care about us,” said Ginny Katz, the founder of HazAdapt, a consultancy that helps disaster officials figure out how to use technology. “AI-generated content does not feel authentic.” There’s also a risk that chatbots could allow emergency managers to send out more alerts, and faster, which could increase the risk of warning fatigue.
As is the case in other areas where AI is being deployed, disaster experts say that for the moment the software is only as capable as the person using it. A seasoned emergency manager might be able to speed up their communication with the public by having a chatbot draft a series of alerts, but an inexperienced one rushing to create an urgent alert won’t know how to evaluate the output of a model like ChatGPT or Claude.
Even though the technology is a ways off from being able to perform without a human expert in the loop, that hasn’t stopped many understaffed emergency management departments from using it. As for how the proliferation of AI-generated content is affecting public trust in government, experts say it’s too early to tell.
“If you had a human sending you a text message versus a computer sending you a text message, which one would you believe is being more accurate?” said Justin Snair, the founder of Preppr, another company that offers AI software to emergency managers.
The answer, he said, depends on the person receiving it.
