Madeira: scientists study how marine protection is restoring ocean life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:49:47 UTC
16:49:47 KST

Nearly 200 scientists are studying the marine environment off Madeira's Desertas Islands, assessing ecosystem health and how ocean protection can safeguard biodiversity and tackle climate change.
A ray glides over the seabed off the Desertas Islands in Madeira. The footage is being analysed by scientists trying to understand how marine protection is affecting ocean life.
Juan Mayorga, a marine biologist with National Geographic’s Pristine Seas initiative, is part of an expedition bringing together around 200 scientists to study the archipelago’s marine environment.
"It’s a good day when we see animals like this!" says the Colombian researcher, who studies underwater images to measure the impact of marine protection.
The scientists, on board around 15 vessels, are surveying marine life across the archipelago, assessing the health of its ecosystems and exploring how they can better withstand climate change.
"As we protect this place, year after year, the fish get bigger and produce more and more offspring. That’s protection working," stresses marine biologist Juan Mayorga, who works for the marine conservation initiative run by the National Geographic Society.
The flagship of the expedition is the 70-metre sailing ship Santa Maria Manuela, which has brought researchers from different parts of the world to the Desertas Islands, a group of three uninhabited rocky islets about 40 kilometres southeast of Madeira.
Aboard vessels such as the Santa Maria Manuela, the team uses baited underwater cameras mounted on metal frames to attract and film fish at depths of between 40 and 50 metres.
The aim is to compare two areas: the southern side of the Desertas Islands, where fishing is completely banned, and the northern side, where it is still allowed in some zones.
"We’re going to put these cameras in these protected marine areas and then also in zones where there is fishing, and we’re going to compare the two," explains Jennifer Caselle, a researcher at the Marine Science Institute at the University of California, Santa Barbara.
The research goes beyond images. The scientists also collect water samples to identify traces of fish DNA from species that may escape the cameras.
On the Desertas Islands, they also measure rock temperatures in the intertidal zone to study the effects of heat on marine organisms and help understand how biodiversity may change as the planet warms.
Studying the response to global warming
Rui Seabra, a 44-year-old researcher from the University of Porto, attaches temperature sensors to rocks exposed at low tide along a small cove.
He wants to understand how crustaceans and sponges behave in sunny and shaded areas, information that could help scientists predict how marine biodiversity will respond to rising temperatures.
"We need to understand how biodiversity will be redistributed, which species will migrate where, what conditions exist here, how they will change and which species we expect to find here in the future," he explains.
The expedition comes at a time when the urgency of protecting marine ecosystems is high on the international agenda.
Emanuel Gonçalves, the expedition leader and scientific director of the Oceano Azul Foundation, acknowledges the importance of international meetings such as the 17th COP on biodiversity, taking place in Yerevan, Armenia, in setting political priorities.
However, he points out that fieldwork cannot wait for political decisions. "We cannot wait. And that’s what science is telling us as well. This emergency for action does not allow us to sit back and wait for decisions that sometimes take decades to be made," he says.
Madeira has long been a pioneer in marine conservation. The archipelago includes the main island of Madeira, the beach destination of Porto Santo, the Desertas Islands and the remote Selvagens Islands.
In 1971 the authorities created a reserve around the Selvagens Islands to protect Cory’s shearwaters, seabirds found around Madeira and other Atlantic islands.
Expanded in 2022, the reserve now covers around 2,600 square kilometres, making it the largest marine protected area in the North Atlantic.
Another reserve set up around the Desertas Islands in the early 1990s helped a colony of Mediterranean monk seals, one of Europe’s most endangered marine mammals, grow from just eight animals to 31.

Finland sees record number of drug deaths in 2025
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
09:45:46 EET
16:45:46 KST

There were a total of 333 drug-related deaths in Finland last year, according to figures published on Thursday by Statistics Finland.
The grim tally marks the highest number of drug-related deaths ever recorded in Finland, the number-crunching agency noted.
The figure for 2025 is also a 35 percent increase on 2024, and continues a sharp upward trend in the number of drug-related deaths in the country — from 138 in 2006 to over 300 in every year of the 2020s so far.
Statistics Finland's Kati Taskinen noted in a press release that deaths increased across all age groups, but in particular among younger people.
For example, 64 individuals between the ages of 15 and 24 died a drug-related death last year, a year-on-year increase of 60 percent.
This makes drugs a significant cause of death among young people, Statistics Finland's report said, as mortality from other causes is low.
The most deaths were recorded among the 25–34 age group, up by 12 from 2024 to 85 last year.
In addition, the share of women among drug deaths grew exceptionally strongly: 94 women died from drugs, 44 more than in the previous year — the highest figure in the history of the statistics.
Large regional differences
Statistics Finland's data also revealed large regional differences, with the number of drug-related deaths varying considerably. The highest number of fatalities were registered in Helsinki (58), Pirkanmaa (30), Southwest Finland (28) and North Ostrobothnia (25).
Relative to population, the mortality rate was highest in Päijät-Häme, where 9.8 drug deaths per 100,000 inhabitants were recorded.

Ikram Kouachi
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
More than 29,000 double-envelope ballots, around 6% of the total, have been counted in Israel’s elections, with the Central Elections Committee expecting the count to conclude by the afternoon, Israeli media reported Thursday.
A total of 29,253 double-envelope ballots have been counted out of nearly 500,000, the daily Yedioth Ahronoth noted.
Double-envelope ballots are used by voters casting their votes away from their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers, and displaced residents.
Officials check identification details on the outer envelope to prevent duplicate voting, then separate it from the anonymous ballot before counting.
The remaining votes could change individual parties’ seat totals and the balance between the rival blocs.
The Central Elections Committee estimates that the double-envelope vote count will conclude by the afternoon, according to the report.
After all regular ballots were counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and 19 for predominantly Arab parties, according to Channel 12.
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
The Joint List was projected to secure 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, giving Arab parties a record combined representation of 19 seats.
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999, according to the election committee.

Germany’s Steinmeier says China must avoid one-sided benefits in economic ties
BEIJING – In its pursuit of economic self-sufficiency, China must not create one-sided dependence in other markets, Germany’s President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged in an address at a top-tier university in Beijing on Oct 29.
Steinmeier, who will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Oct 30, was objecting to the trade imbalance between China and Europe, according to his speech text for delivery at the prestigious Peking University.
“It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences,” he said, but pressed that China’s greater independence must not lead to dependence and vulnerability of others on China.
The European Union has called its widening trade deficit with China unsustainable, and warned in September it will use every possible means to remedy it.
Germany, along with France, has also proposed that the EU enact a new rapid-action measure against countries that harm it, with China likely in focus.
European companies have found themselves with no or little access to the Chinese market, while European markets face large amounts of state-subsidised Chinese imports as well as Beijing’s controls and limits on its raw materials exports, Steinmeier said.
Steinmeier argued that Europe was determined to keep its industrial base, and that he was confident that Brussels and Beijing would be able to find solutions through dialogue.
“We do not want a new bloc confrontation. That would not only be dangerous for international security, but would also be an economic loss for everyone,” said the German president who is on a five-day visit until Oct 31. REUTERS

CEC data leak affects 1,573 candidates in Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:56:16 UTC
16:56:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Administration for Cyber Security Director-General Tsai Fu-longe (蔡福隆) said Thursday that the exposure of candidates’ personal identification numbers on the Central Election Commission’s website may have resulted from poorly designed software developed by contractors.
Taiwan Go Go, an alliance of several small political parties, said at a press conference Wednesday that the CEC had exposed the personal identification numbers of 1,573 candidates on its asset disclosure website, per UDN. Taiwan Obasan Political Equality Party Taipei City Council candidate Li Hui-hsuan (李惠暄) said the CEC had violated the law and should notify both affected individuals and relevant authorities of the incident.
The CEC responded that the incident may have resulted from contractors accidentally entering identification numbers into files that were not intended for public disclosure, per Newtalk. The commission said the file appeared as garbled text that ordinary users could not readily read.
The commission said it temporarily suspended the service Tuesday and reopened it at 7 p.m. after correcting the problem.
Tsai announced the preliminary findings of his administration’s investigation, saying the problem may have stemmed from flaws in the contractor’s software design, per TVBS. He added that the Ministry of Digital Affairs would continue working with the CEC to strengthen the security of the entire system.
New Power Party Chair Wang Wan-yu (王婉諭) criticized the CEC’s response, saying the information could be accessed through the browser’s developer tools on the asset disclosure website, per UP Media. She explained that Chinese characters may become scrambled when the wrong character encoding standard is used, but personal identification numbers consisting only of digits and English letters would remain unchanged.
Wang said her team discovered the issue without any engineers or hackers on staff, warning that others may also have noticed the error. She called on the CEC to investigate how many times the information had been downloaded and where it may have been sent.
DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) commented on the incident Wednesday, saying that encoding personal information would not diminish the severity of a data leak, per SETN. He called on the government to provide a more detailed explanation of the incident to restore public trust.
Taipei City Councilor Yang Chih-tou (楊植斗) also demanded answers, adding that affected individuals should seek compensation from the CEC, per China Times. He urged Shen, a national security expert who was also affected by the leak, to pursue accountability through the legislature.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan sent three handler-and-dog teams to the 30th International Rescue Dog Organization World Championship in Codogno, Italy, with two teams placing seventh and 12th in the rubble search event.
Wu Wei-yi (吳惟逸) and search and rescue dog Aqua, representing the New Taipei Fire Department, placed seventh, while Wen Chih-chin (温智欽) and Clay of the Hsinchu City Fire Department finished 12th among 37 teams, per CNA.
The third team consisted of Luo Hao-fang (羅浩芳) and search and rescue dog A-Mei, also from the New Taipei Fire Department. The three teams traveled to Europe ahead of the competition for acclimatization and training.
The championship ran Oct. 11-16 in Codogno, with competitors tested in search, obedience, and dexterity to assess the working relationship between handlers and dogs.
Hsinchu City covered its team’s competition expenses and presented Wen and Clay with prize money and gifts on their return to recognize their training and performance.
The city plans to invest NT$10 million (US$307,000) next year to expand its search and rescue dog facilities, increasing kennel capacity from seven to 10 dogs and adding an obedience training area. The training ground opened in 2023 and was upgraded in 2024 to meet IRO standards for international training and testing, per UDN.
The Hsinchu City Fire Department said it would continue improving its training system and introducing search and rescue technology and equipment to strengthen the effectiveness of specialized rescue teams and canine search units.

One Nation MP rejects $200,000 staffer as Hanson accuses PM of meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Pauline Hanson accuses Anthony Albanese of trying to divide One Nation with staffing offer
In short:
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of political meddling after one of its MPs rejected an unsolicited offer of a $200,000 staffer.
The dispute has intensified scrutiny of the prime minister's power to allocate parliamentary resources.
What's next?
Pauline Hanson says the current system is "grubby" and wants an independent body to set staffing levels.
One Nation has accused Anthony Albanese of trying to use his power to set parliament staffing levels to divide the party after the prime minister offered new MP David Farley extra resources.
The Farrer MP received a letter from Mr Albanese this week authorising him to hire an additional staffer on a $200,000 salary package, an "unsolicited" offer that Mr Farley has rejected.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has criticised the offer as an attempt by Labor to "exert undue political influence" and split her party, which is in the middle of a broader staffing dispute with Mr Albanese.
"We won't be bought or divided by this prime minister,"
Senator Hanson said.
Staffing levels have emerged as a significant point of contention between some crossbenchers and Mr Albanese, who has ignored calls to increase the resources provided to some independents and One Nation.
All parliamentarians are granted five electorate officers, but the power to decide additional personal staff levels is held by the prime minister.
It is understood the extra staff position offered to Mr Farley was the same as the allocation provided to fellow One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce when he quit the Nationals and moved to the crossbench.
Both parliamentarians are in the lower house and have geographically large regional electorates.
Hanson says staffing power 'open to abuse'
In statement today, Senator Hanson said the staff offer made to Mr Farley showed the system was "grubby".
"This is the type of politics that Australians are sick of," she said.
Senator Hanson has repeatedly asked Mr Albanese to let her hire more staff since One Nation achieved minor party status in the wake of Mr Joyce's defection.
"For months, One Nation has been fighting for fair, transparent and objective allocation of staffing for parliamentarians," she said.
Senator Hanson has called for staffing levels to be determined by an independent body.
"While this power has always been open to abuse, it has, in our view, been weaponised to an unprecedented extent under this Labor government and this prime minister," she said.
Senator apologises for 'clumsy' Haines comment
Earlier this week, independent West Australian senator Fatima Payman revealed she had apologised to Indi MP Helen Haines for her "clumsy wording" in relation to a staffing stoush with Labor.
During a Senate estimates hearing on Monday night, Senator Payman suggested Mr Albanese was waiting for her to suffer an attack similar to Ms Haines before he would grant extra staff.
Senator Payman refused to withdraw the comment at the time, which was described by Special Minister of State Don Farrell as an "outrageous statement".
But yesterday, Senator Payman confirmed she had contacted Ms Haines, who is in hospital recovering from a double amputation after an alleged attack last week, to clarify her remarks.
"I have apologised for my clumsy wording on Monday night, and I have conveyed those apologies directly to Dr Haines and her staff," Senator Payman said.
She maintained her need for additional staff, noting the "toll" on her current team of staff.
Crossbench unites in staffing push
Last month, Senator Hanson, Senator Payman and independent Fowler MP Dai Le teamed up to criticise what they described as "unfair" staffing double standards for some crossbenchers.
The trio called on Mr Albanese to provide a "fair" number of staff and later moved a motion attempting to strip him of the personal power to decide personnel allocations.
Data from May this year showed Senator Payman was the only independent in parliament who did not have any additional personal staff allocated.
Ms Le had one extra staff member, as did independent Bradfield MP Nicolette Boele and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet.
The remainder of the crossbench independents have two personal staff, except Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie, who has three.
The Greens, who have one MP and 10 senators, have 15 personal staff.
One Nation, which has two MPs and four senators, has five additional staff.

Poland hands Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
07:55:07 UTC
16:55:07 KST

- Poland will soon transfer two MiG-29 fighters to Ukraine in a new aid package worth about €50 million, Rzeczpospolita reported.
- One jet has reached the end of its service life and may be used for spare parts, while the other is still flying.
Poland will soon hand Ukraine two more MiG-29 fighter jets as part of a new military aid package worth about €50 million (about $56 million), Polish daily Rzeczpospolita reported on Oct. 29, in a story quickly picked up by Ukrainian defense outlet Milarnyi.
Reserve Lt. Gen. Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Polish Defense Ministry’s Strategy and Defense Planning Department, confirmed the transfer to the newspaper and said the decision had been made, without giving a date beyond “in the near future.” Only one of the two jets is still flying. The other has reached the end of its service life, and Rzeczpospolita reported that Ukraine may use it as a source of spare parts.
The rest of the package is mostly munitions. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland will also send 155 mm and 152 mm artillery shells, 20 mm rounds for the six-barrel cannon fitted to F-16 fighters, which Ukrainian pilots use to shoot down Russian drones, and missiles for the Piorun shoulder-fired air defense system built by Polish manufacturer Mesko. Ukrainian defense officials had said in September that the Polish donation would be worth €50 million and would include air defense equipment. Poland’s Defense Ministry declined to detail the contents, saying only that the package draws on equipment being retired by the Polish armed forces or no longer needed.
The two aircraft are a small addition to a fleet Poland has been feeding since the early part of the war. Poland began openly handing over MiG-29s in March 2023, and by that May then-Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak said Ukraine had received 10 of them, Militarnyi reported. In total, Poland has given Ukraine 14 MiG-29s, Militarnyi said. Rzeczpospolita reported the same figure, adding that the jets were sent in 2022 and 2023 in varying technical condition and with little publicity.
A further transfer has been discussed for more than two years. In July 2024, Poland’s security agreement with Ukraine included a pledge to consider sending at least one more MiG-29 squadron, but Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw could not simply give up jets still flying air policing missions unless allies supplied replacements. At the time, the Polish Air Force still had 14 MiG-29s: 11 single-seat MiG-29As and three two-seat MiG-29UB trainers.
In late 2025, the two governments began talks on the last Polish MiG-29s. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the handover would benefit Poland because Warsaw would receive Ukrainian drone and missile technology in return. That exchange has not happened. As of mid-June 2026, Poland’s deputy defense minister said no aircraft from that batch had been delivered, and Rzeczpospolita reported the technology transfer stalled at the political level after Ukraine’s president named a military unit after heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, a wartime nationalist force whose legacy is deeply contested in Poland.
Poland can spare the jets because their missions are moving to newer aircraft. The MiG-29 has kept a shrinking quick reaction alert role over the Baltic, and Rzeczpospolita reported that its tasks are now handled by Polish F-16s and the first 12 South Korean-built FA-50 light fighters, which reached full operational readiness in 2026.
For Ukraine, every additional airframe matters. The Ukrainian Air Force still relies heavily on the Soviet-designed MiG-29, which it has kept flying through deliveries from Poland, Slovakia and Bulgaria and through cannibalizing retired jets for parts, while losing aircraft to Russian strikes on airfields and in the air.
The new package also follows a separate Polish contribution of Patriot interceptors. Rzeczpospolita reported that Poland has given Ukraine 10 PAC-3 MSE missiles in total, five earlier this year and five more through an international donation led by the United States with NATO. Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland’s donations to Ukraine since 2022 were worth about 16.45 billion zlotys, most of them delivered in 2022 and 2023, and the ministry later declassified the full list of transferred equipment.
